# Method statements

A **method statement** is the paragraph an examiner reads aloud when asked how a finding was produced: what the module read, what it produced, **what it cannot do**, and what it refuses outright. The third and fourth are the half that makes one worth having — a statement that lists only capabilities is a brochure.

**This file is generated** from the module set the product actually builds, by `seance_api::method_statements`. It is not edited by hand: the prose lives in that module beside the code, and a statement for a module the product no longer has fails the build.

**158 of 159 modules have a written method statement. 1 do not, and every one of them is named below.** A module with no statement is not a module with nothing to say about it; it is one nobody has written the paragraph for yet, and listing them is the only honest way to say how far this has got.

## Written

### `container.7z_expander`

**Reads.** The directory of a 7-Zip archive — and only the directory. It subscribes to `Container` and `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::Stream`; an artifact whose `subtype` is set but is not exactly `7z` yields an empty list, and one with no subtype is taken only when its lowercased `name` ends `.7z`. The `7z` subtype is written by `detect_file_type` when the first six bytes are `37 7A BC AF 27 1C`, and by the ingest extension map for `.7z`. It needs `artifact.data` (`InvalidInputFormat`, "7z module requires data source"), reads six bytes at offset 0 with `read_full` and remembers whether they are the signature, then opens the archive with `sevenz_rust2::ArchiveReader::new(SourceCursor, Password::empty())` (sevenz-rust2 0.21.4 — the maintained fork, chosen over `sevenz-rust` because of RUSTSEC-2026-0245/0246). That open seeks to the end for the length, checks the signature and that the major version is 0, then reads the 32-byte start header. If its CRC field is non-zero, or the twenty bytes after it are not all zero, the start header's CRC-32 is verified, the next header is located from it and its CRC-32 verified. If the CRC field is zero and the following twenty bytes are zero — an archive whose writer never finalised the start header — the library instead scans backwards through the last 1 MiB of the file for a `kHeader` or `kEncodedHeader` byte and accepts the first candidate that parses into a non-empty file list, with no CRC check. An encoded (compressed) header is decoded through its folder's coders — LZMA, LZMA2, BCJ and the rest — with the declared size used as a `take` bound rather than a pre-allocation; an AES-256 coder on the header with the empty password is `Error::PasswordRequired`. From the decoded header it reads, per entry, `name()`, `is_directory()`, `has_stream()` and `size()`, and for each folder ("block") whether any of its coders is AES-256-SHA256 (`06 F1 07 01`), mapped to entries through `stream_map.file_block_index`. No entry's bytes are ever kept, and a password is used only when an examiner supplies one for this archive and this run (`POST …/credential` with `kind: sevenz_password`, visible to this module through `seance_core::credential` for one `process` call): the archive is opened with it, and — when the header was plain, so the entries were already listed — `BlockDecoder` decodes the first entry of the first AES folder to a sink, its CRC-32 checked, or only its first MiB when the entry is over 64 MiB.

**Produces.** One `FileEntry` per entry in the archive's file list, parented to the archive, with **no data source**. Its metadata is `name`, `path` and `parent_path` from `entry_path::resolve_sevenz_entry_path` — which first turns every `\\` into `/`, because 7z carries Windows-authored names and `..\\..\\payload` is the exact vector RUSTSEC-2026-0245 was filed for, then resolves `..`, `.` and absolute roots within the archive — `size` (`entry.size()` when `has_stream()`, else 0), `is_directory`, `container: "7z"`, `container_path`, `original_name` holding the stored bytes verbatim whenever resolution or the separator swap changed them, and `path_traversal: true` when the stored name reached outside the root (`test_7z_entry_paths_do_not_escape_the_archive_root` pins `../`, `a/../../`, `/etc/passwd` and the backslash form). Every non-directory entry with a size above zero also carries `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason: compressed` and `content_incomplete_detail: "7z uses solid compression; per-entry content is not extracted by this ingest"`, so a sized entry with no bytes reads as "not extracted" rather than "was empty" (`test_7z_entries_declare_content_not_extracted`). An entry in an AES folder — what `7z a -p…` writes when the header is left plain — carries `encrypted: true`, `scheme: 7z_aes256_sha256` and reason `encrypted` instead, with a detail saying its bytes are encrypted and that 7z content is not extracted whatever the password (`entries_in_an_aes_folder_are_recorded_as_encrypted`, real `7z` output). When the header itself is encrypted (`-mhe=on`), the open fails with `PasswordRequired` and it produces one `ParsedRecord` with `record_type: archive_scan_status`, `name: "<name> (encrypted, not expanded)"`, `encrypted: true`, `encrypted_header: true`, the same `scheme`, and `content_incomplete` and `inventory_incomplete` both with reason `encrypted` — the reason the Needs-attention queue keys on, so the archive is listed there with a field for its password (`a_header_encrypted_7z_is_recorded_as_encrypted_not_unreadable`, real `7z` output). With a supplied password that opens a header-encrypted archive it produces the entries as above — those in AES folders with `password_supplied: true` and reason `compressed`, since the password is no longer what keeps the bytes out — and an `ArchiveScanStatus` of `status: unlocked`, `credential_kind`, `credential_source`, no incompleteness pair, which supersedes the encrypted-header record on the re-run; for an archive whose header was plain, only an `ArchiveScanStatus` of `status: password_verified` with `password_check` (`crc32` or `decoder_prefix`) and `checked_entry`, the entries not being listed twice. A password that does not open the archive is reported back as rejected and the orchestrator records nothing from that run (`a_password_supplied_for_this_run_*`, `a_wrong_password_*`, real `7z a -p…` output). When the archive carries the signature but will not open for any other reason, it produces instead one `ParsedRecord` from `expansion_failed_status`: `type: ArchiveScanStatus`, `record_type: archive_scan_status`, `name: "<name> (not expanded)"`, `container: 7z`, `content_incomplete: true` with reason `sevenz_unreadable`, `inventory_incomplete: true` with reason `unresolved_structure`, `entries_recovered: 0`, and the library error's `Display` — which is its `Debug` form, so the detail reads `NextHeaderCrcMismatch`, `ChecksumVerificationFailed`, `UnsupportedCompressionMethod("…")` and so on — in the three detail keys. The listing is the whole product: nothing inside a 7z is hashed, previewed, parsed, indexed, exported or recursed into, and the API's content resolver has no `7z` arm, so asking for an entry's content after ingest is refused with "Content resolution for '7z' containers is not supported".

**Cannot.** It cannot produce a byte of any entry. That is the whole limitation and the code says so in place: 7z groups entries into solid folders sharing one compressed stream, per-entry random access does not exist, `sevenz-rust2`'s per-name reader decodes every earlier entry in the folder and returns the file whole in memory, and building a windowed, bomb-capped extractor over decoded folders is deferred (marked DEFERRED for 7z in `sevenz.rs`). So the mobile, office, hashing and carving parsers never see what a 7z holds; the `documentation/Container_Formats.md` line "7z — extract member entries", the `COMPARISON.md` row "ZIP / 7z / tar / archives, recursive ✅" and the online help's "contents are expanded and processed recursively" all overstate this module, which lists. A password supplied for an archive lists a header-encrypted one and verifies a content-encrypted one; it brings no entry's content into the case, so the queue row for content-encrypted entries offers no field. Without a password an encrypted-header archive lists nothing at all. The library keeps its own UTF-16 copy of a supplied password for the call, which is freed, not zeroed. It recognises only the AES-256-SHA256 coder as encryption. It cannot check whether the archive is actually solid before saying so: `archive().is_solid` is available and unread, and the detail sentence is stamped on every entry of a non-solid archive too. It cannot read what the header knows about each entry beyond name, directory flag and size: `last_modified_date`, `creation_date`, `access_date`, `windows_attributes`, the per-entry `crc` and `is_anti_item` are all present on `ArchiveEntry` and none is published, so the listing carries no timestamp, no attribute and no digest to compare a later extraction against, and an anti-item (a deletion marker in an update archive) is listed as though it were a file. It cannot bound a listing: there is no cap on entry count, and every entry becomes an artifact. It cannot be certain of a rescued archive: where the start header was never written, the library's backward scan takes the first candidate header that yields entries with no CRC over it, and nothing on the artifact records that the archive was opened that way. It cannot re-open anything for the API afterwards, because there is nothing to re-open. A `.7z`-named file without the signature that fails to open is silent, folded into the "ran and produced nothing" row, as is an artifact whose subtype says `7z` without the signature.

**Refuses.** It refuses to let a stored name become a location: `..`, absolute names and the Windows `..\\` form are resolved and clamped inside the archive, the stored name is kept in `original_name` as evidence of the attempt and as the name that still addresses the entry, and `path_traversal: true` marks it — the defence the advisory was filed for, applied in this crate as well as in the library, because this crate never extracts to disk and its exposure is a path that lies about where an entry lives (`entry_path::resolve_sevenz_entry_path`, `test_7z_entry_paths_do_not_escape_the_archive_root`). It refuses to present a sized entry with no bytes as an empty file: every such entry carries the `compressed` incompleteness pair, so a hash, preview or export that comes back empty is understood as "not extracted" (`test_7z_entries_declare_content_not_extracted`). It refuses to let a signed archive that will not open read as one that held nothing: a corrupt archive, a CRC mismatch, an unsupported coder or an encrypted header all produce an `ArchiveScanStatus` record, never an empty success (`test_7z_corrupted_is_reported_not_silent`), while a `.7z`-named file without the signature is left silent so the stamp does not fire on every mislabelled file (`test_7z_without_signature_is_silent`). It refuses a missing data source with `InvalidInputFormat` — a folded "skipped" row — and any other subtype or name with an empty list. It never supplies a password, never decodes a payload and never writes anywhere; and, like the other expanders, it never returns a `ModuleError` for a bad archive, so its refusals live on the artifact tree under `complete`, not in the processing log's error rows.

### `container.aff4_reader`

**Reads.** An AFF4 container — a ZIP file — and it opens one only when something upstream has already said so. It subscribes to `Container` artifacts, declines in silence any artifact whose `subtype` is not exactly `aff4`, and where no subtype is set at all accepts the artifact only if its `name` ends `.aff4`, case-insensitively. The subtype it keys on is written by `seance_core::file_detection::detect_file_type`, which reads the first 512 bytes and calls a buffer an AFF4 container when it opens with `PK` and the literal filename `container.description` appears inside that window — the first local file header of a real AFF4 — and by the `.aff4` extension map in the ingest fallback. It then needs a real local path: the bytes are read with `File::open` through `zip::ZipArchive`, from the `path` in the artifact's metadata, and the module never spills the artifact's own data source to disk. Inside the container it reads, by exact entry name: `container.description`, whose trimmed contents become the base URN that the turtle subject `:` expands to; `version.txt`, trimmed; and `information.turtle`, parsed by a line-oriented reader that skips `@prefix` and `#` lines, tracks the current subject and accumulates `predicate value[, value]* [;|.]` statements into a subject→predicate→values map, unwrapping `<…>`, dropping a `^^datatype` suffix and stripping quotes. From that graph it takes the first subject whose `a` values include `aff4:Image`, then `aff4:DiskImage`, then `aff4:ContiguousImage`; from it `aff4:size`, which is the logical size of the image served, `aff4:dataStream`, and a hash predicate where the graph carries one — `aff4:md5`, `aff4:sha1`, `aff4:sha256`, or the generic `aff4:hash` whose algorithm is read from its `^^datatype` suffix, all matched case-insensitively; no AFF4 specification is vendored in this tree to pin one true predicate spelling, so this is the plausible set, not a certainty. If that stream's types include `aff4:Map` it is read as a map, otherwise it must itself be a bound `aff4:ImageStream`. Image streams are bound to the container that actually stores their bytes: the directory holding the primary container is scanned for every other file with an `.aff4` extension, each one's ZIP directory and `information.turtle` are read, and a stream is bound to the first of those files whose entry list contains `<prefix>/00000000` — the URL-encoded URN, with only `:` and `/` percent-escaped, as the segment-name prefix. From each stream come `aff4:chunkSize` (default 32,768), `aff4:chunksInSegment` (default 2,048), `aff4:size` and `aff4:compressionMethod`, whose URN is classified by substring on its lowercased form: snappy, or deflate — `deflate`, `1951` or `zlib` — and anything else as stored. A map is read from two segments under the map URN's prefix: `<prefix>/idx`, one target URN per non-empty line, positionally indexed; and `<prefix>/map`, a flat array of 28-byte little-endian records `u64 mapOffset, u64 length, u64 targetOffset, u32 targetId`, sorted by map offset after parsing. Each idx line is resolved against the bound streams, or by suffix on its lowercased URN to a constant-byte symbolic stream (`…#zero`, `…/zero`, `…:zero`, `…symbolicstream00` → 0x00; `…symbolicstreamff` → 0xFF; `symbolicstream<HH>` anywhere in the URN with exactly two trailing hex digits → 0xHH), or to `aff4:UnreadableData`, or to `aff4:UnknownData`, or to nothing. `aff4:mapGapDefaultStream` is resolved the same way and defaults to `aff4:Zero`. Bytes are then served on demand: a logical offset is located in the sorted map by binary search, translated to a target offset with checked arithmetic, and for an image stream turned into a global chunk index; the chunk's bevy is `<prefix>/<bevy:08d>`, its `<prefix>/<bevy:08d>.index` is a flat array of 12-byte `u64 offset, u32 length` records, and the addressed slice is inflated to exactly the expected chunk length — the chunk size, or the remainder of the stream for the last chunk. A slice whose compressed length already equals the expected length is taken raw whatever the stream's nominal method says, because the writer keeps incompressible chunks verbatim. Whole bevies are cached per stream and the last decompressed chunk is cached singly.

**Produces.** Exactly one artifact: a `RawEvidence` artifact parented to the container it was read from, carrying an `Aff4DataSource` that serves the reconstructed logical image, so partition, file-system, carving and hashing code reads an AFF4 image exactly as it reads a raw one. Its metadata carries `size` (the logical image size the turtle declares), `subtype: raw`, `container: aff4`, `container_path` and `path` both set to the container file, a name of `<container name>_extracted`, and an `aff4_metadata` object holding a surface view of the ZIP taken independently of the turtle graph: `container_type: AFF4`, the central-directory entry count as `files_in_container`, the list of every ZIP entry name that would read as `container_files`, the character length of `information.turtle` as `turtle_metadata_size`, the keys `contains_image_stream` and `contains_map` — each present and `true` only where a substring search for `aff4:ImageStream` or `aff4:Map` in that file succeeds, never `false`, and never from the graph — and the trimmed text of `version.txt` as `aff4_version`. Where the data stream is a map and any part of the logical image is not imaged evidence, the artifact carries the standard pair `content_incomplete` with `content_incomplete_reason: unresolved_structure`, and four byte counts measured from the map at open time: `aff4_unreadable_bytes` (`aff4:UnreadableData` — the imager asked the device and did not get the bytes), `aff4_unknown_bytes` (`aff4:UnknownData` — never imaged), `aff4_unmapped_bytes` (covered by no map entry at all, served as the declared gap stream), `aff4_unresolved_bytes` (a target URN or a dangling target id that could not be bound, so those bytes cannot be produced at all), their total as `aff4_non_evidence_bytes`, and a `message` saying in words that those bytes are served as recognisable markers and are not device content. Where a stream or sibling container could not be bound, it carries `inventory_incomplete`, `inventory_incomplete_reason: unresolved_structure`, and `stream_bind_failures`, one string per failure naming the container or stream URN and the error. In the bytes themselves, an unreadable range is served as the repeating 14-byte pattern `UNREADABLEDATA` and a never-imaged range as the repeating 11-byte pattern `UNKNOWNDATA`, both phased on the logical offset so the same offset yields the same byte however a read is split, which is what lets a hash of the image be reproducible. Where a recognised MD5 or SHA-1 hash is found, it is published as `stored_md5`/`stored_sha1` at the artifact's top level, exactly as the E01 reader does, so the ingest's decoded-media verification pass — gated on `stored_md5` being present — now runs for an AFF4 exhibit that records one. A SHA-256 found is published under `aff4_hash_sha256` instead, because that verification pass has no SHA-256 comparison path. Where the graph carries no recognised hash predicate at all, `aff4_hash_baseline: "not recorded in container"` says so explicitly. Nothing else is produced: no parsed records, no timeline events, no per-file inventory.

**Cannot.** It cannot verify against a hash the graph does not carry, or against one in an algorithm the ingest's verification pass does not compare (SHA-256): for either, that second full-pass verification never runs and the Evidence Integrity row has no container-recorded value to compare against. The only integrity check anywhere in this path is one it does not perform itself: the ZIP library checks each entry's stored CRC-32 at the end of the entry, and every segment under the size cap is read whole, so a corrupt segment fails its own read and a corruption in `information.turtle` or `version.txt` fails the open. No test in this module holds that behaviour in place, and a segment refused for exceeding the size cap is never read to its end, so its CRC is never checked. It cannot tell a hole from imaged zeros. A range the map points at `aff4:Zero` or any `aff4:SymbolicStream<HH>` is served as that constant byte and is deliberately **not** counted as non-evidence, so an image whose unallocated or skipped ranges were written as an explicit Zero mapping reads as zeros, carries no `content_incomplete` flag, and is indistinguishable from a device that genuinely held zeros there; only a range covered by no entry at all, or one explicitly marked unreadable or unknown, is counted. Where the data stream is a bare `aff4:ImageStream` rather than a map, no coverage is measured at all: the image is served as one identity range, the container's declared gap stream is ignored in favour of zero, and **no `content_incomplete` flag or byte count can ever be stamped**, however far the declared `aff4:size` runs past the stream's own. Nor is any declared size ever reconciled: the image subject's `aff4:size` is what is served, and a map, or an image stream, declaring a different size is neither checked nor reported. It cannot read encrypted AFF4: no key, passphrase or certificate handling exists in this module. It cannot decompress anything but snappy and deflate/zlib; LZ4 or any other `aff4:compressionMethod` URN falls through to "stored", and its chunks then fail the exact-length check, so the affected region is unreadable rather than wrong. It cannot serve more than one image from a container: the first subject of type `aff4:Image`, `aff4:DiskImage` or `aff4:ContiguousImage` found while iterating a hash map is used, that order is not defined and can differ between runs of the same container, and nothing anywhere records that other images were present. It reads only `aff4:Map` and `aff4:ImageStream` data streams; a logical AFF4 container of file streams is not read, and `aff4:dependentStream` is not consulted. It cannot follow `aff4:stored` or any locator to find a stream's container — it finds segment sets only by scanning the primary container's own directory for files whose extension is `.aff4`, and binds a stream only to the first container it finds holding that stream's `00000000` bevy, so a set spread across directories, one whose members are named otherwise, or one where a single stream's later bevies live in a second container, does not bind; two containers offering the same stream URN are not detected as a conflict. A sibling's metadata is parsed with an empty base URN, so a stream that sibling declares under the base-relative subject `:` cannot bind and, no error having occurred, its absence is recorded nowhere. Equally it cannot tell a member of this set from any unrelated `.aff4` file in the same directory: an unrelated container that will not open is recorded against this image as a bind failure, and this image is flagged `inventory_incomplete` for it. Nor does it probe the file it is handed: an AFF4 whose ZIP does not name `container.description` inside the first 512 bytes and whose filename does not end `.aff4` is detected as a plain ZIP and expanded as an archive by another module, with no AFF4 reconstruction and nothing said. It records no acquisition provenance: no imager name or version, no case or evidence number, no examiner, no acquisition timestamps, no completion state — the only acquisition-side facts published are the trimmed text of `version.txt` and the ZIP entry list, itself silently short of any entry whose header will not read. Its turtle reader is not an RDF parser. `@prefix` lines are skipped and predicates are matched as literal prefixed text, so only the spellings `a`, `aff4:size`, `aff4:dataStream`, `aff4:chunkSize`, `aff4:chunksInSegment`, `aff4:compressionMethod` and `aff4:mapGapDefaultStream` are understood; a container writing those predicates as full URIs or under a differently-bound prefix fails to open, a value containing a comma is split into two values, and there is no handling of blank nodes or multi-line literals. Where two map entries overlap, the part of the earlier entry's range that lies past the later entry's end is treated as covered by no entry and served as the declared gap stream, while the coverage measurement counts it as evidence, so such a range reads as fill with no incompleteness flag. Its ceilings are these: no single ZIP segment may materialise more than 4,294,967,296 bytes, which also bounds the map at 153,391,689 records and a bevy index at 357,913,941 records; `aff4:chunkSize` must be between 1 and 67,108,864, which is also the ceiling on one decompressed chunk; a deflate chunk is inflated under a hard limit of the expected length plus one byte; the decompressed-chunk cache holds exactly one chunk, while the per-stream bevy cache is never evicted, so a full sweep of a large image retains every bevy it has touched — 67,108,864 bytes each at the default geometry. The sibling scan itself has no ceiling: every `.aff4` in the directory has its whole central directory and its whole `information.turtle` read before a byte of image is served. A read at or past the logical end returns zero bytes rather than an error, and a read is satisfied only up to the logical size however large the buffer.

**Refuses.** It refuses to fabricate a byte it was not given, and every refusal below exists because the alternative was a fabricated byte reaching a hash, an export or a preview with nothing left to mark it. A range whose target URN could not be bound to a stream or a symbolic constant fails the covering read with an error naming the URN, rather than degrading to zeros; so does a map entry whose `targetId` is past the end of the `idx` table; and so does a gap whose declared `aff4:mapGapDefaultStream` could not be resolved, which used to quietly become 0x00 — itself a legal declaration, which made an unmet declaration indistinguishable from a met one. That last refusal is deferred to the read that actually lands in a gap, because an image whose map covers every byte never consults the declaration and must not be lost over it. `aff4:UnreadableData` and `aff4:UnknownData` are refused as constant streams: they are served as the `UNREADABLEDATA` and `UNKNOWNDATA` markers and counted into the artifact's coverage, because a zero-filled bad sector is byte-for-byte a sector that held zeros . A chunk that decompresses to anything other than its exact expected length is refused, never accepted and padded; a snappy frame declaring an uncompressed length other than the expected one is refused from its header before any buffer is allocated; a read that a map entry pushes past the declared end of an `ImageStream` is refused rather than zero-filled; and a map entry whose `mapOffset + length` or whose `targetOffset + delta` overflows 64 bits is refused rather than wrapped. A `map` segment or a bevy `.index` segment with any trailing bytes past its last whole 28- or 12-byte record is refused entirely, naming the truncated segment, because the records that did not survive are ranges of the image and dropping them would serve those offsets as gap fill; a chunk whose index record is missing from its bevy, or whose index record addresses bytes outside that bevy's data, is refused by chunk number for the same reason. A ZIP segment larger than the 4 GiB cap is refused rather than truncated at the cap and served as complete, and an `aff4:chunkSize` of 0 or above 67,108,864, or an `aff4:chunksInSegment` of 0, refuses the stream at construction rather than dividing by zero or allocating from hostile metadata. A segment it needs and cannot open — a bevy, an index, the `map`, the `idx` — is refused by that segment's name, though the reason given is always "not found", including where the entry is present but the ZIP reader will not open it. On the way in, a file that is not a readable ZIP, or whose `information.turtle` or `version.txt` is not valid UTF-8, is refused at metadata extraction before the image is opened at all; and a container with no readable `information.turtle`, no image subject, no `aff4:size`, no `aff4:dataStream`, or a data stream that is neither a map nor a bound image stream — a bare `ImageStream` in a sibling that will not open included — refuses to open, the module returning a `ParsingError` naming the reason. An artifact with no `path` returns `InvalidInputFormat` ("AFF4 module requires file path"). Note what that last group does **not** produce: unlike the network and prefetch readers, a container this module cannot open leaves **no** refusal artifact of its own. The reason travels only as the module's error into the case's processing log, so an examiner asked why an exhibit yielded nothing must read that log, not the artifact tree.

### `container.android_backup`

**Reads.** An `adb backup` archive: the ASCII header and the tar it wraps. It subscribes to `RawEvidence` and `FileEntry` — not `Container` — with `InputCapability::Stream`, because a top-level `.ab` is not recognised by `detect_file_type` or the ingest extension map and lands as the undetermined `RawEvidence`, while one found inside another container arrives as a `FileEntry`. An artifact with no `data` is passed over in silence. A `FileEntry` must be named `.ab` (lowercased suffix) before its bytes are looked at; every `RawEvidence` artifact is sniffed regardless of name. The sniff reads 15 bytes at offset 0 with `read_exact_or_fail` and requires them to be `ANDROID BACKUP\n`. It then reads up to 512 bytes from offset 0 with `read_full` and finds the first four line feeds: line two is the format version (parsed as text and copied onto the success summary, otherwise unused), line three is `1` for a compressed payload, line four is the encryption word, and the payload begins after the fourth line feed. If the encryption word is anything but `none` it stops there. Otherwise the payload is a `WindowSource` from that offset to the end of the source, read through `flate2::read::ZlibDecoder` (RFC 1950) when compressed and directly when not, then wrapped in a ceiling of `MAX_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES` = 2,147,483,648 bytes (`CeilingReader`, which at the ceiling asks the stream for one more byte and remembers whether there was one) and walked by `tar::Archive::entries()` (tar 0.4.46) — the same walker the tar extractor uses: header checksums verified, GNU long names and PAX local extensions consumed, an all-zero block ending the walk. From each entry it takes `entry_type().is_file()` (only `Regular`), `entry.size()` — the PAX-aware size the reader is actually bounded by, chosen over the header field so a crafted archive cannot publish one size and deliver another — and `entry.path()` as lossy UTF-8 with a trailing `/` trimmed. An entry of at most `MAX_ENTRY_BYTES` = 536,870,912 bytes (512 MiB) is read whole into memory with `take(MAX_ENTRY_BYTES).read_to_end`; a larger one is not read. No password is ever asked for or used, and no header field beyond the four lines is interpreted.

**Produces.** One `FileEntry` per regular file in the tar, parented to the backup artifact, until the walk ends or the entry cap of `MAX_ENTRIES` = 100,000 is reached. Its data, when the entry was at most 512 MiB and read without error, is a `ByteSliceDataSource` holding the bytes in memory — which is how `mmssms.db`, `msgstore.db`, `contacts2.db` and the rest chain to their parsers at ingest. Its metadata is `name` (the basename), `path` (`/` + the entry path), `parent_path`, `size` (`entry.size()`), `is_directory: false`, `container: "android_backup"` and `container_path` (the backup's `name`). An entry over the per-file cap is emitted with its claimed size, no data, `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason: cap_reached`, `content_omitted: entry_over_size_cap` and `max_entry_bytes`; one whose bytes errored mid-read gets `short_read`, `content_omitted: entry_read_failed` and `read_error`; one that read fewer bytes than its size carries `materialized_size` and `short_read`. Six container-level `ParsedRecord`s exist, all `type: AndroidBackupWarning`, `record_type: android_backup_status`, each named `Android backup (<status>)` and carrying `status`, `entries_extracted`, both incompleteness pairs and the sentence in `content_incomplete_detail`, `inventory_incomplete_detail` and `message`: `EncryptedNotSupported` (reason `encrypted`, with the header's `encryption` word) — the record the Needs-attention queue's `AndroidBackupWarning`/`encrypted` remedy matches, telling the examiner this build has no password field to offer; `HeaderTruncated` and `PayloadMissing` (reason `short_read`); `PayloadUnreadable` (reason `unresolved_structure`) when `entries()` fails; `PayloadTruncated` (reason `unresolved_structure`, with the tar error and the count extracted) when an entry errors mid-walk; and `EntryCapReached` (reason `cap_reached`, with `max_entries`) when the 100,000th entry was reached; and `CapReached` (reason `cap_reached`, with `max_decompressed_bytes`, and — when the ceiling fell inside an entry — `cut_entry_path`, `cut_entry_declared_size` and `cut_entry_bytes_extracted`) when the payload reached the 2 GiB ceiling, taking precedence over the `PayloadTruncated` the cut would otherwise cause. The entry the ceiling fell inside is stamped `cap_reached` with `content_omitted: payload_ceiling_reached` rather than `short_read`. A payload that ends exactly at the ceiling is not called capped. A clean backup carries none of them (`clean_backup_emits_no_status_record`); instead a walk that reached the archive's own end closes the list with one `AndroidBackupSummary` (`subtype: android_backup_summary`, `format_version` from the header, `compressed`, `encryption: none`, `entries_extracted`, `entries_content_incomplete`, and `app_packages` — the distinct `apps/<package>` directories among the file entries), parented to the backup, so a backup that was read is recognisable as a backup and the source-kind label can say so (ROADMAP §1.4). Reaching the end means every entry is listed, not that every entry's content was read: an entry over the 512 MiB per-entry cap, one whose bytes could not be read, or one shorter than its declared size carries its own `content_incomplete` flag, and the summary counts those in `entries_content_incomplete`. Only with that count at zero is its `status` `Extracted` and its name "unpacked whole"; otherwise it is `WalkedToEnd`, named "walked to its end", with a `message` giving the count. Graded on the Magnet 2019 Android CTF's `adb-data.tar` payload behind a restored five-line header: 258 file entries and 62 packages, as Python's `tarfile` counts them. Nothing goes to the timeline, no digest is computed here, and the API's content resolver has no `android_backup` arm, so an extracted file's content is not servable after ingest (see Cannot).

**Cannot.** It cannot serve a file's bytes after ingest. Each entry's content is an in-memory `ByteSliceDataSource` that nothing persists, and `content_resolver::apply_step` routes an artifact tagged `container: android_backup` to `reopen_container`, whose match rejects it with "Content resolution for 'android_backup' containers is not supported" — so a database that was parsed at ingest cannot be viewed in hex, downloaded, exported or handed to an ad-hoc module run afterwards. It cannot read past the 2 GiB payload ceiling, and a backup of a modern phone inflates well past it; the ceiling is a constant, not adjustable per run like `SEANCE_MAX_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES` for gzip, bzip2 and xz, so the `CapReached` record names it but cannot offer a way past it. Both places it can fall — a header boundary and inside an entry — are pinned under a small injected ceiling (`a_ceiling_on_a_header_boundary_is_named_not_read_as_the_end`, `a_ceiling_inside_an_entry_is_named_on_the_entry_and_the_backup`, `a_payload_that_fits_the_ceiling_exactly_is_not_called_capped`), on synthetic backups built to the documented layout; no real 2 GiB backup was on hand. It cannot resolve a hostile name: `path` is `/` + the stored name with `..`, `.` and an absolute root kept, unlike the tar, ZIP and 7z extractors, whose shared `resolve_entry_path` clamps them and flags `path_traversal` — so `../../x` in a crafted backup becomes `/../../x` on the file tree and in the export manifest. It cannot record when a file was written or who owned it: the tar header's `mtime`, `mode`, `uid`, `gid` and owner names are not read here (the tar extractor reads all of them), so nothing from a backup reaches the file timeline and an app's per-UID ownership is lost. It cannot record the backup's own facts: the version line and compressed flag are parsed and only logged, so the artifact tree does not say which `adb backup` format version this was or whether it was compressed. It cannot list a directory, symlink or hard link: non-`Regular` entries are skipped without a record, so `parent_path` is derived, never listed, and a link's target is lost. It cannot decrypt: an `AES-256` backup produces the warning and nothing else, and no password path exists in this crate (an `adb` backup is read only when it is unencrypted). It cannot hold a backup within bounded memory: every entry up to 512 MiB is resident at once, and 100,000 entries under a 2 GiB inflated total is the only bound on the sum. It reads a pre-POSIX (V7) tar payload — unlike the tar extractor it never looks for `ustar`, and `tar-rs` parses old-style headers — but it cannot read past an unrecoverable header after the first fault, and cannot see past a zero block inside the tar. It cannot verify content: the tar checksum covers headers only, the zlib stream's Adler-32 is checked by flate2 at its end and a mid-stream corruption is surfaced as a tar error, but there is no digest of any file.

**Refuses.** It refuses to let a backup that stopped early read as one that was whole, and every way the walk can stop has its own record: a truncated header, a header with no payload, a payload that will not open as tar, a mid-stream tar error and the entry cap each produce an `android_backup_status` record naming the failure and how many entries came out before it, because an examiner reads "not in the case" as "not on the device" (`unreadable_payload_emits_a_status_not_silence`, `mid_stream_tar_error_emits_a_status_alongside_the_partial_entries`, `entry_cap_warning_states_the_extraction_stopped_early`, `header_only_no_payload_reports_the_missing_payload`, `truncated_header_reports_instead_of_vanishing`). It refuses to present an unread file as an empty one: an entry over 512 MiB, one whose read failed and one that read short each carry the incompleteness pair with a reason (`oversized_entry_declares_that_its_content_was_omitted`, `truncated_entry_is_flagged_incomplete`, `complete_entry_has_no_incomplete_flag`). It refuses to leave an encrypted backup out of the completeness census: the encrypted warning carries the standard pair with reason `encrypted` so the court report's not-recovered section and the attention queue both see it (`encrypted_ab_carries_the_standard_incompleteness_pair`). It refuses to trust the header's size over the reader's: `entry.size()` is used so a crafted PAX `size` cannot publish one figure and deliver another. It refuses to be triggered by name alone — the magic must be present — and refuses to sniff the flood of ordinary `FileEntry`s, reading a header only for a `.ab` name or a `RawEvidence` artifact (`non_ab_file_entry_skipped_cheaply`, `garbage_ab_without_magic_returns_empty`). It never panics on a malformed input (`truncated_payload_does_not_panic`), never allocates from a declared size before the bytes arrive, never asks for or stores a password, and never returns a `ModuleError`: an artifact with no data source is an empty `Ok`, so nothing this module declines or refuses appears as an error row in the processing log — the refusals are all on the artifact tree, under `complete`.

### `container.bzip2_expander`

**Reads.** Every bzip2 stream in a file, under the same shape as the gzip expander. It subscribes to `Container` and `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::Stream`; an artifact whose `subtype` is anything but exactly `bzip2` yields an empty list, and one with no subtype is taken only when its lowercased `name` ends `.bz2`, `.tbz2` or `.tbz`. The `bzip2` subtype comes from `detect_file_type`, which claims a file when its first three bytes are `BZh`, and from the ingest extension map for `.bz2`. It needs `artifact.data` (`InvalidInputFormat`, "BZIP2 module requires data source", otherwise), reads three bytes at offset 0 through `read_full` and remembers whether they are `BZh`, then decodes stream by stream (`members::MemberChain`): each stream through `bzip2::bufread::BzDecoder` (bzip2 0.5.2 over libbz2 from `bzip2-sys`) on one buffered, byte-counting `SourceCursor` from offset 0, and after each stream another is decoded only if the next three bytes are `BZh`; anything else ends the walk at that offset. libbz2 checks each block's CRC and the stream's combined CRC as it goes, surfacing a failure as an `InvalidInput` error; a stream that ends before `BZ_STREAM_END` is an `UnexpectedEof` error, "decompression not finished but EOF reached". The output is spilled by `TempBackedSource::from_reader` into an anonymous, already-unlinked file in the system temp directory, in 64 KiB writes, under `limits::max_decompressed_bytes()` — 10 GiB by default, `SEANCE_MAX_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES` read once per process — with the reader wrapped in `take(cap + 1)` so an overrun is detected rather than clipped. When the temp file is complete it reads five bytes at offset 257 of the output and calls the payload a tar if there are at least 262 bytes and they read `ustar`.

**Produces.** One artifact per stream, parented to the compressed artifact: a `Container` with `subtype: "tar"` when the `ustar` test passed, otherwise a `FileEntry` with no subtype; in both cases the temp-backed random-access source is attached. Metadata: `name` — `.tar.bz2` becomes `.tar`, `.tbz2` and `.tbz` become `.tar`, a bare `.bz2` is stripped, and any other name gets `.decompressed` appended — `size` (bytes written), `container: "bzip2"`, `container_path` (the outer name, or `unknown.bz2`), `compressed_members` (streams decoded), the `trailing_bytes_after_last_member` / `trailing_bytes_offset` / `trailing_bytes_all_zero` trio when bytes follow the last stream without beginning another — non-zero ones also setting `content_incomplete: true` with reason `unresolved_structure` (`every_stream_of_a_multi_stream_bzip2_is_expanded`, `bytes_after_the_last_stream_are_recorded_not_dropped`, on real `bzip2` output) — and the ceiling pair `decompression_ceiling_bytes` / `decompression_ceiling_source` (`default` or `SEANCE_MAX_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES`) that the report's ceiling census reads to print `limits::ceiling_statement`, counting this container among those admitted under that figure. On a decode failure with `BZh` present it produces one `ParsedRecord` instead — `type: ArchiveScanStatus`, `record_type: archive_scan_status`, `name: "<name> (not expanded)"`, `container: bzip2`, `content_incomplete: true` with reason `bzip2_decompress_failed`, `inventory_incomplete: true` with reason `unresolved_structure`, `entries_recovered: 0`, the decoder's message in the three detail keys with the cap guidance appended when the ceiling was the cause, and the fixed `message` — with no ceiling stamp. After ingest, the API's `reopen_compressed` runs this `process()` again on a synthetic copy of the parent to serve the inner file or a tar entry inside it, and caches the result per parent id. The end-to-end `.tbz` chain — bzip2 child carrying data, tar extractor windowing its members out — is pinned in `tests/archive_chain.rs::tbz_chain_surfaces_inner_files`. No timeline event, no hash, no record for a name-gated file that was never bzip2.

**Cannot.** It cannot keep the good streams of a file with a bad one: a stream that begins `BZh` and then fails fails the whole expansion closed, the streams before it included. It cannot decode bytes after the last stream that do not begin `BZh`, only count them and say where they start, and it records no stream boundaries inside the child. The multi-stream walk is pinned on a two-stream `cat` of real `bzip2` output; no `pbzip2` or `lbzip2` file was on the machine that wrote it. It cannot recover an inner name or time from the stream: bzip2 has no header fields for them, so the child's name is the outer name with a suffix rule applied and it carries no `modified`, `path` or `parent_path`. It cannot recognise a tar without the `ustar` magic at 257, and the tar extractor cannot either, so a V7 tar inside is never expanded. It cannot work without temp space equal to the decompressed size, cannot bound its work by the compressed size (a ceiling-sized bomb is written in full before it is admitted), and cannot keep the decompressed bytes past the ingest process — the content resolver re-decompresses on the first request. It cannot report an unparseable `SEANCE_MAX_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES` as a choice — that silently becomes the built-in default with `from_env: false` — and cannot pick up a value changed after the first stream of the process was expanded. It verifies nothing beyond what libbz2 verifies: the block and stream CRCs are the library's arithmetic, no test in this module pins that they are checked, and there is no digest of the decompressed output on the record. A `.bz2`-named file without `BZh` that fails to decode produces nothing at all, and an artifact whose subtype says `bzip2` without the magic goes the same way; both are folded into the "ran and produced nothing" processing-log row and are indistinguishable there from a module that read the artifact and found nothing.

**Refuses.** The refusals mirror the gzip tier line for line, and the three tiers share `TempBackedSource` and `limits::expansion_failure_detail` precisely so that they cannot drift. A stream that would pass the ceiling fails closed and is never truncated at it ; a libbz2 error after output has begun fails closed with "decompression failed after N bytes; refusing to serve a truncated stream as complete" rather than serving the prefix; a stream that ends early is an `UnexpectedEof` refusal, not a short success; and a block or stream CRC failure is refused as libbz2 reports it. A file carrying `BZh` that will not expand is recorded as `ArchiveScanStatus` with both incompleteness pairs and never as an empty success, so a corrupt or capped archive cannot read as one that held nothing (`test_bzip2_corrupted_emits_incompleteness_status`), while a `.bz2`-named file without the magic is left silent so the record is not spammed by mislabelled files (`test_bzip2_without_magic_is_silent`). It refuses to stamp a refusal with the ceiling keys, so a stamp means admitted (`test_bzip2_expanded_child_records_the_ceiling_it_was_admitted_under` pins the other half). It refuses a missing data source with `InvalidInputFormat` — a folded "skipped" row with `error_message: None` — and any other subtype or name with an empty list. As with gzip, a bad stream is never a `ModuleError`: the refusal travels as one status artifact under `complete`, on the artifact tree, and an examiner asking why a `.bz2` yielded no files must look there rather than in the processing log's error rows. Nothing is written to evidence; the anonymous temp file is the only file created.

### `container.e01_reader`

**Reads.** An EnCase/EWF evidence file, and it decides for itself only on a name. It subscribes to `ArtifactType::Container` with `InputCapability::FilePath`, and gates twice: an artifact whose `subtype` is anything other than `e01` or `ewf` yields an empty list, and an artifact with no subtype at all yields an empty list unless its `name` metadata ends in an EWF segment extension — exactly three ASCII characters, first `E`, `S` or `L` in either case, then either two ASCII digits other than `00` — segment numbering starts at one, and the ingest layer's own ordinal refuses `.E00` on the same ground — or two **uppercase** ASCII letters, the uppercase requirement being what keeps `.exe`, `.eml` and `.epub` out of the parsing path. The `e01` subtype it usually runs on is not its own work: `seance_core::file_detection::detect_file_type` reads the first 512 bytes of the file in a loop and calls it an E01 container when at least 8 bytes arrived and either the first three are `EVF` or all eight are the logical signature `LVF\x09\x0d\x0a\xff\x00`, and that answer is mapped to a `Container` artifact with subtype `e01`. The file it opens is the `path` metadata, not the `name` it gated on. Before libewf is asked for anything, that file's own first eight bytes are read: `EVF\x09\x0d\x0a\xff\x00` is a physical image and is opened, `LVF\x09\x0d\x0a\xff\x00` is a logical evidence file (`.L01`) and is walked as one, never served as a disk image (the logical route is described at the end of this paragraph) — and a file whose signature cannot be read is left to libewf, which is about to try the same file. Opening runs by default in a separate process: `isolated::open_e01` spawns the `seance-ewf-helper` binary — found at `SEANCE_EWF_HELPER`, else beside the current executable, else one directory up — hands it the path, and the child opens the image with libewf so that a segmentation fault inside a C library on hostile evidence kills only the child. Inside the child, `libewf_glob` is asked for the segment set with format 0 (auto-detect); on success every returned filename is copied out through a lossy UTF-8 conversion before the C array is freed and the whole list is handed to `libewf_handle_open` with read-only access flags, and on glob failure the single named file is opened alone. `libewf_handle_get_media_size` must then answer or the open fails, and `libewf_handle_set_read_zero_chunk_on_error` is asked to turn zero-substitution off so that a chunk libewf cannot decode raises an error rather than being handed up as zeroes — a request whose return code is checked, so that an image on which libewf will not accept it does not open at all. Every segment path is then `stat`ed to measure the set on disk. Metadata is read once, at open: ten UTF-8 header values by the two-call size-then-value protocol — `case_number`, `description`, `examiner_name` (published as `examiner`), `evidence_number`, `notes`, `acquiry_date`, `acquiry_software_version`, `acquiry_operating_system`, `serial_number` and `model`; `libewf_handle_get_number_of_sectors` and `libewf_handle_get_bytes_per_sector`; `libewf_handle_get_format`, naming the EWF variant; `libewf_handle_get_compression_values`, whose out-param — literally named `compression_level` in libewf's own header — is the acquisition-time compression level (`default`/`none`/`fast`/`best`), a different enum from the compression *method* (zlib/DEFLATE vs bzip2), which no call in this crate asks for; `libewf_handle_get_chunk_size` and `get_sectors_per_chunk`, from which a chunk count is computed (never asked of libewf directly — no read-path accessor for it exists in this build's bindings) and labelled as computed; and the EWF hash section's `MD5` and `SHA1` values, trimmed, lower-cased and dropped when empty — the acquisition tool's hashes of the **decoded media**, not of the container file. Twenty-two libewf entry points in all — the format/level code tables are transcribed by hand from `/usr/include/libewf/definitions.h`, since this build's bindgen allowlist does not surface either enum by name. The child then serves random reads over a framed little-endian stdio protocol (handshake: status byte, `u64` size, `u32`-prefixed metadata JSON; request: `u64` offset, `u32` length; response: status byte, `u32` length, bytes), and the parent wraps that pipe in a `CachingDataSource` holding 64 KiB chunk-aligned regions in a 128 MiB LRU — 2,048 chunks — because each read is a process round-trip and each libewf read re-decompresses the whole containing chunk. Reads go through `libewf_handle_read_random`, so no seek position is kept. The same `process()` is also driven outside the orchestrator by the API's content resolver, per content request, on a synthetic artifact built from the stored metadata. A logical evidence file goes by `isolated::open_l01` instead, with the same isolation default, helper discovery and in-process fallback: the helper is started as `seance-ewf-helper --logical <path>`, opens the file exactly as above, and walks its entry tree from `libewf_handle_get_root_file_entry` down through `libewf_file_entry_get_number_of_sub_file_entries` and `libewf_file_entry_get_sub_file_entry`, in pre-order, iteratively (one libewf entry held per level of the current path, freed as each level finishes), and at most 1,000,000 entries and 256 levels below the root. Of every entry it asks libewf the UTF-8 name (two-call, a declared name over 64 KiB not read), type (`d`/`f`), flags, size, media data offset and size, duplicate media data offset, the four times the L01 records — `creation_time`, `modification_time`, `access_time` and `entry_modification_time`, POSIX seconds as libewf returns them — and the MD5 the L01 stores for the entry, where it stores one; a getter that fails is recorded with libewf's words against that field and the walk goes on. The walk crosses the pipe after the handshake as a JSON header and one length-prefixed JSON frame per entry; the parent refuses a count over the million, a frame over 1 MiB, and any entry whose parent link does not point at an earlier entry one level up whose index path its own extends. An entry's bytes are then read through `libewf_file_entry_read_random` on the entry re-found by its index path (the child index at each level), requested by the entry's position in the walk — so libewf, not this crate, decides where an entry's data lives, including data EnCase stored once for duplicate files. The content resolver re-opens one entry the same way, re-walking the file to find it by `l01_index_path`, and keeps up to four entry sources alive.

**Produces.** One `RawEvidence` artifact per container, parented to the container artifact, named `<name>_extracted` — or, where the artifact carries no name, after the file that was opened, with `subtype: "raw"`, `container: "e01"`, `container_path` set to the file that was opened, `size` set to the media size the handshake declared, and a data source over the decoded image — so partitioning, file systems, carving, hashing and search see an ordinary raw disk. Its `e01_metadata` object carries whichever of the ten header values the image held, `sectors` and `bytes_per_sector` where libewf answered, `ewf_format`, `compression_level`, `chunk_size_bytes`, `sectors_per_chunk` and `number_of_chunks_computed` where those calls succeeded, `media_size`, `source_file`, `stored_md5` and `stored_sha1` where the hash section held them, and the set's composition: `segment_count`, `segment_files` as basenames in glob order, and `segment_bytes_total` as the summed on-disk size. `stored_md5` and `stored_sha1` are also written at the **top** level of the artifact, because that is where the integrity path looks: `evaluate_integrity` uses them as the baseline the recomputed media hash is checked against, taken after any `acquisition_*` baseline and before a file's own content digests, and with no SHA-256 on that route. Where a segment named in the set could not be `stat`ed, `segment_bytes_total` is `null`, the partial sum is published under its own name `segment_bytes_known`, the unstatable segments are listed with their OS errors, and `inventory_incomplete: true` with `inventory_incomplete_reason: "unresolved_structure"` plus a sentence saying the set's total size is unknown rather than the partial sum shown — and four of those keys (`inventory_incomplete`, `inventory_incomplete_reason`, `segments_unstatable`, `segment_bytes_known`) are copied up to the artifact's top-level metadata, because every consumer of that incompleteness pair reads the top level and a flag left one level down is written and never rendered ; the null total and the explanatory sentence stay in the nested object. Where the helper's metadata frame did not parse as JSON, the object is empty and the open still succeeds, so the artifact carries no baseline and no header values at all. For a logical evidence file it produces no `RawEvidence` at all. It produces one `LogicalEvidenceInventory` `ParsedRecord` (subtype `ewf_logical_inventory`) carrying `entries_published`, `root_present`, the two ceilings (`entry_cap`, `depth_cap`) and whether each was reached, `entries_not_walked` (a lower bound when the entry ceiling fired), up to 100 of the walk's errors and their count, `unreadable_names`, `entries_with_field_errors`, `directory_data_streams_published`, `directory_placeholder_bytes_not_served`, `directory_placeholder_values_recorded`, `directory_placeholder_spans_checked`, `directory_placeholder_bytes_alone`, `directory_placeholder_bytes_in_shared_span`, `stored_spans_unknown`, `directories_with_data_not_served` (only where a directory's stored data disagrees with its recorded size), `walk_incomplete`, the L01's `media_size`, its `e01_metadata`, `e01_open_mode`, and — where the walk is incomplete — `content_incomplete` with reason `cap_reached` (a ceiling) or `unresolved_structure` (libewf would not hand over an entry or a count) and a sentence naming which. Then one `FileEntry` per entry, parented flat to the container like a ZIP's, in pre-order: `name` as recorded, `path` the `/`-joined names from the root (the NGDC EnCase files' root is `LogicalEntries`), `parent_path`, `size` (libewf's entry size, else its media data size), `is_directory` (type `d`), `container: "ewf_logical"`, `container_path`, `l01_entry_ordinal`, `l01_index_path`, `l01_entry_type`, `l01_flags`, the three media-data values and `l01_sub_entries`; the four times raw under `l01_creation_time`, `l01_modification_time`, `l01_access_time` and `l01_entry_modification_time`, and — where non-zero, 0 being how an L01 says a time was not recorded — projected as RFC 3339 UTC onto `created`, `modified`, `accessed` and `changed` (entry modification being a metadata change) with `timezone: "UTC"`, which the file timeline projects; the entry's stored MD5 as `stored_md5` with `stored_hash_source: "l01_entry"`, the baseline Verify Integrity compares the served bytes against; `l01_field_errors` where a getter failed; and `name_unreadable`, `name_lossy_utf8` or `name_contains_path_separator` where those hold. A file (anything not type `d`) carries a data source serving its bytes to its recorded size through a 64 KiB-chunk, 4 MiB cache; one flagged sparse carries `l01_content_source` — `duplicate_data_offset` where the entry table names one (libewf 20140816's `libewf_file_entry_read_buffer` then reads the recorded size from the media stream at that offset), with the file entry whose data sits there as `l01_duplicate_of_path` and `l01_duplicate_of_ordinal`, else `sparse_one_byte_repeated` (libewf repeats the one stored byte to the recorded size) — a sentence saying which as `l01_content_source_detail`, and `l01_duplicate_content_check`: entries of at most 64 MiB are read at ingest and hashed against the MD5 the L01 stores for them, `stored_md5_matches` lifting any stamp, `stored_md5_differs` stamping `content_incomplete` with reason `unresolved_structure`, and `no_stored_md5` or `not_checked` stamping reason `unvalidated`; one whose stored data is shorter than its size is stamped `short_read`. A directory whose stored data equals its recorded size is followed by a second `FileEntry`, its own stream: `name` and `path` the directory's with `:l01_directory_data` appended, `is_directory: false`, `l01_record_kind: "directory_data"`, `l01_directory_data_of` the directory's path, the directory's index path and media values, `l01_directory_data_decoded: false` and a sentence saying the bytes are not decoded, with a data source serving what libewf reads for that directory entry; the directory itself names it as `l01_directory_data_stream` and still has no data source, and `entries_published` does not count the streams. A directory recording no size and storing one byte — the form libewf reads as an entry with no content — is marked `l01_directory_placeholder_byte`; the walk reads that one byte from the media stream at the entry's own offset and records it as `l01_directory_placeholder_value` (0-255), or the read failure in `l01_field_errors`; one with no usable media offset is not read, and its sentence says so. After a complete walk each placeholder's byte is compared with every walked entry's stored span, and with every sparse entry's read at its duplicate data offset, and marked `l01_directory_placeholder_byte_span` `alone` or `shared`, and only `alone` is described as covered by no other entry's stored data; after an incomplete walk the mark is `not_checked_walk_incomplete`, and where any walked entry's span is not known (libewf would not give its media offset or size, a sparse entry's duplicate offset or flags, or it stores data at no usable offset; counted in `stored_spans_unknown`) the mark is `not_checked_span_unknown`, and no such claim is made. The byte is not served as content and no meaning is given for it: the format defines none. SQLite and registry sidecars among the entries are bundled as for a file system. Where libewf cannot open or walk the file it produces one `ContainerRefusal` `ParsedRecord` instead, subtype `ewf_logical_evidence`, carrying the container path, `content_incomplete` with reason `unresolved_structure`, and a sentence giving libewf's reason and saying the file's contents were not recovered. The artifact's top-level metadata also carries `e01_open_mode` — `isolated_helper` or `in_process`, which of the three ways this image was opened, a custody fact `open_e01` always knows and previously left off the record. It produces no timeline event, no hash of its own, and — apart from that one refusal — no record of any kind for a container it could not open.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell you that the image is intact. It verifies nothing at open: the MD5 and SHA-1 the acquisition tool wrote into the image are copied out and published as a baseline, and this module never computes a hash of the decoded media, never compares one, and emits no integrity record — the comparison happens later, elsewhere, and only when something asks for it. It reads only `MD5` and `SHA1` from the hash section, so an image recording a SHA-256 has no SHA-256 baseline here, and the integrity path it feeds carries `None` for SHA-256 on the stored route. Where the metadata frame did not parse, there is no baseline at all and nothing distinguishes that from an image whose acquisition tool recorded none. It does not verify the EWF chunk checksums itself; that is libewf's arithmetic, and a failure reaches the caller as an I/O error carrying libewf's own words where it gave any (`libewf error at offset N: …`) and saying so where it gave none, so a failed chunk checksum, a missing segment and a truncated file are told apart only as far as libewf's message tells them apart. A read libewf ends early is not an error at all: zero bytes mid-image is taken as end-of-file, the short chunk is logged and not cached, and the caller is handed a short count with nothing on the artifact to say so. It cannot bound the image by anything it checked: `size` is whatever the handshake declared, up to the full range of a `u64`, and it is never cross-checked against the segments' on-disk bytes, nor is `sectors × bytes_per_sector` checked against `media_size`. It cannot say a multi-segment set is whole. It publishes the count and names libewf's glob returned and nothing more: there is no test here that the segments form a contiguous `1..n` run, no missing-segment refusal, and no statement of which segment any byte came from — the well-formed-set check lives in the ingest layer, over the files on disk, and governs whether an acquisition baseline may be recorded, not whether this module opens the image. It cannot report a set's size when a segment cannot be `stat`ed, and a segment whose filename is not valid UTF-8 trips that same flag, because the names are copied out of C lossily and then `stat`ed as the lossy string. It cannot distinguish a sparse or unallocated region of the acquired device from acquired zeroes: it exposes bytes and a length and nothing else, and a run of zeroes is served with nothing marking it absent. It cannot say how the image was compressed: `ewf_format` names the EWF variant and `compression_level` the acquisition-time level, but no call in this crate asks libewf for the compression *method* (zlib/DEFLATE vs bzip2) — there is no such accessor in this build's bindings — so a chunk's actual codec is not on the record (standard EWF only ever uses zlib/DEFLATE regardless of level; bzip2 needs the EWF2/Ex01 format, which `ewf_format` states independently of this). The chunk count is never asked of libewf directly either, since no read-path accessor for it exists; `number_of_chunks_computed` is derived from sectors ÷ sectors-per-chunk and labelled as computed, not reported. It cannot say more about acquisition than five of the ten header values it now reads carry: `acquiry_date`, `acquiry_software_version`, `acquiry_operating_system`, `serial_number` and `model` are read the same two-call way as `case_number` etc., but a header the acquisition tool did not write is a genuine absence — this module cannot tell that apart from a header it failed to ask for. It cannot say more about a logical evidence file's entries than libewf's `file_entry` API exposes: no ACLs, no attributes beyond the flags word, and no hash but the stored MD5. It does not decode the data EnCase stores against directory entries, which it serves as `:l01_directory_data` streams: on the NGDC phone L01s the 192-byte record beside each photo holds the photo's name, its size as text and four 32-bit POSIX times, but those times agree with neither the independent zip export's file times nor any constant offset from them (`L01-1`), and no published description of the record was found, so what they record is not established and nothing in it is presented as a time. It does not serve the single byte a directory with no recorded size stores, and it cannot say what that byte means: it records the value, and on the five NGDC files it was measured to lie in the entry's own span (the stored spans tile the media with no gap or overlap), but its values vary, a one-off probe found no relation to the neighbouring bytes or the entry's name, and the EWF specification requires a size-0 entry to store one byte and libewf never reads it, so the byte has no defined meaning and none is given it. The times it projects have been checked against no real L01 that records one: the only public L01s it was graded on record every time as 0. It cannot vouch for the bytes of a sparse entry with no stored MD5, or larger than 64 MiB, or one libewf fills from its single stored byte (no real L01 here has one) — those stay `unvalidated`; the one sparse entry per NGDC file names a duplicate data offset and its served bytes match its stored MD5. It cannot read an `.Lx01` (EWF2), for which no public sample exists to test against, and a multi-segment `.L01` set is opened through the same glob as an E01 set but has been tested on no real one. It cannot walk more than 1,000,000 entries or below level 256; past either, what was not walked is counted and stated, not read. It cannot read anything encrypted: no key or password call exists in this crate, and an image libewf will not open produces a `ParsingError` and no artifact. It cannot match a four-character extension, so `.Ex01`/`.Lx01` never pass the name fallback and reach this module only when the content check has already labelled them. `.l01` is in no extension map: an `.L01` reaches this module by its signature, and one whose first bytes cannot be read does not reach it at all. It cannot match a segment named past `.EZZ`: the name gate accepts only the prefixes `E`, `S` and `L`, so every `FAA`…`ZZZ` continuation name is rejected by name. It cannot return more than 64 MiB from one read — `MAX_ISOLATED_READ` clamps the request on the parent side and the length again on the child side — so a caller asking for more is given a short read and must loop; the in-process fallback applies no such clamp, and through the artifact's own data source the clamp is never reached, because the cache reads its inner source 64 KiB at a time. Its other ceilings: a frame carrying metadata or an error message that declares more than 64 MiB is refused, while a read response declaring more than the caller asked for is refused outright; the decoded-chunk cache is 2,048 regions of 64 KiB — 128 MiB — per opened image, and the API's content resolver keeps up to eight reopened containers, so up to eight helper processes and about a gibibyte of chunk cache can be alive at once; a short chunk fill is never memoised, so a momentary shortfall does not become the permanent view of that range. It cannot promise the isolation it is named for: with `SEANCE_E01_ISOLATED` set to `false` or `0` it parses in-process with no log line, and with the helper binary absent it warns and parses in-process, where a malformed image can take down the whole server — and `e01_open_mode` records only `isolated_helper` or `in_process`, not which of the two in-process routes was taken.

**Refuses.** It refuses to substitute zeroes for a chunk libewf could not decode, and asks for that refusal at open — `libewf_handle_set_read_zero_chunk_on_error` is set to 0 precisely so that a bad chunk raises an error rather than presenting as a region of zeroes, because zeroes are a finding in their own right and a decode failure dressed as zeroes is unfalsifiable downstream. The return code of that one call is checked: an image on which libewf will not accept the request is not opened at all, rather than read under libewf's own default with nothing on the record to say which governed. It refuses to write: the handle is opened with read-only access flags, and nothing in the crate writes to evidence. It refuses to treat anything coming back from the helper as trustworthy, because the helper exists to hold a C library that hostile evidence can corrupt: a declared metadata or error frame longer than 64 MiB is refused as `isolated frame too large` before a byte is allocated for it, a declared length the child does not then send is an I/O error rather than a read of stale memory, a response claiming more bytes than the caller asked for is refused outright and every later read on that handle is refused with it — clamping to the buffer stopped the overrun but left the surplus in the pipe, so each later frame decoded from the middle of this one and served bytes under an offset they did not come from — and truncation at any point in a frame is an error and never a partial success reported as a whole one, while a frame shorter than the request stays an ordinary short read; and a logical-mode walk declaring more than 1,000,000 entries, an entry frame over 1 MiB, or an entry whose parent link points forward, skips a level or disagrees with its index path is refused before the parent follows it; all pinned by the ten tests in `protocol_tests`, with the same three decoders fuzzed by `fuzz/fuzz_targets/e01_isolated_protocol.rs`. It refuses to fail an otherwise readable image over its metadata: metadata JSON that will not parse becomes an empty object and the open proceeds, because the metadata is descriptive and the media is the evidence — at the cost of the baseline going with it. It refuses to publish a set total it does not have, a segment that cannot be examined on disk leaves `segment_bytes_total` null and the partial sum under a different name, rather than rendering "could not determine" as a smaller, confident number in the custody record. It refuses a name that merely looks like a segment — a lowercase letter-continuation such as `.eaa` is rejected outright so that `.exe`, `.eml` and `.epub` cannot enter the parsing path, and a user with genuinely lowercase continuation segments must rename them or set the subtype explicitly. It refuses to publish a container of files as an image of a device: a logical evidence file is recognised by its own `LVF` signature — not by its `.L01` name, so a physical image named that way still opens — and its media stream, EnCase's packing of the entries' data, is never published as raw evidence; its entries are walked instead, and one libewf cannot open or walk leaves a `ContainerRefusal` record naming what was not recovered, because an exhibit that produced nothing must never read as an exhibit that held nothing. It refuses to identify an entry by its name, which need not be unique: reads, and the content resolver, find an entry by its index path. It refuses to project an L01 time of 0 onto the timeline as 1970. Everywhere else it will not or cannot read, it leaves no artifact: a missing `path` is an `InvalidInputFormat` folded into the artifact's single "skipped" row shared with every module that declined it; a handle that will not initialise, a set that will not open, or a media size libewf will not give produce a `ParsingError` recorded as one `error` row in the processing log with its message; and a subtype it does not claim returns an empty list, which is folded into the "ran and produced nothing" row and is not distinguishable there from a module that read the artifact and found nothing in it. There is no refusal artifact in any of those cases, so on the case record an E01 that was recognised and would not open is not distinguishable from one nobody pointed at — except in the processing log. Its reading of a real image is pinned by two corpus-gated checks, neither fixture present in this tree, both skipping when it is absent: the isolated path decodes `nps-2009-canon2-gen6.E01` to 31,129,600 bytes with MD5 `750b509d8fbed37a5213480aaccfdc61`, and validation case WIN-1 reads `NTFS-HiddenFiles.E01` through the in-process reader and reproduces FTK Imager's 2023 acquisition log — MD5 `e7d5b36a407d5a02d0872d4dd3f3f9d0`, SHA-1 `5edc4c6efda9d266ecabcab5629694d0063e9d7f` — over 101,711,872 decoded bytes. Its walk of a real logical evidence file is pinned by validation case L01-1 (`SEANCE_L01_CORPUS`, skipping when unset): on the five EnCase 7.4.1.10 `.L01` acquisitions of one iPhone in Digital Corpora's 2012 National Gallery scenario, all 59,687 entries libewf's own `ewfinfo` lists are published at the same path and nothing else is, the 55,599 files are each served in full to their recorded size (103,292,662 bytes) and the 646 carrying a stored MD5 match it, and all 30 camera-roll JPEGs of an independent zip export of the same phone match an entry by name, size and MD5.

### `container.gzip_expander`

**Reads.** Every gzip member in a file, and only when something has already called the artifact one. It subscribes to `Container` and `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::Stream` and gates in two steps: an artifact whose `subtype` is set to anything other than exactly `gzip` yields an empty list, and one with no subtype at all is accepted only if its `name`, lowercased, ends `.gz`, `.gzip` or `.tgz`. The `gzip` subtype it keys on is written by `seance_core::file_detection::detect_file_type`, which reads the first 512 bytes and calls a file gzip when bytes 0–1 are `1F 8B` — checked before the tar test at offset 257, so a compressed tarball is gzip first — and by the ingest extension map for a bare `.gz`. It then needs `artifact.data`, and returns `InvalidInputFormat` ("GZIP module requires data source") without one. Before decoding it reads two bytes at offset 0 through `read_full` and remembers whether they are the gzip magic; that flag decides later whether a failure is recorded or kept silent. The stream is decoded member by member (`members::MemberChain`): each member by `flate2::bufread::GzDecoder` (flate2 1.1.5) over one buffered, byte-counting `SourceCursor` from offset 0, and after each member the next two bytes are read and another member decoded only if they are `1F 8B`; anything else ends the walk at that offset. In each member the RFC 1952 header is parsed — `FEXTRA`, `FNAME`, `FCOMMENT` and an `FHCRC` header CRC when present, the last verified — the deflate body is inflated, and at the end of the member the trailer's CRC-32 and `ISIZE` are checked against what was produced, a mismatch failing the read with "corrupt gzip stream does not have a matching checksum" and a missing trailer with `UnexpectedEof`. The decoded bytes are not held in memory: `TempBackedSource::from_reader` streams them in 64 KiB writes into `tempfile::tempfile()` — an anonymous file in the system temp directory, unlinked at creation — under the run's decompression ceiling, `limits::max_decompressed_bytes()`: 10,737,418,240 bytes (10 GiB) unless `SEANCE_MAX_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES` carried a value that parsed (plain bytes or a `K`/`M`/`G`/`T` binary suffix, zero and anything unparseable rejected), read once per process through a `OnceLock`. The reader is wrapped in `take(cap + 1)` so a stream one byte over the ceiling is detected rather than truncated at it. Once the temp file is complete it reads five bytes at offset 257 of the decompressed output and, if there are at least 262 bytes and they spell `ustar`, treats the payload as a tar.

**Produces.** Exactly one artifact per stream, parented to the compressed artifact. When the payload passed the `ustar` test it is a `Container` with `subtype: "tar"`, which is what `container.tar_extractor` subscribes to; otherwise it is a `FileEntry` with no subtype, left for name- and content-based modules to claim. Either way its data source is the temp-file-backed `TempBackedSource`, random-access, alive until the last reference drops. Its metadata is `name` — the outer name with `.tar.gz` and `.gz` cut to leave `.tar` or the bare name, `.tgz` rewritten to `.tar`, `.gzip` stripped, and anything else suffixed `.decompressed` — `size` (the count of bytes actually written to the temp file), `container: "gzip"`, `container_path` (the outer artifact's `name`, or `unknown.gz` when it had none), `compressed_members` (how many members were decoded), and — when bytes follow the last member and do not begin another — `trailing_bytes_after_last_member`, `trailing_bytes_offset` and `trailing_bytes_all_zero`; trailing bytes that are not all zero also set `content_incomplete: true` with reason `unresolved_structure` and a detail naming the count and offset, because they may be a damaged member, while zero padding is counted and not called a gap (`every_member_of_a_concatenated_gzip_is_expanded`, `bytes_after_the_last_member_are_recorded_not_dropped`, `zero_padding_after_the_last_member_is_counted_but_not_a_gap`, all on real `gzip` output). It also carries the two ceiling keys `limits::stamp_ceiling` writes on every successful expansion: `decompression_ceiling_bytes`, the figure that admitted this stream, and `decompression_ceiling_source`, either `default` or the literal `SEANCE_MAX_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES`. Those two keys are what the report's method-qualifications census reads (`seance_api::lib` around the `CEILING_QUALIFICATION_SUBJECT` block) to print `limits::ceiling_statement` — one entry per distinct ceiling, with a count of the gzip/bzip2/xz containers admitted under it — so the sentence a report prints about the ceiling is read off the evidence and never from the reporting process's own environment.
