When decoding fails and the two-byte magic was present, the single artifact is instead a `ParsedRecord` from `status::expansion_failed_status`: `type: ArchiveScanStatus`, `record_type: archive_scan_status`, `name: "<name> (not expanded)"`, `container: gzip`, `container_path`, `content_incomplete: true` with `content_incomplete_reason: gzip_decompress_failed`, `inventory_incomplete: true` with `inventory_incomplete_reason: unresolved_structure`, `entries_recovered: 0`, the decoder's own message in `content_incomplete_detail`, `inventory_incomplete_detail` and `detail` — with `limits::cap_guidance` appended when the error carries the `decompression ceiling reached:` marker, naming the byte figure and the variable that raises it — and a fixed `message` saying the contents are unknown, not absent. A refusal carries no ceiling stamp, so a stamp always means "admitted". The API's content resolver runs this same `process()` on a synthetic copy of the parent (`reopen_compressed`) whenever the inner file or a tar entry inside it is asked for after ingest, caching the temp-backed source per parent id. It emits no timeline event, no hash and no record of its own for a name-gated file that turns out not to be gzip.

**Cannot.** It cannot keep the good members of a file with a bad one: a member that begins with the magic and then fails to decode fails the whole expansion closed, so the members before it are not served either (the status record says the stream could not be expanded). It cannot decode bytes after the last member that do not begin with the magic — a member whose header was overwritten is among them — and can only count them and say where they start. It cannot say which member a byte of the child came from: the members are concatenated into one child with no member boundaries recorded. It cannot record what the gzip header knows: `GzDecoder::header()` exposes `FNAME`, `MTIME`, `OS` and the comment, and none of them is read, so the inner name is invented from the outer name — a `.tgz` whose payload is not a tar is still named `.tar`, a `data.gz` whose header says `report.docx` is named `data` — and the child carries no `modified`, no `path` and no `parent_path`. It cannot tell a V7 or otherwise magic-less tar from a plain file: the only test is `ustar` at offset 257, and the tar extractor applies the same test, so such a payload lands as a `FileEntry` and is never expanded. It cannot expand within memory: every byte is written to the system temp directory before anything reads it, so a stream of N bytes costs N bytes of temp space, a stream that turns out to exceed the ceiling has written up to the ceiling before it is refused, and the content resolver re-decompresses the whole stream on the first request after ingest because the temp file was unlinked at creation and does not survive the ingest process. It cannot bound the work by the compressed size: the ceiling counts decompressed bytes only, and a 10 MiB file that inflates to 10 GiB is admitted at 10 GiB of temp writes. It cannot report the ceiling as a choice unless it was one: a `SEANCE_MAX_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES` value that does not parse is silently the built-in default with `from_env: false`, which is deliberate (a typo must not remove the ceiling) but means the record cannot distinguish "nobody set it" from "somebody set it wrongly". The ceiling is read once per process, so a value changed between two ingests in one server lifetime does not take effect. It cannot verify more than the trailer offers: a CRC-32 and a length modulo 2^32, both computed by flate2 — there is no test in this module pinning that the checksum is checked at all; the guarantee is the library's. It cannot say why a name-gated file was left alone: a `.gz` without the magic that fails to decode yields an empty list, folded into the artifact's "ran and produced nothing" processing-log row, and one with subtype `gzip` set by hand but no magic goes the same way. Its child has the outer artifact's parent chain and nothing else — no `original_name`, no traversal flag, since a gzip has no entry name to resolve — and the ingest extension map sends `.tar.gz` and `.tgz` to subtype `tar`, not `gzip`, in the one case content detection fails, so that fast path would decline them; in practice a real gzip is always caught by its magic first.

**Refuses.** It refuses to serve a partial stream as a complete one, and both halves of that refusal are pinned. A stream that would exceed the ceiling fails closed with `limits::cap_exceeded` — the temp file is discarded, nothing is served, and the status record says which figure was reached and how to raise it (`cap_exceeded_fails_closed`, `a_refused_stream_is_not_stamped_as_admitted_under_the_ceiling`). A decode error after some output has already been written fails closed too, with the message "decompression failed after N bytes; refusing to serve a truncated stream as complete", rather than returning the bytes decoded so far (`mid_stream_error_after_output_fails_closed`), because the tar or file inside would then carry the wrong hash with nothing marking it short. A trailer whose CRC-32 or length disagrees with what was inflated is refused by flate2 and recorded here as `gzip_decompress_failed` with the library's sentence. It refuses to let a failure pass for an empty file: a stream carrying the gzip magic that will not expand produces the `ArchiveScanStatus` record with both incompleteness pairs, never an empty success, so a corrupt or bomb-capped `.gz` cannot ingest exactly like a file that was never gzip (`test_gzip_corrupted_data_emits_incompleteness_status`). It refuses, symmetrically, to stamp a file that was never its own: a `.gz`-named file without the two magic bytes that fails to decode is left silent, because a status that fired on every mislabelled file on a disk would tell an examiner nothing (`test_gzip_without_magic_is_silent`). It refuses to stamp a refusal as admitted: the ceiling keys are written only on a successful expansion, so their presence in a report means the evidence was expanded under that figure and not merely that a ceiling existed. It refuses a missing data source with `InvalidInputFormat`, which the orchestrator folds into the artifact's single "skipped" row with no message, and any other subtype or name with an empty list. Note the shape of every other outcome: the module never returns a `ModuleError` for a bad stream — a refusal is `Ok` with one status artifact, so the processing log shows `complete` with one artifact produced, and the refusal is found on the artifact tree under the container, not in the log. It never writes to evidence; the only file it creates is the anonymous temp file, which is unlinked before a byte is written to it.

### `container.memory_image`

**Reads.** It reads two things about an ingested artifact and nothing else: the first 64 bytes of its A shadow-copy prior version of the file (a `VssPriorVersion` `ParsedRecord`) is read too and named by its `file_name`, since its `name` carries a `[shadow copy ...]` label; everything it yields repeats the snapshot id, label and creation time, and its sidecars are not searched. `DataSource` at offset zero, and what the case declared about it in metadata. From those bytes `seance_memory::format::detect` recognises a Windows crash dump (`PAGE` followed by `DUMP` or `DU64`), a LiME segment file, an AVML image, a QEMU `savevm` stream, VMware snapshot metadata whose declared group table fits inside the file, an ELF64 file whose `e_type` is `ET_CORE` with at least one program header, or a hibernation file signed `hibr`, `wake` or `RSTR` — and returns `Raw`, which is the absence of a detection and never a positive one. From metadata it reads `memory_image`, a boolean meaning "this file is a headerless capture of physical memory, on my authority", and `memory_image_format`, a name that must be one of the strings in `DECLARABLE_FORMAT_NAMES`. An artifact with no `DataSource` attached is passed over without a word. Where the format is decoded, the format reader beneath it reads that format's own geometry — segment tables, `_DUMP_HEADER` physical runs and `_SUMMARY_DUMP` bitmaps, hibernation restore sets and their Xpress page blocks — and the layer's declared size, architecture and notes. A hibernation file's two restore sets, the boot set and the kernel set, are each walked table by table to the page count the file's own header states for the set (`0x58` for the loader pages; `0x238` on the Windows 10/11 layout and `0x1c8` on the 6.2/6.3 layout for the kernel set), because a restore set has no terminator and only the header's count can tell a finished set from a broken one; each table header's size field is read as 21 bits, its bit 29 as an uninterpreted flag, and its Xpress-Huffman flag per layout — bit 30 on Windows 10 and later, bit 31 on 6.2/6.3, where bit 30 means the opposite — with a plain-Xpress block accepted only when it decodes to exactly the page bytes with no back-reference reaching before the output.

**Produces.** It produces exactly one record per artifact it claims. On success that record is a `MemoryImage` carrying the decoded physical address space as its own `DataSource`, so the bulk string and feature scanners, the search index and the hex viewer read memory content with no symbols and no profile: it states `image_format`, `addressable_bytes` against the `file_bytes` on disk, the layer's `declared_size` with a `size_mismatch` flag when the two disagree, the architecture where the format proves one, and the whole serialised `layer_meta` including a crash dump's own `DirectoryTableBase` and `KdDebuggerDataBlock`. It states the acquisition's geometry as `backed_ranges` — ascending, merged where they touch — for any image that is not one unbroken run from address zero, which is what lets the analysis side tell "the machine held nothing there" from "the acquisition never covered that address"; it states `incomplete` with every reason from the whole layer chain and `content_complete` either way, and it stamps `analysis_stage: "physical_only"` with a note saying process, module and network analysis are not part of this stage. For a hibernation file, `hibernation_restore_sets` — for each set its name, the pages its tables described, the count the header states, `complete` (the two agree), where and why it ended, its table count and `tables_with_uninterpreted_bit_29` — beside `hibernation_restored_bytes`, with an `unresolved_structure` incompleteness naming both numbers when a set's described pages and header count disagree and a `compressed` one counting any page whose block did not decode. A hibernation file's state and the moment the machine was suspended, and a crash dump's bugcheck code, its four parameters, build, processor count and `maps_an_address_space`, ride both the successful record and the failure one. Where a declaration named a format, the record carries `declared_image_format` and `format_declaration_mismatch` — stamped `false` too, so corroboration and nobody-said-anything are different states. Where something announced itself as a capture and would not decode, the record is a `memory_image_error` with `decode_failed: true`, the reason in words, and no address space behind it.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell you a headerless file is memory, and does not try: a raw dump has no magic, so `raw` is claimed only because the case declared it, and every statement resting on such an image rests on that declaration being true. It cannot say what bit 29 of a hibernation table header means: it is set on 15,326 of the 31,969 kernel tables of the one Windows 11 corpus (build 26200, 8,499,130,368 bytes), both classes decode with the same codec, and it is recorded per set as uninterpreted. It cannot say what the bytes past a kernel set's stated page count are — on that corpus 7.4 GB of high-entropy bytes with no table header chaining on, taken to be the unwritten remainder of a preallocated file on a decrypted BitLocker volume on the strength of the header count matching, not of any zero run. It has been validated on two real captures only (Windows 11 26200, whose 65,536 `HIBRMARK` marker pages are all restored byte-exact with 551,503 pages and both sets complete against the header's counts, and Server 2012 R2, 16,664 and 113,548 pages), and the plain-Xpress path's own tests are hand-traced streams, only the Huffman path being checked against Microsoft's compressor output. A `hibr`-signed file of between 0x80 and 0x240 bytes reaches the reader (identification accepts 8 bytes) and the kernel-count read at `0x238` or `0x1c8` is not guarded, so such a file panics with an index out of bounds instead of a `FormatError`; no fuzz target covers hibernation. It cannot find a capture that does not begin at offset zero, because detection reads one 64-byte probe there, and it cannot warn about an undeclared one unless the name ends `.mem`, `.vmem` or `.ram` — a `.raw`, `.dd`, `.bin` or `.img` gets no hint at all, and even the hint is a log line, never a record. It cannot report a size mismatch on a declared raw image: `PhysicalLayer::raw` builds a `LayerMeta` with no declared size, so the file's length is taken as the address space without a second figure to check it against. It cannot reconstruct the Windows 7 NT6.1 hibernation layout unless `SEANCE_HIBER_LEGACY=nt61-x64` is set, and what that returns is stamped `Unvalidated` because no Windows 7 corpus exists here; older and 32-bit layouts are identified and not reconstructed. It names only macOS as an operating system this build recognises but does not analyse, from one Darwin banner hit, and a scan that could not finish is reported as no recognition rather than as a failure.

**Refuses.** It refuses to claim any artifact on the strength of its name or its size, and returns nothing for a headerless file nobody declared, because guessing would put a record asserting a memory image on every unrecognised file in every case — and a memory image holds cached MBR sectors, GPT headers and filesystem superblocks, so the partition and filesystem modules would then find structure inside RAM. It refuses to discard a declaration it cannot act on: `memory_image_format` naming no format this build reads, or either key written in the wrong JSON shape, ends the run with a `ParsingError` quoting the word that was not understood and listing the accepted names, and deliberately not with `InvalidInputFormat`, which the orchestrator logs at `debug!` and records as `status: "skipped"` with `error_message: None` — the variant that would delete the sentence the refusal exists to deliver. It refuses to let a declaration overrule the bytes: a header that identifies one format beats a case that declared another, and the disagreement is written onto the record rather than resolved in a log line, because that is usually how a mislabelled exhibit is caught. It refuses a decoded address space that reports no acquired bytes at all, since an empty geometry is read downstream as "flat", meaning full coverage. And it refuses to read a `.vmem` flat when no `.vmss` or `.vmsn` is reachable beside it: the map from guest-physical address to file offset lives in that metadata, a flat read is wrong for any guest whose memory is split into regions, and this path never calls the degraded reading that exists for an examiner who asks for it explicitly.

### `container.ole2_expander`

**Reads.** The directory tree and stream bytes of an OLE2 / Compound File Binary document — the container beneath legacy `.doc`, `.xls` and `.ppt`, Outlook `.msg`, MSI installers, `Thumbs.db` and Jump Lists. It subscribes to `Container` and `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::Stream`; an artifact whose `subtype` is set but not exactly `ole2` yields an empty list, and one with no subtype is taken only when its lowercased `name` ends `.doc`, `.xls`, `.ppt` or `.ole2`. The `ole2` subtype is written by `detect_file_type` when the first eight bytes are `D0 CF 11 E0 A1 B1 1A E1` — so at top-level ingest every compound file of any name gets it — and by the ingest extension map for `.doc`, `.xls` and `.ppt`. It needs `artifact.data` (`InvalidInputFormat`, "OLE2 module requires data source"), reads eight bytes at offset 0 with `read_full` and remembers whether they are the signature, then opens the file with `cfb::CompoundFile::open` (cfb 0.10.0) over a `SourceCursor` — the **permissive** validation mode, not `open_strict`, so a version-3 file with a non-zero directory-sector count is accepted with that field treated as zero. The library reads the 512-byte header, the FAT, the DIFAT, the directory sectors and the mini-FAT. It then walks `comp.walk()` — every entry from the root storage down, in preorder — collecting each entry's `path()` (lossy UTF-8, `/`-rooted, e.g. `/WordDocument` or `/\u0005SummaryInformation`), `is_stream()` and `len()`. For each stream whose length is above zero and at most `MAX_OLE2_STREAM` = 268,435,456 bytes (256 MiB) it calls `open_stream(path)` and `read_to_end` into a `Vec` pre-sized to the directory length, following the FAT or mini-FAT chain through the library.

**Produces.** One `FileEntry` per directory entry, including the root storage itself (`name: "/"`, `is_directory: true`) and every sub-storage, parented to the compound file. Metadata is `name` (the full `/`-rooted path — there are no separate `path` or `parent_path` keys), `size` (the directory's declared length; 0 for a storage), `is_directory` (the inverse of `is_stream`), `is_stream`, `container: "ole2"` and `container_path` (the outer name, or `unknown.ole2`). A stream that materialised in full carries a `ByteSliceDataSource` holding its bytes in memory, so the hasher, the office parsers and everything else subscribing to `FileEntry` runs on the real content at ingest (`test_ole2_attaches_stream_content`), and no incompleteness stamp. A stream that did not carries no data and says why: `content_incomplete: true` with `content_incomplete_reason: cap_reached` when its declared length exceeds 256 MiB; `short_read` with `available_size` (bytes actually read) when `read_to_end` returned fewer bytes than the directory declares, or errored — in the latter case `content_incomplete_detail` carries the I/O message; and `unresolved_structure` with the library's message in `content_incomplete_detail` when `open_stream` itself failed (`test_ole2_unreadable_stream_is_flagged_incomplete`, which truncates a 16 KiB stream and asserts no bytes are served). When the signature is present but `CompoundFile::open` fails, the single product is a `ParsedRecord` from `expansion_failed_status`: `type: ArchiveScanStatus`, `record_type: archive_scan_status`, `name: "<name> (not expanded)"`, `container: ole2`, `content_incomplete: true` with reason `ole2_unreadable`, `inventory_incomplete: true` with reason `unresolved_structure`, `entries_recovered: 0` and the cfb error in the detail keys. Nothing is written to the timeline, no digest is computed here, and the in-memory bytes live only for the ingest: the API's content resolver has no `ole2` arm, so a request for a stream's content after ingest is refused with "Content resolution for 'ole2' containers is not supported".

**Cannot.** It cannot serve a stream's bytes after ingest. The `ByteSliceDataSource` is attached to the artifact in memory and nothing persists it; `content_resolver::apply_step` routes every artifact tagged `container` to `reopen_container`, whose match has arms for `e01`, `aff4`, `vhd`, `vhdx`, `vmdk`, `qcow2` and `sparseimage` and rejects anything else — so a `WordDocument` stream that was hashed and parsed at ingest cannot be viewed in hex, downloaded, exported or re-run through a module by the API afterwards. It cannot say when a stream was created or modified: cfb's `Entry` exposes `created()`, `modified()`, `clsid()` and `state_bits()`, none of which is read, so the directory timestamps that a compound file carries per storage and stream are not on the record and nothing from this module reaches the timeline. It cannot give an entry a flat-model path: `name` holds the whole `/`-rooted path and there is no `path` or `parent_path`, which is the trio every other archive in this tree writes; a stream named with a control character (`\u0005SummaryInformation`, `\u0001CompObj`) keeps it in `name`. It cannot reach a compound file inside a file system unless it is named `.doc`, `.xls`, `.ppt` or `.ole2`: a `FileEntry` has no subtype, so an `.msg`, `.dot`, `.xlt`, `.pps`, `.vsd`, `.mpp`, `.msi`, `Thumbs.db` or `*.automaticDestinations-ms` found on a volume is never opened by this module by name — top-level ingest catches them by signature, a volume walk does not. It cannot read a stream above 256 MiB at all, and cannot read one below it without holding the whole stream in memory: every materialised stream of a document is resident at once until the artifacts are flushed, and there is no ceiling on their sum or on the entry count. It cannot verify anything: CFB carries no checksums, and permissive mode accepts a header strict mode would reject. It cannot recover a deleted or orphaned stream: only entries reachable from the root directory tree are walked, so an unlinked directory entry, a free-but-unwiped sector or a stream whose chain was cut from the tree is not listed. It cannot follow an interpretation: it does not know that `/WordDocument` is Word or `/Workbook` is Excel — that is left to the parsers that run on the children. A `.doc`-named file without the signature that will not open is silent, folded into the "ran and produced nothing" row; so is an artifact whose subtype says `ole2` without the signature.

**Refuses.** It refuses to serve truncated bytes as a stream's content: a stream that read short is left with no data source and stamped `short_read` with the count it did get, never padded and never handed on at its declared length (`test_ole2_unreadable_stream_is_flagged_incomplete`), and a stream over the 256 MiB cap is left as metadata with `cap_reached` rather than buffered or clipped. It refuses to let a sized entry with no bytes read as an empty stream: every stream it did not materialise carries the incompleteness pair with a reason, so a hash, preview or export that comes back empty is understood as "not extracted". It refuses to let a signed compound file that will not open read as one that held nothing: the `ArchiveScanStatus` record is produced with both pairs, never an empty success (`test_ole2_corrupted_data_is_reported_not_silent`), while a `.doc`-named file without the signature is left silent so the stamp does not fire on every mislabelled file (`test_ole2_non_ole2_content_is_silent`). It refuses a missing data source with `InvalidInputFormat` — folded into the artifact's "skipped" row with no message — and any other subtype or name with an empty list (`test_ole2_extension_matching` pins that `.doc`, `.xls`, `.ppt` and `.ole2` are attempted). It never returns a `ModuleError` for a bad file, so a refused compound document is found on the artifact tree under a `complete` row, not in the processing log's errors. It never writes to evidence, never modifies the compound file (cfb is opened over a read-only cursor), and never decodes a stream's contents — it hands the bytes on and interprets nothing.

### `container.qcow2_reader`

**Reads.** A QEMU QCOW2 image, and it does not find one for itself. It runs on `Container` and `FileEntry` artifacts and gates on metadata, not on content: an artifact carrying a `subtype` is read only when that subtype is exactly `qcow2`, and an artifact carrying no subtype at all is read only when its `name` metadata, lower-cased, ends `.qcow2` or `.qcow`. The `QFI\xFB` magic is what classifies an image, but only at the path-based entry points — `seance_core::file_detection::detect_file_type` returns `Qcow2Image` for those four bytes at offset 0, which `seance_api::auto_detect_artifact_type` maps to `Container` with subtype `qcow2` for the HTTP ingest handler and the CLI `scan`, falling back to the `.qcow2`/`.qcow` extension when no magic is recognised — so a qcow2 sitting inside an evidence image reaches this module through its file name and nothing else, and a file merely named `.qcow2` reaches it as a declared qcow2. The artifact must carry a random-access data source of at least 72 bytes. It then re-establishes the image for itself: 104 bytes are read from offset 0 through `read_full`, which loops over short returns because a single `read_at` may legitimately deliver fewer bytes than asked and treating that as a too-small file once made a valid image undetectable behind a chunked source; at least 72 must arrive. Everything it reads from the header is big-endian and is eight fields on a v2 image and nine on a v3: the magic at 0, the version at 4, `backing_file_offset` at 8, `cluster_bits` at 20, the disk `size` at 24, `crypt_method` at 32, `l1_size` at 36, `l1_table_offset` at 40, and on version 3 the `incompatible_features` word at 72. The version must be 2 or 3 and `cluster_bits` must be in 9..=21, giving a cluster of 512 bytes to 2 MiB; `cluster_size` is `1 << cluster_bits`. The L1 table is then staged whole in memory — `l1_size` × 8 bytes read from `l1_table_offset` through `read_exact_or_fail`, which loops over short reads and errors rather than parse a zero-padded buffer — and decoded as an array of 64-bit entries. `l2_entries_per_table` is computed as `cluster_size / 8`. From then on every read is a two-level walk done live against the host file: the logical offset is shifted right by `cluster_bits` to a cluster index, divided by `l2_entries_per_table` to an L1 index and taken modulo it for an L2 index; the L1 entry is masked with `0x00FFFFFFFFFFFE00`, bits 9 to 55, to give the L2 table's host offset; and the single 8-byte L2 entry is read fresh from the host file by `read_exact_or_fail` — no L2 table is ever cached. In that entry it looks at three things and no others, in this order: bit 62, the compressed flag; bit 0, the version-3 "all zeros" flag; and the same bits 9 to 55 for the host cluster offset, to which the offset within the cluster is added with `checked_add`. Nothing else in the file is read. `backing_file_size` at 16, the refcount table at 48 and its cluster count at 56, `nb_snapshots` at 60, `snapshot_offset` at 64, and on version 3 `compatible_features` at 80, `autoclear_features` at 88, `refcount_order` at 96 and `header_length` at 100 are never read; neither is the header extension area, nor any snapshot table, refcount block or L2 bitmap; and bit 63, the `COPIED` flag, is examined on neither the L1 nor the L2 entry.

**Produces.** One artifact, and one only: a `RawEvidence` child parented to the container artifact, whose data source is the decoded guest disk and whose `size()` is the `size` field from the header. Its metadata carries the file name, `container: "qcow2"` — the tag the content resolver later dispatches on to re-open it — `qcow2_version`, `disk_size`, `cluster_size`, and `has_backing_file`. It emits no `ParsedRecord`, no `TimelineEvent`, no finding, no hash, no acquisition attestation, no allocation census, and no incompleteness stamp of any kind: nothing on the child distinguishes an image every cluster of which was read from one whose compressed clusters will error when touched. Everything the case then holds about the guest — its partition table, its file systems, its files, anything carved — hangs off that one child and is produced by other modules. When a nested artifact's content is later re-resolved for export or display, this module is re-run on the same bytes and the decoded source is wrapped in a `DeviceImageSource`, so an offset in the guest disk is reported as an exact physical device offset; that re-open is not cached — the container cache admits only `e01` and `ewf` by name — so the header and the whole L1 table are re-read on every request.

**Cannot.** **It cannot read a compressed cluster, and it will not pretend one held zeros.** On a version-2 image any L2 entry with bit 62 set makes the read fail, naming the logical offset, so an image written with `qemu-img -c` is opened and then yields errors wherever a compressed cluster is touched — partially readable, never quietly zero-filled; a version-3 image written with a non-default compression type sets an incompatible feature bit and is refused at the header instead, never opened at all. It cannot decrypt: `crypt_method` other than 0 refuses the image, it holds no key, password or keyslot reader, and neither the legacy AES header nor a LUKS keyslot is parsed. It cannot follow a backing file, so a differencing image — the ordinary shape of a snapshotted VM, where the unwritten clusters live in the parent — does not open at all, and it cannot assemble a chain of images even when every file in that chain is in the case. It cannot read a snapshot: `nb_snapshots` and `snapshot_offset` are never read, so a QCOW2 internal snapshot is invisible, is not counted, and is mentioned on no record; what it serves is the single view the current L1 table describes. **It cannot tell you that a region of zeros was ever zeros.** An L1 entry of 0, an L2 entry of 0, a cluster index beyond the end of the staged L1 table, and a version-3 cluster with the zero flag all read as zero bytes, and nothing distinguishes any of them from guest sectors that genuinely held zeros: it implements no `physical_map`, so during the ingest pass the projection of any byte read through it is `PhysicalMap::opaque` — no device backing — and the hole extent the framework provides for exactly this is never emitted. It publishes no count of allocated clusters, so a 500 GB disk with 2 GB ever written cannot be told from one that was written and wiped. It publishes no free space, so nothing points the carver at clusters the current L1/L2 tables do not reference, and the refcount table and `COPIED` flag it never reads mean a leaked or doubly-referenced cluster is not detectable at all. **It checks no hash, because the format carries none** — QCOW2 has no checksum over its header, its L1 or L2 tables or its data — and it cross-checks no structure either: an L2 entry is trusted as found, with no check that the host offset is cluster-aligned (the mask discards the low 9 bits rather than rejecting a misaligned entry), no check that it lies inside the file other than the read failing, and no check that two logical clusters do not map to the same host cluster, so cluster aliasing is not detected. It cannot bound what the header claims. The `size` field is published as the disk size unchecked, never compared with the host file's length, never checked against zero, and never compared with the range the staged L1 table can actually cover: an `l1_size` of 0 is accepted, and an `l1_size` too small for the declared disk is accepted, and in both cases the uncovered part of the disk — up to the whole of it — reads as zeros with no error, no flag and no log line. It cannot tell you where in the `.qcow2` file a byte lived: the host cluster offset the L2 entry gave is used for the read and discarded, and the physical coordinate the case reports for guest bytes is the guest disk's own offset. It is a single-file reader: it opens exactly one file, never looks for a sibling or a segment, and an external data file — a version-3 incompatible feature — refuses the image. A read that begins at or past the declared disk size returns zero bytes, and a read is clipped at that boundary; a read spanning several clusters that meets a compressed or unreadable cluster part-way fails whole, discarding the plain bytes already copied, so a consumer cannot obtain the readable prefix of such a range. Its caps are these: 72 bytes of header minimum and 104 required for a version-3 image; `cluster_bits` 9..=21; and 1,048,576 L1 entries, 8 MiB staged. That last cap bounds the table, not the disk — nothing compares the two — so it refuses an image whose header *declares* more than 1,048,576 L1 entries, which at the 512-byte minimum cluster is an image covering more than 32 GiB, while at the 64 KiB cluster QEMU uses by default it does not bind at any real disk size.

**Refuses.** It refuses in three ways, and the differences matter to anyone asked why a case is empty. A hard refusal returns `ModuleError::ParsingError`, produces no artifact, lands as an `error` row in the case's processing log carrying the message, broadcasts a `ModuleError` event, and marks the artifact's processing as failed. It refuses an encrypted image outright — `crypt_method != 0`, on version 2 and version 3 alike, with the method number in the message — rather than read the ciphertext as disk content. It refuses an image with a non-zero `backing_file_offset`, in terms: a differencing image would read as zeros, and fabricating the parent's clusters as zero bytes would put invented evidence in the case. It refuses a version-3 image whose `incompatible_features` word is non-zero, reporting the whole 64-bit value in hex and interpreting no individual bit, because a bit this reader does not implement means the clusters would be addressed by the wrong rules — so a compression-type, extended-L2, external-data-file, dirty or corrupt marking all refuse alike. It refuses a version-3 file that delivers fewer than 104 header bytes, stating how many of 104 arrived. It refuses an L1 table it cannot fill to `l1_size` × 8 bytes — a truncated image fails closed rather than parsing a zero-padded table that would read as a disk of holes — and it refuses an `l1_size` above 1,048,576 before a byte is allocated. At read time it refuses a compressed cluster, refuses an L2 entry it cannot read whole, and refuses an allocated cluster the host file cannot deliver in full, returning `UnexpectedEof` with the byte counts rather than zero-filling the missing tail. A version-3 cluster with the zero flag set is served as zeros **even when it carries a preallocated host offset**, which is a refusal to publish stale preallocated bytes as evidence; the test that pins it writes 0xAB into the preallocated cluster and requires zeros out. The second way is a silent decline that produces no artifact and no reason in the case: a source under 72 bytes, a header short of 72 bytes, a first four bytes that are not `QFI\xFB`, a version other than 2 or 3, and a `cluster_bits` outside 9..=21 — the last two leave a warning in the application log and nothing on the case. Those leave only a zero-yield "ran and produced nothing" row in the processing log naming this module — the same row a file that was never a qcow2 produces. The third way is an artifact with no data source at all, which returns `InvalidInputFormat` and is folded into the log's `skipped` row instead. The order of the checks decides which answer an examiner gets: encryption is tested first, before the version-3 header-length and feature tests, and those before `cluster_bits` and before the backing file — so an encrypted image with an impossible cluster size refuses as encrypted, a version-3 image with an unimplemented feature bit refuses on that bit whatever else is wrong with it, and an unencrypted version-2 image with an impossible cluster size declines silently even if it also names a backing file. Within a cluster the compressed test precedes the zero-flag test, so an entry carrying both errors rather than reading as zeros. **No refusal, hard or silent, leaves a record in the case** — there is no refusal artifact in this crate, and the `SourceUnparsed` record the framework emits for a source nothing in the build claims cannot fire here either: it is confined to a parentless `RawEvidence` artifact and suppressed when a module has failed, and a qcow2 is ingested as a `Container`. So "this image did not open" lives in the processing log and on no report.

### `container.sparseimage_reader`

**Reads.** The 4,096-byte header of an Apple single-file sparse disk image and, on demand, the bands it maps. It subscribes to `Container` and `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, so a `.sparseimage` handed to ingest and one found inside another file system are both opened; an artifact whose `subtype` is set but is not exactly `sparseimage` yields an empty list, and one with no subtype is taken only when its lowercased `name` ends `.sparseimage`. The subtype is written by `detect_file_type` when the first four bytes are `sprs`, and by the ingest extension map for `.sparseimage`. It needs `artifact.data`, and returns `InvalidInputFormat` ("sparse image artifact carries no data source to read") without it. It reads 4,096 bytes at offset 0 with `read_full` — fewer is `InvalidInputFormat` naming the count — and parses them by the layout transcribed from libyal/libmodi's `libmodi_sparse_image_header.c`, every field big-endian: `sprs` at 0x00, sectors-per-band at 0x08, total 512-byte sectors at 0x10 (the logical disk size), and the band index array at 0x40. The version field at 0x04 and the flags at 0x0C are not read. The array is indexed by physical band position in the file and each entry is the 1-based logical band that physical slot holds, or 0 for an unused slot; `N = ceil(total_sectors / sectors_per_band)` entries are read, and because the header is fixed at 4,096 bytes the array is bounded at `(4096 − 0x40) / 4 = 1,008` entries. Reads then go through `SparseImageDataSource::read_at`: a logical offset is split into band and offset-within-band, a mapped band is read at `0x1000 + physical × band_bytes + within` with `read_exact_or_fail`, an unmapped band is filled with zeros, and the read is cut at the logical size. No file other than the artifact's own data source is opened.

**Produces.** Exactly one `RawEvidence` artifact, parented to the container, carrying a `DeviceImageSource` around the `SparseImageDataSource` — so an offset into it is reported as an exact device coordinate, and the partition, file-system, carving and hashing stack reads the contained disk exactly as it reads a raw one. Its metadata is `name` (the container artifact's own `name`, or `disk.sparseimage` if it had none — the child is not renamed `_extracted`), `container: "sparseimage"`, `container_format: "Apple sparse disk image"`, `size` (the logical size, `total_sectors × 512`), `allocated_bands` (the count of logical bands with a physical slot) and `total_bands` (`N`). There is no `subtype`, no `container_path`, no `path`, no stored hash — the format carries none — and no `content_incomplete` stamp of any kind. Every read is served on demand from the container file; nothing is spilled to disk or memory. The API's content resolver re-opens the image after ingest by running this same `process()` on a synthetic copy of the parent (`reopen_container("sparseimage")`) and wrapping the result in a second `DeviceImageSource`. It produces no timeline event, no processing-log record beyond the orchestrator's own, and no refusal artifact.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell a hole from a zero. An unmapped logical band is served as zeros and counted only in `allocated_bands`/`total_bands`; there is no `content_incomplete` flag, no per-band coverage record and no way downstream to distinguish a sector the imager never wrote from one it wrote as zeros — and for a sparse image written by a live imager the two mean different things. It cannot open an image whose band table does not fit the first header: any image with more than 1,008 bands is refused as "not a single-file sparse image", which bounds the logical disk at 1,008 × band size — 1,008 MiB at a 2,048-sector (1 MiB) band, 8,064 MiB (7.875 GiB) at a 16,384-sector (8 MiB) band, and the band size is whatever the writer chose. Whether the images FUJI, RECON and ASLA write for a real Mac fit that bound is not evidenced anywhere in this tree: no `.sparseimage` from any tool exists in the corpus, `Container_Formats.md` cites libmodi rather than a sample, and the reader's eight tests all run against a writer that lives in the same test module and follows the same reading of the layout. It cannot read the version or flags fields, so a future or variant layout is not detected by them — only by the arithmetic failing. It cannot serve a truncated image at all past the truncation: a mapped band whose bytes are not in the file fails the read with an error naming "sparse image band", which is deliberate, but it means a partly copied image yields nothing from the missing bands rather than a flagged partial. It cannot bound band size: `sectors_per_band` is any non-zero u32, so a hostile header can declare a band of 2 TiB and every read then addresses that far into the file. It cannot recover a band the map does not name, cannot detect a physical slot that maps to a logical band beyond `N` except by refusing the whole image, and cannot read the `.sparsebundle` directory form or an encrypted image (`encrcdsa`), the latter being identified elsewhere at ingest. It cannot verify anything: the format has no checksums and none are computed. Its refusals are invisible on the record: every parse failure is `InvalidInputFormat`, which the orchestrator logs at `debug!` and folds into the artifact's "skipped" row with `error_message: None`, so a signed `.sparseimage` with a corrupt or over-long band map is told apart from a file this module never claimed only by the status word — the refusal lands in the artifact's `skipped` fold, a never-claimed file in its `complete` zero-yield fold, and neither row carries the reason — and — unlike the archive expanders — no `ArchiveScanStatus`-style record is left under the container. The `triage` ingestion profile does not list this module, so under triage a `.sparseimage` is never opened.

**Refuses.** It refuses to fabricate zeros for a band the map says is there: a mapped band whose bytes are missing from a truncated file errors on the read that reaches it, never zero-fills, because a truncated capture must not read as a sparse one (`a_truncated_present_band_errors_rather_than_zero_filling`). It refuses a band map in which two physical slots claim the same logical band, naming the band and both slots — last-writer-wins would orphan one payload and silently change which host bytes back a sector, and the refusal is at open, before any read (`a_duplicate_logical_band_map_is_refused_rather_than_last_wins`). It refuses a band reference outside `0..N`, a `sectors_per_band` of zero, a band size or logical size that overflows 64 bits, a band count above 1,008 (`rejects_a_band_table_that_cannot_fit_the_header`), a header shorter than 4,096 bytes, and a file without `sprs` (`rejects_a_file_without_the_signature`) — each with `InvalidInputFormat` and a sentence naming the reason, and each therefore recorded only as a debug log line and a "skipped" row. It refuses to guess by name what the subtype denies, and refuses, in silence, any artifact that is neither subtyped `sparseimage` nor named `.sparseimage` (`ignores_artifacts_that_are_not_sparse_images`). It serves at most the logical size and returns zero bytes for a read at or past it rather than an error. It never writes, never spills, and never opens a sibling file.

### `container.tar_extractor`

**Reads.** An uncompressed ustar-family tar, from whatever source hands it one. It subscribes to `Container` and `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess` and gates three ways: an artifact with no `data` is passed over in silence (an empty `Ok`, not an error); it must then either carry `subtype: "tar"` or have a lowercased `name` ending `.tar`; and five bytes read with `read_full` at offset 257 must spell `ustar` — which both POSIX `ustar\0` and GNU `ustar ` satisfy — or it declines without a word. The `tar` subtype arrives from three places: `detect_file_type`, which claims a file when bytes 257–261 of its first 512 are `ustar`; the ingest extension map, which maps `.tar` — and `.tar.gz`, `.tgz`, `.tar.bz2`, `.tar.xz`, `.tbz2`, `.txz`, though only when content detection returned nothing, which a real compressed file never does — to `tar`; and the gzip, bzip2 and xz expanders, whose child carries `subtype: tar` when their decompressed output passed the same offset-257 test. It walks the archive with `tar::Archive::entries()` (tar 0.4.46) over a `SourceCursor`, wrapped in a reader that remembers whether its last read hit end-of-file. tar-rs reads 512-byte headers in sequence and reports the end the same way for an all-zero header block (`ignore_zeros` is left false) and for end-of-file where a header should be; the wrapper is what tells the two apart. The header checksum is recomputed and a mismatch is an error; a GNU LongName (`L`) or LongLink (`K`) entry and a PAX local extension (`x`) are consumed into the entry that follows, so `entry.path()` returns the long or PAX `path` name; and a PAX `size` override governs how far the walker skips. A PAX global header (`g`), which tar-rs yields as an entry, is skipped. From each entry it takes the entry type (directory, symbolic link, hard link), `entry.size()` — the PAX `size` when one was given, else the header field, octal or GNU base-256 — `raw_file_position()` (the byte offset of the entry's data in the archive), `link_name_bytes()` for a link, the path as lossy UTF-8 with trailing `/` trimmed, and the header's `mtime`, `mode`, `uid`, `gid`, `username` and `groupname`. The path is resolved by `entry_path::resolve_entry_path`: empty and `.` segments dropped, `..` applied and clamped at the archive root, an absolute name or a `..` that walks past the root flagged. A backslash is deliberately an ordinary character here, not a separator, because it is legal in a POSIX file name. The second entry point, `extract_tar_entry_source`, re-walks an archive for one entry by its archive-internal path — the raw header name first, then the resolved form — and is what the API's content resolver calls for any artifact tagged `container: tar`.

**Produces.** One `FileEntry` per surviving entry, parented to the archive artifact, and re-queued by the orchestrator so the office, mobile, hashing and every other `FileEntry` parser runs on it. Its data source, for an entry that is neither a directory nor a link and whose window is non-empty, is a `WindowSource` over the parent at `raw_file_position()` with length `min(entry size, archive length − offset)` — no copy, no extra memory, and a length the archive can actually serve. Its metadata is `name` (the resolved basename), `path` (`/`-prefixed, resolved), `parent_path`, `size` (the entry's declared figure, PAX `size` honoured, kept even when the window is shorter — `a_pax_size_override_is_the_size_published`, on Python `tarfile`'s real header for a 9 GiB member), `is_directory`, `container: "tar"`, `container_path` (the archive's `name`); `original_name` with the stored name verbatim whenever resolution changed it, and `path_traversal: true` when it escaped the root; `modified` as RFC 3339 UTC from the header `mtime` when it is non-zero — zero is tar's "not recorded" and produces no key rather than 1970 — `mode` as octal of the low twelve bits, `uid`, `gid`, and `owner`/`group` when the header's names are non-empty. A symbolic link carries `is_symlink: true`, `symlink_target` (the stored target, verbatim) and `tar_entry_type: symlink`; a hard link `is_hardlink: true`, `hardlink_target` (the member name it links to) and `tar_entry_type: hardlink`; neither gets a data source (`links_are_published_as_links_with_their_targets`, on GNU tar output). Those header fields are what put an archive-sourced case's files on the file timeline at all (`the_header_fields_reach_the_file_entry`). A non-directory whose bytes run past the end of the archive carries `available_size` (the window length), `content_incomplete: true` and `content_incomplete_reason: short_read`. When the walk stops early — a header that will not parse, an entry whose name will not decode, or end-of-file on a header boundary with no end-of-archive block — it appends one `ParsedRecord`: `type: ArchiveScanStatus`, `record_type: archive_scan_status`, `name: "<name> (partially extracted)"`, `container: tar`, `content_incomplete: true` with reason `tar_entry_unreadable`, `tar_entry_name_undecodable` or `tar_end_marker_missing` (`an_archive_with_no_end_of_archive_marker_is_recorded_as_cut_short`, on GNU tar output cut with `head -c`, which GNU tar itself lists without complaint), `inventory_incomplete: true` with reason `unresolved_structure`, `entries_recovered`, the library's message in the three detail keys, and a `message` saying entries missing from the listing are not evidence the archive lacked them. A `tar_unreadable` status exists for an `entries()` failure, but on a fresh cursor `entries()` only errors when the position is not zero, so that branch is not reached in practice. It produces no timeline event of its own, no hash, and no record for a `.tar`-named file without the magic.

**Cannot.** It cannot see past a zero block. The walker treats the first all-zero 512-byte header as the end of the archive, so two tars concatenated, or an archive with a zero block written mid-stream, lose every entry after it, and because that is a normal end rather than an error no `ArchiveScanStatus` is produced — the bytes after the end-of-archive block are not examined. (An archive that stops on a header boundary with no zero block at all is recorded, as `tar_end_marker_missing`.) It cannot expand a GNU sparse entry, and misreads one: for a GNU sparse header `entry.size()` returns the real (expanded) size while `raw_file_position()` addresses the stored compact data, so the window serves the compact bytes and whatever follows them in the archive, up to the real size, as the file's content — no hole is restored and no flag is set. It cannot tell a device or FIFO from a file: directories and links are recognised, and a character or block device or a FIFO is listed as a `FileEntry` like a regular file. It cannot resolve a link: the target is recorded as stored and a hard link is not given the bytes of the member it names. A PAX global header's attributes (the commit id `git archive` writes, for one) are skipped with it, not recorded. It cannot read the archive's V7 form, which has no `ustar` magic, and cannot read PAX `atime`/`ctime` or any timestamp finer than a second. It cannot verify content: the header checksum covers the header only, and there is no digest, length check or trailer over an entry's bytes — a window that is short is flagged, a window that is wrong is not detectable here. It cannot bound itself: there is no cap on entry count or on a header's declared size, only the clamp to the bytes that remain, and every entry becomes an artifact. Names that are not UTF-8 are converted lossily and the original bytes are lost; a name that will not decode at all is dropped from the listing (with the status record saying so). Because it re-walks from the start, `extract_tar_entry_source` costs a header-by-header scan per request and returns `None`, not an error, for a directory, a link, an empty entry, or an entry it cannot reach past a corrupt header. The processing log cannot show this module failing: it never returns a `ModuleError`, so a `.tar` it declined and a `.tar` it read fully appear in the same "ran and produced nothing" fold when the archive was empty.

**Refuses.** It refuses to let an archive's own names state a location outside the archive: `..`, absolute names and doubled separators are resolved and clamped, the entry stays in the listing at its resolved path, the stored name survives verbatim in `original_name` and the attempt is marked `path_traversal: true` — nothing is dropped and nothing is silently rewritten, because the file tree, the `/files` API and the export manifest render `path` as fact (`entry_path_metadata_does_not_escape_the_archive_root`). It refuses to hand out a window that claims bytes the archive does not hold: a truncated entry's window is bounded by what remains, `size` keeps the header's claim, and the shortfall is declared with `available_size` and `short_read` rather than served as zeros later (`truncated_entry_is_flagged_and_windowed_to_the_bytes_present`); `extract_tar_entry_source` applies the same bound on re-open. It refuses to continue past a header that will not parse — tar is sequential and there is no way to find the next header — and refuses to let that stop be silent: what parsed before the fault is kept and the `ArchiveScanStatus` record names the fault and how many entries were recovered (`a_walk_stopped_by_a_corrupt_header_publishes_an_incomplete_archive_record`), and a clean archive publishes no such record so the record keeps its meaning. It refuses to date a file to 1970 for want of an mtime (`an_unrecorded_mtime_is_absent_not_1970`). It refuses to become a second copy of the bytes — every entry is a window over the parent. It refuses, quietly, anything not claimed as tar and anything claimed as tar without `ustar` at 257 (`ignores_non_tar_and_missing_magic`), and an artifact with no data source, all with an empty list rather than an error. Note what that leaves: no refusal of this module ever reaches the processing log as an error row, and a resolved entry is re-openable by the path an examiner is holding (`a_resolved_entry_is_still_reopenable_by_its_stored_path`).

### `container.vhd_reader`

**Reads.** A Hyper-V / Virtual PC VHD, fixed or dynamic, from its footer. It subscribes to `Container` and `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`; an artifact whose `subtype` is set but not exactly `vhd` yields an empty list, and one with no subtype is taken only when its lowercased `name` ends `.vhd`. The `vhd` subtype is written by `detect_file_type` when the first eight bytes are `conectix` — which only a dynamic or differencing VHD has, as the footer copy at offset 0; a fixed VHD begins with the guest's own first sector and is caught only by the `.vhd` extension map. It needs `artifact.data` (`InvalidInputFormat`, "VHD module requires data source"). A file under 512 bytes is declined in silence. It reads the last 512 bytes with `read_full` (a single short `read_at` used to make a valid VHD undetectable); if they do not begin `conectix` it reads 512 bytes at offset 0 instead and takes those if they do, and otherwise declines in silence. From the validated footer it reads two fields, both big-endian: `disk_type` at 60–63 and `current_size` at 48–55, published as `disk_size`. Nothing else in the footer — checksum, features, format version, data offset for a fixed disk, timestamp, creator application, version and host OS, original size, CHS geometry, UUID, saved-state flag — is read or verified. For `disk_type` 3 (dynamic) it reads the 1,024-byte dynamic header at the footer's `data_offset` (bytes 16–23) with `read_exact_or_fail`, requires `cxsparse`, and takes `table_offset` (16–23), `max_table_entries` (28–31) and `block_size` (32–35); the header's checksum, parent UUID, parent timestamp and parent locators are not read. It then reads the whole BAT — `max_table_entries × 4` bytes, at most 1,048,576 entries — into memory. Per read of a dynamic disk it computes the block from `block_size`, reads that block's sector bitmap (`ceil(sectors_per_block / 8)` bytes at `entry × 512`, `read_exact_or_fail`), and serves each 512-byte sector from `entry × 512 + bitmap_size` (bitmap rounded up to a 512 multiple) only when its bit — most-significant first — is set.

**Produces.** One `RawEvidence` artifact, parented to the container, carrying a data source over the virtual disk so the partition and file-system stack reads it as a raw device. For a fixed disk that source is a `WindowSource` over the container from offset 0 of exactly `disk_size` bytes — the footer's figure, not `file_size − 512`, so host padding past the declared size is not served as image and an undersized file still reports the declared capacity (`test_vhd_fixed_honors_footer_disk_size_over_file_padding`). For a dynamic disk it is a `VhdDynamicDataSource` whose `size()` is `disk_size`. The metadata is `name` (the container's own `name`, or `unknown.vhd`), `container: "vhd"`, `vhd_type` (`fixed` or `dynamic`) and `disk_size`. There is no `size` key, no `subtype: raw`, no `container_path` and no `path` — the sibling VHDX reader writes all four — and no stored hash, because the format records none. The source is not wrapped in `DeviceImageSource` at ingest, and `VhdDynamicDataSource` implements neither `physical_map` nor `open_relative`, so a physical location inside a dynamic VHD projects through the default `PhysicalMap::opaque` (no device backing) during ingest; the API's content resolver, re-opening the image by running this same `process()` on a synthetic copy of the parent (`reopen_container("vhd")`), wraps its result in `DeviceImageSource` and so does report exact offsets then. A differencing disk (`disk_type` 4) and a dynamic disk whose header or BAT will not read produce a `ModuleError::ParsingError` — one `error` row in the processing log with the message — and no artifact; an unknown `disk_type` produces an empty list. No refusal artifact is ever produced, no timeline event, and no integrity record. The `triage` ingestion profile lists this module by id, so a VHD opens under triage.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell a block the BAT never covered from one it marked unallocated. `read_at` treats `block_idx >= bat.len()` exactly as it treats an entry of `0xFFFFFFFF`: zeros. So a dynamic disk whose footer declares more capacity than `max_table_entries × block_size` covers — a truncated or lying BAT — reads as zeros for the remainder with no error and no flag, where the VHDX reader in the same crate errors with `UnexpectedEof` for the same shape (`vhdx.rs`, the truncated-BAT test); the `Container_Formats.md` note that no reader "reconciles a declared capacity against the allocation it can actually see" describes this, and understates it for VHD, which silently serves the gap. It cannot tell an unwritten sector from a written zero: an unallocated block and a sector whose bitmap bit is clear are both served as zeros with no coverage record, and nothing on the artifact says how much of the disk was ever written. It cannot verify the footer or the dynamic header: neither checksum is computed, the format version is not checked, and a footer whose `disk_size` disagrees with the BAT, the geometry or the file is not reconciled. It cannot say who made the image or when: the creator application, version, host OS, timestamp, UUID and original size are all in the footer and none is read, so an examiner asking what produced the VHD gets nothing from this module. It cannot open a differencing disk or find its parent, and does not read the parent locators that would name it. It cannot find a fixed VHD by content: `detect_file_type` claims only `conectix` at offset 0, so a fixed VHD not named `.vhd` ingests as `RawEvidence` with its 512-byte footer trailing the disk and this module never runs — the guest is still readable as a raw image, but nothing records that it was a VHD. It cannot bound a fixed disk by the file: the window is `disk_size` whatever the file holds, and a read past the real data returns a short count from the file, not an error from this module; the dynamic source, by contrast, errors on a present sector the file cannot deliver. It cannot serve a dynamic disk with more than 1,048,576 BAT entries — 2 TiB at the default 2 MiB block — and refuses such a header outright. It cannot honour a `block_size` that is not a multiple of 512, and refuses it. It cannot work on a file under 512 bytes or one whose footer will not read in full, and says nothing about either. And a VHD of `disk_type` 0, 1, 5 or 6 — none, reserved, reserved — is declined with a warning in the log and an empty list, folded into the "ran and produced nothing" row where it is indistinguishable from an image that was read.

**Refuses.** It refuses to serve host bytes for a sector the bitmap says was never written: each dynamic block's sector bitmap is read and honoured, absent sectors are zero-filled and present ones read from the block, because the block's slack past the written sectors is stale host data that would otherwise be served as guest evidence (`test_dynamic_vhd_absent_sector_reads_zeros_not_host_bytes`). It refuses to fabricate zeros for a present sector the file cannot deliver: a short read inside an allocated block is an `UnexpectedEof` error naming the physical offset, and a bitmap or BAT that cannot be read in full fails the open (`test_dynamic_vhd_short_block_read_errors`, `test_dynamic_vhd_truncated_bat_errors`). It refuses a differencing disk with a `ParsingError` saying the parent is required and not available, rather than returning an empty success that would look like "processed, nothing found" while the parent's blocks went missing (`test_vhd_differencing_rejected`). It refuses a dynamic header without `cxsparse`, a `block_size` below 512 or not a multiple of 512 — which would make `sectors_per_block` zero or misaligned and every allocated block read back as zeros — a `max_table_entries` of zero, and one above 1,048,576, each with a `ParsingError` naming the fault (`test_dynamic_vhd_invalid_header_magic`, `test_dynamic_vhd_sub_sector_block_size_errors`, `test_dynamic_vhd_zero_block_size`, `test_dynamic_vhd_bat_too_large`). It refuses to serve host padding as image and refuses to shrink the declared capacity to the file, for a fixed disk. It refuses to parse geometry from a buffer that did not pass the magic check (`test_vhd_footer_fallback_parses_validated_copy`), and refuses, in silence, a file too small for a footer, a footer readable at neither end, any other subtype or name, and an unknown disk type (`test_vhd_skip_too_small`, `test_vhd_invalid_magic`, `test_vhd_unknown_type`). Every one of those silent refusals is a "skipped" or "produced nothing" fold in the processing log, and the two loud ones are error rows there: nothing this module refuses leaves a record on the artifact tree, which `Container_Formats.md` states for all four virtual-disk readers.

### `container.vhdx_reader`

**Reads.** A Hyper-V VHDX virtual disk, and it is handed one rather than hunting for it. The module subscribes to `ArtifactType::Container` and to nothing else, and declares `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, which is advisory — the orchestrator prepares nothing on a module's behalf. If the artifact carries a `subtype` it must be exactly `vhdx` or the module returns an empty list in silence; only where there is no subtype at all does it fall back to the name, accepting an artifact whose lower-cased `metadata["name"]` ends in `.vhdx` and nothing else. The subtype is set upstream by `seance_api::auto_detect_artifact_type`, which reads the first 512 bytes through `seance_core::file_detection::detect_file_type` and returns `VhdxImage` when the eight bytes `vhdxfile` stand at offset 0, falling back to the extension table only when detection returned `Unknown` — so a Hyper-V checkpoint named `.avhdx` reaches this module by its magic, there being no `.avhdx` entry in that table. Having been selected, the reader re-establishes the file for itself: eight bytes at offset 0 must read `vhdxfile`; then a fixed 65,536 bytes are read at 0x30000 and must arrive entire, so no file that cannot deliver 262,144 bytes opens at all, and `regi` must stand at its offset 0. The 32-bit entry count at offset 8 of that table is walked for at most 2,047 entries of 32 bytes each, and exactly two region GUIDs are recognised, both compared as the mixed-endian bytes the format stores: the BAT region `2DC27766-F623-4200-9D64-115E9BFD4A08` and the metadata region `8B7CA206-4790-4B9A-B8FE-575F050F886E`. Each contributes a 64-bit file offset and a 32-bit length; the two offsets must be non-zero, and the lengths are taken as given. The metadata region is then read at its declared length, capped at 16,777,216 bytes and required to be at least 32, read whole, and `metadata` must stand at its offset 0. Its 16-bit entry count at offset 10 is walked for at most 2,047 entries of 32 bytes from offset 32, stopping early where an entry would run past the staged region and skipping any entry whose 32-bit item offset — taken as relative to the region start — plus eight bytes would; three items are read and no others: File Parameters `CAA16737-FA36-4D43-B3B6-33F0AA44E76B`, giving the 32-bit block size and the flag word whose bit 0x2 says the disk has a parent; Virtual Disk Size `2FA54224-CD1B-4876-B211-5DBED83BF4B8`, a 64-bit byte count; and Logical Sector Size `8141BF1D-A96F-4709-BA47-F233A8FAAB5F`, 32 bits. Block size and logical sector size must both be non-zero. From them comes the chunk ratio, `(8,388,608 × logical_sector_size) / block_size`, floored at 1 — the number of payload entries the format puts between the interspersed sector-bitmap entries. The BAT is then loaded whole into memory: its declared length divided by 8, capped at 8,388,608 entries (64 MiB of table), read exactly, and parsed into a second in-memory copy as little-endian 64-bit entries. Every subsequent read is served from that table: for a virtual offset the block is `offset / block_size`, its BAT index is `block + block / chunk_ratio`, the state is the entry's low three bits, and where the state is 6 the host offset is the entry masked with `0xFFFF_FFFF_FFF0_0000` — the format's 1 MiB-granular file offset — plus the offset within the block, and that many bytes are read from the underlying source at that physical offset. A read is clamped to the declared virtual size and then either fills its whole length or fails; it never returns short.

**Produces.** Exactly one artifact, and it is not a record — it is the evidence. One `ArtifactType::RawEvidence` child, parented to the container artifact, whose data is a `VhdxDataSource` presenting the decoded guest disk as an ordinary `DataSource` of exactly the declared virtual size, so the partition, file-system, carving and hashing stack runs on it unchanged. Its metadata carries the source name with `_extracted` appended, the virtual size in bytes, `subtype: "raw"`, `container: "vhdx"`, and `container_path` and `path` both set from the parent artifact's `path` — null where the parent had none. It is the `container: "vhdx"` tag, and only that tag, which routes the child back through this module when content is requested later: `seance_api::content_resolver` re-runs `process` on a synthetic copy of the parent for every ranged request — no handle is cached for VHDX, only for E01 and EWF, so the region table, the metadata region and the whole BAT are read again each time — checks the recorded `path` against the evidence-root policy, and wraps the result in a `DeviceImageSource` so an offset into the decoded image is treated as device-absolute. It emits no `ParsedRecord`, no timeline event and no summary of the image: no block counts, no statement of how much of the virtual disk was backed by a present block, no BAT statistics, no report of which virtual ranges were synthesised. In the case's processing log, this module's two outcomes each take a row of their own — a `complete` row with one artifact produced, or an `error` row whose message is the `ModuleError` rendering, `Parsing Error:` and then the reason. The silent empty list, where the artifact was not a VHDX by subtype or name, takes no row of its own: it joins the single folded `complete` row the orchestrator writes per artifact for every module that ran and produced nothing.

**Cannot.** It cannot open a VHDX found inside the evidence. It subscribes to `Container` only, where the VHD, VMDK, QCOW2 and Apple sparse-image readers all subscribe to `FileEntry` as well, and nothing in the pipeline re-types a file entry to a container — so a virtual machine's disk recovered from an acquired file system is listed as a file and never read as a disk. It cannot verify the image's integrity, because it never looks at the parts of the format that would let it. The two VHDX headers at 0x10000 and 0x20000 are not read at all: not their CRC-32C checksums, not their sequence numbers, not the file and data write GUIDs, and not the log GUID. No CRC-32C is computed or compared anywhere in this module — not over a header, not over the region table — so a bit-flip in the region table or the metadata region is read as the value it now holds, and an examiner asked whether the container's own integrity fields agreed must answer that they were not consulted. It computes no digest of the decoded stream or of the container file, and the format carries none over payload to compare against if it did. It cannot replay the log, and cannot say whether there is one outstanding: a VHDX taken from a running or crashed host carries log entries describing metadata and BAT updates not yet applied to the file, and this reader presents the on-disk state without replaying them and without reporting that a log is present, because the header field that names the log is never read. It cannot fall back to the format's second copy of anything: only the region table at 0x30000 is read, so a corrupt primary region table refuses the image even where the backup at 0x40000 is intact, and the newer of the two headers is never chosen because neither is read. It cannot tell an examiner which bytes of the decoded image are real. The code names two states — fully present, 6, and partially present, 7 — and every other value of the low three bits is served as zeros, so a never-written block, a block the guest wrote zeros into, and a state value the format does not define all come out of the decoded image the same, and nothing on the produced artifact marks which virtual ranges were synthesised rather than read. A hole is therefore reported as zeroes, never as absent. It cannot honour the format's `Required` flags: the 32-bit required field at offset 28 of a region-table entry is never read, and neither is a metadata item's flag word, so a file carrying a region or metadata item this build does not know but that the format says must be understood is read anyway rather than refused. It reads no metadata item beyond the three above — the physical sector size, the virtual disk identifier and the parent locator are all left unread, which is why the refusal below can say a parent is required but cannot name the parent it would need; and it is why the differencing refusal rests on a single bit of the File Parameters flag word with no second witness, so an image carrying a parent locator with that bit clear is opened and its parent-backed blocks served as zeros. It validates the declared geometry barely: block size is required only to be non-zero, with no power-of-two check and no upper bound; virtual size is not checked at all, so a metadata region declaring a virtual size of zero opens successfully and yields a child artifact of size zero; and the BAT region's declared length is not checked either, so a region entry declaring length 0 opens the image and then fails every read of it. Where the metadata region's declared length exceeds the 16,777,216-byte cap, an item living past the cap is skipped in silence and the file is then refused for a missing block or sector size — a refusal naming the wrong cause. It decompresses nothing and decrypts nothing: this module performs no payload decompression, and a BitLocker-protected guest volume inside the image reaches the partition stack still encrypted. Its ceilings are: 65,536 bytes of region table at a fixed 0x30000; at most 2,047 region-table entries and 2,047 metadata entries considered; 16,777,216 bytes of metadata region; and 8,388,608 BAT entries, which at the common 1 MiB block and 512-byte logical sector is a chunk ratio of 4,096 and about 8,386,000 addressable blocks — just under 8 TiB of virtual disk, past which every read is a hard error and not a hole. And the reading has never been checked against a VHDX that Hyper-V wrote. There is no VHDX sample in `test_data/`, no known-answer validation, and the four unit tests in the module run only against images the tests build themselves: one 1 MiB fully-present block round-tripping 0xAB, a non-VHDX refusal, a truncated BAT and a wrapping host offset. A fuzz target, `fuzz/fuzz_targets/vhdx.rs`, drives the module over arbitrary bytes; it pins that it does not panic and nothing about what it reads. Nothing pins the differencing refusal, nothing pins the partially-present refusal, and nothing exercises a source that returns short reads.

**Refuses.** It refuses a differencing disk outright. Where the File Parameters flag bit 0x2 is set the module logs a warning and returns a parsing error saying the image is a differencing disk whose parent is required and not available, and produces no artifact at all — because the unwritten blocks of a differencing disk live in its parent, and opening it alone would present the parent's content as zeros and let an examiner read a checkpointed Hyper-V disk as an empty one. That refusal is taken after the image has been fully opened, so a differencing VHDX pays the whole region, metadata and BAT read before it is declined. It refuses a partially-present block, state 7, at read time: the read returns an `Unsupported` error naming the block number and saying its sector bitmap is not reconstructed. A state-7 block holds real payload sectors selected by the interspersed sector-bitmap BAT entry with the rest sourced from a parent, and this reader reconstructs neither the bitmap nor a parent, so zero-filling would silently discard bytes that are present in the file. Because the check is per read and not at open, a partially-present image opens successfully and then fails one read at a time from inside the partition and file-system parsers. It refuses a block that lies inside the virtual size but has no BAT entry, with an `UnexpectedEof` error naming the index, the block and the virtual size, rather than coercing a missing entry to "not present" — coercion is what the reader used to do, and it read real evidence back as zeros (readiness gap C5). It refuses a host offset that carries past the top of the address space: the 44-bit mask leaves bits up to 63 set, so a crafted BAT entry can sit within one block of `u64::MAX`, and `base.checked_add(in_block)` fails with `InvalidData` instead of wrapping round to unrelated bytes near the start of the file and presenting them as this block's content. It refuses a short or truncated image rather than reading it as far as it goes: every structural read — the eight signature bytes, the 65,536-byte region table, the declared metadata region, the whole BAT — is an exact read that errors on a short return, and a present block whose host offset lies beyond the end of the file fails the read rather than returning the zeros a partial buffer would hold. And it refuses each malformed structure by name, so the processing-log row says which: not a VHDX file; bad region table signature; missing BAT or metadata region; metadata region too small; bad metadata signature; metadata missing block or sector size. The one failure that is not an error is a VHDX artifact with no data source attached, which is returned as `InvalidInputFormat` and is recorded by the orchestrator as a module declining its input rather than as a failure — folded, with every other module that declined this artifact, into one `skipped` row.

### `container.vmdk_reader`

**Reads.** A VMware monolithic sparse extent, and it does not find one for itself. It runs on a `Container` or `FileEntry` artifact and selects on metadata before it looks at a byte: where the artifact carries a `subtype` it must be exactly `vmdk`, compared case-sensitively, and anything else is declined in silence; where it carries no subtype the decision falls to the `name` field, lower-cased, ending `.vmdk`. That subtype is written upstream by `seance_api::auto_detect_artifact_type`, which sets it when the first four bytes of the file are `KDMV` (0x564D444B) and otherwise from the `.vmdk` extension alone — so a descriptor-only or flat VMDK reaches this module marked `vmdk` on the strength of its name. An artifact with no data source is refused as an invalid input; a source of fewer than 512 bytes yields no artifact. It then re-establishes the extent for itself: 512 bytes are read from offset 0, looping over short returns, and it reads nine fields out of that header and nothing else — the magic at 0, which must be 0x564D444B; `version` at 4; `flags` at 8; `capacity` at 12 and `grainSize` at 20, both in 512-byte sectors; `numGTEsPerGT` at 44; `gdOffset` at 56, in sectors; `overHead` at 64; and `compressAlgorithm` at 77. The grain count is `capacity` divided by `grainSize`, rounded up, through `checked_add` and `checked_div`, because both numbers come from the evidence; the grain-table width is `numGTEsPerGT`, or 512 when that field is zero; and the grain-directory entry count is the grain count divided by that width, rounded up, capped at 1,048,576. Every other multiplication by 512 — the disk size, the grain size in bytes, the grain-directory byte offset — saturates rather than being checked. The grain directory is then read whole from `gdOffset` × 512 as that many little-endian `u32`s, in one buffer of at most 4,194,304 bytes, and held in memory for the life of the source. Every later read walks two levels per grain: the logical offset gives a grain index, which gives a grain-directory slot and a position within its grain table; a directory entry of zero means that whole table is unallocated; otherwise one 4-byte grain-table entry is read out of the file at the table's sector × 512 plus four times the position, on every access, and an entry of zero means that grain is unallocated. A non-zero entry is a sector number, and the host offset is that sector × 512 plus the offset within the grain. It never touches the file system: it opens no path, seeks no sibling file, and reads `name` only as a selector and a label, so nothing outside the bytes of the one source it was handed is ever consulted.

**Produces.** One artifact and no records: a `RawEvidence` child, parented to the container artifact it read, carrying a data source over the decoded disk and metadata holding the `name` it was given, the `container` as `vmdk`, the `vmdk_type` as `sparse`, the `vmdk_version` exactly as the header declared it, the `disk_size` as `capacity` × 512 and the `grain_size_bytes` as `grainSize` × 512. It carries no subtype, which is why every module that subscribes to raw evidence sees it. That `container: "vmdk"` tag is load-bearing after the run as well as during it: content resolution re-opens the disk by re-running this module over a synthetic copy of the same parent, for every content request, with no cache — the decoded image is never persisted, only re-derived, and each re-derivation repeats the header parse, the grain-directory read and every per-grain metadata read. Nothing inside the disk is this module's output. The partition parser, the file-system parsers, the carver, the hasher and the search index all read through the data source it published, and every file in the case that came out of that virtual disk came out of it through this two-level grain walk. The data source serves exactly the declared `disk_size`: a read starting at or past that offset returns zero bytes rather than an error, and a read crossing the end is answered short.

**Cannot.** It cannot open a VMDK that is not a monolithic sparse extent. The descriptor text file a hosted VM writes, and the `-flat.vmdk` extent it points at, have no `KDMV` magic, and a source without that magic produces no artifact at all — not a partial read, not a refusal record, nothing; and because such a file was typed `Container` on its extension, no partition or file-system parser subscribes to it either, so nothing in the case examines it. It reads no descriptor.
