The nine fields above are all it reads: nothing in the header between offsets 28 and 43, nothing at 48 to 55, nothing at 72 to 76 — which is where the format puts the descriptor's location and size, the redundant grain directory and the unclean-shutdown flag — and no code anywhere in this tree parses a VMDK descriptor. Three things follow from that which an examiner must be told. First, it cannot tell a snapshot delta from a base disk: a child extent carries the same `KDMV` header as a base one, the parent identifier and the disk's declared type exist only in the descriptor, and a delta opened on its own presents every grain that lives in its parent as zeroes — a disk that reads as mostly empty may be a snapshot layer whose content is in a file this module never saw. Second, it cannot assemble a split set: each `-s001.vmdk`, `-s002.vmdk` and so on opens as a disk in its own right, declaring its own capacity, no segment is ever joined to another, and because the module has no notion of a set at all it cannot notice that a segment is missing. Third, it cannot report the disk's declared adapter, geometry or extent layout. It cannot tell a hole from a written zero. An unallocated grain table, an unallocated grain, and a logical offset the grain directory does not reach are all answered with zeroes; no byte range is marked as never-stored; and the module publishes no count of allocated against unallocated grains — so nothing on the record distinguishes a disk one per cent written from one written end to end. It verifies no integrity. The format it reads carries no checksum over its header, its grain directory, its grain tables or its grains, and the module computes none; it does not read the format's unclean-shutdown flag, so an extent a hypervisor closed improperly opens with no remark; and it does not read the redundant grain directory the format provides, so it can neither cross-check the primary directory against it nor fall back to it when the primary is unreadable. It decompresses nothing and decrypts nothing. It does not validate `version`: a header declaring 0, or 99, opens on exactly the same terms as 1, 2 or 3, and the number is published as found. Of `flags` it consults one bit, so the format's convention for a grain explicitly recorded as zeroed is not honoured: any non-zero grain-table entry is taken as a sector number, the value 1 included, and a grain marked by that value resolves to 512 bytes into the file — the extent's own metadata — rather than to zeroes. It reads `overHead` and discards it, so nothing checks that a grain table or a grain lies past the metadata region or inside the file at all; a grain-table entry pointing back into the header or the grain tables is served as disk content, and only a grain the file cannot deliver in full is caught, by the short-read error rather than by a bounds check. Because the multiplications by 512 saturate, a capacity above 2⁵⁵ sectors is clamped to a 16 EiB disk and published as one rather than refused, and a valid magic with a capacity of zero publishes a 0-byte child that is indistinguishable from a disk holding nothing. It cannot tell a failed read from the end of the file: an I/O error inside an allocated grain is reported as a short read of that grain. It says nothing about time: nothing it reads is a timestamp and nothing it produces carries one. Its one geometry ceiling is 1,048,576 grain-directory entries, read as a single 4,194,304-byte buffer; its floor is a source of 512 bytes.

**Refuses.** It refuses compressed grains outright rather than reading them as plain sparse. Flag bit 16 set, or a non-zero `compressAlgorithm`, is a hard error naming the subformat and quoting both fields, and so is a `gdOffset` of 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, the sentinel that says the grain directory is in the footer. All three mean streamOptimized, and all three are refused for one reason: read as plain sparse, every grain in such a file resolves to nothing and the disk would present itself as an expanse of zeroes — evidence fabricated out of a subformat we do not decode. It refuses to parse a zero-padded structure anywhere. A source that reports 512 bytes or more and then fails to deliver a 512-byte header is an error naming the structure, the bytes it got and the offset; a grain directory the file cannot fill is an error rather than a directory of zero entries, which would have served zeroes for every grain it covers; a grain-table entry that reads short is an error; and an allocated grain the file cannot deliver in full fails with the bytes got and the host offset, because fabricating zeroes for an allocated grain would present unread disk as real content. That refusal is deliberately not the same as tolerating a chunked source: an E01-, AFF4- or archive-backed source that hands back seven bytes at a time is looped over, and only a genuine shortfall is a refusal — one short call was once taken for truncation, and behind such a source that meant valid sparse VMDKs never opened at all and nothing inside them was ever examined. It refuses a grain count it cannot compute from the evidence: a `capacity`-plus-`grainSize` sum that overflows a `u64`, the geometry a stored fuzz reproducer drives, and a grain-directory entry count over 1,048,576. Where the header's `grainSize` or `gdOffset` is zero it refuses nothing and produces nothing: it logs a warning and returns empty, as it does for a missing magic and for a source under 512 bytes. Those declines leave no record of their own — they reach the case only as the processing log's folded "ran and produced nothing" entry against this artifact — while a hard refusal reaches it as an error row carrying the reason, and an artifact handed to the module with no data source reaches it as a declined input. Past the point where the disk has opened, a refusal is no longer the module's to make and surfaces to whoever is reading: a host offset that would carry past `u64::MAX` fails the read as invalid data rather than wrapping round to unrelated bytes of the file. If it panics, the orchestrator catches the unwind and the processing log records an error naming the module and the panic message.

### `container.xz_expander`

**Reads.** An xz-compressed stream, and it is handed one rather than hunting for it. The module subscribes to `Container` and `FileEntry` artifacts with `InputCapability::Stream`, and gates on metadata before it touches a byte: an artifact carrying a `subtype` is read only when that subtype is exactly `xz`, and an artifact carrying no subtype at all is read only when its `name` metadata, lower-cased, ends `.xz` or `.txz`. The `xz` subtype is set upstream by `seance_api::auto_detect_artifact_type`, which reads the first 512 bytes through `seance_core::file_detection::detect_file_type` and returns `XzArchive` when the six bytes `FD 37 7A 58 5A 00` stand at offset 0, and falls back to the extension table only when detection returned `Unknown` — where `.xz` maps to subtype `xz` but `.tar.xz` and `.txz` map to subtype `tar`, so a magic-less file with one of those two names goes to the tar extractor and never here. A file entry recovered out of a file system, which carries no subtype, reaches this module through its name alone. The artifact must carry a `DataSource` or the module returns `InvalidInputFormat` (`XZ module requires data source`). It then reads its own six bytes at offset 0 through `read_full` and remembers whether they are the xz magic; that answer decides only what is said on failure, not whether decoding is attempted. Decoding is `xz2::read::XzDecoder::new` — liblzma's single-stream decoder, with no memory limit and without the `CONCATENATED` flag — over a `SourceCursor` walking the source sequentially from offset 0, and every decompressed byte is streamed in 64 KiB reads into an anonymous, already-unlinked `tempfile::tempfile()` in the system temp directory by `TempBackedSource::from_reader`, under the run's decompression ceiling: `SEANCE_MAX_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES`, parsed by `limits::parse_cap` as plain bytes or a `K`/`M`/`G`/`T` binary suffix with zero and unparseable values ignored, read once per process, defaulting to 10,737,418,240 bytes. The reader takes one byte past the ceiling so a stream that would exceed it is detected rather than truncated. liblzma's own block checks — CRC32, CRC64 or SHA-256 as the stream declares — are verified by the decoder as it goes; nothing in this module reads the stream header, the index or the filter chain itself. After a successful expansion it reads five bytes of its own output at offset 257 of the temp file, when that output is at least 262 bytes long, to see whether the literal `ustar` stands there.

**Produces.** Exactly one child artifact per artifact it claims, parented to it and backed by the temp-file `TempBackedSource`, so a downstream reader can address the decompressed bytes at random. Where `ustar` was found at offset 257 the child is `ArtifactType::Container` with `subtype` `tar`, which is what routes it to `container.tar_extractor`; otherwise it is a `FileEntry` with no subtype, and whatever module recognises its name or content reads it next. Its metadata carries `name`, derived from the parent's name by suffix — `x.tar.xz` becomes `x.tar`, `x.txz` becomes `x.tar`, any other `.xz` name loses its last three characters, a name ending in none of those becomes `<name>.decompressed`, and an artifact with no name at all yields `unknown`; `size`, the byte count actually written to the temp file; `container` set to `xz`, the tag the API's content resolver later dispatches on to re-run this same `process()` on a synthetic copy of the parent and cache the result per parent artifact, so a tar inside it or a multi-range download is not re-inflated each time; `container_path`, the parent's name; and two keys stamped by `limits::stamp_ceiling` — `decompression_ceiling_bytes`, the ceiling in force for the run, and `decompression_ceiling_source`, either `default` or the literal `SEANCE_MAX_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES` — which the report's method-qualifications section reads to print, once per distinct ceiling, the sentence in `limits::ceiling_statement` and a count of the containers it governed. Where the xz magic was present and decoding failed it produces instead exactly one `ParsedRecord` built by `status::expansion_failed_status`: `type` `ArchiveScanStatus`, `record_type` `archive_scan_status`, named `<name> (not expanded)`, with `container` `xz`, `container_path`, `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason` `xz_decompress_failed`, `inventory_incomplete: true`, `inventory_incomplete_reason` `unresolved_structure`, `entries_recovered: 0`, the decoder's own message — wrapped by `TempBackedSource` as `decompression failed after N bytes; refusing to serve a truncated stream as complete: <message>`, so that prefix stands before liblzma's wording — under `detail`, `content_incomplete_detail` and `inventory_incomplete_detail` — with the sentence from `limits::cap_guidance` naming the variable appended when the failure was the ceiling — and a `message` saying the stream's contents are unknown, not absent. It emits no hash, no timeline event and no record of the xz header's own fields. The child carries no `path` and no `parent_path`, so a module classifying by location, such as the launchd reader, sees an empty path for anything expanded here.

**Cannot.** It cannot expand a concatenated xz file at all. liblzma is constructed without `LZMA_CONCATENATED`, so on an xz file made by concatenating several `.xz` files — a form `xz` itself produces and accepts — the decoder reaches the first stream footer, `xz2` then fails the read with `corrupt xz stream` because liblzma consumes nothing of the bytes that follow, and `TempBackedSource::from_reader` fails closed: the module emits the `xz_decompress_failed` record and a `warn!` line, and no child at all. The limitation is real, but the failure is recorded, not silent. It cannot say what it did not verify beyond what liblzma checks: the block integrity check is liblzma's arithmetic, a stream declaring a check type this build's liblzma does not support decodes with no check and no word said, and the module computes no digest of the decompressed bytes and compares none, because the format carries none over the whole payload. It cannot tell a truncated stream from a corrupt one except by liblzma's wording: both arrive as an `io::Error` and both become the same `xz_decompress_failed` record, distinguishable only by the `detail` text (`premature eof` against `corrupt xz stream`, or liblzma's own message). It cannot expand a `.tar.xz` or `.txz` that reached the case by extension fallback rather than by magic, because that fallback labels those names `tar`, not `xz`, and the subtype gate declines anything but `xz` in silence. It cannot read a raw `.lzma` (LZMA_Alone) stream at all: the magic check is the six-byte xz header and the decoder is the xz stream decoder, not the auto decoder. It recovers none of the xz header's own facts — no filter chain, no check type, no stream flags, no block count — and the xz format carries no original filename or modification time, so the child's name is derived from the container's name and nothing else. It cannot bound its own disk use below the ceiling: a 10 GiB decompressed stream is 10 GiB in the temp directory for as long as any `Arc` to the child's source lives, and through the resolver's per-parent cache that can be the life of the API process. It cannot detect a tar by anything but `ustar` at offset 257: a pre-POSIX tar, or one written without that magic, comes out as a plain `FileEntry` and is expanded by nothing. A magic-less file named `.xz` is decoded anyway — the decode attempt is made before the magic answer is used — and only its failure is silenced. Its reading is pinned by seven unit tests — four over streams the tests themselves encode with `xz2::write::XzEncoder` at level 1, the other three over no data, plain text, or the raw magic followed by garbage — and by nothing written by another tool: no xz fixture exists in `test_data/`, and no test covers a concatenated or a multi-block stream.

**Refuses.** It refuses to serve a truncated payload as a whole one, and that is the shape of every refusal here. A decode error at any point — after zero bytes or after nine gigabytes — discards the temp file and fails the expansion, because a single-stream format has no already-complete entries to keep, and the partial bytes would otherwise be hashed, indexed and exported as the file. A stream whose decompressed length would exceed the ceiling is refused whole with `decompression ceiling reached: decompressed stream exceeds the <cap>-byte cap` rather than cut at the cap and served as complete; a stream exactly at the ceiling is accepted. It refuses to let a mistyped ceiling remove the ceiling: an unparseable or zero `SEANCE_MAX_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES` falls back to the 10 GiB default and is recorded as `default`, never as a setting the examiner made. It refuses to stay silent about a stream it recognised and could not expand: where the six-byte magic was present, the failure leaves the `ArchiveScanStatus` record above with the decoder's reason, because a corrupt or bomb-capped `.xz` that produced nothing used to ingest exactly like a file that was never xz. And it refuses the opposite too — a file merely named `.xz` that carries no xz magic and will not decode returns an empty list with no record and one `warn!` line, because a failure stamp on every mislabelled file on a disk tells an examiner nothing. An artifact with no data source returns `InvalidInputFormat`, which the orchestrator logs at `debug!` and folds into the artifact's single `skipped` row. Every other decline — wrong subtype, wrong name — is a silent empty list folded into the artifact's `ran and produced nothing` row, indistinguishable there from a module that read the artifact and found nothing. Nothing this module does produces an `error` row in the processing log: it never returns `ParsingError`.

### `container.zip_extractor`

**Reads.** A ZIP archive, selected in two stages. First a cheap gate on what the case already believes: an artifact whose `subtype` is present and is neither `zip`, `docx`, `xlsx` nor `pptx`, and whose name ends in none of thirteen extensions (`.zip`, `.docx`, `.docm`, `.xlsx`, `.xlsm`, `.pptx`, `.pptm`, `.jar`, `.apk`, `.odt`, `.ods`, `.odp`, `.ufdr`), is declined with no byte read, because another handler owns that format. Everything else — a named archive, or any artifact carrying no subtype at all, which is how a `FileEntry` arrives from the filesystem subscription — is probed on content: `read_full` is looped over four bytes at offset 0 (a two-byte return from a windowed or container-backed source is ordinary and is not read as "not a ZIP"), and the archive is accepted only when they are `PK` followed by `03 04` (a local file header), `05 06` (an empty archive's end-of-central-directory) or `07 08` (the spanning marker). Those four bytes are what decide it, so an extensionless archive is read exactly as a named one is; an archive already stamped with some other subtype is not read at all. It is then opened over a seekable `SourceCursor` and its central directory is parsed **exactly once**, that one parse shared by every entry through a cloned `ZipArchive` — a clone is a cursor and a reference count, not a re-parse, because re-opening per entry cost 12 to 40 seconds on the first read of each entry of a 125,327-entry Cellebrite archive, forty-three days for one ingest. Opening each entry seeks to its local header and requires the local-file-header signature to stand there, taking the data offset from the local name and extra-field lengths; every other fact comes from the central directory — the stored name, the uncompressed and compressed sizes (from the Zip64 extra field where the 32-bit fields are saturated), the directory bit, the compression method, the CRC-32, the MS-DOS modification date and time, and the external attributes. Names are decoded by the reader as UTF-8, lossily, when general-purpose bit 11 is set, and as CP437 when it is not. Entry content is not read during listing: each file entry is given a lazily-materialised data source that decompresses the entry into memory only when a downstream parser reads it, pre-sizing its buffer to the declared size capped at 64 MiB, and caching the outcome; decompression covers stored, deflate, bzip2 and zstd, the `zip` 0.6.6 crate's default feature set, and the entry's CRC-32 is checked by that reader as the bytes run out. Stored names are resolved into the flat-model `name`/`path`/`parent_path` trio: backslashes are folded to `/` first, so `..\..\payload` is two traversal segments and not one filename (RUSTSEC-2026-0245); empty and `.` segments are dropped, `..` is applied and clamped at the archive root, and an absolute or root-escaping name is flagged. An entry source can also open a sibling by name suffix (`1.db` → `1.db-wal`) or a neighbour by plain relative path within its own directory, so a SQLite database and its write-ahead log packed side by side are read together.

**Produces.** One `FileEntry` artifact, parented to the container, for every central-directory record the reader accepted, carrying `name` (the basename), `path` (`/`-rooted and resolved within the archive), `parent_path`, `size`, `compressed_size`, `is_directory`, `container: "zip"` and `container_path`. Where resolution changed the stored name, `original_name` carries that name with backslashes already folded to `/`, and `path_traversal: true` marks the attempt. A recorded modification time is emitted as an RFC 3339 string with a `+00:00` offset and a companion `timezone: "local"`, because ZIP stores a local wall clock at two-second resolution in a zone the archive does not carry. A Unix mode is emitted octal, masked to the low twelve bits. A non-directory entry carries a readable lazy data source; a directory carries none. Where entries are password-protected it emits one `EncryptedArchive` `ParsedRecord` (subtype `zip_encrypted`, `evidence_grade: scanned`) naming the archive, the encrypted-entry count, up to fifty sample names — a sample, not the inventory — and `recoverable_with: "seance crack-zip"`, and it still emits a `FileEntry` for every encrypted entry, its name, path and size taken from the central directory without a password, marked `encrypted: true`, `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason: "encrypted"`, with no data source attached; where even that read fails the entry is published under the placeholder name `(encrypted entry #<index>)` with `size: 0`, which is not evidence the file was empty. Where the archive could not be opened at all, where a named archive's first four bytes are short or wrong, or where entries failed to open after a successful parse, it emits an `ArchiveScanStatus` `ParsedRecord` (`record_type: archive_scan_status`, `content_incomplete: true`, reason one of `zip_unreadable`, `zip_magic_unreadable` or `zip_entry_unreadable`) carrying `entries_recovered`, `entries_skipped`, the first underlying error and the sentence that entries missing from the listing are not evidence the archive did not contain them. The crack surface — `ZipCracker`, `verify_zip_password`, `has_encrypted_entry` — returns a `ZipVerdict` of `Correct`, `Wrong`, `NotEncrypted` or `Unreadable` for one candidate password, and nothing else: no recovered file, and no record.

**Cannot.** It cannot decrypt. ZipCrypto and WinZip AES entries are recognised and listed, but their content is never served — the `FileEntry` carries no data source — and `seance crack-zip` recovers a *password*, not the bytes: no path in this product hands a ZIP password back to a parser, so a cracked archive's entries stay contentless in the case. It cannot materialise an entry larger than 4 GiB (`MAX_ENTRY_SIZE`, 4 × 1024³): the reader takes one byte past the cap so an over-cap entry fails closed with `InvalidData` rather than being truncated, and a Zip64 entry above that is listed at its true size and can never be read. Every entry is held wholly in memory, never spilled to disk, and every read materialises the whole entry whatever offset and length were asked for; the cap bounds one entry, not the resident total, and a sibling or neighbour opened twice is decompressed twice because each source keeps its own cache. It cannot serve an entry whose materialised length disagrees with the uncompressed size its central directory declared — a short or long materialisation fails the read rather than being reconciled. It cannot serve an entry that will not inflate: a corrupt deflate stream, a CRC-32 mismatch or an absent name fails with `InvalidData`, the failure is cached and re-raised on every later read, and it is never served as an empty full-size buffer, which would fabricate all-EOF evidence at the claimed size. It decompresses only stored, deflate, bzip2 and zstd; any other method — 1 shrink, 6 implode, 9 deflate64, 14 LZMA, 98 PPMd — is rejected when the entry is opened during listing, so such an entry is counted in `entries_skipped` and **no record of its name is produced at all**. It verifies nothing about the archive as a whole: ZIP carries no archive-level digest, integrity is the per-entry CRC-32 alone, that CRC is checked only when an entry is actually read to its end and never during listing, and no signature is checked — not an `.apk`'s signing block, not a `.jar`'s manifest. It does not reconcile the local file header against the central directory: it requires only that the local signature be present, and takes name, sizes, method, CRC and the encryption flag from the central directory, so a local header that disagrees is neither detected nor reported. Where two records share one stored name, both are listed but both data sources resolve to the later one's bytes; the length check catches that only when the two declare different sizes. It probes for the magic at offset 0 only, so an archive with a prepended stub — a self-extracting ZIP — is refused even though the reader would find its central directory by searching backwards. It reads no multi-volume set: it sees only the one source handed to it, an archive whose end-of-central-directory names more than one disk is refused by the reader, and an earlier segment carries no end-of-central-directory at all; either way the outcome is a `zip_unreadable` status and never the contents. It records only a modification time, and only the MS-DOS field: the extended-timestamp (0x5455) and NTFS (0x000A) extra fields that carry true UTC times at one-second and 100 ns resolution are not parsed, so a precise UTC stamp in the archive is still reported as a two-second local wall clock, and no access or creation time is ever reported; no uid or gid is read. An entry stamped with the DOS epoch (1980-01-01 00:00:00) or a pre-1980 date gets no timestamp — that is the format's "no time recorded", and it is left absent rather than dated to 1980. Its `mode` is not always a recorded permission: for a DOS-made archive — which is every ZIP a Windows tool writes — the reader synthesises `0o664` for a file and `0o775` for a directory from the DOS attribute bits, masking to `0o555` when the read-only bit is set, and the record does not distinguish that from a real Unix mode; where the external attributes are zero no mode is emitted. It publishes no compression method, no CRC-32, and no archive or entry comment. A name stored in a code page other than UTF-8 is transliterated as CP437 and its original bytes are not published. It imposes no nesting-depth limit: a ZIP inside a ZIP is re-expanded through the `FileEntry` subscription, and there is no depth counter here and none in the orchestrator, so a quine or a deeply nested archive is bounded only by the per-entry cap and by memory. An archive that opens and lists no entries produces nothing whatever — no entry, no record — so this module's output does not separate an empty archive from one never examined. A relative-path open cannot climb: a `..`, a backslash or an absolute path returns nothing whatever the archive holds. The crack path has no read cap by design, because the chosen entry must be read to its CRC or HMAC; it verifies against the *smallest* encrypted entry only, so a verdict speaks for that entry's password and not for an archive whose entries carry different ones; it holds the whole archive in memory, and its ceiling is the caller's — the CLI refuses an archive over 2 GiB, runs on CPU only, and requires a wordlist or a mask.

**Refuses.** It refuses AFF4 evidence containers outright — an `.aff4` name or an `aff4` subtype returns nothing at all — because those are ZIP-based but owned by a dedicated reader and must not be double-processed as plain archives. It refuses any artifact carrying a present, non-ZIP subtype (`e01`, `vmdk` and the like), cheaply and without touching a data source, because another handler owns that format. It refuses a file named as an archive but arriving with no data source, returning `InvalidInputFormat` rather than a silent skip, because that is caller error. It refuses to treat a wrong or short magic on a named archive as an empty archive: a `.zip`, `.docx` or `.ufdr` whose first four bytes are not a ZIP signature yields a `zip_magic_unreadable` status stating how many bytes could be read or which bytes were wrong, so a truncated mobile extraction report never reads as a phone with nothing on it. An archive it cannot open leaves a `zip_unreadable` status with `entries_recovered: 0`, and an archive whose entries partly failed to open leaves a `zip_entry_unreadable` status with the recovered and skipped counts and the first error, because files absent from a listing are read as files the archive did not hold. A file that is not named as an archive and whose first four bytes are not a ZIP signature is ignored in silence, so an ordinary `FileEntry` raises no false alarm. In the cracker it refuses to call a candidate correct on anything less than a full decrypt of an encrypted entry read to EOF with its CRC-32 (ZipCrypto) or HMAC (WinZip AES) intact, so a ZipCrypto 1-in-256 check-byte collision cannot pass as a hit; bytes that are not a parseable ZIP are `Unreadable`, an archive with no encrypted entry is `NotEncrypted`, and a run with neither wordlist nor mask is refused rather than reported as a failure to crack.

### `macos.apple_mail`

**Reads.** Apple Mail's own index, `~/Library/Mail/V*/MailData/Envelope Index`, selected only by that name: the final path component of `name`, lower-cased, must be exactly `envelope index`, so `Envelope Index-wal`, `Envelope Index-shm` and any renamed copy are declined. It subscribes to `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, passes over an artifact with no data source, reads through `read_capped` up to 536,870,912 bytes, spills by `TempDb::spill` to `seance_envelope_index_<uuid>.db` with a `-wal` sibling staged whole beside it when the header says WAL mode and the source can open one, requires `SQLite format 3\0`, opens read-only, and probes the catalogue for a table or view named `messages`. One newest-first statement then walks `messages` with a `LIMIT` of 250,001: `m.ROWID, m.message_id, m.date_sent, m.date_received, m.date_last_viewed, m.size, m.read, m.flagged, m.deleted, m.snippet, m.subject_prefix, s.subject, a.address, a.comment, b.url, m.conversation_id, m.type`, left-joining `subjects` on `m.subject`, `addresses` on `m.sender` and `mailboxes` on `m.mailbox`, ordered by `m.date_received DESC`. Every column is named outright with no probe of the column set first. Per message two further cached statements run: `SELECT r.type, a.address, a.comment FROM recipients r LEFT JOIN addresses a ON a.ROWID = r.address_id WHERE r.message_id = ?1 ORDER BY r.position LIMIT 65`, and `SELECT name FROM attachments WHERE message = ?1 ORDER BY name LIMIT 65`. The three date columns are integers read as Unix epoch seconds — a basis the record states rather than assumes — with a value of zero or below treated as not recorded. `recipients.type` 0, 1 and 2 are read as To, Cc and Bcc. The schema these joins were written against is Apple's own DDL, dumped from a real macOS 11 Mail V8 index (database version 4.30006) whose tables were all empty, kept at `seance_plugin_macos_artifacts/tests/fixtures/envelope_index_v8_schema.sql`. Nothing else in the file is read: not `message_global_data`, `message_references` (the reply graph), `conversations`, `labels`, `events`, `properties`, `searchable_messages`, `server_messages` or `summaries`.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per message, `type` `EmailMessage`, `analysis_type` `email` — which is what puts it in the Email view beside PST, EML and mbox messages — `subtype` `apple_mail_index`, `format` `apple_mail_envelope_index`, `container` set to the index's file name, parented to the file entry. It carries `from` (the sender address, trimmed, null when empty), `from_name`, `to`, `cc` and `bcc` as lists rendered `Display Name <address>`, a bare address, `<name> (no address recorded)` or `(no address recorded)`; `recipients_unrecognised_type` for addresses whose `type` was not 0, 1 or 2; `recipient_count` and `recipients_truncated`, with `recipient_count_is_a_floor` when more than 64 were named; `subject` (the stored `subject_prefix` rejoined to the normalised subject) and `subject_prefix` on its own; `date`/`date_epoch` from `date_received`, `date_sent`/`date_sent_epoch`, `date_last_viewed`/`date_last_viewed_epoch` — RFC 3339 and integer, null when zero — and `date_basis`, the sentence saying the integers were read as Unix seconds and that no populated database here confirms it; `size`; `read`, `flagged` and `deleted` as booleans; `mailbox` (the mailbox URL); `conversation_id` (null when −1); `message_type`; `snippet`; `attachment_count`, `attachments`, `attachments_truncated`, `attachment_count_is_a_floor` past 64, and `has_attachments`; `message_id_hash` with `message_id_hash_note` saying it is an integer hash and not the RFC 5322 header; `body_text` and `body_html` as explicit nulls with `body_absent_reason`; `basis` `schema_verified_rows_unverified` with `basis_statement`; and, on every record by construction, `content_complete: false`, `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason` `unvalidated`, and a `content_incomplete_detail` quoting the validation statement. The `name` is `<sender>: <subject>`. Where the walk hit 250,000 messages it appends a `cap_marker` of `type` `EmailParseStatus`, `subtype` `parse_incomplete`, `source_table` `messages`. Where the spill was short, every record is stamped and a `SqliteSpillIncomplete` marker appended. Where the open, the probe, any statement or a row read fails, the output is one `ParsedRecord`, `type` `EmailParseStatus`, `subtype` `parse_incomplete`, `status` `ParseFailed`. The Email view shows `snippet` under the line `The index's own one-line preview · not the message body`. No `TimelineEvent` is emitted and no timeline row is derived.

**Cannot.** **It cannot give you the mail.** The index holds no body and no RFC 5322 header, so every record is a statement of who wrote to whom, when, about what, in which mailbox, with which attachments named, and whether Mail marked it read, flagged or deleted — and nothing more. The body lives in an `.emlx` file this record does not reach and does not name: no `.emlx` path, `document_id` or `remote_id` is read, so the record cannot be joined to the message file by anything but the examiner's own search. It cannot confirm the dates: Apple Mail has written them as Unix seconds in every version examined, but the one real index this project holds has no populated row, and a date read under the wrong epoch is 31 years out while looking ordinary — which is why `date_basis` is on every record. **It cannot say it has been proven on real mail at all**: the joins, the recipient types and the column meanings were written against Apple's DDL and exercised against rows the tests wrote into it, and every record says so under `basis`; `documentation/COMPARISON.md` marks this reader ⚠️ for exactly that reason. It cannot survive schema drift: all seventeen columns are named outright, so a `messages` table from an older Mail generation lacking any one of them — `snippet`, `subject_prefix`, `deleted`, `conversation_id` — fails the statement and the whole index becomes one `ParseFailed` record, where the quarantine reader would have probed and substituted. It cannot reconstruct a thread: `message_references` and `conversations` are not read, so `conversation_id` is an opaque integer and the Email view's `In-Reply-To`/`References` threading has nothing to work from here. It cannot tell a sender's display name apart from an empty one: `from_name` is the raw `comment` and may be an empty string, unlike `from`, which is nulled when blank. It cannot tell whether a message was outgoing or incoming beyond `message_type`, an integer it does not interpret, and it does not read the mailbox's own `source` or counts. It caps recipients and attachments at 64 each, counting one past the cap, so a mailing-list message names 64 addresses and a count of 65 marked as a floor. A store over 536,870,912 bytes opens as its prefix with every record stamped `cap_reached`. It reads live rows only — no freelist, no unallocated pages — and its `deleted` is Mail's own flag, not a recovered row.

**Refuses.** It refuses to render an absent body as an empty one: `body_text` and `body_html` are null with a stated reason, because an empty string reads as a message that had none. It refuses to publish `messages.message_id` under the name the rest of the case uses for an RFC 5322 `Message-ID`; it is an integer hash and goes out as `message_id_hash` with a note. It refuses to guess a recipient's header: a `type` other than 0, 1 or 2 keeps the address out of `to`, `cc` and `bcc` and lists it under `recipients_unrecognised_type`, because a blind copy filed under To would assert that a recipient knew about a copy the sender hid from them. It refuses to render zero as 1970: a date of zero or below is `null`, since every message Mail never displayed has a zero `date_last_viewed`. It refuses to publish an empty address as a blank: a sender with no address is `null`, and a recipient with neither address nor name is the literal `(no address recorded)`. It refuses to present any record as complete or validated — every one carries `content_incomplete: true` with reason `unvalidated`, which the case's incompleteness census counts — and refuses to present a count past 64 as a total. It refuses to read a `-wal` or `-shm` as the index, and it refuses a file named `Envelope Index` that is some other database, or not a database, returning nothing rather than a failure. It refuses to run a `COUNT(*)` per message, reading one row past each cap instead, so a hostile or corrupt index without its `recipients` index cannot make the reader quadratic. It never writes to evidence. Its only `ModuleError` is `ParsingError` (`spill failed: …`); every parse failure is an `Ok` list holding the `ParseFailed` record, and every decline is a silent empty list. It refuses to file its own statements about what it could not read under the messages' subtype: the cap marker and the failure record keep `subtype` `parse_incomplete`.

### `macos.asl`

**Reads.** Apple System Log stores — `/var/log/asl/*.asl`, including the `BB.*` expiring stores — selected by the `ASL DB` magic rather than by name. **This is where macOS's `wtmpx` went**: `utmpx(5)` says those files 'can be replaced with log entries', and the login and logout history is written here under the facilities `com.apple.system.utmpx` and `com.apple.system.lastlog`, carrying the same `struct utmpx` members the binary reader decodes, as text. A store is an 80-byte header then a flat sequence of length-prefixed records; messages are a doubly linked list through their first and last eight bytes, and their string fields are eight-byte slots holding either an offset or, when the high bit is set, the string inline.

**Produces.** One `AslMessage` per record with the time to the nanosecond, the severity, the sending process and its PID, the facility, the host, the message text and every key/value pair the writer attached. From the login-history facilities it also produces one `LoginSession` per reconstructed session — the account, the terminal, the remote address an SSH session came from, and both ends where both are in the store — and one `BootEvent` per boot and clean shutdown. The sessions are paired by the same engine the `wtmp` reader uses (`seance_login_sessions`), so the two readers of this evidence apply one set of rules. An `AslStatus` row carries the facility and severity histograms and every shortfall.

**Cannot.** It cannot pair a session across stores. A login on one day and its logout on the next are reported as an open session and an unpaired logout, and the open one is given no duration. It cannot read the `AUX.<date>/` directories, which hold the payloads some messages point at. It cannot say who may read a message beyond the access-control uid and gid the record carries, and it does not report the `-1` in that field as an account. It cannot tell you that the store is complete: `syslogd` writes only what the configured facilities and severities let through, and a store holding no record of an event is not evidence the event did not happen.

**Refuses.** It refuses to resynchronise, and it refuses to skip a record type it does not know **even though that record's length is stated** — a store holding a third record type is not the format this reader was shown, and reading past it would be reading the rest against a guess. It refuses to use the message's own timestamp for a session: `ut_tv.tv_sec` is when the login happened and the message is timed when `syslogd` wrote it, and the two differ by up to minutes. It refuses to turn a logout with no matching login into a session with an invented start. And where a file named as a store was not read it refuses to stay silent, because on macOS this store is where the login history is and absence here is not evidence that nobody logged in.

### `macos.bom`

**Reads.** A Bill of Materials — the installer receipts at `/var/db/receipts/*.bom`, and a `Bom` file wherever one has been unpacked to disk — selected by the final path component of `name`, lower-cased, ending `.bom` or being exactly `bom`. It subscribes to `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess` and passes over an artifact with no data source. `Staged::read` reads up to 268,435,456 bytes from offset 0, recording the declared size, the bytes delivered and whether the cap cut the read. The first eight bytes must be `BOMStore`. The layout read is the one in hogliux/bomutils, big-endian throughout: `indexOffset` at 16 and `varsOffset` at 24 of the header — `version` at 8, `numberOfBlocks` at 12, `indexLength` at 20 and `varsLength` at 28 are not read — then the block table at `indexOffset`, a count followed by that many `(address, length)` pairs, every one of which must lie inside the staged bytes to be usable; then the named variables at `varsOffset`, a count then `(block index, name length, name)` triples, of which only the one named `Paths` is used — `HLIndex`, `Size64`, `VIndex` and `BomInfo` are walked past. The `Paths` block must be at least 13 bytes and begin `tree`; its `child` at offset 8 is the root `BOMPaths` node. Nodes are walked depth-first from a stack with a visited set: a node block must be at least 12 bytes; `isLeaf` is the 16-bit word at 0 and `count` the word at 2; the `forward` and `backward` links at 4 and 8 are not followed; each of `count` eight-byte entries from offset 12 gives `index0` and `index1`. On a branch node `index0` is pushed as a child. On a leaf, `index0` names a `BOMPathInfo1` block (at least 8 bytes: the path `id` at 0 and the `BOMPathInfo2` block index at 4) and `index1` a `BOMFile` block (at least 5 bytes: the parent id at 0 and the NUL-terminated name from 4). The `BOMPathInfo2` block, where it resolves and is at least 22 bytes, gives the type byte at 0 (2 directory, 3 symlink, anything else read as a file), `mode` at 4, `uid` at 6, `gid` at 10, `modtime` at 14 and `size` at 18 — its `checksum`, `linkNameLength` and link name are not read. The walk stops after 2,000,000 nodes or once more than 5,000,000 entries are held, checked per node rather than per entry. Full paths are then rebuilt by following each entry's parent id through the table of ids, at most 4,096 steps, skipping `.` and empty components, and the chain is rooted only when it reaches parent 0.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per leaf entry, directories included, `type` `BomEntry`, `subtype` `bom`, parented to the file entry, carrying `path` — `/`-joined and given a leading `/` only when the chain reached the root — `path_rooted`, `source_bom` (the file's name), and, where the `BOMPathInfo2` block resolved, `entry_type` (`directory`, `symlink` or `file`), `size`, `mode` rendered in octal, `uid`, `gid`, `modtime` as the raw seconds and `modtime_rfc3339` when non-zero. Where the metadata block was missing or short those keys are absent and the record carries `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason` `unresolved_structure` and a detail naming `BOMPathInfo2`; where the parent chain broke before the root the same pair is stamped with a detail naming the path id and saying `path` is a suffix, not a location. The `name` is `<kind>: <path>`, with `unknown` for the kind when the metadata was absent. Then, at most once per file, a `BomEntryIncomplete` marker, `subtype` `parse_incomplete`, `status` `InventoryIncomplete`, with `entries_emitted` and the `inventory_incomplete` pair whose detail joins every reason that applied: the staging shortfall with its byte counts (`cap_reached` or `short_read`), the walk cap, the count of blocks the tree pointed at that could not be resolved, and the count of path ids that appeared more than once. Where the file was staged short of its first eight bytes, or has no `BOMStore` magic and was staged short, it produces one `BomEntryIncomplete` marker with `status` `NotStagedInFull`. Where the header, block table, variables or `Paths` tree will not parse it produces one `ParsedRecord`, `type` `BomEntry`, `subtype` `bom`, `status` `ParseFailed`, with the error and `content_incomplete: true` / `unresolved_structure` — and because that record shares its `type` with the data, and `BomEntry` matches no rule in the Records view, both the entries and the failure land under 'Other records', while `BomEntryIncomplete` lands under 'What could not be read'. No `TimelineEvent`, no hash and no cross-reference to the file system are produced.

**Cannot.** **It cannot tell you where on the disk a path was installed.** The `/` at the head of a rooted path is the root of the BOM's own tree, and the receipt's install prefix lives in the sibling `.plist` receipt, which this module does not read, so a BOM path is relative to something the record does not state. It cannot verify that anything listed was ever laid down or is still there: nothing here looks up a path in the file system, compares a size or an mtime with a file entry, or reads the per-entry `checksum` the format carries, so a receipt is published as a manifest and never as a finding that the files match it. It cannot name a package: the BOM has no package identifier, version or install date, which live in the `.plist` beside it and in `InstallHistory.plist`, read by `macos.install_history` with nothing linking the two. It cannot give a symlink its target, because `linkNameLength` and the link name after the fixed fields are not read, and it cannot tell a device node or any type byte other than 2 and 3 from a regular file, because both are reported as `file`. It cannot report a size of 4 GiB or more correctly: `size` is the 32-bit field in `BOMPathInfo2` and the `Size64` variable the format keeps for larger files is not consulted, so such a file's size is its low 32 bits. It cannot read hard-link structure (`HLIndex`) or the `VIndex` and `BomInfo` variables. It cannot bound one leaf: the entry cap is tested when a node is taken from the stack, so a single leaf declaring 65,535 entries is read whole past the cap. It does not follow leaf `forward` links, relying on every leaf being reachable through a branch entry, and it treats a branch entry's `index1` as unused. It cannot recover an entry whose blocks lie past the staged 268,435,456 bytes or past the end of a truncated file: those are counted as unresolved and reported, not read. A modtime is a 32-bit unsigned count of seconds, so nothing before 1970 or after 2106 can be expressed, and zero is reported as the number with no RFC 3339 rendering. It reads `.pkg` `Bom` files only where a package has already been unpacked to a directory: there is no xar reader in this tree, so a `Bom` inside a flat `.pkg` is never reached, whatever the module's own header comment says. And it has never been run against a receipt Apple wrote on the record: the format is verified against bomutils' source, the tests build their own two-entry BOM, and no `.bom` is in `test_data/`.

**Refuses.** It refuses to fabricate a file's metadata. An entry whose `BOMPathInfo2` block cannot be resolved used to be filled with zeros, which read as a real 0-byte file owned by root with mode 0 — a statement about what the installer laid down that the BOM never made — so those keys now stay absent and the record says why. It refuses to format a broken chain as an absolute path: a parent chain that does not reach id 0 yields the resolved suffix without a leading `/` and with `path_rooted: false`, because the leading slash is the form an examiner would cite. It refuses to let a short listing read as the manifest: every shortfall — a short or capped stage, the walk cap, an unresolvable block, a duplicated path id — is counted rather than skipped and lands in the single `BomEntryIncomplete` marker, because an examiner reading a receipt has no other way to tell a short list from a complete one. It refuses to let a `.bom` vanish when its first eight bytes were never staged, leaving the `NotStagedInFull` marker rather than treating an unreadable header as 'not a BOM'. It refuses to read a block whose address and length run past the staged bytes, counting it unresolved rather than reading whatever bytes are there; a block *table* that itself runs past the end is a hard failure with `ParseFailed`. It refuses to loop: a node visited twice is skipped, and a parent chain is followed 4,096 steps at most. It never returns a `ModuleError`: every outcome is an `Ok` list, so a BOM that would not parse is a `ParseFailed` record in the tree and never an `error` row in the processing log. Its declines — a name not ending `.bom`, no data source, a whole file without the `BOMStore` magic — are empty lists folded into the `ran and produced nothing` row.

### `macos.install_history`

**Reads.** `/Library/Receipts/InstallHistory.plist`, selected by the final path component of `name`, lower-cased, being exactly `installhistory.plist`, wherever it sits. It subscribes to `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess` and passes over an artifact with no data source. `Staged::read` reads the source from offset 0 through `read_full` up to 67,108,864 bytes and records three facts about the read: the size the source declared, the bytes actually delivered, and whether the cap rather than the file decided where it stopped. The bytes are handed whole to `plist::from_bytes`, which accepts XML and binary property lists alike. The parsed value must be an array; each element that is a dictionary is read for six keys and no others — `displayName`, `displayVersion`, `processName` and `contentType` as strings, `date` as a plist date, and `packageIdentifiers` as an array of which only the string members are kept — and an element that is not a dictionary is skipped and counted. A `date` is converted to Unix seconds through `SystemTime::duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH)`, whole seconds only, and a date before 1970 yields none. Nothing else on the machine is consulted: not the per-package receipts in `/var/db/receipts/` (`.plist` and `.bom`), and not the file system's own timestamps for the file.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per dictionary in the array, `type` `SoftwareInstall`, `subtype` `install_history`, parented to the plist's file entry, carrying `display_name`, `display_version`, `process_name` and `content_type` — each JSON `null` where the key was absent or not a string — `package_identifiers` as a list, empty where absent, and, where a date converted, `timestamp` as Unix seconds and `timestamp_rfc3339`. The `name` is `Installed <display_name, else (unknown package)> <version> via <process>`. Where the file was not staged whole every record is stamped by `Staged::stamp` with `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason` (`cap_reached` when the file exceeded 67,108,864 bytes, `short_read` when the source delivered fewer bytes than it declared) and a `content_incomplete_detail` giving the byte counts, so an install read out of a partial file does not read as the whole timeline. Where the read was short **and** the staged bytes either would not parse as a plist or parsed to an array that yielded no record, it produces exactly one marker: `type` `SoftwareInstallIncomplete`, `subtype` `parse_incomplete`, `status` `NotStagedInFull`, `bytes_staged`, `bytes_declared`, the incompleteness pair and a detail ending `so the OS updates and package installs it records could not be read`. Where the file was staged in full and still cannot be read it produces the same type, `subtype` `parse_incomplete`, with `status` `ParseFailed` (the decoder's error is in the detail) or `UnexpectedLayout` (the root is not an array), `content_incomplete_reason` `unresolved_structure` and a detail beginning `<file> was read in full and`; where the root is an array but some of its elements are not dictionaries, one more such marker with `status` `EntriesUnreadable`, `entries_unreadable` and `entries_total` rides beside the rows. An empty array produces nothing: the file itself says no install was recorded. A short prefix that parses but is not an array gets the `NotStagedInFull` marker. It emits no `TimelineEvent`, so an install's date is on its record and on no timeline; no hash; and no record of the file itself beyond what the file-system parser already made. The Records view files `SoftwareInstall` under 'The device' by word rule and `SoftwareInstallIncomplete` under 'What could not be read'.

**Cannot.** It cannot read an install out of a file that will not parse or is not an array of dictionaries; it says so with a marker and reads nothing from it. It cannot tell you what a package put on the disk: `packageIdentifiers` names the packages, and the file-level manifest is the receipt `.bom`, read by `macos.bom` with nothing here linking the two. It cannot say the list is everything that was ever installed: nothing in this module cross-checks the entries against `/Applications`, `/var/db/receipts/` or any other source, so an application that arrived without an installer package is not something this record can speak to. It keeps only whole seconds of the install date and loses any fraction, and a `date` before the Unix epoch is dropped rather than reported negative. It reads six keys and ignores every other one a dictionary carries, without recording that it did. It cannot distinguish an absent `displayName` from a `displayName` that is not a string: both are `null`. It cannot detect that the plist was edited: there is no signature, checksum or cross-reference to check, and the module compares nothing against the receipts directory. It has no cap on the number of entries, and the memory cost of a file is the file. Its tests are XML plists written by the tests, and one reads the Magnet 2021 macOS image's own `InstallHistory.plist` (15 entries, all read, no marker) where that gitignored corpus is present; no real file is in `test_data/`.

**Refuses.** It refuses to let a short read pass as a short history. A plist read short of its declared size — because the source stopped early or because it exceeded the 67,108,864-byte cap — produces either records stamped `content_incomplete` or, where the prefix would not parse, the `SoftwareInstallIncomplete` marker, because a prefix of a plist normally will not parse and returning nothing would delete the system's software-provenance record from the case without a trace. It refuses to fabricate a date: an entry with no `date`, or with one before 1970, gets no `timestamp` key rather than zero. It refuses to read any file not named `InstallHistory.plist`, so a receipt plist or a preference plist with a similar shape is never reported as an install history. It never returns a `ModuleError` of any kind: every outcome is an `Ok` list, so nothing this module does produces an `error` row in the processing log. It refuses to let a whole file it could not read pass as a machine with no install history: a file staged in full that will not parse, whose root is not an array, or whose entries are not dictionaries leaves a `SoftwareInstallIncomplete` marker.

### `macos.keychain`

**Reads.** Apple keychains of the classic `kych` generation — `login.keychain-db`, `System.keychain` and any `*.keychain` — selected by that magic rather than by name. A keychain is an **encrypted store with a cleartext index**: each item's secret is wrapped under the database's master key, and each item's attributes are not. The file's own relational schema is read first, because it declares every relation and every attribute of every relation with its storage format, and each record is then decoded against that declaration rather than against a hard-coded table.

**Produces.** One `KeychainItem` per password, key or certificate record, carrying the service, the account, the label, the description, the comment, the creator code and the creation and modification dates — all in the clear — with the format the file itself declared for each value. A certificate's bytes are carried out as their own `FileEntry` artifact, because a certificate in a keychain is not encrypted and can be hashed, identified and exported. A `KeychainStatus` row carries the relation inventory, the counts, and the parameters a lawful password-recovery attempt needs: the PBKDF2 salt, the initialisation vector, the iteration count the format fixes and the offset of the wrapped master key.

**Cannot.** **It cannot show a secret.** Every wrapped item is reported locked, with the sentence that an absent password is not evidence the item held none. Decryption needs the keychain password, or `/var/db/SystemKey` for the system keychain. A password supplied as the `macos_keychain_password` credential is checked against the file's `DbBlob` (PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1 then 3DES-CBC, graded on two real keychains with published passwords, `VALIDATION.md` `KEYCHAIN-1`) and the status row says whether it opened; the master key is zeroed and written nowhere. A `/var/db/SystemKey` supplied as the `macos_system_key` credential (its 48 bytes as hex) opens `System.keychain` the same way with no key derivation: bytes 8 to 32 are the 3DES key that unwraps the `DbBlob`. That is graded on one real macOS 11.2.1 `System.keychain` with its own `SystemKey`, against an independent unwrap and chainbreaker (`VALIDATION.md` `KEYCHAIN-3`). With the password or SystemKey accepted, each `ssgp` password item is matched to its symmetric key record by label, its item key unwrapped under the master key and its secret decrypted; that is graded on one real macOS-made keychain with a published answer, four items of four (`VALIDATION.md` `KEYCHAIN-2`). A secret that decrypts is marked `secret_state: withheld` with its length and is written to no record, export or index; it is released one record at a time by `POST /api/v1/cases/{case}/keychain/{item}/reveal` with the keychain password in the body (used for that request and kept nowhere), which re-reads the keychain file, decrypts that one item, writes `macos_keychain_secret_revealed` to the audit log before the value leaves the process, and refuses (audited as `macos_keychain_reveal_refused`) on a wrong password; the Inspector has a password field, a credential list that switches it to a `SystemKey` as hex, and a button for it. `ssgp` password items and private keys (PKCS#8, graded as a valid RSA-2048 key by an independent parser) are decrypted; the symmetric keys that wrap the passwords stay locked, the format is graded on one keychain from one macOS version. It cannot resolve an account number to a name, and it cannot tell you what an item's secret was used for beyond what the item's own description and comment say.

**Refuses.** It refuses to guess a layout: a keychain declaring a version this reader has not been shown is refused outright rather than parsed at nearby offsets. It refuses to sort a relation's attributes by their identifiers, because the password relations number theirs by four-character code and a sorted read puts an account where a date belongs while still producing legible output. It refuses to report an attribute the record does not carry as an empty string — an item with no comment has no comment. And where a table's own record count disagrees with the number of live records found, it refuses to resolve the disagreement silently: it is reported and the items carry the caveat.

### `macos.keychain_data_protection`

**Reads.** `keychain-2.db` — the iOS-style data-protection keychain, which macOS keeps under `~/Library/Keychains/<UUID>/` alongside the classic one. Selected by name and then by the presence of the `genp` table, so a database that merely shares the name is passed over. Its item tables (`genp`, `inet`, `cert`, `keys`), its schema version, and `ckdevicestate` are read; every column is looked up by name and an absent one is reported absent, so a schema from another OS version is read rather than refused. A `-wal` sibling is attached when the source can reach one, because uncheckpointed rows are rows.

**Produces.** One `KeychainItem` per item, carrying what this database actually states: the **access group** — which application or daemon owns the secret — the protection class decoded into words, the iCloud sync view, the creation and modification dates, the sync and tombstone flags and the item's UUID. One `ICloudKeychainDevice` per `ckdevicestate` row: every device the Apple ID's keychain circle has held, with its OS and build, its Secure Object Sync circle status, its Octagon peer id and status, its key state and its current top-level keys, per CloudKit zone. And a `KeychainStatus` row with the item census by kind, by access group and by protection class, the number in the `ThisDeviceOnly` classes (never synced to iCloud Keychain; an `aku`, `cku` or `dku` item is present in an encrypted backup but wrapped under a key derived from the device's hardware UID, so it can be restored only to the same device, while an `akpu` item is not backed up at all and is unreadable once the passcode is removed; each item's note says which), the number that sync, the tombstones, and the bound below.

**Cannot.** **It cannot name an account or a service, and does not pretend to.** Every `acct`, `svce`, `srvr`, `path`, `atyp` and `sdmn` value in this database is a SHA-1 of the attribute — 128 of 128 generic items and 158 of 158 internet items on the one real file measured, with no exceptions — so the value each names is not recoverable from the file. Those hashes are emitted under names ending `_sha1` precisely so nothing downstream can render one where an examiner reads a username. It cannot decrypt a single secret either, and here there is no password that would: each item's payload is wrapped under a class key from the device keybag, which is protected by hardware an image does not carry. Unlike the classic keychain, nothing about this file becomes readable with a password. It also cannot read a certificate: in this database even the `cert` table's subject, issuer and serial are hashed and its data is a wrapped blob, not the DER the classic keychain holds.

**Refuses.** It refuses to report a hash as a value, which is the whole shape of this reader. It refuses to map a protection class it does not recognise onto a nearby one, reporting the code the file holds instead. It refuses to invent a column a schema has not got. And it refuses to read a `-wal` or `-shm` sibling as the database: claiming to have read an account's credentials out of a write-ahead log would be worse than declining.

### `macos.knowledgec`

**Reads.** CoreDuet's `knowledgeC.db` — on macOS at `~/Library/Application Support/Knowledge/knowledgeC.db` and `/private/var/db/CoreDuet/Knowledge/knowledgeC.db`, and on iOS the same file — and the module does not care which. It subscribes to `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, selects by the final path component of `name`, lower-cased, being exactly `knowledgec.db`, and passes over an artifact with no data source. The source is read through `read_capped` up to 536,870,912 bytes and spilled by `TempDb::spill` to `seance_knowledgec_<uuid>.db`, with a `-wal` sibling staged whole beside it when the header says WAL mode and the source can open one; the staged file must begin `SQLite format 3\0`. The database is opened read-only, `sqlite_master` is probed for a table or view named `ZOBJECT`, and one statement is run: `SELECT ZSTREAMNAME, ZVALUESTRING, ZSTARTDATE, ZENDDATE, ZVALUEINTEGER FROM ZOBJECT ORDER BY ZSTARTDATE DESC LIMIT 500001` — five columns named outright, with no probe of the column set first, so a `ZOBJECT` lacking any one of them fails the statement. The walk is newest-first and admits 500,000 rows through a `CapCounter`, the 500,001st row being the probe that proves the table held more. `ZSTARTDATE` and `ZENDDATE` are REAL `CFAbsoluteTime` values converted by `cfabsolute_to_unix_parts` — whole seconds floored, 978,307,200 added, fraction kept to the nanosecond — and a duration is `ZENDDATE − ZSTARTDATE` truncated to whole seconds when both are present and the end is not before the start. Nothing else in the database is read: not `ZSTRUCTUREDMETADATA`, not `ZSOURCE`, not `ZOBJECT`'s `ZUUID`, `ZCREATIONDATE`, `ZSECONDSFROMGMT`, `ZVALUEDOUBLE` or `ZVALUECLASS`, and no other table.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per admitted row, `type` `Activity`, `subtype` `knowledgec`, parented to the file entry, carrying `stream` (`ZSTREAMNAME`, for instance `/app/usage`, `/app/inFocus`, `/display/isBacklit`, `/device/isLocked`), `value` (`ZVALUESTRING`), `value_integer`, `start` and `end` as Unix whole seconds, `duration_seconds`, and — only where the fraction was non-zero — `start_ns` and `end_ns`, plus `start_rfc3339` and `end_rfc3339` with the fraction rendered; each is JSON `null` where the column was NULL or the value would not convert. The `name` is `<stream>: <value> for <duration>s`. Where the walk hit the cap it appends one marker built by `seance_sqlite_util::cap_marker` with `type` `KnowledgeCParseStatus`, `subtype` `parse_incomplete`, `status` `CapReached`, `source_table` `ZOBJECT`, `max_entries` 500000, `rows_read`, `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason` `cap_reached`, and a `content_incomplete_detail` saying the oldest rows were the ones not extracted. Where the main file or WAL was not staged whole, every record is stamped by `TempDb::stamp_incompleteness` and one `SqliteSpillIncomplete` marker is appended. Where the open, the probe, the statement or a row read fails, the whole output is one `ParsedRecord`, `type` `KnowledgeCParseStatus`, `subtype` `parse_incomplete`, `status` `ParseFailed`, with the error text, `content_incomplete: true` / `unresolved_structure` and a `content_incomplete_detail` naming the file and the error. In the Records view the type `Activity` matches no named entry and no word rule, so the activity rows file under 'Other records'; the cap marker and the failure record match the `parsestatus` word rule and file under 'What could not be read'. Nothing is emitted to the timeline: no `TimelineEvent`, and `start` is not a key `seance_db` derives a timeline row from. The IOS-2 validation run in `documentation/VALIDATION.md` answered 'the app with the most screen time' by summing the `/app/inFocus` records' durations from an iOS 15 handset's copy of this file, which is the one real database this reader has been run against on the record.

**Cannot.** It cannot say which device an activity happened on. knowledgeC carries rows synchronised from a user's other devices, and the device is named through `ZOBJECT.ZSOURCE` and the `ZSOURCE` table — a join this module does not make — so every row reads as this machine's. It cannot give an activity a local time: `ZSECONDSFROMGMT` is not read, so every timestamp is UTC with no record of the zone the device was in. It cannot decode anything held in `ZSTRUCTUREDMETADATA`, which the statement never joins: a stream whose content is stored there rather than in `ZVALUESTRING` yields a record with the stream name, the times, and whatever `ZVALUESTRING` and `ZVALUEINTEGER` held, which may be nothing — a record that something happened and not of what. It reports the stream name as the file spells it and interprets none of them: the record does not say that `/app/usage` is foreground time, that `/device/isLocked` with `value_integer` 1 is a lock, or that `/display/isBacklit` 0 is the screen going dark; that reading is the examiner's. It cannot survive a column it did not expect: the five column names are fixed in the statement, so a `ZOBJECT` without any one of them — or a database that merely shares the file name — is reported as a single `ParseFailed` record, and a database whose `ZOBJECT` is absent is passed over in silence. It cannot recover the rows past the cap: 500,000 newest rows are kept, the oldest are dropped, and rows whose `ZSTARTDATE` is NULL sort last in `DESC` order and so are the first to go. It cannot recover a deleted row or a freelist page, and it reads the WAL only when the source can hand it a sibling. Its duration is whole seconds, truncated, so a 0.9-second focus event has `duration_seconds: 0`, and an end before its start yields no duration at all rather than a negative one. A database over 536,870,912 bytes is opened as its prefix and every record is stamped `cap_reached`. The unit tests run against tables the tests build with the five columns and nothing else; the schema has never been graded against Apple's own DDL the way the Mail reader's has.

**Refuses.** It refuses to file a failed catalogue read as an empty history: a `ZOBJECT` the catalogue cannot be asked about is `schema unreadable` and a `ParseFailed` record, not 'this device recorded no activity'. It refuses to report a truncated walk as a complete one — the `LIMIT` is the cap plus one, and the probe row's arrival is what writes the `CapReached` marker, because a query returning exactly 500,000 rows looks the same whether the table held 500,000 or ten million. It refuses to invent a negative duration, and it refuses to move a pre-2001 activity later by casting: the whole seconds are floored, and a NaN, infinite or out-of-range date yields no `start` rather than a fabricated one. It refuses to replay a partial write-ahead log: a `-wal` it cannot take whole is declined and named in `wal_incomplete_reason`. It refuses to read anything but a file named `knowledgeC.db`, so a renamed copy is not read and a `-wal` sibling is not mistaken for the database. It never writes to evidence: the open is read-only and the rollback journal is not staged. The only `ModuleError` it returns is `ParsingError` (`spill failed: …`), an `error` row in the processing log; every other failure travels as an `Ok` list holding the `ParseFailed` record, and every decline — wrong name, no data source, not SQLite, no `ZOBJECT` — is an empty list folded into the artifact's `ran and produced nothing` row. It refuses to file its own statements about what it could not read with the rows they qualify: the cap marker and the failure record carry `type` `KnowledgeCParseStatus`, not the rows' `Activity`, as `cap_marker`'s documented contract requires.

### `macos.launchd_persistence`

**Reads.** Every property list on the disk, and it decides afterwards which ones are launchd jobs. It subscribes to `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess` and takes any artifact whose `name`'s final path component, lower-cased, ends `.plist` — a `.plist` in `/Library/LaunchDaemons`, one in a user's `Library/Preferences`, one inside an application bundle, all alike — and passes over one with no data source. `Staged::read` reads up to 67,108,864 bytes (raised from 4,194,304) from offset 0 through `read_full`, recording the declared size, the bytes delivered and whether the cap cut the read. The bytes go to `plist::from_bytes` (XML or binary); the value must be a dictionary; and the dictionary must carry a `Label` that is a string and at least one of the keys `Program` or `ProgramArguments`, of any type — that pair is the whole of the self-selection, the path playing no part in it. From a job it then reads `Program` as a string, `ProgramArguments`, `WatchPaths` and `QueueDirectories` as arrays keeping only their string members, `RunAtLoad` and `Disabled` as booleans, `StartInterval` as a signed integer, whether `StartCalendarInterval` is present at all, and `KeepAlive` as a boolean or, when it is anything else, the word `conditional`. The domain is classified from the artifact's `path` metadata, or `parent_path` where there is no `path`, lower-cased: a path containing `launchdaemons` is `system_daemon_apple` when it also contains `/system/library/` and `system_daemon` otherwise; one containing `launchagents` is `agent_apple` under `/system/library/`, `user_agent` when it contains `/users/`, and `system_agent` otherwise; anything else, including no path at all, is `unknown`. No other key of the job — `UserName`, `GroupName`, `EnvironmentVariables`, `MachServices`, `Sockets`, `LaunchEvents`, `StandardOutPath`, `LimitLoadToSessionType`, `AssociatedBundleIdentifiers` — is read, and the schedule inside `StartCalendarInterval` is not decoded.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per job plist, `type` `Persistence`, `subtype` `launchd`, `mechanism` `launchd`, parented to the plist's file entry, carrying `label`, `domain`, `program`, `program_arguments`, `run_at_load`, `start_interval_seconds`, `start_calendar_interval` (a boolean saying only that the key exists), `watch_paths`, `queue_directories`, `keep_alive` (true, false, the string `conditional`, or null), `disabled`, and `plist_path` — the path it classified from, or an empty string. Each key is JSON `null` where the plist did not carry it or carried it in a type the reader does not take. The `name` is one sentence, `launchd: <label> runs <target> <trigger>`, where the target is `Program`, else the first `ProgramArguments` element, else `(no program)`, and the trigger is the first of these that applies, in this order: `at load (login/boot)` when `RunAtLoad` is true; `every <n>s` when `StartInterval` is set; `on a calendar schedule`; `when watched paths change`; `kept alive` when `KeepAlive` is present in any form; else `on demand`. Where the plist was not staged whole the record is stamped `content_incomplete` with `cap_reached` or `short_read` and the byte counts. Where the plist was not staged whole **and** could not be ruled in or out — because the prefix would not parse, was not a dictionary, or lacked the `Label`-and-program pair — it produces instead one marker, `type` `PersistenceIncomplete`, `subtype` `parse_incomplete`, `status` `NotStagedInFull`, `bytes_staged`, `bytes_declared`, and a detail ending `so whether it declares a launchd job could not be determined` — unless the artifact's recorded path is outside every `LaunchAgents`/`LaunchDaemons` directory (domain `unknown` from a non-empty path), where it produces nothing; with no path at all the marker stays. A whole plist that is not a job produces nothing. No `TimelineEvent` is emitted; the file's own MAC times are on its file entry, not here. The Records view files `Persistence` under 'The device' by word rule and `PersistenceIncomplete` under 'What could not be read'.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell you whether the job was loaded, enabled, or ever ran. The record is a reading of the plist and nothing else: it consults no other file — launchd's own override database of disabled jobs included — so a job whose plist says nothing about `Disabled` but which the user disabled with `launchctl` reads as enabled, and a `Disabled: true` in the plist that an override re-enabled reads as disabled. It does not check that the program exists on the volume, what it is, whether it is signed, or what it hashes to, and it emits no `Finding`: a `Persistence` record for `/tmp/evil` and one for `/usr/sbin/periodic` are the same shape, and separating them is the examiner's work or another module's. It does not read the other persistence stores at all — `BackgroundItems-v*.btm`, login items, cron tabs, `/etc/periodic`, emond, kernel and system extensions — which `documentation/MACOS_DESIGN.md` lists as open. It names one trigger where a job may carry several: the sentence takes the first that applies, so a job with both `RunAtLoad` and a `StartInterval` is described as `at load` and the interval is on the record but not in the sentence, and `StartCalendarInterval`'s hours, minutes and weekdays are never decoded. Its domain is a substring test on the path: a job anywhere else — an app bundle's `Contents/Library/LaunchServices`, a `/private/var` location, a plist carved from unallocated space, or one expanded out of an archive whose entries carry no `path` — is `unknown`, and any `LaunchAgents` path containing `/users/` is a user agent whatever it actually is. A plist outside every launchd directory that was staged short — over 67,108,864 bytes, or delivered short — and whose prefix does not show a job is passed over without a marker, so a job plist planted outside those directories and padded past the cap is not reported; one inside them, or with no recorded path, still leaves the marker. It keeps only the string members of `ProgramArguments`, so an argument stored as an integer or a nested array is dropped from the list without a count. Its tests are XML plists written by the tests, plus one that reads the Magnet 2021 macOS image's `/System/Library/LaunchDaemons` (every plist a `Persistence` record or nothing, no marker) where that gitignored corpus is present; no CTF validation row in `documentation/VALIDATION.md` graded a launchd answer.

**Refuses.** It refuses to rule a plist in or out from bytes it never saw. A `.plist` in a launchd directory, or with no recorded path, staged short — over the 67,108,864-byte cap, or delivered short — whose prefix will not parse, is not a dictionary, or lacks the label-and-program pair is not silently dropped: it leaves the `PersistenceIncomplete` marker, because silence would state that the file declared no autostart, the one answer nothing in the bytes supports. It refuses to select by path: a job plist copied to a Desktop, a Trash, a backup or an archive is reported as a job, because the plist is the evidence and the directory is only where it was found; the directory contributes the `domain` and nothing else. It refuses to read a plist that names a `Label` but nothing to run as persistence, and a plist with something to run but no string `Label` likewise. It refuses to guess the shape of `KeepAlive`: a dictionary of conditions is reported as `conditional`, not as `true`. It never returns a `ModuleError`: every outcome is an `Ok` list, so nothing it does produces an `error` row in the processing log. Its declines — not a `.plist`, no data source, a whole plist that is not a job or not a plist at all — are empty lists folded into the artifact's `ran and produced nothing` row, where a preference file and a job plist that failed the pair test look the same.

### `macos.notifications`

**Reads.** The Notification Center store `usernoted` keeps at `~/Library/Group Containers/group.com.apple.usernoted/db2/db`. It subscribes to `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess` and selects by name and path: an artifact whose `name`'s final component, lower-cased, contains `usernoted` is taken whatever its path; one whose final component is exactly `db` is taken when its `path` metadata (else `parent_path`), lower-cased, contains `usernoted`; where it has neither, its first 16 bytes are read through `read_full` and it is taken only if they are `SQLite format 3\0`, so a bare `db` from a source that stamps no path is read without spilling every such file. An artifact with no data source is passed over. The source is read through `read_capped` up to 536,870,912 bytes, spilled by `TempDb::spill` to `seance_usernoted_<uuid>.db` with a `-wal` sibling staged whole beside it when the header says WAL mode and the source can open one, and must begin `SQLite format 3\0`. Opened read-only, the catalogue is probed for both a `record` and an `app` table or view, and both must be present. `PRAGMA table_info(record)` is read — case-sensitively, unlike the quarantine reader's lower-cased probe — to choose the delivery column: `record.delivered_date` if present, else `record.date`, else the literal `NULL`. One statement then runs with no row limit: `SELECT app.identifier, <delivered>, record.data FROM record LEFT JOIN app ON record.app_id = app.app_id ORDER BY <delivered> DESC`.
