The delivery time is a REAL `CFAbsoluteTime` converted by `cfabsolute_to_unix_parts` with the fraction kept. Each `record.data` blob is parsed by `plist::from_bytes` and walked recursively to depth 16 — dictionaries and arrays — for the first dictionary carrying a `titl` or `body` key, taking `titl`, `body` and `subt` from it when their values are strings — or, where the blob is an `NSKeyedArchiver` archive, `UID` references that name a string in `$objects` (a reference to `$null` is an absent value); the walk stops as soon as both a title and a body are held. No other column of `record` is read — not `uuid`, `request_date`, `request_last_date`, `presented`, `style` or `snooze_fire_date` — and no other key of the blob is looked at.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per `record` row, `type` `Notification`, `subtype` `usernoted`, parented to the database's file entry, carrying `app_bundle_id` (`app.identifier`, null where the join found no app), `title`, `body` and `subtitle` — each null where the blob was absent, would not parse as a plist, held no dictionary with those keys, or held them as something that is not text — and says which: an absent blob carries `content_note` (`the record carries no data blob…`); a blob that will not parse carries `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason` `unresolved_structure` and a detail giving its length and that it did not parse; a key present whose value is not text and not a `UID` naming a string carries the same pair with a detail naming the keys (`titl`, `body`, `subt`). A blob that parses and has no such keys carries neither. Where the delivery time converted, `timestamp` (Unix seconds), `timestamp_ns` when the fraction was non-zero, and `timestamp_rfc3339` with the fraction rendered. The `name` is `Notification from <bundle id, else (unknown app)>: <title, else body, else (no content decoded)>`. There is no row cap: a store of a million rows is a million records. Where the main file or WAL was not staged whole every record is stamped by `TempDb::stamp_incompleteness` and one `SqliteSpillIncomplete` marker is appended. Where the open, either probe, the pragma, the statement or a row read fails, the output is one `ParsedRecord`, `type` `NotificationParseStatus`, `subtype` `parse_incomplete`, `status` `ParseFailed`, with the error, `content_incomplete: true` / `unresolved_structure` and a `content_incomplete_detail` — a type of its own, which the Records view files under 'What could not be read'; `Notification` itself matches no category rule there and lands in 'Other records'. No `TimelineEvent` is emitted and no timeline row is derived from these records.

**Cannot.** It cannot find a title or body nested deeper than sixteen levels in the blob: those yield `null` with no flag, as does a blob whose text sits under keys other than `titl`, `body` and `subt`. It cannot say whether a notification was ever shown: `record.presented` is not read, so a row delivered to the store and dismissed unseen, one shown as a banner, and one still sitting in Notification Center are the same record. It cannot give the request time, only the delivery time, and where the schema has neither `delivered_date` nor `date` every record is undated and unordered. It cannot name the sender of a message notification: no key of the blob beyond `titl`, `body` and `subt` is read, so an iMessage alert yields the app bundle id and the text and not the handle it came from — unless the sending app put it in the title, in which case it is there as text with no field of its own. It cannot bound itself: there is no row cap and no per-blob size cap beyond the 536,870,912 bytes the whole database is staged under, and a database over that is opened as its prefix with every record stamped `cap_reached`. It reads only live rows through SQLite — no freelist, no unallocated pages — and takes the `-wal` only when the source can hand it a sibling. Its name gate is strict: a file named `db` under a path not containing `usernoted` is never looked at, a pathless `db` that is any SQLite database is still spilled and probed for `record` and `app`, and a copy renamed to anything not containing `usernoted` is missed. Its tests build the two-table schema themselves and write `req` dictionaries with `plist::to_writer_binary`, and one reads plaso's `mac_notificationcenter.db` (six real records, every title and body decoded) where that gitignored reference tree is present; no real store is in `test_data/`, and no validation row in `documentation/VALIDATION.md` graded a notification answer.

**Refuses.** It refuses to file a catalogue that would not answer as a store with no notifications: an `Undetermined` probe of either table bails into the `ParseFailed` record rather than into an empty list, and a store with a `record` table but no `app` table — or the reverse — is declined as not this database rather than half-read. It refuses to fail a store over one blob: a `data` value that will not parse produces a record with null content, stamped as unread, not a parse failure, because the app and the delivery time are still evidence. It refuses to substitute a wrong column for the delivery time: where neither `delivered_date` nor `date` exists the time is `NULL`, never `request_date` or another column that means something else. It refuses to move a pre-2001 delivery later by truncation, and refuses to render a non-finite or out-of-range time. It refuses a `-wal` it cannot take whole, naming the reason, and never writes to evidence. The only `ModuleError` it returns is `ParsingError` (`spill failed: …`); everything else is an `Ok` list, so a store that would not parse is a `ParseFailed` record in the artifact tree and never an `error` row, and every decline — name and path not matching, no data source, not SQLite, a table absent — is an empty list folded into the `ran and produced nothing` row.

### `macos.openbsm`

**Reads.** OpenBSM audit trails — `/var/audit/<start>.<end>`, the `.not_terminated` trail still being written, and the `.crash_recovery` ones `auditd` leaves behind — selected by **content**, so a trail carved out of free space or renamed is still read. A trail is a flat sequence of records and a record is a sequence of length-prefixed tokens; two independent facts bracket every one, because the header token states the record's byte count and the trailer token repeats it behind the magic `0xB105`. Each record's tokens are walked and must tile exactly into the space between the two.

**Produces.** One `AuditEvent` per record carrying the event identifier and its symbolic name, the audit class, the time, whether the system said yes or no, the account by number (audit, effective and real), the process, the audit session, the terminal port, the remote address and — on Darwin — the code-signing identity of the binary that asked, with its cdhash. A refused **credential** attempt additionally produces a `FailedLogin`, the same record type a Linux `btmp` produces, so 'was there a brute force' is one screen on both platforms. An `AuditTrailStatus` row carries the event histogram, the counts and every shortfall.

**Cannot.** It cannot give you a session. BSM records events, and a loginwindow login and the logout that ended it are written by different processes, so pairing them would be inference dressed as a record: no duration is reported and the status row says why. It cannot name an account: the trail identifies one by number, and the daemon's own message — `invalid password for user eliflatt` — is quoted verbatim as the text token it is rather than parsed into a username, because its wording is specified nowhere. It cannot name an event outside its shipped table of login, authentication and administration identifiers; such a record is reported by number with its class, which is what decides whether it is a login record, marked unknown. Where one number carries two names in Apple's own table, it cannot say which was meant and shows both.

**Refuses.** It refuses to resynchronise. A trail whose records stop tiling stops being read and the remaining bytes are reported as a count with the reason, because scanning forward for the next plausible header would turn a fragment of some other file into a set of confident audit records. It refuses to report an outcome for a record that carries no return token — silence about an outcome is not success, and such a record is not evidence of a failure either. And it refuses to call a refused Security Server *authorization* a failed login: those fail routinely on a machine nobody attacked, they are counted under their own name, and filing them as login attempts would bury the ones that were real.

### `macos.quarantine`

**Reads.** The LaunchServices download-quarantine database, `com.apple.LaunchServices.QuarantineEventsV2`, kept per user under `~/Library/Preferences/`. It subscribes to `FileEntry` artifacts with `InputCapability::RandomAccess` and selects by name alone: the final path component of the artifact's `name` metadata, lower-cased, must contain `quarantineeventsv2`, so a renamed copy matches and so do a `-wal` or `-journal` sibling. An artifact with no data source is passed over in silence. The source is read through `read_capped` up to 536,870,912 bytes and spilled by `seance_sqlite_util::TempDb::spill` to `seance_quarantine_<uuid>.db` in the system temp directory, removed on drop; when the database's own header byte 18 says it is in WAL mode and the source can open a `-wal` sibling, that sibling is staged beside it — whole, up to 536,870,912 bytes — so committed-but-uncheckpointed rows are seen. The staged file must begin `SQLite format 3\0` or the module returns nothing. The database is opened read-only (`SQLITE_OPEN_READ_ONLY | SQLITE_OPEN_NO_MUTEX`), `sqlite_master` is asked whether a table or view named `LSQuarantineEvent` exists, and `PRAGMA table_info(LSQuarantineEvent)` gives the column set, lower-cased. Eight columns are then selected by name where the table has them and as the literal `NULL` where it does not: `LSQuarantineEventIdentifier`, `LSQuarantineTimeStamp`, `LSQuarantineAgentName`, `LSQuarantineAgentBundleIdentifier`, `LSQuarantineDataURLString`, `LSQuarantineOriginURLString`, `LSQuarantineSenderName` and `LSQuarantineSenderAddress`, ordered by `LSQuarantineTimeStamp DESC` when that column exists and unordered otherwise, with no row limit. The timestamp is a REAL `CFAbsoluteTime` — seconds since 2001-01-01 UTC — converted by `cfabsolute_to_unix_parts`, which floors the whole seconds, adds 978,307,200, keeps the fraction to the nanosecond, and yields nothing for a NaN, infinite or out-of-range value. No other column of the table is read: `LSQuarantineTypeNumber`, `LSQuarantineOriginTitle` and `LSQuarantineOriginAlias` are not selected, and no other table is opened.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per row, `type` `Download`, `subtype` `quarantine`, parented to the database's file entry, carrying `event_identifier`, `agent_name`, `agent_bundle_id`, `data_url`, `origin_url`, `sender_name` and `sender_address` exactly as the row holds them — JSON `null` where the column was NULL or where the schema lacked the column — and, where the timestamp converted, `timestamp` as Unix whole seconds, `timestamp_ns` as Unix nanoseconds only when the fraction was non-zero, and `timestamp_rfc3339` with the fraction rendered. Where the table lacked any of the eight columns, every record also carries `schema_absent_columns`, the list of those names, so a null read from a column this macOS never had is not read as a value recorded empty. The `name` an examiner sees is `Downloaded via <agent>: <data URL, else origin URL, else (unknown source)>`. Where the main file or its WAL was not staged whole, `TempDb::stamp_incompleteness` adds `content_incomplete: true` with `content_incomplete_reason` (`cap_reached` or `short_read`) and/or `wal_incomplete_reason` to every record and appends one `SqliteSpillIncomplete` marker, `subtype` `parse_incomplete`, `status` `DatabaseNotStagedInFull`, with `records_recovered`. Where the open, the catalogue probe, the column probe, the statement or a row read fails, it produces exactly one `ParsedRecord` in place of everything: `type` `Download`, `subtype` `quarantine`, `status` `ParseFailed`, the error text, `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason` `unresolved_structure`. Because that failure record carries the same `type` as the data, the Records view's word rules file it under Activity beside the downloads rather than under 'What could not be read'. No `TimelineEvent` is emitted and no timeline row is derived — `seance_db` derives timeline rows only from `TimelineEvent` artifacts, `chat_message` records and file entries — so a download's time is on its record and on no timeline.

**Cannot.** **It cannot name the file that was downloaded.** `LSQuarantineEvent` records the download, not the destination: no path, no filename and no size are in the eight columns, and the link from an event to a file on disk is the `com.apple.quarantine` extended attribute each file carries, whose value names the event UUID — which this module does not read and does not correlate with the `event_identifier` it publishes. An examiner holding a `Download` record and a file must join the two by UUID themselves, through whatever the file-system parser recorded of that attribute. It cannot say the history is complete: a row absent from the table is the absence of a row, not evidence that a download did not happen, and the module makes no claim either way. It cannot read the older database whose name lacks `V2`, because the gate requires `quarantineeventsv2`, nor the per-file attribute's own fields. It cannot recover a deleted row: it reads live rows through SQLite and nothing else; freelist and unallocated-page recovery is the generic SQLite parser's work, and the WAL is staged only when the source can reach a sibling — a bare byte buffer, or a source that cannot enumerate neighbours, parses without it and, where the header said WAL mode and the source could not be asked, carries `wal_incomplete_reason` `wal_not_reachable`. It publishes `sender_name` and `sender_address` verbatim with no interpretation, and `LSQuarantineTypeNumber` — the one column that says which kind of transfer a row was — is not read, so a web download, a mail attachment and an AirDrop transfer are told apart only by what their agent and URL columns happen to hold. It applies no row cap and no per-row error tolerance: one undecodable row fails the statement and the whole database becomes the single `ParseFailed` record above, so a database of ten thousand downloads with one corrupt row yields none of them. A file over 536,870,912 bytes is opened as its prefix and every record is stamped `cap_reached`. It cannot distinguish a database whose `LSQuarantineEvent` is absent from a file that is not the quarantine database: both return nothing, and neither leaves a record. It cannot place a download in local time: every timestamp is UTC as the column stores it, and nothing here reads the machine's zone. Its tests run only against databases the tests themselves build with the documented eight-column schema and its subsets; no real `QuarantineEventsV2` is in `test_data/`, and none of the CTF validation runs in `documentation/VALIDATION.md` graded a quarantine answer.

**Refuses.** It refuses to answer a failed schema query as a finding. `probe_table` is three-valued: an `LSQuarantineEvent` the catalogue lists is read, one the catalogue says is absent returns nothing, and a catalogue that would not answer — a damaged page 1 — bails with `schema catalogue unreadable` into the `ParseFailed` record, because reading `SQLITE_CORRUPT` as 'no such table' would manufacture 'this user downloaded nothing' out of a read error. It refuses to substitute NULL for a column it could not list: `probe_columns` returning an error is a failure, not an absence, so a download URL is never silently replaced by NULL and presented as complete. It refuses a table wearing the name with none of the provenance columns — timestamp, agent name, agent bundle id, data URL and origin URL all absent — and reports that as a failure naming the missing columns rather than emitting rows of nulls. It refuses to stamp a schema absence as a recorded blank, which is what `schema_absent_columns` is for. It refuses to move a pre-2001 timestamp later by truncation: the whole seconds are floored, and a non-finite or out-of-range value yields no timestamp rather than a date at the end of time. It refuses a `-wal` sibling it cannot take whole — one over 536,870,912 bytes or one delivered short — and says so with `wal_incomplete_reason` instead of replaying a prefix of the log as if it were all of it. It never writes to evidence: the connection is read-only and the rollback journal is deliberately not staged, because a hot journal makes a read-only open fail and its pre-images are the forensic SQLite parser's business. It refuses to fail the ingest: the only `ModuleError` it can return is `ParsingError` (`spill failed: …`) when the temp file cannot be written, an `error` row in the processing log; every parse failure is an `Ok` list holding the failure record. And it refuses to speak about a file it did not claim: a non-matching name, a missing data source, a non-SQLite file with the right name, and a SQLite file without the table all return an empty list, folded into the artifact's `ran and produced nothing` row with nothing to distinguish them.

### `macos.spotlight_store`

**Reads.** A Spotlight version-2 metadata store — `.Spotlight-V100/Store-V2/<UUID>/store.db` — selected by its own `8tsd` magic and never by its name, because `store.db` is one of the most-reused file names on a disk. The first 512 MB are staged. The header gives the flags, the 4,096-byte page granularity the blocks are laid out at, the 16 KiB block size and the five chain heads at offset 0x30. Blocks are found by scanning every page for the `2pbd` tag rather than by following those chains, because the chains reach only the structured kinds — twelve of the 86 blocks in the larger of the two stores measured — and the `2mbd` block on page 1, which lists the item blocks, is then read as a **second, independent statement** of that population: on both corpus stores the scan and the map name the same pages, and where they disagree the pages are named. It reads the property table (`0x11`) — an id, a property type, a value type and a name; the category table (`0x21`) — an id and a string; **two** `0x81` tables, which are separate namespaces told apart only by which chain reaches them, one mapping an id to a list of category ids and the other to the same label once per language; and the item blocks (`0x09`, `0x4009`), which are **zlib streams beginning at block offset 20** with the uncompressed length at offset 16 counting those twenty bytes. Inside an inflated block the records are a little-endian `u32` byte count then that many bytes, opening with the item id, a flag byte, one number whose meaning is not established, the parent item's id, and the time the index wrote the record in microseconds since the Unix epoch. Then the attribute stream: pairs of a delta added to a running property id and a value whose shape comes from the type that id declares. Every number in the format is big-endian behind a leading-ones length byte, which is what makes sibling item ids come out consecutive; a little-endian reading of the same bytes yields plausible nonsense.

**Produces.** One `SpotlightItem` per indexed file or folder — 14,934 from the larger corpus store — carrying what Spotlight recorded about it: the file name, the display name, the content type and its whole type tree resolved against this store's own tables, the localised kind, the logical and physical sizes, the owning uid and gid, where a download came from, the creation, modification, added and last-used dates, the use count, the bundle identifier and version, and **every other attribute the record holds under its own `kMDItem…` name**. Each item also carries a path assembled from the parent chain, with a flag saying whether that chain reaches a root this store holds. One `SpotlightStore` record per store with the header's figures, the block census by declared kind, the map-against-scan agreement, the item census and every shortfall. One `SpotlightProperty` per named attribute the index held and one `SpotlightContentType` per content type it knew about. A `SpotlightStoreStatus` row where a file inside a Spotlight store directory would not read at all. Every record names the store it came from.

**Cannot.** **It cannot say that an item is a file that exists.** Spotlight indexes files that have since been deleted, which is much of why the store is worth reading, so an item is a record of what the index knew and not of what is on the volume now — and the reverse holds: a file absent from the store is not a file Spotlight never indexed. It cannot assemble a path for an item whose parent chain leaves this store: a volume's index is split across stores, 967 of the larger store's items name a parent it does not hold, and those are reported without an absolute path rather than with a partial one dressed as absolute. It cannot tell you which of two records for one item id is current without their index times — four ids in that store carry two records each, the older a stub — so both are emitted with their own times. It cannot compare an id between stores: the two on one machine hold 44 property ids in common that carry different values, because the tables are built up per volume as Spotlight meets things. It cannot interpret four things it reads: the record's flag byte, the number between the flags and the parent reference, the leading byte of each localised-label entry, and `value_type`'s bits other than `0x02` and `0x80` — each is published as what was seen rather than dropped. And it cannot vouch for the widest variable-size number form, `0xff` and eight bytes: the byte count is pinned, the value is not, it occurs once in the corpus, and a value read through it is emitted flagged rather than as a number. Its ceilings are 512 MB staged, 200,000 blocks, 100,000 property entries, 1,000,000 category entries, 5,000,000 item records, 64 MB per inflated block, 4,096 bytes per name and 32 sampled display labels, each recorded on the record when it fires.

**Refuses.** It refuses to read past a value it cannot decode. The attribute stream has no terminator and states no length to skip to, so one value read at the wrong width desynchronises every attribute after it — a record reaching a property type this reader has not established keeps what was read before that point, says which type stopped it, and reads nothing further. It refuses to read an item record against the next record's bytes for the same reason, and it publishes the bytes of each inflated block the record walk did not consume — zero on every block in the corpus — so a layout read wrongly shows up as a remainder rather than as fewer items. It refuses to merge the two `0x81` tables, which both number their entries from 1: merging them makes a folder's `kMDItemKind` read as a content-type list. It refuses to render a number it may have read wrongly as a date — an index time outside 2004 to 2100, or a `CFAbsoluteTime` outside 1970 to 2100, is reported as unusable rather than formatted — and it refuses to print a timestamp to nanoseconds when the `f64` behind it resolves to about a quarter of a microsecond. It refuses to report the widest number form as a parent id of 18,446,744,073,709,551,615: that is the file saying "no parent". It refuses to emit the category table's localised display names as content types — 3,703 localisation strings against 397 content types on the larger store — or to emit a localised value's thirty-one spellings as thirty-one observations about a file. It refuses to render a blob as lossy text, because a property list shown that way is a string nobody can check. It refuses to substitute Apple's own published attribute table for what the file says, because emitting a shipped constant as evidence is the worse error. It refuses to apply an entropy threshold to a payload too short to support one — entropy over 256 symbols is bounded by log2(n) — and it applies that threshold to one thing only: a block it does not decode, where it says whether the bytes look compressed or look like structure that was missed. And where a file inside a Spotlight store directory would not read, it refuses to stay silent: a store that could not be parsed must never render as a volume that was never indexed.

### `macos.tcc`

**Reads.** The macOS Transparency, Consent and Control database, `TCC.db`, and it selects one by name alone. It subscribes to `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, takes the artifact's `name`, keeps the final `/`- or `\`-separated component lowercased, and proceeds only when that is exactly `tcc.db`; an artifact with no attached data source is passed over in silence. It never looks at the path, so the system store under `/Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/` and each user's store under `~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/` are read identically and nothing on the record says which one a row came from. The bytes are staged through `seance_sqlite_util::TempDb::spill` with a 512 MiB ceiling (`MAX_DB_BYTES`): the source is read from offset zero up to that cap, written to `seance_tcc_<uuid>.db` in the temp directory, and where the source can open a `-wal` sibling that log is staged beside it so uncheckpointed rows are seen — whole or not at all, with its own 512 MiB cap — while a `-journal` is deliberately not staged. The spilled file must begin `SQLite format 3\0` or the module returns nothing. It opens the database read-only, asks `sqlite_master` whether a table or view named `access` exists, and then reads `PRAGMA table_info(access)` to learn the schema: the presence of an `auth_value` column selects the Big Sur (11+) reading, its absence the legacy `allowed` reading, and `last_modified` is read only where the column exists. One statement is run — `SELECT service, client, client_type, <auth_value|allowed>, <auth_reason|NULL>, <last_modified|NULL> FROM access` — with no `LIMIT`, no `ORDER BY` and no `WHERE`, and every row is decoded: `auth_value` 0/1/2/3 as `denied`/`unknown`/`allowed`/`limited` and anything else `other`; legacy `allowed` 1 as `allowed` and every other value as `denied`; `auth_reason` 1 through 12 as `error`, `user_consent`, `user_set`, `system_set`, `service_policy`, `mdm_policy`, `override_policy`, `missing_usage_string`, `prompt_timeout`, `preflight_unknown`, `entitled`, `app_type_policy`, anything else `unspecified`; `client_type` 0 as `bundle_id`, 1 as `absolute_path`, else `other`; and `last_modified` as whole Unix seconds. Those decodings are the published community tables, not an Apple specification, which is why the raw integer travels beside every label.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per `access` row, subtype `tcc`, parented to the database file, carrying `type: "Permission"`, `subtype: "tcc"`, `service`, `client` and `client_type` exactly as stored (each `null` where the column was NULL), `client_type_label` where the type was not NULL, `schema` (`auth_value` or `allowed`, naming which reading was applied), `auth_value` (the raw grant integer under both schemas — the legacy `allowed` value lands under this key too), `auth_value_label` where the value was not NULL, `granted` (a boolean that is `true` only for the labels `allowed` and `limited`, and `false` for `denied`, `unknown`, `other` and NULL), `auth_reason` with `auth_reason_label` where the modern column held a value, `timestamp` (Unix seconds) with `timestamp_rfc3339` where `last_modified` was present, and a `name` of the form `<client> granted <service>` or `<client> denied <service>`, with `(unknown client)` and `(unknown service)` standing in for NULLs. Where the spill was short — the file over the 512 MiB cap, the source delivering fewer bytes than it declared, or a WAL it could not take whole — every record gains `content_incomplete: true` with `content_incomplete_reason` (`cap_reached` or `short_read`) and/or `wal_incomplete_reason`, and one further `parse_incomplete` record of type `SqliteSpillIncomplete` is appended carrying `status: "DatabaseNotStagedInFull"`, `records_recovered` and a sentence. Where the open, the schema probe or the query fails, it emits exactly one `ParsedRecord` with `type: "Permission"`, `subtype: "tcc"`, `status: "ParseFailed"`, the error text, and `content_incomplete: true` with reason `unresolved_structure` — that record carries no `name` key and is not given the artifact-level subtype the row records get. It produces no `TimelineEvent`: the `timestamp` key sits on a `ParsedRecord`, and the timeline table is fed only by `TimelineEvent` artifacts, chat messages and file MAC times, so a TCC grant's date is visible on the record and absent from the case timeline. The Analysis screen files `Permission` records under the device category. A count of grants is written to the log at `info`.

**Cannot.** It cannot say which store a grant came from: the path is not on the record, so a per-user `TCC.db` and the system one differ only in their parent artifact. It cannot say what an automation grant was over — `kTCCServiceAppleEvents` rows name the target application in `indirect_object_identifier`, which is not selected — nor read `flags`, `auth_version`, `policy_id`, `pid`, `pid_version`, `boot_uuid`, `last_reminded` or `expired_at`, and it does not read the `csreq` code-signing requirement, so the `client` string is what TCC stored and nothing here verifies that a binary of that name is the one the user consented to. Under the legacy schema `prompt_count` is not read, and every `allowed` value other than 1 — including a NULL — is labelled `denied`. Under the modern schema an `auth_value` of 1 is labelled `unknown` yet renders in the record's `name` as `<client> denied <service>`, and so does a NULL grant, because the name's verb is chosen from `granted` alone; an examiner reading the name rather than the label is told a denial the row does not state. The `auth_reason` and `auth_value` tables are community decodings that vary between published sources, which is why the raw integers are kept; a value outside the table is `other` or `unspecified`, not an error. `last_modified` is read as whole Unix seconds with no sub-second part and no timezone question asked of it. It reads live rows through SQL only: a revoked or deleted grant that survives in a freelist page, in unallocated space or in a `-journal` pre-image is not recovered here — that is the generic forensic SQLite parser's job on the same file — and rows sitting only in a WAL the source cannot reach are missing with the stamp saying so, never silently. Its ceilings are 512 MiB for the database and 512 MiB for its WAL; a bigger database is parsed as a prefix, stamped `cap_reached`, and SQLite answers from whichever pages that prefix reaches, so the row set is a subset with no statement of which rows were lost. A file named `TCC.db` whose schema has no `access` table produces nothing at all — no record, no marker — and is indistinguishable in the case from a store that was never there. No real `TCC.db` from a Mac is in this tree; both schemas are pinned by databases the tests build themselves.

**Refuses.** It refuses every file whose basename is not `tcc.db`, and it refuses in silence: a file that passes the name test but does not begin with the SQLite header returns an empty list rather than a failure, because a file that was never a database is not a parse failure. A database whose catalogue can be read and has no `access` table is also declined in silence (`Presence::Absent`), while a catalogue that cannot be read at all (`Presence::Undetermined`) is a `ParseFailed` record with the SQLite error, because "the store did not have that table" and "the store could not be asked" are opposite findings. It refuses to present a partial spill as a whole one: a database over the cap, a short read, or a WAL that could not be staged whole stamps every emitted record and appends a `parse_incomplete` marker, so a store from which no rows were recovered still leaves a record that the file was there and was not read in full. It refuses to replay a WAL it holds only part of, because a prefix of the frames replays as an arbitrary earlier state with nothing to mark it. It refuses to hide the value it interpreted: every label is emitted beside its raw integer and a value its table does not know is carried as `other`/`unspecified` rather than dropped. It opens the spill read-only and never writes to evidence; the temp file and any `-wal`/`-shm` beside it are removed when the handle drops, on the error path as well as the success path. A `spill` that cannot write its temp file at all is the one case that returns a `ModuleError::ParsingError` instead of a record, and lands in the processing log rather than the artifact tree.

### `macos.unifiedlog`

**Reads.** An Apple Unified Log `.tracev3` file — the firehose store under `/var/db/diagnostics/` or a `.logarchive`. It subscribes to `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, passes over any artifact with no data source, and first reads 16 bytes at offset zero. It stages the file when either the lowercased basename ends `.tracev3` or the first four bytes, little-endian, are `0x1000` — the Header chunk tag. The stage is `Staged::read` with a 512 MiB ceiling. It then walks 16-byte chunk preambles — `tag: u32`, `sub_tag: u32`, `data_size: u64` — from offset zero, the first of which must be a Header, advancing by `16 + data_size` rounded to 8 bytes, and stops with a flag at 5,000,000 chunks, at a size that overflows or runs past the staged bytes, or at an end that does not advance. Inside the walk it reads two chunk kinds. A **Catalog** (`0x600b`): its UUID table, subsystem strings, process entries (pid, effective uid, main-binary and shared-cache UUIDs, subsystem/category pairs) and sub-chunk table, and it checks the catalog's own arithmetic — the process entries must end at the sub-chunk offset the header states and the sub-chunk table at the end of the chunk. A **Chunkset** (`0x600d`): its LZ4 `bv41` and raw `bv4-` blocks up to the `bv4$` marker, decompressed with `lz4_flex` under a 16 MiB ceiling per chunkset, and then the entries inside — firehose (`0x6001`), oversize (`0x6002`), statedump (`0x6003`), simpledump (`0x6004`) — each padded to 8 bytes of its own size; where the padded position holds no entry and the unpadded one does, the entry is taken and counted as unpadded (132 entries of one corpus file are laid out that way). Every firehose entry is parsed to its tracepoints: the 24-byte header (activity type, log type, flags, format-string offset, thread, continuous-time delta, data size), the type-specific fields the flags select, the formatter fields that say where the format string lives, and the argument items. A file matched by the header tag alone must show a Catalog or Chunkset chunk before it is claimed; a file named `.tracev3` is claimed on the name. The layouts follow the community reading in Mandiant's `macos-UnifiedLogs` and libyal's notes, checked against the six corpus archives rather than taken as the answer. When the source answers `supports_ancestors()` — a loose file on disk, or a ZIP entry — it also reaches the file's own tree through `DataSource::open_from_ancestor`, at most three directories up and then a plain relative path: for each UUID a Catalog names, `../<XX>/<rest>` or `../dsc/<UUID>` (a `.logarchive`), else `../../uuidtext/<XX>/<rest>` or `../../uuidtext/dsc/<UUID>` (`/var/db/diagnostics` beside `/var/db/uuidtext`), each file opened by name and read whole under a 512 MiB ceiling; and the Header chunk's boot UUID (sub-chunk `0x6102`), timebase and clock anchor, with the boot looked up in `../timesync/`. A file at the tree's root (`logdata.LiveData.tracev3`) is looked up one level less, and `catalogue_tree.levels_up` records which held. The timesync database's sequence-named files are probed from 0 upward, stopping after 16 misses past the last hit and at 256. Parsed catalogue files are shared through a process-wide cache keyed by path under a 1 GiB budget.

**Produces.** Exactly one `ParsedRecord` per claimed file, subtype `tracev3`, carrying the chunk counts (`chunk_count`, `header_chunks`, `catalog_chunks`, `chunkset_chunks`, `other_chunks`), `bytes`, `chunksets_decompressed` and `chunksets_not_decompressed`, entry counts by kind (`firehose_preambles`, `oversize_entries`, `statedump_entries`, `simpledump_entries`, `other_entries`, and `entries_without_padding` where any were), the tracepoint count and its split by kind (`tracepoints_by_kind`: log, activity, signpost, trace, loss), `tracepoints_not_read_whole`, `format_string_locations` (main executable, shared cache, absolute, UUID-relative), `entries_lost_per_loss_records` — the log's own statement that it dropped entries — where it has loss records, the catalogs' `catalog_uuids`, `catalog_process_entries`, `catalogs_self_consistent`, a list of up to 512 distinct processes (pid, euid, main and shared-cache UUIDs) and up to 512 subsystem names. On the corpus, every chunkset in the 125 `.tracev3` files of six archives (High Sierra to Tahoe) decompresses, every catalog tiles, and all 9,900,644 firehose tracepoints read whole; per archive, tracepoints plus statedump and simpledump entries equal the totals Mandiant's tests pin (569,796; 747,616; 2,397,109) — for Big Sur, 747,294 tracepoints, the figure those tests quote from Apple's own `log raw-dump` — and on Tahoe this reader counts one entry fewer (4,288,583 against 4,288,584), not yet attributed. Every file record carries `catalogue_tree` — `reachable`, `source_can_climb`, `layout` (`logarchive` or `diagnostics`), catalogue files loaded and unparsed, UUIDs not in the tree, timesync files seen, `boot_uuid` and `boot_in_timesync` — and `messages_decoded`, true only when the tree was reached. Then it also carries a `messages` block (resolved, dynamic-format, unresolved, loss records, arguments rendered raw, records emitted, not emitted over the cap, and up to 16 unresolved reasons with counts) and is followed by one `ParsedRecord` per tracepoint, subtype `unifiedlog_message`, parented to the file's record, up to 150,000 per file: `message` (the format string rendered with the entry's arguments, `%{public}`/`%{private}` honoured, a withheld private argument shown as `<private>`), `format_string`, `activity_type`, `level` for log entries, `thread_id`, `pid`, `euid`, `process` and `process_uuid`, `image` and `image_uuid`, `subsystem`, `category`, `continuous_time`, and `timestamp`, `timestamp_ns` and `timestamp_rfc3339` with `time_source` — `timesync` when the file's boot is in the timesync database (the last anchor at or before the time, through the boot's timebase), else `tracev3_header` from the file's own clock anchor. Every message record carries `dated`; one neither source can date has no timestamp, `dated: false`, and says it could not be dated in `content_incomplete`. An unresolved message carries `resolved: false`, `unresolved_reason` and `content_incomplete`; a loss record carries `lost_entries`. A tracepoint whose arguments are in an oversize entry (`0x6002`) is joined to it by process pair and `data_ref` once the file is read and says `arguments_from_oversize`; statedump (`0x6003`) and simpledump (`0x6004`) entries are message records of their own (`activity_type` `statedump`/`simpledump`) — a simpledump's subsystem and text, a statedump's title, object type, decoder library and data, a property list decoded to JSON and any other kind kept as `data_hex` (first 4,096 bytes) with `data_decoded: false`. With them, entries per archive equal Mandiant's pinned totals (High Sierra 569,796; Big Sur 747,616; Monterey 2,397,109). On the Big Sur archive's `Persist/0000000000000004.tracev3` read where it lies: 110,836 resolved, 108 dynamic, 8 unresolved and 1 loss record, 110,953 records — Mandiant's count for the file, a comparison and not ground truth — the first reading `opendirectoryd (build 796.100) launched...` dated 2022-01-16T03:32:13.964503310Z, within 2 s of the header's own clock. When the tree is not reached, `messages_decoded: false` and the reason are the last entry of the record's `content_incomplete` detail.

**Cannot.** It cannot decode a message from a `.tracev3` whose source cannot climb to the rest of its tree (one inside a disk image reaches its tree only through the APFS or HFS+ volume listing, which is tested on listings and has not been run on a real image), so the record says `tree not reachable, not decoded` and no message is emitted. A loose file whose tree is not beside it emits none either and says the catalogue was not found. It cannot resolve a reference whose catalogue file is absent or whose offset falls outside its ranges; that message is emitted with the reason and no text. It does not see a timesync file whose sequence name is far off the run it probes, and a file whose boot is not found is dated from its own header anchor and labelled so. It joins an oversize entry only within the same file, so an argument the log wrote to another file shows as missing, with the reason. It does not decode a statedump's protocol-buffer or custom-object data (Big Sur: 66 of 322), nor the Header chunk's build fields. It does not interpret `sub_tag`. A format string's width or precision is clamped to 4,096. A `%c` argument that is not a Unicode scalar value is shown as `<invalid character 0x…>` and counted as rendered raw. Messages past 150,000 in one file are counted and not emitted. It cannot claim a file on the header tag alone, so a genuinely empty log under another name is not reported; it reports nothing for a `.tracev3`-named file whose first chunk is not a Header. Its ceilings are 512 MiB staged, 5,000,000 chunks, 16 MiB decompressed per chunkset, 65,536 process entries per catalog, and 512 listed processes and subsystems per record, each stated where hit.

**Refuses.** It refuses to claim a file on four bytes. It refuses to erase a log over one bad field: a broken preamble stops the walk with the chunks already counted kept and flagged `unresolved_structure`. It refuses to report counts from partial bytes as the whole log: a short stage stamps `short_read` or `cap_reached`. It refuses to count a chunkset whose blocks do not decompress — a bad LZ4 stream, a missing `bv4$`, a declared size past the ceiling — and says how many did not, as `compressed`; it refuses to keep a partial block's bytes. It refuses to guess past broken entry framing inside a chunkset: an entry that neither the padded nor the unpadded position explains stops that chunkset's walk, flagged. It refuses to read a tracepoint, argument or private value past its entry's bytes: such an argument is `missing`, the tracepoint is counted as not read whole, and the reason is in the detail. It refuses to render an unresolved message as empty text, or a statedump's undecoded bytes as text, and to present a file whose tree was not reached as a decoded log: `messages_decoded: false` is carried into the standard incompleteness keys. It refuses to climb more than three directories or down any path that is absolute or holds `..`, and a ZIP entry never climbs above its archive's root. Nothing is written to evidence.

### `macos.unifiedlog_catalogue`

**Reads.** The unified log's format-string catalogue, under `/var/db/uuidtext`, in both of the forms it takes. A **per-image entry** — at `uuidtext/<first two hex digits of the binary's UUID>/<the other thirty>`, magic `0x66778899` — is a 16-byte header, a table of `u32 offset, u32 size` ranges, each range's bytes in order, and then that binary's path as the one NUL-terminated string left in the file. A **shared cache** — `uuidtext/dsc/<32 hex digits>`, magic `hcsd` — is a 16-byte header (`u16` major, `u16` minor), `range_count` range entries and `image_count` image entries, and then the strings and the paths. Version 1 (to Big Sur) has 16-byte ranges (image index, range start, data offset, range size) and 28-byte images (load address, size, a 16-byte UUID, a path offset); version 2 (Monterey and later) has 24-byte ranges (a 64-bit range start, data offset, size, a 64-bit image index) and 32-byte images (a 64-bit load address, then the same). Selection is by magic alone, because every file in this tree is named in hexadecimal and a hex name is not a claim about content. The first 256 MB of a file are staged.

**Produces.** One `UnifiedLogCatalogue` record per file with its kind, its format version, its range, image and format-string counts, and whether its own arithmetic came out. One `UnifiedLogImage` per binary the catalogue covers — 527 from each of the corpus's shared caches and one per entry file — carrying that binary's path, its UUID, its load address and size where the format states them, how many format strings the catalogue holds for it, and a bounded sample of those strings. Taken together that is an **inventory of the code on the machine that logs**, which survives the log files: on the corpus image the `diagnostics` tree holds no `.tracev3` at all while this tree is intact, so the catalogue is the only thing left on it saying what was running.

**Cannot.** **It cannot produce a single line of log text**, and nothing it emits is a log message. A format string is a sentence the operating system would have substituted arguments into — `"connection from pid_t: %d"` — and this tree says nothing about whether any of them was ever written; the messages are in `.tracev3` files elsewhere. It cannot tell you a binary was executed: a catalogue entry means the machine held logging metadata for that binary, which is a weaker statement, and every record says so. It cannot match a per-image entry to a log reference unless the file's own path survived: **that UUID is nowhere in the file**, it is the directory name plus the file name, so a copy under another name loses it — and the record then says it cannot be matched rather than omitting the field. It cannot count binaries by counting files: twelve of the corpus's 274 entry files name a path another file already named, under a different UUID, so 274 files are 262 binaries. And it cannot resolve a reference into an image the cache holds no strings for — 33 of the corpus cache's 527 — which is reported as a count rather than left to be inferred from an absence. Its ceilings are 256 MB staged, 1,000,000 ranges, 200,000 images, 4,096 bytes per path, and 8 sampled strings of 240 bytes per image.

**Refuses.** It refuses to emit the format strings as records. There are 848,768 of them across the corpus tree; they are Apple's own source text rather than observations about this machine, and one record each would bury a case under them — so they are counted, sampled and read in full for a decoder's use, and not filed as evidence. It refuses to accept a lower-case hexadecimal file name as a UUID, because the tree's own names are upper case and a UUID that does not match the tree's is worse than none. It refuses to report its counts without publishing whether the file's own arithmetic came out: an entry file's ranges must land on a tail holding exactly one NUL-terminated path, and a shared cache's image table must end at exactly the byte its first range's data begins at, and a file failing either is reported with what was read and the reason rather than as a whole read. It refuses to read a range or a table past the bytes staged. And it refuses to select on a file name, because in this tree there is nothing in a name to select on.

### `macos.unifiedlog_timesync`

**Reads.** The unified log's timesync database, `/var/db/diagnostics/timesync/*.timesync` (and a `.logarchive`'s `timesync/`). It is a flat run of little-endian records: a 48-byte **boot record** — `u16` signature `0xBBB0`, `u16` header size (48), `u32` unknown, the 16-byte boot UUID, the mach timebase as `u32` numerator and `u32` denominator, the boot's wall-clock time as `i64` nanoseconds since 1970, then `u32` timezone offset in minutes and `u32` daylight-saving flag — followed by that boot's 32-byte **sync records** — `u32` signature `"Ts \0"`, `u32` flags, `u64` continuous time, `i64` wall time in nanoseconds, `u32` timezone offset and `u32` daylight flag. A file named `.timesync` is claimed on its name; any other file only when it opens with a boot record whose own size field says 48 and a sync record straight after, because two bytes of signature are too common to claim a file on. The first 64 MB are staged. The layout was read from the corpus files and agrees with Mandiant's `macos-UnifiedLogs` reading, which is a comparison, not the source.

**Produces.** One `UnifiedLogTimesync` record per file with its boot and anchor counts, and one `UnifiedLogBoot` record per boot record: the boot UUID (32 upper-case hex digits, the form the uuidtext tree uses), the timebase numerator and denominator, the boot's wall-clock time in nanoseconds and as RFC 3339 (and as the record's timestamp, so the boot sits on the timeline), the timezone offset and daylight flag, the byte offset of the record, and every **anchor** — continuous time, wall time in nanoseconds and RFC 3339, timezone, daylight flag and flags. On the Big Sur corpus archive's file that is 5 boots and 23 anchors; all ten timesync files in the six corpus archives read to their last byte.

**Cannot.** **It dates no log entry.** An anchor is the table a decoder converts a `.tracev3` entry's continuous time through; this module reads the table and converts nothing, and no unified-log message is dated anywhere in the product by it. It cannot say the machine's clock was right: an anchor is what the machine believed the time was when it wrote the record. It does not interpret the boot record's unknown field or a sync record's flags; both are carried raw. It lists at most 10,000 anchors per boot, keeping the exact count and saying where the list was cut.

**Refuses.** It refuses to attribute anything to a boot when the file does not open with a boot record, and a file named `.timesync` that does not is reported as unread with the reason rather than dropped. It refuses to read past a record it does not recognise or a boot record whose size field is not 48: the walk stops there, keeps the boots and anchors already read, and says in the record's incompleteness detail at which byte it stopped. It refuses to read a record that runs past the bytes staged, and says so as a short read.

### `macos.wifi_known_networks`

**Reads.** The macOS Wi-Fi known-networks preference files, selected by name and read as property lists. It subscribes to `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, lowercases the final path component of the artifact's `name`, and proceeds when that basename contains `known-networks` (the Big Sur and later `com.apple.wifi.known-networks.plist`) or `airport.preferences` (the older `com.apple.airport.preferences.plist`); an artifact with no data source is passed over. The file is staged whole through `Staged::read` with a 16 MiB ceiling (`MAX_PLIST_BYTES`), and the staged bytes are handed to `plist::from_bytes`, which reads XML and binary property lists alike. The top-level value must be a dictionary. Two shapes are walked in one pass: every top-level key beginning `wifi.network.ssid.` whose value is a dictionary is a modern network entry, and a top-level `KnownNetworks` dictionary's dictionary-valued members are legacy entries, so a file carrying both yields both. For each network the SSID is taken from `SSID_STR` where that is a string, else `SSID` where that is a string or a data blob (decoded as lossy UTF-8), else the key with the `wifi.network.ssid.` prefix stripped. `AddedAt` is read as a plist date; a last-joined date is taken from the first present of `JoinedByUserAt`, `JoinedBySystemAt`, `LastAutoJoinAt` and `UpdatedAt`, in that order; each date becomes whole Unix seconds and a date before 1970 becomes nothing. `SupportedSecurityTypes` is read as an array of strings or a single string. Nothing else in the entry is read.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per network, subtype `known_network`, parented to the plist, carrying `type: "WifiNetwork"`, `subtype: "known_network"`, `ssid`, `added_at` and `last_joined` (Unix seconds, or `null` where the key was absent, not a date, or pre-1970), `added_at_rfc3339` and `last_joined_rfc3339` where the seconds exist, `security_types` (an array, present only when non-empty) and a `name` of `Wi-Fi network: <ssid>`. `WifiNetwork` is the same record type `plugin.windows.wlan_profiles` emits, so both platforms' answers sit together under the device category on the Analysis screen. Where the stage fell short of the declared size — the file over 16 MiB, or the source delivering fewer bytes than it declared — every network parsed from the partial bytes carries `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason` (`cap_reached` or `short_read`) and a `content_incomplete_detail` sentence naming the bytes staged against the bytes declared. Where a short stage yields no network at all — a plist keeps its trailer or closing tags at the end, so a prefix usually does not parse — one `ParsedRecord` of type `WifiNetworkIncomplete`, subtype `parse_incomplete`, is emitted instead, with `status: "NotStagedInFull"`, `bytes_staged`, `bytes_declared`, the same pair and detail, and a `name` saying the file is incomplete and the networks this machine joined could not be read from it. Where the file was staged in full and still cannot be read, the same type is emitted with `status` `ParseFailed` (the decoder's error in the detail) or `UnexpectedLayout` (the top level is not a dictionary), `content_incomplete_reason` `unresolved_structure`, and a detail beginning `<file> was read in full and`. It produces no timeline event: `added_at` and `last_joined` are keys on a `ParsedRecord`, not `TimelineEvent` artifacts, so a join date is on the record and not on the case timeline. A count of networks is logged at `info`.

**Cannot.** It cannot say when the machine was last on a network. `last_joined` is the first present of four keys in a fixed order, not the latest of them: where an entry holds both `JoinedByUserAt` and a later `JoinedBySystemAt`, the earlier user-initiated join is reported as `last_joined`, and where neither join key exists the value may be `UpdatedAt`, which is a preference write and not a join at all. Nothing on the record says which key supplied the figure. It cannot place the machine: no BSSID, channel, `BSSList` per-access-point join history, `ChannelHistory` or previous-SSID list is read, so a network is a name and two dates, and the network's password is not here — that lives in the keychain, which `macos.keychain` reports as locked. It does not read whether the network was hidden, captive, auto-join-disabled or shared, nor the `__OSSpecific__` block, nor a legacy file that keeps its networks under any key other than `KnownNetworks` (older releases wrote a `RememberedNetworks` array, which yields nothing). A dictionary that parses in full and carries neither shape — an empty known-networks file among them — produces no record and no marker, so a file of an unknown layout that is still a dictionary reads as no networks. Dates lose their sub-second part and any date before 1970 is dropped as if absent. An SSID stored as bytes that are not UTF-8 is rendered lossily with replacement characters, and the record does not carry the raw bytes. Its name gate is a substring test, so any file whose basename contains `known-networks` or `airport.preferences` is attempted, and a modern file that happens to be XML or binary is not distinguished on the record. The ceiling is 16 MiB staged, stated on every record it affects. Both shapes are pinned by XML fixtures the tests write, and one test reads the Magnet 2021 macOS image's own `com.apple.wifi.known-networks.plist` (one network, no marker) where that gitignored corpus is present; no real file is in this tree.

**Refuses.** It refuses to let a file it selected by name vanish: a stage that fell short and would not parse leaves a `WifiNetworkIncomplete` record with the byte counts, because returning nothing for a plist this parser claimed would delete the machine's join history from the case with no trace; a partial read that produced no network leaves the same marker, and so does a file staged in full that will not parse or whose top level is not a dictionary. It refuses to present a network read from a partial plist as part of a complete history: each such record carries the standard pair and the sentence, since the networks after the cut are missing. It refuses to invent a date: an absent, non-date or pre-1970 value is `null`, and no RFC 3339 string is written for it. It refuses a `security_types` key when there is nothing to put in it, rather than an empty array. It does not refuse an unrelated plist loudly: a `.plist` whose name does not match, or a matching file with neither network shape, is returned as an empty list and folded into the orchestrator's 'ran and produced nothing' row. It never writes to evidence and holds at most 16 MiB of the file in memory.

### `plugin.analysis.encryption_detector`

**Reads.** The first 512 bytes of an artifact, up to 192 KiB of it for an entropy figure, and one metadata flag another module wrote. It subscribes to `Partition`, `RawEvidence`, `FileEntry` and `Container` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, passes over any artifact with no data source or with `is_directory: true`, and returns nothing when the source is shorter than 6 bytes or delivered fewer than 6. The header is read with `read_full`, so a windowed source that answers a few bytes per call still fills the window. What it looks for depends on the artifact type. On a `Partition` or `RawEvidence` it tests three volume signatures: the eight bytes `-FVE-FS-` at offset 3, which is the OEM name BitLocker writes into an NTFS-style boot sector; the six bytes `LUKS\xBA\xBE` at offset 0, with the big-endian `u16` at offset 6 read as the LUKS version, or 0 when the header delivered fewer than 8 bytes; and Apple Core Storage, taken as `CS` at offset 0 with a non-zero big-endian version at offset 2 and a big-endian `u32` block size at offset 8 that is a power of two between 512 and 65,536 inclusive. On a `FileEntry` or `Container` it tests two: a ZIP local file header `PK\x03\x04` at offset 0 whose general-purpose flag (little-endian `u16` at offset 6) has bit 0 set, and the metadata key `efs_encrypted: true`, which `plugin.ntfs.mft_parser` writes when the MFT record carries a `$LOGGED_UTILITY_STREAM` attribute named `$EFS` and which this module trusts without reading a byte. On every type, when the source holds at least 64 bytes, it reads `min(size, 196,608)` bytes from offset zero and computes Shannon entropy over them; that figure is used only when it exceeds 7.9 bits per byte. It reads the artifact's `name` for the record and for a suffix list — `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.png`, `.mp4`, `.mp3`, `.zip`, `.gz`, `.bz2`, `.xz`, `.7z`, `.rar`, `.webm`, `.flac`, `.aac`, `.avi`, `.mkv` — that suppresses the entropy finding.

**Produces.** Zero or more `ParsedRecord` artifacts parented to the examined artifact, one per detection, each carrying `analysis_type: "encryption_detection"`, `subtype: "EncryptionDetection"`, `encryption_type`, `description`, `confidence` and `source_name` (the artifact's name), and every signature record also `is_encrypted: true`; there is no `type` key, so the DB's record-type derivation falls through to the subtype. The signature detections are `BitLocker` (`BitLocker Drive Encryption detected (BDE boot sector)`, confidence 1.0, with `volume_artifact_id` — the volume's own artifact id, which every record the BitLocker decryptor writes for the volume also carries — `unlock_status_reported_by: "plugin.crypto.bitlocker_decryptor"` and an `unlock_status_note` deferring the unlock status to the decryptor's record, and no incompleteness pair of its own), `LUKS` (`LUKS encrypted partition detected (version N)`, confidence 1.0, with `luks_version`, `volume_artifact_id` — the volume's own artifact id, which every record the LUKS decryptor writes for the volume also carries — `unlock_status_reported_by: "plugin.crypto.luks_decryptor"` and an `unlock_status_note` saying this record states only that the volume is LUKS and that the decryptor's record states whether it was unlocked; it carries no incompleteness pair of its own, so the volume is on the Needs attention queue once, by the decryptor's record ), `FileVault 2` (`Possible Core Storage / FileVault 2 encrypted volume`, confidence 0.7), `Encrypted ZIP` (`ZIP archive with encrypted entries`, confidence 1.0) and `NTFS EFS` (`NTFS EFS-encrypted file`, confidence 1.0). Where entropy over the sampled prefix exceeds 7.9 and no signature matched and the name is not on the compressed-suffix list, one more record, `Unknown (high entropy)`, is emitted with confidence 0.8 on a volume (`Volume has very high entropy (x.xxx) — possibly encrypted`) or 0.5 on a file or container (`File has very high entropy (x.xxx) — possibly encrypted or compressed`), carrying `entropy` rounded to three decimals and NOT carrying `is_encrypted`, because it is a lead and not a finding (pinned by `entropy_only_record_does_not_assert_encryption`); where a signature did match, the same figure is written as `entropy` onto each signature record instead and no separate record is made. These records carry no `content_incomplete`/`inventory_incomplete` pair, so none of them reaches the case's Needs attention queue, which is fed only by records stamped `encrypted` on that pair. They are read by the `Encrypted Files` saved filter (`is_encrypted = true` or `efs_encrypted = true`, so the entropy leads are not in it) and by `count_encrypted_files`, which folds every record with `is_encrypted = 1` onto its parent and counts that parent as an encrypted file — so only a signature-backed record reaches that figure. A `debug` line names the detections per artifact. No timeline event and no data source is produced.

**Cannot.** It cannot detect BitLocker To Go, and the test `test_bitlocker_only_on_volumes` pins the narrower half of that: `-FVE-FS-` is tested only on `Partition` and `RawEvidence`, and a To Go volume's boot sector is a genuine FAT32 BPB reading `MSWIN4.1` at offset 3 with the BitLocker GUID at `0x1a8`, which this module never reads — `plugin.crypto.bitlocker_decryptor` is the only component that sees such a volume. Identification of To Go volumes does not come from this module. It cannot detect VeraCrypt or TrueCrypt and does not claim to: a volume header is random by design, and the variant that once named the detection without any code path emitting it was deleted; a VeraCrypt volume gets at most the generic `Unknown (high entropy)` lead, which never says VeraCrypt. It cannot tell encrypted from compressed, and says so by leaving `is_encrypted` off the high-entropy record: a `.docx`, a `.pdf`, a `.xz` under another name or any high-entropy `FileEntry` whose suffix is not on the sixteen-entry list gets that lead, and it is not counted into the case's `encrypted_files` figure. The mirror case is an `encrcdsa` Apple image that measured 7.940 over its first 4 MiB and got no record while the EWF container beside it at 7.994 did. That figure comes from a different window than this module's 192 KiB and would clear today's 7.9 threshold; what the case shows is that the heuristic is arbitrary, not where its floor lies. The threshold is a fixed 7.9 over at most the first 192 KiB from offset zero, so a whole-disk image whose first sectors are an MBR never trips it however encrypted the partitions are, and the sample is not stated on the record. It reads only the first ZIP local header's flag, so an archive whose first entry is stored in the clear and whose later entries are encrypted is not flagged, and it cannot tell ZipCrypto from WinZip AES. It cannot see an encrypted APFS volume, an `encrcdsa` image, a FileVault-era `CS` volume on a `RawEvidence` whose first sector is a partition table, an encrypted `adb backup`, or an encrypted iOS backup — every one of those is detected elsewhere or not at all. The Core Storage test is a plausibility check on three fields and is labelled `Possible` at 0.7 for that reason. `efs_encrypted` is taken on trust from metadata and no byte of the file is read for it. Detection on a `Container` reads the container file's own first bytes — an E01 or AFF4 wrapper — not the image inside it.

**Refuses.** It refuses to test a volume signature on a file or a file signature on a volume: the BitLocker, LUKS and Core Storage checks run only for `Partition` and `RawEvidence`, the ZIP-flag and EFS checks only for `FileEntry` and `Container`, so a BitLocker VBR carved into a file, or a `.vhd` ingested as a file, is not reported as a BitLocker volume here. It refuses to emit two records for one finding: where a signature matched, the entropy figure is appended to that record and no `Unknown (high entropy)` record is added. It refuses the entropy finding on a name whose suffix says compressed media or archive, and refuses it on anything under 64 bytes, because a figure over a few bytes means nothing. It refuses an artifact under 6 bytes, a directory, and an artifact with no data source, all in silence. It refuses to raise a `FileVault 2` finding on `CS` alone: the version must be non-zero and the block size a power of two in range, pinned by two tests that build the failing shapes. Every refusal here is an empty list, folded into the orchestrator's 'ran and produced nothing' row; this module never errors on content and leaves no refusal record of its own, so an examiner cannot tell from the artifact tree that a volume was examined and found clean. It never writes and never decrypts.

### `plugin.analysis.file_analyzer`

**Reads.** The head of every file, a bounded prefix of it for entropy, and — for two image formats — the whole file. It subscribes to `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess` and returns nothing for an artifact with no `name`, with `is_directory: true`, with no data source, or shorter than 4 bytes. An extension is taken as the text after the last `.` in the name, lowercased, provided it is under 10 characters and is not the whole name. It reads `min(512, size)` bytes at offset zero with `read_full`, so a chunked source still yields a full window, and hands them to `magic::detect_content_type`, a fixed ordered list of some three dozen signatures: JPEG (`FF D8 FF`), PNG, GIF (`GIF8`), BMP (`BM`), TIFF (both byte orders), WEBP and WAV and AVI (`RIFF` plus the form at 8), ICO (`00 00 01 00`), PDF, RTF, OLE2, RAR, 7Z, GZIP (`1F 8B`), BZIP2 (`BZh`), ZIP — refined to `DOCX`/`XLSX`/`PPTX` when the first local header's filename starts `word/`, `xl/` or `ppt/`, and, when it is `[Content_Types].xml` or `_rels/.rels`, by inflating that member (stored or deflated, at most 64 KiB of text) and reading which one of `word/document`, `xl/workbook` or `ppt/presentation` it names; when the member's bytes are not there or name none or more than one, the label is `OOXML`. Because Word pads that member's header with a 520-byte extra field, a file labelled `OOXML` from the 512-byte head is re-read from offset zero up to 16 KiB and detected again — TAR (`ustar` at 257), MP3 (`ID3`, or an MPEG Layer III frame header: sync, a version that is not the reserved `01`, layer `01`, a bitrate index that is not `1111` and a sample-rate index that is not `11`), FLAC, OGG, MP4 (`ftyp` at 4), MKV, FLV (`FLV`), PE (`MZ`), ELF, Mach-O (four magics), SQLite, ESE (`EF CD AB 89` at 4), Registry (`regf`), EVTX and LNK; the first match wins. For entropy it reads `min(size, 196,608)` bytes from offset zero when the file is over 512 bytes, else reuses the head, and computes Shannon entropy over what came back. For a detected `JPEG` or `PNG` of between 4 bytes and 128 MiB it reads the whole file and walks it to its logical end: for JPEG, marker by marker — skipping length-prefixed segments, stepping through entropy-coded scan data honouring `FF 00` stuffing and `RSTn` markers — to the first `FF D9` EOI outside a scan; for PNG, chunk by chunk to `IEND`, trusting each declared length and checking no CRC. Bytes past that end are sniffed with the same signature list.

**Produces.** Exactly one `ParsedRecord` per examined file, parented to it, with `type: "FileSignatureAnalysis"`, `analysis_type: "file_analysis"`, `subtype: "FileSignatureAnalysis"`, `filename`, `magic_bytes_hex` (the first 8 bytes), `entropy` (rounded to three decimals), `entropy_classification` (`very_high` above 7.9, `high` above 7.0, `medium` from 4.0, else `low`), `entropy_bytes` (bytes measured), `entropy_file_bytes` (the file's declared size), `entropy_sampled` (true when the window was smaller than the file), and `entropy_note` where the figure is a prefix sample or short — the sampling sentence deliberately without the `content_incomplete` pair, since sampling by design is not unreadable content and stamping it would put every file over 192 KiB into the court-facing incompleteness count, while a window that came back short of what was asked does get `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason: "short_read"` and a `content_incomplete_detail` sentence. `detected_type` and `detected_extension` are present where a signature matched — except that the undetermined `OOXML` label carries no `detected_extension`, since it names no single one — `actual_extension` where the name had one, and `signature_mismatch` is always present: `true` only when a type was detected, the name had an extension, and that extension is not in the type's accepted list. The overlay outcome is on `trailing_data_check` on every record — `found` (with `trailing_data: true`, `trailing_offset`, `trailing_size` and `trailing_detected_type` where the tail sniffed as something), `none` (with `trailing_data: false`), `undetermined` (with `trailing_data_undetermined: true` and a reason: `cap_reached` for a file outside 4 bytes–128 MiB, `short_read` with `bytes_read` and `declared_size` where the whole-file read fell short, `unresolved_structure` where the walker could not find the end), or `not_applicable` with `trailing_data_not_applicable_reason` of `content_type_not_identified` or `no_logical_end_walker_for_format`. The Analysis screen's `trailingCheck` and `ENTROPY_SCOPE` readers key on exactly these names. No timeline event, no hash and no data source is produced.

**Cannot.** It cannot identify a file it has no signature for, and it says so with `not_applicable`; and where its signature is too short it identifies the wrong thing. `MZ`, `BM`, `FLV`, `BZh` and `ID3` are two- and three-byte tests, and the MP3 frame-header test is four header fields wide, not a decode of a second frame — a UTF-16LE byte-order mark `FF FE` and an `FF FF` run are refused (both decode as Layer I, pinned by `utf16le_bom_and_ff_ff_are_not_mp3`), but a non-audio file that happens to begin with a valid Layer III header is still `MP3`. The Office family is read from the first ZIP member only; when that member is `[Content_Types].xml` or `_rels/.rels` and its bytes cannot be inflated from the first 16 KiB, the label is `OOXML`, which accepts every Word, Excel and PowerPoint OOXML extension — so a Word document renamed `.xlsx` is caught only when the family was read. Macro-enabled and template variants are accepted within a family and not told apart. A package whose first member is none of those (a `docProps/` part first) is labelled `ZIP`, which accepts every OOXML extension as well as the archive and OpenDocument ones, so no family is checked for it at all. It cannot read a container's own type: an OLE2 file is `OLE2` whether it is a `.doc`, `.xls`, `.msi` or `.msg`, and it has no signatures for HEIC, AVIF, PSD, DMG, VHD/VHDX, E01, plist, XML, HTML, script or plain text. Its entropy is a prefix figure: at most the first 192 KiB from offset zero, a sample the record states but a classification (`low: not encrypted`) that describes those bytes only — an installer with a plaintext manifest ahead of a packed payload measures low. The `compute_entropy` sampler's three-window mode above 1 MiB is never reached from here because the window is already capped. Overlay detection walks JPEG and PNG only; every other format is `not_applicable`, and for those two it cannot tell a concealed payload from a legitimate appended trailer — a Samsung or Google motion photo (an MP4 after the EOI), an MPO second frame, or an XMP extended block — all of which are reported `found` with the sniffed type. The JPEG walk stops at the first EOI outside scan data, and a JPEG whose first segment declares a length past the file, or a PNG whose declared chunk length overruns, is `undetermined`; PNG CRCs are not checked and a truncated IEND reads as `none`. Its ceilings are 512 bytes for signature detection (16 KiB for an OOXML family), 192 KiB for entropy, 128 MiB read whole for the overlay walk, and a 4-byte floor below which no record exists at all, so a 3-byte file is not analysed and nothing says so.

**Refuses.** It refuses to report a file as clean that it did not walk. The four outcomes of the overlay check are four distinct values on one declared key, because three of them used to render identically as a blank cell under a 'Signature OK' tile: a file over the 128 MiB cap is `undetermined` (`cap_reached`), never `none`; a whole-file read that stopped short is `undetermined` (`short_read`) with the counts, because the tail it would have to inspect is exactly the part it never saw; a walker that cannot find the end is `undetermined` (`unresolved_structure`); and a type with no walker, or no type at all, is `not_applicable` with the reason named. It refuses to call a file a mismatch without an extension to disagree with, and refuses to stamp the case-wide incompleteness pair on a measurement that was merely sampled by design, stating the sample on its own keys instead, while it does stamp the pair where the bytes it asked for were not there — both shortfalls, where both hold, appear in one `entropy_note` rather than the second overwriting the first. It refuses a directory, a nameless artifact, an artifact with no data source and a file under 4 bytes, all in silence with no record. It never errors on content, never writes, and never reads past 128 MiB of any file.

### `plugin.apple.imessage`

**Reads.** Apple's Messages store — iOS `sms.db` and macOS `chat.db` — selected loosely by name and strictly by schema. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `SystemArtifact` with `InputCapability::Stream`, lower-cases the artifact's `name` and opens any file whose name ends `chat.db`, `sms.db` or `chat.db-wal`, or contains `imessage` or `mobilesms`, so a renamed or backup-hashed copy is still tried. A directory entry yields nothing. An artifact with no data source is not opened and leaves an identification record. A source whose first 16 bytes did not all arrive is a short read of this tool's, never a finding about the file: it yields only the stager's `SqliteSpillIncomplete` record (`content_incomplete_reason: short_read`) where the source declared more than arrived (the shared gate `stage_named_store`, ROADMAP §5.11). Otherwise the whole file is spilled by `TempDb::spill` under a 2 GiB cap (`MAX_DB_BYTES`) with its `-wal` sibling where the source can open one; the staged copy's first 16 bytes must be `SQLite format 3\0` or the file is passed over in silence. The copy is opened read-only and the claim is made through `sqlite_master`: a table named `message` must exist, and a catalogue that will not answer is an error, not an absence. The schema version is Apple's own, not SQLite's: `_SqliteDatabaseProperties` is looked for through `probe_table` and its `_ClientVersion` row is read as a number and compared with the validated window `9005..=15009`, every endpoint read from a real store — 9005 in plaso's `test_data/imessage_chat.db`, 14005 in the Magnet 2021 macOS CTF `chat.db`, 15009 in the Magnet 2022 CTF iPhone 8 `sms.db`; `PRAGMA user_version` is 0 on all three and is not consulted. The presence of `handle`, `chat`, `chat_message_join`, `attachment` and `message_attachment_join` is probed with `SELECT COUNT(*) > 0 FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table'`, each probe keeping "absent" apart from "could not tell", and the optional `message` columns `associated_message_guid` (iOS 10+), `reply_to_guid` (iOS 14+) and `attributedBody` are probed through a `SchemaProbe` that records a failed `PRAGMA table_info` rather than answering "absent". Every other column is resolved through a `FieldMap` against `PRAGMA table_info`, each from one candidate name — `message` (`ROWID`, `guid`, `text`, `date`, `date_read`, `date_delivered`, `is_from_me`, `is_read`, `service`, `cache_has_attachments`, `handle_id`), `handle` (`ROWID`, `id`), `chat` (`ROWID`, `chat_identifier`, `display_name`), `chat_message_join` (`chat_id`, `message_id`), `attachment` (`ROWID`, `guid`, `filename`, `mime_type`, `total_bytes`, `created_date`, `transfer_name`, `uti`, `is_outgoing`), `message_attachment_join` (`message_id`, `attachment_id`) — with a column list that will not read an error for the parse. Messages are walked in one statement, `message` LEFT JOINed to `handle` on `handle_id` and to `chat` through a scalar subquery taking the lowest `chat_id` in `chat_message_join` for the message (so a message filed under several chats yields one row), `ORDER BY m.date DESC LIMIT` one past the 500,000-record cap (`MAX_MESSAGE_ENTRIES`); an unresolved column is `NULL AS <field>` in the SELECT. Attachments are walked first, `attachment` LEFT JOINed through `message_attachment_join` to `message`, newest `created_date` first, under the same cap. Every Cocoa timestamp is read as seconds since 2001-01-01 when at or below 10^12 and nanoseconds above it, with 0 or negative as "unset"; a message whose `text` is NULL or empty has its body taken from the `attributedBody` typedstream by `seance_core::typedstream::extract_message_text`, which finds the `NSString` scaffolding and the `01 2B` length marker and drops U+FFFC attachment placeholders.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per message, `type: "iMessage"`, `subtype: "chat_message"`, `source_table: "message"`, with `rowid`, `guid`, `text` (from `text`, else decoded from `attributedBody`, else null), `date`, `date_read` and `date_delivered` in whole Unix seconds (null when unset) with `date_ns`, `date_read_ns`, `date_delivered_ns` beside them when the sub-second part is non-zero, `is_from_me` and `is_read` as booleans or null, `direction` (`sent`/`received`, null when `is_from_me` was NULL), `service` as stored (`iMessage`/`SMS`), `contact` (the handle's `id` — a phone number or e-mail — or null), `chat_identifier`, `chat_display_name`, `has_attachments` (from `cache_has_attachments`, null when NULL), `associated_message_guid`, `reply_to_guid`, and a `name` of `<direction or "message">: <contact or "Unknown"> — <first 80 characters or "(attachment)">`. One `iMessageAttachment` (`subtype: "chat_attachment"`, `source_table: "attachment"`) per attachment row with `rowid`, `guid`, `filename`, `mime_type`, `total_bytes`, `created_date` (+ `created_date_ns`), `transfer_name`, `uti`, `is_outgoing`, `message_rowid` and `message_guid` from the join (null for an orphan), and a `name` of `Attachment: <transfer_name, else filename, else "unknown">`.
