Per-message incompleteness is stamped on the message itself: when the attachment inventory failed, could not be probed, or lost a column, every message whose `cache_has_attachments` is 1 or NULL carries `attachment_inventory_incomplete: true`, `attachment_inventory_error` and the standard pair (`content_incomplete: true`, reason `unresolved_structure`); when an optional-column probe failed, every message carries `schema_probe_incomplete: true`, `schema_probe_error` and the same pair. After the messages, in order: a `CapReached` marker (`iMessageIncomplete`, `subtype: parse_incomplete`, `max_entries`, `rows_read`, `truncated`, `content_incomplete` pair with reason `cap_reached`) when the walk stopped; a `RowsUndecodable` marker (`rows_dropped`, `records_recovered`, `first_error`, both pairs) when any row would not decode; a `SchemaUndetermined` marker (`schema_probe_failed`, `schema_probe_detail`, both pairs) when the optional-column probe failed; then the schema findings, all `type: "ParserStaleWarning"`, `subtype: "parser_stale"`, `app: "imessage"`: `SchemaOutsideValidated` (the shared marker with `seen_schema_version`, `supported_range: "9005..=15009"`, `message`, detail and name post-stamped; a disclosure with no incompleteness claim) when `_ClientVersion` is outside the window and the rows still parse; `SchemaVersionNotRecorded` with no incompleteness pair when the properties table or the `_ClientVersion` row is absent; `SchemaVersionUndetermined` with the pair when the catalogue would not answer, the row would not read, or the value is not a number — each of the three carrying `validated_against` naming plaso's `imessage_chat.db` (9005), the Magnet 2021 macOS `chat.db` (14005) and the Magnet 2022 iPhone 8 `sms.db` (15009); and one `SchemaFieldsUnresolved` per table (`source_table`, `unresolved_fields`, `records_recovered`, the `content_incomplete` pair) for any table whose fields did not all resolve. Then the attachment records, their own `RowsUndecodable` and `CapReached` markers under `iMessageAttachmentIncomplete`, and, when the attachment tables exist and could not be inventoried, one `iMessageIncomplete` record with `status: "AttachmentInventoryFailed"`, the error, and both incompleteness pairs. An artifact with no data source yields one `iMessage` record with `status: "Identified"`; a file carrying the SQLite header that would not open, whose catalogue or column list would not read, or whose query would not prepare or run yields one `iMessageIncomplete` record with `status: "ParseFailed"`, the error, both pairs and a detail sentence saying the messages' absence here is not evidence they were absent from the device. Every record from a short-staged or WAL-refused copy is stamped `content_incomplete: true` with its reason and one `SqliteSpillIncomplete` marker is appended.

**Cannot.** It cannot see past the five-hundred-thousandth message or attachment: both walks are newest-first, so a cap drops the oldest, and the marker says so. It cannot name a correspondent beyond the handle: `contact` is the phone number or e-mail in `handle.id`, no address book is joined, and a group chat's other participants (`chat_handle_join`) are not read, so a received group message names only its sender and a sent one names whichever single handle `handle_id` pointed at. It cannot decode every body: `attributedBody` is read by a scaffolding-and-marker scan, not a typedstream decoder, so a body whose string is split across runs, uses a class the scan does not recognise, or is stored under a different archive shape yields null with nothing on the record to say a blob was present, and a message that is only a tapback, edit or sticker has no text at all. It cannot say whether a message was delivered or read beyond the raw dates and flags. It cannot tell a tapback from a message except by `associated_message_guid`, which is passed through undecoded, and it does not read `message_summary_info`, `payload_data`, `balloon_bundle_id`, `expressive_send_style_id`, `thread_originator_guid`, `date_edited`, `date_retracted` or the `deleted_messages` and `recoverable_message_part` tables, so an unsent or edited message reads as it last stood. It records an attachment's metadata only: the bytes are never carried, `filename` is a path on the device that the backup may not contain, and an attachment in the table but under no surviving message has no `message_rowid`. Its schema window is three points wide (9005, 14005, 15009) and every field has exactly one physical name, so a store on iOS 17/18's client versions is disclosed as beyond the window and parsed on the assumption its columns mean the same; a rename is an unresolved field until a candidate is added. The join takes the lowest chat id for a message filed under several, so a merged conversation's alternate thread is not shown. It does not read `chat.db-wal` on its own (the name is accepted but the file has no SQLite header and is passed over), and it recovers no deleted rows.

**Refuses.** It refuses to file a corrupt store as a device with no messages: a catalogue that will not answer, a column list that will not read, and a query that will not prepare or run all reach the `ParseFailed` record with both incompleteness pairs and a sentence saying absence here is not absence from the device; only a file with no SQLite header, or a readable catalogue with no `message` table, is passed over in silence. It refuses to answer a probe that failed as "absent": a table probe that errored seeds the attachment-inventory error so every message that may carry media is stamped, and an optional-column probe that errored is stamped on every message and declared once as `SchemaUndetermined`, because on modern iOS the body lives only in `attributedBody` and a substituted NULL there reads as a message with no text. It refuses to guess direction, read state or media presence: a NULL `is_from_me`, `is_read` or `cache_has_attachments` stays null, never `received`, `false` or `false`. It refuses to let a message claim media the inventory could not confirm as clean — the stamp fails closed on an unknown flag. It refuses to fan a message out into one record per chat, resolving the chat with a scalar subquery so counts are of messages, not join rows. It refuses to place an unset Cocoa date at 2001-01-01, and refuses to drop the nanoseconds a modern store records. It refuses to compare `PRAGMA user_version` to anything — it is 0 on every real store seen — and refuses to spend an absent `_ClientVersion` as "older than 9005" or a failed read as in range; it refuses to widen the window past the three files opened. It refuses to substitute a guess for an unresolved column, naming it instead. It refuses to file any marker, cap, failure or attachment-inventory record under the type `iMessage`, because the conversation summary groups on that key and would count it as a message in an `unknown` thread. And it refuses to count a marker as a recovered record, taking `records_recovered` over `chat_message` rows before the markers join the list.

### `plugin.browsers.chrome_cache`

**Reads.** Two Chromium disk-cache formats, each selected by its own first bytes and never by a file name — which matters because the modern format names its files by a hash of the key (`f9a1c3d4e5f6a7b8_0`) and the legacy one names them `data_0`..`data_n`. It runs on `FileEntry` and `FileContent` artifacts, declares `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, passes over any artifact whose metadata says `is_directory: true` or which carries no `DataSource`, and reads 20 bytes at offset 0; fewer than 4 arriving ends it with no record. If the first eight of those bytes are the little-endian u64 `0xfcfb6d1ba7725c30` — `SimpleFileHeader::initial_magic_number` — the file is one Simple Cache entry: the header's `version` (u32), `key_length` (u32) and `key_hash` (u32) are read, and then `key_length` bytes from offset 20, which are the cache key. Nothing after the key is read: the cached response body and the `SimpleFileEOF` records that follow it are not examined. If instead the first four bytes are the little-endian u32 `0xC104CAC3` — `disk_cache::kBlockMagic`, the value the in-tree dtFabric specification at `reference/plaso/plaso/parsers/chrome_cache.yaml` pins for `chrome_cache_data_block_file_header`, and spelled out literally in the test `the_block_file_magic_is_the_one_chromium_writes` because the constant once held `0xC0F0`, a value Chromium never wrote, which made this whole branch unreachable on evidence — the file is a blockfile `data_#`. Up to 512 MiB of it are staged in a single allocation. Of the 8,192-byte `BlockFileHeader` it reads `this_file` (u16 at offset 8), `entry_size` (the block size, u32 at 12), `num_entries` (u32 at 16) and the 8,112-byte allocation bitmap from offset 80 (block i is bit i % 8 of byte i / 8). Only a file declaring 256-byte blocks is walked for entries, because Chromium allocates every `EntryStore` from one; a file declaring 36 (rankings, `data_0`), 1,024 or 4,096 yields nothing of its own. The bytes from 8,192 onward are walked at the declared 256-byte stride, each block read as a candidate `EntryStore`: the key hash as a u32 at offset 0, the key length as an i32 at offset 32, the creation time as a u64 at offset 24, the `long_key` cache address as a u32 at offset 36, and the key itself from offset 96. A key of 160 bytes or more runs past the first block into the following blocks of the same entry, and where such a key is published, `blocks_for_key` — Chromium's `EntryImpl::NumBlocksForEntry` — says how many blocks the entry owns and the scan steps over them rather than rereading them as entries. A key longer than 927 bytes (`kMaxInternalKeyLength`, `4 * 256 - 96 - 1`) is not in the entry at all; the `long_key` word is then decoded as a `disk_cache::Addr` — bit 31 initialized, bits 28-30 file type, bits 26-27 reserved, bits 24-25 the block count less one, bits 16-23 which `data_#` file, bits 0-15 the first block — and where its file selector equals this file's own index the key is read from `8192 + start_block * block_size`, with `block_size` 256, 1,024 or 4,096 for file types 2, 3 and 4, and published only if the NUL Chromium writes sits exactly where `key_len` puts it and the key hashes to the entry's value. A block is an entry when its key — inline or long — hashes by SuperFastHash (`disk_cache::Hash`, checked against hashes Chromium wrote in the plaso corpora) to the u32 at offset 0 and carries its NUL; a key that does not verify is still read when NUL-terminated and of a recognised form. The key is then taken apart: a bare URL; `<n>/<n>/<url>`; the split-cache form `<n>/<n>/_dk_[s_]<top-frame site> [<frame site> ]<url>`; or a sparse child `Range_<key>:<hex>:<hex>` of any of them; the URL must open with `http://`, `https://`, `ftp://`, `ws://` or `wss://`. The bitmap is read for each entry's blocks. Where the selector names a different `data_N`, the module asks the `DataSource` it was handed for that file by name through `open_relative` — only where the source says it can open siblings — reads its first 16 header bytes, requires all three of the magic at offset 0, `this_file` at offset 8 and `entry_size` at offset 12 to match the file and block size the address implies (a file checked good for 1 KiB blocks says nothing about a 4 KiB address naming the same index, so each pair is checked on its own), and then reads `key_len + 1` bytes at `8192 + start_block * block_size` of that sibling under the same NUL, hash and form tests. A file-system parser that bundles a directory's `data_#` files onto each other (`attach_sibling_bundles`) makes that lookup work for a cache inside a disk image as it does for a loose directory or a ZIP. An external `f_` file is never opened.

**Produces.** One `BrowserCacheEntry` per recovered entry, subtype `browser_cache_entry`, as an `ArtifactType::ParsedRecord` parented to the file artifact and carrying no `DataSource` of its own. Every one states `browser: "Chrome/Edge"`, `cache_format` (`simple` or `blockfile`), the `url` recovered from the key, and a `name` of the form `Cached URL: <url>`. A Simple Cache record additionally carries the header's `version` and its `key_hash` as eight lowercase hex digits. A blockfile record carries `creation_time` when the entry held one: the u64 at offset 24 read as microseconds since 1601-01-01 — `base::Time`, the same epoch Chrome history uses — converted by `seance_core::time::webkit_us_to_unix_secs` to a bare integer count of **whole Unix seconds**, the microseconds discarded by a floor division. A record whose URL came from the separate `long_key` allocation rather than from the entry's own block says so explicitly with `key_source: "long_key_same_file"` and `key_length`, because a 1,000-byte tracking URL assembled from a second location in the file should be readable as such; one whose URL was read out of a sibling block file says `key_source: "long_key_other_file"` with `key_file`, `key_block`, `key_offset` and `key_length`. Every blockfile record also carries `key_hash` (the stored value, eight hex digits), `key_hash_verified`, `key_block_in_file`, `allocation` (`allocated`, `free` or `partly_free` by the bitmap, with `allocation_detail` and a name `Cached URL (freed entry): <url>` when not allocated) and `cache_key_form` (`url`, `prefixed` or `double_keyed`); a key that is not the bare URL adds `cache_key` as stored, a split-cache key adds `top_frame_site`, `frame_site` and, for `_dk_s_`, `subframe_document_resource: true`, and a sparse child adds `sparse_signature` and `sparse_child_id`. A key that does not hash to the entry's value is stamped `content_incomplete` saying so. A key that verifies by its hash but is of no recognised form is published with no `url`, its `cache_key` as stored, `url_unrecoverable_reason: "cache_key_form_not_recognised"` and a sentence, and counted in `entries_key_form_not_recognised`. An entry whose key lies in a sibling or external file that could not be read is still published as a `BrowserCacheEntry` with **no `url` field** — `creation_time` where the entry held one, `key_source`, `key_file`, `key_block`, `key_offset`, `key_length`, `url_unrecoverable_reason` as one of `sibling_lookup_unsupported`, `sibling_not_present`, `sibling_header_mismatch`, `sibling_short_read`, `sibling_key_not_terminated_at_length`, `sibling_key_hash_mismatch` or `external_file_not_opened`, the `content_incomplete` pair with the reason in words, and a `name` of `Cached URL not read from this file: <N>-byte key at data_X block B` (or `f_%06x`) — so an examiner can go and read it. A key holding bytes that are not valid UTF-8 is still published — a damaged URL is evidence of a fetch — with `url_encoding_lossy: true` and a sentence on `content_incomplete_detail` saying the string carries a replacement character where each invalid byte was and is therefore not exactly the URL the browser requested. Beside the entries, one or two `BrowserCacheParseStatus` records (subtype `browser_cache_incomplete`) per recognised cache file that yielded less than its whole listing — including a file delivered whole whose entries could not all be read — each carrying `browser`, `cache_format`, `file_name`, `entries_recovered`, `bytes_read`, `declared_size`, `max_cache_bytes`, the `content_incomplete` / `content_incomplete_reason` pair, a `name` of the form `Browser cache (partially parsed): <file> — <detail>`, and the same sentence on both `content_incomplete_detail` and `detail`. Where entries were seen and their URLs could not be produced, that record also carries `entries_unreadable`, `long_key_entries_unresolved`, `long_key_entries_in_other_file` (only the entries whose sibling key was not reached), `long_key_entries_unread_here`, `long_key_entries_recovered`, `long_key_entries_recovered_from_other_file`, `spanning_key_entries_truncated` and `entries_key_form_not_recognised`, and every entry record in the same file is stamped with the listing's shortfall — a URL that came out whole says "this URL was recovered whole, but … so the listing it belongs to is short", and one whose own bytes were substituted keeps its own more specific sentence and has the listing sentence appended to it rather than replacing it.

**Cannot.** **It cannot produce a single cached response body, and it reads no HTTP response metadata at all.** In the Simple Cache it stops at the end of the key; in the blockfile it never reads the four `data_stream_sizes` at offset 40 or the four `data_stream_addresses` at offset 56, so no cached image, page, script or JSON is located, hashed, typed, scanned or exported by this module, and no external `f_` file is ever opened. There is no status code, no response header, no content type, no content length and no response time on any record it writes. **It cannot date a Simple Cache entry** — none of the three header fields it reads is a time — so on the format that is Chromium's modern default, including Android and Linux, the URLs come out with no timestamp of any kind, and the `key_hash` it publishes is never checked against the key it read, so it cannot say the key belongs to the header above it. Where a blockfile entry does carry a time it is the entry's `creation_time` and nothing else: there is no last-used and no last-modified time, and `reuse_count` and `refetch_count` at offsets 12 and 16 of the in-tree specification are not read, so nothing says whether the resource was fetched once or a hundred times. That time is emitted as an integer of whole Unix seconds; the module renders no instant and states no zone, and a value of zero, a negative value, any value below the 1601-to-1970 difference, or a u64 too large to be an i64 causes the field to be **omitted entirely** rather than shown as 1601 or 1970. **A cache entry is not a visit.** It says the URL was in the browser's cache; it does not say a person typed it, that a page was displayed, or that a response was even successful. It reads nothing about how the fetch was initiated, so a top-level navigation, a subresource, an advert, a tracking pixel, a prefetch, a preload and a background or service-worker fetch are indistinguishable in the record beyond what a split-cache key says — the top-frame and frame sites the resource was fetched under, and the `s_` marker of a subframe document — and there is no referrer. It cannot attribute an entry to a user, a profile or a particular browser: `browser` is the fixed string `"Chrome/Edge"` on every record, and the entry record carries neither the cache file's name nor its path — that is on the status record only, and the link back to the file is the artifact parent. It cannot read either cache's index — not the Simple Cache's `index-dir/the-real-index` and not the blockfile `index`, whose own magic `0xc103cac3` this parser does not match — so it cannot state how many entries the cache held and cannot enumerate from anything but a byte scan. **An empty result from this parser means "not a cache", "a block file that holds no entries by design" (`data_0`, `data_2`, `data_3`), or a `data_#` whose header declares no allocations; a 256-byte block file whose header declares allocations and yields nothing gets a record, but the header's `num_entries` counts stream-data allocations as well as entries, so it cannot be reconciled with the listing.** A freed entry is told from a live one only by the allocation bitmap: a block Chromium freed and then reused for stream data holding bytes that happen to hash is not distinguishable from an entry, though the odds are 2^-32. `state` at offset 20 and `self_hash` at offset 92 are not checked, and no hash table or rankings list is walked. A block size other than 36, 256, 1,024 or 4,096 is reported and not walked. It still opens no external `f_` file, naming `f_%06x` on the record instead; and it cannot read a key through a block-file address needing more than 16,384 stored bytes, since `required_file_type` names no block file above `4096 * 4`. A key form Chromium may write that is not among the four it recognises — `_cn_` or any later isolation prefix — yields no URL: the key is shown as stored and counted, never split by guesswork. The Simple Cache path applies no form parsing and publishes the key bytes verbatim under the field name `url` whatever they are, and its `key_hash` is not verified. A spanning key cut off by the end of the scan is counted as a loss only where the bytes still present open like a cache key (a scheme, `Range_` or `<n>/<n>/`), and a key of 160 bytes or fewer can never be cut, so that counter speaks only for declared lengths of 161 to 927. Its records never reach the unified timeline: they are `ParsedRecord`s, and `seance_db` writes a `timeline_events` row only for `TimelineEvent` artifacts, `FileEntry` projections and parsed records with `subtype: "chat_message"`, so a blockfile entry's `creation_time` is absent from the timeline, from date-range queries and from the report's chronology. Its ceilings are 512 MiB (536,870,912 bytes) staged, held in memory and scanned per block file, a declared key length of at most 65,536 bytes, 16,384 stored bytes as the largest long-key allocation it will follow, 927 bytes of key held inside an entry, 160 bytes held in its first block, an 8,192-byte header of which the block size, allocation count, file index and bitmap are read, a 256-byte record stride, 20 header bytes for a Simple entry and 4 bytes minimum read before it will look at a file at all.

**Refuses.** It refuses to produce anything for a file whose first bytes match neither magic — no record, no status row — because the empty result is reserved for "this is not a cache", and a status record on every unrelated file in an image would put a spurious finding beside every one of them. A Simple Cache entry cut off inside its own 20-byte header, one declaring a key length of 0 or over 65,536, one whose declared key runs past the end of the file, and a source that supplies fewer key bytes than it declared each leave a `BrowserCacheParseStatus` saying which, because "this entry's URL could not be read" and "there was no cached entry here" must never render the same. A block file smaller than its own 8,192-byte header plus one 256-byte record does the same — the guard tested `size <= 8,192` while its message spoke of the header plus an entry, so a file of 8,193 to 8,447 bytes returned the empty vector reserved for "this is not a cache". It refuses to present an over-cap or under-delivered scan as a complete listing: an over-cap file is reported as `cap_reached` in preference to `short_read`, because the cap is why the rest was never attempted, and every entry in the file is stamped with the listing's shortfall — the wrong answer it exists to prevent is a 700 MiB `data_1` scanned to 512 MiB presenting a clean list of URLs from which an examiner concludes a site was never fetched. It refuses to publish a long key on the strength of an address alone: the NUL Chromium writes after the key must be exactly where `key_len` puts it and the key must hash to the entry's value, or the entry is counted as a loss instead, because publishing whatever lies at that offset would attribute some other cached URL to this entry's timestamp, which is a fabricated fetch. Where the two bytes at offset 8 that name this block file were not delivered, it refuses to claim any key is in "this file": every in-file address is then reported as being elsewhere, since a scan that cannot say which file it holds must not answer that question. It refuses in the other direction too, and for the mirror reason: a `long_key` word that Chromium could not have written — the initialized bit clear, an undefined file type above 4, the rankings file type 1 which never holds a key, a reserved bit 26 or 27 set on a block-file address, an allocation too small for `key_len + 1` bytes, or a block-file type that is not the one `Addr::RequiredFileType` picks for that length — is treated as not an entry at all and is **not** counted as a lost URL, because a false "evidence was lost" puts a fetch that never happened in front of an examiner and is as wrong as a silent drop. An external `f_` address is the exception: it is a real allocation out of reach, and is counted as a loss whatever length it claims. It refuses to read a key out of a sibling whose own header does not say it is the block file the address names with the block size the address implies — `data_2` beside `data_1` is otherwise just a name, and a key read from the wrong file would be attributed to this entry's timestamp — and refuses to call a sibling absent when the source could not look for it, naming `sibling_lookup_unsupported` and `sibling_not_present` apart. A free block (key length 0), a block whose key length reads negative or absurd, and a blockfile key over 65,536 bytes are likewise not entries and are not counted. It refuses to discard a key with invalid bytes, and refuses to present the substituted string as an exact URL. And it refuses to leave its sentence on `detail` alone: the sentence is written to `content_incomplete_detail`, the one key `frontend/src/lib/incompleteness.ts` reads, as well as to `detail`, because a record reaching an examiner as the bare token `cap_reached` says neither which file nor how much of it was read nor what is therefore missing.

### `plugin.browsers.history_parser`

**Reads.** Browser profile files, selected by **file name alone** — the `name` field of the `FileEntry` or `SystemArtifact` it is offered, never by a magic number, a path or a schema probe. Thirteen names are claimed: `History` (Chrome/Edge), `places.sqlite` (Firefox) and `History.db` (Safari) as history; `Cookies` and `cookies.sqlite` as cookie jars; `Web Data` and `formhistory.sqlite` as autofill; `Login Data` as saved logins; `sessionstore.jsonlz4`, `recovery.jsonlz4` and `previous.jsonlz4` as Firefox session restore; and `Preferences` / `Secure Preferences` as the Chrome/Edge extension inventory. A shadow-copy prior version of the file (a `VssPriorVersion` `ParsedRecord`) is read too and named by its `file_name`, since its `name` carries a `[shadow copy ...]` label; everything it yields repeats the snapshot id, label and creation time, and its sidecars are not searched. Anything else is declined in silence. The eight SQLite names are staged through `TempDb::spill` to a uuid-named file in the system temporary directory at a 500 MB ceiling and opened `SQLITE_OPEN_READ_ONLY`; the spill also stages the database's `-wal` sibling when the source can reach one and it is 512 MB or smaller, so rows committed but not yet checkpointed are read. The `-journal` sibling is deliberately not staged: a hot journal makes a read-only open fail outright with `SQLITE_READONLY_ROLLBACK`, and a journal holds pre-images rather than current rows. Every table is probed three-valued against `sqlite_master` (`type IN ('table','view')`); no column list and no schema version is read anywhere in this module, so each query stands or falls as written. Each walk binds its row budget as `LIMIT ?1` with a deterministic `ORDER BY` that breaks ties on the identity columns it already selects beyond the timestamp. Chrome/Edge history is `visits` joined to `urls` — `u.url`, `u.title`, `v.visit_time`, `u.visit_count`, `v.transition`, newest first — falling back to `urls` alone (`url`, `title`, `visit_count`, `last_visit_time`) where `visits` is absent; `downloads` is read for `target_path`, `tab_url`, `total_bytes`, `start_time`, `end_time`, `danger_type` and `opened`, with the first and last hop of `downloads_url_chains` by `chain_index` where that table exists. Firefox history is `moz_historyvisits` joined to `moz_places` (`url`, `title`, `visit_date`, `visit_count`, `visit_type`), falling back to `moz_places WHERE visit_count > 0` on `last_visit_date`; bookmarks are `moz_bookmarks` rows of `type = 1` joined to `moz_places` on `b.fk = p.id` with `p.url IS NOT NULL`, for `title`, `url`, `dateAdded` and `lastModified`. Safari history is `history_visits` joined to `history_items` (`hi.url`, `hv.title`, `hv.visit_time`, `hi.visit_count`), falling back to `history_items` ordered by `visit_count DESC`. Cookies come from Chrome's `cookies` (`host_key`, `name`, `value`, `encrypted_value`, `path`, `creation_utc`, `expires_utc`, `last_access_utc`, `is_secure`, `is_httponly`) and Firefox's `moz_cookies`; logins from Chrome's `logins` (`origin_url`, `username_value`, `password_value`, `date_created`, `date_last_used`, `times_used`); typed form values from Chrome's `autofill` (`name`, `value`, `count`, `date_created`, `date_last_used`) and Firefox's `moz_formhistory` (`fieldname`, `value`, `timesUsed`, `firstUsed`, `lastUsed`). The two non-SQLite shapes are read whole or not at all: a session-restore container must be at least 12 bytes, carry `mozLz40\0` in its first eight and a declared decompressed length in the next four, is read at a 256 MB ceiling and expanded by LZ4 to at most 512 MB, and the JSON is walked `windows[] → tabs[] → entries[]`, taking the entry at the tab's 1-based `index` — or the last entry where `index` is absent or out of range; a `Preferences` file is read at a 64 MB ceiling and must hold `/extensions/settings` as a JSON object or it is not treated as a profile at all. **Four time treatments, three of them converters.** Chrome/Edge, and the extension `install_time` Chrome holds as a decimal string, are WebKit microseconds since 1601-01-01, shifted by 11,644,473,600,000,000 µs. Firefox is PRTime — microseconds since the *Unix* epoch, no shift. Safari's `visit_time` is a Core Data REAL: seconds since 2001-01-01, shifted by 978,307,200 s, with the fraction split off and floored to microseconds. Chrome's `autofill.date_created` / `date_last_used` and Firefox's `moz_cookies.expiry` are already Unix **seconds** and are passed through on a `> 0` guard alone. Before each SQLite walk it reads the store's schema version — Chromium's from the `meta` table's `version` row (`PRAGMA user_version` is 0 on every real Chromium store) with its `last_compatible_version` beside it, Firefox's and Safari's from `PRAGMA user_version` with 0 read as "not recorded" — and compares it with a range every endpoint of which was read out of a real store on this machine: Chrome/Edge `History` 20..=70 (plaso's `chrome_history` at 20, 32, 33, 36; a Chromebook at 41; android2022 at 51; a 2026 desktop profile at 70), `Cookies` 5..=24, `Web Data` 77..=152, `Login Data` 24..=43, Firefox `places.sqlite` 10..=82 (plaso at 10 and 23, `places118.sqlite` at 75, a 2026 profile at 82), `cookies.sqlite` 5..=16, `formhistory.sqlite` 5..=5 (one real store), Safari `History.db` 13..=16 (plaso at 13, macos2021 at 15, ios2022ffs at 16). Every column each walk reads is resolved through a candidate list against `PRAGMA table_info` before the query is written — `full_path` is meta.version 20's name for a download's target and `secure`/`httponly` meta.version 5's for the cookie flags, while a download's `tab_url`, `end_time`, `danger_type`, `opened` and `url`, a cookie's `encrypted_value` and a login's `date_last_used` are optional because a named real store lacks them and are read as NULL there — and a walk whose required field no candidate resolved is skipped while the other walks of the same file still run.

**Produces.** `ParsedRecord`s typed by what they came from, each parented to the file artifact. One `BrowserHistory` record with subtype `browser_visit` per visit row — the browser, the URL, the title, `visit_time` in Unix seconds and `visit_time_us` in Unix microseconds, `visit_count`, and `transition_type` resolved to a name (`link`, `typed`, `auto_bookmark`, `auto_subframe`, `manual_subframe`, `generated`, `auto_toplevel`, `form_submit`, `reload`, `keyword`, `keyword_generated`, else `other` for Chrome; `link`, `typed`, `bookmark`, `embed`, `redirect_permanent`, `redirect_temporary`, `download`, `framed_link`, `reload`, else `other` for Firefox). Each dated visit also gets a `TimelineEvent` carrying `timestamp` as Unix seconds, `timestamp_desc: "Web Visit"`, `source_module: plugin.browsers.history_parser`, the browser, the URL and the title. One `BrowserDownload` per `downloads` row with the target path, `total_bytes`, `start_time`/`start_time_us` and `end_time`/`end_time_us`, the raw `danger_type` integer, `was_opened`, the raw `url_chain_start`, `url_chain_final` and `tab_url`, and — this is the part that matters — `source_url` beside `source_url_origin`, which states whether that URL is the final hop of the redirect chain (`url_chain_final`), its first hop (`url_chain_start`), the initiating tab (`tab_url`) or `unknown`, because `downloads.tab_url` is only the page that started the download and is frequently a different host or empty. One `BrowserBookmark` per Firefox bookmark with `date_added`/`date_added_us` and `last_modified`/`last_modified_us`. One `BrowserCookie` per jar row with host, cookie name, path, creation, expiry and last-access times in whole seconds, `is_secure`, `is_httponly`, `value` where plaintext is actually present, and `value_encrypted` — computed on the Chrome jar from an empty plaintext column beside a non-empty `encrypted_value` blob, and stamped `false` unconditionally on the Firefox jar, which stores values in the clear. One `BrowserLogin` per saved login with the origin, the plaintext username, `times_used`, `date_created` and `last_used`, and `has_saved_password` / `password_encrypted` both set from whether a blob is actually stored, because claiming encryption over an empty column read as "a password is here, sealed by the OS key" when nothing was. One `BrowserAutofill` per typed value with the field name, the value, `use_count`, `first_used` and `last_used`. One `BrowserSession` per open tab with its URL, title and 1-based window number. One `BrowserExtension` per `extensions.settings` entry with the extension id and, where the profile states them, the manifest name, version and description, the declared permissions, `enabled` (`state == 1`), `from_webstore`, the install path and `install_time`. Every count is qualified rather than implied: a walk that reached its budget appends a `parse_incomplete` marker typed `BrowserHistoryIncomplete`, `BrowserDownloadIncomplete`, `BrowserBookmarkIncomplete`, `BrowserCookieIncomplete`, `BrowserLoginIncomplete` or `BrowserAutofillIncomplete` with status `CapReached`, the source table, `max_entries` and `rows_read`, its sentence on `content_incomplete_detail` and `detail`; a walk that fetched rows it could not decode appends one with status `RowsUndecodable` carrying `rows_dropped`, `records_recovered` and the decoder's first error on both `content_incomplete_detail` and `inventory_incomplete_detail`, so the record count is published as a floor; a non-SQLite file read short leaves `BrowserSessionIncomplete` / `BrowserExtensionIncomplete` with `FileNotReadInFull`, `declared_bytes` and `bytes_read`, and one with no data source at all leaves `FileNotRead`; and a database staged short — or whose `-wal` was refused or could not be reached — stamps `content_incomplete: true` with `content_incomplete_reason` / `wal_incomplete_reason` on **every record it produced** plus a `SqliteSpillIncomplete` marker, which carries its sentence on a bare `detail`. A file with no data source yields a `BrowserHistoryParseStatus` record with status `Identified`; a database SQLite could not read yields the same type with status `ParseFailed` and the error text; a `downloads` or `moz_bookmarks` table that exists and will not read yields a `BrowserDownloadIncomplete` or `BrowserBookmarkIncomplete` record with status `ParseFailed`, while the history already recovered is kept. Beside them, `ParserStaleWarning` records with `subtype: "parser_stale"`, the `app` (`chrome-history`, `chrome-cookies`, `chrome-webdata`, `chrome-logins`, `firefox-places`, `firefox-cookies`, `firefox-formhistory`, `safari-history`), `store`, `parser_record_type`, `validated_against` naming the real files, `detail` and a `name`: `SchemaOutsideValidated` (the shared `StaleWarning` marker with `seen_schema_version`, `supported_range` and `message` — a disclosure with no incompleteness claim — carrying `chromium_last_compatible_version` on a Chromium store and, only when that floor is past the validated maximum, a sentence that Chromium itself states a reader written for anything older cannot read the file, with `content_incomplete: true` under reason `unvalidated` and that sentence as `content_incomplete_detail`), `SchemaVersionNotRecorded` (no incompleteness claim), `SchemaVersionUndetermined` (`content_incomplete: true`, reason `unresolved_structure`), and `SchemaFieldsUnresolved` per table whose required field no candidate matched — `source_table`, `unresolved_fields`, `present_columns`, `records_recovered: 0`, both incompleteness pairs under `unvalidated` — with that walk skipped and the rest of the file still read. None of those four carries the type of the records it failed to produce, and the case index groups by record type, so a profile with no downloads and an unreadable `downloads` table does not read as a profile with one download.

**Cannot.** **It cannot tell you who was at the keyboard.** A visit row is a record that this browser profile stored a navigation; it names no account, no session and no person, and nothing in it distinguishes a navigation someone chose from one the page performed — `auto_subframe`, `manual_subframe`, `embed` and `framed_link` are sub-document loads, `redirect_permanent` and `redirect_temporary` are the server's doing, and `reload` may be automatic. It cannot say how the browser qualified a Chrome visit beyond its core type: `transition & 0xFF` is kept and the raw integer is not published, so the high-order qualifier bits — forward/back, from the address bar, client- or server-redirect, chain start and end — are discarded, and a back-button revisit is reported as `link`. A Firefox `visit_type` outside 1-9 collapses to `other` with the number not published, so a type Firefox adds later cannot be told from a corrupt one. It cannot give a Safari visit a transition at all: the schema has none. It cannot link a visit to the visit that led to it — `visits.from_visit` is not read, so no referrer chain is built — and `visit_duration` is not read, so no record says how long a page was open. `visit_count` is the URL's lifetime aggregate from `urls` / `moz_places`, repeated on every visit row for that URL: it is not a count of the visits listed and can exceed them. Where `visits` or `moz_historyvisits` is absent the fallback is not a visit list at all — one record per URL, carrying only the last visit instant and no transition, so a URL visited fifty times contributes one record; the Safari `history_items` fallback carries no timestamp of any kind and `visit_time` is null on every record of it. **It recovers no deleted rows.** It reads the live B-trees through SQLite only: a freeblock, a freelist page, unallocated page slack and the rollback journal's pre-images are outside it, and a history entry the user cleared is simply not here — the forensic SQLite parser is what reads those. It cannot mark which rows came from the write-ahead log: SQLite replays the staged `-wal` into the query, so an uncheckpointed row is indistinguishable from one in the main file, and where the log was refused or unreachable the records say so by `wal_incomplete_reason` — `cap_reached` for one over 512 MB, which is not staged at all rather than truncated, `short_read` for one the source under-delivered, and `wal_not_reachable` for a database whose own header says WAL mode beside a source that cannot produce siblings. It renders no instant: every time it publishes is an integer count from a fixed epoch — Unix seconds, or microseconds in the `_us` fields — carrying **no time zone and no formatted string**, so any wall-clock reading, and any zone applied to it, comes from whatever displays the record. Cookie, login and autofill instants are published as whole seconds only, with no `_us` companion, although the source columns are microseconds, so two cookies created inside the same second cannot be ordered from the records. Its Safari sub-microsecond remainder is floored, not rounded, because an f64 of seconds-since-2001 resolves to about 100 ns at present-day values; flooring can place a visit fractionally early, never late. Only visits reach the timeline: downloads, bookmarks, cookies, logins, autofill values, open tabs and extensions produce no `TimelineEvent`. Its schema knowledge stops at the newest real store it was validated on — Chrome `History` 70, `Cookies` 24, `Web Data` 152, `Login Data` 43, Firefox `places` 82, `cookies` 16, `formhistory` 5, Safari `History.db` 16 — and a store past that is parsed on the assumption its columns mean the same, with the `SchemaOutsideValidated` marker beside the rows; every field but a download's target and the two Chrome cookie flags has one candidate name, so a rename is a skipped walk named on a `SchemaFieldsUnresolved` marker rather than a substituted column. A column list that will not read is the same failure as an unreadable catalogue and takes the `ParseFailed` path; an unanswerable catalogue probe for `downloads` or `downloads_url_chains`, made after the visits walk has run, does the same. Coverage is narrower than "the browser": no Safari downloads and no Safari or Chrome/Edge bookmarks — Chrome keeps bookmarks in a JSON file this module does not claim — no Firefox download history, no Chrome `keyword_search_terms`, no Safari `Cookies.binarycookies`, no Firefox `logins.json`, no Chrome `autofill_profiles` or `credit_cards`, no `moz_bookmarks` folder hierarchy or tombstones, and no favicon, Top Sites or Shortcuts store. A download record cannot say whether the download finished: `received_bytes`, `state`, `interrupt_reason` and `mime_type` are not read, `total_bytes` is the size expected rather than received, and `danger_type` is published as its raw number, unmapped. A cookie record cannot name the page that set it or the request that used it, does not say whether the cookie was persistent — `has_expires`, `is_persistent`, `samesite` and `source_port` are not read — and decrypts nothing: Chrome's `encrypted_value` is bound to an OS key this module never touches. A login record recovers which account was saved for which site and when, never the password, and nothing on it says why a blob is absent: `blacklisted_by_user`, `signon_realm` and `date_password_modified` are not read. An open-tab record carries no timestamp of any kind and is the tab's *current* entry only — back/forward entries, closed tabs and closed windows are not emitted, and a tab with no `entries` array, an empty one, or a chosen entry with an empty URL is passed over, so the records are not a count of the tabs that were open. A bookmark whose `moz_places` row is missing is dropped by the join, and a Firefox place with `visit_count = 0` is excluded from the places fallback outright. The undecodable-row count is exact only for the columns a walk binds with `?`: the history, download and bookmark walks take every column that way, but the cookie, login and autofill walks default most of theirs, so a blob or a NULL where a timestamp belongs becomes a zero and then an omitted time, counted nowhere. Its ceilings are: 100,000 rows for each history, download, cookie, login and autofill walk, 10,000 for the Firefox bookmark inventory, 500 MB for a staged database, 512 MB for its `-wal`, 256 MB for a session container and 512 MB for its expansion, and 64 MB for a `Preferences` file — each recorded on a marker when it fires. The row caps drop the oldest rows, save in the Safari `history_items` fallback, which is ordered by `visit_count DESC` and therefore drops the least-visited while its marker's sentence is written in newest-first terms; `source_table` is what tells the examiner which ordering applied. Display strings are truncated on character boundaries: the URL in a record's `name` at 80 bytes, a value or origin at 60, a timeline label at 100 characters.

**Refuses.** It refuses to guess which file it is looking at. Selection is by exact file name, so a history database renamed, carved, or offered under any other name is not read — and equally, a file merely *named* `History` is put to SQLite rather than assumed to be Chrome's. It refuses to answer a question it could not ask: a schema probe that fails — `SQLITE_NOTADB`, a carved fragment, a first page overwritten — is an error and not "the table is not there", because those two used to give the same answer and an empty artifact list reads as "this browser held no history"; the failure becomes a `BrowserHistoryParseStatus` record with status `ParseFailed` instead. Where the catalogue does read and the root table is genuinely absent, nothing is produced and no marker is left: that absence is the finding, and it is recorded only in the log. It refuses to let a cap look like a total: every walk binds one probe row past its budget and latches truncation the moment that row appears, so "this profile held exactly 100,000 visits" and "we stopped after 100,000" can never be the same answer. It refuses to leave undefined which rows survive a cap: ordering on `visit_time` / `dateAdded` / `start_time` alone let SQLite's sorter decide, and two runs over the same evidence could list different sites, so every walk breaks ties on the identity columns it already selects — the URL first wherever there is one. It refuses to skip a row the decoder rejected: the row is admitted against the budget, counted, and declared with the decoder's reason, because a blob where `visit_time` should be an integer used to leave a `debug!` line and a listing that read as exact. It refuses to let schema drift in the `downloads` or `moz_bookmarks` table pass quietly: a table that exists and will not read produces its own `ParseFailed` record while the history already recovered is kept, because both were once discarded by `if let Ok`, which rendered exactly like a profile with no downloads and no bookmarks. It refuses to fabricate a date: a WebKit value of 0 or below the 1601→1970 gap, a PRTime of 0 or below, and a Core Data 0.0, negative, non-finite or out-of-range value are all omitted from the seconds fields and from the timeline rather than rendered as 1601, 1970 or 2001-01-01. It refuses to expand a container that declares an unusable size: a `mozLz4` header claiming 0 or more than 512 MB decompressed is refused with a marker saying so, because the magic has already established that this *is* a session file and an empty return would assert the profile had no open tabs. It refuses to equate "not read" with "nothing there" wherever it holds the bytes to know the difference: over a byte ceiling, short of a declared size, or with no data source attached, the session store and the `Preferences` file leave an explicit marker rather than an empty list, and an LZ4 block that will not decompress or a body that is not JSON is returned as an error into the processing log for the same reason. It refuses to treat a generic `Preferences` file as a profile without checking the bytes — no `/extensions/settings`, no records, and the same silence for a body that is not JSON at all — and it refuses to inventory component extensions the browser ships (`location == 5` with no manifest name), which are noise in an installed-extension list. It refuses to read a file under 12 bytes, or one without the `mozLz40\0` magic, as a session container: neither is a session file, and neither leaves a record. And it refuses to stage the rollback journal beside the database, because a hot journal makes the read-only open fail entirely and a journal's pre-images are older data, recovered elsewhere. It refuses to spend `PRAGMA user_version` 0 as "older than the range" — on every real Chromium store it is 0 and the version lives in `meta` — and refuses to spend a version that would not read as in range. It refuses to widen a validated range past the files actually opened, and refuses to substitute a column for a required field no candidate matched, skipping that walk and naming the field instead.

### `plugin.browsers.leveldb_storage`

**Reads.** A Chromium DOM-Storage LevelDB, and it finds one by name and path rather than by content: the artifact's `path` metadata, lower-cased, must contain `leveldb`, `local storage` or `session storage`, and its `name` must end `.log` (read as the write-ahead log) or `.ldb`/`.sst` (read as a compacted SSTable). Nothing in the bytes selects it, and nothing else is examined, which is what keeps it off the unrelated `.log` files an evidence tree is full of. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent` and asks for random access. The bytes are staged in one buffer through `read_capped` up to `MAX_LOG_BYTES`, 268,435,456 bytes, with no external LevelDB library in the path — the framing is walked byte by byte, and `snap` is used for Snappy and nothing else. The log is read as 32,768-byte blocks of physical records, each a 7-byte header of `[u32 crc][u16 length][u8 type]` and then `length` payload bytes; fewer than 7 bytes left in a block is trailer padding and is stepped over, a type-0 record skips to the next block boundary and discards any fragment being assembled, and types 1, 2, 3 and 4 are FULL, FIRST, MIDDLE and LAST, reassembled into logical records. The CRC field is read past and never checked — this is extraction, not integrity checking. Each logical record is read as a LevelDB `WriteBatch`: the leading `u64` sequence number is stepped over unread, the operation count is the little-endian `u32` at offset 8, and then that many operations of `[u8 tag][varint32 key length][key]`, with `[varint32 value length][value]` following when the tag is 1 (a put); tag 0 is a deletion and carries a key only. Varints are LEB128, read to five bytes for a varint32 and ten for a varint64; a continuation byte past that is refused, and so is a value whose last byte carries more significant bits than the width can hold — the loop used to keep `(b & 0x7f) << 28` and drop that byte's top three bits, so an over-wide length read back as a small one and was used as though the file had said so. A table is read from its 48-byte footer: the last 8 bytes must equal the LevelDB magic `0xdb47_7524_8b80_fb57`, then two BlockHandles as varint64 (offset, size) pairs inside the 40 bytes before it. The metaindex handle is decoded and discarded — no filter, bloom or metadata block is read — and the index handle is followed. The index block's every value is read as a handle to a data block; each block is taken as its `size` content bytes, with the one byte immediately after them deciding what they are: 0 stored as-is, 1 decompressed with `snap`'s raw Snappy decoder. Inside a block the entries are prefix-compressed — `[varint32 shared][varint32 non_shared][varint32 value length]`, the key built from that many bytes of the previous key plus the suffix — running up to a restart array whose entry count is the block's last 4 bytes. Each key is an `InternalKey`: the user key is everything before its 8-byte trailer, and the first byte of that trailer is the value type, 0 meaning a deletion tombstone. From either path the same schema gate applies. A key is a storage value only if its first byte is `_` (0x5f) and it contains a NUL: the origin is the bytes between them and the storage key is everything after the first NUL, each through a lossy UTF-8 conversion. A value's first byte is the Chromium encoding marker — 0x00 means the remainder is UTF-16LE, read as little-endian pairs; 0x01 means the remainder is Latin-1/UTF-8; any other first byte and the whole value including that byte is read as UTF-8.

**Produces.** One `LocalStorageItem` `ParsedRecord` per decoded entry, subtype `local_storage`, parented to the file artifact it came from, carrying `browser` (always the string `Chrome/Edge`), `origin`, `storage_key`, `deleted`, the decoded `value` where there was one, and a `name` of the form `localStorage <origin> [<key>]`. And, where the read stopped short of the whole file in one of the ways the module detects, exactly one `LevelDbParseStatus` record, subtype `local_storage_incomplete`, carrying `browser`, `file_name`, `content_incomplete`, `items_emitted`, `bytes_read`, `declared_size`, `max_log_bytes`, the reason token — `cap_reached`, `short_read` or `unresolved_structure` — and one sentence saying what was not read, written once and published on both `content_incomplete_detail` (the key the examiner-facing reader displays) and `detail`, with a `name` repeating the file and that sentence. The same `content_incomplete`, `content_incomplete_reason` and `content_incomplete_detail` triple is stamped on every storage item recovered from that file, so the shortfall travels with each value wherever it is exported and not only on a summary row.

**Cannot.** It cannot date anything. Not one timestamp is read from this format: the module emits no date, no time, no zone and no timeline event, and the two sequence numbers the format does carry are discarded — the `u64` at the head of every WriteBatch is stepped over, and of the `InternalKey`'s 8-byte trailer only the type byte is used, the 56-bit sequence being dropped. So it cannot say when a value was written, when it was deleted, or which of two records for the same origin and key is the later one. It cannot say who did anything: a `localStorage` value is what script running on a page wrote for that origin, not an act by a person and not a visit — the origin names whose storage the value belongs to and nothing about how the browser came to be there. A record marked `deleted` is the deletion, not the value deleted: a log delete operation carries the key alone and a table tombstone's value bytes are dropped, so the module can say a key was removed and can never say what it held. It performs no version resolution and no deduplication — the same key recovered from a `.log` and from a `.ldb`, several versions of it inside one table, and a data block an index names twice all come out as separate equal records — and it reads no `MANIFEST`, `CURRENT`, `LOCK` or LevelDB info `LOG`, so it cannot say whether a table it read is still live or was superseded by compaction. A storage item carries no file name and no offset; which file a given value came from is recoverable only through the record's parent artifact, not from the record's own fields. It decodes one key schema and no other. Only `_<origin>\0<key>` is recognised, so `META:` and `VERSION` keys are skipped for want of the leading `_` — the database's own schema version and its per-origin metadata are therefore never decoded — and a key whose first byte is `_` but which holds no NUL, or whose origin part is empty, is dropped without a note. Any LevelDB under a matching path whose keys are shaped some other way is admitted by the gate, walked, and yields nothing; where such a file parses structurally cleanly there is no status record either, so "this origin stored nothing" and "this is a schema this reader does not decode" render identically. It verifies no CRC — neither the log record header's nor a block trailer's, of which only the single compression byte is read — so framing that happens to look well-formed is read as a record, and a bit-flipped value is published as a value. It does not resynchronise after damage: in a log, a header claiming more payload than the file holds, a length above 32,768 bytes, or an undefined record type abandons the entire remainder of the file rather than restarting at the next block boundary, and a block's prefix-compressed entries stop at the first varint that will not read, because every later key is built on the one before it. It reads only data blocks the index block names — a block whose index entry is unreadable is skipped, and there is no scan for orphaned blocks. Three ways of losing entries it does not report at all, and an examiner should be told them: an unterminated FIRST or MIDDLE fragment that the next FULL, FIRST or type-0 record discards is lost silently, and only a fragment still pending at the end of the file is marked; a tail of one to six bytes, too short to hold a header, ends the walk unmarked; and a `WriteBatch` whose header declares zero operations is reported complete with every operation byte after that header unread. Where it does report, it reports coarsely: one flag is folded across the whole file, so the status record cannot say which batch, which block or at what offset the parse stopped, and its `bytes_read` is the number of bytes staged, not the point of failure. The reason is coarse too — a cap or a short read is set first and a structural failure cannot replace it, so a file that was both truncated and unparseable reports only `cap_reached` or `short_read`. Its decoding is lossy by construction: origins, keys and values go through lossy UTF-8 or UTF-16 conversion, so invalid bytes and unpaired surrogates become U+FFFD; an odd trailing byte of a UTF-16 value is dropped; a value whose marker byte is neither 0x00 nor 0x01 is rendered with that byte included in the string; a value of no bytes and a value of one marker byte both render as the empty string, which no stored empty string can be told from; and the original bytes are not kept on the record, so the rendered string cannot be compared back to what was stored. Its ceilings, each with its number: 256 MiB (`MAX_LOG_BYTES` = 268,435,456 bytes) staged per file, and a file larger than that is parsed only to that point with `cap_reached` on every record; 32,768 bytes as the log block size and the largest physical record length believed; 48 bytes of footer and 40 bytes of block handles in a table; five bytes for a varint32 and ten for a varint64. There is no cap on the number of entries emitted, no cap on the number of data blocks an index may name, no cap on a single value's length, and no cap on the size a Snappy block may inflate to.

**Refuses.** It refuses to look at a file whose path does not contain `leveldb`, `local storage` or `session storage`, or whose name does not end `.log`, `.ldb` or `.sst`, and it refuses a file artifact that carries no readable source at all; both refusals are silent — no record of any kind. A LevelDB copied out of its directory, or a storage database recovered by carving without its path, therefore produces nothing; the gate exists because a parser that read every `.log` on a disk as Chromium storage would report on files it has no business reading. It refuses to present the shortfalls it does detect as a whole read, which is the defect the status record exists for (pinned by the tests in this crate). A FIRST/MIDDLE fragment still unterminated at the end of the file, a WriteBatch that decodes fewer operations than its own count declares, a record header pointing past the end of the file, a record length above the block size, an unknown record type, an unknown operation tag, a block under 4 bytes or one whose declared restart array does not fit, a block cut mid-entry, an entry claiming to share more prefix bytes than the previous key holds, a data block that cannot be located or will not decompress, and a `.ldb` whose footer magic is wrong or which is shorter than its own 48-byte footer all mark the file `unresolved_structure` and emit the status record — with `items_emitted: 0` where nothing decoded at all, because a file under a Local Storage path whose framing is unreadable is a finding, not an empty profile. A source that delivers fewer bytes than it declared is `short_read` and says how many of how many arrived. The counterweight is enforced: a file that parses whole carries no incompleteness keys anywhere, and an empty `.log` produces nothing and no status record — though an empty `.ldb` or `.sst` is refused as a table and does produce one, since a file too short to hold a footer is not a table this reader can say anything about. It refuses to decompress a block whose compression byte is anything but 0 or 1: that block's keys are not read, and the table is marked structurally unresolved rather than reported short. It refuses to attribute an entry whose `InternalKey` is shorter than its own 8-byte trailer to any user key, dropping it and marking the table. And it contains no unsafe code and no panicking path: the crate is `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, and garbage bytes recover nothing rather than aborting the examination.

### `plugin.browsers.webcache`

**Reads.** The Internet Explorer / legacy-EdgeHTML web cache index, `WebCacheV01.dat`, which is an ESE (Extensible Storage Engine) database, and it finds one by content rather than by name. The module subscribes to `FileEntry`, `FileContent` and `ParsedRecord` artifacts (the last only for a shadow-copy prior version: it is read on the same terms as a live file, everything it yields repeats the snapshot id, label and creation time and states that the version's sidecars were not searched, and a `ParsedRecord` that is not a prior version is declined before its data is touched; for such a version the name tested below is its `file_name`, since its `name` carries a `[shadow copy ...]` label); an artifact with no attached data source is declined in silence. Every other candidate passes one gate: `seance_core::file_detection::detect_file_type` over a looped read of the first 512 bytes must return `EseDatabase`, which means the four bytes `EF CD AB 89` stand at offset 4 — not the extension, not the path, so a `WebCacheV01.dat` carved out of free space or renamed reads the same as one under `AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\WebCache`. That gate admits every ESE database on the machine, `SRUDB.dat` included, so the file's `name` metadata is consulted for exactly one purpose: whether its basename, ASCII-lowercased, contains `webcache`. That decides only whether a failure is reported or passed over; it never decides what is parsed. The database is then staged whole, because libesedb opens by path: the size must be non-zero and no more than 4 GiB (`4 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024`), the whole file is read into memory through `read_exact_or_fail` with short reads looped, and a read that cannot be completed fails the parse rather than staging the readable prefix . The bytes are then written a second time, to a uuid-named `seance_webcache_<uuid>.dat` in the system temp directory, behind an RAII guard that removes them on every exit path, unwinding panic included. libesedb (the crate `libesedb` 0.2, the same engine behind the SRUM and User Access Logging readers) opens the staged copy. What separates a WebCache database from any other ESE file here is a single schema probe: a table literally named `Containers` must open. The table catalog is then enumerated once, and if a single table's name will not read the whole catalog is withheld rather than returned short, because the catalog is only ever used to assert that something is absent. `Containers` is the inventory: each row gives `ContainerId`, read through signed and unsigned integer coercions, and `Name` as text — the label `History`, `Content`, `Cookies`, `MSHist…`. Each declared id then names the table `Container_<id>`, opened by that name and walked row by row. Of each row it reads four columns, located by case-insensitive name, and no others: `Url`, `AccessedTime`, `ModifiedTime`, `AccessCount`. A `Url` that ESE keeps outside the row arrives as `Value::Long`, which carries no bytes at all, and is fetched from the long-value tree and decoded as UTF-8 — that variant is resolved rather than dropped, because dropping it lost exactly the longest URLs, the ones carrying the query strings a case turns on. Both time columns are read as Windows FILETIMEs — unsigned counts of 100-nanosecond ticks since 1601-01-01 UTC — either from an ESE `DateTime` cell or by integer coercion. The `Url` value is published as it stands but for one decoration: the exact prefix `Visited: ` is stripped, and where the remainder holds an `@` whose tail begins `http`, `res:`, `about:` or `ftp`, everything up to and including that first `@` is dropped.

**Produces.** One `WebCacheEntry` parsed record, subtype `webcache_entry`, per container row that holds a non-empty URL, parented to the file artifact the database came from, carrying `browser` (always the literal `Internet Explorer / Edge`), `container` — the label verbatim from the `Containers` row, not a classification of this module's making — `url`, and `raw_url` only where cleaning changed the string, so the decoration that was removed stays on the record. `accessed_time` and `modified_time` are RFC 3339 instants with an explicit `+00:00` offset, carrying whatever sub-second part the FILETIME held at 100-nanosecond resolution, and each is present only where it decoded; `access_count` is present only where the column held a non-negative integer. `name` is `{container}: {url}`, which is the one line a listing shows. There is no container id, no entry id and no path on the entry record. And at most one `WebCacheParseStatus` record, subtype `parse_incomplete`, of two distinct shapes. Where the file never opened, it carries `status` `DatabaseNotStaged` or `DatabaseNotOpened`, `entries_recovered: 0`, the failure's own message, both incompleteness flags set, and nothing about containers — there were none to count. Where the walk ran and did not give up everything the database names, it carries `status` `DatabaseNotReadInFull` when bytes this database holds were refused (an unreadable container table, a refused row, or a `Containers` table that would not iterate) and `ContainerRowsWithoutTables` when the only fault is an inventory gap, plus `containers_declared`, `entries_recovered`, `rows_skipped`, `container_list_unreadable`, `catalog_enumerated`, an `unreadable_containers` list naming each container by `container_id` and label with its `reason` (`table_not_opened` or `records_not_iterated`), and an `orphan_containers` list with `reason: table_absent_from_catalog` — so an examiner reads which containers the database declared and this walk did not publish, rather than a bare flag. Each stamp carries a written sentence on `inventory_incomplete_detail`, and on `content_incomplete_detail` where that flag is set; those are the keys the examiner-facing reader displays, and a database whose only fault is an inventory gap carries no content sentence at all. Every surviving entry is stamped `inventory_incomplete` whenever anything at all was not read — a declared container that produced nothing, or a single refused row — because the entry list is the only surface an examiner opens. `content_incomplete` is stamped only where bytes this database holds were refused, so a container row whose table is simply gone never brands the recovered URLs as partial.

**Cannot.** **It cannot say that a person visited a URL.** A row in the `Content` container is a fetch the WinINET stack cached; a row in `History` is a URL the index recorded. Either can be written by a page's own subresources, a redirect, a preload, or a program that is not a browser at all, and there is no user, session or profile on the record — no account name, no profile path, nothing but the parent link to the file the database was read from. The one account name WebCache does carry, the `Visited: user@` decoration, is removed from `url` and survives only in `raw_url`. That removal is cruder than it reads: it strips at the **first** `@` anywhere in the value whether or not the `Visited: ` decoration was there, so a cached URL whose query embeds an absolute URL after an `@` is published with the embedded host as its `url` and its `name`, and only `raw_url` holds what the row said. It reads four columns of a container row and two of the `Containers` table, and nothing else: no cache entry's on-disk filename, no expiry, no creation or sync time, no cookie name or value, no container directory — a `Cookies` row is published as a URL like any other — and it decodes nothing from the container label itself, so an `MSHist01…` name's date window is not read. It does not deduplicate: the same URL in two containers is two records, and the record count is not a count of distinct URLs. Its schema probe is one table name, so any ESE database carrying a table called `Containers` has its rows published as Internet Explorer / Edge entries. It recovers nothing that ESE has freed: it opens the one staged copy and nothing beside it, so no transaction log or checkpoint file is replayed, an uncommitted write is not seen, a deleted row is not recovered, and nothing is carved out of page slack. It writes no timeline event, so a decoded `accessed_time` sits on the record and not on the case's unified timeline, beside Chrome and Firefox visits that are on it. Absence of a timestamp is not absence of activity: a FILETIME of 0, anything before the Unix epoch, and anything at or past 253,402,300,800 Unix seconds — the first instant RFC 3339 cannot express, which is what catches Windows's far-future `never` sentinel — all produce an omitted field rather than a date, and a negative value in a signed column is refused rather than reinterpreted, because reinterpreting `-1` as unsigned yields a visit dated 30828 AD that passes every range check and sorts to the end of any timeline. A negative `AccessCount` is refused the same way (through the shared `seance_ese_util::value_to_u64`), because 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 visits published as a count is a finding the evidence does not support. **On schema drift it is loud in one direction and quiet in the other**, and an examiner should know which: the `Url` column being absent, or holding a value this decoder cannot turn into text, counts every such row into `rows_skipped` and raises the content-incompleteness banner — but `AccessedTime`, `ModifiedTime` and `AccessCount` are located by name with no record kept when the name is not there, so a build meeting a schema that renames or drops them publishes entries with no dates and no count and says nothing about it. A container whose `Name` will not read publishes its entries with an empty container label, uncounted. A `Containers` row the ESE layer refuses, or one whose `ContainerId` will not coerce, counts as **one** skipped row and its whole `Container_<id>` table is then never opened — so a `rows_skipped` of 1 can stand for every URL in a container, and that figure mixes inventory rows with content rows in one number. Selection is only as good as the detector: `detect_file_type` returns the first signature that matches and tests roughly twenty offset-0 magics, several of them two or three bytes, before the offset-4 ESE test, and an ESE database's first four bytes are a page checksum rather than a constant — a database whose checksum opens with one of those magics is classified as an archive and never reaches this module. A file that fails the ESE gate produces nothing at all, not even a refusal, however it is named, because the name is consulted only after the gate passes. It cannot run at all in a build without the `esedb` feature: the parser is registered behind `#[cfg(feature = "esedb")]`, which is in the default set but is selected by neither published Windows asset — x86_64 builds `--no-default-features --features e01` because `libesedb-sys` does not compile under MSYS2 gcc, and Windows/ARM64 builds with no native-C features at all — and with it off a `WebCacheV01.dat` inside a disk image yields nothing whatever, not even a refusal, because the refusal record lives in this module. A panic inside libesedb is caught by the orchestrator and recorded as a `FatalError` row in the case's processing log, but it leaves no WebCache record at all; the staged copy is still removed. Its ceilings are few and exact: a zero-length file refused, no more than 4 GiB staged per database — which is also, because the file is held in memory and written again to the temp directory, roughly 4 GiB of resident memory and 4 GiB of temp space per database, with no check that the temp filesystem has room — and no cap of its own on containers, rows or entries, every recovered entry being held in memory until the walk ends. A database over the 4 GiB bound is refused whole rather than read in part.

**Refuses.** It refuses to read a database it cannot stage in full. A short read of the evidence is an error naming the file, not a smaller database — a staged prefix would let libesedb open a partial file and publish whatever subset of containers it could still parse as if the whole WebCache had been recovered. It refuses to let an unreadable database look like a browser that was never used. Where the file's own name says WebCache, a staging failure leaves a `DatabaseNotStaged` record and a failure to open or walk leaves `DatabaseNotOpened`, each with `entries_recovered: 0`, the failure's own message, and the sentence *this WebCache database was recognised but could not be read; the absence of browsing history below is not evidence that the browser was never used* . It refuses to make that claim about an ESE database that is not a WebCache: the identical failure on a `SRUDB.dat` produces nothing at all, because a browsing-history warning there would be a false statement about the machine — and the same silence therefore covers an unnamed or renamed WebCache database, whose failure is passed over. It refuses to call a container's table absent unless it saw the whole catalog — one unreadable table name withholds the catalog entirely, an unopenable container is then reported as unreadable rather than orphaned, and `catalog_enumerated: false` says on the record that absence was never established. It refuses, equally, to treat every quiet container as damage: a `Containers` row whose `Container_<id>` table is simply not in the catalog is a row that outlived its table — an inventory gap — and is reported as one without branding the recovered URLs, because a warning that fires on ordinary Windows evidence is a warning an examiner stops reading, and it then fails on the case where it mattered. That distinction was measured once, not assumed: on a real Windows 8.1 `WebCacheV01.dat` of 33 MB, `Containers` declared ids 1-8, 10-17 and 19-23 and the catalog held exactly those 21 tables, with 1,549 rows and not one orphan row or unreadable `Url`; the gaps at 9 and 18 are containers Windows scavenged, and scavenging removes the row and the table together. That database is not carried in this repository, so the test that re-checks the measurement skips wherever the fixture is absent — through the corpus gate, so the skip is announced and `SEANCE_REQUIRE_CORPUS=1` turns it into a failure. For the same reason it refuses to count a blank or ESE-NULL `Url` as a loss — WebCache keeps placeholder rows, and counting them as refused put a content-incompleteness banner on every entry of a perfectly healthy database — while a value that is present and will not decode is counted, because that is a URL that existed and was not recovered.

### `plugin.bulk.aes_keys`

**Reads.** The bytes of a decoded memory image — the physical address space the memory tier hands on as the data source of its own `MemoryImage` record — or a raw evidence stream directly, read in 8 MiB windows that overlap by 240 bytes so a key schedule straddling a window boundary is still seen whole in the next window. It reads nothing else about the image: no page tables, no process list, and not one field of the record it is given beyond the `subtype` marker that says the record is a memory image at all. At every single byte offset it takes the following 176, 208 or 240 bytes as a candidate AES-128, AES-192 or AES-256 key schedule, expands the leading 16, 24 or 32 bytes by the FIPS-197 key-expansion recurrence, and compares every derived word against what is actually in memory, abandoning the offset at the first word that disagrees — which is what makes a byte-by-byte sweep of gigabytes tractable. A hit is therefore arithmetic rather than a heuristic: the expansion is anchored to the FIPS-197 Appendix A.1 and A.3 vectors by test, and a 100,000-byte pseudo-random buffer with no schedule planted in it yields nothing.

**Produces.** One `RecoveredKey` record per verified schedule, carrying the algorithm and its size in bits, the absolute offset in the scanned source where the schedule begins, and the key itself as lower-case hex — the first 16, 24 or 32 bytes of the schedule. Each carries `evidence_grade: "scanned"` and a note in as many words that the schedule was verified in memory, that confirming it against a volume header is the decryptor's job, and that only then is it `Validated`. Beside them, where anything was found, the scan cap was reached or some range would not read, one `RecoveredKeySummary` giving the number of keys, `bytes_scanned` — the bytes the sweep actually covered, not the limit it set out to reach — the declared `source_size`, `scan_capped` for the 8 GiB cap, and `short_read`, which when set comes with `content_incomplete: true` and `content_incomplete_reason: "short_read"`. The summary also lists each unreadable range as `unreadable_ranges` with `unreadable_range_count`, `unreadable_ranges_listed_all` and `unreadable_bytes` . Keys are deduplicated by offset and size, so the same schedule seen twice through the window overlap is reported once, while one key resident at two addresses is reported twice — once per address, which is what the evidence shows. The key is written into the case record verbatim: `key_hex` is not one of the metadata names the ingest redactor strips, so it persists and is served back like any other field.

**Cannot.** It cannot recover a key that is not sitting in RAM as a forward-expanded schedule in order from the key: a stored inverse (decryption-order) schedule, an implementation that keeps only the key and expands into registers, and a schedule interleaved with anything else all verify as nothing, and their absence from the results is not evidence no cipher was live. It tolerates no bit errors whatsoever — one mismatched four-byte word rejects the region — so a decayed cold-boot capture yields nothing rather than a degraded answer. It reads at most 8 GiB of any one source. A range it cannot read — a hole in a crash dump, LiME, AVML, QEMU or hibernation layer, which refuses rather than splice two regions together, or a bad sector — is stepped over and the sweep resumes past it; each such range is listed by exact offset and length in `unreadable_ranges` (at most 1,024 listed, all counted in `unreadable_range_count` and `unreadable_bytes`), and `short_read` is set . A readable run shorter than 4 KiB lying wholly between two unreadable 4 KiB probes is counted as unreadable, never as scanned. It cannot say whose key it is: there is no owning process, no virtual address, no volume and no timestamp on the record, only a physical or file offset, so a recovered key raises no timeline event and names nothing it belongs to. And it cannot hand the key to anything — the BitLocker decryptor accepts only a password or a recovery key and the LUKS decryptor only a passphrase — supplied for one run through `POST …/credential` or at start, or for reading through `POST …/unlock` — so a recovered key is a record an examiner reads, not an unlock this product performs.

**Refuses.** It refuses to run on ingest. Sweeping every byte of a multi-gigabyte source is worth its cost when an examiner wants keys and is pointless latency on every raw disk, so it is registered as opt-in, is never attached to an artifact type in the pipeline, and runs only when triggered against a named artifact.
