It refuses to scan a parsed record that is not the memory tier's decoded image — a record of any other kind produces nothing at all, not even a note saying it was declined — and it refuses to produce anything for an artifact with no data behind it. It refuses to call a verified schedule the key to anything: the schedule is mathematically real, "this is the volume key" is only proven by decrypting the volume header, and every record says the grade is `scanned` and names who would have to raise it.

### `plugin.bulk.decode_rescan`

**Reads.** The content of a file — it subscribes to `FileContent` and `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::Stream` — looking for encoded or obfuscated spans it can lift out into child buffers for the orchestrator to re-queue through the whole parser and carver set. It is opt-in, triggered per artifact, because it multiplies the pipeline's work. An artifact with no data source yields nothing, and one whose `decode_generation` metadata is 8 or more (`MAX_DECODE_DEPTH`) yields nothing, which is what stops a gzip-of-gzip or an XOR child re-queued into this module from recursing forever. The first 64 MiB (`MAX_INPUT`) of the source is read and the tail beyond it left unscanned. A stretch below that the source will not deliver — a bad sector, a gap in a memory image — is found to the byte, recorded and stepped over, and every readable run either side of it is read; runs are never joined, so no encoded span is decoded across a gap. Three decoders run over each run. Single-byte XOR keys are recovered by proof, not guessed: XOR preserves byte-to-byte deltas, so one pass compares each adjacent pair's delta against the first delta of eleven plaintext witnesses — the PE/DOS header `MZ\x90\x00\x03\x00`, the DOS stub text, a ZIP local header, `%PDF-1.`, the PNG signature, `GIF89a`, `SQLite format 3\0`, the OLE2 signature, ELF32 and ELF64 headers, and `http://` — each at least six bytes so a chance match under a wrong key is about one in 2^40 per position, and a candidate key is confirmed only by XORing the whole witness back out; a key of zero is rejected. Base64 spans are runs of at least 24 base64 characters, trimmed to a multiple of four, decoded with the standard alphabet, kept when the result is at least 16 bytes, under ceilings of 4,096 decoded spans (`MAX_BASE64_SPANS`) and 64 MiB of decoded output (`MAX_BASE64_TOTAL_OUT`) — a span past either is counted and not decoded, and the span the output ceiling falls inside is cut at it and marked truncated. Gzip members are found at every `1f 8b 08` and inflated, under a total output budget of 512 MiB across all members and at most 4,096 attempts, each member read one byte past the remaining budget so a cut stream can be told from a whole one.

**Produces.** One `FileContent` child per decoded span, up to 256 (`MAX_CHILDREN`), each carrying an in-memory data source of the decoded bytes and `type: "DecodedBuffer"`, `decode_method` (`xor`, `base64`, `gzip`), `parent_offset` (the span's offset in the scanned buffer), `byte_size`, `decode_generation` one more than the parent's, and a `name` of `decoded_<method>_<offset>` — or, for an XOR child, `decoded_xor_<key>` with `xor_key` as `0x<hh>` and `xor_evidence` naming the witness that proved it, so the deobfuscation can be checked rather than taken on trust. A gzip member or base64 span cut by its output budget carries `content_incomplete: true` and `truncated_reason: "decode output cap reached"`, so a downstream parser does not treat a partial buffer as a whole file. XOR children come first, at most two (`MAX_XOR_KEYS`) whole-buffer copies, so the 256-child cap can never drop a proven deobfuscation in favour of the 256th base64 span. One `DecodeRescanSummary` (`subtype: "summary"`) is emitted only when something was withheld: when the input was larger than 64 MiB (`input_capped: true`, `bytes_scanned`, `source_size`), when some of it would not read (`short_read: true`, `unreadable_ranges` by offset and length, `unreadable_bytes`, and the `content_incomplete` pair with reason `short_read`), or when more decodable spans or proven keys were found than emitted (`children_found`, `children_emitted`, `children_dropped`, `xor_keys_found`, `xor_keys_emitted`), or when the base64 decoder's own ceilings were reached (`base64_decode_capped`, `base64_spans_not_decoded`, `base64_span_cap`, `base64_output_cap`; the undecoded spans count in `children_found`). A file with nothing to decode yields nothing.

**Cannot.** It cannot deobfuscate what it cannot prove: a single-byte XOR key is emitted only when one of eleven plaintext signatures XORs back out of the buffer, so an XOR-obfuscated file whose plaintext carries none of those witnesses — a text document, a script, a configuration file — is left as it is, and multi-byte, rolling or RC4-style keys are not attempted at all. It cannot decode base64 that uses the URL-safe alphabet, is broken across lines, or is shorter than 24 characters, and it drops any decoded span under 16 bytes; a base64 run inside a larger alphanumeric run — an identifier, a hash — is decoded to noise if it happens to decode, and no test of plausibility beyond length is applied. It cannot inflate zlib, deflate-raw, bzip2, xz, zstd or LZ4 — only gzip members with deflate method 8 — and it stops after 4,096 members or 512 MiB of output with nothing on any record but the summary's `children_dropped`. It does not scan past the first 64 MiB. It cannot say what a child is; that is the re-queued parsers' job, and a child none of them claims is a buffer of decoded bytes with a method and an offset. It emits at most 256 children per buffer and at most two XOR keys, disclosing the rest as dropped. A child's `parent_offset` is its offset in the source; an XOR child's is the start of the readable run it transforms — 0 unless a gap came before it, when its name carries that offset too. It cannot see bytes the source will not deliver, nor an encoded span that crossed one; those ranges are named, not scanned. It bounds recursion by generation only: eight generations of 256 children each is still a very large fan-out, and nothing here bounds the total.

**Refuses.** It refuses to guess an XOR key: every key on every byte "succeeds", and a guessed key would bury the case under a buffer of noise per file, so a whole-buffer child is produced only for a key the bytes themselves prove, with the witness named on the child. It refuses key zero, which is the buffer in the clear and would otherwise be XORed back and forth forever. It refuses to recurse without bound, stopping at generation 8. It refuses to present a budget-cut gzip member as whole, stamping `content_incomplete` on the child. It refuses to drop a child in silence: an input over 64 MiB, a span past the 256th, or a proven key past the second is counted and disclosed on the summary, because silence would read as "the whole buffer was scanned and these are all the children". It refuses to let a base64 or gzip span outrank a proven XOR key under the cap. And it refuses to run on ingest.

### `plugin.bulk.features`

**Reads.** Raw bytes, not records: an `UnallocatedSpace` artifact, or a `ParsedRecord` that is the decoded memory image `seance_memory` emits, recognised by its `subtype: "memory_image"` and nothing else. It streams the artifact's data source in 8 MiB windows that overlap by 1,024 bytes on each side, and each start offset in the source is owned by exactly one window — a hit whose start lies outside the window's owned range is discarded as the neighbour's, or as one the window edge cut short — and it stops after 8 GiB (`SCAN_CAP`); a range that will not read ends the window at the byte it starts, is recorded by exact range, and the sweep resumes on its far side with no window spanning it. Over each window it runs eleven compiled byte-regex selectors — `email`, `url`, `ipv4`, `mac`, `btc`, `ccn`, `phone`, `ssn`, `iban`, `vin` and `gps` — five of which then have to pass a semantic check before the hit is kept. Every kept hit is tallied into a `FeatureHistogram` as it streams past, keyed on the pair (kind, exact value), so the counts are complete even once the per-occurrence records are capped; the histogram holds at most 100,000 distinct values (`MAX_DISTINCT_VALUES`), and a hit that would introduce a new value beyond that ceiling is counted as dropped while an already-tracked value's count climbs regardless. The `UnallocatedSpace` artifacts it reads are the inter-partition gaps the partition module declares (each a window over the parent image from a gap of at least 512 bytes) and, since `ROADMAP` §5.4, the free-cluster runs the NTFS parser proves free from `$Bitmap`. It runs automatically, on every such artifact, because it declares no `execution_mode` and the trait's default is `ExecutionMode::Automatic`.

**Produces.** One `Feature` record per hit, carrying four fields and no more: the selector `kind`, the matched text as `value`, the `device_offset` it was found at, and `subtype` set to the same kind — at most 20,000 per artifact (`MAX_FEATURE_RECORDS`), the lowest offsets first, with the same value found at two offsets being two records. Beside them, when anything was found, the scan cap was hit or some range would not read, one `FeatureSummary` giving `features_found` — the true total, counted whether or not a record was emitted for it — with `records_emitted`, a `by_kind` count over the whole sweep, `records_capped`, and the sweep's coverage: `bytes_scanned` (the bytes actually covered, not the limit), `source_size`, `scan_capped`, and `short_read`, which when set comes with `content_incomplete: true` and `content_incomplete_reason: "short_read"`, and `unreadable_ranges` with `unreadable_range_count`, `unreadable_ranges_listed_all` and `unreadable_bytes`. And, when anything was found, one `FeatureHistogramSummary` per scan: `total_hits`, `distinct_values`, `hits_dropped`, `capped` with `max_distinct_values` = 100,000 named on the record, `top_n` = 100, the 100 most-common `(kind, value, count)` entries as `top` with `top_omitted` giving how many distinct values the table left out, `by_kind` with `hits` and `distinct_values` per selector, the same coverage fields, and a `note` in words — a capped histogram says so, gives the exact number of hits not tallied, and states that counts for the tracked values are exact while the distinct-value total is a floor. A card number is reported only if Luhn passes and the digits match a real issuer prefix at a length that issuer uses; an IBAN only if mod-97 gives 1; a VIN only if the ISO 3779 check digit in position 9 agrees; an SSN only outside the ranges the SSA never issued; a GPS pair only if latitude and longitude are in range.

**Cannot.** It cannot give you a device offset, despite the field being called `device_offset`: the number is an offset inside the artifact that was scanned. On an inter-partition gap it is an offset into that gap's window, and the gap's own `offset_bytes` lives on the parent record, not on the `Feature`; on a memory image it is an address in the decoded physical layer, which is not an offset in the capture file. It can see a filesystem's free clusters where the NTFS parser emits them, but it still cannot see **file slack**, the unused tail of a cluster a live file owns: the NTFS, FAT, exFAT, ext4, HFS+ and APFS parsers publish it as `SlackSpace` regions, and this module does not subscribe to that type; and it does not subscribe to `RawEvidence`, so a raw RAM or hibernation capture the memory tier cannot decode is swept for AES keys by `plugin.bulk.aes_keys` and never for selectors. It cannot match text stored as wide characters: every selector is a non-Unicode byte pattern over ASCII classes, so a UTF-16 email or URL in memory produces nothing, which is the same class of false absence recorded against case search as `SEARCH-002`. Its selectors are narrower than their names: a phone number must begin with `+`, an SSN must be written dashed as 3-2-4, an IBAN must be unspaced and upper-case, and a GPS pair must be two decimal degrees with at least three decimal places separated by a comma. It cannot tell you which 20,000 hits you are looking at once `MAX_FEATURE_RECORDS` is reached — the kept records are the lowest offsets reached first, so a whole selector kind can appear in `by_kind` with no record behind it, though the histogram's `top` and `by_kind` still count every hit — and past 100,000 distinct values it cannot say what the dropped values were, only how many hits they carried. It cannot date any hit, because a `Feature` carries no timestamp and nothing from which one could be derived. It cannot scan bytes the source will not deliver; each unreadable range is listed on the summary, and a readable run under 4 KiB lying wholly between two unreadable 4 KiB probes is counted as unreadable. Finally, when nothing was found, no cap was hit and every byte was read it emits no record at all, so scanned-and-clean and never-ran look identical in the case.

**Refuses.** It refuses to publish a syntactic match that fails its own arithmetic, which is most of what a byte pattern this loose finds on real evidence: a digit run that fails Luhn or carries no real issuer prefix at a length that issuer uses, an IBAN whose mod-97 is not 1, a seventeen-character run whose ISO 3779 check digit disagrees, a 3-2-4 group in an area the SSA never issued or with a zero group or serial, a coordinate pair outside latitude 90 or longitude 180, and a uniform run of one repeated character offered as a card or a VIN. It refuses to report a hit a window edge cut short, deferring every start offset to the one window that owns it, so a match is never reported as a shorter value at a wrong offset or twice. It refuses to present a capped histogram as complete: the record states the ceiling, the exact number of hits not tallied, and that the distinct-value total is a floor. It refuses to sweep any other `ParsedRecord`: a record from another module returns an empty result immediately, because running selectors over already-parsed record JSON is `seance_api::entities`'s job and doing it twice would put two counts of one fact in the case. It refuses to scan an artifact carrying no data source, returning nothing rather than a record saying a scan happened. And it refuses to emit a value it cannot render as valid UTF-8, dropping the hit rather than publishing bytes as text.

### `plugin.bulk.net_carve`

**Reads.** A memory image or a raw evidence stream, byte by byte, looking for IPv4 packet headers that prove themselves. It is opt-in — triggered per artifact from the modules UI or API, never on ingest — and subscribes to `ParsedRecord` and `RawEvidence` with `InputCapability::Stream`: a `ParsedRecord` is accepted only when its `subtype` is `memory_image` (the decoded address space `container.memory_image` emits), and an artifact with no data source yields nothing. The source is read in 8 MiB windows with a 64 KiB overlap on each side — a packet's total length fits in 16 bits, so a packet whose header lands near a window boundary is seen whole by the window that owns its start — up to a scan cap of 8 GiB (`SCAN_CAP`); a range that will not read ends the window at the byte it starts, is recorded by exact range, and the sweep resumes on its far side with no window spanning it. At every offset, `seance_bulk::net::packet_at` accepts a packet only when the version nibble is 4, the IHL is 5..=15, the total length is at least the header length, at least 20, and within the buffer, the protocol is 1, 6 or 17 (ICMP, TCP, UDP — nothing else, to keep false positives near zero), and the IPv4 header checksum verifies as a ones-complement sum of 0xffff; after a hit the scan advances past the whole packet so a payload cannot re-match, and a hit whose start is outside the window's owned range is discarded as the neighbour's or as one the edge cut short.

**Produces.** Nothing at all when no packet was carved from a sweep that read every byte up to its limit; when none was carved from a sweep the 8 GiB cap cut short or in which a range would not read, the `NetworkCarveSummary` alone, with `packet_count` 0. Otherwise exactly two artifacts: one `FileEntry` named `carved_packets.pcap` (`type: "CarvedPcap"`, `subtype: "pcap"`, `packet_count`, `byte_size`, and a `note` saying capture timestamps are unknown and recorded as zero) carrying an in-memory data source with a pcap 2.4 file of link type 101 (`LINKTYPE_RAW`, raw IP with no link-layer header), snaplen 65,535, every record's `ts_sec` and `ts_usec` written as 0, `incl_len` the bytes copied and `orig_len` the header's total length, each packet's exact bytes copied from the window it was carved in — so it appears in the file grid, exports, and can be re-parsed by the pcap module; and one `NetworkCarveSummary` (`subtype: "summary"`) with `packet_count`, `bytes_scanned` (the bytes the sweep actually covered — every readable byte; unreadable ranges are listed in `unreadable_ranges` with `unreadable_range_count`, `unreadable_ranges_listed_all` and `unreadable_bytes`), `source_size`, `scan_capped` (whether the source was larger than 8 GiB), `short_read` (whether any range would not read, with `content_incomplete` and reason `short_read` when it did), and `endpoints`, the first 200 packets' source and destination addresses, protocol number and absolute offset in the source. No timeline event: a carved packet has no time.

**Cannot.** It cannot date a packet. Nothing in a raw IP header says when it was sent, so every pcap record carries a zero timestamp and the file's own note says so; a consumer that reads the pcap as a chronological capture is reading a fabrication of its own making. It cannot carve IPv6, nor any IPv4 protocol other than ICMP, TCP and UDP — GRE, ESP, SCTP and the rest are left in the image. It cannot reassemble a TCP stream, decode a payload, or tell a packet the machine sent from one it received, from one that sat in a buffer copied out of a file: a packet-shaped structure anywhere in memory or on disk — a cached pcap, a driver ring buffer, a swapped page — carves alike and the summary attributes it only by offset. It cannot see past the 8 GiB scan cap, and says so; nor into a range the source will not deliver, which it steps over and lists (`short_read`, `unreadable_ranges`). It keeps every carved packet's bytes in memory until the pcap is written, so a source dense with packets costs memory in proportion. It carves on a memory image's physical address space, not on a process's virtual view, so a packet split across non-contiguous physical pages is not found. It lists only the first 200 endpoints on the summary; the pcap holds them all. A checksum-valid header over 20 random bytes is possible and, at roughly one in 65,536 windows that also pass the version, IHL, length and protocol tests, a very large image may carry a handful of false packets.

**Refuses.** It refuses to invent a capture time, writing zero rather than the acquisition time or the current time, because a carved packet has no capture time and inventing one would put it on a timeline. It refuses a packet whose header checksum does not verify, and refuses any protocol but ICMP, TCP and UDP, because the value of a carved packet is that it proved itself. It refuses to report a hit a window edge cut short, deferring it to the window that owns it. It refuses to run on ingest: the sweep reads up to 8 GiB and writes a file, so it is opt-in. And it refuses to emit an empty pcap, or a summary when nothing was carved from a sweep that read everything, so an absence of the record means the sweep read the whole source and found nothing, not that it did not run — the processing log says which.

### `plugin.calendar.ical_parser`

**Reads.** An iCalendar stream (RFC 5545), chosen by content first and name second. It subscribes to `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::Stream` and `ExecutionMode::Automatic`, passes over `is_directory: true` and any artifact with no data source, and reads a 512-byte probe at offset zero with `read_full`. The probe admits the file when, after an optional UTF-8 byte-order mark and ASCII whitespace, it begins `BEGIN:VCALENDAR` case-insensitively; failing that, the file is admitted only if its lowercased name ends `.ics`, `.ical` or `.ifb`. Two further facts are taken from the same probe: whether `BEGIN:VCALENDAR` appears anywhere in the window, and whether the probe delivered fewer bytes than the file declares (up to 512), which is treated as 'unknown', not 'no'. The whole file is then streamed, starting after the byte-order mark and leading whitespace, a preamble measured on the stream itself: when the whole probe is preamble the run is followed in 64 KiB reads to its first other byte, and the content tests above — the short-read test included — are made on a fresh 512-byte window from there, a short read of that window judged against what the file declares past the preamble. The stream is fed through `SourceCursor` and a `BufReader` into the `ical` crate's parser with no byte cap and no event cap: that parser unfolds continuation lines, requires the first non-empty line to be exactly `BEGIN:VCALENDAR`, walks components by `BEGIN`/`END`, and yields one calendar per `VCALENDAR` block or an error. Every `VEVENT` of every calendar that parsed whole is read for `SUMMARY`, `DESCRIPTION`, `LOCATION` (each with RFC 5545 text escapes decoded), `DTSTART` with its `VALUE` and `TZID` parameters, `DTEND` with `TZID`, `ORGANIZER` and every `ATTENDEE` with `CN` and a `mailto:` prefix stripped, `STATUS`, `UID`, `RRULE`, `CREATED`, `LAST-MODIFIED` and `SEQUENCE`; the calendar's `X-WR-CALNAME`, `PRODID` and `VERSION` are read from the first calendar carrying each. Dates are reformatted, not converted: `YYYYMMDD` becomes `YYYY-MM-DD`, `YYYYMMDDTHHMMSS` becomes `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS` with a trailing `Z` kept where the value had one, and any other shape is passed through as it was.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per `VEVENT`, parented to the file, with `type: "CalendarEvent"` and whichever of `summary`, `description`, `location`, `dtstart`, `dtstart_tzid`, `dtend`, `dtend_tzid`, `organizer` (`CN <address>` or the bare address), `attendees` (an array in the same form), `status`, `uid`, `recurrence` (the raw `RRULE` text), `created`, `last_modified`, `sequence` (an integer where it parses, else the text) and `calendar_name` were present, plus `all_day`, which is always present and true when `DTSTART` carried `VALUE=DATE` or was eight digits. Absent properties are omitted, never fabricated. Then one `CalendarSummary` record per file with `calendar_name` (`X-WR-CALNAME`, else the file name), `event_count`, and `prodid` and `version` where found; where the parser stopped at a malformed block after at least one calendar parsed, the summary also carries `content_incomplete: true` and `inventory_incomplete: true`, both reasons `unresolved_structure`, `parse_stopped: true`, `parse_error` and a `message` copied to both `_detail` keys saying the events after that block were not read. Where no calendar parsed at all and either the probe held the marker or the probe was short, one `CalendarParseStatus` record (subtype `ical_not_parsed`) is emitted instead, with `status` of `ContentUnreadable` (reason `short_read`) when the probe was short, `ParseFailed` (reason `unresolved_structure`, with the parser's error) when the parser stopped, or `NoCalendarBlock` otherwise, plus `file_name`, `content_incomplete: true`, a `message` and the same sentence in `content_incomplete_detail`. The Analysis screen files `CalendarEvent` under 'Calendar Events' and the tree under 'Calendar'. No `TimelineEvent` is produced and no Unix timestamp is written, so an appointment appears on the record and not on the case timeline. None of these records is given an artifact-level subtype.

**Cannot.** It cannot put an event at a moment in time. `dtstart` is a reformatted string: a UTC value keeps its `Z`, a floating value has no offset, and a `TZID` is copied verbatim beside it and never resolved, so `2021-07-04T15:30:00` with `dtstart_tzid: Europe/London` is not converted to an instant, and no `VTIMEZONE` block is consulted; nothing is written that the timeline could sort on. It cannot expand a recurrence: `RRULE` is kept as text, `RDATE`, `EXDATE`, `EXRULE` and `RECURRENCE-ID` are not read, so a series is one record and an overridden instance is indistinguishable from its master. It cannot give an end to an event expressed as `DTSTART` plus `DURATION`, which is not read, and it reads no `CATEGORIES`, `PRIORITY`, `CLASS`, `TRANSP`, `URL`, `ATTACH`, `GEO`, `DTSTAMP`, `X-` property or `VALARM`. It reads `VEVENT` only: `VTODO`, `VJOURNAL` and `VFREEBUSY` components are parsed by the crate and discarded here, and a `.ifb` free-busy file therefore yields a summary with `event_count: 0` and nothing else. It cannot recover part of a calendar block: the crate yields a `VCALENDAR` whole or as an error, so a calendar of a thousand sound events followed by one malformed line, one truncated `VEVENT`, or one component it does not know — `BEGIN:VAVAILABILITY`, `BEGIN:VPOLL`, any vendor `X-` component, or any sub-component of a `VEVENT` other than `VALARM` — loses every event in that block, and reports `ParseFailed` (if it was the only block) or a stopped summary (if a sound block preceded it). It cannot tell a truncated file from a non-UTF-8 one from a read error: the crate's line reader turns an I/O error or an invalid UTF-8 byte into end-of-stream, so a Latin-1 accent in a `DESCRIPTION` ends the file there and is reported as a malformed block (`NotComplete`), not as an encoding problem, and the same is true of a source that fails mid-read; the module's own doc comment says only that such input 'never panics'. `calendar_name` and `prodid` come from the first calendar carrying them, so a concatenated export of several calendars files every event under the first name. It has no byte ceiling and no event ceiling: the bytes are streamed, but the parsed calendar tree of a large `.ics` is held whole in memory before a record is written. A UTF-8 byte-order mark is skipped only at the start of the file. Its behaviour is pinned by four fixtures in `tests/fixtures/` written for the tests — `bom_crlf.ics` is `normal.ics` given the BOM and CRLF line ends Outlook writes, by script — and no calendar exported by a real client is in this tree.

**Refuses.** It refuses to invent a diary from a name. A file admitted on its `.ics`/`.ical`/`.ifb` extension whose probe holds no `BEGIN:VCALENDAR` anywhere and was read in full is returned as nothing — no status record — because a note or placeholder named `.ics` is not a calendar this parser failed to read, and a warning that fires on ordinary files is one an examiner learns to skip. It refuses the opposite silence too: where the content already said calendar, or where the evidence delivered fewer probe bytes than it declares, an empty result is replaced by a `CalendarParseStatus` record, and a short probe is `ContentUnreadable` rather than `ParseFailed`, because seven bytes of a declared four kilobytes cannot say the file held no appointments (fail closed). It refuses to present a fragment as the whole: a parse that stopped part-way stamps both incompleteness pairs and the error on the summary, so `event_count` cannot be read as the custodian's full diary . It refuses to fabricate a UTC instant from a floating or zoned time, and refuses to fabricate any property the event did not carry. It never errors the pipeline on content — every outcome is `Ok` with records or without — and never writes.

### `plugin.crypto.bitlocker_decryptor`

**Reads.** Every `Partition` and `RawEvidence` artifact with a data source, and it decides for itself from the first 512 bytes. `is_bitlocker` reads the volume boot record with `read_exact_or_fail` — a source under 512 bytes is not BitLocker — and looks for one of three 16-byte identifiers at either of two positions: the standard volume GUID `4967d63b-2e29-4ad8-8399-f6a339e3d001`, the BitLocker To Go GUID (`…d011`) or the mid-conversion GUID `92a84d3b-dd80-4d0e-9e4e-b1e3284eaed8` that Windows writes while a volume is still encrypting, at `0xa0` (Windows 8 and later) or `0x1a8` (Vista and 7 and To Go media), the first layout tried first. The three 8-byte little-endian FVE metadata block offsets follow at `0xb0` or `0x1b8` respectively, and `bytes_per_sector` is read from the BPB at `0x0b`. This test comes before the credential is looked at: whether a volume is encrypted is a fact about the evidence, whether anyone can open it a fact about the run. Without a credential, `describe_bitlocker` reads the first metadata block whose offset is non-zero and whose `read_block` succeeds: `-FVE-FS-` at its start, a metadata size at `+0x40` between 0x30 and 16 MiB, the encryption method at `+0x64`, the volume GUID at `+0x50`, and the typed entry list from `+0x70`, from which every VMK entry's protection type at `+0x1a` is read and labelled — clear key, TPM, startup key, TPM and PIN, recovery password, password, or `unknown (0x….)`. With a credential — first one an examiner supplied for this volume and this run (`POST …/credential`, kind `bitlocker_password` or `bitlocker_recovery_password`, visible to this module through `seance_core::credential` for one `process` call on that artifact only), else the `--bitlocker-password`/`SEANCE_BITLOCKER_PASSWORD` or `--bitlocker-recovery-key`/`SEANCE_BITLOCKER_RECOVERY_KEY` given to `seance_cli` once at start, password winning when both are set — `unlock_bitlocker` parses the first block that yields an FVEK AES-CCM blob and at least one VMK protector carrying a stretch-key salt and an AES-CCM blob, plus the volume-header entry (type `0x000f`) saying where the file system's real boot sectors were relocated to. A password is UTF-16LE, SHA-256 hashed twice; a recovery password is eight groups of six digits, each divisible by 11 and under 0x10000 after division, decoded to 16 bytes and hashed once; either is stretched 1,048,576 rounds of SHA-256 with the protector's salt, and the VMK then the FVEK are unwrapped with AES-256-CCM, whose MAC is what authenticates a correct credential.

**Produces.** For a BitLocker volume with no credential: one `ParsedRecord` (type `VolumeDecryption`, subtype `detected_locked`, `status: "NotUnlocked"`, `scheme: "BitLocker"`, `volume_name`, `volume_artifact_id` — the volume's artifact id, which the encryption detector's BitLocker record for a `-FVE-FS-` volume also carries, and which every record below carries too ) carrying `bitlocker_encryption_method` (the cipher label, or `unknown (FVE metadata unreadable)`), `bitlocker_key_protectors` (an array of labels in metadata order, empty where no block read), and, where a block read, `bitlocker_volume_identifier` in the mixed-endian GUID form `manage-bde` and escrow records use and `sector_size` from the BPB; with `content_incomplete` and `inventory_incomplete` both `true` with reason `encrypted`, the same sentence in both `_detail` keys and in `detail`, and a `name`. That pair and scheme are what the Needs attention queue keys on, where the row takes the recovery password or the password for this volume. For a successful unlock: one artifact of the parent's own type (`Partition` or `RawEvidence`), parented to it, named `<name> (BitLocker decrypted)`, with `bitlocker_decrypted: true`, `bitlocker_encryption_method`, `volume_artifact_id`, `offset_bytes: 0`, `size_bytes` and `sector_size: 512`, carrying a decrypting `DataSource` — AES-XTS-128/256 with the sector index as tweak for methods `0x8004`/`0x8005`, or AES-CBC with the Elephant diffuser for `0x8000`/`0x8001` — wrapped in `BitlockerVolumeSource`, which serves the relocated boot sectors at offset zero from their ciphered location and passes the three 64 KiB FVE metadata regions through from the raw volume, so the partition, file-system and carving modules read it as an ordinary volume; and beside it a `VolumeDecryption` record, subtype `unlocked`, `status: "Unlocked"`, with `bitlocker_encryption_method`, `credential_kind`, `credential_source` (`supplied_for_this_run` or `process_start`) and `decrypted_volume_artifact_id`, no incompleteness pair — the record whose re-run supersedes the earlier locked one. With a supplied credential it reports back accepted when the key hierarchy unwraps and rejected (with the error, never the secret) when it does not, and a rejected run's records are not persisted, so the locked record stands. For a credential that unlocks nothing: a `VolumeDecryption`/`unlock_failed` record with `status: "UnlockFailed"` and `error` (`no volume master key could be unlocked with the supplied credential`, `invalid recovery key: …`, `malformed FVE metadata: …`, or an I/O error) and the same pair. For keys recovered under a cipher this build does not decrypt — plain AES-CBC `0x8002`/`0x8003`, an unknown method, or an XTS volume whose BPB sector size is not 512 — a record with `status: "CipherNotDecryptable"` and the method. A decrypted source refuses a read whose ciphertext came back short rather than decrypting the zero fill. Warnings go to the log; the credential never does.

**Cannot.** It cannot open a volume without a credential, and the ordinary seized laptop has none it can use: a TPM, TPM-and-PIN or startup-key protector carries no stretch-key salt and no password-unwrappable blob, so with a password supplied such a volume fails with `malformed FVE metadata: no VMK protectors` — the volume is well formed; the error names the wrong thing. It cannot recover an FVEK from a memory capture and nothing in the tree hands it one. It cannot decrypt plain AES-CBC without the diffuser: the keys are recovered and the sectors are not, and the record says so. It cannot decrypt an XTS volume on any sector size but 512, because the tweak is per sector and a 4Kn volume decrypted at 512 yields bytes for every sector and correct bytes for none; it refuses instead, but the `CipherNotDecryptable` record it leaves says the cipher `is not implemented for sector decryption in this build`, which is true of the sector size and false of the cipher, and only the log line says which. The diffuser path makes no such check — it decrypts 512-byte sectors whatever the BPB declares — and both successful paths stamp `sector_size: 512` on the child from a constant rather than from the volume. Its decrypted volume cannot be re-read from the evidence after the run on its own — the key is not retained — so the content resolver refuses it and everything beneath it rather than serve ciphertext, until an examiner unlocks it for reading (`POST …/unlock`, kind `bitlocker_password` or `bitlocker_recovery_password`, audited by kind), which re-derives the FVEK from the volume's own metadata and holds the decrypting view in process memory for that case only, for a TTL (8 h default, `SEANCE_UNLOCK_TTL_SECS`), never on disk; lock, expiry, case deletion or a restart forgets it and the refusal returns. The FVEK, and the diffuser's AES and tweak keys, are held in zeroizing buffers wiped when the source drops; the stretched password key and the VMK are ordinary buffers for the length of the unlock. The plaintext size is the ciphertext size, so no bytes are trimmed and none are added. Where none of the three metadata blocks will read, the locked record still exists but names no cipher, no protectors and no identifier, and a converting volume is reported as BitLocker without the record saying conversion was incomplete or how much of it is still plaintext. Its real-image evidence is two corpora, neither in the repository: `test_data/bdetogo.raw` (a Vista/7-era To Go volume, AES-CBC-128 + diffuser, password `bde-TEST`, FVEK asserted byte-for-byte, the relocated FAT boot sector decrypting to `0x55AA`/`mkdosfs`) and a 64 GiB Windows 11 25H2 XTS-AES-256 system volume opened by its Windows-generated recovery password, with a partial-conversion image of the same machine at 56%; both suites skip silently when the file is absent; the per-run credential path is pinned on both (password and recovery password, each with a wrong one rejected). One stale statement stands in its own source: `source.rs` says the relocated boot sectors and metadata regions are 'surfaced verbatim' pending a vector, which `BitlockerVolumeSource` now remaps.

**Refuses.** It refuses to let a locked volume be silence. The BitLocker test runs before the credential is consulted, because an earlier version returned early on the missing credential and a locked volume was byte-for-byte what an unencrypted one produced; the `detected_locked` record now exists precisely so the absence of files under the volume reads as a missing key and not as an empty disk, and it is the only report a To Go volume gets anywhere in the tree, since the generic detector looks for `-FVE-FS-` at offset 3 and a To Go boot sector says `MSWIN4.1` there. It refuses to guess at a sector size: an XTS volume declaring anything but 512 is reported as detected and left undecrypted. It refuses to decrypt zero fill: a short ciphertext read is an `UnexpectedEof` error naming the sectors, never plausible plaintext. It refuses to cipher what was never encrypted, serving the FVE metadata regions raw, and refuses to leave noise at offset zero where a relocated boot sector exists. It refuses a recovery password that fails its own arithmetic — wrong group count, non-digits, a group not divisible by 11 or over range — and reports the reason. It refuses every metadata block without the `-FVE-FS-` signature or with a metadata size outside 0x30..16 MiB, and an entry list whose entry size is under 8 bytes or overruns its buffer ends iteration rather than looping. It refuses to carry the credential anywhere but process memory: `Debug` prints only its kind, it is never read from or written to artifact metadata, a supplied one arrives through the per-run channel and never through metadata or the environment, and a `Credential`'s text is zeroed when it drops. It is silent, deliberately, on a volume that is not BitLocker, with or without a credential, because every partition in the case reaches it and the credential may belong to another one.

### `plugin.crypto.luks_decryptor`

**Reads.** A LUKS1 or LUKS2 volume, with or without a passphrase. It subscribes to `Partition` and `RawEvidence` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, passes over an artifact with no data source, and then — before it looks at the passphrase — `is_luks` reads six bytes at offset zero for `LUKS\xBA\xBE`. The passphrase is, first, one an examiner supplied for this volume and this run (`POST …/credential`, kind `luks_passphrase`, visible through `seance_core::credential` for one `process` call on that artifact), else the one constructed from `--luks-passphrase`/`SEANCE_LUKS_PASSPHRASE` by `seance_cli` once at start. The big-endian `u16` at offset 6 selects the version, and `header::parse` reads either the 592-byte LUKS1 header — cipher name, cipher mode, hash spec, payload offset in 512-byte sectors, key bytes (1..=1024), the master-key digest with its salt and iteration count, the UUID, and eight 48-byte keyslots each with its active marker (`0x00AC71F3`), iterations, 32-byte salt, key-material sector offset and stripe count — or the LUKS2 binary header's `hdr_size` (big-endian `u64` at 8, which must exceed 4096 and not exceed 4096 + 16 MiB), followed by the NUL-terminated UTF-8 JSON area from offset 4096 to `hdr_size`, deserialised for `keyslots`, `segments` and `digests`. It accepts only `aes` ciphers containing `xts` (LUKS1 `cipher-mode`, LUKS2 segment and keyslot-area `encryption`), hash specs `sha1`, `sha256` and `sha512`, LUKS2 keyslots of type `luks2` with a `raw` area, KDFs `pbkdf2`, `argon2i` and `argon2id`, digests of type `pbkdf2`, the first segment of type `crypt` in key order with `sector_size` 512, 1024, 2048 or 4096, and anti-forensic geometry of 1..=1024 key bytes and 1..=4000 stripes. For each usable keyslot it derives the slot key from the passphrase bytes, reads the slot's key material rounded up to whole 512-byte sectors (zero-padding a short read), decrypts it with AES-XTS at tweak zero, AF-merges it down to a candidate master key with the slot's hash, and accepts the candidate only when PBKDF2 over it reproduces the stored digest — every digest covering that slot in LUKS2, the single `mk_digest` in LUKS1.

**Produces.** On a verified master key: one artifact of the parent's own type (`Partition` or `RawEvidence`), parented to it, named `<name> (LUKS decrypted)`, with `luks_decrypted: true`, `offset_bytes: 0`, `size_bytes` (the volume size minus the payload offset), `sector_size: 512` — a constant, written even when the LUKS2 segment declared 4096 — and `source_name`, `volume_artifact_id` (the id of the volume it decrypts, which the encryption detector's LUKS record for the volume also carries), carrying a `LuksDecryptingDataSource` whose byte zero is the first payload byte, which widens every read to whole cipher sectors, decrypts them with AES-XTS (128, 192 or 256 by key length) under `plain64` tweaks numbered from the segment's `iv_tweak` (zero for LUKS1), and slices back to the request; the partition, file-system, carving and hashing modules then read it as a plain volume. Beside it, a `VolumeDecryption` record, subtype `unlocked`, `status: "Unlocked"`, `credential_kind`, `credential_source`, `decrypted_volume_artifact_id`, no incompleteness pair, which on a re-run supersedes the locked record; a supplied passphrase is reported back accepted or rejected, and a rejected run's records are not persisted. A ciphertext read that comes back short of the bytes being returned is refused with an `UnexpectedEof` error naming the sectors rather than decrypted from zero fill. On any failure — no keyslot verifying (`no keyslot could be unlocked with the supplied passphrase`), an unsupported cipher, hash, KDF, digest type or LUKS version, malformed or truncated header, unparseable JSON, or an I/O error — one `ParsedRecord` of type `VolumeDecryption`, subtype `unlock_failed`, `status: "UnlockFailed"`, `scheme: "LUKS"`, `volume_name`, `volume_artifact_id`, `error`, with `content_incomplete` and `inventory_incomplete` both `true` with reason `encrypted`, the sentence in both `_detail` keys and in `detail`, and a `name` — the shape the Needs attention queue keys on, where the LUKS row takes the passphrase for this volume, or points to `crack-luks`. With no passphrase, on a LUKS volume, the same record shape with subtype `detected_locked` and `status: "NotUnlocked"`, and `luks_version`, `luks_cipher`, `luks_uuid` (LUKS1 only; `null` for LUKS2) and `luks_active_keyslots` from the plaintext header (all `null`, and the detail saying why, when the header does not parse), so a locked volume reaches the same queue row. A `warn` line records a failed unlock and an `info` line a successful one; the passphrase reaches neither.

**Cannot.** Its decrypted volume cannot be re-read from the evidence after the run on its own — the key is not retained — so the content resolver refuses it and everything beneath it, until an examiner unlocks it for reading (`POST …/unlock`, kind `luks_passphrase`, audited by kind), which runs the keyslot KDF again and holds the decrypting view in process memory for that case only, for a TTL (8 h default, `SEANCE_UNLOCK_TTL_SECS`), never on disk; lock, expiry, case deletion or a restart forgets it and the refusal returns. The master key is held in a zeroizing buffer wiped when the source drops; the slot key and the AF-merged candidates are ordinary buffers for the length of the unlock. It cannot read a LUKS2 volume's UUID into the locked record (the binary header's UUID field is not parsed). It cannot decrypt anything but AES-XTS: `aes-cbc-essiv:sha256`, Serpent, Twofish, Camellia, and every authenticated mode are `unsupported parameter`, as are `ripemd160` and `whirlpool` hashes and any digest type but `pbkdf2`. It cannot use a detached header, a keyslot whose area is not `raw`, a `reencrypt` keyslot, a LUKS2 volume with dm-integrity (the `integrity` object is not deserialised, so the tag-interleaved layout would be decrypted as if it were plain sectors and refused only if the cipher name fails the XTS test), a token, or a keyfile. It cannot bound Argon2: `memory`, `time` and `cpus` are taken from the JSON as written, so a hostile header can demand gigabytes per keyslot and the allocation is attempted; the AF geometry is bounded and Argon2 is not. It cannot tell a wrong passphrase from a truncated image: key material past the end of the device is zero-padded, the AF-merge yields a wrong key, and the record says `no keyslot could be unlocked`. It reads the primary header only, verifies no header checksum, and does not honour a LUKS2 segment's fixed `size`, so plaintext runs to the end of the device. It does not verify the decrypted payload holds anything: a verified digest proves the key, not the sectors. Its plaintext view is validated by round trips against images the tests build with the crate's own encryptor — LUKS1/PBKDF2, LUKS2/PBKDF2 and LUKS2/Argon2id — and the PBKDF2 vectors of RFC 6070. Its header, keyslot and AF reading and the passphrase path are also checked against LUKS1 and LUKS2 volumes the real `cryptsetup luksFormat` writes on a file at test time (`tests/cryptsetup_credential.rs`, skipped where `cryptsetup` is absent): the master-key digest verifies under the passphrase and a wrong one is rejected. The payload of those volumes is never opened through dm-crypt, so no kernel-written plaintext has been compared.

**Refuses.** It refuses to let a locked volume look like an unencrypted one: with no passphrase a LUKS volume is still reported, with both incompleteness pairs. Given one, it refuses to let a failed unlock look like an unencrypted volume: every error path emits the `VolumeDecryption` record with both incompleteness pairs. It refuses a verification bypass — an empty stored digest, which would match any candidate, is `invalid LUKS2 metadata: empty master-key digest`. It refuses keyslot geometry it cannot bound — zero or over-large key sizes and stripe counts, a `key_size × stripes` that overflows, a segment `sector_size` outside the four LUKS values, a `hdr_size` outside its window — before any allocation sized from it, because a multi-terabyte allocation aborts past `catch_unwind`. It refuses to decrypt zero fill where the ciphertext being returned came back short. It refuses every cipher, hash, KDF and digest it does not implement, by name, in the record's `error`. It refuses a header whose 592 bytes or JSON area cannot be read in full: a truncated header is an I/O error, never parsed from zero padding. It refuses to carry the passphrase anywhere but process memory — `Debug` prints only whether one was supplied, it is never read from artifact metadata, a supplied one arrives through the per-run channel, and the process-level one is zeroed when the module drops — and it refuses, deliberately, to say anything about a volume that is not LUKS, with or without a passphrase, because the passphrase may belong to a different volume in the same image.

### `plugin.detection.yara`

**Reads.** An examiner's own YARA rules, and the bytes of the single artifact it was dispatched on — now on eight surfaces rather than one. Séance ships **no rules of its own**: the set comes from the path named by `SEANCE_YARA_RULES` — one rule file, loaded whatever it is called, or a directory searched recursively for `*.yar` and `*.yara` — compiled once by `yara-x` before any evidence is touched, with symlinks followed to files and directories so a rule tree assembled out of links loads whole, and the file list sorted and de-duplicated so the same set compiles in the same order on every machine. It subscribes to `FileEntry`, `FileContent`, `UnallocatedSpace`, `SlackSpace` and `ParsedRecord`, and because it is opt-in that list is what the API offers it against, not a dispatch rule. What it reads about the artifact decides the surface: a `carved: true` producer flag (with `carving_signature`, `carving_offset`, `carving_offset_absolute`, `carving_validated`, `carving_source`, `parent_file`); a `FileEntry`'s `is_ads`, `stream_name`, `parent_file`, `path` and `deleted`; an `UnallocatedSpace`'s `offset_bytes`, `size_bytes`, `offset_basis`, `filesystem` and `source` (or `partition_scheme`, read as a partition gap); a `SlackSpace` region's `offset_bytes`, `size_bytes`, `offset_basis`, `filesystem`, `source`, `parent_file`, `parent_path`, `owner_artifact_id`, `logical_size` and `cluster_size`, as `seance_core::slack` publishes them; a `Partition`, `FileSystem`, `RawEvidence` or `Container`'s type and bounds; and a `RegistryHive` record's `all_values` inventory — each value's `key_path`, `value_name`, `value_type`, `raw_data_size`, its rendering and `value_data_b64` — together with the record's own `key_inventory_complete` and `content_incomplete`. A byte surface is read best-effort through `read_capped` from the artifact's own data source, up to 256 MiB (`MAX_SCAN_BYTES`), under a 60-second per-artifact timeout. A registry value is scanned on its stored bytes, `value_data_b64`, which the parser publishes for every value except one over 64 bytes past the hive's own per-hive cap (`exact`); a record without them — an older build's, or a capped value — has its bytes rebuilt from a lossless hex rendering or a little-endian DWORD/QWORD at its own width (`rebuilt_from_rendering`), or, for a string, its decoded text re-encoded as UTF-16LE without its terminator (`reencoded_utf16le`), or, for a `REG_MULTI_SZ`, the elements of its `value_data_list` re-encoded as the stored list — each UTF-16LE with its terminator, then the list terminator (`reencoded_utf16le_elements`) — within a per-hive byte budget of 256 MiB. Every region scanned is also handed to `seance_bulk::decode`, which lifts base64 spans of at least 24 characters and gzip members out of it, one level deep, under ceilings of 256 spans and 64 MiB of decoded bytes per region, and each decoded buffer is scanned as a child of the region. Scanning an address space rather than a file is a different driver, `memory::MemoryYaraScanner`, over the same compiled rule set, and is not this module.

**Produces.** Every record about scanned bytes carries `surface` — one of `file`, `ads`, `registry_value`, `unallocated`, `carved`, `deleted_file`, `volume`, `slack` — and `surface_means`, one sentence saying what a hit there is and is not (in free space it is not a hit in any live file; in a carved object the bounds are the carver's inference; in a deleted file the clusters may have been reallocated; in a volume it is attributed to no file; in slack it lies past the named live file's logical end, is not that file's content, may be an earlier file's, and a string split across the region's edge is not matched whole), plus the region's own context keys copied from the producer. One `YaraMatch` per rule that fired, with the rule's identifier, `namespace`, `tags`, `rules_in_set`, `bytes_scanned`, `declared_size`, `entropy_bits_per_byte` (Shannon, to four decimals) with `entropy_bytes` (the population it was computed over), and where and how often its strings fired: `pattern_matches` — up to 64 entries (`MAX_PATTERN_MATCHES_RECORDED`) of `pattern`, `offset_in_region`, `length`, and `offset_in_parent` where the region can be placed in its parent's coordinate space (a partition's `offset_bytes`, a free run's, a slack region's (into its file system), a carver's `carving_offset` when it is into the parent and not into slack; never a file system's copied offset) — with `pattern_match_count` as the true total, `pattern_matches_recorded`, `pattern_matches_truncated`, and `matched_without_pattern: true` for a rule true with no string found (`condition: true`, a `filesize` test). A hit on decoded bytes says so — `bytes_are_decoded`, `decoded_via` (`base64` or `gzip`), `decoded_from`, the span's offset, `decoded_bytes`, `decoded_truncated`, `decoded_depth: 1`, a `decoded_means` sentence, and `offset_in_decoded` in place of `offset_in_region`. A registry hit carries `key_path`, `value_name`, `value_type`, `raw_data_size` and `value_bytes_basis` (`exact`, `rebuilt_from_rendering`, `reencoded_utf16le` or `reencoded_utf16le_elements`) with its statement. A slack hit names the file as `base_file` and `path`, with `owner_artifact_id`, `logical_size`, `cluster_size` and `region_source` (`file_slack`). One `YaraRegionScanned` per ADS, unallocated, slack, carved, deleted-file or volume region read end to end, matched or not, with `bytes_scanned`, `declared_size`, `matches`, `scan_complete`, the entropy pair and the decode counts (`decoded_spans_found`, `decoded_spans_scanned`, `decoded_bytes_scanned`, `decoded_cap_reached`, `decoded_engine_errors`); a live file scanned whole yields no such record, so on the file surface alone an empty record set means one thing — the object was read end to end and no rule fired. One `YaraRegistryCoverage` per hive (`values_total`, `values_scanned`, `values_scanned_exact`, `values_scanned_rebuilt`, `values_scanned_reencoded` (which counts both re-encoded bases), `values_not_scanned` with `not_scanned_reasons` counted as `multi_sz_rendering_is_lossy`, `parser_could_not_read_value`, `rendering_does_not_reproduce_bytes`, `big_endian_dword_rendering_order_unknown` or `byte_budget_reached`, `values_engine_error`, `bytes_scanned`, `byte_budget`, `byte_budget_reached`, `matches`, `value_bytes_means`), with the hive record's own incompleteness carried onto every record. One `YaraDecodeCoverage` on a plain file only when a decode ceiling or a decoder engine error occurred. And exactly one coverage record whenever a byte surface was not examined whole: `YaraNotScanned` when no content was attached, the source declared bytes and returned none, a hive record carries no `all_values`, or the artifact type has no surface here (a non-hive `ParsedRecord`, a `TimelineEvent` — refused with `refused_artifact_type` and deliberately **no** `surface`); `YaraScanError` when the engine did not complete; `YaraPartialScan` with `bytes_scanned`, `declared_size`, `max_scan_bytes` and `matches_in_scanned_prefix` when only a leading prefix was readable. Each says in words that no conclusion may be drawn from the absence of matches.

**Cannot.** It cannot detect anything the examiner's rules do not describe, and a match is not a verdict — it is a flagged aid whose worth is entirely the worth of the rule behind it, which is why no rule set ships with the product. It reaches file slack only through the `SlackSpace` regions the NTFS, FAT, exFAT, ext4, HFS+ and APFS parsers publish, so it cannot scan slack the producer did not publish: an all-zero tail, a resident, compressed, encrypted or deleted file's, a tail that could not be read in full, clusters allocated past the one holding the last byte, slack on any other file system, or regions past the producer's ceiling of 250,000 per volume — so a run with no slack hit means none in the slack that was published, and the volume's `slack_space_summary` record (its unread-tail, past-ceiling and `files_not_located` counts — the last for live files whose tail the parser could not locate because the run list or chain was incomplete or the allocation compressed or encrypted — and `content_incomplete`) says where the producer could not look. A slack hit's `offset_in_parent` is into the file system, not the evidence: on a partitioned image the partition's own offset must be added to reach an image offset, and this module does not compose it (DFTT #2 and #3, the graded images, are bare volumes). It cannot match a string that crosses a slack region's edge — begun in the file's own content and ended in its slack, or run from the slack into the next cluster (DFTT #2's `1slack1` and `2slack2`, pinned by a test): each region is scanned on its own, and only a `volume` scan of the whole image finds such a string, attributed to no file. It cannot scan the stored bytes of a registry value whose record does not carry them — a value over 64 bytes past the hive's per-hive cap: a string there is its decoded text re-encoded as UTF-16LE — an inference, labelled `reencoded_utf16le`, that reproduces the stored bytes only for a well-formed string with one terminator; a `REG_MULTI_SZ` is its element list re-encoded — an inference, labelled `reencoded_utf16le_elements`, that reproduces the stored bytes only for a well-formed list, since the registry parser drops empty elements and replaces unpaired surrogates — and a `REG_MULTI_SZ` with no `value_data_list`, a `REG_DWORD_BIG_ENDIAN`, a value the parser could not read, or one whose rendering cannot reproduce its bytes is counted by reason and not scanned. It cannot list more than 64 offsets for one rule, though it always says how many there were. It cannot look past 256 MiB of a single artifact, past 256 decoded spans or 64 MiB of decoded bytes per region, or decode more than one level deep — a gzip inside a base64 span inside a file is not reached — and it cannot say a hit on decoded bytes was ever stored in that form: the bytes it matched were produced by this module's decoder, not read from the evidence. It cannot distinguish a truncated file from a device that errored partway through one — `read_capped` breaks identically on a zero-length read and on an I/O error, so both arrive as a short read. It does no decryption and no decompression beyond gzip, so a rule written for plaintext does not fire on the same content inside an archive or an encrypted container unless another module produced the decoded child artifact. It cannot place a hit in the parent's coordinates from a `FileSystem` (its `offset_bytes` is the partition's, copied) or from an object carved out of slack, and says nothing rather than guessing. And it cannot sweep a case by itself: as `ExecutionMode::OptIn` it is absent from the orchestrator's artifact-type registry entirely, and runs only when an examiner dispatches it by module id against one named artifact at a time.

**Refuses.** It refuses to exist without rules. There is deliberately no scanner holding an empty rule set, because a module that is listed, reports success and produces nothing reads as "scanned, nothing found"; with `SEANCE_YARA_RULES` unset the module is not registered and `plugin.detection.yara` is absent from the module list, and a rule set that **was** named and will not load ends the run rather than hunting with fewer rules than the examiner believes. It refuses to half-load one: an unreadable path, a directory holding no `.yar` or `.yara` file, a source that compiles to zero rules, and a dangling symlink that carries a rule extension are each fatal, and any rule that fails to compile fails the whole load with the engine's diagnostic for every bad file rather than the first. It refuses to stamp `file` on anything but a live file's own content — `file` is the narrow case, not the default — and refuses to stamp any surface on an artifact type that has none, because the only truthful sentence there would be that the provenance is unknown. It refuses to let a hit in free space, a carved object, a deleted file or a stream read as a hit in a live file: `surface` and `surface_means` are on every record. It refuses to invent a `false` for a producer that never wrote `deleted`, carrying `entry_deleted` only where it was written. It refuses to let an engine failure read as a clean object — the fault comes back from `scan` on its own `Err` channel so a caller counting the match vector cannot count it as a match. It refuses to place a hit in a parent by a wrapped addition, leaving `offset_in_parent` absent rather than at a plausible small address. It refuses to present a truncated pattern list as the whole, publishing the total beside it. And it refuses to return nothing for a surface it did not read end to end: every path out of `process` either scanned the whole region — and, on every surface but a live file, said so with a `YaraRegionScanned` — or emitted a record saying why it did not.

### `plugin.disk.filesystem_detector`

**Reads.** It reads the first bytes of a volume, and nothing else. Handed a `Partition` artifact — whose data source the partition parser has already windowed to that partition — or a whole-image `RawEvidence` artifact, it reads up to 4,096 bytes from offset 0 of that source and matches a fixed table of magic values at fixed offsets: the OEM name at byte 3 for `NTFS ` and `EXFAT `, the FAT type strings at bytes 54 and 82, the ext superblock magic `0xEF53` at `0x438`, the F2FS magic `0xF2F52010` at 1024, `NXSB` at 32 for APFS, `H+`/`HX` at 1024 for HFS+ and HFSX, `XFSB` at byte 0, and `hsqs` at byte 0 for SquashFS. Where the FAT32 type string is absent it also accepts a FAT32 boot sector whose sector count is carried only in the non-standard 64-bit field at byte 82 — FAT32-shaped BPB, `0x29` extended boot signature, both standard counts zero, a nonzero count and the `0x55AA` signature. Because four signatures live outside that window it then reads four more fixed places directly: `CD001` at `0x8001` for ISO9660, the UFS magic at 8192+1372 and at 65536+1372, and `_BHRfS_M` at `+0x40` in the Btrfs superblock at 64 KiB and its mirrors at 64 MiB and 256 GiB. It declares `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, runs automatically on every `Partition` and `RawEvidence` artifact the pipeline produces, and reads no file system content, no directory, no inode and no partition-table entry of its own.

**Produces.** It produces one `FileSystem` artifact per signature it matched, parented to the artifact it was given and carrying that artifact's data source unchanged, so the parser that picks it up reads exactly the bytes the detector probed. Each carries `filesystem_type` as the name of the matched signature, `subtype` as its lower-case form — which is the string the FAT, XFS, Btrfs, ext and F2FS parsers gate on, so this field is what decides whether a volume is walked at all — plus the `offset_bytes` and `size_bytes` its parent declared, the parent's id, and the evidence path where the parent names one. Where more than one signature matched it emits an artifact for each, and every one of them carries `filesystem_overlap`, the full `overlapping_filesystems` list and an `overlap_warning` naming the others; the non-primary ones are additionally flagged `hidden`, which is how a second filesystem in one partition reaches its own parser rather than being named and dropped. Nothing it emits is a record about the filesystem's contents: it is a routing decision, published as an artifact, that some named filesystem begins at byte 0 of this volume.

**Cannot.** A detection here is a magic-string match and nothing more — it validates no checksum, reads no second field for agreement, and does not require the volume to be mountable, so a formatted-over volume with a residual superblock, a carved fragment, or a file that merely contains those bytes at those offsets produces a `FileSystem` artifact indistinguishable from a live filesystem's. It cannot tell ext2 from ext3 from ext4, because all three carry the same magic, and labels every one of them `ext4` — so on the classic NTFS+ext2 hidden-filesystem case the record names a filesystem version the volume does not have. It cannot detect a FAT volume that omits the optional file-system-type string in its BPB, since that string is the only thing it looks at for FAT12 and FAT16 and, outside the 64-bit-count shape above, for FAT32. It names SquashFS only inside a `Partition`: a whole-image SquashFS `RawEvidence` is left to the SquashFS reader's own subscription, so it is not walked twice. It names neither ReFS, ZFS, an LVM physical volume, a Linux swap area, nor the `-FVE-FS-` and LUKS signatures that BitLocker and LUKS volumes carry at those same offsets — those two are other modules' work, and this one simply finds nothing. Detecting UFS1 or UFS2 buys an examiner nothing beyond the name: no module in this build consumes a `ufs1` or `ufs2` subtype, so the artifact is emitted and never walked. It cannot say which of two overlapping filesystems is the genuine one; `primary` means first in its own probe order, not first in time or most likely, and the flag carries no evidential weight. When it matches nothing it emits no record at all — only a log line — so from the artifact set alone an examiner cannot tell a volume that was probed and found unrecognisable from one no module ever saw.

**Refuses.** It refuses to process a `Partition` artifact whose metadata does not state `offset_bytes` and `size_bytes`, failing with `InvalidInputFormat` naming the missing field rather than assuming zero and the whole source: a filesystem reported at a position nobody recorded is a finding with no place on the disk. It refuses any artifact that is neither `Partition` nor `RawEvidence`, and any artifact with no data source, returning empty or an `InvalidInputFormat` instead of probing what it was handed. It refuses to treat the zero tail of a short read as evidence: the signature window is truncated to the bytes that actually arrived and a warning says how many of how many were readable, because a signature absent from bytes that never arrived is not a signature that is absent. And it refuses to probe a Btrfs superblock mirror that lies past the partition's declared end, skipping the 64 MiB and 256 GiB copies on volumes too small to hold them, because reading past the end would return the same nothing a missing magic does and the two must not be confused.

### `plugin.disk.partition_parser`

**Reads.** The first sector of a `RawEvidence` image, read whole or not at all, and then whichever of three schemes the bytes prove. It looks for GPT first, by the `EFI PART` signature at LBA 1 probed at 512-byte and then 4096-byte sectors, because a GPT disk carries a protective MBR that would otherwise read as an MBR disk; then for MBR, by `0x55AA` at bytes 510 and 511 and the four 16-byte entries at byte 446, from which it reads only the boot byte, the type byte, the 32-bit starting LBA and the 32-bit sector count; and where an entry is an extended container it follows the extended-boot-record chain, treating every extended-type slot as a link and every other non-empty slot as a logical partition rather than assuming the conventional slot 0 and slot 1. Failing both, it looks for a Linux `md` software-RAID superblock in three placements — v1.1 at offset 0, v1.2 at 4 KiB and v1.0 at the end of the device — and accepts one only if the superblock's own checksum verifies, so a coincidental magic in carved or nested data produces nothing. It reads no filesystem and no file: what is inside a partition is `plugin.disk.filesystem_detector`'s work and the parsers below it.

**Produces.** One `Partition` artifact per entry, each carrying a `WindowSource` over the parent image at the offset and length the table declares, so every downstream module reads the partition without a copy being made. Each carries its scheme, its id, its type — a GUID with a name for GPT, a type byte with a name for MBR — its first and last LBA or starting LBA and sector count, its byte offset, its byte size and the sector size the geometry was computed at; a logical partition is additionally flagged `logical` with an `extended_container` back-reference to the primary it came from. Beside them it produces `UnallocatedSpace` artifacts, also as windows, for the gaps around and between partitions and for the free space between logical partitions inside an extended container, flagged `small_gap` below 1 MiB and `trailing` for the space after the last partition. Where a GPT's own CRC does not verify it still produces the partitions: the entries are decoded from the header's own figures, every partition carries `partition_table_verified: false` with a sentence saying which of the two checksums failed and why that matters, and a `GptPartitionTableUnverified` record carries both digests — declared and computed, header and entry array — so a reader can check the claim rather than take it. Where anything was dropped it produces the record that says so, `GptPartitionTableIncomplete` or `MbrExtendedChainIncomplete`, naming the guard that fired, the count emitted and the count missing, and it stamps `inventory_incomplete` on the partitions that did survive so one exported alone still says the map it came from is short. An image that is a RAID member rather than a disk produces a `RaidMember` record naming the level, the disk count, the chunk size and the `scan-raid` and `assemble-raid` commands that reconstruct the array.

**Cannot.** It cannot find a GPT whose primary header is gone. It probes for `EFI PART` only at byte 512 and byte 4096 and never at the backup header at the end of the device, so a disk whose primary header was wiped is read as its protective MBR — a single partition of type `0xEE` spanning the whole disk, which is a materially wrong partition map and not an empty one. It cannot work at any logical sector size other than 512 or 4096, and for MBR it assumes 512 unconditionally. It does not read the CHS triplets in an MBR entry at all, only the 32-bit LBA and sector-count fields, so an entry that describes its partition only in CHS terms yields no usable extent and no partition beyond the reach of those 32-bit fields can be described. On the unverified-GPT path it produces no unallocated-space windows and no `partition_type_name`, because that path decodes the entry array by hand and never reaches the free-sector arithmetic and GUID table the verified path uses. It drops any gap smaller than `MIN_GAP_BYTES`, 512 bytes, so sub-sector slack is not in the map, and it stops an extended chain at `MAX_EBRS`, 1,024 links, and refuses an unverified GPT header declaring more than 4,096 entries or an entry size outside 128 to 4,096 bytes. It does not bounds-check a primary MBR entry against the image the way it bounds-checks a logical one, does not report two primaries whose extents overlap as the finding that would be, and recognises no Apple Partition Map, BSD disklabel or Sun VTOC — an image carrying one of those, or a bare LVM physical volume, produces no artifact and no record saying why, only a log line.

**Refuses.** It refuses to answer "no partition table" for a read it could not complete: a source long enough to hold the GPT signature that will not deliver those eight bytes is returned as an I/O error, because an empty partition map for a disk nobody could read is indistinguishable on a report from a genuinely unpartitioned disk. It refuses to treat a failed integrity check as an absence of partitions — a CRC mismatch is what carved, truncated and deliberately damaged evidence looks like, and the strict parser's refusal turned a readable 2,098,028,544-byte disk whose header CRC verifies (`0x6e47e4e5`) and whose entry-array CRC does not (declared `0xf87a9ff9`, computed `0x11726dec`) into one artifact, where `mmls` reads its four partitions regardless. It refuses, on that same path, to decode a table whose header could not be read directly, whose declared entry count or entry size this build will not read, or whose entry array is not fully readable at the LBA the header names — each is returned as an error naming the byte counts, because decoding past the end of the image would invent partitions rather than recover them. It refuses to emit an extended container as a data partition, since it is a container and not evidence of a volume. It refuses to publish the free space inside an extended container whose walk stopped short: sectors the walk never accounted for are unknown, and calling them unallocated would assert something that was not established. And it refuses to claim a RAID member is as large as its superblock says when the capture is smaller, clamping to the image and recording the declared size and the short read beside it.

### `plugin.documents.office`

**Reads.** A modern office document — an OOXML or OpenDocument ZIP — and it reads one only after a name or a content-types part has said what it is. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent` artifacts with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, passes over any artifact whose `is_directory` metadata is `true` and any artifact with no data source, and then gates on the `name` metadata: the last dot-separated segment, lower-cased, is looked up in a fixed table — `docx`/`docm`/`dotx`/`dotm` are Word, `xlsx`/`xlsm`/`xltx`/`xltm` are Excel, `pptx`/`pptm`/`potx`/`potm`/`ppsx` are PowerPoint, `odt`/`ott`, `ods`/`ots` and `odp`/`otp` are the three OpenDocument families. A name carrying any other extension is skipped without a byte being read; a name with no extension at all, or no name, is read and identified from inside. Up to `MAX_CONTENT_BYTES` (256 MiB) of the source is read through `read_capped`, and a buffer shorter than 4 bytes or not beginning `PK` is dropped as not a ZIP. The buffer is opened with `zip::ZipArchive` (zip 0.6) in memory. For an extension-less file the family is sniffed by substring: `[Content_Types].xml` containing `wordprocessingml`, `spreadsheetml` or `presentationml`, else `mimetype` containing `opendocument.text`, `opendocument.spreadsheet` or `opendocument.presentation`; anything else yields nothing. Every part is fetched by its exact entry name through `read_entry_capped`, which inflates at most `MAX_ENTRY_BYTES` (128 MiB) plus one byte — a member that delivers that extra byte is discarded whole and recorded as `cap_reached`; a member that exists but will not open or inflate (a CRC failure on a stored member, for instance) is recorded as `unresolved_structure`; a member that is simply absent is recorded nowhere — and every part is decoded as lossy UTF-8. Word text is `word/document.xml`: the character data of every element whose local name is `t`, with a newline pushed at the close of every element whose local name is `p`. PowerPoint text is every entry whose name starts `ppt/slides/slide` and ends `.xml`, sorted by a natural key so `slide2` precedes `slide10`, walked by the same `t`/`p` rule with a newline between slides. Excel text is `xl/sharedStrings.xml` — one string per `si`, its `t` runs concatenated — resolved against every `xl/worksheets/sheet*.xml` in natural order: a `c` whose `t` attribute is `s` has its `v` parsed as an index into that table (a miss yields an empty cell), an `is`/`t` inline string is taken as it stands, and any other `v` is taken literally; non-empty cells are tab-joined per `row` and rows newline-separated. The worksheet is the only part whose attributes are read, and they are read through `seance_xml_util::XmlGuard`, which caps attributes at 256 per element and counts duplicates and unparseable ones (RUSTSEC-2026-0194). OpenDocument text is everything inside `content.xml`'s `body` element, with a newline at the close of `p`, `h` and `table-row`. Properties come from `docProps/core.xml` (`title`, `subject`, `creator` as `author`, `lastModifiedBy` as `last_modified_by`, `created`, `modified`, `keywords`) or `meta.xml` (`title`, `subject`, `creator` as `author`, `initial-creator` as `initial_creator`, `creation-date` as `created`, `date` as `modified`), first non-empty occurrence of each, trimmed, matched by local name only. Every XML walk uses quick-xml 0.31 and records whether it reached `Eof` or stopped on a parse error, because a stopped walk has produced a prefix.

**Produces.** Exactly one `ParsedRecord` per document it claims, subtype `office_document`, parented to the input artifact, with `type: OfficeDocument`, `format` (`Word`, `Excel` or `PowerPoint`), `container` (`OOXML` or `OpenDocument`), `name` in the form `<Format> document: <title>` where the title is the `title` property or, failing that, the file name, `file_name`, `text`, `char_count` and `word_count` (both counted on the full extracted text, by `chars()` and by whitespace splitting, before any cut), and `text_truncated`. The stored `text` is cut at `MAX_TEXT_BYTES` (4 MiB) on a character boundary, and when it is cut the record carries the standard pair `content_incomplete: true` with `content_incomplete_reason: cap_reached`, `text_bytes_stored`, `max_text_bytes` and a `message` saying the text below is the leading portion. When the outer read fell short of the source's declared size the record carries `content_incomplete` with reason `cap_reached` if the declared size exceeds 256 MiB and `short_read` otherwise, plus `bytes_read`, `declared_size`, `max_content_bytes` and a `message` saying parts beyond the read were not parsed. When any declared part could not be read in full the record carries `content_incomplete` and `parts_incomplete: true`; where the outer read did not already explain the shortfall it also carries the reason — `cap_reached` if any part hit the member cap, else `unresolved_structure` — with `max_entry_bytes` and a `message`; and it lists `skipped_parts` as `{part, reason}` objects, `xml_truncated_parts` as `{part, error}` objects for parts whose XML walk stopped early so the text is a prefix, and `xml_anomalies` as `{part, detail}` objects for a worksheet that tripped the attribute guard or carried malformed attributes. Properties are merged in last and never overwrite a key already set. A file that begins `PK` but whose ZIP directory will not open produces instead one record with `status: container_unreadable`, `name` of the form `Office document (unreadable): <file>`, `format` and `container` where the extension gave them, `content_incomplete` (reason `short_read` where fewer bytes were read than declared, else `unresolved_structure`), `inventory_incomplete: true` with reason `unresolved_structure`, `bytes_read`, `declared_size`, `open_error` carrying the zip library's message, an empty `text`, and a `message` saying this is not evidence the document was empty or not an office document. Because the search indexer serialises record metadata into its content field, the `text` is what makes the document full-text searchable. It produces no `TimelineEvent`, no `FileEntry` for embedded objects, no hash and no separate record for properties; the `created` and `modified` values are copied as the strings the document held.

**Cannot.** It cannot read the legacy binary formats — `.doc`, `.xls`, `.ppt` are OLE2 compound files, carry a non-office extension by this module's table, and are skipped before a byte is read. It cannot see a password-protected OOXML document: Office writes those as an OLE2 `EncryptedPackage`, so the file fails the `PK` check and the module returns nothing — no record, no encryption marker, no distinction from a text file — and a document renamed `.zip`, `.bak` or `.txt` is never read at all, while a document with its extension stripped is read only if its content types name a family. It reads a fixed set of parts and only those: no headers or footers, footnotes, endnotes, comments, notes slides, chart data, embedded objects, `docProps/app.xml` (application name, revision count, total editing time, company) or `vbaProject.bin` — a `.docm` or `.xlsm` is read as text and nothing on the record says it carries a macro project. In Word it takes every element whose local name is `t`, so `w:t` runs, `a:t` in drawings and text boxes, and both the `Choice` and `Fallback` halves of an `mc:AlternateContent` block are all included — the last of those duplicating text — while tracked deletions (`w:delText`) are silently excluded and tracked insertions silently included. In Excel it publishes the cached `v` of a formula cell and never the formula, dates as their serial numbers, booleans and errors as raw tokens, and it neither names sheets nor distinguishes hidden sheets, rows or columns; a shared-string index past the table yields an empty cell with nothing to say so.
