In OpenDocument it does not expand `table:number-columns-repeated`, and everything under `body` — including notes and hidden text — is one stream. Property dates are copied verbatim: no normalisation, no timezone reconciliation (ODF dates carry none), no check that created precedes modified, and no timeline event is raised from either. The text extraction is not an XML parser in the schema sense: namespaces are ignored, entities are unescaped and nothing else, and a walk that stops on a syntax error keeps what it had as a prefix. Its ceilings are a 256 MiB outer read, a 128 MiB decompressed member, a 4 MiB stored text, and 256 attributes per worksheet element; a document larger than 256 MiB has its central directory beyond the cap, so `ZipArchive::new` fails and it is published as `container_unreadable` with reason `short_read` and no `max_content_bytes` key (`unreadable_container_record` at `seance_plugin_office/src/lib.rs:826-834`), where the same shortfall on a document that did open is called `cap_reached` (`build_record`, 940-946). The zip library checks a member's stored CRC-32 only at the end of a full read, so a stored member is caught but a member skipped for size is never checked. The word count is a whitespace split of the extracted text and counts CJK text as one word per run. It cannot say how many documents it looked at and declined: every non-document path returns an empty list, indistinguishable in the processing log from a document it read and found empty. Nothing in this tree pins its reading of a real Office-authored file — every fixture in `seance_plugin_office/src/tests.rs` is a ZIP built in the test from hand-written XML.

**Refuses.** It refuses to file a damaged document beside the text files: a `PK`-prefixed file whose archive directory will not open is published as `container_unreadable` with the library's error, because a corrupt `.docx` and a `.txt` must not read the same. It refuses to publish an unreadable part as an empty part: a member the archive declares but the parser could not inflate, or refused for size, is named in `skipped_parts` and flags the record, because the caller substitutes empty text for it and an unflagged record would read as a genuinely blank document. It refuses to return any part of an over-cap member: a member that inflates past 128 MiB is dropped whole rather than truncated, so an over-cap part is never mistaken for the whole part. It refuses to publish clipped text as whole , a partially read archive as fully parsed, or a prefix from a stopped XML walk as a short document. It refuses to read attributes without a bound: the worksheet path, the one place a crafted attachment can reach quick-xml's quadratic duplicate-name check, goes through `XmlGuard`, pinned by `a_worksheet_with_a_hostile_attribute_count_parses_in_bounded_time` at under two seconds where the unguarded reader took about 29. It refuses to mistake a plain ZIP for a document, and refuses to read a file whose extension is not in its table. It refuses to emit a `null` property — an absent field is omitted. And it never returns an error: every failure path is `Ok`, so nothing this module declines or fails on reaches the processing log as an error row; the only trace of a document it could not read is the `container_unreadable` record, and the only trace of one it declined is silence.

### `plugin.email.parser`

**Reads.** Mail, from `FileEntry` and `Container` artifacts only. A `Container` labelled `mbox` goes straight to the mbox splitter; a `Container` labelled `ole2` is considered only if the name ends `.msg`, because OLE2 — signature `D0 CF 11 E0 A1 B1 1A E1` — is the same compound-document container as `.doc`, `.xls` and `.ppt`; any subtype other than `mbox`, `ole2`, `eml` or `msg` is declined in silence. Where there is no subtype and no mail extension (`.eml`, `.emlx`, `.msg`, `.mbox`, `.mbx`, `.pst`, `.ost`) the file is content-probed first: 1,024 bytes from offset 0 through a loop over short reads, because a windowed source hands back a handful of bytes per call and a 40-byte "header" failed the format gate and dropped a valid mail store. Selection then runs in one fixed order, and it is a name test as often as a byte test: `!BDN` at offset 0 is a PST or OST; failing that a `.pst` or `.ost` name, with no content test at all; then eight bytes at offset 0 matching `D0 CF 11 E0 A1 B1 1A E1` **together with** a `.msg` name; then `From ` at offset 0 as an mbox; then an `.emlx` name (which covers `.partial.emlx`), or, for a file with no such name, the whole Apple Mail wrapper — a decimal count line in those 1,024 bytes and `<?xml` starting exactly where the count says the message ends, looked for inside the probe or, when the counted offset lies past it, by one five-byte read at that counted offset, since a digits-only first line alone is common text; then a `.eml` name; then, in the first ten lines of the first 1,024 bytes, one **identity-bearing** header — `From:`, `To:`, `Cc:`, `Received:`, `Message-ID:`, `Message-Id:`, `Return-Path:` or `Delivered-To:`; and last a `.mbox` or `.mbx` name. The whole file is then staged in memory: at most 512 MiB (536,870,912 bytes), measured against the size the source **declares**. An `.eml` is parsed by the `mail-parser` RFC 5322 reader, which supplies the first `From` address and display name, the whole `To`, `Cc` and `Bcc` address lists, the subject, `Message-ID`, `In-Reply-To`, `References`, the first text body part, the first HTML body part, the `Date`, and the MIME attachment parts with their content type, `Content-Disposition` filename and decoded bytes. An mbox is split on separator lines of the form `From <sender> <asctime date>` — weekday, three-letter month, one- or two-digit day, `HH:MM:SS`, four-digit year, with any trailing zone — and the date is what tells a separator from prose, because requiring a blank line before it lost every message whose body ends without one: a Thunderbird mailbox of 49 messages yielded 4. The separator line itself is discarded, `>From ` at the start of a body line is unescaped to `From `, and each split message is handed to the same RFC 5322 reader with its index. An Apple Mail `.emlx` is three things end to end and only the middle one is mail: a decimal byte count on the first line (space-padded as Apple Mail writes it, `701 `), exactly that many bytes of RFC 5322 message, handed to the same reader as an `.eml`, and an XML property list, which is parsed and never reaches `body_text` or `body_html`. From the plist it reads `date-received`, `date-last-viewed`, `date-sent`, `flags`, `conversation-id`, `remote-id` and `original-mailbox`. A `.partial.emlx` is one Mail did not download whole: each MIME part left as a stub — a leaf with an `X-Apple-Content-Length` header and an empty body — lives beside it as `<id>.<section>.emlxpart`, the section being the part's 1-based position, dotted through nested multiparts (`message/rfc822` parts are not descended into, and nesting is walked 16 deep). Only the part files the message itself declares are asked for, by name, from the source's own directory; the directory is never listed. A part that is found is spliced into the message where its body belongs before the message is parsed, so a reunited attachment is extracted like any other, and its length with CRLF line ends is compared with `X-Apple-Content-Length`, which is what that header counts (on the hoover-testdata file: 75,521 bytes and 981 line ends make 76,502). A PST or OST is identified from its own header before any reader is asked to open it: `!BDN`, the client tag at offset 8 (`SM` a PST, `SO` an OST, anything else "unknown client") and `wVer` at offset 10, which this build's gate admits only for versions 14, 15, 23 and 36. **Version 36** — the Outlook 2013-and-later layout with 4 KiB pages, which the linked reader refuses — is read in memory by this crate's own reader (`ost4k`, ROADMAP §2.6a), written from the format as it lies in the one real file held, the NIST Data Leakage suspect's OST: both header CRCs are checked and `bCryptMethod` must be 0; the node and block B-trees are walked iteratively from the header's two roots, each 4,096-byte page checked for its CRC over bytes 0..4072, its page type, its BID and signature, and its entry size, count and level, with a visited-page set and a depth cap of 8; a page past the bytes supplied or of all zeros is named as never written (on an image, not initialised) rather than walked; every block the block B-tree names is then read once — trailer, BID, signature and CRC over the stored bytes — and zlib-inflated where its stored and inflated sizes differ, the inflation stopped one byte past the stated size. Folders and messages are the node B-tree's normal-folder (type 2) and normal-message (type 4) nodes, each read as a property context through the heap-on-node and its B-tree-on-heap (XBLOCK/XXBLOCK data trees and SLBLOCK/SIBLOCK subnode trees followed), placed by the parent NID the node B-tree records — **not** by walking the folders' hierarchy and contents tables — with each folder's `PidTagContentCount` compared against what was found under it; attachments are the message's attachment subnodes (type 5). A property whose value would not read is listed, not dropped: a fixed-width value of the wrong length, an odd-length UTF-16 string, a value past a read budget equal to the heap's own size, and a tag that a second record names again (the first value is kept and the repeat is listed, so a conflict is never settled by arrival order) each go to `properties_unreadable`. An 8-bit string that is valid UTF-8, ASCII included, is read as a string; any other 8-bit string is kept as stored and decoded afterwards in the message's code page (see Cannot). For versions 14, 15 and 23 the staged bytes are handed to the linked `outlook-pst` reader as an owned in-memory copy; nothing is written to disk. The store is opened as Unicode first and ANSI second, and the refusal of the reader that matches the header's version is the one reported. `IpmSubTreeEntryId` is read from the store properties, and the hierarchy is walked depth-first from it: each contents-table row is turned into an entry id from its node id and read as a message, each hierarchy-table row into a subfolder, and each folder node is entered once — a hierarchy row naming a folder already entered is counted as a cycle and skipped, so its messages are not published twice. Over the same bytes, and without the linked reader, the module's own reader of the 512-byte-page layouts (`pst512`) then scans for deleted mail (see Cannot). Per message, on every version, it reads `Subject 0x0037` (Outlook's two-character prefix marker, U+0001 and a length, removed), the sender — name `0x0C1A`, address `0x5D01` then `0x0C1F` — and the party it was sent on behalf of — name `0x0042`, address `0x5D02` then `0x0065` — of which one party supplies both the name and the address, the sender when it has a usable address and otherwise the represented party, the other being published as `sent_on_behalf_of` only where the sender leads and the two visibly differ, display recipients `0x0E04`/`0x0E03`/`0x0E02`, `Body 0x1000` and `BodyHtml 0x1013` (the text rendered from the HTML where there is no plain body, and `body_source` saying which), whether `RtfCompressed 0x1009` is present (it is not decoded), `MessageClass 0x001A`, `HasAttachments 0x0E1B`, `InternetMessageId 0x1035`, `InReplyToId 0x1042`, `InternetReferences 0x1039`, `InternetCodepage 0x3FDE` (the code page of the HTML body's bytes), `MessageCodepage 0x3FFD` (that of the message's 8-bit text), and for the time `ClientSubmitTime 0x0039` then `MessageDeliveryTime 0x0E06` then `CreationTime 0x3007`. Each message's attachment table is read row by row for `AttachLongFilename 0x3707`/`AttachFilename 0x3704`/`DisplayName 0x3001`, `AttachSize 0x0E20`, `AttachExtension 0x3703`, `AttachMimeTag 0x370E` and `AttachMethod 0x3705`. A message whose full read fails is re-read, on the Unicode and the ANSI layout alike and through one function, with eight properties only — subject, sender name, sender address, sender SMTP address, `PidTagDisplayTo`, submit time, creation time and message class — and published from those, marked `read_fallback`; a message that not even that opens is asked of this crate's own reader (`pst512`), which needs no recipient table (the linked reader refuses a message that has none, as an Outlook 2000 welcome message does): one it opens is published with `read_by: own_reader`, its recipient table listed when it has one and the summary's `messages_read_by_own_reader` counting it; one that opens in neither reader is counted in `messages_unreadable`. Threading is derived in one place for every format that reaches a record, from the RFC 5322 identifiers only: angle brackets and folding whitespace are stripped and case is **not** folded, since the local part of an address is case-sensitive by the standard; the key is the first usable entry of `References` (the ancestry, oldest first), else the parent named in `In-Reply-To`, else the message's own `Message-ID`.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per message, `type: EmailMessage`, `subtype: email_message`, `analysis_type: email`, parented to the artifact it was read from. It carries `from` and `from_name`, the `to`, `cc` and `bcc` lists, `subject`, `message_id`, `in_reply_to`, `references`, `body_text` and `body_html` each cut at 65,536 bytes on a UTF-8 boundary with a `...[truncated]` marker appended, `body_truncated` (set when either was cut), `attachment_count`, an `attachments` array, `attachments_incomplete`, `has_attachments`, the `container` it came from, and the time twice: `date` as an RFC 3339 string and `date_epoch` as Unix seconds beside it, because the conversation views sort and page on one integer expression across every channel and casting this format's ISO string to an integer yields the *year*. An mbox message carries its `message_index`; a PST message carries `format: pst`, its `folder_path` within the store, its `message_class` and `body_source` (`text`, `html`, `rtf_not_decoded` or `none`), `body_html_codepage` (the code page the message named for its HTML, else null) and `body_decoding_lossy`, `legacy_8bit_text` where any 8-bit text was decoded in a code page, and `sent_on_behalf_of` where the sender is a delegate; a message published from the eight-property fallback adds `read_fallback`, `read_fallback_error` and `properties_unreadable`; a version-36 message also carries `store_version: 36` and its `node_id`. `properties_unreadable` names any property whose value would not read, on any version, and marks the record `content_incomplete` with reason `unresolved_structure`, as does an unreadable attachment row or an HTML body decoded with replacement characters. A message recovered from unallocated space carries the fields set out under Deleted mail in Cannot. An `.emlx` message carries `format: emlx`, `emlx_byte_count`, `emlx_plist_present` and `emlx_plist_parsed` (with `emlx_plist_error` where it would not parse), the plist values as `emlx_date_received`, `emlx_date_last_viewed`, `emlx_date_sent`, `emlx_flags`, `emlx_conversation_id`, `emlx_remote_id` and `emlx_original_mailbox` where present, `emlx_flags_decoded: false`, and `emlx_plist_other_keys` naming any other key by name; a count larger than the file adds `emlx_bytes_available` and `content_incomplete` with reason `short_read`, and a missing or unparseable plist sets reason `unresolved_structure`. A `.partial.emlx` adds `emlx_partial: true` and `emlx_parts`, one entry per stub with its `section`, the part `file` looked for, `declared_length`, and `status` — `reunited` (with `bytes` and `declared_length_agrees`), `absent`, `source_cannot_look`, `over_cap` or `read_failed` — and every part not reunited is named in `attachment_absent_reason` and sets `content_incomplete`. Every record carries `email_thread_key`, `email_thread_basis` — `references_root`, `in_reply_to` or `own_message_id` — and `email_thread_basis_note`, a sentence stating what that basis is worth, or, where the message carries none of the three identifiers, `email_thread_unavailable_reason` and **no key**. Each `.eml`, `.emlx` and mbox attachment whose bytes were read becomes a child `FileEntry` parented to the message record, carrying the decoded bytes, the reassembled `main/subtype` content type, `source: email_attachment` and the subject and `Message-ID` of the message it came from, so the modules that subscribe to `FileEntry` — the hasher and the file-type detector — see it. The inline `attachments` summary states per attachment whether that happened, in `bytes_extracted`. One `TimelineEvent` per message that yielded a usable time, parented to the source artifact, stamped `timestamp_desc: "Email Sent"`, `event_type: email_message`, `source_module: plugin.email.parser`, with the from, to, subject and a one-line description. One `PstSummary` record per store (`subtype: pst_summary`), carrying `pst_variant` (`unicode`, `ansi` or `ost_v36`), `message_count` and `folder_count` — **what was recovered, not what the store holds** — the caps `max_messages` and `max_folders`, and every way the walk fell short counted separately: `depth_limited_folders`, `messages_unreadable`, `entry_ids_unresolved`, `folders_unreadable`, `root_unreachable`, `messages_partial` (messages published from the eight-property fallback) and `folder_cycles` (hierarchy rows naming a folder already entered). `message_count` counts live messages only; messages recovered from unallocated space are counted apart. Where any of those fired it also carries `truncated`, `inventory_incomplete`, `message_cap_reached`, `folder_cap_reached`, the standard `content_incomplete`/`content_incomplete_reason` pair, and a `message` naming each shortfall in words. The summary of every layout also states what the deleted-mail scan found and what it could not read: `recovered_messages`, `recovered_fragments`, `recovered_entries_without_data`, `recovered_copies_of_live`, `superseded_copies`, `unreferenced_pages`, `unreferenced_blocks`, `blocks_found_by_scan`, `recovery_capped`, `unreferenced_pages_unvalidated` and `unreferenced_blocks_unvalidated` (offsets whose trailer matched and whose CRC or metadata did not: counted whole, the first 100 listed) and `property_contexts_not_decoded` (unreferenced blocks that carry the property-context signature and did not decode, with block, offset and reason), each also said in the `store_note` sentence. On versions 14, 15 and 23 it adds `recovery_scanned_version`, or `recovery_not_run` with the reason where the scan could not be made. A recovery listing that stopped at its cap sets `recovery_capped` and marks the summary `content_incomplete`, with reason `cap_reached` unless a more specific reason is already there, and adds a sentence to `message`; it does not set `truncated` or `inventory_incomplete`, because the live inventory was not cut short. A version-36 summary adds `store_version`, `store_client`, `header_file_eof` beside `bytes_supplied`, `btree_pages_walked`, `page_faults` and `pages_unwritten`, `blocks_in_bbt`, `blocks_verified`, `blocks_inflated`, `blocks_unwritten` and `block_faults`, `folder_count_mismatches`, `messages_with_unreadable_properties` and a `store_note` sentence; any page fault, block fault, unreadable node or property, or folder holding fewer messages than it says sets the incompleteness pair (`short_read` where something was never written) and names it in `message`, and its display name reads "OST (version 36): N messages from M folders" ("PST: N messages from M folders" on the other layouts), followed by ", K recovered from unallocated space" where any were. And where a file was identified as mail and not turned into messages, a status record instead of silence: `type: EmailParseStatus`, `subtype: email_not_parsed`, with `status` one of `OverSizeCap` (declared size and the cap), `ReadFailed`, `ShortRead` (`bytes_read` against `declared_size`), `FormatUnrecognised`, `NotParsable` (with `bytes_skipped` and, inside an mbox, the message index), `InvalidCompoundFile` or `EmlxNoByteCount` (with `format: emlx`) — each with `content_incomplete` and a reason of `cap_reached`, `short_read` or `unresolved_structure`, and a display name reading "Email not parsed: <file>", or "Email partially read: <file>" for a short read. A PST that was recognised and produced nothing leaves a record whose `subtype` is `parse_failed`, naming the store and the reason, titled "OST not parsed" over an `.ost` and "PST not parsed" over a `.pst`; that record carries **no `type` key and no `status`**, so a consumer selecting on `type: EmailParseStatus` does not see it.

**Cannot.** **It cannot tell you that a header is true.** `From`, `To`, `Cc`, `Subject`, `Date` and `Message-ID` are what the file says, and the file was written by whoever sent it. This module verifies no DKIM signature, checks no SPF or DMARC result, reads no `Received` chain — it does not extract `Received` headers at all — and publishes no `Authentication-Results`. A message record is evidence of what a mailbox held, not proof that the named person wrote it or that the named recipient read it. For the same reason it publishes no raw header block and no other header: an examiner who needs the transport path, the `X-` headers, the `Return-Path`, the reply-to, the user agent or the original `Content-Type` must go back to the file, and for a message inside an mbox or a PST no artifact holds that message's own bytes at all. It cannot read an Outlook `.msg` whose name does not say `.msg`: the compound-document signature it tests — `D0 CF 11 E0 A1 B1 1A E1` — is shared with Word, Excel and PowerPoint, so the name must agree before the bytes are read as mail. It cannot say where a message was when it was read, or in whose hand it was. A file is a file; it proves the file existed at that path. **Zones and precision.** An `.eml` `Date` header is converted to an instant and rendered as UTC: the offset the sender's client wrote — which is what shows whether a message was sent at 9am or at midnight where the sender was — is not published, and RFC 5322 carries no fraction, so an `.eml` time is seconds at best. A PST time is a FILETIME, UTC by definition, rendered at its full 100-nanosecond precision in `date`, but `date_epoch` is whole seconds, so two PST messages a quarter of a second apart carry the same integer and any consumer paging on it orders them by nothing. The two fields come from one decision over one property: the calendar conversion decides for both, so a time past the year 10000 (the Windows "never" sentinel is one) and a FILETIME landing exactly on the 1970 boundary are each refused for both fields rather than for one. **Which time.** Every timeline event is labelled `Email Sent` whatever supplied it, and the record does not name the property that did. For a PST the second and third choices are `PidTagMessageDeliveryTime` and `PidTagCreationTime`, so a message with no submit time produces an event reading "Email Sent" at a time that is not when it was sent. Where no usable time survives, `date_epoch` is **absent rather than zero**, `date` is empty and **no timeline event is produced at all**, so an undated message appears in no timeline. **What a PST message may be missing.** A message whose full property read failed is published from eight properties only: no body, no `cc` or `bcc`, no `Message-ID`, `In-Reply-To` or `References` — so no thread key — no delivery time, and no attachment inventory. The record says so, on the Unicode and the ANSI layout alike: `read_fallback`, `read_fallback_error` and `properties_unreadable` name the failure, the record is `content_incomplete` with reason `unresolved_structure`, and the summary counts it in `messages_partial` and is itself marked incomplete (before that date the Unicode path published such a message unmarked and counted it with the messages read whole, and the ANSI path had no fallback and counted it lost). It is still counted in `message_count`. A message that not even the fallback opens exists only as the count `messages_unreadable`; no record names it. **Threading.** `In-Reply-To` alone threads two levels and no further: a reply to a reply keys on its own parent, so one exchange appears as more than one thread, and the record says so in `email_thread_basis_note`. It cannot group by subject line, and does not try — "Re: invoice" is not evidence that two messages are the same exchange. A message carrying none of the three identifiers is grouped into nothing. A thread of one means no reply was recovered, not that none was sent; and a thread is only ever as complete as the mailbox in hand. **Recipients.** For a PST or OST of any version the `to`, `cc` and `bcc` lists come from `PidTagDisplayTo`, `PidTagDisplayCc` and `PidTagDisplayBcc` split on `;`. Those are **display strings**: they often hold names rather than addresses, and where an address is not in them there is none on the record. The reader does not open the message's recipient table, so a recipient's SMTP address is not recovered from a live PST message by it; the messages this crate's own reader publishes (a live one the linked reader refused, a version 36 one, and a recovered one) carry `recipients`, one record per recipient-table row with its type, name, address type, address and SMTP address, graded against libpff on five public stores. On the `.eml` path a `Bcc` header is read where it is present, which in a received message it usually is not — a blind copy is a fact about delivery that the delivered message does not record. **Bodies.** Only the first text part and the first HTML body part of an `.eml` are read; alternatives, inline parts beyond the first and nested message parts are not published as bodies. For a PST or OST `body_html` is `PidTagBodyHtml` decoded in the code page `PidTagInternetCodepage` names where this build can decode it (UTF-8 and UTF-16, Windows 874 and 1250 to 1258, Shift-JIS, GBK, GB18030, Big5, EUC-KR, EUC-JP, ISO-2022-JP, Macintosh, KOI8-R, KOI8-U, ISO-8859-1 to 9 and ISO-8859-15) and otherwise as UTF-8, with `body_html_codepage` recording what the message named. A byte that could not be mapped is replaced, and then `body_decoding_lossy` is set and the record is `content_incomplete`: the text is not the stored body. An HTML body stored as a string property was decoded by the reader that produced it, not by this rule. Where there is no `PidTagBody` the text is rendered from that HTML and `body_source: html` says so (tested on the version 36 OST; versions 14, 15 and 23 go through the same extractor, but no test yet holds a PST of those versions with a binary HTML body). No compressed-RTF body is decoded on any path, so a message holding only `PidTagRtfCompressed` — Outlook's own synchronisation logs in the Data Leakage OST are three — has an empty body and `body_source: rtf_not_decoded`, and is marked `content_incomplete` with reason `compressed`: its body is present and was not read. `body_source: none` means no body property at all. Every body over 65,536 bytes, text or HTML, is cut and carries `body_truncated` with the standard `content_incomplete`/`cap_reached` pair (on a PST record an unreadable attachment row or property, or a lossy HTML decode, takes the reason `unresolved_structure` instead, and `body_truncated` still says the body was cut); the `...[truncated]` sentinel inside the text is prose, and the flags are what a consumer reads. **Attachments.** A PST attachment is **inventory only**: filename, size, extension, MIME tag and attach method are published, and its bytes are never carried into the case, so it is never hashed, previewed or exported. Its `attachment_count` is the number of rows in the attachment table and the `attachments` list holds only the rows that read, so the list can be shorter than the count, with `attachments_incomplete` and the `content_incomplete` pair the signs (a recovered message names the first ten attachments that would not read in `recovery_gaps`, with node, block and reason, and counts the rest); and an attachment row with none of `AttachLongFilename`, `AttachFilename` or `DisplayName` is published with an empty filename. An `.eml` attachment over 67,108,864 bytes, or one that decodes to no bytes, is left as a row with `bytes_extracted: false` and no reason beside it. No attachment is ever reached by the carver, which subscribes to file systems and unallocated space only. An embedded message attachment is not parsed as a message on any path. **Apple Mail `.emlx`.** The plist `flags` integer is published raw and **not decoded** into read, flagged, deleted or any other state: its bit layout is Apple-private and no file held here confirms any published description of it. The Envelope Index reader reports read, flagged and deleted state for the rows of Mail's own index, and those rows are not joined to any `.emlx` by this tool — neither reader names the other's record — so matching the two is the examiner's own search. The plist dates are published as the integers Mail wrote, not converted and not put on the timeline; the timeline event is still the `Date` header's. A `.partial.emlx`'s parts are reached only on a source that can open a file beside the one being read, which is a host directory or a ZIP entry and nothing else. A file served out of an NTFS, APFS, HFS+ or ext4 file system inside a disk image cannot (`supports_siblings` is false there), so on the commonest shape of this evidence, a Mac's disk image, every stub part of a `.partial.emlx` is `source_cannot_look`, as it is for a carved or in-memory copy — **could not look, which is not the same as absent** — the stub parts stay empty and no attachment is extracted from them. A part file over 64 MiB is not read (`over_cap`). A `X-Apple-Content-Length` that disagrees with the part is reported in `declared_length_agrees: false` and the part is still used. A stub inside a `message/rfc822` part, or nested more than 16 multiparts deep, is not looked for. An `.emlx` whose name was lost is recognised by its wrapper alone, so one whose count line is damaged, or whose plist is missing or does not start at the counted offset (a carve cut short, say), is not read as `.emlx`: it reaches the `.eml` path only if an identity-bearing header sits in its first ten lines, with the count line read as a header and whatever follows the message as body, and otherwise yields no record at all, in silence. The reader was checked against three files Apple Mail wrote — PRONOM_Research `2.emlx` and `9.emlx` (Mail 13.4, held locally, no licence, so not committed; the tests skip and say so when they are absent) and hoover-testdata `1498.partial.emlx` with its `1498.3.emlxpart` (MIT, committed) — and a Mail version that writes the wrapper differently may fail a check and say so. **Deleted mail.** From a version 36 store, and from version 14, 15 and 23 stores (below). The bytes supplied are walked again with the allocation map ignored: on version 36 every 4 KiB-aligned page and every 512-byte block slot whose trailer signature and CRC match its own offset is read, and node B-tree leaf pages no live tree references yield the entries of message nodes the live tree no longer holds, whose blocks are looked up among every block found. Each recovery is published by the same code on every layout, with `recovered: true`, `allocation: unallocated`, `recovery_source` (`stale_node_entry` or `unreferenced_block`), its page and block offsets in `recovery_offsets`, `recovery_other_versions` (the other versions of the same node entry, each with the reason it did not read where reading it was tried; when no version reads, each carries its own reason) and `recovery_completeness` (`complete`, or `partial` with `recovery_gaps` saying what was lost, such as an overwritten subnode tree or an attachment that would not read; a `partial` message record is `content_incomplete`); an entry whose data block is not found anywhere is named in the summary's `recovered_entries_without_data`, not published as a message. A message property context no entry names is a `partial` fragment whose folder and subnodes are unknown. A recovery is `deletion_status: deleted` only where the live walk was whole; where a live B-tree page or a live message node could not be read, it is `undecided` and `could_be_live` says why, because the message may still be live under a node the walk never reached. A recovery matching a live message's class, subject and two times is counted as a copy, not reported as deleted; the match needs a subject and at least one of the two times, so a message without a subject, or with neither time, has no identity and is never merged. Unreferenced folder-associated items (views, rules, configuration) are not mail: the version 36 summary counts them and the other layouts skip them. A recovery listing stops at 10,000 messages and, separately, 10,000 fragments, and says so on the summary. **What the scan could not read is stated, not skipped.** An offset whose trailer signature matched but whose CRC or metadata did not is counted and located (a signature match is a 16-bit check, so some are chance, but a damaged page or block is among them, and nothing stored there was read), and so is an unreferenced block that carries the property-context signature and would not decode or whose read the budget refused, with its block, offset and reason; "nothing more was found" cannot be read off a scan that was blind in those places. A recovery's folder path on versions 14, 15 and 23 that cannot be followed to the root (a missing parent, a parent that is not a folder, nesting past 64 levels) starts with a marker saying where it stopped, and a version 36 folder path does the same, with one more marker for a chain of parents that loops. A version 36 folder whose 8-bit name is not UTF-8 is decoded in Windows-1252, an assumption since a folder declares no code page, and listed on the summary as `folders_8bit_name_decoded`. On the Data Leakage OST it recovers the key's "It's me" whole; the three other deleted messages it recovers there are not in the key and are not graded, and the fragment rule is pinned only on a synthetic store. **Versions 14, 15 and 23** are walked the same way by a reader of their own 512-byte-page layouts (every 512-byte offset tried as a page, every 64-byte boundary as a block's end, 64-byte block slots, 12-byte ANSI or 16-byte Unicode trailers, permutative and cyclic encoding decoded (cyclic graded on synthetic re-encodings only), B-trees 8 levels deep and 4,096 data blocks under one node at most), and published by the same code, so a record reads the same whichever layout it came from; the scan is made only over a store the linked reader opened, and the summary says it was scanned (`recovery_scanned_version`) or, when it could not be (a version 36 store, for one), `recovery_not_run` with the reason. The ANSI layout is graded on a real Outlook 2000 mailbox against libpff: all 258 live messages read as libpff reads them, and with the 62 that have a stale node entry cut from the live tree, 61 come back with libpff's subject, folder and attachment count and the 62nd, whose data blocks were overwritten, is named as an entry without data. **The Unicode (version 23) layout is graded on a real 59 MB mailbox: all 543 live items read as libpff reads them. Three messages deleted from it are recovered, but libpff cannot recover from that file, so their existence is not corroborated; recovery after a live entry is cut from the tree is graded on altered copies of the real bytes. Version 15 has no sample.** Attachments are read, the recipient table is read for versions 14, 15, 23 and 36 (graded against libpff on five public stores, one of them version 14 and one version 36), and a deletion that left no stale node entry behind is not found, because the live block tree still names its block. On versions 14, 15 and 23 (not on version 36, which makes no such check) a fragment that shares its subject and delivery time with a live message says it may be an earlier state of that message: the one fragment in the real mailbox is an unsent draft of a live sent message. It examines nothing past the bytes supplied, reassembles no message whose blocks are all overwritten, and carves nothing that is not a whole, CRC-valid block. **Encryption and signatures.** It decrypts nothing and verifies nothing: an S/MIME or PGP message's protected body is whatever the file holds in that part, and there is no code in this module for either. It does not deduplicate: the same message in two mailboxes is two records. It normalises an mbox to LF line endings and decodes a non-UTF-8 mbox lossily, so a mailbox in an 8-bit legacy encoding reaches the reader with replacement characters; a PST binary property of even length and at least two bytes is read as UTF-16LE and otherwise as UTF-8, both lossily. **Legacy 8-bit text in a PST or OST.** A string stored as 8-bit text is in the message's own code page. On version 36, and on every message recovered from unallocated space whatever the version, 8-bit text that is valid UTF-8 (ASCII included) is read as UTF-8, and any other 8-bit text is kept as stored and decoded in the code page `PidTagMessageCodepage` declares where this build can decode it, and where it declares none in the non-Western Windows code page its locale (`PidTagMessageLocaleId`) or its transport code page (`PidTagInternetCodepage`) implies (Japanese 932, Simplified Chinese 936, Korean 949, Traditional Chinese 950, Thai 874 and the Cyrillic, Greek, Turkish, Hebrew, Arabic, Baltic, Vietnamese and Central European pages), an inference that is taken only if it decodes the bytes without replacing one, and otherwise in Windows-1252, which is an assumption; `legacy_8bit_text` names the tags so decoded (`tags`), the `codepage`, whether the message declared it (`codepage_declared`), how it was chosen (`codepage_basis`: `declared`, `message_locale_id`, `internet_codepage`, `store_messages` or `assumed`) and a note, so the characters read as a decoding of bytes and not as stored Unicode. Its limits: text that is valid UTF-8 is not flagged even where the message's code page would read the same bytes differently; a declared code page this build cannot decode is treated as undeclared; text that is not UTF-8 is also decoded lossily where the code page cannot map a byte, and the replacement character is then in the text. An attachment carries no code page of its own, so its 8-bit names are decoded in the code page of the message that holds it, and an attachment entry carries the same `legacy_8bit_text` marker when it was decoded. **For a live message in a version 14, 15 or 23 store** the linked `outlook-pst` reader supplies the stored bytes and this build applies the same rule to them, in place of the reader's own widening of each byte to the Unicode code point of the same value (Latin-1). That rule is pinned by unit tests on bytes and graded on one real mailbox with non-Western text: an Outlook 97-2002 store holding a Japanese contact, whose Unicode twin is the answer, reads character for character as the twin once the page its locale implies (Shift-JIS) is used, where it read as Windows-1252 mojibake before. That is one language and one double-byte page; the Cyrillic, Greek and other mappings are pinned on the locale table by unit tests, not by a real store. A live folder's name in a version 14 or 15 store is decoded in the page the store's messages agree on, sampled with this crate's own reader (up to 64 live messages; one page is taken only if every sampled message that names one names it, recorded on the summary as `folders_8bit_codepage`), else in Windows-1252, and listed on the summary; the mechanics are also pinned on a SYNTHETIC version 14 store, the Jean fixture with one byte of a folder name patched to 0xE9. The same name in a version 23 store is stored as UTF-16 and read as stored. **Version 36 specifically.** It reads an unencoded store only: a `bCryptMethod` other than 0 is refused by value. Folder-associated (hidden) messages, node type 8, are not read. Because messages are placed by their node's parent rather than by the folder's contents table, a message node the table no longer lists would still be published under the folder; `folder_count_mismatches` is where that shows, and it marks the summary incomplete only where a folder holds fewer messages than it says, not more. The reader was built and validated against one real file (the Data Leakage OST: 351 nodes, 381 blocks, 123 compressed, 14 messages, each of the 11 the NIST answer key lists found with its folder, subject and time, its sender matching the key's address on 6 and only by display name on the informant's own 5, which hold no SMTP address); a store written by a later Outlook in a way that file does not exercise may fail a check and say so. Reading a version 14, 15 or 23 PST holds a second in-memory copy of the store for the linked reader (made again for the second attempt where the first reader refused it); nothing is written outside the process. And it never tells you that a mailbox is complete: a store with a thousand messages read is a store this tool read a thousand messages out of. Its ceilings, each recorded on the record it touches: 512 MiB (536,870,912 bytes) staged per mail store, measured against the declared size — **any PST, OST, mbox or message larger than that produces one `OverSizeCap` status record and no messages**; 65,536 bytes of body text and of body HTML; 67,108,864 bytes per extracted attachment; through the linked reader (versions 14, 15 and 23) 100,000 messages and 10,000 folders per PST, with the walk stopping at either, and a PST folder nesting depth of 32 counting the IPM root as zero, past which the subtree and every message in it is abandoned and counted; on version 36 every folder found is listed, and the message cap is reported only where messages were left over; 10,000 recovered messages and 10,000 recovered fragments per store, and 100 listed offsets or blocks per list of unvalidated or undecoded finds, whose counts stay whole; for version 36, a node or block B-tree 8 pages deep, a B-tree-on-heap 8 levels deep that names no node twice, a data tree no deeper than an XXBLOCK that names no block twice and whose leaves hold exactly each level's `lcbTotal`, a subnode tree that names no block twice, node reads assembling at most 8 times the inflated bytes the block B-tree holds plus 1 MiB across the whole store (past that a node is named unreadable), a block inflated to at most its stated size, and a folder path of 64 names; 1,024 bytes and the first ten lines for content detection. The message and folder ceilings are PST-only: nothing caps the number of messages taken from one mbox, or the number of attachments on one message, beyond the 512 MiB stage.

**Refuses.** It refuses to consider an OLE2 compound document as mail unless the name says `.msg`, because that container is shared with Word, Excel and PowerPoint, and reading a spreadsheet as a message would put property streams it does not have on a record shaped like a message. It refuses to guess where an `.emlx` message ends: a file named `.emlx` that does not open with the decimal byte-count line leaves one `EmlxNoByteCount` status record and no message, because without the count the message cannot be told from the property list after it. It refuses to call a file mail because a header merely *says something about* a message. Android writes crash dumps under `/data/system/dropbox` with a header block of `Process:`, `Subject:` and `Build:`, and matching any one RFC-822-looking header turned twenty Java stack traces into twenty emails with no sender, no recipient, no date and a `wtf` trace as the body, on a case whose examiner is asked questions about the custodian's email. The match must be an identity-bearing header — who it is from, who it is to, or what names it as a message that travelled. RFC 5322 makes `From:` mandatory and real mail carries `Received:` and `Message-ID:` as well. It refuses to call a valid store malformed. A store of any format version other than 14, 15, 23 and 36 is named by its client and version with the sentence "this build's readers open versions 14, 15, 23 and 36 only, so none of it was read; the store is not malformed", because reporting the Data Leakage OST (version 36) as "Not a valid PST file" was a false statement about the evidence ; a version-36 store that is encoded is refused with its `bCryptMethod` named in the same terms, and one whose header fails its CRC or version check names what failed. A store whose header names a supported version and which the reader for that version refused is named by client and version with the reader's own reason — "its signature and version were recognised, but this build's reader refused its structure (...). The store is not shown to be malformed, and none of it was read" — and the record carries the incompleteness pair; it is not called "Not a valid PST file", which survives only for a file with no `!BDN` signature at all (or under 12 bytes), which both readers then refuse. It refuses to let a store it could not read look like a machine with no mail on it. An over-cap store, a store that would not read, an `.eml` whose bytes yield no header and no body, a file identified as mail whose content matches no format it reads, and a store whose IPM subtree or root folder will not open each leave a record saying what was found and what stopped it — the last of these titled "PST: identified but not readable", never "PST: 0 messages from 0 folders". The control is deliberate: a file nothing ever claimed was mail is skipped in silence, so a status record keeps meaning something. An mbox whose content holds no separator line leaves a `NoMessagesFound` status record saying what was looked for. **Two gaps remain in that rule, and an examiner should hear them: any bytes standing before the first separator in an mbox are dropped with nothing said, and a `.pst` or `.ost` handed to the tool as an evidence source in its own right is read by no module at all.** It refuses to invent a thread key. A message with no `Message-ID`, no `In-Reply-To` and no `References` gets none, and says why — a fabricated key would collect every header-less message in a mailbox into one "conversation" that never existed. For the same reason an empty leading `References` entry is skipped rather than taken as the root, and two spellings of one id (`<a@b>` and `a@b`) are one thread while two casings are two, because the standard makes the local part case-sensitive. It refuses to invent an attachment: a PST message with no attachment table reports zero rather than the one that `PidTagHasAttachments` alone once implied, and a row it could not read is counted and flagged rather than dropped. It refuses to publish an Exchange X.500 distinguished name as a sender address where a real one exists: `PidTagSenderSmtpAddress` and `PidTagSentRepresentingSmtpAddress` win over the legacy `*EmailAddress` properties, a present-but-blank property does not mask a good one further down the chain, a DN is published only where the leading party has no usable address, and where it has nothing at all the field is empty rather than fabricated ; and it refuses to pair a delegate's name with the principal's address, publishing one party's name and address together and the other as `sent_on_behalf_of`. It refuses to publish a message whose full read failed as a whole one (`read_fallback`, `messages_partial`), a recovery it cannot rule out as live as deleted (`undecided`), and two messages without a subject, or with neither time, as one (no identity, never merged); it refuses to publish a folder's messages twice where a hierarchy points back at an ancestor (`folder_cycles`), and to say a recovery scan found nothing more where it was blind (the unvalidated and undecoded counts). And it refuses to treat a prefix as a mailbox. Where the source delivered fewer bytes than it declared, the messages that parsed are emitted **and** a `ShortRead` record states the bytes read against the declared size, because a mailbox read to its first two thirds is not the mailbox.

### `plugin.executable.pe_signature`

**Reads.** The Authenticode signature of a Windows PE: its certificate table, the digest the signature commits to, and the digest of the image as it is on disk.

**Produces.** Whether the image's own bytes reproduce the digest inside its signature, with the signer's certificate details and the ranges that were and were not hashed.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell you the certificate chains to a root the machine trusts, that the certificate was valid when the file was signed, or that the signer is who the certificate says. It reports whether the bytes match the digest, which is a narrower claim than "signed by Microsoft" and must not be read as the wider one.

**Refuses.** It refuses to hash the bytes after the certificate table. Authenticode covers the image up to `FileLength - SizeOfCertTable`, and hashing further made 231 carved executables report as modified after signing, because a carver's window overshot the end of the file by between 8 and 97,824 bytes. Every one of those 231 matched once the digest stopped where the format says it stops.

### `plugin.filesystem.apfs`

**Reads.** An APFS container, and it does not find one for itself. It runs only on a `FileSystem` artifact whose `subtype` metadata is exactly `apfs` — the label the partition parser writes when `NXSB` stands at offset 32 of the 4,096-byte signature window it reads from the start of a partition or of a whole raw image, truncated to what actually arrived — and an artifact carrying any other subtype is declined in silence. It then re-establishes the container for itself: up to 4,096 bytes are probed from offset 0 of that window, at least 200 must arrive, and `NXSB` must stand at offset 32 or the module produces no artifact and the failure is recorded in the case's processing log. `nx_block_size` at 36 must be a power of two in 512..=65536 before a single allocation is sized from it, and where the block is larger than the probe returned the whole block is re-read and that re-read must succeed entire. Block 0 is the superblock written at format time, so the checkpoint descriptor ring is scanned for a newer one — `nx_xp_desc_blocks` at 104, `nx_xp_desc_base` at 112, up to 4,096 slots, each read whole, each required to carry object type 0x0001 and `NXSB`, the highest `xid` adopted — but block 0 stays the candidate of record and is what gets used when the ring holds nothing newer, when `nx_xp_desc_base` is zero, and when the descriptor area is in tree form. From the adopted superblock come `nx_omap_oid` (160), `nx_max_file_systems` (180) and the `nx_fs_oid` array from 184. Each non-zero volume OID is resolved through the container object map — a B-tree whose keys are read as a fixed 16 bytes of (oid, xid) and values as a fixed 16 bytes of (flags, size, paddr), hardcoded rather than taken from `btree_info_t` — taking the highest `xid` that is not flagged `OMAP_VAL_DELETED`. The volume superblock must hold `APSB` at 32; from it come `apfs_incompatible_features` (56), `apfs_omap_oid` (128), `apfs_root_tree_oid` (136), `apfs_num_files` (184), `apfs_num_directories` (192), `apfs_vol_uuid` (240), `apfs_fs_flags` (264) and the 256-byte `apfs_volname` at 704. The volume's object map gives `om_snap_count` (36) and the tree at 48, and the file-system tree root is resolved through it. That tree is walked depth-first, each physical node visited once, to a depth of 16; where the node is flagged `BTNODE_HASHED` — which is every sealed volume, so every macOS 11 or later system volume, Intel included — each index value's 8-byte child reference is an offset from the tree's own root oid and is rebased before the object map is asked for it, because resolving the raw field found none of the children and cost the whole 203,258-file inventory of a real macOS 13.7.4 system volume. In the leaves it reads four record types by the top four bits of `obj_id_and_type` and no others: inode (3) — the parent id, the data-stream id `private_id`, all four timestamps, the internal flags, the link count, uid, gid, mode, the `uncompressed_size` field, and the logical size from the `DSTREAM` extended field (x_type 8) in the extended-field blob at 92; directory entry (9), read always as `j_drec_hashed_key_t`, the name length from the low ten bits of the u32 at offset 8 and the name from offset 12; file extent (8), sought first under the data-stream id and only then under the inode number, because the two diverge for clones, with the length as the low 56 bits of `len_and_flags` and the `crypto_id`; and extended attribute (4), of which exactly two names are kept, `com.apple.decmpfs` and `com.apple.ResourceFork`. Paths are then built by a breadth-first walk of the directory entries from inode 2, descending only into an entry whose directory-entry type is `DT_DIR`. For a transparently compressed file it reads the `fpmc` decmpfs header out of the attribute and decodes the file whole — compression types 1 and 9 (stored inline), 3 (zlib inline), 4 (zlib in the resource fork), 7 (LZVN inline) and 8 (LZVN in the resource fork) — in the format's fixed 64 KiB chunks, LZVN through an in-tree decoder built to Apple's own 256-entry opcode dispatch table and checked against a tail chunk of a `ditto --hfsCompression` resource fork macOS itself produced. Every name it reads — file name, attribute name, volume name — is decoded through a lossy UTF-8 conversion.

**Produces.** **File slack**: for each live regular file in an unencrypted volume whose whole-block run list is complete and whose logical size is not a whole number of blocks, the bytes from its logical end to the end of its last allocation block are read, and a `SlackSpace` region is published (filesystem `apfs`, `source: file_slack`, offsets in the container's own coordinate space) when any of them is non-zero; a file reached under several names is offered once per inode; a slack summary counts the files offered, the tails that were all zero, the tails that could not be read and the files whose tail could not be located (a compressed or encrypted file, or one whose extent list was cut). Graded on the APFS partition of the CFTT string-search unix image against the extents libfsapfs reports, where every real tail is zero, and on tails planted in memory over that partition; not graded on a real macOS volume that holds a non-zero tail. One `FileSystem` record per volume, carrying the volume name and UUID, its index, the block size, and `apfs_num_files` and `apfs_num_directories` **as the superblock declares them**, so the count the volume claims can be set against the count recovered. The index is this parser's own position in the list of non-zero volume OIDs, not the container's `nx_fs_oid` slot and not `apfs_fs_index`. One `FileEntry` per inode that a directory entry names: the name, the absolute path, the parent path, the inode number, mode, uid, gid, size, and all four APFS inode timestamps — `created`, `modified`, `changed` and `accessed`, each a signed count of nanoseconds since the Unix epoch rendered as RFC 3339 — plus, where the entry's own directory record carries one, `date_added`: the instant it was added to that directory, a fifth timestamp the volume root never carries. `is_directory` and `is_symlink` are both derived from the inode's mode rather than from the directory entry, and the volume it came from. It writes no timeline events of its own; the storage layer projects those four onto the unified timeline for every producer at once. Where one inode is reachable under several names the alternates are published as `hardlink_paths`, and where the inode's link count exceeds one it also carries `hardlink_paths_known` and `hardlink_paths_complete`, with `inventory_incomplete_reason: apfs_hardlink_names_unresolved` when the count exceeds the names found; before that only the last name survived and "this file was never at path X" could be answered falsely . None of it is published for a directory, whose link count counts children rather than names. A regular file's content is attached as a data source over its extents and the same byte runs are persisted as `data_runs` with `data_runs_complete` beside them, so the file is still readable, hashable and exportable after ingest. A compressed file instead carries `compression: apfs_decmpfs`, the compression type and the format, algorithm and storage labels, the compressed length, the decmpfs logical size, the resource-fork stream id and `compressed_data_runs` where the bytes are in a fork, and the decmpfs attribute itself base64-encoded — the attribute is the content location, it lives in a B-tree nothing re-walks, and without it every compressed file on a macOS volume had no retrievable content at all. A volume whose walk fell short says so on itself and names which shortfall: `apfs_max_dir_entries` (as `directory_parse_incomplete`), `apfs_max_inodes`, `apfs_unwalked_subtree` with the count and `inventory_outcome: partial`, `apfs_volume_not_enumerated` with `inventory_outcome: not_enumerated` where subtrees were lost and nothing at all was recovered, `apfs_volume_walk_failed` with the error, or `apfs_snapshots_not_enumerated`. A volume whose walk returned also carries `snapshot_count` and `snapshots_enumerated: false` whether or not it has snapshots; a FileVault volume and a volume whose walk failed carry neither. A file whose bytes were not reconstructed carries `content_incomplete` and one of fourteen reasons — `apfs_file_too_large`, `apfs_no_extent_records`, `apfs_max_extents`, `apfs_extent_offset_overflow`, `apfs_extent_encrypted`, `apfs_decmpfs_header_unreadable`, `apfs_decmpfs_size_mismatch`, `apfs_decmpfs_unsupported_algorithm`, `apfs_decmpfs_too_large`, `apfs_decmpfs_decode_failed`, `apfs_decmpfs_resource_fork_missing`, `apfs_decmpfs_resource_fork_too_large`, `apfs_decmpfs_resource_fork_no_extents` or `apfs_decmpfs_resource_fork_unreadable` — with a sentence of detail, because a sized entry with no bytes and no reason is indistinguishable from a file that held nothing . An encrypted file also carries `content_encrypted`, `encryption: apfs_per_extent_crypto`, the encrypted extent count and each encrypted extent's logical offset, length, physical offset and `crypto_id`: the bytes are withheld, where they live is not. One `ParsedRecord` of subtype `parse_incomplete` is emitted where the container's own volume inventory is short — slots beyond the 100-volume cap or outside the superblock block, or named volumes that would not resolve or whose superblock would not parse — naming the declared slot count, the skipped count, the unreadable count, the number reported and the first error, because the volumes lost there produce no artifact to stamp.

**Cannot.** **It cannot recover a deleted file, and it does not try.** It reads the live file-system tree of one checkpoint and nothing else: no free B-tree record, no reaped inode, no private directory, no unallocated block, no snapshot. Every entry it emits is a live entry, there is no `deleted` marker anywhere in what it produces, and the absence of a file from its inventory is not evidence that the file never existed. It cannot read a snapshot: `om_snap_count` is published, but a file version that exists only in a snapshot — including anything deleted since that snapshot was taken — is not in the case . It cannot read an encrypted volume's files at all and does not decrypt anything: not a FileVault volume, not a per-extent-encrypted file, and it holds no key, password or recovery-key path; a FileVault volume's record says `encrypted: true` and does **not** say `inventory_incomplete`, so the case's incompleteness census does not count a volume whose entire inventory was unreachable. It publishes no free space, so nothing points the carver at an APFS volume's unallocated blocks — the space manager is never read. **It cannot tell you that a volume it walked to the end was walked completely.** It publishes the superblock's `apfs_num_files` and `apfs_num_directories` and compares them with nothing; only five conditions raise an incompleteness flag — the inode cap, the directory-entry cap, an unwalked subtree, a failed walk and a non-zero snapshot count — and every other way a record goes missing leaves the volume reading as fully enumerated. Those other ways are real and each is silent: an inode record shorter than 92 bytes, a directory entry whose key or value will not parse, an extent value shorter than 24 bytes, an attribute declaring neither embedded nor stream storage, an inode that no directory entry names, a directory whose directory-entry type is not `DT_DIR` and therefore the whole subtree beneath it, and a B-tree node whose table of contents fails a bounds check mid-node — which truncates that node and returns the prefix as a success, dropping every remaining file, directory entry and extent in it with no counter and no flag. It cannot say where a symlink points: the target lives in an extended attribute it discards, and a symlink's size, like a directory's, is reported as 0; a FIFO, socket or device node is emitted with `is_directory` and `is_symlink` both false and a size of 0, indistinguishable from an empty file. Of the extended attributes on a volume it keeps two by name; a quarantine flag, a Finder attribute, an ACL and every other attribute are read past and appear on no record, and the inode's own `default_protection_class` and `bsd_flags` are skipped without being decoded. It resolves no firmlink, so the synthesised System-plus-Data root a modern macOS presents is not reconstructed, and it decodes every directory-entry key as the hashed form, never consulting the `apfs_incompatible_features` word it parses — so it applies no case folding and no Unicode normalisation either. It verifies no checksum on any object it walks: the Fletcher-64 is computed only while choosing a checkpoint superblock, and even there only when block 0's own checksum reproduces, so a corrupt B-tree node, object map or volume superblock is parsed on its magic and its declared offsets alone; nothing on any record says a container was read from the format-time block 0 because the ring was in tree form or would not read. It reads the object map's keys and values as a fixed 16 bytes each rather than from `btree_info_t`, so a map declaring any other geometry is parsed against the wrong offsets. Where the superblock block is too small to hold a field, that field reads as zero without comment: the volume name is published as an empty string below 960 bytes and the UUID as all zeros below 256. **A name on its records is the file system's bytes put through a lossy UTF-8 conversion**, so a name that is not valid UTF-8 is published with replacement characters and nothing marks it; the path is this tool's reconstruction, built by a breadth-first walk from inode 2, and where an inode has several directory entries the canonical `path` is the first that walk discovered and not a choice APFS made. Its timestamps are published to nanosecond precision exactly as the inode holds them and are never range-checked; one that will not convert to a date is emitted as an empty string rather than as null. The inode's internal flags are decoded and on no record it emits. `date_added` — the fifth APFS timestamp, the instant the entry was added to its directory — is now published alongside `created`/`modified`/`changed`/`accessed`, but only where the entry has a directory record of its own to read it from; the volume root, which has none, carries no `date_added` rather than a fabricated one. A regular file with no `DSTREAM` extended field is sized from the inode's `uncompressed_size` field, and where that is zero it is published as a zero-byte file with no flag. Where the container superblock or the container object map will not read, it produces no artifact at all — not even an incompleteness record — and the only trace is the error row in the case's processing log. Its caps are real and each names itself on the record it truncates: 100 volumes per container, a B-tree depth of 16, 1,000,000 inodes and 500,000 directory entries per volume, 100,000 extents per data stream, 4,294,967,296 bytes (4 GiB) above which a file's real bytes are not mapped, 67,108,864 bytes (64 MiB) of decoded output for a decmpfs file and the same ceiling on a decmpfs **resource fork's** declared length — an inline compressed payload is bounded only by the attribute's own 16-bit length — and 4,096 checkpoint descriptor slots scanned. LZFSE — decmpfs types 11 and 12, common on modern macOS — is not decoded, and those files are named as undecoded rather than served.

**Refuses.** It refuses a volume whose `APFS_FS_UNENCRYPTED` bit is clear. A FileVault volume is emitted as a `FileSystem` record with `encrypted: true` and its file-system walk is not attempted, because the records are ciphertext and decoding them would produce invented names and times. It refuses to serve ciphertext as content anywhere, at three independent points: an extent whose `crypto_id` is neither 0 nor `APFS_UNASSIGNED_CRYPTO_ID` has its byte runs withheld, its data source withheld, and a read of it through the file source refused outright with the logical offset and the `crypto_id` in the error — fixing only the first would leave the next caller free to hash and export encrypted blocks as plaintext. Those two sentinel values are treated as clear on the strength of a recorded negative control: every extent of three real volumes was measured at `crypto_id == 0`, and a rule without that control would have flagged every file on every normal volume. It refuses to read physical block 0 as file data: APFS writes block 0 for a hole, block 0 of the container is the container superblock, and serving it would hand an examiner container structures to hash as the file's own bytes, so the range reads as zeros and persists as a sparse run. It refuses to zero-fill what it could not locate: past the last extent of a list the 100,000-extent cap truncated, the source short-reads instead of fabricating a sparse tail, and an extent whose physical offset overflows is persisted as a hole **and** the runs declared incomplete. It refuses a block it could not read whole — callers decode records across the entire block, and a zero-padded tail would be parsed as records that were never there — it refuses to re-read a short superblock into a padded buffer, and it refuses to adopt a checkpoint descriptor slot that did not read whole. It refuses a deleted (ghost) object-map mapping even when its transaction id is the highest, because a stale ghost would shadow the live object and point at a reclaimed block. It refuses to serve a compressed file's compressed bytes under any circumstance: a decmpfs attribute that is a data stream rather than an embedded value, one without the `fpmc` magic, an inode and a decmpfs header that disagree about the file's length, an algorithm it does not decode, a decoded size or a resource fork above its 64 MiB ceilings, a missing, capped, unlocatable, encrypted or short resource fork, or a decode that does not produce exactly the declared size — each returns no content and its own reason. The rebuild after ingest refuses on the same terms and two more: a run list the parser already declared short, and a run list that accounts for fewer bytes than the resource fork is long; and an artifact carrying no `decmpfs_attribute_b64` is refused with the instruction to re-ingest rather than served something else. Underneath, the LZVN decoder returns no bytes at all on an undefined opcode, a stream that ends without end-of-stream, a match distance of zero or one reaching before the start of the block, or an expansion of the wrong length, because a prefix that happened to decode would be exported and hashed as though it were the file. It refuses to rebase a non-hashed index node's child reference, which would break every volume that reads correctly today. It refuses a block size that is not a power of two in 512..=65536. And it refuses to report a short inventory as a complete one — or a total failure in the language of a partial one: where subtrees were lost and nothing was recovered the volume says it was not enumerated rather than that it is a subset, because "a subset of the volume" over an empty listing reads as a mostly-complete listing with gaps.

### `plugin.filesystem.btrfs`

**Reads.** A Btrfs volume, and only when the partition layer has already called it one. It subscribes to `FileSystem` artifacts with `InputCapability::RandomAccess` and gates on `subtype` being exactly `btrfs` — not on `filesystem_type` — a subtype the partition module's detector writes after finding `_BHRfS_M` at `+0x40` of a superblock copy at 64 KiB, 64 MiB or 256 GiB. Without a data source it returns `InvalidInputFormat`. It reads the 4,096-byte superblock from the first of those three offsets that lies inside the source and parses — a copy beyond the end is skipped, a short read or wrong magic tries the next — and keeps the raw bytes of the copy that parsed, because the system chunk array and the device's own id are read from that same copy (a mirror paired with the primary's chunk array pairs a live `chunk_root` with a stale array). From it: `fsid` at `0x20`, `generation` `0x48`, `root` `0x50`, `chunk_root` `0x58`, `total_bytes` `0x70`, `bytes_used` `0x78`, `num_devices` `0x88`, `sectorsize` `0x90`, `nodesize` `0x94`, the 256-byte label at `0x12b`, `sys_chunk_array_size` at `0xa0` and the array itself at `0x32b` (17-byte key, 48-byte chunk item, 32-byte stripes of `devid`, `offset`), and `dev_item.devid` at `0xc9`. Every B-tree node is read whole at `nodesize` — refused outside 4,096..=262,144 — with `read_full`, and a short node is an error, never a zero-filled parse; the 101-byte header yields `bytenr`, `generation`, `owner`, `nritems`, `level`; internal nodes are 33-byte key pointers, leaves 25-byte items indexing a data area. Walks are bounded by a visited set, a depth of 8 and 1,000,000 nodes. Logical addresses resolve through the chunk map: the system chunks bootstrap the chunk tree walk at `chunk_root`, whose `CHUNK_ITEM` (type 228) records extend the map; for each range the profile flags choose the arithmetic — SINGLE/DUP/RAID1 take any stripe, preferring a device it has; RAID0 interleaves by `stripe_len`; RAID10 stripes across `num_stripes/2` columns of two mirrors; RAID5/6 locate the data column with the kernel's `(row + col) % num_stripes` rotation and never touch parity. The root tree at `root` yields every `ROOT_ITEM` (type 132) for objectid 5 and for 256..=u64::MAX-255, taking the tree's root bytenr at `+176`. Each file tree is walked for `INODE_ITEM` (type 1: generation, size, nlink, uid, gid, mode, atime/ctime/mtime/otime seconds), `DIR_INDEX` (type 96: location key, name, type), and `EXTENT_DATA` (type 108: inline payload, or `disk_bytenr`, `disk_num_bytes`, `extent_offset`, `num_bytes`, with `compression` and `encryption` bytes). Paths are built breadth-first from inode 256 along `DIR_INDEX` entries; an entry whose location is a `ROOT_ITEM` is a subvolume or snapshot mount and is queued as a separate tree under its mount path; trees no mount names are walked under `/<subvolume_N>`. A sibling device image is found by scanning up to 64 regular files in the primary image's directory (when the artifact carries `path`, `source_path` or `container_path`) for a primary superblock with the same `fsid`, keyed by its `devid`. Zlib and zstd extents are decompressed in memory through `seance_core::compression::btrfs_decompress_blob` for files up to 256 MiB.

**Produces.** A second `FileSystem` artifact, child of the input and sharing its data source, with `filesystem_type: Btrfs`, `total_bytes`, `bytes_used`, `generation`, `num_devices`, `sector_size`, `node_size`, `label`, the `fsid` as a UUID string, `superblock_offset` and `superblock_is_mirror`; it carries no `subtype`, so it is not re-dispatched to this module. On it, when the walk stopped short: `inventory_incomplete: true` with `inventory_incomplete_reason` one of `btrfs_max_btree_nodes`, `btrfs_btree_subtree_unreadable` or `btrfs_subvolume_unresolved`; `directory_parse_incomplete` with reason `btrfs_max_dir_entries` when the 500,000-entry cap dropped names; `unresolved_subvolumes` listing root object ids the trees name but the root tree does not carry; and when the walk failed outright, `inventory_incomplete_reason: btrfs_tree_walk_failed` with the error text in `inventory_error`. Then one `FileEntry` per inode reachable by a name, parented to the **input** artifact rather than to the new `FileSystem` record or to its directory: `name`, `path`, `parent_path`, `inode`, `mode`, `permissions` (octal of the low 12 bits), `uid`, `gid`, `size`, `nlink`, `changed` (ctime — the inode change time, labelled so), `modified`, `accessed`, `is_directory`, `is_symlink`, and `created` from `otime` only when it is non-zero. A file with more than one name carries `hardlink_paths`, `hardlink_paths_known` and `hardlink_paths_complete`, and `inventory_incomplete` with reason `btrfs_hardlink_names_unresolved` when `nlink` exceeds the names found. A regular file with a non-zero size gets a `DataSource` — a `ByteSliceDataSource` for a single plain inline extent, otherwise a `BtrfsFileSource` that serves holes and prealloc extents as zeros and refuses to serve anything still compressed — and a persisted location: `data_runs` with `data_runs_complete` for plain on-disk extents, a `btrfs_extents` descriptor array with `compression: btrfs` for zlib/zstd files, or `resident_data_b64` for inline or mixed files up to 16 MiB; plus `compressed`, `has_prealloc_extents`, `compression_unsupported` for an LZO or otherwise undecodable codec, `encrypted` with `content_ciphertext: btrfs_extent_encryption` and the standard pair with reason `encrypted`, `data_incomplete_multi_device` with `content_incomplete_reason: btrfs_missing_device` when a stripe lives on a device it does not have, or `btrfs_extent_off_primary_device` when the persisted runs had to leave a hole for a sibling device the content resolver will not have , and `content_incomplete` with reasons `btrfs_file_too_large` (over 4 GiB, with `content_incomplete_limit`), `btrfs_no_extent_records`, `btrfs_max_extents`, `btrfs_compressed_not_decompressed` or `btrfs_resident_short_read` . It produces no `TimelineEvent`, no record for an orphan inode, no record of deleted files, and no record of the subvolume a file belongs to beyond its path prefix.

**Cannot.** It cannot recover anything deleted. There is no scan of free space, of stale tree generations, of the log tree, or of the superblock's backup roots (`super_roots`); an inode with no `DIR_INDEX` naming it is skipped as an orphan and left off the case, and a directory entry to a missing inode is silently dropped, and this parser has no directory-slack path. It cannot verify integrity: the node header's checksum and `fsid`, the superblock checksum, `csum_type` and the whole checksum tree are never read, so a node whose bytes are corrupt but whose header still parses is walked as good, and the superblock copy used is the first that parses, not the newest by generation — a stale mirror is flagged as a mirror but not compared. It walks only the committed state named by the superblock's `root`: an unreplayed log tree, a transaction in flight at acquisition, and every earlier generation are invisible. It cannot read LZO: the codec is refused rather than served, and files under it have no content anywhere. It cannot reconstruct RAID5/6 parity — a missing device on a striped profile leaves those ranges zero-filled in the served bytes and flagged, never rebuilt — and it can only find a sibling device that sits in the same directory as the primary image, is a regular file, and is among the first 64 entries scanned; a sibling behind a container path is never found. Every timestamp is whole seconds: the nanosecond fields are not read; and `changed`, `modified` and `accessed` are rendered unconditionally through `format_timestamp` (`seance_plugin_btrfs/src/lib.rs:2282-2284`, 2607-2611), so a zero field prints as `1970-01-01T00:00:00+00:00` and a value `chrono` rejects prints as an empty string, while only `otime` is guarded against zero. It reads no symlink target, no extended attribute, no `INODE_REF`, no `DIR_ITEM` (only `DIR_INDEX`), no free-space cache, no quota, no device stats, and does not record which subvolume or snapshot an entry belongs to except by the path prefix; a directory's `size` is the raw Btrfs value (twice the sum of its name lengths), published as if it were a byte count. Its ceilings are 500,000 directory entries per walk, 100,000 extents per file, 8 tree levels, 1,000,000 nodes per traversal, 4 GiB per file for content, 256 MiB for in-memory decompression and 16 MiB for a resident copy; a compressed extent whose `disk_num_bytes` or `ram_bytes` exceeds 256 MiB is treated as unsupported rather than read. One failure loses the whole inventory: `walk_filesystem` applies `?` to every `walk_fs_tree` call (lib.rs:2534 and 2571), so a single subvolume or detached snapshot whose root node cannot be resolved or read discards every `FileEntry` already gathered from the healthy trees and publishes the volume as metadata only with `btrfs_tree_walk_failed` — the comment at 2554-2556 says detached subvolumes are walked so nothing is silently dropped, and here the drop is flagged but total. A directory entry cap that trips mid-tree leaves entries missing from whichever directories came last in leaf order, with only the volume-level flag to say so. Nothing in this tree reads a real `mkfs.btrfs` volume: every test in `seance_plugin_btrfs/src/lib.rs` is a hand-built superblock, node or chunk map, `VALIDATION.md` lists no Btrfs case, and `LINUX_DESIGN.md` says `Output: FileEntry` where the module also emits a `FileSystem` artifact.

**Refuses.** It refuses to serve bytes it did not get. A logical range that resolves to a device it does not have, to no chunk at all, or that a device delivers short is an `UnexpectedEof` error from the file source, never zero-fill handed up as content; a prealloc extent and a hole are served as zeros because the kernel serves zeros there, and the residual bytes at a prealloc extent's `disk_bytenr` are never read as file content. It refuses to serve a still-compressed extent, inline or on disk, as plaintext — the read returns an `InvalidData` error naming the codec, because a hash over a compressed blob is indistinguishable from the hash of a different file — and refuses to feed an encrypted extent to the decompressor. It refuses to fabricate a sparse tail past a truncated extent list: a read there short-reads instead. It refuses a superblock `nodesize` outside 4,096..=262,144 before allocating, because a value in 1..=100 once passed the zero check and panicked the slice of the node header, losing the whole volume (MEM-BTRFS-001), and it refuses a short superblock or a short node rather than parse zero-padding as pointers. It refuses to wrap: stripe offsets, chunk lengths, extent offsets and logical addresses are combined with saturating arithmetic so a hostile value reads past the device end instead of landing on unrelated bytes. It refuses to present a partial inventory as complete — every cap, unreadable subtree, unresolved subvolume and missing hardlink name is stamped on the volume or the file — and refuses to publish a sized file with no content and no reason. It refuses to persist an off-primary run as a complete location, because the content resolver only ever reopens the primary device .
