It refuses a `FileSystem` artifact whose subtype is not `btrfs` with an empty list, an artifact with no data source with `InvalidInputFormat`, and a volume with no readable superblock copy with a `ParsingError`, producing no artifact at all, so the only record of that refusal is the processing log. A volume whose superblock reads but whose system chunk array is empty fails the tree walk instead, and the `FileSystem` artifact is still published, stamped `inventory_incomplete_reason: btrfs_tree_walk_failed` with the error under `inventory_error` (`a_failed_tree_walk_marks_the_filesystem_inventory_incomplete`).

### `plugin.filesystem.directory_walker`

**Reads.** A **live directory on the examiner's own machine** — an unpacked extraction, a Google Takeout, a logical acquisition, a mounted share, a triage collection — selected not by any content probe but by metadata already on the artifact: it subscribes to `RawEvidence` and does nothing unless that artifact carries `is_directory: true` and a `path` that `Path::is_dir()` still answers true for at the moment the walk runs. That test follows a link, so the tree it is pointed at may itself be a symlink. Two entry points write that shape — `seance scan` on a directory and `ingest_directory` in the API — and both write the same keys so a case does not depend on which loaded the evidence; the API canonicalises the path first and the CLI records it as typed. There is no image, no superblock, no allocation bitmap and no on-disk structure of any kind. The structures are `fs::read_dir`, `fs::symlink_metadata` and, on a link, `fs::read_link`; no file's bytes are read here. The walk is depth-first from an explicit LIFO stack of `(directory, depth)` pairs, and `symlink_metadata` does **not** follow a link, so a link is described as itself. From each entry's metadata it records the size (`meta.len()`), the modification time, the access and creation times, and **on Unix only** the permission bits masked to `0o7777`, the uid, the gid, the link count and the inode number. For each regular file it builds a **deferred** `FileDataSource`, which stats the path a second time — with `std::fs::metadata`, which does resolve a link — and opens it only at the first read, because one eager open per file held a descriptor per file and, past the host's `ulimit -n`, failed silently and left files the case had examined and found empty. The walked directory is the stack's seed and is not itself listed. Before walking anything it tests the handed directory for a shape another parser owns: a directory holding both `Manifest.plist` and `Info.plist` as files is an iOS backup and is not walked.

**Produces.** One `FileEntry` artifact per file, directory and symlink found below the root, each parented directly to the evidence artifact — the tree is carried in the metadata, not in the artifact parentage. Each entry carries `name`, `path` and `parent_path` as `/`-rooted paths relative to the walked directory, `is_directory`, `size` for anything not a directory, `source_path` — the path on this machine, rooted exactly as the ingest named it, which is what lets the API serve and export a folder-sourced file later without re-walking — and `source: "directory"`. The timestamps are recorded under names that say **whose times they are**: `modified` alone, and only `modified`, is written as a device time, because the collection tools preserve mtime — `cp -p`, `rsync -a`, `tar` and `zip` all carry it — while the access and creation times on a copy record when the *copy* was read and written. Those two are kept, where the platform supplies them, as `accessed_on_collection_media` and `created_on_collection_media`, and every entry carries a `times_note` saying in words that they belong to the copy and not to the device. This is the reason the case does not show the examination as device activity: recorded as `accessed`, the atime this very walk set became an "Accessed" timeline event dated to the moment of ingest — 38,000 of them on the ChromeOS image, sorted to the top of the evidence. Downstream, the database's own projection raises one timeline row per entry that carries a `modified` value, stamped `Modified` and attributed to `filesystem.mac_times`; the collection-media times match no key in that vocabulary and so raise nothing. A symlink is recorded with `is_symlink: true`, its target under `symlink_target` (or the literal `(unreadable)` where `read_link` failed), no data source, and `content_omitted: "symlink_not_followed"`. A file that cannot be stated as a regular file — a FIFO, a socket, a device node, a file whose path has gone — is listed with `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason: "unresolved_structure"`, `content_omitted: "file_could_not_be_opened"` and the operating system's own error text under `open_error`, rather than losing its bytes without a word. Where the walk fell short of the folder it produces one `DirectoryWalkStatus` `ParsedRecord` carrying `entries_listed`, `unreadable_directories`, `undecodable_entries`, `directories_too_deep`, `inventory_incomplete: true`, an `inventory_incomplete_reason` of `cap_reached` or `unresolved_structure`, `content_incomplete: false` with a null reason, and a detail sentence naming each shortfall and the first five unreadable directories with the reason each gave. Where it stood aside it produces one `DirectoryWalkSkipped` record naming the owner (`iOS backup`) and saying why walking it here would put the same evidence in the case twice, once unusably.

**Cannot.** **It cannot recover a deleted file, and it cannot see that one ever existed.** It reads a directory through the operating system's own directory API: an entry the file system has unlinked is not returned to it, there is no unallocated space, no slack, no orphaned inode and no free-list to walk, and no record it emits is ever marked deleted. A folder that has been through a copy is only what the copying tool carried, so **absence from this listing is not evidence of absence from the device** — it is evidence about the collection. It cannot tell you that the listing is complete: the status record exists only when something fell short, so a case with no `DirectoryWalkStatus` cannot be distinguished from a case where the walk never ran. **It cannot report that it could not look.** Where the ingested `path` is missing, is not marked as a directory, or is no longer a directory when the walk runs — the folder moved, renamed or unmounted, or a non-UTF-8 path that reached it as an empty string — it produces nothing at all and no record saying so, and the source is then described as one no module in this build parses, which is a different statement from the true one. Every name and path it reports is decoded with `to_string_lossy`: a name that is not valid UTF-8 is recorded with U+FFFD replacement characters in place of the bytes that were there, silently, and is **not** counted as undecodable — so a name in the record may not be the name on the medium, and nothing on the record says so. It cannot tell an entry whose directory record would not read from one whose metadata could not be stated: both increment the same counter and both surface as `undecodable_entries`, and either can be a file that was deleted under the walk. A symlink whose target could not be read is counted nowhere and is published as a link to `(unreadable)`, which reads the same as a link to a path of that name. It cannot read what a file system knows beyond `stat`: no extended attributes, no ACLs, no alternate data streams, no resource forks, no birth time where the platform does not supply one (the key is then simply absent, because a file dated to the epoch because `stat` said nothing is a date the evidence never carried), and no allocated-block count — `size` is the apparent length, so a sparse file reads as its declared size. **On anything but Unix it records no `mode`, `uid`, `gid`, `nlink` or `inode` at all**; where it does, the `mode` is masked to `0o7777`, which drops the file-type bits, so it cannot say from the mode whether an entry was a socket, a device or a pipe. A symlink's `size` is the byte length of its target string, not the size of any file. It cannot deduplicate a hard link: a file reachable under three names is three entries, and `nlink` and `inode` are published — on Unix — so a reader can join them by hand. It keeps no record of where it has been and compares no device number, so it cannot detect that it is walking the same directory twice: a bind mount or a mounted ancestor inside the tree is listed again under a second path until a ceiling stops it, and a mounted share or image below the walked folder is listed as part of it with nothing saying it came from another volume. It cannot vouch that the bytes later read are the bytes it sized: the size is taken at walk time by one `stat` and the deferred source opens the path at first read after a second `stat`, so a tree that changes under the analysis yields content the record does not describe and nothing detects the difference. It does not hash, type, or classify anything — those are other modules over the entries it emits. Its ceilings are `MAX_ENTRIES = 2,000,000` entries per walk, counting directories, and `MAX_DEPTH = 64`: a directory is descended only while its own depth is 64 or less, so the deepest entries recorded are 65 levels below the root, and `directories_too_deep` counts the directories at that boundary whose contents were never read — not the entries inside them, which are unknown and uncounted. A walk truncated by the depth limit alone is published under the reason `unresolved_structure`, not `cap_reached`, so it does not declare itself as a capped one. When the entry cap fires the walk stops where it stands: the unread remainder of the directory it was reading and **every directory still on its stack are neither listed nor counted anywhere** — the status record says the cap was reached and how many entries were listed, and does not and cannot say how much of the folder was never reached. The walked directory itself gets no entry, so its own time, mode and ownership are not in the case. The stand-aside test is applied once, to the directory it was handed, and never to a directory inside it: an iOS backup one level down inside a walked tree is listed as its content-addressed blobs. Neither ceiling is exercised by any test in this module.

**Refuses.** It refuses to follow a symlink. A link to `/etc` would pull the examiner's own machine into the case, and a link to its own parent would not terminate, so the target is written down, `content_omitted: symlink_not_followed` says why there are no bytes, and the walk stays inside the tree it was pointed at — tested by `a_symlink_is_recorded_and_not_followed`, which plants both a link to `/etc` and a loop back to the walk's own root and asserts that no `passwd` entered the case and that the walk ended. The refusal governs entries found inside the tree; it does not govern the root, which is accepted through a link. It refuses to walk a directory whose own reader produces better artifacts than a raw listing: an iOS backup's files are content-addressed blobs that only its `Manifest.db` can name, so where both `Manifest.plist` and `Info.plist` are present the walker stands aside and emits a record saying so rather than emitting the blobs beside the named output. That list is deliberately one entry long, because adding a shape to it is a decision to hide raw files. It refuses to report a directory it could not list as an empty one — the failure and the operating system's reason are counted and named on the status record; `an_unreadable_directory_is_declared_not_skipped_in_silence` asserts that where the permission bits held, and asserts nothing where the process could read the directory anyway. It refuses to report a short walk as a whole one: the entry cap, the depth limit, every unlistable directory and every unstatable entry are counted and declared with the inventory-incompleteness pair. And it refuses to write the examination's own footprints into the exhibit under the names the timeline reads: the access and creation times of a copy are never published as `accessed` or `created`, a refusal pinned by `the_examination_does_not_write_itself_into_the_timeline`, which asserts both of those keys absent and `accessed_on_collection_media` and the `times_note` present.

### `plugin.filesystem.fat_parser`

**Reads.** A FAT-family volume, handed to it as a `FileSystem` artifact the partition layer already windowed, and gated on that artifact's `subtype` — `fat12`, `fat16`, `fat32`, `fat` or `exfat`, and nothing else; an artifact carrying no subtype at all is attempted, and any other subtype is passed over without a word. Selection is therefore inherited, not made here: `plugin.disk.filesystem_detector` finds FAT12/16/32 only by the optional `"FAT12 "`/`"FAT16 "`/`"FAT32 "` string at byte 54 or 82 — or, for FAT32, by the 64-bit sector count that can stand in its place — so a volume whose formatter omitted that field never reaches this module. What this module reads for itself is the first 512 bytes of the volume, gathered in a loop until all 512 are in hand rather than in one `read_at` (a chunked windowed or E01-backed source left the tail zeroed, the `0x55 0xAA` at 510 read as absent, and a sound volume was reported as no filesystem at all). `EXFAT ` at bytes 3..11 diverts the whole read to the exFAT path. Otherwise it decodes the BIOS Parameter Block from offset 11 — bytes per sector, sectors per cluster, reserved sectors, FAT count, root entries, both total-sector fields, media descriptor, and — only on a FAT32-shaped BPB carrying the `0x29` extended boot signature with both standard counts zero, the condition `dfir_ntfs` uses — the non-standard 64-bit sector count at byte 82, named as `total_sectors_source: bs_totsec64` on the allocation map ; `sectors_per_fat_16`, geometry and hidden sectors — and derives the layout from the BPB shape — `sectors_per_fat_16 = 0` is FAT32, read with 32-bit entries even under 65,525 clusters — and, for a FAT12/16 layout, the entry width from the cluster count: under 4,085 clusters FAT12, otherwise FAT16, never FAT32; where the count alone would name another width the allocation map carries `fat_type_note`. In the extended BPB at offset 36 the drive number, the volume id and the extended boot signature are read unconditionally; the signature `0x29` is what declares that the 11-byte label and the filesystem-type string exist, and without it those two are left unset rather than decoded (FAT-001). The label, the filesystem-type string and every 8.3 short name are OEM bytes with no encoding declaration and are decoded through **CP437**, the table named on the record whenever a byte outside ASCII was interpreted. The first FAT is then read into memory from `reserved_sectors * bytes_per_sector`, its declared length clamped to the volume's own size and then required to arrive in full. The FAT12/16 root directory is read as `root_entries` fixed 32-byte slots at `reserved_sectors + num_fats * sectors_per_fat_16`; a FAT32 root is a cluster chain like any directory. Inside a directory it reads each slot one at a time, exactly 32 bytes or not at all, classifying by raw bytes before parsing: `0x00` in byte 0 ends the directory, `0xE5` marks it deleted, `0x0F` in byte 11 makes it a long-name slot. Long-name slots are buffered, their 13 UTF-16 code units taken from the three runs at +1, +14 and +28, and attached to the following 8.3 entry only when every buffered slot carries the same checksum byte and — for a live entry — that byte equals the rotate-and-add checksum of the entry's own raw 11-byte name. The VFAT case-info byte at offset 12 is honoured: bit 3 lowercases the base, bit 4 the extension. Cluster chains are followed through 12-, 16- or 32-bit FAT entries (FAT32 masked to `0x0FFFFFFF`), each entry classified as next, end-of-chain, free, reserved, bad or outside the table. Subdirectories are descended by first cluster, and each cluster number is descended once on the whole volume. On the exFAT path it validates `BytesPerSectorShift` in 9..=12 and `SectorsPerClusterShift` at most 15 with their sum at most 25 before any shift is performed, then reads the FAT offset and length, the cluster heap offset, the cluster count, the root cluster, the FAT count, the volume serial and the volume flags, reads the first FAT whole, scans the root directory for the Allocation Bitmap entry (`0x81`, first-bitmap flag clear) and reads that bitmap through its chain as file content. Directory entry sets are read by index across the **whole FAT chain**, not within a cluster, so a set that begins in a cluster's last slot continues in the chain's next cluster and not the physically adjacent one: a primary file entry (`0x85`, or `0x05` with its InUse bit cleared), then its declared `secondary_count` entries — the stream extension for flags, name length, `ValidDataLength`, first cluster and `DataLength`, then the name entries, 15 UTF-16 code units each, taken by position. Where a listing holds a file and an in-image sidecar of it (`-wal`, `-journal`, `.LOG`, `.LOG1`, `.LOG2`), the base file's source is republished carrying its sidecars so registry log replay and WAL-aware SQLite reach them inside the image.

**Produces.** One `FileEntry` artifact per directory entry — file and directory alike, `.` and `..` excluded — parented flat to the `FileSystem` artifact with the hierarchy carried in `path` and `parent_path`, because the content resolver walks the parent chain and a directory has no runs of its own. On FAT it carries `name` (the long name where one was validated, else the short name), `short_name`, `size` from the 32-bit directory field, `first_cluster`, `is_directory`, and `read_only`/`hidden`/`system`/`archive` from the attribute byte; `created`, `modified` and `accessed` as RFC 3339 strings, with `timezone: "local"` on any record that carries one, and `path_decode: "cp437"` where a name held a byte this build had to interpret. On exFAT it carries `name`, `size` (`DataLength`), `valid_size` (`ValidDataLength`), `first_cluster`, `is_directory`, `is_contiguous`, `in_use`, the five attribute bits, and the three timestamps converted to true UTC where the per-stamp offset byte's valid bit is set, with `timezone: "local"` where any of the three was not. A file with locatable content gets a live data source plus `data_runs` — coalesced `[offset, length]` pairs measured from the start of the volume — and `data_runs_complete`. Where the clusters are not certainly the file's own, or do not span its recorded size, the FAT record carries `content_incomplete` with a `content_incomplete_reason` naming which: `chain_entry_free`, `chain_entry_reserved`, `chain_entry_bad_cluster`, `chain_entry_out_of_range`, `chain_cycle`, `chain_cap_reached`, `chain_points_below_first_cluster`, `chain_yielded_no_clusters`, `deleted_contiguous_assumed`, `deleted_clusters_assumed_in_order` or `deleted_reconstruction_short`, alongside `cluster_chain_incomplete`. A deleted FAT entry carries `deleted` and `deleted_recovery_source: "fat_directory"`, and — only where a contiguous reconstruction was actually built, so not for a deleted directory or a deleted zero-length file — `deleted_recovery_method: "contiguous_assumed"`, or `"unallocated_clusters_in_order"` with `deleted_clusters_skipped` when clusters the FAT calls allocated now lay in the old run and were stepped over. A deleted exFAT set carries `deleted`, `deleted_recovery_source: "exfat_directory_entry"`, `content_incomplete` with reason `unresolved_structure`, and a `content_incomplete_detail` saying in words that its name, size and timestamps are as the directory recorded them but its clusters were freed and may hold another file's data. An exFAT file whose `ValidDataLength` is short of its `DataLength` carries `has_unwritten_tail` and `unwritten_tail_bytes`, and its tail is persisted as a **sparse** run so the resolver zero-fills it; a `ValidDataLength` of zero on a non-empty file is published as `valid_data_length_zero` and the clusters are still served. A directory whose own listing stopped early carries `directory_parse_incomplete` with `fat_chain_incomplete`, `fat_deleted_directory_unverified`, `fat_deleted_directory_zeroed`, `fat_deleted_chain_unverified`, `exfat_chain_incomplete`, `exfat_deleted_directory_unverified`, `exfat_deleted_directory_zeroed` or `exfat_deleted_directory_sets_refused` (HUNT-278). A deleted directory whose first cluster is free and entirely zero carries `directory_content_zero` and its `_zeroed` reason: Windows 11's FAT32 and exFAT drivers were observed to zero a deleted directory's clusters, so the volume does not hold its names, and an empty directory looks the same, which the volume cannot tell apart; one whose first cluster is now the first cluster of another directory, or holds file bytes, is `_unverified` (`directory_content_reallocated` or `directory_content_unrecognised`). One `ParsedRecord` per volume of `type: "allocation_map"` carries the geometry this module no longer mints a `FileSystem` for — on FAT the `fat_type` (`Fat12`, `Fat16`, `Fat32`), the boot sector's `volume_label` with `path_decode` where the table was used, bytes per sector, sectors per cluster, total sectors and sectors per FAT; on exFAT `fs_type: "exFAT"`, the sector and cluster figures, the cluster count and the volume serial as eight hex digits, plus `allocation_map_incomplete` where the bitmap's chain was cut or its 64 MiB ceiling bit — plus the downsampled allocation picture: `allocation_bitmap_b64`, one byte per bucket holding the allocated fraction scaled to 0–255, with `allocation_clusters_per_bucket`, `allocation_total_clusters` and `allocation_cluster_size`, plus `allocation_fat_covered_clusters` where the FAT holds entries for fewer clusters than the BPB declares. That record also carries the free-space census — `free_runs_found`, `free_regions_emitted`, `free_bytes_emitted`, `free_runs_dropped`, `free_bytes_dropped`, the region and byte ceilings and whether each was reached, `free_space_unassessed_clusters`, `free_space_unassessed_bytes`, `free_space_complete`, and where the pass fell short `free_space_incomplete` with a reason of `cap_reached` or `unresolved_structure` and a sentence stating what was not carved — and, where the root listing was cut short, `directory_parse_incomplete` with `fat_root_chain_incomplete`, `fat_root_cluster_invalid` (a FAT32 root cluster below 2), `fat_bpb_layout_inconsistent` (a BPB mixing the FAT32 and FAT12/16 root fields) or `exfat_root_chain_incomplete`; where no allocation map exists to carry that flag, a bare `fat_volume_walk` or `exfat_volume_walk` record is minted to carry it instead, because a flag that appears only when another artifact happens to exist is not a flag. Finally one `UnallocatedSpace` artifact per run of free clusters, each windowed to its own bytes and carrying `first_cluster`, `clusters`, `cluster_size`, `offset_bytes`, `size_bytes`, its index in the set, `source: "allocation_bitmap"`, the filesystem name (`FAT12`, `FAT16`, `FAT32` or `exFAT`), the pass's own shortfall, and the sentence that the offsets are measured from the start of this volume and not the start of the evidence — the regions the automatic carver reads. On FAT those bits are synthesised from the FAT itself: a zero entry is free, any other value is in use, and the bad-cluster marker and the reserved value 1 are never offered as free. On FAT12/16/32, after the live walk, the free clusters are also scanned for **orphaned directories**: a free cluster whose first two entries are `.` naming that very cluster and `..` is read as a directory whose own entry in its parent is gone, and its entries are published as deleted files carrying `recovered_from_free_space`, `orphan_fat_state: free`; allocated clusters no walked directory leads to are tried the same way afterwards, and what is found there is `orphan_fat_state: allocated`, unreachable and **not** called deleted (tested on a synthetic volume only); a free orphan is read on into later clusters by the same contiguity assumption as any deleted directory, and says `orphan_directory_listing_incomplete` when that stopped short, `orphan_directory_cluster`, `orphan_parent_cluster` and a `path` of the form `/[orphaned directory, cluster N]/NAME` with a `path_basis` sentence saying the path names a cluster and not a folder. The scan is bounded at 1,048,576 clusters examined, free clusters first and allocated clusters from what remains; the allocation map carries `orphan_directory_scan` with the counts (the budget is `max_clusters_examined`) and, where the bound was reached or a candidate cluster could not be read, `orphan_directory_scan_incomplete` with `orphan_directory_scan_incomplete_reason` of `bound`, `unreadable_clusters` or `bound_and_unreadable_clusters`. After it, the free clusters that nothing anchors are tried once more as **headless** directory clusters (HUNT-278): a free cluster not already read, whose first slot passes the plausibility test and in which every slot before the end marker passes it too, with at least two short entries (not long-name slots, not `.`/`..`), is read as directory entries, every one deleted, under a `path` `/[headless directory entries, cluster N]/NAME`, `orphan_directory_headless: true`, `recovered_from_free_space` and a `path_basis` that says the path names a cluster and not a folder; a cluster whose `.`/`..` pair is present and whose `.` names a different cluster says so in `orphan_directory_dot_names_cluster`. The later clusters of a deleted multi-cluster directory are found this way, as clusters of their own, not as continuations. The allocation map carries `headless_directory_scan` with the counts. Graded on RM#2 of the Data Leakage case against The Sleuth Kit (23 root-level deleted pictures, every one recovered, none extra) and on seven other FAT volumes (none published).

**Cannot.** **It cannot give a deleted file's first character.** FAT overwrites the first byte of the 8.3 name with `0xE5`, and this module substitutes an underscore in its place, as The Sleuth Kit does: `MULT.DAT` is reported as `_ULT.DAT`. The underscore is this tool's reconstruction and nothing in the record says so — no field marks the substitution — and the same loss makes the 8.3 checksum unmatchable, so for a deleted entry the long-name chain is accepted on internal consistency alone and an adjacent chain from another deleted file can be attached as this file's name; on DFTT #9 that is how the deleted entry `_EWFOL~1` comes out named `New Folder`. It cannot vouch that a deleted file's content is that file's content: the FAT no longer records where its clusters were, so recovery reads them from the start cluster upward in order, stepping over any cluster the FAT now calls allocated (as The Sleuth Kit does), and a fragmented original re-serves another file's bytes under this name — the runs span the recorded size and are published `data_runs_complete: true` for that reason, with `content_incomplete` and `deleted_contiguous_assumed` (nothing in the way) or `deleted_clusters_assumed_in_order` (clusters stepped over, counted in `deleted_clusters_skipped`) as the only warning. The span is clamped to the volume's data clusters, and a deleted entry whose recorded first cluster lies outside them yields no run and `deleted_reconstruction_short`; inside them, nothing says a free cluster it reads was not the property of another file since. On the six generations of a Canon camera card it recovered seven of 26 erased photos exactly, the seven The Sleuth Kit recovers, and none of the other 19 is presented as whole. It cannot say what an entry behind a directory's first `0x00` was: past that marker it reads only the rest of the marker's own cluster, and publishes a slot only if it passes a strict plausibility test (legal 8.3 or long-name bytes, no reserved attribute bits, in-range dates, a cluster inside the volume); a passing slot is published `deleted` with `recovered_from_directory_slack` and a basis saying its state is unknown, never as live, a refused slot is counted in `directory_slack_slots_rejected`, and the later clusters of the directory and the FAT12/16 fixed root are not examined at all. It cannot recover a deleted FAT directory whose first cluster was reallocated or overwritten: the first cluster must still open with a `.` naming itself and a `..`, else nothing is read and the record says `directory_content_reallocated` or `directory_content_unrecognised`, and its later clusters are not found. It cannot know where a deleted FAT directory went on: its chain is freed, so it is extended over the *next* clusters only while they are free and plausible, each record so read is stamped `directory_chain_basis: contiguous_assumed`, and a directory that grew non-contiguously stops at the gap and says `fat_deleted_chain_unverified`; the later clusters are found as headless directory clusters, and a long name cut by a cluster boundary is joined to the end of the nearest earlier directory cluster only when every slot carries the same 8.3 checksum and the first byte that checksum implies for the deleted short name is the upper-case form of the name's first character (`long_name_basis: stitched_across_clusters`), or, where the driver freed the directory without marking its slots (Haiku's and ReactOS's), only when the ordinals count down without a gap from the head, which opens the chain, to the short entry and the checksum is the one of the short entry's own name; a deleted name whose last slot has no terminator is flagged `long_name_possibly_truncated`, because deleted slots lose their ordinal, and where the ordinals were kept a name whose first slot does not open its chain is flagged from the ordinal itself. All of this is graded on synthetic volumes, on four volumes written by Windows 11's own FAT32 and exFAT drivers, where deleted files of a live directory were recovered by name 260 of 260 and a deleted directory left nothing to read, and on four volumes written by Linux's `vfat` and `exfat` drivers, which leave a deleted directory's names and from which every name of three deleted directories came back whole, and on two volumes each written by Haiku's and by ReactOS's FAT drivers, from which every name of three deleted directories came back whole once the ordinals they leave were read. It reads a **deleted exFAT** directory whose first cluster is free in the allocation bitmap over `DataLength` consecutive clusters when its stream extension carried NoFatChain, or through the FAT entries the driver left behind when it did not (`directory_chain_basis: stale_fat_chain`, stopping short and flagged at a cluster in use again), keeping a set only if its `SetChecksum` verifies (`directory_content_basis: set_checksum_validated`, refusals counted as `directory_entry_sets_refused`); a reallocated one is flagged. It also looks once, in the free clusters of an exFAT volume whose allocation bitmap it read whole, for a deleted directory that no entry points to: a free cluster that starts a deleted file entry set with its stream and name entries, and that no free cluster's stale FAT link leads to, is read as the head of such a directory, along the stale chain, with every set gated by its `SetChecksum`, and what it lists that no listing already reached is published under `/[orphan cluster N]/` with `orphan_directory_head_cluster` and `orphan_directory_basis`. Its name, its path and its length are unknown and the listing runs to the end of the chain, a cut chain is not told from a finished one, and only the first 2,000,000 free clusters are examined (an `exfat_orphan_scan` record says so when more were skipped). Behind an exFAT directory's end-of-directory marker it reads the rest of the marker's own cluster, keeps an entry set only if it lies whole in that cluster and its `SetChecksum` verifies, and publishes it as deleted with `recovered_from_directory_slack`, state unknown; later clusters are not read. **It cannot tell an exFAT chain that ended from one that was cut.** On FAT12/16/32 a free, reserved or bad entry mid-chain, or a cluster outside the FAT, each stops the walk with its own reason and marks the file incomplete; the exFAT reader collapses free, bad, end-of-chain and out-of-table into one "no next cluster" answer and reports the chain **complete**, so a truncated exFAT file is published with `data_runs_complete: true` over a prefix — a defect the FAT reader does not have, and which is not closed here. A deleted, fragmented exFAT file is the worst case of it: its FAT entries are zero, so the chain is its first cluster alone, reported complete, and the resolver zero-fills the rest of the recorded size and serves that as the file. And where the exFAT walker *does* know it stopped early — a cycle, or the 100,000-cluster cap — it sets only `cluster_chain_incomplete`, not the `content_incomplete` that the API, export and integrity-verify paths read. It cannot check an exFAT file's clusters against the volume's own records where the stream extension sets the no-FAT-chain flag: the clusters are then synthesised consecutively from the first cluster with neither the FAT nor the allocation bitmap consulted, bounded only by the volume's length. It cannot refuse an exFAT first cluster the FAT does not cover: that cluster is collected before the table is consulted, so its bytes — an unrelated region of the image — are served as the file's first cluster, where the FAT path refuses the same cluster before collecting it. It cannot report a name in its original bytes. An 8.3 name, the volume label and the filesystem-type string are OEM bytes read through an assumed CP437; the same bytes on a volume formatted under another OEM code page spell a different name, which is why `path_decode` names the table rather than the name being offered as literal. It cannot restore the `0x05` escape: a live file whose name genuinely begins with byte `0xE5` is stored with `0x05` there and is reported with a leading U+0005 control character, unflagged and with no `path_decode`, because the byte is below 0x80 and nothing was interpreted. Long and exFAT names are assembled with `from_utf16_lossy`, so an unpaired surrogate becomes U+FFFD. It cannot report the volume label a FAT root directory holds: entries with the volume-id bit are skipped whole, label and timestamps alike, and the only label published is the boot sector's — on DFTT #9 that means `LABEL1` is reported and the root directory's own `LABEL2` is not reported at all, though the two disagreeing is that image's whole point; and on exFAT the `0x83` volume-label entry is skipped too, so an exFAT volume's label is never reported. It cannot publish a FAT volume's serial number: the volume id is decoded off the disk and carried on no record. It cannot say which slot a long name came from, or that the chain was whole: sequence numbers and the last-slot bit are decoded only in tests, so a chain with a missing middle slot passes the checksum test and yields a name up to 13 characters short, and no 255-character ceiling is enforced on what it assembles. It cannot check an exFAT entry set: the `SetChecksum` and the name hash are decoded and never verified, and the secondary entries are read by position with no test of their type bytes, so a corrupt set yields a plausible size, first cluster and name. It cannot tell a short exFAT name from a whole one: the name is exactly `NameLength` code units of whatever the name entries supplied, so a set declaring more than it carries is published under a silently shortened name, one declaring zero is published with an empty name, and a zero code unit anywhere inside a name entry is dropped rather than ending the name. It cannot give a FAT timestamp better than the format does: modification and access are two-second resolution, creation is refined only by `DIR_CrtTimeTenth` in 10 ms units (0–199), the year is seven bits from 1980 so nothing before 1980 or after 2107 can be expressed, and **the access field carries no time of day at all** — it is decoded against a zero time word and rendered as midnight, which is this tool's filler and not a recorded hour. It cannot say what zone a FAT timestamp was written in: FAT records local wall-clock time, nothing on disk records the offset, no conversion is performed, and the digits are published unconverted with `timezone: "local"` — but rendered as RFC 3339 with a `+00:00` designator, so a reader who takes the string and not the flag reads a wall-clock hour as UTC. On exFAT it converts to true UTC only where the per-stamp offset byte's valid bit is set, in 15-minute units; the `timezone: "local"` flag is all-or-nothing across the three stamps, so a record with one valid offset and two invalid is marked local entire, every stamp is rendered with the same UTC designator either way, and the 10 ms increment is truncated to whole seconds. It cannot detect that the FAT copies disagree: `num_fats` is read, the active-FAT and mirroring flags in the FAT32 extended BPB and the exFAT `VolumeFlags` are decoded and never consulted or published — so the volume-dirty and media-failure bits are read off the disk and never reported, the second FAT is never read or compared, and on a volume whose active-FAT bit names the second table the first is read with nothing saying so. It cannot read the FSInfo sector, the exFAT UpCase table, the exFAT Volume GUID entry, or the TexFAT second bitmap. **It cannot list the root directory of a BPB that mixes the FAT32 and FAT12/16 layouts, or of a FAT32 volume whose root cluster is below 2.** A volume is read by its layout — `sectors_per_fat_16 = 0` is FAT32, with 32-bit entries even under 65,525 clusters, and `fat_type_note` on the allocation map says where the cluster count disagrees — but a FAT32 layout with a non-zero `root_entries`, a FAT12/16 layout with none, or a root cluster of 0 or 1 does not say where the root is, so the root listing is empty and flagged `directory_parse_incomplete` with `fat_bpb_layout_inconsistent` or `fat_root_cluster_invalid` instead of being reported complete. It cannot say why a directory has no children when another directory claimed its first cluster first: each cluster number is descended once per volume and the second entry is left with an empty listing and no flag — on DFTT #9 both `/dir1` and the deleted `/New Folder` name cluster 2. It cannot mark a FAT shorter than its own header short: the declared table length is clamped to the volume's size before the read is required to complete, so a BPB naming a FAT longer than the volume is accepted with a truncated table, and the shortfall appears only as per-file `chain_entry_out_of_range` and as unassessed clusters in the census. It cannot mark the downsampled FAT allocation picture short: a cluster with no FAT entry is drawn as free in `allocation_bitmap_b64` and no `allocation_map_incomplete` is set on the FAT path, though the free-region route counts the same clusters as unassessed — so two figures on one record disagree. It offers slack only as its own `SlackSpace` type — one region per live, non-directory file whose persisted run list is complete and whose last cluster's tail holds a non-zero byte, never for a deleted entry, whose contiguous chain is a guess, nor for an exFAT file whose `ValidDataLength` falls short of its `DataLength` — with one `slack_space_summary` per volume; on DFTT #2 the regions cover `3slack3` and the slack halves of `1slack1` and `2slack2` at their published offsets. It cannot distinguish "not found" from "could not look" at the volume level: every reason it declines a volume before the FAT is read — a boot sector that would not deliver 512 bytes, a missing `0x55 0xAA`, geometry that is not a power of two, an exFAT shift out of range, a FAT table that read short — produces **no artifact and no refusal record**, which on the case is indistinguishable from a volume that held nothing; a volume declined after that point keeps its allocation map and free regions and loses only its files; and on exFAT a bitmap entry that is missing, or a root slot that would not read whole, simply omits the allocation map and every free region with nothing saying why. Its ceilings are all real and all recorded where they fire: 512 bytes of boot sector required whole; bytes per sector a power of two in 512..=4096 and sectors per cluster a power of two; exFAT sector shift 9–12, cluster shift at most 15 and the two summing to at most 25, so a 32 MiB cluster; **10,000 clusters per FAT12/16/32 chain** — 5,120,000 bytes on a 512-byte-cluster volume, 327,680,000 on a 32 KiB-cluster FAT32 — and **100,000 per exFAT chain**, past which the file is a marked prefix; **512 data runs** persisted per file on the cluster-chain path and **4,096** on the exFAT unwritten-tail path, past which `data_runs_complete` is false and the resolver will not serve the file; a deleted file's contiguous reconstruction clamped to the volume's data clusters; per-cluster work (the allocation bitmap, the orphan scan) bounded by the entries the FAT holds, not the BPB's declared cluster count; a FAT file size that is a 32-bit field, so nothing above 4 GiB less one byte can be recorded; the whole first FAT held in memory, bounded only by the volume's length; **64 MiB** of exFAT allocation bitmap read; **65,536 buckets** in the downsampled allocation map; **4,096 free regions** and **128 GiB** of free bytes per volume by default (`SEANCE_FREE_REGION_CAP` and `SEANCE_FREE_BYTE_CAP` change them, and the record states the ceilings applied), largest runs first, with no run dropped for being small — one cluster is a region; an exFAT name of at most 255 UTF-16 code units across at most 254 name entries, both because the declaring fields are one byte. There is no ceiling at all on the number of file entries emitted, and none on the length of a long name assembled from LFN slots.

**Refuses.** It refuses to invent geometry. A boot sector the source cannot deliver in full is refused rather than parsed with a zeroed tail, because the cluster size, the cluster heap offset and the cluster count all sit past the bytes that would be missing and a partial sector places every later read at a fabricated offset. It refuses a boot sector without `0x55 0xAA` at 510, a `bytes_per_sector` or `sectors_per_cluster` that is not a power of two, a sector size outside 512..=4096, and an exFAT shift pair outside the spec's range — the last checked **before** any `1u16 << shift` is executed, because an out-of-range shift panics in a debug build and silently masks in release, yielding plausible geometry that corrupts every downstream offset. It refuses to read the FAT short: a zero-padded tail would read as free and terminated clusters and would silently truncate every chain running through the missing region, so a FAT that cannot be gathered to its clamped length fails the volume closed . It refuses to parse a directory slot it could only partly read. A zero-padded half slot would either fabricate a file's cluster and size out of sixteen bytes or forge the `0x00` end-of-directory marker, so the read fails, the listing is marked a prefix and the slot becomes no file — and an exFAT set whose name entry could not be fully read is dropped entire, and the listing marked, rather than recorded under a silently shortened name. It refuses an exFAT entry set declaring more secondary entries than the directory's clusters hold, because emitting it would mean inventing the missing entries, and marks the listing short where it stops; it also drops a primary entry declaring no secondary entries at all, because nothing then describes the file's data — but that drop is silent, and the listing is not marked. It refuses to attach a long name it cannot tie to its file: a buffer whose slots disagree on the checksum byte, or whose checksum does not match the 8.3 entry it precedes, yields no long name rather than another file's name on this file's record . It refuses to invent a volume label. Absent the extended boot signature `0x29` — which many FAT12 floppies lack — the eleven bytes at that offset declare nothing and are left unset; decoding them through CP437 made this worse than the old mangling, because arbitrary bytes stopped looking like garbage and started reading as a name somebody chose (FAT-001). It refuses to follow anything that is not a cluster number: the bad-cluster marker `0x?FF7` is not followed (doing so reads an unrelated region of the image as this file's content), nor is the reserved value 1 or the reserved band below the end-of-chain threshold, nor a cluster the FAT does not cover, nor a cluster already visited — and on FAT12/16/32 each of those stops the walk with its own named reason rather than as a clean ending, because collapsing them publishes a truncated file as a whole one. It refuses to publish a chain the walker cut as a complete run list, even when the clusters coalesce to a single run well under the run cap, because the content resolver treats any shortfall against the recorded size as a sparse hole and zero-fills it, which would serve fabricated zeros in place of real clusters. It refuses to leave a sized FAT file whose chain yielded nothing looking empty: such a record carries `data_runs_complete: false`, `content_incomplete` and the reason the chain failed, because a bare entry reads as a file that had no content. It refuses to present a prefix of a directory as the directory: a listing cut by a cyclic chain, the safety cap or an unreadable slot is stamped, because an examiner who cannot see the difference will testify that a file was not in that folder . It refuses to serve exFAT bytes past `ValidDataLength`: the spec (7.4.4) says those bytes are not file data and read back as zeros, so they are persisted as a sparse run and zero-filled, since serving the residue of the clusters' previous tenant disagrees with every operating system reader and poisons the file's hash — with one deliberate exception, a `ValidDataLength` of zero on a non-empty file, which is as likely an implementation that never maintains the field as a genuine preallocation, so the ambiguity is recorded and the clusters are served rather than a whole real file being blanked. It refuses to descend a deleted exFAT directory, because its clusters may since have been reallocated and what they hold now is not that directory's listing. It refuses to descend a directory cluster twice, so a directory pointing back at an ancestor or at itself cannot loop. It refuses to allocate against a header field: the FAT length is computed with checked arithmetic and clamped to the volume's size, and a deleted file's or a contiguous exFAT stream's cluster count is clamped to the clusters the volume could hold, because an inflated length would otherwise be an out-of-memory kill of the worker rather than a caught error. It refuses to offer a cluster the FAT marks bad, or the reserved value 1, as free space to the carver, and refuses to report clusters past the end of the FAT as free rather than unassessed — a short FAT would otherwise report the rest of the volume as never written to. And it refuses to mint a `FileSystem` artifact of its own: the partition layer owns that, and a second one would re-trigger this module on its own output and cascade without bound.

### `plugin.filesystem.hfsplus`

**Reads.** A whole HFS+ or HFSX volume, and only when something upstream has already said that is what it is. The module subscribes to `ArtifactType::FileSystem` alone and declares `InputCapability::RandomAccess`; it runs only where that artifact's `subtype` is exactly `hfsplus` or its `filesystem_type` reads `HFS+`, `HFSPLUS` or `HFSX` case-insensitively. In this build nothing ever writes that `subtype` — it appears only in the fuzz target and this crate's own tests — so in the product the module rests entirely on `filesystem_type`, written by `seance_plugin_partition` from a two-byte match of `H+` or `HX` at byte 1024 of the partition and nothing else. It performs no probe of its own to decide whether to run, and anything else handed to it leaves with an empty list. Given the volume it reads 512 bytes at offset 1024 through `seance_core::io::read_exact_or_fail`, so a source that ends inside the header errors rather than parsing a zero-padded buffer. From that header it takes four fields and no others: the signature at +0, which must be 0x482B (`H+`) or 0x4858 (`HX`); the block size at +40; `totalBlocks` at +44, which is logged and never published or checked against the length of the image; and the catalog fork's 80-byte `HFSPlusForkData` at +272 — its `logicalSize` and the eight extent descriptors from +16, keeping those whose `blockCount` is non-zero. The catalog B-tree's bytes are then reconstructed by concatenating those extents at `startBlock × blockSize`, each read clamped both to the fork's remaining logical size and to what the source physically holds past that extent's start, so a `blockCount` of 0x08000000 at a 4,096-byte block — a 512 GiB extent claimed by a two-kilobyte volume — allocates nothing beyond the fork's own declared size. Inside the reconstruction it reads two fields of the header node's `BTHeaderRec`: `firstLeafNode` at +14+10 and `nodeSize` at +14+18, at those absolute offsets, taking on faith that node 0 is the header node without reading its kind byte. It then follows the **leaf chain** by each node's `fLink` at +0, starting at `firstLeafNode` and bounded by `catalog.len() / nodeSize` visits so a corrupt chain cannot cycle; it never descends the tree from its root, and a node whose kind byte at +8 is not -1 is skipped to its own `fLink`. In a leaf it reads `numRecords` at +10, clamped to 8,192, and takes each record from the offset array that grows backward from the node's end. In a record it reads `keyLength` at +0, the key's `parentID` at +2 and the `HFSUniStr255` name at +6 — a u16 code-unit count clamped to 255, decoded from UTF-16BE — then the data at `2 + keyLength`, whose first u16 is the record type. A folder record (type 1) gives `folderID` at +8; a file record (type 2) gives `fileID` at +8 and the 80-byte data fork at +88; a folder or file thread record (types 3 and 4) gives the object's real parent CNID at +4 and its name at +8, filed under the key's `parentID`, which for a thread record is the object's **own** CNID. Three of the record's five dates are read from every folder and file record — `createDate` at +12, `contentModDate` at +16 and `accessDate` at +24, each a u32 of seconds since 1904-01-01 GMT, converted by subtracting 2,082,844,800. A regular file's data-fork extents are finally projected onto byte runs in the volume: up to 256 MiB is materialised in memory through the same fail-closed reader, and above that the file is served lazily from those runs when and only when the eight descriptors reach its logical size.

**Produces.** **File slack**: for each live regular file whose data fork is fully described by the volume header's eight extent descriptors and whose logical size is not a whole number of allocation blocks, the bytes from its logical end to the end of its last allocation block are read, and a `SlackSpace` region is published (filesystem `hfsplus`, `source: file_slack`, offsets in the volume's own coordinate space) when any of them is non-zero; a slack summary counts the files offered, the tails that were all zero, the tails that could not be read and the files whose tail could not be located (a compressed file, whose data fork is empty by design, and a file whose extents continue in the overflow tree, which this parser does not follow). Graded on the HFS+ partition of the CFTT string-search unix image against The Sleuth Kit, where every real tail is zero, and on tails planted in memory over that partition at offsets `icat -s` confirmed. One `FileEntry` artifact per catalog file or folder record whose CNID is 16 or above, parented to the volume artifact, carrying the catalog's `name`, an assembled `path` and `parent_path`, the `cnid` and `parent_cnid`, `is_directory`, `size` (the data fork's logical size, and 0 for every folder), `filesystem_type` fixed at the string `HFS+`, and `created`, `modified` and `accessed` as RFC 3339 UTC strings — each omitted entirely where the catalog field was the zero sentinel, so an unset date is absent rather than published as 1904-01-01. A regular file whose record was long enough to hold its 80-byte data fork also carries `extent_count`, and — unless that fork is zero-length — its `data_runs` (adjacent runs coalesced, so the list is not a one-to-one statement of the fork's descriptors) and `data_runs_complete`, with an attached content `DataSource`: the bytes themselves under 256 MiB, or a `RunListDataSource` over the volume above it. Where the reconstruction fell short the shortfall is stamped in the keys the rest of the product reads as well as the HFS+-private one: `content_truncated` with `content_incomplete`, `content_incomplete_reason` (`short_read` when the volume would not deliver an extent, `unresolved_structure` when the eight in-catalog extents do not reach the logical size), `content_bytes` and `logical_size`, and where the catalog itself was short, `catalog_incomplete`, `catalog_incomplete_reason`, `inventory_incomplete`, `inventory_incomplete_reason` and, on folders, `directory_parse_incomplete`. A short catalog also produces one volume-level `ParsedRecord` of type `HfsPlusCatalogIncomplete`, subtype `parse_incomplete`, status `CatalogNotReconstructedInFull`, carrying `catalog_bytes_read`, `catalog_logical_size`, `entries_listed` and a sentence saying in words that only the volume header's eight extent descriptors are followed and that the listing is a prefix of the volume — so the fact survives a walk that reached no record at all, **provided** the short catalog still yielded a usable node size; where it did not, the volume ends in an error and no marker is emitted. The module emits no timeline event of its own; the three dates it writes onto each entry are what `seance_db` projects onto the unified timeline under `filesystem.mac_times`. Separately, an unallocated-space pass over the volume's free blocks recovers a deleted file's catalog record where an orphaned leaf node survives, publishing it as an ordinary `FileEntry` with `deleted: true` and `deleted_recovery_source: "hfsplus_orphaned_catalog_leaf"`, plus one of `content_recovered`, `content_not_recoverable_reallocated` or `content_not_recoverable_unreadable` stating exactly what could be attached and why.

**Cannot.** **It cannot say the live catalog held no deleted file — only that none was recovered.** The live-tree walk reads live leaf records and nothing else, and produces no deleted flag or deletion time of its own. A separate unallocated-space pass now recognises an orphaned catalog leaf node — one whose blocks the allocation-file bitmap marks free — through the exact record decoder the live walk uses, and reconstructs a deleted file's name and, where its data blocks are confirmed still free, its content; a block since reallocated or an inconsistent extent is reported as such rather than substituting the wrong bytes or the new occupant's content. That pass requires the volume's allocation-file fork, and where it is absent or unreadable the pass does not run rather than guess "free" for blocks never checked — so absence from either inventory remains silence about deletion, not a finding that nothing was deleted. **It cannot read a compressed file's contents.** HFS+ compression (`decmpfs`) keeps the data in the attributes B-tree or the resource fork, and this module reads neither — the attributes B-tree is not opened at all, and the resource fork at +168 of a file record is never touched. A compressed file has an empty data fork, and it is recognised from the `UF_COMPRESSED` bit in its own record's `permissions.ownerFlags` and stamped `compression: hfsplus_decmpfs` with `content_incomplete` and reason `compressed`, so it is not published as a zero-byte file that reads as whole — but its bytes are still not recovered and its real length, which lives in the decmpfs header, is not known: the size on the record is the data fork's, which is zero. The same gap removes every extended attribute and every resource fork, where classic Mac applications and some document formats keep the real data. A file record too short to hold its 80-byte data fork is likewise published as a zero-byte file, with no runs, no `extent_count` and no flag. It cannot follow the extents-overflow B-tree: only the eight extent descriptors inside the catalog record are read, so a file fragmented beyond eight extents is served as a prefix whose source still reports the full logical size and is marked `unresolved_structure`, and above 256 MiB with short coverage no content is attached at all; above 256 MiB the runs it does publish are never checked against the length of the image, so `data_runs_complete: true` can stand over runs naming bytes the image does not hold. It cannot read the journal, so an uncheckpointed transaction is not recoverable here; it cannot read the allocation file, so HFS+ free space is not published as a carvable region; it reads neither `attributeModDate` nor `backupDate`, so two of the five dates in every catalog record are absent from the case; and it reads no permissions, uid, gid or mode, no Finder info, no text encoding, no record flags — so the flag bit that marks a file as carrying attributes or compression is never consulted — and no folder valence or folder count, which means **it cannot say that a directory it listed has all of its children**. It does not resolve hard links, so an indirect node under the HFS+ private data directory is listed as the file the catalog names. It cannot tell you that a volume was HFSX: the `HX` signature is accepted and then every record is stamped `filesystem_type: "HFS+"`, and the volume's case-sensitivity and key-compare type are never read. Its paths are its own assembly, not the file system's: they are built purely from thread records, and where the chain to the root breaks the components gathered so far are joined and prefixed with `/`, which is indistinguishable from an absolute path, while a parent with no thread record at all puts the file at `/` — at the volume root — with nothing marking either case. The chain is walked at most 256 deep. Where a catalog holds two thread records for one CNID the second silently replaces the first, so the path is built from whichever the walk met last. A name containing a `/` cannot be told from a path separator, because components are joined with `/` and nothing is escaped; a name is decoded with a lossy UTF-16 conversion and no normalisation, so an unpaired surrogate becomes U+FFFD and the name is emitted in whatever decomposition the volume stored; a name declaring more than 255 code units is published as its first 255; and **a name that will not decode at all is published as the empty string**, so a record whose name field is truncated is inventoried under no name and at a path ending in a bare separator, with nothing saying the name is this tool's substitute rather than the catalog's. It drops every CNID below 16, the root folder's own record included, and it does not deduplicate entries: two records for one CNID are emitted twice. **It cannot tell you where a corrupt structure stopped it, and it cannot promise that what it did list is even a prefix.** An extent that begins past the end of the source is skipped and the next extent's bytes are appended in its place, so after any such gap the byte at `node × nodeSize` is no longer that node of the B-tree and records are read out of whatever landed there; the only thing said about it is that the catalog was short. Every other mid-walk fault is skipped silently and counted nowhere: a node whose extent lies past the end of the reconstructed catalog ends the walk; a non-leaf node in the leaf chain is followed by its own `fLink`, which can carry the walk off the leaf level; a record whose offset pair does not ascend, or runs past its node, is skipped; a record whose key length, key parent or record type will not read is dropped; an unrecognised record type is ignored; and a node declaring more than 8,192 records has the excess discarded. None of this appears on any record — the only incompleteness marker is the short-catalog one — so a catalog that reconstructs to its full length but whose `firstLeafNode` is zero, or whose chain breaks at once, produces no `FileEntry` and no marker whatsoever: "this volume held no files" where "the catalog could not be walked" is the truth. Nor does it check its own walk against the catalog's own arithmetic: `BTHeaderRec` states `leafRecords` at +6 and `totalNodes` at +22, eight and twelve bytes from fields this module does read, and neither is consulted — the visit budget is `catalog.len() / nodeSize`, derived from the reconstruction rather than from the tree. Its ceilings are 512 bytes of volume header, 512 MiB of catalog fork (`MAX_CATALOG_BYTES`), 256 MiB of in-memory file content (`MAX_CONTENT_BYTES`), eight extents per fork, 8,192 records per node (`MAX_RECORDS_PER_NODE`), `catalog.len() / nodeSize` nodes visited, 255 code units per name, 256 path components (`MAX_PATH_DEPTH`) and 4,096 coalesced data runs written into metadata (`MAX_METADATA_DATA_RUNS`). And nothing in this build pins it against a real HFS+ volume: every fixture is a synthetic volume built in the test module, and the two stored fuzz reproducers, though checked in, are replayed as `Partition` artifacts that the gate rejects before a byte is read, so they assert nothing about this module at all.

**Refuses.** It refuses to identify the file system it parses. Where the artifact does not already declare HFS+, HFSPLUS or HFSX it returns an empty list rather than probing the bytes, which the orchestrator folds into a row recording a module that ran and produced nothing — so if the upstream two-byte probe misses a volume, this module is silent about it and leaves no refusal behind. It refuses to read a zero-padded structure: the volume header and every file extent go through `read_exact_or_fail`, so a truncated image, or a file extent the volume will not deliver in full, fails rather than being filled with zeros and served as content; a *catalog* extent past the end of the source is not refused but skipped, and surfaces only as a short catalog. It refuses a volume outright in nine places, each with a message naming what it saw: a signature other than `H+` or `HX`, quoted as the hexadecimal found; a block size of zero or under 14 bytes, as implausible; an empty catalog fork; a catalog fork whose logical size exceeds 512 MiB, naming both the size and the cap; an extent whose physical offset or byte length overflows; a catalog too short to hold the B-tree header's `nodeSize` or its `firstLeafNode`; and a node size under 16 bytes or larger than the catalog itself. Each of those ends the whole volume: no `FileEntry` and no record are produced — including, on the last three, no `HfsPlusCatalogIncomplete` marker even where the catalog was known to be short — and the reason survives only as the processing log's `error` status carrying that message. An artifact with no data source is refused as an unsupported input, which the log records as `skipped` with no message at all. It refuses to present a partial file as a whole one: a short reconstruction is wrapped in a source whose `size()` is the file's real logical size and whose missing tail short-reads instead of returning fabricated zeros, so the hasher records a short read rather than a digest of a prefix stored under a full-size entry; and for a file above the 256 MiB ceiling whose eight extents do not cover it, no source is attached at all, because a source sized to the covered bytes would hash as a complete small file. It refuses to let a prefix listing read as a whole volume: every entry a short catalog produced is stamped incomplete in both the HFS+-private and the standard keys, and a volume-level `HfsPlusCatalogIncomplete` record is emitted even when the walk reached zero records, because an empty artifact list is indistinguishable from an empty volume. It refuses to publish the 1904 epoch: a zero date is omitted rather than converted into a fabricated 1904-01-01 timestamp. And it refuses to trust a length field from the evidence — an extent's byte length is bounded by the fork's logical size, the source length and a 512 MiB cap; a record count is clamped to 8,192; a name length to 255; and every offset derived from a key length is read through accessors that return nothing rather than index out of bounds — which is what keeps a two-kilobyte hostile volume from driving a 512 GiB allocation or an arithmetic underflow in the record-offset walk.

### `plugin.filesystem.iso9660`

**Reads.** An ISO 9660 (ECMA-119) volume, from a `FileSystem` artifact the partition layer has labelled. It subscribes to `FileSystem` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess` and runs when `subtype` is `iso9660` or `filesystem_type` is `ISO9660`, `ISO 9660` or `CD9660` case-insensitively; the partition module writes both after reading five bytes at `0x8001` and finding `CD001`. An artifact with no data source returns `InvalidInputFormat`. It reads the volume descriptor set from sector 16 in 2,048-byte sectors, at most 64 of them, each with `read_exact_or_fail` — a short descriptor read fails the volume — and each must carry `CD001` at byte 1 or the volume fails with a `ParsingError` naming the sector. The first type-1 descriptor is the Primary Volume Descriptor; the first type-2 descriptor whose 32-byte escape-sequences field at `+88` contains `%/@`, `%/C` or `%/E` is taken as the Joliet Supplementary Volume Descriptor (DOC-013); type 255 ends the set. From the descriptor it walks — the Joliet one when present and parseable, else the primary — it takes the little-endian logical block size at `+128` (any non-zero `u16`), the volume space size at `+80` (logged, not published) and the embedded root record at `+156`: extent LBA at `+2`, data length at `+10`, little-endian copies only. A directory is its whole extent, read with `read_exact_or_fail`, at most 64 MiB; records are walked by their length byte, a zero length skipping to the next block boundary; each record yields extent LBA, data length, the 7-byte recording date at `+18` (year since 1900, month, day, hour, minute, second, GMT offset in signed 15-minute units) converted to RFC 3339 with its stored offset or dropped when it does not form a date, flags at `+25` (bit 1 directory, bit 7 not-final), and the identifier at `+33` for the length at `+32`, clamped to the record. Identifiers `0x00` and `0x01` are the self and parent entries and are skipped. A name is UCS-2 big-endian in the Joliet tree — a trailing odd byte is dropped — and lossy UTF-8 in the primary tree, with everything from the last `;` stripped for files and nothing stripped for directories. Records with the multi-extent flag are joined with the records that follow while each carries the same identifier and is not a directory (ECMA-119 9.1.6). The walk is bounded to depth 64, 200,000 records and one visit per directory extent. A regular file's extents are read whole into memory with `read_exact_or_fail` when their total is at most 256 MiB. Rock Ridge: the primary root's `.` record is read, and when its System Use area — the bytes after the identifier and its padding byte — opens with an `SP` entry (check bytes `0xBE 0xEF`) followed by an `ER` naming RRIP or IEEE P1282, or by any RRIP entry, the primary tree is walked with Rock Ridge even when a Joliet tree exists, the choice the Linux kernel makes. Each record's System Use area, past `SP`'s skip length, is read entry by entry to `ST` or its end, following `CE` continuation areas up to 32 of them and 64 KiB per record; `NM` (continued names joined, the `.`/`..` flags ignored), `PX` (mode, links, uid, gid, and the serial number when the entry is 44 bytes), `TF` (creation, modification, access and attribute-change times, 7-byte or 17-byte form), `SL` (the link target, `.`, `..` and root components included) and `CL`/`RE` are decoded: a record marked `RE` is not listed, and a `CL` placeholder is walked as the directory at the extent it names, its length taken from that extent's own `.` record.

**Produces.** One `FileEntry` per directory record, every one parented to the input `FileSystem` artifact rather than to its directory, with `name`, `path`, `parent_path`, `is_directory`, `size` (the sum of the extents' data lengths, `0` for a directory), `extent_lba`, `filesystem_type: ISO9660`, `name_source` (`rock_ridge`, `joliet` or `iso9660`, so a court-facing name can be traced to the structure it came from), `extent_count` when more than one, and `modified` and `recorded` — the same recording timestamp under both keys — when the record carried a valid one. On a Rock Ridge walk a record with an `NM` name also carries `iso9660_name`, the level-1 name of the same record; `PX` adds `mode` (raw `st_mode`), `nlink`, `uid`, `gid` and `inode` where recorded; `TF` adds `created`, `accessed` and `changed` and replaces `modified` with the file's own modification time, `recorded` keeping the directory record's; `SL` adds `is_symlink: true` and `symlink_target`; a `CL` placeholder is published as a directory with `extent_lba` the relocated extent and `rock_ridge_relocated_from_lba` its own; a record carrying `PN`, `SF` or `ZF` lists those signatures under `rock_ridge_entries_not_read`, a `ZF` file also carrying `content_incomplete` with reason `compressed` and an `SF` file with reason `unresolved_structure`; and a System Use area whose continuation could not be read, or ran past the budget, is stamped `rock_ridge_incomplete: true`, what was read before it kept. A regular file carries `data_runs` (byte offsets within the volume, `lba × block size`) and `data_runs_complete`, and an attached `ByteSliceDataSource` holding its bytes; a file whose extents total more than 256 MiB is published with `content_too_large: true`, `data_runs_complete: false` and no content; a file whose extent read fell short is published with `content_truncated`, `data_runs_complete: false`, `content_incomplete` with reason `short_read` and no content; a multi-extent file whose final record never appeared carries `content_incomplete` with reason `unresolved_structure`. A directory whose own walk stopped short carries `directory_parse_incomplete: true` and `directory_parse_incomplete_reason` — one of `max_depth`, `cyclic_extent`, `directory_too_large`, `extent_read_failed`, `record_budget_exhausted` or `relocated_directory_unreadable` (a `CL` placeholder whose relocated directory's `.` record will not read, stamped on the placeholder itself). When any directory anywhere stopped short, the module adds one `ParsedRecord` with no subtype, parented to the volume: `type: iso9660_walk`, `directory_parse_incomplete: true`, `entries_emitted`, `records_seen`, and `directory_parse_incomplete_reason` when it was the root itself that stopped — because the root has no `FileEntry` of its own to carry the flag, and an inventory that ends at a budget looks exactly like a disc that held nothing more. It produces no `FileSystem` artifact of its own, no volume-level record of the volume identifier or its dates, no `TimelineEvent` (the recording date rides the `FileEntry`), no hash and no deleted entries.

**Cannot.** Of Rock Ridge it does not decode `PN` (device numbers of a device node), `SF` (sparse files: such a file's content is its recorded extent, not the sparse whole) or `ZF` (zisofs: such a file's content is the compressed bytes), stamping the signature and the incompleteness pair on the record instead; it reads no other SUSP extension than RRIP, and it reads the Rock Ridge only of the primary tree, so the relocation directory itself (`rr_moved`) is still listed, empty of what it relocated. It cannot read El Torito — no boot catalog, no boot image — and it does not read UDF, which is `plugin.filesystem.udf`'s: on a UDF-bridge disc the partition layer publishes both halves, each stamped `udf_bridge: true` and neither marked hidden, and this module walks the ISO tree alone, which on a Windows install ISO holds only `README.TXT`. It publishes nothing from the descriptor beyond what it needs to walk: no volume identifier, system identifier, publisher, application, or the volume creation, modification, expiration and effective dates; no volume set information; and it reads only the first primary and the first Joliet descriptor. When a Joliet tree exists without Rock Ridge the primary tree is never walked, so the ISO-9660 rendering of each name is not on the record at all, and when Rock Ridge exists the Joliet tree is never walked, so a Joliet name that differs from the Rock Ridge one is not on the record; when the Joliet descriptor is present but will not parse, the module falls back to the primary tree with only a log line to say so. Only the little-endian copies of the both-endian fields are read and never checked against the big-endian ones. It does not handle interleaved files (unit size and gap at `+26`/`+27`), extended attribute records, the hidden flag (bit 0) or the associated-file flag (bit 2) — an associated file is listed as an ordinary file — and it does not follow multisession discs: only the descriptor set at sector 16 is read, so on a disc with several sessions the files of the later sessions, which the drive would present, are absent. Without Rock Ridge the only timestamp it has is the recording date; there is no creation or access time, the year is `1900 + u8`, and a record with an invalid date has no timestamp and no note. A file's content is materialised whole in memory, up to 256 MiB per file, and every entry of the volume is held in one `Vec` until the walk finishes, so a disc of many large files costs its size in RAM; a file over 256 MiB gets no content and is stamped `data_runs_complete: false` although its runs are complete, and with the bespoke key `content_too_large` rather than the standard `content_incomplete` pair (`seance_plugin_iso9660/src/lib.rs:837-842`), so it is invisible to the completeness census and to any consumer that reads only the standard flag. Every `FileEntry` is a flat child of the volume, so the artifact tree does not reflect the directory tree. It recovers nothing deleted or unallocated: no orphaned directory records, no earlier sessions, no slack. Its reading of a real disc is not pinned in this tree — `PRODUCTION_READINESS_GAPS.md` records DFTT #14 as `detected + extracted` but that image is not checked in. Rock Ridge alone is graded on real discs: three `xorriso -as mkisofs -R` images (one also with Joliet, one with a relocated deep directory, also read with that directory's sector zeroed) under `seance_plugin_iso9660/tests/fixtures/`; every other test builds its volume in memory.

**Refuses.** It refuses to serve zero-filled bytes as directory or file content: every structural read goes through `read_exact_or_fail`, so a truncated or out-of-range extent is a `warn` and a flagged entry with no content, never a padded one. It refuses to fabricate a date from an all-zero or out-of-range recording field. It refuses to let a stray multi-extent flag swallow the next file — a continuation record must carry the same identifier or the file is closed short and flagged — and refuses to publish a half-assembled multi-extent file as whole. It refuses to walk a directory extent twice, because a crafted image whose records point back into an ancestor would otherwise re-emit the same entries up to the record budget from a few kilobytes; a repeat is reported as `cyclic_extent`. It refuses a directory larger than 64 MiB, a tree deeper than 64 and more than 200,000 records, and every one of those refusals is stamped on the directory's own entry and on the volume-level `iso9660_walk` record, pinned by `exhausting_the_record_budget_publishes_a_walk_incomplete_marker` and its counterweight `a_fully_enumerated_directory_reports_no_incompleteness`. It refuses the whole volume — a `ParsingError`, no artifacts — when a descriptor sector lacks `CD001`, when no primary descriptor is found, when the logical block size is zero, or when a descriptor cannot be read in full; it refuses an artifact with no data source with `InvalidInputFormat`; and it returns an empty list for a `FileSystem` artifact that is not ISO 9660. Those refusals leave no artifact of their own: the reason travels only into the processing log.

### `plugin.filesystem.udf`

**Reads.** A UDF (ECMA-167 / OSTA UDF) volume, from a `FileSystem` artifact whose `subtype` is `udf` or whose `filesystem_type` is `UDF` case-insensitively; it subscribes to `FileSystem` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`. The partition layer writes that subtype when the Volume Recognition Sequence, 2,048-byte descriptors from byte 32,768 (at most 64; 4,096-byte steps when the 2,048-byte slot after the first is blank, as on 4 KiB-sector media), holds a `BEA01` followed by `NSR02` or `NSR03` before the `TEA01` that closes it; an `NSR` outside that pair is not believed, and the sequence may open with ISO 9660's `CD001` descriptors. When `CD001` and UDF are both present the two `FileSystem` artifacts are stamped `udf_bridge: true` and neither is marked hidden or overlapping. An artifact with no data source is `InvalidInputFormat`. The Anchor Volume Descriptor Pointer is looked for at sector 256, then the last sector, then N-257, in 2,048-byte sectors, then the same three places in 512-, 1,024- and 4,096-byte sectors; the first that passes sets the sector size every later descriptor is read in. A 512- or 1,024-byte-sector volume still carries its Volume Recognition Sequence in 2,048-byte steps, so the partition layer calls it `udf` and the anchor tells the size. A descriptor whose CRC length runs past one sector (a Logical Volume Descriptor on 512-byte sectors) is read across the sectors it needs, up to 64 KiB. Every descriptor read is verified: the tag checksum over the 16-byte header, the CRC-ITU (polynomial `0x1021`, initial 0) over the `crc_length` bytes after it, the tag identifier, and, for volume descriptors, anchors, File Set Descriptors, File Entries and Allocation Extent Descriptors, the recorded tag location. The main Volume Descriptor Sequence is read to its Terminating Descriptor, following up to 8 Volume Descriptor Pointers and at most 256 descriptors, keeping the Primary, Logical Volume and Partition Descriptors with the highest sequence number; a descriptor that fails a check fails that sequence and the reserve sequence is read instead. From the Logical Volume Descriptor it takes the block size (which must equal the anchor's sector size), the domain identifier and its UDF revision, the File Set Descriptor's `long_ad`, and the partition maps, each resolved to a translation from a (partition reference, block) address to an absolute block. A Type 1 (physical) map is its Partition Descriptor's start plus the block. A `*UDF Sparable Partition` map (rewritable media) reads its sparing tables at the absolute sectors the map names, sized by each table's own entry count rather than the map's size field (NetBSD `makefs` records the whole sparing area there), verifies each tag (identifier 0, its location, CRC) and its `*UDF Sparing Table` identifier, and believes the verified table with the highest sequence number: a block in a relocated packet is read at the sector the table names, every other block as physical.
