A `*UDF Virtual Partition` map (write-once media) is read through the Virtual Allocation Table: the last block of the evidence that is not all zeros (trailing zeros skipped for up to 64 MiB) and the 15 before it are tried as the VAT's File Entry in the underlying partition, newest first, and the first that is a UDF 2.00+ VAT (file type 248, header then entries) or a UDF 1.50 VAT (entries then the `*UDF Virtual Alloc Tbl` identifier and the previous-VAT pointer) is believed, up to 64 MiB; each virtual block is the underlying block its entry names, and `0xFFFFFFFF` is unmapped. The previous-VAT pointers are followed, up to 64 and never in a loop, to locate earlier VATs. A `*UDF Metadata Partition` map (UDF 2.50+) is read through the metadata file (an Extended File Entry of file type 250 at the block the map names), or through its mirror (file type 251) when the main file will not read or its extents are incomplete; a metadata block is the corresponding block of that file's content. Blocks translated one at a time through a virtual partition are bounded to 2^26 per volume. The File Set Descriptor gives the root directory's ICB. A File Entry (tag 261) or Extended File Entry (tag 266) with ICB strategy 4 is read for its file type, information length, uid, gid, permissions, link count, unique id, access, modification and attribute times and, on an Extended File Entry, creation time, each with its recorded timezone offset. Its allocation descriptors are read as short, long or embedded (ICB flags 0, 1 and 3), following Allocation Extent Descriptor chains (extent type 3) up to 4,096 of them and 1,048,576 extents per file; a zero-length descriptor ends the list. A directory is its File Identifier Descriptors (tag 257), read in full up to 64 MiB and walked in order, each checked by tag checksum and CRC; the parent entry is skipped. A name is OSTA CS0: compression 8 is one byte per character, 16 is UTF-16 big-endian. The walk is bounded to depth 64, 200,000 records and one visit per directory ICB.

**Produces.** One `FileEntry` per File Identifier Descriptor, each parented to the input `FileSystem` artifact, with `name`, `path`, `parent_path`, `is_directory` (from the File Entry's file type, or from the identifier's directory bit when the File Entry will not read), `size` (the information length, `0` for a directory), `filesystem_type: UDF`, `icb_lbn`, `icb_partition_reference`, `uid` and `gid` unless recorded as `0xFFFFFFFF`, `udf_permissions` (the raw ECMA-167 permission word), `nlink`, `udf_unique_id`, `udf_file_type`, `udf_extended_file_entry`, and `accessed`, `modified`, `changed` (the attribute time) and, from an Extended File Entry, `created`, as RFC 3339 with the recorded offset; a time whose zone the disc left unspecified is published without an offset and the entry carries `timestamps_timezone_unspecified: true`; a time that is recorded (not all zero) but out of range, a month of 13 say, is not published and is named in `timestamps_undecodable` (`invalid_timestamp_is_named_not_silently_dropped`), while an all-zero time is simply absent. A file carries `data_runs` (byte offsets within the volume, `null` for an unrecorded extent), `data_runs_complete`, and content served from those runs through a `RunListDataSource` cut to the information length: nothing is read into memory, so a file of any size is served whole, and an allocated-but-unrecorded extent reads as zeros. An embedded file's run points into its File Entry. `hidden: true` is stamped when the identifier's hidden bit is set; `deleted: true` and `deleted_icb_may_be_reused: true` when its deleted bit is set; `is_symlink: true` and `symlink_target_not_decoded: true` for a symbolic link; `udf_extended_attribute_bytes_not_read` when the File Entry carries extended attributes; `udf_stream_directory_not_read` when an Extended File Entry names a stream directory; `name_decode_failed` and `name_cs0_compression_id` with the name as hex when the compression id is not 8 or 16. It adds one `ParsedRecord` per volume, `type: udf_volume`, parented to the volume: `anchor_sector`, `volume_descriptor_sequence` (`main` or `reserve`, with `main_volume_descriptor_sequence_error` when the reserve was used), `volume_identifier`, `volume_set_identifier`, `recorded`, `logical_volume_identifier`, `domain_identifier`, `udf_revision`, `sector_size`, `block_size`, `partition_start`, `partition_length`, `partition_contents`, `partition_map_kinds` (each map as `physical`, `sparable`, `virtual` or `metadata`), `file_set_identifier`, `entries_emitted`, `records_seen`, `partition_extends_past_evidence` and `evidence_size` when the partition runs past the end of the evidence (on a VAT volume, where the partition spans the whole disc and nothing after the VAT was written, `partition_unrecorded_after_vat: true` instead). A sparable volume adds `sparing_packet_length`, `sparing_tables_recorded`, `sparing_tables_verified`, `sparing_table_sequence`, `sparing_relocated_packets` and `sparing_tables_not_believed` with each failed table's reason. A VAT volume adds `vat_block`, `vat_icb_lbn`, `vat_form` (`1.50` or `2.00+`), `vat_entries`, from a 2.00+ header `vat_number_of_files` and `vat_number_of_directories`, `vat_found_before_trailing_zeros` when the evidence runs on past it in zeros, and, when the VAT names a predecessor, `vat_earlier_icb_lbns`, `vat_earlier_states_not_walked: true` and `vat_earlier_chain_stopped` with the reason the chain ended early. A metadata volume adds `metadata_duplicate_flag`, `metadata_file_read` (`main` or `mirror`) and `metadata_main_file_error` when the mirror was used. And `directory_parse_incomplete` when the walk stopped anywhere, with `directory_parse_incomplete_reason` naming the root's own reason or, failing that, the first reason met anywhere in the tree. It produces no `TimelineEvent` of its own and no hash.

**Cannot.** Its virtual, sparable, metadata and non-2,048-byte-sector reading is graded only on self-made volumes, not on a real burned or pressed disc: UDF 1.50, 2.01 and 2.50 images written by NetBSD `makefs` and by `mkudffs` 2.3 (two of them populated by the Linux 5.15 kernel) from one synthetic payload, where every file matches the payload's SHA-256 (`UDF-VARIANTS-1` in `VALIDATION.md`, env-gated on `SEANCE_UDF_IMAGES`; lean copies are committed as `seance_plugin_udf/tests/fixtures`). No image in that set has a relocated sparing packet, an unreadable main metadata file or an earlier VAT: those three paths are pinned by editing a copy of a writer-made image in memory. No 1,024-byte-sector volume has been read, and no volume with the metadata duplicate flag set. Of multisession: on a VAT volume the newest VAT describes the last session written, so an image that holds every session in order is read as last written; earlier VATs are located and counted but the volume as it stood under them is not walked, so a file present in an earlier session and gone from the last is not listed. If the image ends before the last session, an earlier VAT is the last one in it and that earlier state is what is read, with nothing to mark it. A multisession disc not joined by a VAT is read only as the session the anchor names; other sessions are neither read nor detected, because an image file carries no session table. The UDF 1.50 VAT's logical-volume extension (its file counts) is not read. It does not read ICB strategies other than 4 (UDF 2.00 strategy 4096 for write-once media), extended allocation descriptors, extended attributes, named streams or the stream directory, or symbolic-link targets, and it does not decode CS0 compression ids 254 and 255. It recovers nothing deleted beyond the identifiers marked deleted: no unallocated space, no orphaned File Entries, no earlier Volume Descriptor Sequences. A deleted identifier's File Entry is read as it stands and may since belong to another file; a deleted directory is listed but not walked, and says so with `directory_not_walked: deleted`. The Logical Volume Integrity Descriptor, the Unallocated Space Descriptor and the Implementation Use Volume Descriptor are not read, and no descriptor other than the File Set Descriptor's first is followed. The identifier CRC is checked but not its tag location. Every `FileEntry` is a flat child of the volume. Graded on one real disc: Microsoft's Windows 11 25H2 ISO, a UDF 1.02 bridge (`UDF-BRIDGE-1` in `VALIDATION.md`, env-gated on `SEANCE_WIN11_ISO` and never committed). There it lists the 976 files and 94 folders 7-Zip lists, reads the 6,225,286,811-byte `sources/install.wim` whole, and matches 7-Zip's SHA-256 on five extracted files, `install.wim` among them. The remaining tests build their volume in memory from ECMA-167 and OSTA UDF 1.02. On a UDF-bridge disc the ISO 9660 and UDF halves are not compared, so halves that list different files raise no signal.

**Refuses.** It refuses a volume it cannot believe with a `udf_volume` record, never with silence and never with a guess: `udf_unreadable: true` and `udf_unreadable_reason` when no anchor passes its checks (the reason names each location and what it failed), when both descriptor sequences fail, when the Logical Volume Descriptor's block size differs from the sector size the anchor was found at, when the File Set Descriptor will not verify, and when a partition map cannot be resolved: a Type 2 map of a kind other than virtual, sparable or metadata, or a map type ECMA-167 does not define, stamps `udf_unsupported_partition_map` with its name (`type2_partition_map_of_an_unknown_kind_is_refused_and_named`); a known kind whose structures cannot be read stamps `udf_partition_map_unresolved` with the reason (`virtual_allocation_table_not_found` with what each tried block held, `sparing_table_unreadable` with each table's failure, `metadata_file_unreadable` with the main and mirror failures; `virtual_partition_without_a_vat_is_refused_and_named`), because a relocated packet, an unmapped virtual block or a metadata block read in the wrong place would be a guess. A virtual block whose VAT entry is unmapped, or a metadata block outside the metadata file, is refused as content like an extent outside its partition, below. It refuses a File Entry that fails its tag, has an unsupported strategy or uses extended allocation descriptors. The entry is still listed, with `icb_unreadable` and `icb_unreadable_reason`, and with `content_incomplete` for a file or `directory_parse_incomplete` for a directory. It refuses to serve an extent outside its partition as content: that run reads as zeros and the entry carries `content_incomplete` (`unresolved_structure`), `udf_content_problem: extent_outside_partition` and `data_runs_complete: false`. The same pair marks allocation that is shorter than the information length, whether in extents or in the bytes embedded in the File Entry (`embedded_data_shorter_than_information_length_is_flagged`), or an Allocation Extent Descriptor that will not read; the missing tail reads as zeros that are not on the disc. An identifier whose ICB extent has length zero (the Linux driver zeroes a deleted identifier's ICB) is listed with `icb_unreadable_reason: icb_not_recorded` rather than read at block 0 (`deleted_fid_with_zeroed_icb_says_icb_not_recorded`). An extent inside its partition but past the end of the evidence (a truncated acquisition) is served as far as the evidence goes, and the entry carries `content_incomplete` (`short_read`), `udf_content_problem: extent_past_end_of_evidence` and `data_runs_complete: false` (`extent_past_end_of_truncated_evidence_is_flagged_short_read`). It stops a directory at the first identifier that fails its tag (`file_identifier_descriptor_invalid`), and it refuses to walk a directory ICB twice (`cyclic_icb`), past depth 64 (`max_depth`), past 200,000 records (`record_budget_exhausted`) or larger than 64 MiB (`directory_too_large`). Each of those reasons is stamped on the directory's own entry; the volume record carries `directory_parse_incomplete` and the first reason, however deeply it was met. It returns an empty list for a `FileSystem` artifact that is not UDF.

### `plugin.filesystem.xfs`

**Reads.** An XFS volume, from a `FileSystem` artifact whose `subtype` is exactly `xfs`; it subscribes to `FileSystem` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, ignores `filesystem_type`, and the subtype it keys on is written by the partition module after seeing `XFSB` at byte 0 of the volume. No data source is `InvalidInputFormat`. The superblock is 512 bytes at offset 0, read with `read_exact_or_fail`: magic big-endian `0x58465342`, `blocksize` `+4`, `dblocks` `+8`, `rblocks` `+16`, `uuid` `+32`, `rootino` `+56`, `agblocks` `+84`, `agcount` `+88`, `versionnum` `+100`, `sectsize` `+102`, `inodesize` `+104`, `inopblock` `+106`, the 12-byte label `+108`, `agblklog` at byte 124, `features2` `+200` OR-ed with `bad_features2` `+204` (the kernel repairs the old misalignment the same way) for the v4 `FTYPE` bit `0x200` under `MOREBITS`, and on v5 (`versionnum & 0xf >= 5`) `features_incompat` `+216` for `FTYPE` `0x1`, `BIGTIME` `0x8` and `NREXT64` `0x20`. It refuses a zero `blocksize`, `sectsize`, `inodesize`, `inopblock` or `agblocks`, a `blocksize` that is not a power of two in 512..=65,536, an `agblklog` of 64 or more, or an `inodesize` not a power of two in 256..=2,048. An inode number is split at `ceil_log2(agblocks) + ceil_log2(inopblock)` bits into allocation group and index, and the inode is read whole at `inodesize` with `read_full`, refused if short: magic `0x494E`, `mode` `+2`, data-fork `format` `+5`, `onlink` `+6`, `uid` `+8`, `gid` `+12`, `nlink` `+16` (falling back to `onlink` when zero), the three 8-byte timestamps at `+32`, `+40`, `+48` kept raw, `crtime` at `+144` on v5 only, `size` `+56`, the extent count as a 64-bit `+24` under `NREXT64` or 32-bit `+76` otherwise, and `forkoff` at byte 82 in 8-byte units bounding the data fork so an attribute fork is never read as extents or directory entries. Formats: `LOCAL` keeps the fork bytes; `EXTENTS` unpacks 16-byte records (bit 127 unwritten, 54-bit logical block, 52-bit start block, 21-bit count) up to 100,000; `BTREE` reads the root in the fork (level, numrecs, 16-byte keys then 8-byte pointers) and on-disk `BMAP` (24-byte header) or `BMA3` (72-byte header) blocks to depth 8 with a visited set. Every filesystem block number is decoded as `(agno << agblklog) | agbno` into `agno × agblocks + agbno` before it becomes a byte offset . Directories: a `LOCAL` shortform list (count, `i8count`, a 4- or 8-byte parent, then `namelen`, 2-byte tag, name, the `ftype` byte when the feature is set, and a 4- or 8-byte inode); an `EXTENTS`/`BTREE` directory whose first block is `XDB3`/`XD2B` (single block, header 64/16, its entries scanned only up to the leaf array whose start the block tail's leaf count gives — a tail that gives no usable bound leaves the scan unbounded and the directory marked `directory_parse_incomplete`) or `XDD3`/`XD2D` (multi-block, header 64/16), walking logical blocks `1..size/blocksize` up to 262,144, skipping unmapped holes, and any other magic parsed raw as salvage; an entry is an 8-byte inode, `namelen`, name, the `ftype` byte when set, a 2-byte tag, padded to 8, with `0xFFFF` marking a free span. Each free span is searched at 8-byte steps for an entry the kernel freed into it: a name length, a name with no NUL or `/`, an `ftype` of 1..=8 where the volume stores one, and a trailing tag equal to the candidate's own offset or an 8-aligned earlier offset in the same span (the start the span had when the entry was merged into it). After the walk, each allocation group's AGI (`XAGI`, one sector at `2 × sectsize`) gives `agi_root`, and the inode B+tree (`IAB3` 56-byte or `IABT` 16-byte headers, 16-byte leaf records of start inode, sparse hole mask and 64-bit free mask) is walked with a visited set, depth 8 and 1,000,000 blocks per AG; every inode marked free and not in a hole is read. Timestamps are decoded per the superblock: under `bigtime` each is one 64-bit nanosecond count from 1901-12-13 20:45:52 UTC (`XFS_BIGTIME_EPOCH_OFFSET` = 2^31 s, `fs/xfs/libxfs/xfs_format.h`), zero meaning unset; otherwise the high 32 bits are whole seconds since 1970 and the low 32 bits are discarded. The walk is bounded to depth 64 and 500,000 directory entries.

**Produces.** One `FileSystem` artifact, child of the input and sharing its data source, with `filesystem_type: XFS`, `version`, `blocksize`, `total_blocks`, `allocation_groups`, `sector_size`, `inode_size`, `filesystem_name`, `uuid` and `root_inode`; when the 500,000-entry budget was exhausted it also carries `directory_parse_incomplete: true` with reason `xfs_max_dir_entries`; when the depth-64 cap stopped a descent, `directory_parse_incomplete: true` and `directory_depth_capped: 64`; when the root inode would not read, `root_inode_readable: false`, `root_inode_error` and the `inventory_incomplete` pair with reason `unresolved_structure` and a sentence that the absence of files is a failure to start the walk; and always a `freed_inode_scan` block (`ags_scanned`, `ags_unreadable` with each reason, `free_inodes_examined`, `freed_inodes_reported`, the 100,000-record cap, `complete`). Then one `FileEntry` per name reached from the root inode, each parented to the **input** artifact, with `name`, `path`, `parent_path`, `inode`, `mode`, `uid`, `gid`, `size`, `nlink`, `is_directory`, `is_symlink`, `data_format` (`local`, `extents`, `btree` or `unknown`) and `extent_count`. Timestamps: `changed` (ctime, the inode change time, deliberately not `created`), `modified` and `accessed`; on a `bigtime` v5 volume also `created` from `crtime` when non-zero, each field omitted when its raw value is zero and listed in `timestamps_unsupported` if it individually fails to decode (ROADMAP §5.7); on a legacy volume the three are always present and a zero field renders as an empty string. A regular file with extents, or a fully sparse one, carries `data_runs` — absolute byte offsets within the volume, `None` for holes and for unwritten extents — `data_runs_complete`, `has_unwritten_extents` when any extent was preallocated, and an attached `XfsFileSource`; a `LOCAL` file carries `resident_data_b64` and a `ByteSliceDataSource` over its fork bytes cut to `size`. Where the extent list is not the whole on-disk list — a capped or short fork, a failed B-tree walk, an inline file shorter than its size, a rejected record, or a format this parser does not decode — the entry carries `data_runs_complete: false`, `extents_incomplete` and the standard `content_incomplete` pair with reason `short_read`, `cap_reached` or `unresolved_structure` . A directory whose listing stopped short carries `directory_parse_incomplete: true` and, for a shortform directory that failed to parse, `directory_parse_error` with the message; so does a directory any of whose live names points at an inode that will not read or is unallocated, a directory whose extent list is empty or whose fork format is not decoded, and one with an unmapped block under a truncated extent list. Deleted entries, each a `FileEntry` with no data source, `deleted: true`, `size: null` and the `content_incomplete` pair (`unresolved_structure`, with a sentence that XFS clears a freed inode's size, extent count and data fork, so no content is attached): one per name recovered from a directory free span, `deleted_recovery_source: "xfs_directory_free_space"`, with `name`, `path`, `parent_path`, `directory_entry_offset_in_block`, `directory_entry_file_type`, `is_directory`, and `inode` with `inode_number_basis` — `intact_in_entry`, or `low_32_bits_volume_inode_numbers_fit_32_bits` when the free tag overwrote the high half and the volume's inode numbers provably fit in 32 bits, else `inode: null` with `inode_low_32_bits` — and `inode_state`: `free` (then `uid`, `gid` and the freed core's timestamps with a `timestamps_basis` sentence), `allocated` (reused, or a rename's old entry; nothing read from it is attributed), `unreadable` or `unknown`; and one per freed inode the B+tree scan found with a non-zero timestamp that no recovered name already reports, `deleted_recovery_source: "xfs_freed_inode"`, `name: null`, `path: null`, `name_recovered: false`, a `name_note`, `inode`, `inode_state: free`, `uid`, `gid` and the timestamps. It produces no `TimelineEvent`, no symlink target, no extended attribute and no hardlink cross-reference.

**Cannot.** It cannot recover a deleted file's content: on the Linux 6.8 volume it is graded on, the kernel zeroes a freed inode's size, extent count and data fork, so where the data lay is not recorded in anything this parser reads, and the recovered records say so. It cannot recover a name removed from a shortform (inline) directory — the kernel compacts that list and zeroes the slack — so such a file surfaces only as a nameless freed inode. A freed inode that has since been reused, or whose chunk was freed back to the AG, is not found; nor is a freed inode whose timestamps are all zero. It does not read the AGI unlinked lists (inodes unlinked but still open at acquisition) or the free-inode B+tree. A free-span name whose inode is allocated again is reported with `inode_state: allocated` and nothing from that inode, because a reused inode and a rename's old entry cannot be told apart here. The recovery was graded on one real v5 volume made in a Linux 6.8 guest with 13 files deleted (`seance_plugin_xfs/tests/real_deleted_volume_test.rs`): all 10 names removed from block and leaf directories recovered with the inode numbers recorded before the deletion, the 3 from shortform directories as nameless freed inodes, and no record for anything live; no v4 volume, node-form directory or pre-6.8 kernel has been graded. It cannot see an unreplayed journal: the log is never read, so a volume acquired after an unclean unmount is presented as its on-disk state. It verifies nothing: the v5 CRCs on the superblock, inodes, B-map blocks and directory blocks, and the per-block UUID and owner fields, are not checked, so a block that parses is a block that is believed. It cannot read a symlink target — `is_symlink` is stated and the fork that holds the target is not published — nor any extended attribute, quota or project id. It has no realtime device: `rblocks` is read and discarded, and a file carrying the realtime flag has its extents decoded as data-device block numbers and served from the wrong place with nothing to say so. Legacy timestamps lose their nanoseconds, treat the 32-bit seconds as unsigned so a pre-1970 value reads as a date after 2038, and render a zero as an empty string rather than omitting the key; v4 has no creation time at all. A hardlinked inode is parsed once per name and published as that many independent entries with the same `inode` and content, with no cross-reference. A block-directory entry with a zero inode or zero name length stops that block's scan, silently dropping every entry after it. Directory data is read only from the low logical range, which is correct for leaf and node directories but means a corrupt `di_size` truncates the listing to what it names. Its ceilings are 100,000 extents per file, 262,144 data blocks per directory, 500,000 entries per volume, depth 64 for the tree and 8 for a B-map. One real `mkfs.xfs` volume is read (the graded fixture above); every other test in the crate builds its volume by hand, and `VALIDATION.md` lists no XFS case.

**Refuses.** It refuses to parse zero-padding as structure: a short superblock, a short inode or a short B-map block is an error, never a fabricated empty record. It refuses a superblock whose geometry would divide by zero, allocate a 4 GiB block buffer, shift by 64 or index past a 256-byte inode, returning `ParsingError` and producing no artifact. It refuses to wrap: extent starts, counts and B-map pointers are combined with saturating arithmetic so a hostile record reads past the device end rather than landing on unrelated bytes and hashing them as this file's content. It refuses to serve the residual bytes of an unwritten extent — they read as zeros, as the kernel serves them — and refuses to serve a sparse tail past a truncated extent list, short-reading instead of fabricating a hole, while a genuine sparse tail is served as zeros to `i_size` . It refuses to read the attribute fork as data or as directory entries, pinned by `a_shortform_directory_stops_at_the_attribute_fork`. It refuses to publish a sized regular file with no located stream as an empty file, a capped extent list as complete, or a short directory listing as a full one; and it stamps the volume itself when the global entry budget or the depth cap stops the walk, or the root inode will not read, so an unreadable volume is never an empty one. It refuses to invent: a freed inode whose name did not survive is published with `name: null`, a recovered name whose inode number's high half was overwritten carries `inode: null` unless the volume's geometry proves that half zero, and a recovered name whose inode is allocated again is given nothing from that inode. It refuses to trust the version number for the directory entry layout: the `ftype` byte is taken from the feature bit in each format's own place, because assuming it from v5 misaligns every entry on an image written without it. It returns an empty list for any `FileSystem` artifact whose subtype is not `xfs`, and `InvalidInputFormat` for one with no data source; neither leaves a refusal artifact.

### `plugin.findings.asep`

**Reads.** Nothing from the evidence directly: it declares `InputCapability::Stream` and never opens a data source. It subscribes to `ParsedRecord` artifacts and acts only on those whose `type` metadata is exactly `AsepEntry` — the records `seance_plugin_asep` writes for every autostart extensibility point it enumerated from a registry hive, the Task Scheduler store, a Startup folder or the WMI repository — and skips any whose `read_status` is `unread`, because an entry the enumerator could not decode has no image to judge. From a record it reads: `target_lookup_path`, the enumerator's normalised form of the image (lower-case, forward slashes, drive letter removed, `\??\`, `\SystemRoot\`, `%SystemRoot%` and `%windir%` rewritten, a bare `system32/` or `syswow64/` prefix moved under `/windows/`, a leading `/` guaranteed) written by `attach_target_resolution`; `image_path`, the image the enumerator separated from its arguments, and `command` as the display fallback; `category_label` or `category` for what the entry is; the evidence fields `category`, `asep_location`, `asep_value_name`, `image_path`, `command`, `arguments`, `scope`, `user`, `runs_when`, `mitre_technique`, `installed_time` and the boolean `enabled`; `target_path_expansion`; and for the second detection `target_exists`, `target_exists_basis`, `target_index_capped` and `target_index_executable_names`, all four written by the enumerator's `EvidenceIndex::resolve` against the files it had seen when the entry was built. The judgement it makes for itself — the only one — is which directory an image sits in. The raw `image_path` decides whether there is a path at all: the first whitespace token, quotes stripped, must carry a drive letter or a separator, so a bare `regsvr32.exe` or a `BootExecute` line whose argument holds the separators is not a path. The normalised lookup path is then split at its last `/`; a lookup containing `%` or not starting `/` is not classified. The directory is tested first against fourteen `UNEXPECTED` substrings — `/appdata/local/temp/`, the two Internet Explorer cache paths, `/windows/temp/`, `/winnt/temp/`, `/winnt/debug/`, `/temp/`, `/tmp/`, `/$recycle.bin/`, `/recycler/`, `/perflogs/`, `/users/public/`, `/downloads/`, `/windows/debug/` — then, as prefixes, the `STANDARD` set (`/windows/system32/`, `/windows/syswow64/`, `/program files/`, `/program files (x86)/`, `/windows/`, `/winnt/`, `/progra~1/`, `/progra~2/`, `/programdata/microsoft/windows/start menu/`, the three Start Menu Startup paths) plus any path containing `/start menu/programs/startup`, then the `USER_WRITABLE` prefixes (`/appdata/roaming/`, `/appdata/local/`, `/programdata/`, `/users/`, `/documents and settings/`, `/docume~1/`); a file at the volume root is unexpected, and anything else is a user-writable tier of its own.

**Produces.** Up to three `Finding` records per `AsepEntry`, each a `ParsedRecord` with `type: Finding`, parented to the ASEP record, whose `subject_artifact_id` is the ASEP record's own parent — the `RegistryHive` record or the task or Startup-folder file it was enumerated from — and whose `device_offset` is always `null`, because no ASEP record carries an offset key. `persistence_in_unexpected_location` is raised at `Confidence::Notable` (rank 1) for the unexpected tier and `Confidence::Weak` (rank 2) for the user-writable tier, never for the standard tier; its title reads `<Category> runs <image> from <what the directory is>`, its observation names the `asep_location`, the image as shown and the lookup path it resolves to, its evidence carries the twelve base fields present — eleven strings and the boolean `enabled` — plus `target_lookup_path` and `target_path_expansion`, its inference — only on the notable tier — says persistence pointing outside an install directory was not set up by an install, and its qualification says in the notable case that the directory was judged and not the program, naming installers run from a temporary copy, portable applications and vendors that ship this way, and in the weak case that the tier fires on healthy machines and is ranked last accordingly. `persistence_target_not_recovered` is raised at `Confidence::Weak` only when `target_exists` is exactly `not_observed`, `target_index_capped` is not `true`, and `target_index_executable_names` is a positive number; its observation states the image and that no file was recovered at the lookup path among that many executable names, its evidence adds `target_exists`, `target_lookup_path`, `target_index_executable_names` and the enumerator's own `target_exists_basis` sentence, it carries no inference, and its qualification says the ordinary cause is an uninstaller that leaves the run key behind and that the comparison was against executable-like files only. `service_binary_unrecognised_in_system_directory` is raised at `Confidence::Weak` for a `service` entry with `service_start_type` 2, an own-process `service_type` (bit 0x10, no driver bits), `target_exists` exactly `observed_at_path` and a raw `image_path` that is a literal drive-letter path under `\Windows\System32\` or `\Windows\SysWOW64\` ending `.exe` and not `svchost.exe`; stock services spell that path `%SystemRoot%\system32\...`, which this rule does not match. It carries no inference, its evidence adds `service_start_type`, `service_type`, `service_account` and `target_exists`, and its qualification says the file, its signature and its hash were not examined, that vendor services also live in System32, that the spelling is trivially evaded, and states the measured hit counts. Every finding carries `grade: investigative_lead`, the standard `grade_note`, `confidence_rank`, `source_module: plugin.findings.asep`, and `name` set to the title so the record table and search index show it. All three detections are declared in `seance_api::FINDING_DETECTIONS`, so an empty triage list can say this build looked for them.

**Cannot.** It cannot say whether an entry is unwanted, whether the image ever ran, or what the image is: nothing here opens the file, checks a signature or reads prefetch, Amcache or any execution artifact, and both qualifications say so. It cannot classify a path it does not have. An entry whose image carries an environment variable this build does not expand — anything but `%SystemRoot%` and `%windir%` — is never classified, and neither is a bare program name or a DLL Windows resolves from the system directory, which is deliberate: on the CFReDS Hacking Case the classifier once raised 742 leads from COM servers, `KnownDLLs`, shell extensions and print monitors that named no path at all, and five more from the default Startup folder. The classification is a string match on a hand-written list: an install to `C:\Tools` or a game library is the weak tier by construction; a `temp` segment anywhere in a program's own directory is the notable tier; `/progra~1/` is accepted as Program Files on convention, not fact, and the error there is towards silence; a Windows installed to a drive other than the one the entry names, a non-English profile root, a junction, or a path with an unusual separator is classified as its text reads; and a directory not on any list is called `a directory outside the system and program directories`. It cannot tell a scheduled task's image from a task whose definition was not read, beyond the enumerator's `read_status`. The absent-target detection is bounded by what the enumerator indexed: a name-keyed table of files with one of 23 executable-like extensions (`exe`, `dll`, `sys`, `com`, `bat`, `cmd`, `scr`, `ps1`, `vbs`, `vbe`, `js`, `jse`, `wsf`, `wsh`, `cpl`, `ocx`, `msc`, `jar`, `pif`, `hta`, `msi`, `efi`, `drv`), at most 400,000 basenames and 8 paths per basename, filled as the volume is walked and consulted at the moment the entry was built — so a target enumerated after the entry, a target on a second volume, in an unreadable region or without one of those extensions, is `not_observed` and the finding says only that the tool did not see it; a capped index or an empty one suppresses the finding entirely. It reads `enabled` as a fact from the record and does not weigh it: a disabled task in a temporary directory is raised exactly as an enabled one. It cannot group: one image referenced from ten autostart points is ten findings. And it cannot say when a service was installed: the ASEP record carries no per-key write time and the 7045 event is not joined. It does compare two other times: the creation time the file system recorded for the service's image in a Windows system directory (`target_created`) and the system's install time from the live SOFTWARE hive's `InstallDate` (`os_install_time`, never a zero and never the `SOFTWARE.SAV` backup), and the service-binary detection raises nothing for a file created at or before that time. Both times are the evidence's own and the creation time is writable by the program it describes, so a back-dated implant is not seen; the install time is stamped only if the SOFTWARE hive was read before the entry was built, and a service read from a hive processed earlier says so and is judged without it, except that a service read from the setup-time copy of the SYSTEM hive under `\Windows\repair` is not raised at all, since setup registered it before the install finished. cannot place a finding on the device — `device_offset` is `null` for every one, and the subject it names is the hive record or file, not the key.

**Refuses.** It refuses to judge a value that is not a path, and the run that taught it is on the record: `is_a_path` consults the raw `image_path`, not the normalised one, so a bare token is declined even though `normalize_target` gives it a leading `/` and the shape of a file at the volume root (pinned by `a_bare_program_name_is_not_a_file_at_the_root_of_the_volume` and `an_argument_that_looks_like_a_path_does_not_make_the_image_one`). It refuses to accept `command` as an image — a command line is not a path — and refuses to classify an unexpanded variable or a lookup that does not start with `/`. It refuses to raise anything for the standard tier, including the default Startup folder in either era's spelling, because that is where startup items belong and the enumerator's own `startup_folder_not_default_location` observation already says when one is elsewhere. It refuses to read a record whose `read_status` is `unread`, and any record whose `type` is not `AsepEntry` — which includes every entry the enumerator recovered from an unallocated hive cell, written as `RecoveredAsepEntry`, so a deleted autostart entry is never judged for location or absent target. For the absent-target detection it refuses every `target_exists` value but `not_observed` — `no_file_index`, `observed_by_name_only`, `unresolved_environment_variable`, `not_applicable` and `observed_at_path` are questions that were not asked or were answered — and refuses to raise it when the index was capped or empty, because `not observed` is then an artefact of the search and not a fact about the volume. It refuses an inference on the weak tier, because any reading of a user-writable location would be this tool's invention. It refuses to re-derive anything the enumerator established: the category, the split of image from arguments, the normalisation and the resolution are the enumerator's and are quoted. And it never returns an error and never reads bytes, so it leaves no row in the processing log beyond the findings themselves.

### `plugin.findings.hive`

**Reads.** Metadata only — `InputCapability::Stream`, no data source ever opened. It subscribes to `ParsedRecord` and acts on records whose `type` is exactly `RegistryHive`, which `seance_plugin_registry` writes once per on-disk hive file it parsed (memory-resident hives produce no such record). From that record it reads the `all_keys` array and, for each key, three things the registry plugin wrote from `seance_hive`: `subkey_count_disagrees_with_index`, stamped `true` by `seance_plugin_registry/src/lib.rs:1099-1103` when the key node's own `subkey_count` differs from `SubKeyNodes::listed_len()` — the number of offsets its subkey index actually names, counted before iteration; `subkey_count`, the count the key declares; and `subkeys_listed`, the index's count, which is absent rather than zero for a key that declares no subkeys because there is then no index to have counted. It also reads each key's `key_path`, the record's `hive_type` (the hive's file name as ingested — `SOFTWARE`, `NTUSER.DAT`) or `name`, `total_keys`, and each key's `subkeys_incomplete`, which the registry plugin sets when part of a key's subkey list could not be read at all. It also reads the replay provenance the registry plugin stamps on the hive record — `logs_replayed`, `hive_dirty`, `replay_reason` and `log_entries_applied` — to word its qualification. It reads nothing else from the hive record — not `key_inventory_complete` — and it does not open `seance_hive` itself: both numbers are the registry plugin's transcription, and this module's whole job is to notice when the two accounts of one key differ.

**Produces.** At most one `Finding` record per hive, never one per key. It is a `ParsedRecord` with `type: Finding`, `finding_kind: hive_subkey_count_discrepancy`, parented to the hive record, with `subject_artifact_id` set to the hive record's parent — the hive file — and `device_offset: null`, because a hive record covers a whole file and offset zero is a real place on the device. Its `confidence` is `notable` (rank 1). The title reads `A key in <hive> declares a different number of subkeys than its index names` or `<N> keys in <hive> declare a different number …`; the observation states the hive, how many keys disagree, how many of them declare more than their index names, and that the enumeration in the hive's record is the index's answer. The evidence carries `hive`, `keys_disagreeing`, `keys_declaring_more_than_the_index_names`, `keys_walked_in_this_hive` from `total_keys`, then up to `MAX_NAMED_KEYS` (10) key paths each valued `declares <d>, index names <l>`, sorted so keys that declare more than they list come first, then by the size of the gap, then by path; when more than ten disagree a further row `keys not named above` states the remainder and that the hive record's `all_keys` carries every one stamped `subkey_count_disagrees_with_index`; and when any key also has `subkeys_incomplete`, a row `keys whose subkey index would not read` states that count and that those keys are short for a different reason — an unreadable sublist is a hole, not a discrepancy; and each of `logs_replayed`, `hive_dirty` and `replay_reason` the hive record carries. The inference says a key that counts more children than its index names has lost them and that a deleted key's name and values may still be in the hive's unallocated cells; the qualification says this does not establish deletion or tampering, names an unflushed hive with its recent writes still in `.LOG1`/`.LOG2` and corruption from a bad shutdown or failing disk as ordinary causes, says what was done with the logs as the hive record states it — replayed before the hive was read and the discrepancy survived (with the entries applied), replayed but stopped early (with the reason), not replayed on a dirty hive (with the reason), a clean flush with nothing to replay, or, where the record carries no provenance, that it does not say — and states that what is established is only that the hive as read gives two answers. Every finding carries `grade: investigative_lead`, the standard `grade_note`, `confidence_rank`, `source_module: plugin.findings.hive` and `name` set to the title. The detection is declared in `seance_api::FINDING_DETECTIONS`.

**Cannot.** It cannot say which of the two counts is right, and does not try: the direction of the disagreement is reported, not resolved. It cannot name a lost subkey — that is `seance_plugin_registry`'s unallocated-cell recovery, published as its own record types and never joined to this finding — and it does not check whether such a recovery succeeded for the keys it names, so the inference that the name `may still be in the hive's unallocated cells` is stated without looking. What it says about the transaction logs is only what the hive record's replay provenance says; it does not check the logs itself, and it cannot say which keys the replay changed, because the registry plugin does not compute that (`replay_changed_keys_computed: false`). It cannot distinguish a hive walked to completion from one the registry plugin stopped at its 100-level depth cap or that lost subkey lists to read errors: `key_inventory_complete` is not consulted, so on a damaged hive the finding counts the keys the walk reached and no others. It sees only on-disk hives with a `RegistryHive` record: a hive carved from memory, a hive the registry plugin refused as unparsed (`RegistryHiveUnparsed`) or published as `RegistryHiveIncomplete`, and a transaction log file, produce no finding. It reads the `subkeys_listed` and `subkey_count` numbers as the record has them and skips any key where either is missing or not an integer. It cannot rank one hive's damage against another's — every hive with any disagreement is `notable` — nor separate the two directions into two findings; a hive with a torn index root and a hive with one deleted key read alike in grade. Its grounding on real evidence is a null result: on the CFReDS Hacking Case run (`VALIDATION.md`, HACK-1) it raised zero leads, which was the right answer for that image, and no image with a planted deletion has been run against it. And it cannot place a finding: `device_offset` is `null` by design, and the subject it names is the whole hive file.

**Refuses.** It refuses to raise one finding per key. A torn index root produces hundreds of disagreeing keys from one cause, and the module raises one finding per hive, names ten keys, and always states the full count so the cap cannot be mistaken for the total — pinned by `one_cause_produces_one_finding_however_many_keys_it_damaged`. It refuses to conflate a discrepancy with a hole: a key whose sublist could not be read is counted separately in the evidence and never as a disagreeing key. It refuses to reconcile the two counts or prefer one, because a reader that silently trusted the index would present a key's contents as settled while the hive itself disagreed. It refuses to act on any record whose `type` is not `RegistryHive`, on a record with no `all_keys` array, and on a key without the boolean flag or without both integers. It refuses to fabricate an offset — `device_offset` is `null`, never zero. It never reads the hive bytes, never re-derives a count from `seance_hive`, and never returns an error, so nothing from this module reaches the processing log except the findings it raises.

### `plugin.findings.kernel_tamper`

**Reads.** The `MemoryTamperChecks` record the Windows memory tier's kernel-side tamper stage writes. It reads no memory image and no bytes of evidence: every signal it reports was established by that stage, which read the structures, applied the exclusions, and had each of its seven groups' false-positive count measured on a clean Windows 11 capture before the rule shipped.

**Produces.** Ranked leads for a triage screen: a kernel pointer landing inside the freed range of a driver the kernel unloaded, a timer whose DPC routine no loaded module owns (never one the stage published as PatchGuard-shaped), a kernel thread starting outside every loaded module, a thread carrying an armed hardware breakpoint on an address outside the null page, a patched ETW write export, and a patched `cryptdll!CDLocateCSystem` inside `lsass.exe`. Each carries the values it rests on, what it may indicate, and what it does not establish.

**Cannot.** It cannot grade any of these as strong, and does not: not one of them is hard to produce innocently. A driver that unloaded legitimately, a debugger, and an endpoint-protection product patching the same bytes for its own reasons each produce one of these shapes, and every lead names that cause. It cannot tell you a machine is clean when it raises nothing: six of the eight checks behind it can be silent because a symbol, a process list or a structure was missing, and the stage's own record says which -- read that before reading an empty list as an answer. It cannot see a patch further into a function than its first sixteen bytes, or one that preserves the prologue.

**Refuses.** It refuses to raise a lead for a suspended thread, however many times it was suspended: the platform suspends packaged apps, debuggers suspend, and `CREATE_SUSPENDED` is how nearly every injector starts a thread, so the stage reports suspension as a listing and promoting it would be the mistake that once produced 4,054 false timestomps here. It refuses to raise an orphan kernel thread whose four exclusions were not all assessable -- such a row is published by the stage as an observation, and grading it would state a claim with one of its own controls silently unapplied. And it refuses to re-derive any signal for itself: a second implementation would drift from the one with a measured false-positive rate, and two numbers for one fact from one tool is indefensible.

### `plugin.findings.pe`

**Reads.** Only the analysis record another module already wrote: it declares `InputCapability::Stream`, never opens a data source, subscribes to `ParsedRecord`, and acts on records whose `type` is exactly `PeSignature` — the record `seance_plugin_pe` (`plugin.executable.pe_signature`) emits, parented to the executable, for every `FileEntry` or `FileContent` that begins `MZ` and that goblin will parse, and also the `PeSignature` record it emits for an `MZ` file that would not parse, which carries `analysis_incomplete` and none of the analysed fields. From the record it reads `source_name` or `name` for the file's name; `signature_integrity`, which the PE plugin writes as `valid (bytes match the signed digest)`, `MISMATCH — file does not match its signature`, or one of several `unverified (…)` sentences, and which it tests only by the prefix `MISMATCH`; the boolean `analysis_incomplete`, which the PE plugin sets when it read fewer bytes than the file declares (the certificate table sits at the end of a signed image, capped at 256 MiB); `in_alternate_data_stream`, `stream_name` and `parent_file`, which the PE plugin copies from the source artifact only when the MFT parser had stamped it `is_ads`; `source_deleted`, copied from the source's `deleted`; `carving_source` and `parent_file` from a carver; `likely_packed`, which the PE plugin sets when `max_section_entropy` — the Shannon entropy in bits per byte of the highest-entropy section — exceeds 7.2, with `max_entropy_section` naming it; `version_info`; and as supporting evidence whichever of `publisher`, `cert_issuer`, `digest_algorithm`, `cert_not_before`, `cert_not_after`, `imphash`, `subsystem` and `machine` the record holds. For a device offset it looks for `device_offset`, `physical_offset`, `carving_offset_absolute` or `offset` on the record. Nothing here parses a PE, recomputes a digest or measures entropy, because a second opinion from this crate could only disagree with the record it points at.

**Produces.** Up to four `Finding` records per `PeSignature` record, each a `ParsedRecord` with `type: Finding`, parented to the PE record, with `subject_artifact_id` set to the PE record's parent — the executable's own `FileEntry` — so the triage list opens the file rather than the record about it. `pe_signature_mismatch` at `Confidence::Strong` (rank 0): title `Signature does not match the bytes of <name>`, observation that the file carries an Authenticode signature and the digest recomputed from its bytes does not equal the digest inside it, evidence `signature_integrity` plus any of `publisher`, `cert_issuer`, `digest_algorithm`, `cert_not_before`, `cert_not_after`, `imphash`, inference that the bytes were modified after signing, and a qualification naming appended data and a partial acquisition as ordinary causes and stating the comparison is Séance's own recomputation, not an operating-system trust decision. `pe_in_alternate_data_stream` at `Notable`: observation that the content of the named stream parses as a PE and a directory listing gives no indication it is there, evidence `stream_name`, `parent_file`, `signature_integrity`, `publisher`, `imphash`, `subsystem` and `source_deleted` where present, inference that a stream is a place to keep an executable an ordinary listing does not show, and a qualification naming `Zone.Identifier` and backup, antivirus and build products as legitimate users and stating that nothing here examined execution. `carved_executable_in_slack` at `Notable`: observation that a PE was recovered from the slack past the logical end of `parent_file`, evidence `carving_source`, `parent_file`, `signature_integrity`, `publisher`, `imphash`, `machine` and the offset, an inference that — because a file starts on a cluster boundary and the start of that cluster is the live file's content — under this volume's cluster size the executable is not the start of a former file and is either embedded in a former file's content or was placed in slack deliberately, stating that a reformat with a larger cluster size or an earlier file system could leave a former file starting there and that nothing excludes it, and a qualification that the carve stops at the end of the cluster, so its signature and imphash describe the bytes recovered, not a whole executable. `high_entropy_executable` at `Weak` (rank 2): observation that section `<name>` has an entropy of `<x>` bits per byte above the 7.2 threshold, evidence the section, the entropy to three decimals, `publisher`, `signature_integrity`, `imphash` and `version_info` — or the literal `absent — the image carries no version resource` — inference that a section this uniform holds compressed, packed or encrypted data, and a qualification calling it the weakest lead Séance raises and close to worthless on its own. Every finding carries `grade: investigative_lead`, `grade_note`, `confidence_rank`, `source_module: plugin.findings.pe`, `name` set to the title, and `device_offset`, which on every record the PE plugin actually writes is `null`. All four kinds are declared in `seance_api::FINDING_DETECTIONS`.

**Cannot.** It cannot place a finding on the device. `device_offset_of` reads four keys none of which the PE plugin writes — `carry_provenance` (`seance_plugin_pe/src/lib.rs:229-250`) copies `is_ads`, `stream_name`, `parent_file`, `carving_source` and `deleted` and no offset — so `device_offset` is `null` on every finding this module raises in a real ingest, and the test that asserts `Some(1_048_576)` (`seance_plugin_findings/src/pe_tests.rs:173-183`) supplies `carving_offset_absolute` by hand on a record shape no parser produces. It raises `carved_executable_in_slack` only for an executable the automatic carver recovered from a `SlackSpace` region: so only on NTFS, FAT, exFAT, ext4, HFS+ and APFS, only in the slack of a live file, and only where the carve fits the slack window — under one cluster, at most about 3.5 KiB on 4 KiB clusters — so the detection rarely fires and an empty result does not say that no executable was ever in slack. It cannot see an executable in an alternate data stream on anything but on-disk NTFS: `is_ads` is stamped by the MFT parser alone, so a stream reached through a memory image, a carved file or another file system never produces the finding, and a stream that is not itself a PE never reaches the PE plugin. The signature verdict is bounded by what the PE plugin computes: a catalog-signed file (no embedded certificate table) is `signed: false` and raises nothing; an unsupported digest algorithm, an unparseable PKCS#7, a missing indirect-data digest and a file read short are all `unverified` and raise nothing; and `MISMATCH` says only that the bytes differ from the signed digest — no certificate chain is built, no trust root, revocation, expiry or countersignature timestamp is examined, and a self-signed certificate over intact bytes is `valid`. It cannot tell a benign mismatch from a malicious one: appended data after the certificate table, which some self-extracting installers write to themselves, produces the same `Strong` finding as a patched binary. The entropy threshold is a fixed 7.2 over the single highest-entropy section, with no allowance for a resource section holding compressed images or a `.NET` metadata stream, so ordinary software raises the weak finding constantly and the qualification says so; it cannot name the packer. It cannot say anything about execution — no prefetch, Amcache or shimcache is consulted — nor about what a packed section decompresses to. It never groups: a file with all four patterns is four findings, and a thousand packed installers are a thousand rows. Its grounding on real evidence is a null result: on the CFReDS Hacking Case (`VALIDATION.md`, HACK-1) `pe_signature_mismatch`, `pe_in_alternate_data_stream` and `carved_executable_in_slack` raised zero leads, which was right for that image (and that run predates the slack producer), and no image with a planted mismatch has been run. That the slack detection is reachable is shown only on a synthetic NTFS volume, parser to carver to PE plugin to finding (`carved_executable_in_slack_fires_on_enumerator_produced_shape`); no held image carries an executable in file slack, so it is not graded on real evidence.

**Refuses.** It refuses to raise the strongest claim it makes from a partial read: a record with `analysis_incomplete: true` never yields `pe_signature_mismatch`, because a digest over fewer bytes than the file holds cannot match and the PE plugin has already withdrawn the `signed` verdict for it. It refuses to match `MISMATCH` anywhere but as a prefix, so an `unverified (…)` explanation that happened to contain the word could not raise it. It refuses to raise the ADS finding unless the record says `in_alternate_data_stream: true`, the slack finding unless `carving_source` is exactly `slack`, and the packed finding unless both `likely_packed` is `true` and `max_section_entropy` is a number — a claim of packing with no number behind it is dropped. It refuses to grade the packed finding above `Weak`, and says in the finding's own words that it is close to worthless alone. It refuses to act on any record whose `type` is not `PeSignature`, refuses to re-derive a digest, an entropy or a provenance, and refuses to guess an offset — absent is `null`, never zero. It never reads bytes and never returns an error, so it leaves no row in the processing log beyond the findings it raises.

### `plugin.findings.timestomp`

**Reads.** Metadata only, and only from `FileEntry` artifacts: it declares `InputCapability::Stream` because the enum has no variant for reading nothing, subscribes to `ArtifactType::FileEntry` alone, and never opens a data source. From an entry it reads the boolean `timestomp_suspected`, acting only when it is exactly `true`; `timestomp_reasons`, an array of strings; `name` or `file_name`; the `$SI` timestamps the MFT parser writes as `created`, `modified`, `mft_modified` and `accessed`, and the `$FN` timestamps `fn_created`, `fn_modified`, `fn_mft_modified` and `fn_accessed`, where present; the `timestamp_indicators` array of `{reason, strength, also_produced_by}` objects; and for an offset `device_offset`, `physical_offset`, `carving_offset_absolute` or `offset`. Every one of those keys is the vocabulary of `seance_core::ntfs_timestamps::detect_timestomp_indicators`, the one rule shared by the on-disk MFT parser and the memory MFT sweep, which compares the `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` and `$FILE_NAME` FILETIMEs and grades five indicators: three weak — `SI Created` before `FN Created` (a move or rename), `SI Modified` before `FN Created` (a copy), and a whole-second `SI Created` against a sub-second `FN Created` (a FAT-sourced copy or an installer) — and two strong — all four `$SI` times equal to the second with a differing `FN Created` (bulk-set), and a whole-second `$SI` ChangeTime older than a sub-second `FN Created`, which the filesystem never writes whole and always writes after the name entry (measured at one whole-second hit among 4,231 older-ChangeTime records on DFIR Madness Case 001 and none among 84,674 on the NIST Data Leakage image). `timestomp_suspected` is true only for a strong indicator; `timestomp_reasons` holds the strong reasons only. This module re-derives nothing: the naive rule flagged 4,054 of 25,018 files on the CFReDS Hacking Case's stock Windows XP install, and a second implementation would drift from the one with the measured false-positive rate.

**Produces.** One `Finding` record per qualifying entry: a `ParsedRecord` with `type: Finding`, `finding_kind: timestomp`, parented to the input entry, `subject_artifact_id` set to the entry itself (the file), `confidence: notable` (rank 1) — never `strong`, because `no ordinary operation produces this` is not `a person did this` — with title `Timestamps reordered on <name>`, an observation stating that the `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` and `$FILE_NAME` timestamps of the file are inconsistent in a way ordinary operations do not produce and quoting the strong reasons joined by `; `, evidence consisting of an `indicator` row with those reasons, one row per timestamp the entry held — each `$SI` value labelled `si_created`, `si_modified`, `si_mft_modified` or `si_accessed` — and one `indicator (strong)` or `indicator (weak)` row per entry of `timestamp_indicators`, an inference that rewriting `$SI` is how the time of an action is hidden and leaves `$FN` — which the Win32 API cannot reach — holding the original, and a qualification stating that a restore from backup, an archive extraction and some filesystem-level copy tools reorder the fields the same way, that the weak asymmetries occur on roughly a sixth of a stock install and were not the grounds, and that the named indicator and the timestamps should be read before relying on it. It carries `grade: investigative_lead`, the standard `grade_note`, `confidence_rank`, `source_module: plugin.findings.timestomp`, `name` set to the title, and `device_offset`. The detection is the first entry of `seance_api::FINDING_DETECTIONS`, so the Findings screen, the report and the API tell the examiner this build looks for it.

**Cannot.** It cannot see a verdict the memory MFT sweep finds: that sweep writes `timestomp_suspected` on each record nested inside the `records` array of one `ParsedRecord` (`seance_plugin_memory_windows/src/mftscan.rs`), never on a `FileEntry`, so a timestomped file seen only in memory raises no lead. The path from parser to lead is pinned by `seance_plugin_mft`'s `the_parsers_file_entry_raises_the_timestomp_lead`, on a synthetic record; it has not been measured on a real image with a stomped file. Beyond that: it cannot judge the weak indicators, and will not — a tool that rewrites one `$SI` field to a full-precision value leaves a weak indicator and no verdict, and that cost is accepted; it cannot see a timestomp on FAT, ext4, APFS or HFS+, where there is no `$FN` to compare; it cannot use the `$I30` slack copies, the USN journal or `$LogFile` to corroborate; it cannot distinguish a restore, an extraction or a copy tool from a person; it cannot say when the change was made or by whom; and it cannot grade above `notable`. `device_offset` depends on the record carrying one of four keys, and a `FileEntry`'s `mft_offset` is not among them.

**Refuses.** It refuses to raise anything from weak indicators alone, whatever their number, pinned by `weak_indicators_alone_raise_nothing`. It refuses to raise a verdict it cannot show the grounds for: `timestomp_suspected: true` with an empty or missing `timestomp_reasons` yields nothing, because a finding that could say only `the parser said so` is not one an examiner can check or an opponent can test. It refuses a `timestomp_suspected` that is anything but the boolean `true`, refuses to re-derive the comparison from the timestamps on the record, and refuses to grade the finding `strong`. It refuses to fabricate an offset — absent is `null`. It never reads bytes and never returns an error, so the only rows it can add to a case are findings.

### `plugin.fs.ext4`

**Reads.** An ext2, ext3 or ext4 volume, reached as a `FileSystem` artifact with a random-access `DataSource`. Selection is by declaration, not by probe: the module accepts the artifact when its subtype, or its `filesystem_type` metadata, spells `ext2`, `ext3` or `ext4` in any case, and it declines silently when either names something else — the only content test it applies is the superblock magic `0xEF53` at absolute offset 1080, and a volume the partition reader labelled `ext4` on that magic alone is what it is usually handed. The whole 1,024-byte superblock at offset 1024 is gathered before any field is believed, and from it: `s_inodes_count`, the block count (the high half at 336, and the group-descriptor size at 254, read only when the `64BIT` incompat bit `0x80` is set — otherwise a 32-byte descriptor is assumed), `s_log_block_size` (which must be 0 through 6, giving a 1 KiB to 64 KiB block), `s_rev_level` at 76 (revision 0 has no inode-size field and its inodes are 128 bytes), `s_inode_size` at 88 (which must be a power of two from 128 to the block size), the compat, incompat and ro-compat feature words at 92, `s_journal_inum` at 224 and `s_first_meta_bg` at 0x104. The group-descriptor table follows — the legacy contiguous table at block 2 when the block size is 1,024 and block 1 otherwise, or, when `META_BG` (`0x10`) is set, one descriptor block per meta-group from `s_first_meta_bg` upward located through the `SPARSE_SUPER` 3/5/7 rule (the meta-groups below it are read from the classic table) — and the table is truncated to the number of groups the image can physically hold, itself capped at 4,194,304. From each descriptor it takes the block-bitmap and inode-table block numbers, with their high halves at 0x20 and 0x28 when the descriptor is 64 bytes or larger, and the group flags, which it honours for `BLOCK_UNINIT` only on a volume with `uninit_bg` or `metadata_csum`; the inode bitmap's contents are never read, only its block number, to place a `BLOCK_UNINIT` group's own metadata. Then it walks the directory tree from inode 2, and reaches an inode only through a directory entry — the journal inode, read by its number, is the sole exception: there is no sweep of the inode table. An inode is read in full from its group's inode table, and past the 128-byte base — and only as far as `i_extra_isize` at 128 says the extended area reaches — it reads `i_ctime_extra`, `i_mtime_extra`, `i_atime_extra`, `i_crtime` and `i_crtime_extra`, whose low two bits extend the epoch by multiples of 2³² seconds and whose upper thirty carry nanoseconds. Extended attributes are read from both places ext4 keeps them: the in-inode area at `128 + i_extra_isize` and the block named by `i_file_acl` (its high half taken from `l_i_file_acl_high` at 118), each behind the `h_magic` `0xEA020000`, each entry's name prefixed from the seven `e_name_index` values the table knows. File content is served two ways by the inode's own `EXTENTS_FL` (`0x80000`): an extent tree, magic `0xF30A`, descended through index nodes to leaves, refusing a tree that names a child block twice, spans more than 65,536 blocks or holds more than 1,048,576 extents; or the legacy direct pointers `i_block[0..11]` with the single, double and triple indirect chains at `i_block[12]`, `[13]` and `[14]`. An inode with `EXT4_INLINE_DATA_FL` (`0x10000000`) is read as neither: its `i_block` holds content bytes, not pointers, and it is served from `i_block` plus the `system.data` xattr (see Produces). A directory is walked as `htree` when `EXT4_INDEX_FL` (`0x1000`) is set — the `dx_root`'s fixed 12-byte `.` and `..` fake dirents validated, `dx_root_info` at 24 gate-checked (reserved word zero, hash version at most 6, `info_length` at least 8, at most two indirect levels), and the entry count taken from the `dx_countlimit` overlay on `entries[0]` rather than by scanning for a zero pair — and linearly otherwise. Every entry's slack is then read: the bytes between an entry's real record length and where its `rec_len` points are where the kernel hides the entries it deleted, and they are walked twice, once along the hidden `rec_len` chain and once as a 4-byte-aligned carve. Finally it reads every block group's block bitmap (not that of a `BLOCK_UNINIT` group, whose on-disk bitmap is not valid and which is derived instead, see Produces; on a volume with the `BIGALLOC` ro-compat feature, `0x200`, each bit is read as a cluster of `1 << (s_log_cluster_size - s_log_block_size)` blocks, believed only where `s_clusters_per_group` agrees with `s_blocks_per_group`), and the internal JBD2 journal — the inode named by `s_journal_inum`, or 8 — whose every integer is big-endian: superblock magic `0xC03B3998`, whose block size must equal the file system's, then the log from `s_start` as descriptor blocks (tags of 8 or 12 bytes by the `64BIT` journal feature, 10 or 14 under `CSUM_V2`, 16 under `CSUM_V3`, each followed by a 16-byte UUID unless it is flagged `SAME_UUID`, the list ending at the tag flagged `LAST_TAG`), revoke blocks and commit blocks, the ring cursor stepping over each descriptor's journaled data blocks.

**Produces.** One `FileEntry` per inode the directory walk reaches, parented to the volume, carrying the name and the assembled path, the parent path, the inode number, the raw `i_mode`, uid, gid, the 64-bit size, `is_directory`, and the times: `changed` from `i_ctime` — labelled the inode change time, never "created" — `modified`, `accessed`, and `created` only where the inode actually carries a non-zero `i_crtime`, each to nanosecond precision where the extended fields are present. One record per **name**: a hard-linked inode is emitted once for each directory entry that names it, and no link count is published. A regular file with a non-zero size carries `data_runs`, a list of (byte offset, length) pairs in logical order — offsets in the volume's own coordinate space, not the evidence's — with contiguous runs coalesced and sparse runs offset-null, plus `data_runs_complete`; its artifact carries a `DataSource` that re-serves the bytes through the same mapping, and a directory carries one too. Where the inode carries any extended attribute, an `xattrs` object maps each name to its value, binary values as `base64:…` so nothing is rendered lossily. A file with preallocated extents carries `has_unwritten_extents`. An fscrypt inode (`EXT4_ENCRYPT_FL`, `0x800`) carries `encrypted`, `content_ciphertext: "ext4_fscrypt"` and `content_incomplete`, so the digest of ciphertext never travels the export and integrity-verify paths as a file's plaintext hash. A deleted entry — an inode with `i_dtime` set or `links_count` zero, or any name found in slack — carries `deleted`, `deleted_recovery_source`, `deleted_time` where `i_dtime` is set, and always `deleted_content_caveat: "blocks_may_be_reallocated"` with `content_incomplete`; where the name came from slack but its inode now looks live, `inode_reused` and a sentence saying the bytes reached through it belong to that other file. A name recovered with its inode number zeroed produces a name-only record: inode null, no size, no times, no data source, `metadata_unavailable` and a sentence saying so; so does a slack name whose nonzero inode now yields no record (cleared, unreadable or past the recursion limit) and a slack name whose `file_type` is a directory, each keeping the inode number the directory recorded. All carry `deleted_recovery_source: "directory_slack"` whether the entry was hidden in slack or standing in the live chain, so that field states the shape of the recovery, not reliably where the bytes sat. A slack name is recorded and never descended, whatever its inode is now. A **live** directory entry that could not be resolved — an inode out of range, past the descriptor table, short-read, or carrying no file type (`i_mode` 0) — is published name-only as well, not deleted: its name and inode number, `metadata_unavailable`, `content_incomplete` (`unresolved_structure`) and a sentence saying nothing about the file could be read through it; a live name containing `/` or NUL, or empty, is published percent-escaped (`%2F`, `%00`) with `name_invalid: true` and is not followed. A directory whose listing is known not to cover the whole directory carries `directory_parse_incomplete` with `directory_parse_incomplete_reason` (`unresolved_structure`, or `cap_reached` where the recursion limit stopped a child) and, where live entries could not be resolved, `directory_entries_unresolved` counting them. An inode with `EXT4_INLINE_DATA_FL` on a volume that declares the `INLINE_DATA` feature is published with `inline_data: true`. A regular file is served from its `i_block` (up to 60 bytes) followed by the `system.data` xattr, cut to `i_size`, with `inline_data_bytes_in_inode` and `inline_data_bytes_in_xattr` and no `data_runs`, because no block holds it; if the bytes that exist fall short of `i_size` it serves what exists and carries `content_incomplete` naming the shortfall. An inline directory's first four bytes are its parent inode (`inline_dir_parent_inode`, with no `.` or `..` entry emitted), then its entries are read from the rest of `i_block` and, separately, from `system.data`, each region ending at its own end; a real gap stamps `directory_parse_incomplete`. A deleted inline inode's data lies in the freed inode body and is not recovered. A live directory entry is checked the way the kernel checks it: `rec_len` a multiple of four, large enough for its own name and ending inside its block, else that block is not read further and the directory is stamped; an entry whose `file_type` byte names a different type from its inode's mode is kept and carries `dirent_file_type_mismatch`; a directory reached a second time under another name carries `duplicate_directory_visit` and is not listed again; and a walk cancelled before it finished leaves an `ext4_walk_status` record (`inventory_incomplete: true`, reason `cancelled`) and stamps the directory that lost a child. A regular file whose extent tree or indirect-block chain would not read keeps its size, mode and times and carries `data_runs_error` and `content_incomplete` (`unresolved_structure`). If the root inode itself cannot be used — past the image end, unallocated (mode 0), not a directory, or stopped by the recursion limit — an `ext4_root_status` record carries `root_inode_readable: false`, `root_inode_error` and `inventory_incomplete`, and the passes that do not need the tree still run. One `ParsedRecord` of type `allocation_map` stitches every group's block bitmap into a downsampled 65,536-bucket map with the cluster size, the bucket stride and the total, marked `allocation_map_incomplete` with `allocation_blocks_declared` where the superblock declares more blocks than the descriptors, or the image itself, can describe, and where a group's bitmap was read short (reason `short_read`) or a `BLOCK_UNINIT` group's layout could not be derived (`allocation_block_uninit_groups`). A `BLOCK_UNINIT` group has no valid bitmap on disk, so its bitmap is **derived, not read**, the way libext2fs and the kernel derive it: the group's backup superblock, descriptor blocks and reserved descriptor blocks, plus the block bitmap, inode bitmap and inode table of every `BLOCK_UNINIT` group wherever the descriptors place them. The map says so (`allocation_block_uninit_groups_synthesized` and `allocation_block_uninit_basis`). It derives all or none: group 0, a `META_BG` group that carries descriptor duties or a superblock backup, or any location outside the volume leaves every such group unassessed. On a `BIGALLOC` volume the map and the free regions are published per cluster, so a free region starts and ends on a cluster boundary and a partly used cluster is in use; only a bigalloc volume whose cluster fields disagree with its block fields gets an `ext4_free_space_status` record (`allocation_map_unavailable: true`, `content_incomplete`) saying the map, the free regions and the orphaned-directory scan are omitted and that their absence is not evidence of no free space; beside the map, up to 4,096 `UnallocatedSpace` regions (the default; `SEANCE_FREE_REGION_CAP` changes it and the record states the ceiling applied), largest first and then in address order, one per run of blocks the bitmaps prove free, each a window the carver reads, each labelled `ext4` and each stating that its offsets are relative to the start of this volume and not to the evidence. That pass publishes its own census — `free_runs_found`, `free_regions_emitted`, `free_bytes_emitted`, `free_runs_dropped`, `free_bytes_dropped`, the two ceilings and whether each fired, `free_space_complete`, and a sentence naming which ceiling fired — and, where a group bitmap was read short or a `BLOCK_UNINIT` group's layout could not be derived, `free_space_blocks_short_group_bitmaps` with the sentence that those blocks are not free space and no region covers them. It also publishes **file slack**: one `SlackSpace` region per live regular file whose last block's unused tail — from the file's logical end to the end of that block — holds any non-zero byte, each carrying the owning file and its logical size and labelled `ext4`, and one `slack_space_summary` record counting the tails offered, emitted, all-zero, unreadable and not located. A file reached under two names is one inode and is offered once; a file whose run list is incomplete, that is fscrypt-encrypted or that has no block-mapped data (inline data) is counted as not located, never as having no slack. This is graded on one 2 MiB volume `mke2fs` wrote, with known bytes planted in two tails — a synthetic plan, not evidence from a case. One `ParsedRecord` of type `ext4_journal` carries the journal inode, the log's block size, `maxlen`, `first`, `sequence` and `start`, whether the log is clean, and each committed transaction's sequence with the filesystem blocks its tags journaled and the blocks it revoked; where the walk stopped early it carries `journal_walk_incomplete` with its reason alongside `content_incomplete` and `inventory_incomplete`. In-image sidecars (`-wal`, `-journal`, `.LOG`, `.LOG1`, `.LOG2`) are attached to their live parent files so a SQLite or registry reader downstream sees them. An unallocated-space pass separately recognises a deleted directory's own first block by content — a `.`/`..`-opening `ext4_dir_entry_2` chain whose `rec_len` fields land exactly on the block boundary — and, for each name recovered from it, either resolves the inode into an ordinary `FileEntry` (only when the inode's type still agrees with the dirent and the inode itself carries its own deletion marker) or reports it as an orphaned name with `inode_status` (`unallocated`/`reused`/`unreadable`) and no content, never merged into the live listing. That pass reads runs of consecutive free blocks (up to 256 per call), skips a free block it could not read whole, and, when it found a block or hit its cap of 100,000 entries, leaves an `orphaned_directory_scan` record counting the blocks found and entries recovered (with `content_incomplete`, reason `cap_reached`, where the cap fired).

**Cannot.** **It cannot find a deleted file whose directory entry is gone.** The walk starts at inode 2 and descends; an inode is reached only through a directory entry — live, zeroed-inode, or hidden in slack — so an orphaned or unlinked inode whose name no longer survives anywhere is never enumerated and never counted. There is no inode-table sweep and no inode bitmap is read, so the absence of a file from this output is not evidence the inode is empty. It cannot read an inode whose `i_mode` was cleared: the file type cannot be told, so nothing about it is read, and where a directory entry still names it the entry is published name-only with its inode number; an inode no entry names is not found. **And it cannot promise that a name it did not emit was not there**. A live directory entry whose inode will not parse is published name-only and its parent directory is stamped `directory_parse_incomplete`; a `rec_len` under 8, or a name running past the data, ends that walk and stamps the directory (a linear directory is read as one run, so everything after the break in it goes unread; a hash-tree directory loses the rest of that leaf block); a file whose extent tree will not parse keeps its size, mode and times, loses its `data_runs` and says so (`data_runs_error`); an entry more than 20 levels below the root gets no record at all, and the directory that holds it is stamped `directory_parse_incomplete` with reason `cap_reached`; and a root inode that will not parse leaves an `ext4_root_status` record. A live entry whose `rec_len` is misaligned, too short for its name or runs past its block is not walked and the rest of that block is not read, so a name after it in the same block is not listed. A `file_type` that disagrees with the inode's mode is marked, not resolved: which of the two was altered is not decidable here. If the superblock or the group-descriptor table will not parse, the module returns a parsing error to the case's processing log and publishes no record at all, which on the case is what an unexamined volume looks like.
