It cannot say that a recovered deleted file's blocks still hold its content: the extents name where the blocks were, ext4 frees them on unlink, and a reallocated block serves another file's bytes under this name, with this name's size and timestamps beside them; that is why every deleted record carries the caveat and `content_incomplete`, and why an examiner hashing one against a known-file set must not read a non-match as the file itself differing. **A name recovered from slack is the directory's record, not the file system's live answer**: pass one of the slack walk follows the hidden `rec_len` chain, but pass two visits every 4-byte offset and emits, name-only, anything that parses as a plausible dirent — an inode number no greater than `s_inodes_count` (zero included), a 4-aligned `rec_len` at least the record's real length, and a name of at least one byte with no NUL, no slash and no byte below 0x20 that fits — so a name carved that way is a name those bytes contained, and nothing more. Deduplication is per slack span, so the same deleted name surviving in two entries' slack is emitted twice: the record count is a count of records, not of files. The slack walk cannot recover a deleted directory's contents: a hidden entry whose `file_type` is 2 is recorded, by both passes, as a name-only entry (its inode number kept, `is_directory: true`) and never descended, so nothing under it is read through that name. A slack name whose inode now looks live is emitted as that inode's record marked `inode_reused`, and where that inode is a live directory it is not descended either, so its children are not attributed to the stale path. A separate, unallocated-space pass now recovers a deleted directory's *contents* where its own dirent block survives unoverwritten — see Produces — but it is scoped to that block's first block only (the one opening `.`/`..`) and requires the recovered inode to carry its own deletion marker before attaching content; a reused or unreadable inode is reported as an orphaned name and nothing more. It cannot give a symlink's target: only regular files and directories get a data source, so a fast symlink's target sitting in `i_block` is not decoded, and a symlink, device node, FIFO or socket appears as `is_directory: false` with its type recoverable only from the raw `i_mode` number. It cannot report a uid or gid above 65,535 correctly: `i_uid` and `i_gid` are read as 16-bit fields and `l_i_uid_high`/`l_i_gid_high` at 120 and 122 are not read, so a uid of 100,000 is published as its low half with no marker. It cannot recover a **deleted** inline-data file or directory: its bytes lived in the inode body, which the kernel reuses and zeroes when it frees the inode, and an inline file whose bytes spilled to an xattr block rather than the in-inode `system.data` is served only as far as the in-inode part reaches and says so. Inline data is graded on one synthetic `mke2fs` volume, not on real evidence. It cannot recover free space inside a partly used **bigalloc** cluster: the bitmap calls the whole cluster in use, so the unused blocks of a cluster that holds any data are neither offered as free space nor scanned for orphaned directories. Bigalloc is graded on one synthetic volume. It cannot derive a `BLOCK_UNINIT` group's bitmap on a `META_BG` volume where that group carries a superblock backup or descriptor block, on group 0, or where a descriptor names a location outside the volume: those blocks are unassessed, never free. Derivation is graded on four synthetic volumes (flex_bg, no flex_bg, meta_bg without such duties, and 4 KiB blocks with backup-superblock groups flagged through `debugfs`), not on real evidence. It cannot state an xattr value it did not inline: a value held in a separate EA inode is published as its name with an **empty** value, an attribute whose `e_name_index` is outside the seven known ones is published with no prefix and so under a name that is not its full name, and an xattr block read short is parsed to whatever arrived with nothing said. It cannot render a time it cannot represent: an unset `i_atime`, `i_ctime` or `i_mtime` of zero is published as `1970-01-01T00:00:00+00:00` as though it were a real instant, and a value outside the representable range is published as an empty string rather than as null with a reason. It verifies no checksum anywhere — not the superblock's, not `metadata_csum` on a group descriptor, inode, extent block or dirent, and not the journal's — and it reads no backup superblock, so a corrupt primary superblock is the end of the volume. It cannot tell ext2 from ext3 from ext4: the three share the magic, the upstream detector labels every one of them `ext4`, and this module reports the features the superblock declares rather than a version. It publishes no volume-level record — no label, no UUID, no mount or write time, no free-block or free-inode count — only file entries, the allocation map, the free regions, the slack regions, the journal and the status records named above. It cannot descend past 20 directory levels: an entry deeper than that gets no record and its parent directory is stamped `cap_reached`; a directory reached a second time in one walk is emitted but not re-descended, with no marker. It cannot enumerate a **linear** directory larger than 1 MiB of dirents: only the first 1,048,576 bytes are scanned, and that directory is stamped `directory_parse_incomplete`; an htree directory is bounded instead by 65,536 blocks per index level and by its own `dx_countlimit`. It cannot serve the residual disk bytes behind a preallocated extent, and does not try: an `ee_len` above 32,768 marks an unwritten extent, and both its served content and its data run are zeros, so such a file's hash covers zeros where `fallocate` reserved blocks that were never written. It reads no external journal device: the journal is the volume's own inode, and a volume whose journal lives elsewhere reports its journal unreadable. It does not replay the journal, does not reconstruct a superseded version of a file or an inode from it, and reports no timestamp for a transaction — a transaction is a sequence number and a list of block numbers, not a dated event — and it raises no timeline event of any kind. Its ceilings are stated and each fires in the open: 1,024 bytes of superblock and no more; block sizes 1 KiB to 64 KiB only; 4,194,304 block groups, and no more than the image's own size can hold; 1,048,576 bytes of dirents per linear directory; 20 directory levels; extent trees 5 levels deep, 65,536 distinct tree blocks and 1,048,576 extents per file (a tree past either is an error and the file says so, never a partial run list); 100,000 entries from the orphaned-directory scan; 65,536 blocks per hash-tree index level and at most two htree indirect levels; 512 data runs per file, past which `data_runs_complete` goes false; 1,048,576 logical blocks walked for a legacy block-mapped file's run list; 512 slack entries per live entry per pass; 4,096 xattr entries per area; 65,536 buckets in the allocation map; 4,096 free regions per volume and 128 GiB of free space by default (`SEANCE_FREE_REGION_CAP` and `SEANCE_FREE_BYTE_CAP` change them), whichever bites first — and on the 67 GB ext4 partition of the Magnet 2022 Linux CTF image the region ceiling declines 1,356,359 of 1,360,455 free runs, 14,379,802,624 bytes, 37.6% of that volume's free space, which the record states rather than presenting the remainder as the whole; and in the journal, 100,000 transactions, 8,192 tags per descriptor, 8,192 revokes per block, 1,048,576 blocks per transaction, and a ring walk no longer than the smaller of `s_maxlen` and the journal file's own block count.

**Refuses.** It refuses to parse a structure it could not read in full. A short superblock, a short group-descriptor block, a short extent-tree block, a short htree root or index block, or a short journal superblock or journal record is rejected outright rather than decoded against its own zero tail — a zero-padded superblock still passes the magic test while the block size, inode size and 64-bit halves come back fabricated, a reused descriptor buffer re-presents the previous meta-group's bitmaps as this group's, a truncated extent node still carries `0xF30A` while the entries cut off it map as holes and serve real content as zeros, a short htree block's zero tail reads as dx entries pointing at block 0, and a partial journal block's tag list both loses tags and desynchronises the ring for every record after it. An inode that will not come back whole is refused for the same reason: its zero tail would decode as a real, empty size and an empty extent list. It refuses an inode number of zero, and an inode whose group lies beyond the descriptor table it built. It refuses a `s_log_block_size` above 6, a `blocks_per_group` or `inodes_per_group` of zero, an `s_inode_size` that is not a power of two from 128 to the block size, and — in the `META_BG` layout, where it is a divisor — a descriptor size of zero or larger than a block. It refuses to read an inline-data inode's `i_block` as extents or block pointers, and an extent tree that names a block twice or exceeds its block or extent bound, because a truncated extent list would be recorded as sparse runs over real content. It refuses an htree hash version above 6, more than two htree indirect levels, a `dx_root_info` whose reserved word is not zero or whose `info_length` is under 8, a `dx_countlimit` whose count is zero or exceeds its limit or its block, and a block size too small to hold an htree root at all; and it refuses to walk the same leaf block twice, however many times a crafted tree names it. Where an htree yields nothing usable, it refuses to accept that as an empty directory and re-reads the directory linearly; where both fail, the directory is flagged. **It refuses to publish an allocation map or a single free region when there are no group descriptors, when `blocks_per_group` is zero, or when any one block group's block-bitmap block number is zero or cannot be read at all, or on a bigalloc volume whose cluster fields disagree with its block fields** — a zero bit means free, a bitmap that was not read is all zeros, and a volume whose bitmaps could not be gathered has no free space anybody established. Where a bitmap came back short, or a `BLOCK_UNINIT` group's layout could not be derived, the blocks it does not reach are synthesised as **in use** and counted, so no region carves a byte nobody assessed; where the superblock declares more blocks than the descriptors or the image describe, the map covers what they cover and says on the record that it does, rather than letting the remainder render as space nothing was ever written to. It refuses to step past a journal descriptor block with no terminating tag: the count of journaled data blocks is then unknown, so the next record's position is unknown, and guessing it would mis-attribute every later transaction — the walk stops and says the ring position is unrecoverable. It refuses to let a volume that declares a journal report nothing about it: when the `HAS_JOURNAL` compat bit is set and the journal inode, its zero size, its superblock, its magic or a block size that disagrees with the file system's will not read, an `ext4_journal` record is emitted anyway carrying `journal_unreadable` and the reason, because a clean journal reports `clean: true` and an unread one must never be indistinguishable from it. It refuses to let an unusable root, a live name it could not resolve, a name no path can represent, or a file whose extent structure would not read vanish from the listing: each is published or stamped and says what could not be read. And it refuses to descend into a deleted directory found in slack, to read an extent tree deeper than five levels, or to re-enter a directory graph that loops back on itself, because past those points it would be reporting whatever now occupies the blocks as the evidence of what once did.

### `plugin.fs.f2fs`

**Reads.** An F2FS volume — the `/data` partition of a modern Android device — and only one that something upstream has already called F2FS. It subscribes to `FileSystem` artifacts and declines in silence any whose `subtype` is set to something other than `f2fs`, or whose `filesystem_type` is non-empty and not `f2fs`, both compared case-insensitively; an artifact carrying neither key is accepted and left to the magic check. The keys it gates on are written by `seance_plugin_partition`, which calls a partition F2FS when the little-endian `u32` at byte 1024 of it is `0xF2F52010`, and stamps `filesystem_type: F2FS` and `subtype: f2fs` on the `FileSystem` artifact it emits with a data source windowed to the partition. Every offset below is relative to that window. It reads 4,096 bytes from offset 1024 in a short-read loop and requires at least 2,184 of them, because the highest field it uses sits at superblock offset 2180: the magic at 0, `log_blocksize` at 16 (which must be 12), `log_blocks_per_seg` at 20 (at most 30), `nat_blkaddr` at 84, `root_ino` at 96 and `feature` at 2180. It then walks the tree from `root_ino`. A node id is resolved through the NAT directly: 9-byte entries, 455 to a 4 KiB block, the block chosen as the primary copy by `nat_entry_offset` with the checkpoint's `nat_bitmap` assumed all-zero, and the entry gathered with `read_full` so a windowed source's short read is not mistaken for a NAT miss. The node block is read whole with `read_exact_or_fail`. From an inode it takes `i_mode` at 0, `i_advise` at 2, `i_inline` at 3, `i_size` at 16, the three timestamps at 32/40/48 with their nanosecond halves at 56/60/64, `i_flags` at 80, and — only when `feature` bit `0x0008` (extra attributes) is set — `i_extra_isize` and `i_inline_xattr_size` at 360 and 362, clamped so the pointer array stays inside the block. `i_addr` begins at 360 plus the extra-attribute size and holds 923 slots less the extra words and, when `i_inline & 0x01`, the inline-xattr words; `i_nid[5]` sits at 4052 and is walked as two direct nodes, two single-indirect and one double-indirect, each node holding 1,018 addresses or node ids. Regular files with `i_inline & 0x02` hold their bytes inline from the second `i_addr` slot, at most `4 × (slots − 1)` bytes and never more than `i_size`; otherwise `i_size` rounded up to blocks is resolved to a run list, with a block address of 0 or `0xffffffff` recorded as a hole. Directories with `i_inline & 0x04` hold an inline dentry table whose geometry (entry count, bitmap size, reserved padding) is derived from the inline payload size as the kernel derives it; block directories are read one 4 KiB dentry block at a time — a 27-byte bitmap, 214 eleven-byte entries (hash, ino, name length, type) at offset 30, and 8-byte name slots at 2384 — visiting only set bitmap bits and advancing by the entry's slot count.

**Produces.** One `FileEntry` per inode reached from the root, the root itself included as `/`, every one parented to the `FileSystem` artifact rather than to its directory. Its metadata carries `name`, `path`, `parent_path`, `inode` (the node id), `size` (`i_size`, for directories too), `is_directory`, `mode` (the raw 16-bit `i_mode`) and `modified`, `changed`, `accessed` as RFC 3339 UTC strings with nanoseconds — an all-zero or out-of-range timestamp is written as the empty string, which the timeline projection in `seance_db` reads as not recorded. A regular file with inline data carries `resident_data_b64` and an in-memory data source of those bytes. Any other regular file carries `data_runs` — adjacent runs coalesced, serialised as `[offset | null, length]` pairs, at most 4,096 of them — and `data_runs_complete`, plus a `RunListDataSource` clamped to `i_size` so the last block's slack is never served; a `null` run is served as zeros. Where any node subtree could not be resolved the entry carries `content_incomplete: true` with `content_incomplete_reason: unresolved_structure`, and the subtree's logical span is held open as holes so every later block keeps its offset; a file over the 2,097,152-block (8 GiB) cap carries the pair with reason `cap_reached` instead, plus `file_blocks_mapped` and `file_blocks_total`. A directory reached a second time through a corrupt or cyclic graph is not emitted again: the path it was reached by is appended to `also_reached_at` on its first entry. An inode whose `i_advise` bit `0x04` is set carries `encrypted: true`, `content_ciphertext: f2fs_fscrypt` and, unless a reason was already stamped, the pair with reason `encrypted`; one whose `i_flags` bit `0x00000004` is set carries `compression_unsupported: f2fs` and the pair with reason `compressed`. A directory whose listing is a subset carries `directory_parse_incomplete: true` and `directory_parse_incomplete_reason` — `cap_reached` past 65,536 data blocks or 5,000,000 entries, `unresolved_structure` when its node tree would not resolve, `short_read` when a dentry block was past the end of the image or would not read whole. If any inode was dropped — a subtree past the depth cap, the file cap, or a name whose inode could not be read — the walk ends with one `ParsedRecord` of `type: f2fs_walk_status`, parented to the volume, carrying `walked: true`, `files_emitted`, `subtrees_past_depth_cap`, `file_cap_reached`, `unresolved_inodes`, and both `inventory_incomplete` and `content_incomplete` with the reason `cap_reached` where any cap fired and `unresolved_structure` otherwise. A superblock that fails its checks yields that record alone, with `walked: false`, `files_emitted: 0`, `superblock_error` holding the reason, and `inventory_incomplete` with reason `short_read` for a short superblock and `unresolved_structure` otherwise. The type name is the one the frontend's `walk_status` rule files under what could not be read. It emits no timeline events of its own: the three timestamps are projected onto the timeline by the `filesystem.mac_times` projection in `seance_db`, and the hasher digests the served content unless the ciphertext or compression markers tell it not to.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell whether the NAT block it read is the current one. F2FS keeps two copies of each NAT block and the live checkpoint's `nat_bitmap` says which is current; this parser never reads a checkpoint — `cp_blkaddr` is not even parsed — so it takes the primary copy always, consults no NAT journal, and on a volume that has been updated in place a node id can resolve to a stale block, which is then served as that file's content with no flag and a digest to match. Apart from one small `mkfs.f2fs` + `sload.f2fs` volume (`tests/fixtures/sload_f2fs.img.gz`) the tests in this crate are synthetic images built by `tests.rs`; no real Android volume is in the fixture set, so nothing in the tree measures how often that happens. It reads only the primary superblock at byte 1024 and does not try the backup copy in the next block. It reads only 4 KiB-block volumes. It decrypts nothing and decompresses nothing: an fscrypt inode's blocks are served as ciphertext behind the markers above, and the names in an encrypted directory are ciphertext bytes decoded lossily as UTF-8 with no marker on the name itself. It reads no `i_crtime`, so no `created` time is ever published; no uid, gid, link count, xattrs or project id; and it distinguishes only regular files and directories — a symlink, device node, FIFO or socket is emitted as an entry with no content and no target. It recovers nothing deleted: only set bits of a dentry bitmap are read, unset slots and the tail of a partly used block are never examined, orphan inodes are not sought, and there is no unallocated-space pass, so no deleted entry is recovered from directory slack. A hole is served as zeros and is indistinguishable from stored zeros. Its ceilings are 5,000,000 entries, a recursion depth of 100 (the 101st level is abandoned and counted), 2,097,152 blocks — 8 GiB — per file, 65,536 blocks per directory and 200,000 node reads per file; a file over the 8 GiB cap is served short, stamped `cap_reached`. The walk status carries no `name`. Nothing here is reconciled against the SIT, the checkpoint's valid-block counts, or `f2fs_super_block.block_count`.

**Refuses.** It refuses to parse a padded buffer as evidence, and every refusal below is a fail-closed read. An inode block, a node block or a dentry block that cannot be read in full is not parsed: a partial inode means the name that pointed at it is counted in `unresolved_inodes` and its subtree is dropped; a partial node block means the subtree it addresses is reserved as holes and the file stamped `content_incomplete`; a partial dentry block is skipped and the directory stamped `short_read`. It refuses to shift a file's later blocks leftward over a subtree it could not resolve, holding the span open instead so a surviving byte stays at its true offset. A NAT entry that cannot be read whole, a node block whose address lies past the end of the image, and an inode whose mode is zero are each treated as a node that could not be recovered, never as a node that does not exist. It refuses to serve or hash ciphertext or compressed clusters as plaintext without saying so: the `encrypted`, `content_ciphertext` and `compression_unsupported` markers and the `content_incomplete` pair are what make the hasher skip them. It refuses to present a capped or partly resolved walk as a complete inventory — the walk status exists for that — and refuses to let a run list truncated to 4,096 entries claim `data_runs_complete`. It refuses a `FileSystem` artifact with no data source with `InvalidInputFormat`, which the processing log folds as a skipped input; it declines, silently and by design, any volume the detector did not call F2FS; and it refuses a superblock whose magic is not `0xF2F52010`, whose `log_blocksize` is not 12, whose `log_blocks_per_seg` exceeds 30, or which reads short, on the record — the `walked: false` walk status above — rather than with an empty result that would read as a volume with no files.

### `plugin.fs.squashfs`

**Reads.** A SquashFS 4.0 image, recognised by its own bytes. It subscribes to `RawEvidence` and `FileEntry` artifacts — a standalone image file, or an image lying as a file inside another filesystem — with no name, extension or subtype gate, and to `FileSystem` artifacts whose `subtype` is `squashfs`, which `plugin.disk.filesystem_detector` emits for a partition whose first four bytes are `hsqs`; a `FileSystem` of any other subtype is declined. An artifact without a data source is declined in silence, and so is one whose first four bytes are not `hsqs`. The read length is the superblock's `bytes_used` rounded up to 4 KiB, or the source's size if smaller, so a volume inside a larger partition is read to its own end. An image larger than 4,294,967,296 bytes is not read at all. Anything smaller is pulled into memory whole, in a short-read loop that stops at the first zero-length read, and the buffer truncated to what arrived is what is parsed. From the 96-byte superblock it takes `inode_count` at 4, `block_size` at 12, `fragment_count` at 16, the compression id at 20, the version major and minor at 28 and 30, `root_inode_ref` at 32, `bytes_used` at 40, `id_table_start` at 48, `inode_table_start` at 64, `directory_table_start` at 72 and `fragment_table_start` at 80. The block size must be a power of two between 4,096 and 1,048,576 and the codec must be gzip (id 1). Two metadata regions are inflated eagerly: the inode table from `inode_table_start` to `directory_table_start`, and the directory table from `directory_table_start` to the least of `fragment_table_start`, `id_table_start` and `bytes_used`. Each region is a chain of metadata blocks with a 2-byte little-endian header whose top bit means stored and whose low fifteen bits are the on-disk size, each inflated to at most 8,192 bytes, the region as a whole to at most 512 MiB. The fragment table is `ceil(fragment_count / 512)` little-endian `u64` pointers, each to a metadata block of 16-byte entries (`start u64`, `size u32`, unused `u32`). From the root reference — `block_offset << 16 | offset_in_block` — it reads inodes of type 1 and 8 as directories, 2 and 9 as regular files and 3 as a basic symlink, treating every other type as an unnamed other. A directory listing is read from the declared size less three bytes: a 12-byte header (`count`, `start_block`, `inode_base`) then `count + 1` entries of `offset u16`, `inode delta i16`, `type u16`, `name_size u16` and `name_size + 1` name bytes, the child reference being `start_block << 16 | offset`. A file inode yields `blocks_start`, its fragment index, `block_offset`, `size` and its `block_sizes` array — `ceil(size / block_size)` entries with no fragment, `floor` with one — where the low 24 bits of each are the on-disk size and bit 24 says stored. File content is not read at walk time: each regular file at or under 268,435,456 bytes is given a `SquashFileSource` that, when read, locates block *n* by summing the on-disk sizes before it, inflates it alone under a ceiling of `block_size` and keeps the last eight in an LRU; an on-disk size of zero is served as a block of zeros; the tail fragment is inflated once from the fragment table entry and its `block_offset` applied.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` of `type: SquashFsVolume` parented to the input, with `subtype: filesystem`, `compression` (the Debug name of the codec), `block_size`, `inode_count` and `entry_count`. Then one `FileEntry` per entry the walk reached, the root directory itself excluded, each parented to the input and carrying `name`, `path` — relative to the image root with no leading slash, `docs/note.txt` — `is_directory`, `size` (0 for a directory or an other; the target length for a symlink), `mtime` and `modified` both holding the inode's raw 32-bit epoch seconds — or, where that is zero, neither of them and `mtime_not_recorded: true` instead — `filesystem: squashfs`, and `symlink_target` when the entry is a basic symlink. A regular file at or under 256 MiB has the lazy source attached, so the hasher, the carver, search and every parser that reads content see the inflated bytes; a larger file is metadata only. The integer `modified` is what the `filesystem.mac_times` projection in `seance_db` puts on the timeline, and the file grid sorts on it. Where the image cannot be read as SquashFS three things are said instead: an image over 4 GiB yields one `ParsedRecord` of `type: SquashFsSkipped` with `reason` and `size`; a superblock or metadata region that fails — an unsupported version, a codec other than gzip named as `unsupported compression: xz`, a block size out of range, a metadata block past the end or inflating past its ceiling — yields one `type: SquashFsError` record with `error` holding the message, which the frontend files under what could not be read; a source read error, or any failure inside the tree walk, returns `ParsingError` and produces nothing but a processing-log row. Nothing else is produced: no timeline events of its own, no ownership, no permissions, no inode numbers.

**Cannot.** It finds a SquashFS only where it begins a whole artifact or a partition the partition table names; one at another offset inside a partition, or behind a container the tree does not open (an Android sparse image, a dynamic `super` partition), is not found. It inflates only gzip; lzo, lzma, xz, lz4 and zstd are named and refused, and the `xz.sqfs` and `zstd.sqfs` fixtures pin that. It reads only version 4.0. It publishes no uid, gid, mode, inode number, link count or xattrs, and the format records no access or change time, so `mtime` is the only instant a file has. A zero there — what reproducible firmware builds routinely write — is published as not recorded, not as 1970-01-01; a nonzero instant is published raw, and one that is merely implausible is not questioned. An extended symlink (type 10), a device node, a FIFO or a socket is emitted as an ordinary entry with `is_symlink: false`, `size: 0` and no target. A hard link is two entries with nothing to say they share an inode. A file over 256 MiB carries no content and no marker saying content was withheld; the hasher then emits nothing for it, so it sits with blank hash columns and no `hash_skipped`, the state the orchestrator's own comment says must not exist. A `SquashFsSkipped` or `SquashFsError` record carries neither `content_incomplete` nor `inventory_incomplete`, so the incompleteness census does not count it, and `SquashFsSkipped` matches none of the frontend's category rules. The walk is all or nothing: one inode reference outside the table, one directory extending past its region, a nesting past 64 or a tree past 5,000,000 entries fails `entries()` as a whole, and every file already walked is discarded with it — the case receives no entry and no record, only the processing-log error. A source that delivers fewer bytes than it declares is parsed as the shorter image and nothing records the shortfall; what is missing surfaces, if at all, as a region-past-end error at open or at the first read of a file whose blocks lay beyond the cut. The whole image, up to 4 GiB, is resident in the worker's memory for the duration. The directory index of an extended directory, the entry's own `type` field and its inode delta are read past and not used. Its doc comments still describe a `SquashReader::read_file` that no longer exists.

**Refuses.** It refuses to reconstruct a file that would read as complete when it is not, and every ceiling below is the format's own maximum rather than a guess. A metadata block that inflates past 8,192 bytes, or is stored uncompressed and longer than that, is refused; so is a data or fragment block that inflates past `block_size` or is stored longer than it — the inflate is stopped one byte past the ceiling so exactly-at-limit and over-limit are told apart and nothing beyond is allocated. A metadata region that would grow past 512 MiB across its chain of blocks is refused rather than half loaded, because a half-loaded table resolves inode references to the wrong bytes. A fragment tail whose `block_offset + length` does not fit inside the inflated fragment block is refused at read time rather than returned short. Any region whose start or length overflows or lies past the end of the image is refused by name (`region extends past image end`, `metadata header past end`, `fragment index past end`). A fragment index outside the table, an inode reference outside the inode table, a directory reference outside the directory table, a root or child reference that does not resolve to a directory, a nesting deeper than 64 and a tree past 5,000,000 entries each refuse the walk. A block size of zero, or one that is not a power of two in [4 KiB, 1 MiB], is refused before anything divides by it; a version other than 4 is refused by number; a codec other than gzip is refused by name so the examiner learns the image needs a build with that codec, not that it held no files. A `fragment_count` of billions is not trusted for an allocation: the table reserves at most 65,536 entries and grows only as blocks actually exist. A block that inflates shorter than the offset a read needs stops that read rather than looping. And an artifact with no data source, or whose first four bytes are not `hsqs`, is declined without a record, as is an image whose superblock is shorter than 96 bytes yet opens with the magic — that one is a `SquashFsError`.

### `plugin.generic.sqlite_parser`

**Reads.** A SQLite database, chosen by its own bytes and never by its name. The module subscribes to `FileEntry`, `SystemArtifact` and `ParsedRecord` — a `ParsedRecord` is read only when it is a shadow-copy `VssPriorVersion`, every row recovered from which repeats the snapshot label, id and creation time and states that its sidecars were not searched — and declares `Stream`: it walks pages through `read_at` on the artifact's data source and makes no temporary copy and no driver connection. Two gates admit a file: the shared detector's exact `SQLite format 3\0` at offset 0, or this crate's own `looks_like_sqlite_source`, which reads the first 65,536 bytes and scans them byte by byte for that same 16-byte magic — so a database embedded in a larger file or carved at an offset is found and its offset published as `base_offset`, though a magic beginning in the last fifteen bytes of that window is past the scan — and then requires the 100-byte header to parse. The header is re-read as 4,096 bytes from `base_offset`. A signature that is not exact is tolerated on four grounds and each leaves its own warning on the record: fewer than sixteen bytes available at all; all sixteen zeroed; a fuzzy match differing in one to three bytes; or a signature that is none of those, where the page-1 b-tree type byte at index 100 is one of `0x0D`, `0x05`, `0x02`, `0x0A` **and** the page-size field is one of the eight common sizes — anything else is not read. The page size is the big-endian `u16` at offset 16, with `1` meaning 65,536, required to be a power of two in 512..=65,536; where it is not, it is inferred from the length of the buffer the header parser was handed — which this module caps at 4,096 bytes — against `[4096, 2048, 8192, 1024, 16384, 32768, 65536, 512]`, taking the first that divides that length exactly and otherwise the first that fits. The reserved-space byte at 20 gives the usable size, from which the leaf payload bounds are derived as the file format does (`usable - 35` and `((usable - 12) * 32 / 255) - 23`). The schema comes from walking the `sqlite_master` b-tree at page 1 and reading each five-column row as type, name, `tbl_name`, `rootpage` and SQL, with column names extracted from the `CREATE TABLE` text by paren-depth splitting, skipping `CONSTRAINT`/`PRIMARY`/`UNIQUE`/`FOREIGN`/`CHECK` clauses. Every table with a root page above zero is then walked depth-first to a depth of 100, each physical page visited once, interior-table cells followed by their four-byte child pointers and the rightmost pointer at header offset 8; a cell is a payload-length varint, a rowid varint and a record whose header names its serial types, with an overflow chain followed through each page's leading four bytes, cycle-guarded, when the payload exceeds the local maximum. Recovery then runs from six labelled sources. Over every page including a trailing partial one — and only where that page is a leaf-table or interior-table page, an index page being carved not at all — a live-allocation map is built from the page header, the cell-pointer array and each live cell's extent; the freeblock chain is walked from the two-byte head at content offset +1, cycle-guarded; record-shaped runs are then carved from bytes outside that map (payload length above zero and under 16,384, a clean decode with no corruption note, no overlap with a live cell) and labelled **freeblock** where the run begins inside a freeblock and otherwise by the page's own origin — **unallocated** on a live page, **freelist** on a freelist page; each freeblock body not already claimed is put through the header-realignment reconstructor, which skips up to 12 residual bytes looking for the alignment at which the surviving serial-type header and its column bodies consume the region *exactly*, at most 40 columns, accepted only with two or more non-null columns, at least one convincingly textual, and no control or replacement byte inside a text column; and what is still unclaimed is scanned for runs of five or more bytes in `0x20..=0x7E`, labelled **freeblock** or **slack** by where the run began. The freelist is walked from the trunk head at header offset 32 for as long as fewer leaves have been gathered than the count declared at offset 36, and each freelist page is first re-parsed as an intact leaf-table page — SQLite does not zero freed pages without `secure_delete` — and only carved when that yields nothing, labelled **freelist**. A `-wal` and a `-journal` are located by **name** beside the database, from the artifact's `source_path` or the source's underlying path, and failing that as a sibling through the data source itself so a database and its log inside one container are still paired; each is staged up to 512 MiB. The WAL is read as a 32-byte header — magic `0x377F0682` or `0x377F0683`, page size at offset 8 — and a run of 24-byte frame headers each carrying a page number, a commit-marking database size and two salts; a zeroed magic or a zeroed page size is recovered from the database's own page size. The rollback journal is read as a 28-byte header, sector size at 20 (a power of two no greater than 65,536, else 512) and page size at 24, with records starting at the first sector boundary and each being a page number, a page image and a four-byte checksum; a zero page number is treated as padding and resynchronised to the next sector boundary within one sector, and a page number above 4,000,000 stops the walk. Each WAL frame and each journal pre-image is decoded as a leaf-table page in its own right, labelled **wal** or **journal**. Finally, on a schema declaring both a `message` and a `handle` table, up to 512 MiB of the file from `base_offset` is read into memory and scanned for `streamtyped` signatures, each decoded through the shared Apple typedstream extractor over an 8,192-byte window, recovering iMessage bodies of two characters or more from `attributedBody` blobs that the record carver never reconstructs cleanly.

**Produces.** One `SqliteRow` `ParsedRecord` per row, live or recovered, parented to the database artifact, carrying the table name where one is known, the rowid where one survived, the 1-based page the bytes were found on — 0 on a body recovered from a raw `attributedBody` blob, which belongs to no page — `deleted`, the `recovery_source` as one of `freeblock`, `freelist`, `unallocated`, `slack`, `wal` or `journal`, a `confidence` from 0 to 100, the decoded columns as a name-to-value map, the decoder's own `corruption_notes`, and the database's identity — its name, its artifact id and its path — so a "message" table in a case of many databases is attributable. Values are published as the record encoded them: integers, floats, text, NULL, and blobs as full base64 at 256 bytes or under and otherwise as a 64-byte (128-character) hex preview with the true size and `truncated: true`. Confidence starts at 100 and is reduced by 15 for each corruption note, by 20 where more than half the columns are NULL or 10 where more than a quarter are, and by the source — slack 35, unallocated 30, freelist 20, freeblock 15, journal 15, WAL 10 — so a slack salvage cannot present itself with the authority of a live read. One `SqliteDatabaseForensics` summary per database carries the page size, the page count derived from the readable length, the text encoding as decoded, whether the signature was clean, the `base_offset` the database was found at, the table list, the full schema with each object's type, `tbl_name`, root page, column names and SQL, the live, deleted and carved row counts, the freelist page count, whether a WAL and a journal were present and how many frames each held, how many records were emitted, and every warning the header, WAL and journal parsers raised. Those three row counts are not a census of the emission: a row recovered from the WAL is counted in none of them, and a freelist row re-parsed from an intact page counts as deleted but not as carved, so they do not sum to `records_emitted`. Where the emission cap fired, the summary carries `records_truncated` alongside `inventory_incomplete`, `content_incomplete`, `content_incomplete_reason: cap_reached`, `max_records` and a sentence saying the rows not emitted are absent from this result and not from the database — before that it carried only the bespoke key, which the API and export honesty paths never read, and a capped recovery presented as the whole of what the database held. Where the source could not deliver the last byte of the size it declares, the summary carries `source_short_read`, `content_incomplete`, `content_incomplete_reason: short_read` and a sentence naming the byte count, because this parser never buffers the file and so had nothing else to compare against. Where a sidecar could not be staged whole it carries `sidecar_truncated`, the reason as `cap_reached` or `short_read`, and a sentence saying the page versions past that point were not searched, so rows that lived only there look like rows that never existed. On the four chat schemas — iMessage `chat.db` (a `message` plus a `handle` table), WhatsApp iOS (`ZWAMESSAGE`), WhatsApp Android (`messages`/`message` plus one of eight `msgstore` marker tables) and Android SMS (`sms`) — recovered rows **that carry a table** are threaded into `chat_message` records the conversation viewer renders — attribution, not recovery, is the condition, so an orphaned freelist row is published as a row and threaded into nothing, typed `iMessage`, `WhatsApp` or `AndroidSms`: the body, the correspondent resolved through the surviving `handle`, `jid` and `chat` rows, the thread key published as `chat_identifier`, `conversation_id` and `contact_jid` so each viewer groups on the field it reads, the direction, and the provenance — `recovered: true` always, `deleted` only where the row really was deleted, the recovery source, the confidence, and the source table and rowid. Timestamps on those records are decoded and stated as whole Unix seconds in `date`, with the full-precision instant beside it in `date_ns` as Unix nanoseconds when there is a fraction to carry: an iMessage `date` integer is seconds since 2001 at or below a threshold of 1,000,000,000,000 and nanoseconds since 2001 above it, both shifted by the Cocoa epoch of 978,307,200; a Core Data `ZMESSAGEDATE` REAL is seconds since 2001 with its fraction preserved; an Android `timestamp` or `date` is milliseconds where its magnitude exceeds 1,000,000,000,000 and seconds otherwise. `date_ns` is what reaches `timeline_events.timestamp_subsec_nanos`, and only where its own whole-second part agrees with `date`; it is the only thing that orders two recovered messages inside one second, since a recovered row has no live b-tree position to fall back on. An `attributedBody` body, which carries no recovered timestamp at all, instead gets a monotonic `recovery_index` in file order so the viewer can present those deterministically rather than at random.

**Cannot.** **It cannot say that a recovered row was ever a row of the table it is filed under.** A carved row's table is the table whose live b-tree the walk found owning the page the bytes sat on — not the table the row was inserted into — so a page freed by one table and reused by another attributes its residue to the current owner, and where two walks reached one page the first table to reach it wins. A row recovered from the freelist carries **no table name at all**, and its columns are placeholders `c0, c1, …` — a rollback-journal row is now attributed through the same page-to-table map the WAL path uses, and says on the record that the attribution is an inference from the database as it is now, because the journal holds the page as it was before the transaction and a page reused since would be misattributed: on the freelist's intact-leaf path the count is the maximum observed across that page's rows, with a note stating the count and the percentage of rows that agreed; on the journal path and the freelist carve fallback the placeholders come with no such note and nothing says where the count came from. It cannot read a `WITHOUT ROWID` table, or any index: only page type `0x0D` yields rows, `0x05` yields child pointers, and the index pages such a table keeps its data in are neither walked nor carved — nor is any freeblock or slack byte on them, so that space is not recovered either, and no record says a table was skipped for that reason. It cannot read a view, a trigger or a virtual table's declared root, which is zero, and it cannot see a table whose `sqlite_master` row decoded to fewer than five values or to an empty name: that table is absent from the schema, its b-tree is never walked, and the summary does not say a schema row was unreadable. It cannot honour the database's declared text encoding: the field at header offset 56 is reported on the summary — as UTF-8 where the field was zero, which is this parser's default and not the database's statement — and never used; every TEXT value is instead decoded by a per-value heuristic, a UTF-16 byte-order mark or a zero-byte count over a quarter of the value's whole length taken from its first 100 bytes only, with the result over 80% printable, falling through to a lossy UTF-8 conversion otherwise, so a UTF-16 value of 200 bytes or more with no byte-order mark is always published as mojibake. It cannot salvage non-ASCII text from freed space: the slack and freeblock text pass keeps only runs of bytes in `0x20..=0x7E`, so a Cyrillic, CJK or emoji body that survived intact is not recovered as text. It cannot publish a record of more than 200 columns at all — such a cell is dropped with a corruption note and no values — and it does not carve the last ten bytes of any page. It cannot state a `SqliteRow`'s timestamp, or interpret any column as a date: a row's values are published exactly as encoded, an integer date column arrives as an integer, **nothing on a row record carries a zone or a rendered instant**, and no `SqliteRow` reaches the unified timeline at all — only the reconstructed `chat_message` records do, and only those of them that carry a date, so every `attributedBody` recovery is off the timeline entirely. Where it does decode a time, it decodes to Unix seconds and nanoseconds and offers no local offset, because none of these columns record one; a 0 or negative value is published as no date rather than as 1970 or 2001. **A recovered message proves a row existed in a file, not that a person sent or read one.** A WAL frame is a page version that was never checkpointed, not a deletion, and is marked `deleted: false` for that reason; a freeblock or slack recovery proves the bytes were there when the image was taken and says nothing about who put them there or when they were freed. It cannot tell two versions of one row apart beyond their bodies: a WAL reconstruction that repeats a live row's table, rowid and body is dropped as a duplicate, and one that keeps the rowid with a different body is kept as a change to that row — but the frame index and the commit flag are decoded and discarded, so a recovered row cannot be tied to a frame or to a transaction. The salts are read: a frame whose pair differs from the log header's was written before the last checkpoint or reset, every row from such a frame carries a note saying it is older than the live database, and the parse counts and states how many frames were in that position — what it still cannot do is say which generation a frame belongs to beyond current-or-earlier, or order two earlier generations. It cannot decide which of two identical WAL rows is which: the cross-frame de-duplication keys on the decoded values alone, with no table, page or rowid, so two distinct rows anywhere in the log carrying the same values collapse into one. It cannot keep a WAL row through the emission cap: WAL rows are counted in neither the live nor the deleted census and carry `deleted: false`, so the cap's sort treats them as live and they are the first rows discarded. It cannot recover a coalesced freeblock holding more than one record — that is deliberately not attempted and the region falls back to text salvage — and it cannot restore a deleted record's leading columns at all: a freeblock header overwrites them, so a reconstruction is right-aligned onto the table's **trailing** columns and the rowid-alias and anything before the clobber boundary are gone. It cannot thread a freelist-recovered or journal-recovered chat row into a conversation, because those rows carry no table name and the conversation reconstructor selects by table. It cannot attribute a bare `message` or `messages` table to WhatsApp without one of eight `msgstore` marker tables, because a `message` table is not evidence of WhatsApp; a Signal marker suppresses the WhatsApp Android and Android SMS branches, but not the iMessage or WhatsApp iOS ones, which are selected by their own table sets. It cannot recover a message body shorter than four characters or holding fewer than three letters through the generic path, nor one shaped like an identifier — an unbroken hex-alphabet run carrying a digit or a separator — though a body that breaks into whitespace-separated tokens or is a bare URL is admitted whatever its letter ratio, which is the fix for the phone numbers, addresses and links that a 50% letter test had been silently dropping . It cannot recover an `attributedBody` body that matches any text value on any live row of the database, or one under two characters: both are dropped before they reach a record. It cannot count two identical messages twice: reconstructions sharing a thread key and a body are collapsed to one. It cannot bound an embedded database's extent: where the magic was found at a non-zero offset, the database is assumed to run to the end of the containing source, so the page count over-reports and the carve walks bytes beyond it. It cannot compare what the database declares against what was recovered — the header's own page count at offset 28, its change counter, its `largest_root_page`, its schema format, its auto-vacuum mode and its writer's version number are all decoded and published nowhere. Its ceilings, every one real: 50,000 records emitted per database; 512 MiB staged per `-wal` or `-journal`; 512 MiB read into memory and scanned for `attributedBody` blobs, in 8,192-byte windows; 65,536 bytes scanned for a displaced magic; 4,096 bytes of header read, which is also the length the page-size guess is made against; 16,384 bytes of carved payload; 200 columns in a record and 40 in a carved or reconstructed one; a b-tree depth of 100; 12 skipped bytes in a freeblock realignment; a five-byte minimum salvaged text run; the freelist's own declared leaf count; a journal page number of 4,000,000; and 256 bytes of blob published inline, above which 64 bytes of hex preview and the true size are all that is kept.

**Refuses.** It refuses to fire on a name. The gate is content only, and a file that is not a database — or whose header is damaged past the four tolerated cases — produces no artifact rather than an empty database. It refuses to read past a page it cannot make sense of: a clobbered page costs that page and not the file, which is what lets a database with page 2 destroyed still return the rows on page 3, and no input of any length or fill has ever been allowed to panic the reader — that is asserted directly, because the orchestrator catches a panic and a caught panic is a silent absence. It refuses to accept a page size it cannot establish: where neither the header field nor the inference from the bytes read yields one, the database is refused outright. It refuses to publish a carved record on a guess. A candidate must decode with no corruption note, must not overlap a live cell, must hold between two and forty values of which at least two are non-null and at least one is convincingly textual, and must not be more than half NULL; a freeblock reconstruction must consume its region exactly and must not put a control or replacement byte inside a text column — the signature of an alignment that split a field mid-value — and where nothing fits, the region is published as salvaged text rather than as a confident wrong split. It refuses to invent a date: a zero or negative Cocoa, Core Data or Android timestamp is published as no date, never as 2001-01-01 or 1970-01-01, and a recovered `attributedBody` body with no timestamp is published undated with a recovery index rather than with a borrowed one. It refuses to attribute a row to an app it cannot identify — a Signal store, or a generic `messages` table with no WhatsApp marker, is left as loose recovered rows, because a row published under the wrong service name puts an examiner's conclusion on the wrong app. It refuses to drop a WAL row because its body appears somewhere live: the duplicate test is table, rowid and body together, since matching any live text anywhere deleted real uncheckpointed messages whose bodies happened to equal a common phrase, another chat's message, or a live handle string; a recovered row with no rowid cannot be proven a duplicate and is kept, on the reasoning that a visible flagged duplicate is recoverable by an examiner and a silently dropped message is not. It refuses to let a live table crowd the deleted rows out of a capped result: the cap stable-sorts deleted rows to the front before truncating, so on a database with 300 live rows and a 50-record cap the kept set is recovered rows — a WAL row, which is not deleted, gets no such protection. It refuses a WAL whose magic is neither valid value nor zeroed, by number, and stops a journal walk at an implausible page number rather than reading misaligned bytes as a page. And it refuses to present any shortfall as a complete answer — a cap reached, a sidecar staged short, a source that cannot reach its own declared end — each is stamped with the shared `content_incomplete` pair and a sentence saying in words what is missing from the result and not from the database. The one thing it does not refuse cleanly: a database that was detected and then would not parse yields a parsing error in the case's processing log and **no record at all**, which on the case is indistinguishable from a database that held nothing.

### `plugin.hash.file_hasher`

**Reads.** The attached content of every `FileEntry` that enters the pipeline, and nothing else — it does not subscribe to `FileContent`, `RawEvidence` or `ParsedRecord`. It declines in silence an entry whose metadata `is_directory` is `true` and one with no data source at all. Before reading a byte it reads the parent's honesty markers: `encrypted: true`, `efs_encrypted: true` or a non-null `content_ciphertext` mean the bytes are ciphertext; a non-null `compression_unsupported` means they are clusters no parser could inflate; and, as the fallback contract every producer writes, `content_incomplete: true` with a `content_incomplete_reason` that parses to `encrypted` or `compressed` — any other reason, `unmapped` or `cap_reached` or `short_read`, does not stop the hash, because a sparse file's zeros really are its content. It then takes the source's declared `size()` and, if that is at most 2,147,483,648 bytes, streams the content once through a `SourceCursor` in 1 MiB buffers — a reader thread and a hashing thread ping-ponging two buffers — computing MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 in that single pass and counting the bytes the source actually delivered. It reads nothing from disk directly, has no path, and reads no stored or expected hash to compare against.

**Produces.** Exactly one `ParsedRecord` of `type: file_hash` per file it accepts, parented to the `FileEntry`, and that record is never persisted: the orchestrator intercepts every produced artifact whose metadata `type` is `file_hash`, buffers it, and on the writer's flush applies it to the parent, retrying while the parent is not yet persisted — for at most `MAX_HASH_APPLY_ATTEMPTS`, 60 tries, about 30 s at the 500 ms flush cadence; past that it logs an `EVIDENCE LOSS` error and writes a processing-log row against the file — this module's id, status `error` — whose message carries the three digests, or the `hash_skipped` reason, and says they were not stored on the file. The outcome is then held in memory, keyed by the file's artifact id and case, for up to `MAX_LATE_HASHES` (65,536) files: when the writer saves a batch holding that file's record, the held digests or skip stamp are merged into the record and written by the same insert, in the same transaction, and a second processing-log row (status `complete`) says the earlier error row is superseded. A give-up past the cap is not held, the store lives only as long as the orchestrator run, and a record that never arrives is never written; in each of those cases the error row is the only record of the digests. With all three digests present the parent's `md5_hash`, `sha1_hash` and `sha256_hash` columns are set and `md5`, `sha1`, `sha256` — lowercase hex — are merged into its metadata, scoped by case id so a corrupt parent id cannot write digests onto another case's evidence; hash-set matching, the known/notable counts and the report read those columns. Without digests the record carries `hash_skipped` with one of four reasons and the orchestrator marks the parent instead: `size` (the source is over 2 GiB; `size` is carried), `short_read` (the source delivered fewer bytes than it declared; `size` and `bytes_hashed` are carried), `encrypted` or `compressed` (from the markers above; `size` carried). The DB then stamps the parent with `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason: hash_skipped_<reason>` and `hash_skipped: <reason>`, so a file with blank hash columns always says why; a `file_hash` record that somehow carries neither digests nor a reason is applied as `unrecorded`. An empty file is hashed — `d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e` — not skipped. A directory, and an entry with no data source, produce nothing at all. It writes no timeline events and no artifacts an examiner can open; the file's own row is where its work shows.

**Cannot.** It cannot say anything about a file it was never given content for. An entry with no data source — a file over a filesystem parser's content cap, a metadata-only entry, an inline file whose bytes did not fit — is skipped without a record, so the parent keeps blank hash columns and no `hash_skipped`, which is exactly the state the orchestrator's interceptor comment says must not exist for a file that was hashed and matched nothing. Nor can it distinguish that from a file whose read failed: an I/O error mid-stream is returned as `IoError`, the module's row in the processing log says `error`, and again the parent carries no marker. It cannot verify: it compares against no stored, container-recorded or previously computed hash; a second run over the same evidence overwrites the columns and nothing records that the values agreed. It hashes what the parser served, so a run list that resolves stale blocks, a hole served as zeros, or a compressed cluster the parser inflated wrongly all digest cleanly — the markers it honours are the parser's, and a parser that attached ciphertext without setting them gets a ciphertext digest filed as the file's. The 2 GiB ceiling is fixed at registration; `with_max_bytes` exists for tests only, so a 3 GiB video on a real exhibit is never hashed by this module. The parent-side stamping has two costs of its own: a fully readable file over 2 GiB is marked `content_incomplete: true`, though its content is complete and only the digest is absent; and the parser's own `content_incomplete_reason` — `encrypted`, `compressed`, `unresolved_structure` — is overwritten with `hash_skipped_encrypted` and the like, strings that `IncompleteReason::from_str` does not parse, so a consumer gating on the parsed reason, such as the content resolver's ciphertext check where the pair was the only marker, no longer sees it (noted at the time in the changelog, not in the defect register). It computes no CRC-32, SHA-512, ssdeep, TLSH or perceptual hash — those are other modules' work — and it does not hash `FileContent` artifacts such as decoded spans, alternate views, or the volume, partition and unallocated-space artifacts. It cannot tell a source that delivered more than it declared: only a shortfall is checked. And its record is invisible by design, so an examiner cannot find the `file_hash` artifact in the tree; the digest, or the reason there is none, must be read off the file.

**Refuses.** It refuses to record a digest that is not the digest of the file's own bytes, and each of its four refusals exists because the alternative was a wrong hash in the same columns as a right one. Content a parser declared opaque — ciphertext behind fscrypt, EFS or btrfs encryption, or clusters nobody could inflate — is not streamed at all; the record says `encrypted` or `compressed` and the hash columns stay blank rather than hold a digest of ciphertext that a known-file lookup would report as a non-match. A source that stops short of its own declared size is refused after the fact: the digests it computed are thrown away and `short_read` recorded with the byte count, because a digest of a partial read would look authoritative and a later re-hash of the same truncated view would falsely verify. A source over 2 GiB is refused before a byte is read, with `size`, rather than hashed to a cap and presented as whole. And a `file_hash` record with no parent id is refused by the orchestrator — logged as an error naming the record and dropped — because a digest that cannot be attributed to a file must not be attributed to one by accident. Everything else it declines — directories, entries without content — it declines without a word, which is the gap named above.

### `plugin.ios.calendar_db`

**Reads.** iOS's Calendar and Reminders store, `Calendar.sqlitedb`, selected by basename and magic through the crate's shared front end `with_db`: it subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, lower-cases the last path segment of the artifact's `name` and acts only on exactly `calendar.sqlitedb`; a directory entry or an artifact with no data source yields nothing. The first 16 bytes are read with a looping `read_full` and must be `SQLite format 3\0`, else the file is passed over in silence. The file is spilled by `TempDb::spill` under a 1 GiB cap (`MAX_DB_BYTES`) with its `-wal` sibling where the source can open one, and the copy opened read-only. `probe_table` must list `CalendarItem`. Two fixed statements are run, both `CalendarItem` LEFT JOINed to `Calendar` on `calendar_id`: `SELECT ci.summary, ci.description, ci.start_date, ci.end_date, ci.all_day, c.title … ORDER BY ci.start_date` for events, and `SELECT ci.summary, ci.due_date, ci.completion_date, ci.priority, c.title … WHERE ci.start_date IS NULL ORDER BY ci.due_date` for reminders, which share the table as rows with no start date, after `probe_columns` has listed `CalendarItem`. `completion_date` is the column's name on the one real store held (the Magnet 2022 iPhone 8, iOS 15). No column map is used and no row limit applies. Every date column is a REAL of Cocoa seconds since 2001-01-01, converted with its fraction; 0, a negative, a non-finite value or one that would overflow is "unset".

**Produces.** One `CalendarEvent` (`subtype: "calendar_event"`, `source: "Calendar.sqlitedb"`) per `CalendarItem` row with a non-NULL `start_date`, in the iCalendar plugin's shape so the existing calendar viewer renders it: `summary`, `description`, `calendar_name` (the joined `Calendar.title`), `all_day` as a boolean (JSON `null` when NULL), `dtstart` and `dtend` as RFC 3339 strings rendered to the nanosecond, and `date` in whole Unix seconds with `date_ns` beside it when the store recorded a fraction; a start that decodes as unset yields a record with no `dtstart` and no `date`. One `Reminder` (`subtype: "reminder"`, `source: "Calendar.sqlitedb"`) per row with a NULL `start_date`: `title` (the summary, else the literal `Reminder`), `due` and `due_ns` when set, `completed` as a boolean true only when `completion_date` decodes to a real instant (a raw 0 is not completed), `completed_date`/`completed_date_ns` when it does, `priority` only when non-zero (iOS uses 0 for none), `calendar_name`, and `name` the title. After each walk, a `RowsUndecodable` marker under `CalendarEventIncomplete` or `ReminderIncomplete` (`subtype: parse_incomplete`, `source_table: "CalendarItem"`, `rows_dropped`, `records_recovered`, `first_error`, both incompleteness pairs with reason `unresolved_structure`) when the engine refused to step a row. A reminders statement that would not prepare or run yields one `ReminderIncomplete` record with `status: "DatabaseUnreadable"`, `source_table: "CalendarItem"`, SQLite's message as `sqlite_error`, both pairs and `records_recovered: 0` (a column list that would not read, `StoreUnreadable`) beside the events. Last, one `CalendarSummary` (`platform: "iOS"`, `source`, `source_table`, `events`, `event_rows_undecodable`, `reminders` — `null` when the reminders statement did not run, never 0 — `reminders_status` `read` or `query_did_not_run`, `records_recovered`, `name`) for every store whose `CalendarItem` was walked, zeros included, so a present and empty table is a record . A `Calendar.sqlitedb` carrying the SQLite header that could not be staged or opened yields one `IosArtifactParseStatus` record with `status: "DatabaseUnreadable"`, both pairs under `unresolved_structure` and the error. A readable catalogue holding none of the tables this reader is built on yields one `IosArtifactParseStatus` with `status: "ExpectedTableAbsent"`, `expected_tables`, both pairs under `unresolved_structure`, `records_recovered: 0` and a sentence saying this is not a schema this reader knows — not a finding that the device held none; a catalogue that would not read, and a fixed `SELECT` that would not prepare or run, each yield one `DatabaseUnreadable` record naming SQLite's error. Every record from a short-staged or WAL-refused copy is stamped `content_incomplete: true` with its reason and one `SqliteSpillIncomplete` marker is appended, even when nothing parsed. No timeline event of its own.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell you where an event was, who was invited, whether it repeats, or in which time zone it was entered: `Location`, `Participant`, `Recurrence`, `Alarm`, `Attachment`, `ExceptionDate`, `ci.location_id`, `ci.time_zone`, `ci.unique_identifier`, `ci.status`, `ci.availability` and `ci.creation_date`/`last_modified` are not read, so a recurring event appears once at its first occurrence and an all-day event's local date depends on a zone the record does not carry. It cannot read a generation that renamed a column of its fixed event `SELECT`: there is no column map, so that store is reported `DatabaseUnreadable` rather than read for what remains; the reminders `SELECT` is fixed the same way, so a generation without `due_date`, `completion_date` or `priority` has its reminders reported unread, not read in part. On the one real store held no `CalendarItem` row has a NULL `start_date`, so the reminder mapping has been checked against real data for its column names only, not a real reminder. It cannot distinguish a reminder from an untimed event with no start date: every NULL-start row is emitted as a `Reminder`. It cannot say a reminder was deleted. It has no row cap. It recovers no deleted rows and reads no `-journal` sibling.

**Refuses.** It refuses to file a store it recognised and could not stage or open as a device with no calendar, emitting `DatabaseUnreadable` with both incompleteness pairs. It refuses to read a short probe as "not SQLite". It refuses to place an unset Cocoa date at 2001-01-01: a 0 or negative `start_date`, `end_date`, `due_date` or `completion_date` writes nothing, and a reminder with a raw 0 completion date is not marked complete. It refuses to drop the fraction a REAL column records, publishing `_ns` beside the seconds and rendering the string to the nanosecond so the two cannot disagree. It refuses to report a priority of 0 as a priority. It refuses to let a row the engine would not step vanish, counting it into the `RowsUndecodable` marker. And it refuses to present a partially staged database as whole, stamping every record and an empty result with the spill's incompleteness.

### `plugin.ios.healthkit`

**Reads.** HealthKit's sample store, `healthdb_secure.sqlite`, with the source name resolved from `healthdb.sqlite` beside it, selected by basename and magic through the crate's shared front end `with_db`: it subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, lower-cases the last path segment of the artifact's `name` and acts on exactly `healthdb_secure.sqlite`; a directory entry or an artifact with no data source yields nothing. The first 16 bytes are read with a looping `read_full` and must be `SQLite format 3\0`. The file is spilled by `TempDb::spill` under a 1 GiB cap with its `-wal` sibling where the source can open one, and the copy opened read-only. `probe_table` must list both `samples` and `objects`. `PRAGMA user_version` is compared through the shared `check_schema_version` with the single-point range `15043..=15043`, the generation validated (iOS 15.0.2, 19A404, the Magnet 2022 iOS 15 device). The neighbour is asked for only when the source can open siblings: `healthdb.sqlite` is opened relative to the artifact, spilled under the same cap, and its `sources` (`ROWID, name, bundle_id, product_type`) and `source_devices` (`ROWID, name, manufacturer, model, hardware, firmware, software, localIdentifier`) read into maps; each step that fails leaves a named resolution (`source_cannot_open_neighbours`, `sibling_not_found`, `sibling_not_staged`, `sibling_not_opened`, `sibling_has_no_sources_table`). `metadata_values JOIN metadata_keys` is read into a per-object map under a 2,000,000-row cap (`MAX_METADATA_ROWS`). Samples are walked by one fixed statement joining `samples` to `objects` on `data_id`, LEFT JOINed to `data_provenances` (product type, build, iOS version, `tz_name`, `source_id`, `device_id`, local product and build), `quantity_samples` (`quantity`, `original_quantity`, `original_unit`), `category_samples` (`value`) and `unit_strings`, `ORDER BY s.start_date DESC, s.data_id DESC LIMIT` one past the 500,000-sample cap (`MAX_HEALTH_SAMPLES`). Dates are Cocoa REALs converted with their fraction. The census — `count(*) GROUP BY data_type`, the total, `objects.type = 2` and the deleted-sample join — is taken over the whole table, not the capped walk. On the iOS 15 schema both deleted counts are answered from the partial index `objects_deleted`, so a damaged index page can fail them while the walk still reads.

**Produces.** One `HealthSample` (`subtype: "health_sample"`, `platform: "iOS"`, `source: "healthdb_secure.sqlite"`) per sample, newest first, up to 500,000: `data_id`, `data_type` as the integer the file holds, and — for exactly three types, 7 `step_count`, 8 `distance_walking_running`, 12 `flights_climbed` — `data_type_name` with `data_type_name_basis: "asserted"`, because those meanings are corroborated by the value shapes on the device held (131 whole-numbered type-7 samples 2..958 summing to 21,285 over a month; type 12 integer 1..8; type 8 running 0.96..682.83 beside the steps), and `data_type_name_unknown: true` for every other type; `start`, `date`, `end` and `created` in Unix seconds with `_ns` and a `_source` naming the column and its 2001 epoch; `duration_seconds` when the end is not before the start; `quantity` with `unit` from `unit_strings` or `unit_not_recorded: true` (that table is empty on the device held, so every quantity says so and none is given HealthKit's canonical unit for a guessed type); `original_quantity`, `category_value`, `deleted` (`objects.type` is 2), `object_type`, `uuid` as hex, `origin_product_type`, `origin_build`, `origin_os_version`, `recording_timezone` (the valuable one), `local_product_type`, `local_build`; `source_id` with `source_name`, `source_bundle_id`, `source_product_type` when the neighbour resolved it, else `source_name_unresolved: true` with the reason (`source_id_not_in_sources` or the resolution named above); `device_id` with `source_device` and a `source_device_join` sentence saying the match on `source_devices.ROWID` is an inference the file does not declare, or `source_device_unresolved_reason` (`device_id_not_in_source_devices` when the table was read and does not hold the id, else the device resolution that failed, such as `sibling_source_devices_query_did_not_run`); `metadata` as a key→value map (string, number, a dated object naming its Cocoa source, or `{data_bytes, decoded: false}`), or `metadata_unread: true` with `metadata_unread_reason` when the metadata join did not run; and a `name` of `Health <type name or "data_type N">: <quantity>`. Then a `HealthSampleIncomplete` `CapReached` marker (`max_entries: 500000`, `rows_read`, `content_incomplete` pair with reason `cap_reached`) when the walk stopped, and a `RowsUndecodable` marker when any row would not decode. Before the samples, one shared `ParserStaleWarning` schema record (`app: "HealthKit healthdb_secure.sqlite"`, `subtype: "parser_stale"`, `supported_range`, `schema_version_locator: "user_version"`, `validated_against` naming the Magnet 2022 iPhone 8 file, `message`, `detail` and `name`) unless the version is inside `15043..=15043`: `status: SchemaOutsideValidated` with `seen_schema_version` and no incompleteness claim (a disclosure) for any other recorded version; `SchemaVersionNotRecorded` with `schema_version_recorded: false` and no incompleteness claim for a `PRAGMA user_version` of 0; `SchemaVersionUndetermined` with `schema_version_detail` and the content pair (reason `unresolved_structure`) for a pragma that would not read. Then one `HealthKitSummary` (`samples` walked, `sample_rows` in the table, `data_type_histogram_status` — `counted` with `data_type_histogram` over the whole table, `partial` with the rows read before the census failed kept in `data_type_histogram` and `data_type_histogram_query_error`, or `query_did_not_run` with `data_type_histogram_query_error` — `named_data_types`, `unnamed_data_types`, `data_type_names_basis` in words, `deleted_samples` and `deleted_objects` (the second counts every deleted object, sample or not, published apart), `deleted_samples_basis` (`whole_table`, or `walked_samples` when the join would not run, with `deleted_samples_census_error` and `deleted_samples_is_lower_bound` — true when the walk was capped or dropped a row), `deleted_objects_census_error` in place of `deleted_objects` when that count would not run, `samples_walk_failed` with an `inventory_incomplete_detail` sentence and a name reading `sample walk failed, N read` when a sample row failed — the walk sorts before it returns a row, so a failure can cost rows on either side of it — row counts or `_table_absent` flags for `workouts`, `workout_events`, `category_samples`, `sleep_schedule_samples`, `unit_strings`, `data_provenances`, `ecg_samples`, `location_series_data` — a count that would not read is neither: it is named in `lookup_failures` (as is a `sample_rows` count or a histogram that did not complete), which also stamps the summary `content_incomplete` with reason `unresolved_structure` and a `content_incomplete_detail`, and the display name then says `workouts not counted` rather than `workouts table absent` — `workouts_decoded: false`, `sleep_decoded: false`, an `undecoded_detail` sentence, `metadata_status` (`read`, `tables_absent` or `query_did_not_run`) with `metadata_rows` and `metadata_rows_capped`/`metadata_cap` at the cap, `metadata_tables_absent`, or `metadata_query_error`, `source_name_resolution`, `sources_rows`, `sources_query_error`, `source_device_resolution`, `source_device_rows`, `source_devices_query_error`, `schema_version`, `records_recovered`, and `inventory_incomplete: true` with reason `cap_reached` or `unresolved_structure` when capped, lossy or metadata-capped). A store whose sample statement will not prepare or run — a generation missing a column — yields one `IosArtifactParseStatus` `DatabaseUnreadable` record with both pairs and SQLite's error; one that could not be staged or opened yields the same. Every record from a short-staged or WAL-refused copy is stamped `content_incomplete: true` with its reason and one `SqliteSpillIncomplete` marker is appended.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell you what most samples measure: `samples.data_type` is Apple's private enum, its meaning is not in the database and it moves between releases, so only three types are named — each marked asserted, not read — and the mobility types on the same device (182, 187, 188, 194) and every other type carry only their number. It cannot give a unit the file did not record: `unit_strings` was empty on the device held, so a `quantity` is a bare number with `unit_not_recorded` and no canonical unit is guessed from the type. It cannot decode a workout, a sleep sample, an ECG or a location series — those tables are counted and left unread because no held device has a row in them to check a decoder against — and it cannot read `category_samples` beyond the raw `value`. It cannot name a source unless the neighbour resolves: without `healthdb.sqlite`, or from a source that cannot open siblings, every sample says `source_name_unresolved` with which of the five reasons applies, and `source_cannot_open_neighbours` is not "not there". Its device join is an inference and is labelled as one. Its schema knowledge is one point (15043 from one iOS 15.0.2 device); the version check goes through the shared `check_schema_version`, which reads a `PRAGMA user_version` of 0 as not recorded rather than older, and a pragma that will not read as undetermined rather than in range; no column map exists, so a renamed column fails the fixed statement and the store is reported unreadable rather than by field. It cannot see past the five-hundred-thousandth most recent sample, though the histogram and totals on the summary are over the whole table. A metadata `data_value` blob is measured, not decoded. It does not read `healthdb.sqlite`'s own `sources` beyond the four columns, nor `healthdb_secure.hfd`, nor the `ACHAchievements` or `activity_caches` tables. It recovers no deleted rows beyond the objects HealthKit itself marks deleted.

**Refuses.** It refuses to name a data type it cannot corroborate from the file itself, publishing the number on every record and naming only three with `asserted` beside each, so an examiner never reads a private enum value as a fact HealthKit stated. It refuses to supply a unit the store did not record. It refuses to decode workouts, sleep, ECG and location series it has never seen a real instance of, counting their rows and saying so in words. It refuses to conflate "the neighbour is not there" with "the source could not look", naming the resolution on every unresolved sample and on the summary. It refuses to present the device join as declared when it is inferred. It refuses to take the census from the capped walk unannounced: the histogram, the total and both deleted counts are over the whole table, so the histogram is the truth even when the list is not all of it — except that when the deleted-sample join will not run, `deleted_samples` is the count the walk saw and `deleted_samples_basis: walked_samples` says so, with the error and whether the walk was whole; and a deleted-object count that will not run is not published, its error is . It refuses to present a store whose statement would not run as one with no samples. It refuses to place an unset Cocoa date at 2001-01-01 and refuses to drop the fraction a REAL records. It refuses to present a capped, lossy or metadata-capped walk as whole, stating the cap and the reason. And it refuses to present a partially staged store as whole, stamping every record with the spill's incompleteness.

### `plugin.ios.notes`
