**Reads.** The two property lists that answer what machine a Mac is, recognised by path. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent`, takes `path` or, failing that, `name`, normalises backslashes and lowercases, and accepts the artifact only when that string ends with `/system/library/coreservices/systemversion.plist` or `/library/preferences/systemconfiguration/preferences.plist` — a suffix match, so a volume-UUID or mount prefix still resolves, and a path with no leading slash does not. A directory, and an entry with no data source, are declined. It then issues one `read_at` from offset 0 for the lesser of the declared size and 4,194,304 bytes and hands whatever that single call returned to `plist::Value::from_reader`, which reads XML and Apple binary property lists alike; the tests pin both. From `SystemVersion.plist` it takes the top-level strings `ProductName` as `os_name`, `ProductVersion` as `os_version` and `ProductBuildVersion` as `build_id`. From `preferences.plist` it follows three dictionary paths to a string: `System → Network → HostNames → LocalHostName` as `host_name`, `System → System → ComputerName` as `computer_name` and `System → System → HostName` as `dns_host_name`. A key that is absent, or whose value is not a string, contributes no fact.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per file, of `type: HostDeviceInfo` with `platform: macos`, parented to the file, with a `name` of `macOS version and build` or `macOS machine names`, `source_file` (the matched path), `source_kind` (`system_version_plist` or `system_configuration_preferences`), a `facts` object and a `fact_sources` object that names each fact's key — `ProductBuildVersion`, or the dotted dictionary path `System.Network.HostNames.LocalHostName`. The computer name a person typed and the local host name the network sees are two facts and are never collapsed into one; on the Magnet 2021 image they are `Eli’s Mac mini` and `Elis-Mac-mini`. The device-facts endpoint, `GET /api/v1/cases/:id/device_info`, fetches every `HostDeviceInfo` record, files this one under the platform the record itself names, and folds it beside the phones, so the System Info screen renders it without picking a winner where two files disagree. Where the single read was short of the declared size or the file was over 4 MiB but the bytes still parsed, the record carries `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason: short_read` and a `content_incomplete_detail` sentence with the byte count. Where the bytes do not parse as a property list, or parse and state none of the identity keys, a record with `subtype: identity_unread`, empty `facts`, `content_incomplete_reason: unresolved_structure` and a detail sentence saying which of those it was — and, when the read was short, that only so many of the file's bytes were acquired — is emitted so the one file that names the machine does not vanish from the summary. No timeline events, no hashes.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell the system's own identity from a copy of it: the suffix match claims a `SystemVersion.plist` inside a macOS installer package, a Time Machine backup, a second bootable volume or an iOS Simulator runtime as this machine's version, and only `source_file` distinguishes them. A Mac with two system volumes on one image yields two records and no reconciliation, by design. It reads three keys of `SystemVersion.plist` and no others — not `ProductUserVisibleVersion`, not `ProductVersionExtra` (the Rapid Security Response suffix), not `iOSSupportVersion`, not `ProductCopyright` — and three of `preferences.plist`, so the network services, locations and interface configuration that file also holds are not read here. It reads no serial number, hardware model, board id or UUID (none of which those files hold), no `/Library/Preferences/.GlobalPreferences.plist` locale or time zone, no user accounts (`/var/db/dslocal` is not read), no install date, no FileVault or SIP state, and no time at all — nothing reaches the timeline. The read is one `read_at`, not `read_full`, and the core I/O module says a single call may return fewer bytes than asked; on a windowed or container-backed source a fully readable plist can therefore be handed to the parser short, fail to parse — a binary plist keeps its trailer at the end — and be recorded as `identity_unread`, with a detail saying only part of the file was acquired when all of it was there. A plist over 4 MiB is cut at the cap and meets the same fate. Values are taken as the strings they are; nothing validates that a `ProductVersion` looks like a version. Where a key holds a non-string — an array, a number — the fact is simply absent and `fact_sources` does not say why. `FileContent` is subscribed to, but a decoded span carries a generated name rather than an identity path, so none matches in practice.

**Refuses.** It refuses to pass over the file that names the machine. A property list at either path that will not parse, or that parses and states none of the keys the identity is kept under, is recorded as `identity_unread` with the reason in words, rather than left out of the case as though a Mac had no version. It refuses to claim the machine's identity from a `preferences.plist` anywhere else — every application bundle can ship one — by matching the full path suffix and not the name. It refuses to merge the computer name and the local host name, or to prefer one file's answer over another's. It refuses a directory at the path and an entry without content, silently. It refuses to present a partial read that happened to parse as a whole file: the `short_read` pair and detail say the record covers the first N bytes only. A read error from the source is returned as `ParsingError` naming the path, which the processing log records as an error against the artifact.

### `plugin.macos.installed_apps`

**Reads.** The `Info.plist` of every application bundle on a Mac, recognised by path. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent`, takes `path` alone (there is no fallback to `name`), normalises backslashes, and accepts the artifact only when the path ends with `/Contents/Info.plist` — case-sensitively — and the directory above `Contents` ends with `.app`, again case-sensitively, and that bundle path, with its `.app` removed, contains none of `.app/`, `.framework/` or `.bundle/`; so `Safari.app/Contents/Info.plist` is Safari, while an XPC service, a helper application or a framework inside it is a part of Safari and not a second installation. Where the bundle path says, its location is classified in this order: a path containing `/system/applications/` or `/system/library/coreservices/` is `system`, then one containing `/applications/` is `applications`, then one containing `/users/` or `/home/` is `user`, and anything else — a subtree ingested on its own, `/Safari.app/Contents/Info.plist` — is left unsaid. A directory at the path, and an entry with no data source, are declined. It then issues one `read_at` from offset 0 for the lesser of the declared size and 16,777,216 bytes and hands whatever that single call returned to `plist::Value::from_reader`, XML or binary. The top level must be a dictionary. From it eight string keys are taken, each only when present and non-empty: `CFBundleIdentifier` as `package`, `CFBundleDisplayName` as `display_name`, `CFBundleName` as `bundle_name`, `CFBundleShortVersionString` as `version`, `CFBundleVersion` as `build_version`, `CFBundleExecutable` as `executable`, `LSMinimumSystemVersion` as `minimum_system_version` and `DTSDKName` as `built_with_sdk`.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per application bundle, of `type: InstalledApp` with `subtype: InstalledApp`, `analysis_type: installed_app` and `platform: macOS`, parented to the `Info.plist`. It carries `source: Info.plist`, `source_file` (the plist's path), `bundle_path` (the `.app` folder), `installed_in` only where the path said (`system`, `applications` or `user`), the eight fields above where the plist stated them, and `name`: the display name, else the bundle name, else the folder's own name without `.app`, which is what Finder shows. An application with no `CFBundleIdentifier` is not dropped: `package` is set to the folder name and `package_source: bundle folder name` says so. On the Magnet 2021 image this is how Finder is answered as version `11.1`, build `1350.2.10`, in `/System/Library/CoreServices`. A bundle whose `Info.plist` will not parse, or parses to something other than a dictionary, is still inventoried — it is installed either way — as the same record type with `name` and `package` from the folder, `package_source: bundle folder name`, `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason: unresolved_structure` and a `content_incomplete_detail` sentence carrying the parser's error or saying the plist is not a dictionary. The frontend files these under The device as Installed Apps. No timeline events, no hashes, no summary record: the Android inventory's `InstalledAppSummary` has no macOS counterpart.

**Cannot.** It cannot say when an application was installed, by whom, whether it was ever launched, or whether it is still present: it reads no receipt, no `InstallHistory.plist` (that is `seance_plugin_macos_artifacts`), no launch-services database, no quarantine attribute, no code signature, no notarisation ticket, and it does not hash or even locate the executable it names. It publishes no install provenance of the kind the Android inventory does, so the comparison table's provenance row is about Android. It counts only `.app` bundles at the top level of their path: command-line tools, launch agents and daemons, kernel and system extensions, preference panes, Safari extensions, Homebrew casks without a bundle and packages installed under `/usr/local` are not installed applications to it; a `.app` inside `/Library/Application Support` is. Its location field is coarser than its own description: a per-user `~/Applications` folder — `/Users/<name>/Applications/X.app` — is classified `applications` because that test precedes the `user` test, so a bundle a person installed for themselves reads as a system-wide install. The path tests are case-sensitive where the volume is not: a bundle at `Foo.APP/contents/info.plist` on a case-insensitive APFS or HFS+ volume is not matched. It reads eight keys and no others — not `CFBundlePackageType`, not `LSUIElement`, not the document types, URL schemes or entitlements an application declares — and takes them as strings, so a version stored as a number is absent. The read is one `read_at` with no accounting: a plist over 16 MiB is cut at the cap, and a windowed or container-backed source that returns short hands the parser a partial file; either then fails to parse and is recorded as `did not parse` with `unresolved_structure`, never as a short read or a capped read, so the examiner is told the bundle's plist is broken when the tool read only part of it. `FileContent` is subscribed to but a decoded span has no bundle path, so none matches. Nothing here reaches the timeline.

**Refuses.** It refuses to make one application read as thirty: every `Info.plist` beneath a bundle's own — its XPC services, helpers, frameworks and plug-ins — is declined by path. It refuses to drop an application from the inventory because its description of itself is broken or has no identifier: an unparseable plist is inventoried with the reason, and a missing `CFBundleIdentifier` is replaced by the folder name with `package_source` saying so. It refuses to guess where an application lived when the path does not say — answering `elsewhere` for `/Safari.app/Contents/Info.plist` would be a finding drawn from silence — and omits `installed_in` instead. It refuses an ordinary property list (`com.apple.dock.plist`) and any file whose path does not end in `.app/Contents/Info.plist`, silently. It refuses a directory at the path and an entry without content. A read error from the source is returned as `ParsingError` naming the path, which the processing log records as an error against the artifact. What it does not refuse, and what the section above records, is a partial read: that is passed to the parser as if it were the whole file.

### `plugin.macos.plist_parser`

**Reads.** Apple property lists, binary or XML, wherever a file entry carries one. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `SystemArtifact` with `InputCapability::Stream`, which is advisory, and it selects by content, never by name: an artifact with no data source returns an empty list without a word, and the `name` metadata is read only to label what it produces (`unknown` where there is none). It first reads 256 bytes at offset 0 through `read_full`, which loops over short reads, and asks `is_plist` of them: at least 8 bytes, and either `bplist` at offset 0, or `<?xml` at offset 0 with the literal `<plist` somewhere in the first 200 bytes decoded as UTF-8, or `<plist` at offset 0. That probe decides only whether a file it is about to decline deserves a record. A source larger than `MAX_PLIST_BYTES`, 104,857,600 bytes, is not read at all; otherwise the whole declared size is pulled through `read_capped`, and a buffer shorter than the declared size is refused rather than parsed. The full buffer is put through `is_plist` again — a file that fails here is passed over in silence — and then decoded once by `plist::from_bytes::<plist::Value>`, the same call for both encodings. The value tree is walked twice without re-parsing: once by `collect_blobs`, which lifts out every `Data` value of 1,024 to 67,108,864 bytes that does not begin `bplist`, addressed by a dotted key path with `[i]` array indices, stopping at 64 blobs that qualify (a qualifying 65th raises the cap flag; ordinary values after the 64th do not), and recording by key path and size every non-plist `Data` value over 67,108,864 bytes it leaves behind; and once by `content_of`, which renders the tree to JSON — booleans, integers as signed then unsigned then a decimal string, reals, strings, dates as `to_xml_format` RFC 3339, arrays, dictionaries, `Uid(n)` as the string `UID(n)`, and a `Data` value through `nested_or_opaque`: where it is at least 8 bytes, begins `bplist`, and the nesting depth is below `MAX_NESTED_PLIST_DEPTH` (8), it is decoded as a plist of its own; a `bplist` value at the bound is described with `byte_length`, `hex_preview` and a note that it sits at the nesting bound and was not opened; anything else is described as `<data N bytes: hex>` with the first 32 bytes in hex. Where the root dictionary carries `$archiver` equal to `NSKeyedArchiver`, a `$objects` array and a `$top` key, `keyed_archive::resolve_in` follows the UID graph from `$top` with `MAX_DEPTH` 64 per walk. One `keyed_archive::Budget` is made per file and shared by every resolution in it — the top-level archive (resolved first) and every archive nested inside a `Data` value on either the literal or the resolved path — holding `RESOLVE_NODE_BUDGET` of 20,000 output nodes, `MAX_RESOLUTIONS` 100,000 and `MAX_TRANSIENT_BYTES` of 4 MiB, charged by string leaves and, inside a walk, by the bytes of every nested plist the walker opens. The walker renders a non-string leaf at its own plist nesting depth, so an archive inside an archive is opened one level deeper and the 8-level bound holds across archives. In the pipeline its input comes from the filesystem parsers, the archive expanders and the iOS backup readers; a bare `.plist` handed to the API's ingest is typed `RawEvidence` because no `.plist` entry exists in the extension table, and `RawEvidence` is not a type this module subscribes to.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per plist it parses, parented to the file, with `type: PlistFile`, `filename`, `source: PlistParser`, and, for a dictionary root, `key_count`, `sample_keys` (the first ten keys in file order) and a `plist_type` chosen by four key tests — `Bundle Info` where `CFBundleIdentifier` is present, `User Preferences` where `LastUsedDate` or `RecentApplications` is, `Bookmark` where both `Items` and `Name` are, and `Generic` otherwise; an array root is `plist_type: Array` with `array_length`. A keyed archive is classified from the archive, not from this module's wrapper: `plist_type: Keyed Archive`, `archive_format: NSKeyedArchiver`, `key_count` and `sample_keys` from the resolved `$top` dictionary (`[root]` for the usual archive), and `archive_root_class`, the `$classname` of the object under `$top.root`, where it has one. `data_blobs_extracted` counts the blobs carried out; where a qualifying blob was met past the 64-blob cap `data_blobs_capped: true`, and where a blob exceeded 67,108,864 bytes `data_blobs_oversize` lists each one's `key_path` and `size`; either rides with `inventory_incomplete: true`, `inventory_incomplete_reason: cap_reached` and a detail sentence naming what was left behind. The rendered tree is stored as `content` only when its serialised JSON measures at most `CONTENT_CAP_BYTES`, 100,000 bytes — measured by a counting writer that stops at the cap, never by building the string; past it the record carries `content_size_at_least: 100000`, `content_note`, a `content_preview` of the first ten keys fitting inside 8,000 bytes (a value too large for what is left becomes an `$omitted` marker, with `$keys_not_shown` and `$values_omitted` counts), and the standard pair `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason: cap_reached`. For a keyed archive `content` is an object of two members: `keyed_archive` — `root` (the resolved graph), `resolved_from: NSKeyedArchiver`, `object_count`, `truncated` and `truncation_reason` (`nesting depth`, `resolution count`, `output size` or `transient bytes`, whichever bound was met first — in this walk or, because the budget is shared, in an earlier resolution of the same file) — and `raw`, the literal rendering, kept so an examiner can check the resolution against what was on disk. When any resolution in the file — the top-level one or an archive nested inside a `Data` value — was stopped by a bound, the record carries `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason: cap_reached` and a `content_incomplete_detail` naming the bound even when `content` is stored whole under the cap. The same pair is stamped, with a detail naming the plist nesting bound, when a nested binary plist was left unopened at that bound — in an ordinary plist as in an archive. Inside a resolved graph a reference already open on the path becomes `{$cycle_to_object: n}`, one past the end of `$objects` becomes `{$dangling_reference: n}`, the `$null` object becomes JSON null, and a `Data` value that begins `bplist` but will not parse is rendered with `byte_length`, `hex_preview` and the note that it claimed to be a plist and did not parse. Each blob carried out is a second artifact: a `FileEntry` parented to the record, with a `ByteSliceDataSource` over the bytes and `type: PlistDataBlob`, `name: <filename>:<key_path>`, `key_path`, `size`, `source: plist_data`, `source_file` — so the hasher, the signature reader and the gallery see an embedded picture or certificate as a file. Where it declines a file its magic says is a plist, it leaves a `ParsedRecord` with `type: PlistParseStatus`, `subtype: plist_not_parsed`, a `status` of `OverSizeCap`, `ShortRead` or `ParseFailed`, `content_incomplete: true` with reason `cap_reached`, `short_read` or `unresolved_structure`, `content_incomplete_detail` and `message` carrying the same sentence, `file_name`, `declared_size`, `max_size` (104,857,600), a `name` of `Plist not parsed: <file>`, and for `ParseFailed` the decoder's own `error` text. It emits no timeline event, computes no hash, and returns `Err` from no path at all.

**Cannot.** It cannot classify what it read beyond four key tests and the keyed-archive test; an archive's `plist_type` says only that it is one, and its `archive_root_class` names the encoded class without interpreting it. It cannot see a plist that does not open with its magic — a UTF-8 byte-order mark, leading whitespace, or an OpenStep or JSON property list all fail `is_plist` and are passed over in silence, indistinguishable from a text file — and an XML plist whose `<plist` element lies past byte 200 is missed the same way. It cannot open a plist nested more than eight `Data` values deep, on either path; the ninth is described, not read. It cannot carry out a blob over 67,108,864 bytes: it is described in `content` as `<data N bytes: …>` and named on the record by key path and size. A blob under 1,024 bytes stays in the record only as its first 32 bytes of hex. A nested plist that fails to parse is described but never extracted, so its bytes cannot be hashed or exported from this record. Past the 100,000-byte content cap the values are gone: a preference file of eleven keys keeps ten in the preview and a keyword search over the case does not see the eleventh, which is exactly why the pair is stamped. The top-level archive resolution stops at 20,000 output nodes — sized to the content cap, not to the file — so a large archive's `keyed_archive.root` is a prefix with `truncated: true`. Because the budget is one per file, archives nested inside `Data` values share it with the top level and with each other, and the later ones in a file resolve to a prefix or to a `$truncated` marker: on the Magnet 2021 image's `com.apple.notificationcenterui.plist` (183 KB, widget archives nested three deep) 23 nested resolutions stop at `output size`, where each once had 200,000 nodes of its own — the record's content exceeds the 100,000-byte cap either way. It reads dates as strings and raises no timeline event from them; a `LastUsedDate` in a preference file is searchable text and nothing more. It does not know which plist it is reading: no domain, path or bundle is inferred, and `plist_type` is the whole of its interpretation — the meaning of a login-items list or a recent-documents archive is left to other modules or to the reader. It never returns `Err`, so the processing log holds a `complete` row for every file it touched, plist or not. The `SystemArtifact` subscription is dead in practice: nothing in the ingest layer types a plist `SystemArtifact`, and a plist handed straight to the API is `RawEvidence`, which it does not subscribe to. Its ceilings are 104,857,600 bytes of file, 100,000 bytes of stored content, 8,000 bytes of preview, 64 blobs of 1,024 to 67,108,864 bytes each, one budget per file of 20,000 resolved nodes, 100,000 references and 4 MiB of transient leaf content, eight levels of nested plist, and one full decode of the file held in memory beside its JSON rendering. The integration test against a real Apple plist (`test_data/sample.plist`) skips because the file is not in the tree; every other test builds its fixture in code.

**Refuses.** It refuses to parse a plist it could not read whole: a buffer shorter than the declared size is dropped, because a truncated binary plist can decode as valid with a tail of fabricated zeros, and the `ShortRead` marker says so rather than leaving a file that held settings looking like one that held none. It refuses a file over 104,857,600 bytes before allocating for it, and leaves an `OverSizeCap` marker only when the 256-byte probe said it was a plist, so the case is not filled with markers for every large file that was never one. It refuses to let a decode failure vanish: a file whose magic is a plist and whose bytes will not decode leaves a `ParseFailed` marker with the decoder's error, because returning nothing made a corrupt plist indistinguishable from a file that was never a plist. It refuses to carry out a `Data` value that begins `bplist` as a blob, since its contents are already in the record and a second copy would be the same evidence twice; it refuses more than 64 blobs and says it did; and it refuses to inline a resolved archive it has no room for, measuring the JSON against the cap without materialising it. Inside a keyed archive it refuses to follow a reference already open on the path, emitting `$cycle_to_object` instead of recursing, refuses a reference outside `$objects` as `$dangling_reference` rather than a silent null, and stops the walk at the first bound met, marking the container rather than emitting a truncation marker per element. It refuses to let a nested archive restart the bounds: a walker opening an `NSData` member charges its bytes to the file's one budget before opening it, and resolves it one nesting level deeper. It refuses to leave a blob too large to carry out unmentioned. It refuses to restructure a plist that is not an archive: all three of `$archiver`, `$objects` and `$top` are required, so a file that merely has a `$objects` key is rendered as its author wrote it. It refuses to drop a large unsigned integer to null, falling back to the unsigned form and then to a decimal string. And it refuses nothing else out loud: an artifact with no data, or a file that is not a plist, returns an empty list rather than `InvalidInputFormat`, so both are folded into the orchestrator's 'ran and produced nothing' row and are not told apart from a plist that parsed to nothing.

### `plugin.media.exif_parser`

**Reads.** The embedded metadata of a still image, selected by content. It subscribes to `FileEntry` only, declares `InputCapability::RandomAccess` (advisory) and `ExecutionMode::Automatic`, returns an empty list for an artifact whose `is_directory` is `true` or that has no data source, and then reads 16 bytes at offset 0 through `read_full`, which loops over short reads so a windowed source cannot fail the gate. `is_supported_image` admits four signatures and no others: JPEG (`FF D8 FF`), TIFF in either byte order (`II*\0`, `MM\0*`), the 8-byte PNG signature, and an ISO-BMFF file whose bytes 4..8 are `ftyp` with a brand of `heic`, `heix`, `mif1` or `mif2` at bytes 8..12. The artifact's data source is wrapped in a `SourceCursor` inside a `BufReader` and handed to `kamadak-exif` 0.6.1 as `Reader::new().read_from_container`, which finds the Exif segment in a JPEG APP1, reads a TIFF as its own IFD structure, reads the PNG `eXIf` chunk and walks HEIF boxes for the Exif item. From the primary IFD (`In::PRIMARY`) it takes exactly these tags: `Make`, `Model`, `LensModel`, `DateTimeOriginal`, `DateTime`, `Orientation`, `PixelXDimension`, `PixelYDimension`, `ExposureTime`, `FNumber`, `PhotographicSensitivity`, `FocalLength`, `Software`, `GPSLatitude` with `GPSLatitudeRef`, `GPSLongitude` with `GPSLongitudeRef`, `GPSAltitude` with `GPSAltitudeRef`, `GPSDateStamp` and `GPSTimeStamp`; ASCII fields are lossily decoded and trimmed of NULs and whitespace, unsigned fields taken with `get_uint(0)`, rationals as the first element with a zero-denominator guard, and a GPS coordinate as degrees + minutes/60 + seconds/3600, negated when the reference byte, case-folded, equals `S` or `W`. Independently of Exif it asks the `image` crate (0.25, built with `png`, `jpeg`, `gif`, `bmp` and `webp` decoders and nothing else) for the bitstream's own dimensions through `ImageReader::with_guessed_format().into_dimensions()`, a header read and never a decode. It then iterates every field the container carries, in both the primary and the thumbnail IFD, for a raw dump.

**Produces.** At most one `ParsedRecord` per image, parented to the file, with `type: exif` and an `exif_status` of `read`, `not_present` or `exif_unreadable`. Where an Exif block was read it carries `has_exif: true`, `source_name` (the file's `name` metadata), and whichever of `make`, `model`, `lens`, `datetime_original`, `modify_date`, `orientation`, `exposure` (the display string), `fnumber`, `iso`, `focal_length` and `software` the block held — an absent tag is an absent key, never a default. Dimensions come in two layers: `width`, `height`, `actual_width` and `actual_height` are the bitstream's own where the decoder could read them, and `exif_width`/`exif_height` are the declared `PixelXDimension`/`PixelYDimension`; where both exist `dimensions_mismatch` is `true` or `false`, so an image whose declared size disagrees with its pixels is flagged as a tamper signal. Where the decoder could not read the bitstream — a TIFF or HEIC, for which no decoder is built — `width` and `height` are the declared values and `actual_width`/`actual_height` are absent. Every record carrying `width`/`height` names where they came from in `dimensions_source`: `decoded` or `exif_declared`. `gps_lat` and `gps_lon` are signed decimal degrees, emitted only when both resolve, and then `gps_altitude` (negated when `GPSAltitudeRef` is 1, below sea level) and `gps_datetime` (`GPSDateStamp` plus the three `GPSTimeStamp` rationals as `HH:MM:SS`) ride with them; `has_gps` is always present and is `true` only when both coordinates were read. `raw_exif` is an object of every field in the container keyed by kamadak's tag name, thumbnail-IFD fields suffixed ` (thumbnail)`, each value the display form with its unit, the first occurrence of a repeated key winning. `camera` is `<make> <model>` from whichever parts exist, trimmed. Timestamps are the Exif strings verbatim — `2021:07:04 15:30:00` — with no zone, because Exif records none. Where the reader reports no Exif segment (`NotFound`) but the bitstream's dimensions could be decoded, it emits the same record type with `has_exif: false`, `exif_status: not_present`, `metadata_status: 'No EXIF metadata present (stripped in transport or never written)'`, `source_name`, `width`/`height`/`actual_width`/`actual_height`, `dimensions_source: decoded` and `has_gps: false`, so a WhatsApp or Messenger re-encode is documented rather than blank. Where the reader returns any other error — a damaged APP1, a broken marker chain, a truncated file — it emits `exif_status: exif_unreadable` with `exif_error` (the reader's message), a `metadata_status` sentence saying the EXIF could not be read and is not shown to be absent, `content_incomplete: true` with reason `short_read` for an I/O error and `unresolved_structure` otherwise and the same sentence as `content_incomplete_detail`, no `has_exif` key (presence is unknown when the error came before the segment was found), and the decoded dimensions where the bitstream still yields them (pinned by `a_damaged_app1_is_reported_unreadable_not_absent` on a Pillow-written JPEG with its APP1 byte-order mark overwritten). Where no Exif segment exists and no dimensions could be decoded, or the Exif block yielded no field at all, it emits nothing. Downstream, the geo map takes a point from every `exif` record whose `has_gps` is `true` and whose `gps_lat`/`gps_lon` are finite, targeting the parent file for the thumbnail; the gallery and the artifact page join a record to its image by `parent_id`, falling back to `source_name` only where that name is unique in the case; `datetime_original` is the 'taken' time those surfaces show and sort by. It raises no timeline event of its own.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell an examiner when a picture was taken in any zone but the camera's own: `datetime_original` and `modify_date` are copied as written, `OffsetTimeOriginal` is not read, and nothing here converts, validates or orders them — a camera set to the wrong date is reported at that date. It cannot say what a damaged Exif segment held: an unreadable one is reported as unreadable, with nothing recovered from it. It cannot verify the dimensions of a TIFF or a HEIC — the `image` crate here is built without `tiff` or any HEIF decoder — so for those formats `width` and `height` are the declared Exif values, `dimensions_mismatch` is never computed, and `dimensions_source: exif_declared` says so. It cannot read a WebP, GIF or BMP at all, though kamadak reads WebP Exif and the decoder is built for all three, because `is_supported_image` admits none of them. A GPS coordinate whose reference tag is missing is reported positive — northern and eastern — with nothing to say the hemisphere was assumed; `gps_datetime` truncates fractional seconds; and a coordinate of exactly 0,0 is passed to the map as a fix. It decodes no MakerNote, no XMP, no IPTC and no ICC profile, so a phone's model-specific fields, an editor's history and a colour space are not on the record; it extracts no thumbnail, though it names the thumbnail IFD's tags; and it computes no hash and reads no orientation into the dimensions. `raw_exif` keeps the first of two fields with the same tag name and silently drops the second. It applies no byte cap of its own: what kamadak reads is what kamadak decides to read, and for a TIFF that is the whole file. It cannot say an image was edited beyond the one dimension comparison: `software` is published but not interpreted. It never returns `Err`, so a corrupt image and a non-image leave the same `complete` row in the processing log. Its ceilings are the 16-byte probe and whatever the two libraries allocate; its tests build their own TIFF and JPEG fixtures in code, one JFIF and one PNG through the `image` encoder, and one JPEG written by Pillow (with a damaged copy), and no image from a real camera or phone is checked in.

**Refuses.** It refuses to invent a coordinate: `gps_lat` and `gps_lon` are written only when both `GPSLatitude` and `GPSLongitude` parsed as at least three rationals with non-zero denominators, and `has_gps` is `false` whenever either is missing, so a record with one coordinate and not the other carries neither. It refuses to fabricate a zone, publishing the Exif strings as they are. It refuses a rational with a zero denominator — `fnumber`, `focal_length`, `gps_altitude` and each DMS element fall out rather than divide — and refuses an empty or NUL-only string as a value. It refuses to trust `PixelXDimension`/`PixelYDimension` where the bitstream can be read, taking the decoded size as `width`/`height` and keeping the declared size beside it as `exif_width`/`exif_height` with `dimensions_mismatch` stating the comparison. It refuses to go blank on a stripped image, because the absence of Exif is itself a finding about how the file travelled, and refuses to call an unreadable Exif segment absent. And it refuses in silence everywhere else: a directory, an artifact with no data, a file outside the four signatures, a file with no Exif segment whose pixels cannot be decoded, and an Exif block with no usable field all return an empty list and never an error, which the orchestrator folds into the 'ran and produced nothing' row shared with every image it read and found empty.

### `plugin.media.ocr`

**Reads.** The pixels of a raster image, on request. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent`, declares `InputCapability::RandomAccess` (advisory) and `ExecutionMode::OptIn`, which means it is absent from the orchestrator's automatic registry and runs only when an examiner dispatches it by module id — `POST /api/v1/cases/{id}/artifacts/{id}/run_module` for one artifact, or `run_module_batch` with a list of artifact ids, which is what the gallery's opt-in module buttons call — with the target's content resolved by the API for each run. It returns nothing for an `is_directory: true` artifact or one without a data source. The image's name is `name`, else `path`, else the artifact id. Two gates, either sufficient: the name's extension, case-insensitively, is one of `jpg`, `jpeg`, `png`, `gif`, `bmp`, `webp`, `tif`, `tiff`; or 16 bytes at offset 0, read through `read_full`, begin with JPEG `FF D8 FF`, the PNG signature, `GIF87a`/`GIF89a`, `BM`, TIFF `II*\0`/`MM\0*`, or `RIFF` with `WEBP` at bytes 8..12. A zero-length source returns nothing; one over `MAX_IMAGE_BYTES`, 33,554,432 bytes, is not read. Otherwise the whole declared size is read into memory with `read_full`; fewer than 8 bytes returns nothing, and fewer than the declared size stops the run. The bytes are decoded by the `image` crate (0.25, with `png`, `jpeg`, `gif`, `bmp`, `webp` and `tiff`) via `load_from_memory` into RGB8, and handed to `ocrs` 0.12 on the `rten` 0.24 runtime: `ImageSource::from_bytes`, `prepare_input`, `get_text`. The engine is built once per process from two models compiled into the binary with `include_bytes!` — `models/text-detection.rten` (2,510,284 bytes) and `models/text-recognition.rten` (9,716,568 bytes), the models the `ocrs` project publishes, whose SHA-256 digests are recorded in `models/README.md` — and held behind a `Mutex`, so inferences run one at a time and a poisoned lock is taken over rather than refused. No external binary, library, network call or installed model is used.

**Produces.** For an image in which the engine found text, one `ParsedRecord` parented to the image with `type: OcrText`, `analysis_type: ocr`, `subtype: OcrText`, `text` (the engine's output, trimmed), `char_count` (Unicode scalar values of the trimmed text) and `source_image`. The record is what the search index and the analysis views group on — the frontend labels the type 'OCR (Text in Images)' — so text inside a screenshot becomes searchable. For an image that was selected and not examined, one `ParsedRecord` with `type: OcrParseStatus`, `analysis_type: ocr`, `subtype: ocr_not_examined`, a `status` of `OverSizeCap`, `ShortRead`, `EngineUnavailable`, `DecodeFailed` or `InferenceFailed`, the standard pair `content_incomplete: true` with `content_incomplete_reason` of `cap_reached`, `short_read` or `unresolved_structure`, `source_image`, `declared_size`, `bytes_read` (0 for the size cap), `max_image_bytes` (33,554,432), a `message` written for the examiner — for `DecodeFailed` and `InferenceFailed` carrying the library's own error — and a `name` of `OCR not performed: <image>`. For an image the engine examined and in which it found no text, or only whitespace, it produces nothing at all. It emits no bounding boxes, no per-line or per-word structure, no confidence, no language, no rotation, and no timeline event; nothing is written to disk. Because it runs as an ad-hoc job, its outcome is also a job row: the API records the job, and a target whose content could not be resolved is recorded as a job that did not run rather than a module that found nothing.

**Cannot.** It cannot say that a picture was examined and held no text. `OcrFailure::NoText` produces no record by design, so across a gallery sweep an image the engine looked at and found blank leaves exactly the same trace as an image the examiner never dispatched — none — and the case cannot distinguish 'no writing here' from 'nobody looked'; the only witness is the ad-hoc job row, which names the artifact and not the finding. It cannot tell an examiner how sure the engine was: `get_text` returns a string, and no confidence, no word geometry and no line order is kept, so a recognised `Passw0rd` cannot be located on the image or ranked against a doubtful reading. It reads whatever script the two published models read; nothing in this tree states their language or script coverage, no model is selectable, and no language is declared on the record. It OCRs images only: there is no path from a PDF, an Office document, a scanned-document container or a video frame to this engine, and `documentation/COMPARISON.md` line 856 ('OCR over images and documents', a full tick) claims a document capability the code does not have. It applies a byte cap of its own and no pixel cap of its own: the only bound on the decoded picture is the `image` crate's default allocation limit of 512 MiB, so a 30 MB PNG that decodes to a hundred megapixels is decoded whole into an RGB8 buffer three bytes per pixel before the engine sees it, and one whose buffer would pass 512 MiB is refused by the decoder and recorded as `DecodeFailed`. A multi-page TIFF or an animated GIF yields its first frame only. The `BM` gate is two bytes, so any file beginning `BM` with a `.bmp`-less name is selected and then recorded as `DecodeFailed`. It reads no Exif orientation, so a screenshot stored rotated is examined as stored. It cannot run automatically: as `OptIn` it never joins an ingest, and an image that entered the case before an examiner ran a sweep is un-examined until one does. Recognition quality is not measured anywhere in this tree beyond three words: the only end-to-end test asserts that `FELT`, `2026` and `WAREHOUSE` come back from one 640×160 rendered PNG, with no accuracy figure, no real screenshot and no handwriting. Its ceilings are 33,554,432 bytes per image, one inference at a time per process, and the first build of the engine on first use, which parses about 12 MB of models.

**Refuses.** It refuses to report a failure to look as a finding about the picture: an engine that will not build, bytes that will not decode, and an inference that errors each leave an `OcrParseStatus` record naming which, with a sentence saying this is not a finding that the image holds no text — and `EngineUnavailable` is worded to say that no image in the run was examined. It refuses to OCR a truncated image: a read shorter than the declared size ends the run with a `ShortRead` record carrying `bytes_read` and `declared_size`, because the decoder would render what it has and the result would read as the page's text. It refuses an image over 33,554,432 bytes before allocating for it and says so with `OverSizeCap` rather than silently leaving the gallery. It refuses to emit a record for empty or whitespace-only output, so a record present always carries text. It refuses to run without being asked, and refuses to hold more than one inference at a time. And it refuses in silence — no record, no error — for a directory, an artifact without data, a file that passes neither the extension nor the magic gate, a zero-length source, a source shorter than 8 bytes, and an image in which the engine found no text; none of those returns `Err`, so on the case record they are one 'produced nothing' outcome.

### `plugin.media.perceptual_hash`

**Reads.** Every image a file entry carries that it can decode, and it decides by magic. It subscribes to `FileEntry` only, declares `InputCapability::Stream` (advisory), and runs automatically. An artifact with no data source, or one of size zero, yields nothing. It then reads 16 bytes at offset 0 with a single `read_at` — not `read_full` — and declines unless at least 12 bytes came back and they begin with JPEG `FF D8 FF`, the PNG signature `\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n`, `GIF87a`, `GIF89a`, `BM`, or `RIFF` with `WEBP` at bytes 8..12. Past that sniff the file is treated as an image and every exit leaves a record. A source over `MAX_IMAGE_BYTES`, 67,108,864 bytes, is not read. Otherwise the whole declared size is read in a loop of `read_at` calls that stops on a zero-length read or an I/O error, and the buffer is decoded by the `image` crate (0.25, built with `png`, `jpeg`, `gif`, `bmp` and `webp`) through `load_from_memory`; the decoded picture is converted to 8-bit luminance by the crate's own `to_luma8`, and that buffer with its width and height is handed to `seance_vics`: `PdqHash::from_luminance` area-averages the luminance to 64×64, takes a 16×16 DCT block and thresholds the 256 coefficients at their median into 256 bits; `AHash::from_luminance` averages to 8×8 and thresholds at the mean; `DHash::from_luminance` compares neighbouring cells; `PHash::from_luminance` reduces to 32×32, takes an 8×8 DCT and thresholds. All four hash the same luminance buffer.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per image, parented to the file, and one of two shapes. Where a hash was computed: `type: PerceptualHash`, `subtype: pdq`, `algorithm: pdq`, `pdq_hex` (64 lower-case hex characters, the 256-bit PDQ), `width` and `height` of the decoded picture, `evidence_grade: scanned`, a `note` stating that a small Hamming distance is a lead for review and not an identification, and where each companion computed — in practice always, when PDQ did — `ahash_hex`, `dhash_hex` and `phash_hex` of 16 hex characters each; then, stamped last by `seance_vics::stamp_pdq_interop` so nothing above can weaken it, `pdq_variant: pdq-seance-v1`, `pdq_reference_validated: false` and `pdq_interop_note`, the sentence that this pipeline has not been validated against Meta's reference vectors, area-averages where the reference box-filters, and differs in the median rule and the bit packing. Where no hash was computed: `type: PerceptualHash`, `hash_skipped` naming why — `size`, `short_read`, `io_error`, `undecodable`, `zero_dimensions` or `pdq_unavailable` — `size`, the standard pair `content_incomplete: true` with `content_incomplete_reason` of `cap_reached`, `short_read` or `unresolved_structure`, a `note` saying an image was detected here and near-duplicate and PDQ-set matching do not cover it, `hash_skipped_detail` carrying the I/O or decoder error where there was one, `bytes_read` for a short or failed read, and no hash key of any kind. Downstream, `seance_db` lists every record whose `type` is `PerceptualHash` and carries `pdq_hex`; `GET /api/v1/cases/{id}/near_duplicate_images` parses those and clusters them transitively with `seance_vics::cluster_pdq` at a Hamming threshold defaulting to 31 bits, which the REPL's `/duplicates near` and the Duplicates page show; and a VICS hash set with PDQ values is matched against the same field. It emits no timeline event and no hash of the bytes.

**Cannot.** It cannot match against another tool's PDQ and say the answer means anything: the record says so itself, and a non-match against an externally supplied set may be nothing but two different filters. It cannot hash a TIFF, a HEIC or an AVIF — none passes the sniff and no decoder for them is built — so the default photo format of a modern iPhone leaves no `PerceptualHash` record and no skipped record either, and near-duplicate grouping over such a case is silent about every one of those pictures. Its magic probe is a single `read_at` of 16 bytes: a windowed or chunked source that legitimately returns fewer than 12 bytes on that call, and a probe that returns an I/O error, both read as 'not an image' and leave nothing, the same defect the Exif and OCR modules fixed with `read_full`. It computes no rotated or flipped variants, so a mirrored copy of a picture is not a near-duplicate here, where reference PDQ's dihedral set would catch it. The luminance it hashes is the `image` crate's `to_luma8`, not the Rec.601 integer conversion `seance_vics::rgb_to_luminance` documents as the single conversion every perceptual hash keys on, so a PDQ computed elsewhere in this product from RGB pixels through that function would not be bit-identical to one from this module for the same picture. It hashes the first frame of an animated GIF only, ignores alpha, and does not downscale before decoding, so a 60 MB PNG is decoded whole; the decoded pixel count is bounded only by the `image` crate's default 512 MiB allocation limit, not by anything this module sets, and a picture whose RGB/RGBA8 buffer would pass it is refused by the decoder and recorded as `hash_skipped: undecodable` with the limit error in `hash_skipped_detail`. It does not compare, cluster or grade anything itself: `evidence_grade: scanned` is fixed on every record, the 31-bit threshold lives in the API, and nothing here reads a hash set. It does not check `is_directory`, relying on a directory having no data source. It never returns `Err`, and a record's `size` is the source's declared size, not a measured one. The `pdq_unavailable` exit is unreachable in practice, since the buffer it hands over always matches the dimensions it states. Its ceilings are 67,108,864 bytes of file and one full decode in memory; no picture from a real camera is checked in, the resize test uses a synthetic gradient rendered at 256 and 128 pixels, and no test measures a false-positive rate.

**Refuses.** It refuses to hash part of a picture: a read that ends short of the declared size, or that errors partway, withholds every digest and records `short_read` or `io_error` with how far the read got, because a perceptual hash of a prefix looks like the picture's hash, fails to match a complete copy, and would be confirmed by re-hashing the same truncated view . It refuses to publish a hash without its provenance: `stamp_pdq_interop` overwrites `pdq_variant`, `pdq_reference_validated` and `pdq_interop_note` on every hashed record, so a bare `pdq` label that reads as reference output cannot leave this module . It refuses to let a detected image vanish: past the sniff, an oversize, unreadable, undecodable or zero-dimension image always leaves a record naming why, since silence reads as 'this picture was hashed and has no near-duplicates'. It refuses to compute any hash on an image of zero width or height. And it declines in silence, with no record and no error, an artifact without data, an empty source, and a file that does not pass the six-signature sniff — which, because the probe is one unlooped read, includes an image whose first read came back short.

### `plugin.media.properties`

**Reads.** The movie header of an ISO base media file — MP4, M4A, M4V, MOV, 3GP and, because the gate is the `ftyp` box alone, every other file in that family. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent`, declares `InputCapability::RandomAccess` (advisory), and runs automatically. An artifact with no data source, or with `is_directory: true`, yields nothing. `major_brand` reads one box header at offset 0 — 16 bytes through a single `read_at`, at least 8 of which must arrive — and requires the type to be `ftyp` with a payload of at least 4 bytes; the 4-byte major brand is read, lossily decoded as UTF-8, and the count returned by that read is not checked. A file that is not `ftyp` at offset 0 is not this module's, whatever its name. `find_mvhd` then walks the top-level boxes from offset 0 while the current offset is below `min(size, MAX_SCAN_BYTES)` — 268,435,456 bytes — reading each header the same way: a 32-bit size of 1 means a 64-bit largesize follows, 0 means the box runs to the end of the source, a value of 8 or more is the box's length, and anything below 8 stops the walk because the next box cannot be located. Inside `moov` it walks the children for `mvhd`, reads that payload up to `MAX_BOX_BYTES`, 67,108,864 bytes, and stops at the first `moov` whether or not it held one. `parse_mvhd` reads version 0 — 32-bit creation and modification times at payload offsets 4 and 8, the 32-bit timescale at 12, the 32-bit duration at 16 — or version 1 — 64-bit times at 4 and 12, timescale at 20, 64-bit duration at 24 — and no other version. Times are seconds since 1904-01-01 UTC and are converted by subtracting 2,082,844,800; a stored 0 is treated as never set. No other box, track, sample table, codec or tag is read.

**Produces.** Exactly one `ParsedRecord` for every file whose first box is `ftyp`, parented to it, with `type: MediaProperties`, `name: Media properties: <name>`, `source_file` (the `path` metadata, else `name`), `container: iso_bmff` and `major_brand`. Where a version-0 or version-1 `mvhd` was found it adds `timescale` and `duration_units` as read, `duration_seconds` (units divided by timescale) and `duration_hms` (`HH:MM:SS`, rounded to the nearest second), and `created` and `modified` as RFC 3339 with a `+00:00` offset, each present only where the header's value was non-zero — an unset time is an absent key, never 1904. Where the timescale is 0 the duration keys are omitted and the record carries `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason: unresolved_structure` and a `content_incomplete_detail` saying the timescale of zero makes the duration unconvertible. Where no `moov`/`mvhd` was found, or its version was neither 0 nor 1, the record carries the same pair and a detail sentence saying the file has no readable movie header, that an interrupted recording looks exactly like this, and that how long it runs and when it was recorded are not in the evidence rather than being zero. The analysis views render the record under 'Files and media' with a Duration column. It attaches no data, computes no hash, raises no timeline event — `created` and `modified` are read by no timeline builder in this tree — and never returns `Err`.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell a still photograph from an interrupted recording. HEIC and HEIF — the default iPhone photo format — AVIF, and Canon CR3 all begin with `ftyp` and carry `meta` rather than `moov`, so every one of them receives a `MediaProperties` record stamped `content_incomplete` with the sentence that it has no readable movie header and that 'an interrupted recording looks exactly like this'; a folder of iPhone photos is a folder of incompleteness stamps for a defect that does not exist. It cannot find a `moov` written after a large `mdat`, which is the ordinary layout of a camera or phone recording: the top-level walk stops once the current offset passes 268,435,456 bytes, and a 300 MB MOV whose header is at the end is reported with the same interrupted-recording sentence, not as 'the header lies past the scan cap'. It reads nothing but `mvhd`: no track headers, so no video resolution, frame rate, codec, audio channel count, sample rate, bit rate, language or rotation matrix; no `udta`, `meta` or `ilst`, so no `©xyz` location, no `©mak`/`©mod` device make and model, no title, artist or encoder tag, and no Apple `com.apple.quicktime.creationdate` with its zone; no `mvex` or fragment boxes, so a fragmented MP4 whose `mvhd` duration is 0 is reported as running zero seconds with no flag; and no `edts`, so a trimmed clip's duration is the header's, not the edit list's. It cannot read MP3, WAV, FLAC, OGG, MKV, WebM or AVI: nothing outside the ISO family produces a record. Its box reads are single `read_at` calls, so a windowed source that returns short on a header ends the walk as if the file had no header, and the brand is published even where the 4-byte read returned fewer bytes. It cannot say whose clock set the times: `mvhd` times are what the writer stored, in UTC by the specification and in local time by many writers, and the record does not say which. `duration_hms` rounds, so a 0.4-second clip is `00:00:00` beside a non-zero `duration_seconds`. The record is stamped on the first `moov` met, so a file with a corrupt first `moov` and a good second is read as headerless. It never returns `Err`, so a header the module could not read and a header that was not there are the same processing-log row. Its ceilings are 268,435,456 bytes of scan and 67,108,864 bytes of `mvhd`; every fixture is built in the tests, and no recording from a real device is checked in — the CTF podcast that motivated it is reproduced by a synthetic `M4A ` box with its numbers.

**Refuses.** It refuses to date a recording to 1904: a stored time of 0 is treated as 'the writer had nothing to store' and produces no key, because reading it as a Unix time or as the epoch itself would put a wall of false events on the timeline. It refuses to divide by a zero timescale, publishing the units and the incompleteness pair instead of a zero-second duration. It refuses to guess at a header version it does not know — version 2 or any other value is treated as no header — because the fields move between versions and a version-1 header read at version-0 offsets gives a confident wrong duration. It refuses a box whose stated size cannot hold its own header, stopping the walk rather than mis-locating the next box, and refuses to read more than 67,108,864 bytes of any one box. It refuses to claim a file on its name: `.mp4` with no `ftyp` yields nothing. And it refuses to report a missing header as a zero: a file with no `moov` gets the incompleteness pair and a sentence, not `duration_seconds: 0`. Every refusal above is a record, not an error — the only silent exits are a directory, an artifact with no data, and a file whose first box is not `ftyp`.

### `plugin.memory.linux`

**Reads.** The decoded physical address space the container stage attached to a `MemoryImage` record, and nothing else: it never re-detects a format, never opens raw evidence, and returns nothing for a record of any other type or one whose metadata says the decode failed. Which kernel produced the capture is established from the image itself — a sweep for the bytes `Linux version ` yields every distinct banner and the physical addresses each copy sits at, and that banner is matched against the `linux_banner` of an ISF symbol file in the directories `SEANCE_SYMBOL_DIRS` names. Where no symbol file in the lab describes that kernel, it reads the kernel's own account of itself out of the evidence over the first 16 GiB — the BTF type information, accepted only when it declares at least 20,000 types so that a module's BTF cannot stand in for the kernel's, and the `kallsyms` table — and assembles them into a symbol document identified by its SHA-256 rather than a path, carrying the BTF's structs, unions and named enumerations (a name two different enumerations share is emitted for neither, and a member typed by an enumeration not emitted is read at its width and sign without names). With symbols in hand it walks kernel structures through a page-table root derived from `init_level4_pgt`, `swapper_pg_dir` or `init_top_pgt`, and reads user memory through each process's own `mm_struct.pgd`, resolving a page the kernel swapped out only through a swap area the examiner attached as `index=path` with `SEANCE_SWAPFILES`. It reads each process's argument bracket, `mm_struct.arg_start` to `arg_end`, through that process's own page tables, up to 4,096 bytes. It reconstructs a file's path the way the kernel's `prepend_path` does: from `file.f_path.{dentry, mnt}` up `d_parent` to the mount root, across `mnt_mountpoint` into `mnt_parent` (`struct mount` through the container offset of `mount.mnt` on 3.3+, or the `vfsmount` itself before it, both shapes bound by ordered candidates), stopping at the process root read from `task->fs->root` or at the global root; a dentry whose `d_op->d_dname` is `sockfs_dname`, `pipefs_dname` or `anon_inodefs_dname` is rendered as the kernel renders it. It reads `sys_call_table` (with `ia32_sys_call_table` and the x32 table where declared) sized by the next symbol, `ftrace_ops_list` to `ftrace_list_end` with each ops' filter and notrace hashes bucket by bucket and its trampoline, the `direct_functions` hash as (function, target) pairs, `kprobe_table`'s 64 buckets, and `prog_idr` walked as the xarray it has been since 4.20, attributing every address against a code map built from `_stext`..`_etext` and each module's extent (`core_layout`, or on 6.4+ `mem[MOD_TEXT]` — decoded by the module stage through the symbol table's own `mod_mem_type`, or, when the table declares no such enumeration, read by the hooks stage at index 0 with that assumption stated). On 6.4+ the module stage publishes every `mem[]` region by its `mod_mem_type` name, the core size as the sum of the regions not named `MOD_INIT_*` and the init size as the sum of those that are; without the enumeration it decodes none and says so on the row.

**Produces.** Before any stage runs, a stage manifest naming all twelve stages this build can run with the sentence describing each, and a profile record carrying the banner, the release, the page-table root and kernel shift, the symbol origin and the discovery report — including the paging depth that was demonstrated and why. Then one record per stage: the task list walked from `init_task`, each process's capability sets decoded to named capabilities, the loaded kernel modules, the `dmesg` ring, the kernel hooks cross-view, each process's memory areas, open file descriptors and sockets, the mounts of each mount namespace with their absolute mount points, each process's command line, shell history recovered from a shell's own heap, and each process's environment. Every path-bearing row carries `path_scope` — `mount_crossing` with `path_scope_detail` saying how many mount points were crossed and where the walk ended (the process root, the global root, disconnected, or bound), `dentry_tree_relative` with the reason when `f_path.mnt`, the mount chain or the `fs_struct` would not read and the reduced in-mount walk was used, or `pseudo` for a socket, pipe or anon-inode rendering where no walk was made — and `path_kind` (`socket:[inode]`, `pipe:[inode]`, `anon_inode:<name>`, or `pseudo_unresolved` naming any other `d_dname` symbol with the raw walk beside it, never as a file); each process row carries its root. A command-line row carries the argument vector split at NUL with empty middle arguments kept, `argv_rewritten` when the bracket's last byte is not a NUL (the `setproctitle` shape), `argv_short_read` with the bytes missing and `last_argument_cut` when a page was not acquired, and a kernel thread as a non-gap. The kernel-hooks record carries four cross-views, each naming its sources and listing under `not_checked` every check whose symbol or member was absent or whose bytes would not read: the system-call table with every entry attributed to kernel text (nearest symbol plus offset), a named module's extent, or nothing known (a candidate), trailing nulls reported as padding and the `x64_sys_call` switch-dispatch caveat stated; every `ftrace_ops` with its callback attribution, decoded flags (`IPMODIFY` and `DIRECT` called out), an empty filter on an enabled ops stated as every function, and each direct call read against the eBPF programs' attach targets (`explained_by_bpf_program`, `module_direct_call`, `unexplained`); each kprobe with its probed address and pre/post handler attribution; and each eBPF program's id, name, type (from the symbol table's enum, else the UAPI table, source stated), tag, `len`, `jited_len`, `bpf_func` as a JIT image, `attach_func_name` and `load_time`, with `aux->id` cross-checked against the registry index. The process list and the module list each carry a `cross_view` from an independent physical sweep, with `corroborated_by_second_method` saying whether that second method ran at all. Every record is stamped with `profile_evidence` and `symbols_verified`, and a stage that stopped short carries `content_complete: false` with `content_incomplete_reason` naming each reason — the task walk's own reasons folded in, so a shell survey that examined every process it was handed does not read as complete over a list that never reached the shell. A stage that could not run produces a `MemoryStageFailure` record of its own rather than silence, and when the task list will not walk, the seven stages that hang off it get one such record naming all seven and the reason.

**Cannot.** It has never profiled an ARM64 Linux capture taken from hardware. Discovery offers the arm64 kernel regimes (4, 16 and 64 KiB granules at the `ARM64_VA_BITS` widths Linux builds, 36 to 48 bits) to the same banner proof as the Intel depths. Three QEMU-emulated kernels have been profiled and their process lists and mapping offsets graded structurally: a Debian 4.19 guest (4 KiB), a Debian 6.12 kernel (16 KiB) and an Ubuntu 6.8 kernel (64 KiB), the last two booted under QEMU for the purpose; every other stage after discovery was written and checked against x86-64 kernels. The translation core agrees with an independent walker on all 11,663 leaves of two QEMU-emulated AArch64 guests (MMUShell dataset, 4 KiB granule, 39- and 48-bit), on every leaf of the 16 KiB kernel (35,417 pages and 8 blocks, then 90 pages) and of the 64 KiB kernel (13,203 and 26 pages), and on the Debian guest the root that `SYMBOL(swapper_pg_dir) - NUMBER(kimage_voffset)` in the kernel's own `VMCOREINFO` names is the `TTBR1_EL1` the emulator recorded, proved by reading `init_uts_ns` back through it — emulated, not hardware. It cannot read an arm64 swapped page — it cannot even tell one from an empty entry, and the profile's swap block says the tool could not look rather than that nothing was swapped — nor a 52-bit or LPA2 regime, nor an arm64 process whose user space is wider than its kernel's. An arm64 capture with no matching symbol file and no in-image BTF, such as the 4.19 MMUShell guests, stops at `SymbolsNotFound`, and that refusal does not name the architecture. It cannot tell an arm64 kernel from an x86-64 one when the symbol table declares no symbol only one architecture defines (a `kallsyms` table without `KALLSYMS_ALL` has no `kimage_voffset`) and the image holds no agreeing `VMCOREINFO`: such an arm64 image whose tables read as valid x86-64 ones and prove under no arm64 regime it decodes is profiled as x86-64, with only the discovery note that the arm64 regimes did not prove. It cannot compare the kernel's text against a pristine copy, so an inline patch to a function that no table, ops list, kprobe or program references is invisible to the hooks stage; it walks no perf-event list, no `dyn_ftrace` records, and decodes no BPF trampoline, and it reads the eBPF registry only in its 4.20+ xarray shape — the 4.11–4.19 radix tree and the layered IDR before it are refused by name. It cannot attribute an address beyond the code map it built, and that map's limits are published on the record: a module loaded after the module list was written, or a 6.4+ module whose `mem[]` index the symbol table does not enumerate, is attributed on a stated assumption. It cannot enumerate a process or module hidden from the kernel's lists, and both cross-views say so in as many words — the task signature confirmed 576 of 587 processes on a real 15 GiB capture but also matched several thousand structures that are not tasks, so the scan-only structures are counted and deliberately not reported, and an unlinked `task_struct` or `struct module` would therefore not be surfaced. A path whose mount chain fails midway is published as far as it was walked, with the reason. It cannot recover shell history from a kernel of 6.1 or later, where the bash stage's required `mm_struct.mmap` is gone for the `mm_mt` maple tree, nor from any shell not named `bash`, `sh` or `dash`, nor from one started without `HISTTIMEFORMAT`, because an entry is found by the `#`-prefixed timestamp string; it does not decode the 5.10-and-later `printk_ringbuffer`. It cannot date a process: Linux stores an offset from boot, this tier does not establish the boot wall-clock time, and the raw value is published with its unit and `start_time_is_wall_clock: false` rather than as a date. It stops at caps that are recorded when they fire — 8,192 bytes of one process's environment area, 4,096 bytes of one process's argument bracket, 65,536 memory areas or mounts, 65,536 tasks, 16,384 modules, 8 MiB and 200,000 lines of kernel log, 64 MiB of one shell's heap, a 16 GiB sweep for image-derived symbols, and 8 distinct banners with 64 shift attempts — and a page whose swap area was never attached stays a gap counted against a stage's completeness.

**Refuses.** It refuses to read a single structure until the page-table root has been proved by translating `linux_banner` back to the physical address the sweep found it at, at a paging depth demonstrated rather than assumed; when no candidate location and depth does that, discovery ends at `PageTablesUnproved` naming both counts, because an unproved root does not fail — it walks bytes that are not a page table and yields addresses that are plausible and wrong. It offers a kernel only its own architecture's paging when the symbol table declares a symbol one architecture alone defines (`kimage_voffset` for arm64; `phys_base`, `init_top_pgt` or `init_level4_pgt` for x86-64), because a simple arm64 4 KiB hierarchy is also a valid x86-64 four-level one; with no such symbol it requires one family alone to prove, sweeps the image's `VMCOREINFO`, and when both families prove ends at `ArchitectureUndetermined` unless every copy of that note agrees, on a complete sweep, in naming one architecture; the refusal says what the check found, or that it could not look. An arm64 kernel — by those symbols or by an agreed `VMCOREINFO` — whose tables prove under no regime offered is refused as `UnsupportedArchitecture` naming arm64 and every regime tried, not left at `PageTablesUnproved`; and when only an x86-64 depth proves an unhinted table while any `VMCOREINFO` copy found names arm64, even in a sweep cut short or whose copies disagree, that proof is not taken and the kernel is refused as `UnsupportedArchitecture` naming both. An x86-64 reading it does take says what the `VMCOREINFO` check found, and that the architecture rests on the page-table proof alone unless an agreed note names x86-64. It refuses to report "no hooks" for a check it could not make: a check whose symbol or member is absent, or whose bytes would not read, is listed under `not_checked` by name, and the record's completeness says so. It refuses to run the BTF layout-agreement gate over symbols read out of the image, recording `not_applicable` with the reason instead, since comparing that table against the BTF it was built from would pass every time and manufacture a corroboration that never happened. It refuses to return a profile carrying a symbol table the admission gates rejected, so no symbol-dependent stage can run on one. It refuses to guess a swapped page: both x86-64 swap-entry layouts are decoded and the page is read only through the attached area whose bounds one layout's offset falls inside, and an entry that no area corroborates or that two would stays a hole. It refuses to read past `arg_end` into the environment area for a rewritten argv, and refuses to call a bracket cut by an unacquired page a rewritten one. It refuses to render a socket, pipe or anon-inode dentry as a file path, and refuses to render any other `d_dname` at all, naming the symbol instead. It emits nothing at all in exactly one case — a sweep that covered every acquired byte and found no kernel banner, which is what "this is not a Linux capture" looks like — and refuses to treat a sweep that could not finish as that case, because saying "not Linux" would rest on the part of the image nobody looked at.

### `plugin.memory.macos`

**Reads.** It reads the decoded physical address space of a memory image, and only ever through the `MemoryImage` `ParsedRecord` the container stage emits — never raw evidence, so it never re-decides the image's format — together with Apple Kernel Debug Kit symbol packs found, first hit wins, in `SEANCE_SYMBOL_DIRS`, `<exe dir>/symbols`, `./symbols` and `reference/volatility3/volatility3/symbols`, where this repository holds 129 real packs of which 117 are 64-bit. macOS publishes no header to read a profile out of, so it sweeps physical memory for the `Darwin Kernel Version …` string, matches a pack on that banner exactly, and takes the kernel slide as the distance between where the banner is and where the pack declares the `version` array to be. It then reads six symbols and nothing else to establish the profile: `version`, `version_major` and `version_minor` for the cross-check, `BootPML4` to bootstrap an address space, `IdlePML4` for the running page-table base, and `_mh_execute_header` for the kernel load address. With that address space it walks three kernel structures — the null-terminated `allproc` list of `proc`, the circular Mach `tasks` queue resolved through each task's `bsd_info`, and the `kmod` chain of `kmod_info` — and every member offset it reads comes from the pack in hand rather than from a constant, because `proc.p_pid` sits at offset 16 on Darwin 12 through 17 and at 96 on Darwin 18, and `p_start` at 1048, 1064, 960 and 928 across four packs here.

**Produces.** It produces a manifest of the four stages this build can run, emitted before any of them runs and whether or not discovery succeeded, and a `MemoryProfile` carrying the banner, the slide, the page-table base and the kernel base — each graded `validated` rather than `confirmed`, because reaching `IdlePML4` at all depended on the scanned anchor — beside the discovery report: the banner sweep and its completeness, the pack index, and every banner copy tried as a slide anchor with the sentence saying where its chain stopped. From the two listings it produces `MemoryMacProcessList` and `MemoryMacTaskList`, one row per process with the `proc` address, pid, ppid, uid, gid, both names (`p_comm` and `p_name`), `p_start` as whole seconds and microseconds, the raw `p_stat` and the task pointer, plus the kernel's own `nprocs` counter where the build declares it. `MemoryMacProcessCrossView` then states, per pid, which of the two listings saw it, and `MemoryMacKernelExtensions` gives the `kextstat` inventory — bundle identifier, version, load address, size, header size, reference count, kernel id, `kmod_info` version and the start and stop entry points. Every stage record carries the walk's own verdict (`terminated`, `cycle`, `cap_reached` or `unreadable` with the address it stopped at, and never an invented `0x0`), a `content_complete` flag with the reason when it is false, and the build binding saying which declared member each column resolved to, so a `not_declared` cell is an answer about the kernel build and not a gap in the analysis. A stage that could not run produces a `MemoryStageFailure` of its own rather than silence, because a stage that found nothing and a stage that never looked are opposite findings. And every record without exception carries `validated_against_real_capture: false`, `validation_state`, the basis it was built from and the examiner-facing notice, stamped last so nothing earlier can weaken it.

**Cannot.** It has never been run against a real macOS memory capture, and every record it emits says so in as many words: no Mac image and no oracle existed here, so the walks are transcribed from the symbol packs and from Volatility 3's macOS plugins read as source, and a process list produced that way looks exactly like one produced by validated code. It cannot analyse Apple silicon at all — `seance_memory::translate` implements Intel modes only and no pack in the store is an ARM64 kernel — nor any release past macOS 10.15.4, because the 129 packs are x86 and stop there, and it cannot read compressed or swapped pages, since macOS uses a memory compressor rather than a pagefile and that decoder is not written. It cannot tell you a process or a kernel extension was hidden: the cross-view reports which listing held each pid and deliberately does not interpret the difference, because a rootkit's unlinking, an acquisition that caught the machine mid-`exit` and a walk that stopped early all produce the same shape, and the kext stage has no second listing to compare against at all, so it cannot produce a concealment finding for a kext and does not pretend to. It does not compare the kernel's `nprocs` against the number of entries it walked, because whether that counter counts exactly the `allproc` entries has not been verified against a capture, and a tool making that comparison on this evidence would be guessing in a report. It cannot place any process start time on a timeline — the seconds and microseconds are reported exactly as the kernel held them, with no timezone and no rendered date — and it does not translate `p_stat` into a state name, because that enumeration is not in the symbol pack. Its counts are floors when a cap fires: 65,536 processes, 4,096 kernel extensions, 64 banner copies as slide anchors, 4,096 symbol files opened and identified, and eight directory levels searched.

**Refuses.** It refuses to produce a single record for an image whose sweep was complete and found no Darwin banner, returning nothing at all rather than filing "macOS analysis failed" against every Windows dump in a case — and it refuses to extend that silence to a sweep that could not examine everything, which is reported as a failure because the bytes that would have said "macOS" may simply never have been acquired. It refuses a near-miss symbol pack: the match is on the banner and is exact, there is no nearest-build fallback and there will not be one, because the closest pack to a kernel is a different kernel; it refuses a pack whose declared identity is not the banner found in the image, and refuses one whose admission gate did not pass even when it is the only pack available. It refuses 32-bit macOS by name — Mac OS X 10.6 and 10.7, whose kernels need a different virtual base and a different bootstrap symbol — rather than attempting a walk that would yield a plausible and wrong process list. It refuses a slide that is not page-aligned, one at which `version_major` and `version_minor` disagree with the numbers inside the banner string, and one whose resulting address space does not read the banner back at the address the pack declares plus the slide: each of those rejects the whole chain and moves to the next copy of the banner, and the copies in a cached kernel file, a log line or a `sysctl` buffer are exactly what they reject. It refuses a short read where a value would be completed by bytes nobody acquired — three bytes of a page-table base and one byte of nothing is a number, parses, and is wrong — refuses to transliterate a non-UTF-8 process or kext name, reporting the bytes in hex instead, and refuses to reinterpret a negative signed value as an unsigned one.

### `plugin.memory.pattern_scan`

**Reads.** The `MemoryImage` record the container stage emits, and nothing else: that record's attached decoded address space, the `image_format` it declares, and the geometry the container recorded for it, rebuilt into a `PhysicalLayer` so a sparse reconstruction's holes are known rather than read as unreadable evidence. It never touches the evidence file behind a decoded image and never re-detects a format the container stage has already decoded, so a file whose format was decided upstream is searched as that format or, where the record declares none it can parse, as `Raw`. What it searches for is whatever the registration site was given — a compiled YARA rule set named by `SEANCE_YARA_RULES`, one regular expression named by `SEANCE_MEMORY_REGEX`, or both — held as a `PatternSet` with the engine behind it, so the same compiled rules drive this scan and the Windows tier's per-process one. It plans over the whole image's mapped memory through `derive_sections`, which is the only route available for a capture with no page tables to plan from: a reconstructed hibernation file, a swap area, an acquisition whose operating system could not be profiled.

**Produces.** One `MemoryImagePatternScan` record per image, parented to the image record, listing each match in ascending address order with the pattern that found it, the engine kind, the address as a number and again as hex — because a JSON number is an IEEE double and an address above 2^53 reaches a client rounded — and the match length. Beside the rows, counts that stay exact whether or not the rows do: the total, the total per pattern, and per pass the regions planned, the bytes examined, the bytes that were mapped and would not read, and — kept separate, because nothing could have been found in them — the address space never mapped at all. Every record says what an address in it *is* for that format: a physical address in a reconstructed hibernation image and explicitly not an offset in `hiberfil.sys`, a physical address as a crash dump's run table places it, a physical address as a segment map places it, or for a raw blob an offset in the image as the case declared it — a memory address only if that declaration is true. It publishes each pattern set's own caveat, the chunks the engine refused with the address and the engine's reason, the rules that fired with no string of their own found, and a statement that a scan matching nothing is this pattern set over the memory this capture holds and this build could read, which is not the same as nothing to find.
