The backup-level records are all `type: IosBackupInfo`: `subtype: ios_backup_incomplete` with `status: encrypted_no_password`, both incompleteness pairs with reason `encrypted`, the device's `device_name`, `product_type`, `product_version`, `build_version`, `serial_number`, `unique_identifier`, `version`, `date` and `is_encrypted: true`, and a message inviting the password; `status: PartialExtraction` with `files_without_content` and `entries_without_metadata`; `status: PartialDecryption` with `files_not_recovered`; `status: ManifestTruncated` with `records_recovered`, `stopped_at_offset` and `parse_error`; and `subtype: ios_backup_decrypted`, `status: decrypted`, `supersedes_status: encrypted_no_password`, `manifest_entries`, `files_recovered` (`manifest_entries` less the failures, so directories and symlinks count as recovered), `files_not_recovered` and a sentence saying the earlier no-files record describes the state before the password was given. The `encrypted_no_password` record is what the attention queue matches — `IosBackupInfo` with reason `encrypted` — to offer 'The backup's password' as a `SupplySecret` remedy that sends it to the credential route as kind `ios_backup_password`; and the device summary compiles its `ios` device from `IosBackupInfo` records. From the keychain it emits one `ParsedRecord` per item, parented to the `keychain-backup.plist` file entry, with `type: IosKeychainItem`, `table`, `item_kind` (`generic_password`, `internet_password`, `certificate`, `key`), `keychain_class` and `keychain_class_name`, `this_device_only`, `persistent_ref`, `index_in_table` and `state` (`read`, `device_bound`, `key_unwrap_failed`, `no_class_key`, `authentication_failed`, `attributes_undecodable`, `unsupported_version` or `malformed`); an item not read carries `state_detail`, `secret_state: locked`, `secret_present: null` and the incompleteness pair with reason `encrypted`; a read item adds `access_group`, `account` (or `account_hex` when the bytes are not UTF-8), `service`, `server`, `label`, `kind_description`, `comment`, `view_hint`, `uuid`, `path`, `security_domain`, `synchronizable`, `tombstone`, `port`, `created` and `modified` as RFC 3339, `protection_domain` and its name, every other attribute typed under `attributes`, `secret_present` and `secret_state` (`withheld` or `absent`). One `IosKeychainSummary` beside them counts items by table, class and state, with `secrets_withheld`, the file's `keybag_uuid` and a sentence; a keychain file that will not read as one gives a summary with `state: not_read` and the reason. A failure to parse at all is `ModuleError::ParsingError` with the reason, an `error` row in the processing log and no artifact.

**Cannot.** It cannot say whose phone an unencrypted backup came from. The device fields it reads from `Manifest.plist` are published on the `encrypted_no_password` record and nowhere else: the unencrypted path and the decrypted path emit no `IosBackupInfo` carrying `device_name`, `product_type`, `serial_number` or `unique_identifier`, the two-row `sqlite_basic` fixture produces exactly two artifacts and no device record, and the device summary — which compiles iOS devices from `IosBackupInfo` — therefore shows no device for an ordinary backup folder. It cannot decrypt a legacy backup: an encrypted backup is taken down `parse_encrypted_backup`, which reads `Manifest.db` only, so an encrypted iOS 3–9 backup with `Manifest.mbdb` fails with 'Encrypted backup missing ManifestKey' or a read error and produces nothing. It cannot survive a wrong password gracefully: the RFC 3394 integrity failure on the first passcode-wrapped class key is a `ParsingError` for the whole run, and no artifact — not even the `encrypted_no_password` record — is left behind to say the backup is there. It cannot open a class key the keybag wraps with the device key (`WRAP` bit 1, with or without bit 2 — 5 of the 14 classes on the Hickman iOS 17 backup, classes 5, 9, 10, 11 and 19): a backup does not carry that key, so a file or keychain item in such a class is refused as device-bound. It cannot verify what it decrypted: the manifest's `Digest` is never read at all, the mbdb's data hash is read but never compared to the produced bytes, the decrypted length is never checked against the manifest's `Size`, and no digest of a produced file is computed here. It cannot avoid the host disk: a decrypted `Manifest.db` is written to a `NamedTempFile` in the system temporary directory for rusqlite to open, so a plaintext manifest of an encrypted backup exists outside the case for the length of the parse. The `date` on the `encrypted_no_password` record is `format!('{:?}')` of a `plist::Date` — a Debug rendering, not the RFC 3339 every other date in this crate uses, and not a value-format contract. It reads `Info.plist` on no path, so the IMEI that only `Info.plist` carries is absent from a backup ingested this way. It writes no `path` on a file entry — `domain` and `relative_path` only — and reconstructs no tree, so an entry is found by name and not by where it lived. It reads `Status.plist` on no path either, so the device's own statement of whether the backup completed (`IsFullBackup`, `SnapshotState`) is never consulted and the manifest is trusted as the inventory. Of the keychain it cannot read the items in the ThisDeviceOnly classes 9, 10 and 11: they are in the backup, but their item keys are wrapped under a key derived from the device's hardware, which a backup does not carry, so they are listed as `device_bound` with their table and class only (715 of 1,368 items on the Hickman iOS 17 backup). It releases no keychain secret: the `v_Data` attribute — saved passwords, tokens, private keys, certificate bodies — is withheld from every record, and so is `sha1`, the keychain's digest over the item including its secret; a record says whether a secret is present, never its value or length. A secret leaves only through the API's audited per-record reveal (`POST …/keychain/{record}/reveal`), which re-derives it from the backup through `UnlockedBackup::keychain_secret` while the backup is unlocked for reading, checks the item's `v_PersistentRef`, and writes the audit row before returning it. It reads no `keychain-2.db` from a full-file-system extraction, whose class keys are hardware-bound, and it reads the keychain on ingest only, not on re-read after an unlock. Its file reads are `FileDataSource`s opened at construction, so a blob that is missing or unopenable fails at parse — that is the `backup_blob_unreadable` path — and, the descriptor being already open, a blob deleted after ingest is still readable on Unix for as long as the source lives. It keeps nothing after its run: the password and every key it derived are gone when the run ends, so the files of an encrypted backup are refused afterwards by stream, hex, export and re-hash — the only bytes on disk are ciphertext — until an examiner unlocks the backup for reading (`POST …/artifacts/{id}/unlock`, kind `ios_backup_password`). That re-derives the class keys through this crate's own `unlock_backup` and opens each file through the same per-file step as ingest (`open_encrypted_file`), so a file ingest could not open — no per-file key, no protection class, no class key — is refused on re-read too; like ingest, the unlock writes the decrypted `Manifest.db` (names, domains, wrapped per-file keys) to a temporary file, deleted when the check returns. The API holds the class keys in process memory for that one case, 8 hours by default (`SEANCE_UNLOCK_TTL_SECS`); an expired unlock is never returned and is dropped by the next keyring operation or the expiry sweep, at most a minute later. After expiry, `DELETE` on the route, deleting the case or a restart the refusal returns. The per-file key of a whole-file read and the AES schedule inside a streaming read are not zeroed by this crate. The real-backup tests in `test_data/ios_backup` skip because the folder is not in the tree; the encrypted path is exercised against a backup the tests synthesise, with keys the tests wrap; one real encrypted backup, Hickman's public iOS 17 Finder backup, is exercised by a test gated on `SEANCE_IOS17_BACKUP` (IOS-KEYCHAIN-1) that CI does not run.

**Refuses.** It refuses to exhibit ciphertext as a file's content, and every refusal on the encrypted path exists for that: a row with no usable per-file key, no protection class from either carrier, no class key for that class, a key that will not unwrap, or bytes that will not decrypt leaves an `ios_backup_undecrypted` record with no data attached and names which; protection class 0 is refused in `decrypt_file` rather than returning the input unchanged; and a row carrying an `EncryptionKey` inside a backup that did not declare itself encrypted is left without content on the unencrypted path too. It refuses to resolve a `fileID` that is not a bare ASCII-alphanumeric name against the backup directory, because a manifest is evidence and `../../etc/shadow` walked out of the evidence root; on the encrypted path the entry is recorded as `InvalidFileId`, and on the unencrypted `Manifest.db` and mbdb paths the same refusal is recorded as `content_omitted: backup_blob_unreadable` with the refusal sentence in `open_error`, or as `symlink_has_no_stored_content` when the row is a symlink. It refuses to default `IsEncrypted` to false where the flag is missing, inferring it from `ManifestKey` instead. It refuses a streamed ciphertext whose length is not a multiple of 16 or whose final block does not carry valid PKCS#7 padding, rather than serving pad bytes as plaintext. It refuses to let a manifest walk that desynced look complete, stamping `ManifestTruncated` with the offset, and refuses to let a missing blob open as an empty file, stamping the entry and the backup. It refuses to count a symlink as a hole. It refuses to leave the no-files statement standing once a password has opened the backup, emitting the `decrypted` record that supersedes it. It refuses to present a keychain item whose AES-GCM tag does not verify: the item is `authentication_failed` with no attributes, because unauthenticated bytes may not be what was stored; a `v_Data` of another version or a malformed header is recorded as such, not guessed at. And it refuses to read anything without the password — an encrypted backup with none leaves the device's identity and the invitation, and nothing else — while a wrong password refuses the whole run as a `ParsingError`, and a missing `path` refuses as `InvalidInputFormat`, folded into the orchestrator's `skipped` row.

### `plugin.mobile.ios_backup_manifest`

**Reads.** The three manifests of an iOS backup when they are inside the evidence rather than on the examiner's disk — a laptop image holding `~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup/<UDID>/`, or a ZIP of that folder. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess` (advisory) and runs automatically, and it gates three times before reading a byte: the `name` metadata, case-insensitively, must be `manifest.plist`, `info.plist` or `manifest.db`; `is_directory` must not be `true`; and the parent folder of `path` (else `name`), with backslashes normalised, must be 40 hexadecimal characters or the newer 25-character UDID `XXXXXXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX` — because `Info.plist` is in every application bundle on a Mac and only the folder makes it a backup manifest. An artifact with no data source yields nothing. For the two plists it reads `min(size, MAX_MANIFEST_BYTES)` — 67,108,864 bytes — with a single `read_at`, truncates to what came back, and parses with `ManifestPlist::from_bytes`, the same reader the directory parser uses, so the device fields come from the top-level spaced keys or the `Lockdown` dictionary and `IMEI` from `Info.plist`'s own key; a plist that names no `display_name`, `product_type`, `serial_number`, `unique_identifier` or `imei` is not claimed. For `Manifest.db` it refuses a source over `MAX_MANIFEST_DB_BYTES`, 1,073,741,824 bytes, reads the rest whole with a single `read_at`, writes it to a temporary file and opens it with rusqlite through `ManifestDb::parse_from_bytes`, reading the same `Files` columns and metadata blobs as the directory parser. It then asks the data source whether it can open its neighbours — `supports_siblings`, true for a host `FileDataSource` and a ZIP entry and for the caching wrappers over them, false for a file served from a filesystem inside a disk image — and, where it can, opens each row's blob as `<ab>/<fileID>` then `<fileID>` through `open_relative`, which refuses a path that climbs.

**Produces.** For `Manifest.plist` or `Info.plist`, one `ParsedRecord` parented to the file with `type: IosBackupInfo`, `subtype: manifest_in_evidence`, a `name` of `iOS backup of <device>`, `source_file`, `source_kind`, `backup_path` (the folder), `device_name`, `product_type`, `product_version`, `build_version`, `serial_number`, `unique_identifier`, `imei`, `encrypted`, `backup_version`, `date` as RFC 3339 where the manifest has one, and always `inventory_incomplete: true` with reason `unresolved_structure` and a detail saying this record names the device and nothing else, and that the inventory is the `manifest_db_in_evidence` record for the same `backup_path` — the device summary compiles an `ios` device from it, and the IMEI on it is how the Magnet 2021 question is answered. For `Manifest.db`, one `ParsedRecord` per `Files` row with `type: IosBackupFile`, `subtype: reparented_from_evidence`, `name` (the basename), a `path` of `<backup_path>/<domain>/<relative_path>`, `file_id`, `domain`, `relative_path`, `flags`, `is_directory`, `size`, `mode`, `last_modified`, `birth`, `modified`, `created`, `inode`, `user_id`, `group_id`, `protection_class` and `backup_path`: a directory is a `ParsedRecord`; a symlink is a `FileEntry` with `content_omitted: symlink_has_no_stored_content`; a row with a per-file key is a `FileEntry` with no data, the pair with reason `encrypted`, `content_omitted: stored_blob_is_ciphertext` and a message naming the keybag and password as what is missing; a row the source could not look for is a `FileEntry` with the pair, reason `unresolved_structure`, `content_omitted: source_cannot_open_neighbours` and a message saying the blob is in the case under its hashed name; a row whose blob opened is a `FileEntry` carrying that neighbour as its data source and `stored_path`, which is what lets `sms.db` be parsed as `sms.db`; and a row whose blob was not found is a `FileEntry` with `content_omitted: backup_blob_unreadable`. A row whose metadata blob would not decode carries a stamp saying the metadata could not be decoded. Then one summary `ParsedRecord`, `type: IosBackupInfo`, `subtype: manifest_db_in_evidence`, with `manifest_entries`, `files_reparented`, `files_missing_from_evidence`, `files_ciphertext`, `directories`, `symlinks`, `entries_with_undecodable_metadata` and `encrypted` (true when any row carried a key), and one of three stamps: `inventory_incomplete` with reason `unresolved_structure` where the source could not look and stated files outnumber ciphertext ones, or where any file was missing; else `content_incomplete` with reason `encrypted` where any file is ciphertext. Over the 1 GiB cap the summary alone is emitted with reason `cap_reached`. A read error is `ModuleError::ParsingError`; nothing else returns `Err`.

**Cannot.** It cannot put a backup's files back at their device paths when the backup is inside a disk image. `supports_siblings` is false for a file served out of an NTFS, APFS, HFS+ or ext4 filesystem in an image — only a host directory and a ZIP entry can look sideways — so on the commonest shape of this evidence, a laptop image, every row is `source_cannot_open_neighbours`, no `sms.db` is attached, and the summary says so; a backup found inside a laptop image yields the device identity and the inventory and not the files. It cannot decrypt anything, and the case may offer to: the `manifest_db_in_evidence` summary for an encrypted backup carries `IosBackupInfo` with `content_incomplete_reason: encrypted`, which is exactly what `seance_api::REMEDIES` matches to offer 'The backup's password' and re-run `plugin.mobile.ios_backup` against the record's parent — the `Manifest.db` file entry, whose `path` is a path inside the image, not a directory on this machine — so that run returns `InvalidInputFormat` or nothing, and the queue's guidance that the backup 'is decrypted and extracted in place' is not true of a resident backup. It cannot read `Manifest.mbdb` in the evidence, so a legacy backup inside an image yields its device identity and no inventory. Its reads are single `read_at` calls — up to 64 MiB for a plist and up to 1 GiB for the database — so a source that returns short hands a truncated buffer to the plist reader or to SQLite, which reads it as far as it goes with nothing to say it was cut. It writes the manifest database to a temporary file on the host to open it. It cannot recognise a backup folder renamed or copied out of the UDID-named directory: the folder test is the whole of its provenance check, and a manifest sitting in `Backup/copy/` is not a backup. It produces two identity records for one backup when both `Manifest.plist` and `Info.plist` are present, differing in `source_kind` and in which of them carries the IMEI, and nothing merges them. It reads no `Status.plist`, so a backup's completeness on the device's terms is unknown. It verifies no digest, computes no hash, and does not check that a reparented blob's length matches the manifest's `Size`. It raises no timeline event; `modified` and `created` are carried for the grid. Its ceilings are 67,108,864 bytes of plist, 1,073,741,824 bytes of database, and one copy of the database in memory beside one on disk; every test stages its backup in a temporary directory built by the test, and no manifest from a real device is checked in.

**Refuses.** It refuses to claim a plist on its name alone: the folder must be UDID-shaped, and a plist in such a folder that names no device is left unclaimed rather than put on the device summary as an empty phone. It refuses to attach a stored blob it cannot vouch for: a row with a per-file `EncryptionKey` is described, dated and sized and its ciphertext is not attached, because those bytes are not the file's content and would be hashed and exhibited as if they were. It refuses to report every file missing when the source simply cannot look, stamping `source_cannot_open_neighbours` on the rows and one `inventory_incomplete` on the summary instead of a count of absences that would read as a device that never held them. It refuses a `fileID` that is not ASCII alphanumeric — `stored_blob_candidates` returns nothing for it, so it is recorded as missing rather than resolved — and `open_relative` refuses any relative path containing `..`. It refuses a `Manifest.db` over 1,073,741,824 bytes before reading it, leaving the capped summary. It refuses to invent an inventory from a SQLite file that is not a backup manifest — a `Manifest.db` that will not parse as one yields nothing rather than an empty backup. And it declines in silence a file with a different name, a directory, a file outside a backup-shaped folder, a plist that will not parse, and a manifest with no device fields; only a read error is an `Err`.

### `plugin.network.pcap_parser`

**Reads.** A packet capture, recognised by its own first bytes — a libpcap file in either byte order at microsecond or nanosecond resolution, or a pcapng file — and never by its extension. The first 256 MB of it are staged; the walk then runs twice, because a pcapng packet names its interface by index and the interface table is only complete when the walk ends. Each frame is decoded by its interface's LINKTYPE (Ethernet, raw IP, Linux cooked capture; anything else is refused by number), through any stack of 802.1Q tags, to IPv4 or IPv6 and then to TCP, UDP or ICMP. Every TCP segment's payload is offered to a reassembler keyed by the conversation the flow table put it on; the reassembled bytes before each stream's first gap are read as HTTP/1.x or TLS by their own start bytes, on any port. ARP frames are read for the address they claim. Port 53 payloads are decoded as DNS.

**Produces.** One `NetworkCapture` record per file carrying the format, the capture engine's own attestations and every count below it; one `NetworkFlow` per conversation with per-direction packet and byte counts, the TCP state derived from flags alone, and the reassembled streams with their gaps and conflicts; a `TimelineEvent` at each flow's first timestamped packet; `DnsResolution` records; one `HttpTransaction` per request-and-response pair carrying the URL, the headers, the decoded form fields and the basis the pairing rests on, with each message body handed on as its own `FileEntry` artifact — inflated where it crossed the wire gzip'd — so YARA, the hasher, the file-type detector and the search index see it (not the carver, which subscribes to file systems and unallocated space only); one `TlsSession` per encrypted conversation carrying the server name the client asked for, the version and cipher agreed and the client's JA3 fingerprint; one `TlsCertificate` per certificate a server presented in the clear, with a timeline event at each end of its validity window; and one `ArpBinding` per address, listing every hardware address that claimed it.

**Cannot.** It cannot read what is encrypted. Inside TLS it reads the handshake and nothing else: from TLS 1.3 even the certificate is encrypted, and a session with no certificate says which of three reasons applies -- encrypted by TLS 1.3, absent from a cleartext that should have held it, or no ServerHello in the cleartext at all so the version is not even known -- rather than showing an empty chain. It does not read HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, a CONNECT tunnel's contents, QUIC, SMB, mDNS or DNS over TCP. It recognises TLS only where a stream's first byte begins a handshake record, so TLS behind a preamble -- RDP's X.224 connection request, a STARTTLS exchange -- gets no session record, and neither does a later connection on a five-tuple reused within the capture. It reads no message across a gap in a stream: only the bytes before the first missing byte are offered to a parser, so a conversation with packet loss can hold fewer transactions than took place. It never guesses a protocol from a port number — a binary protocol on 80 is not read as HTTP, and that is deliberate. It verifies no certificate signature, builds no chain and consults no trust store. It does not defragment IP: a non-initial fragment is counted on its address pair and its transport header is not inferred. Its ceilings are stated on every record they touch: 256 MB staged per file, 500,000 flows, 262,144 reassembled streams within a 256 MB total reassembly budget, 100,000 DNS messages, 10,000 HTTP transactions and 131,072 TLS session records per capture; a conversation the stream table had no room for, in one direction or both, says on its own flow record which direction's bytes were not read. Stage 2 is graded on one real capture, DFIR Madness Case 001 (NET-4): the implant's body read off the wire hashes to the MD5 and SHA-256 the publisher's autorunsc recorded on disk. One capture is not a population, and a capture unlike it may show a ceiling this one did not.

**Refuses.** A file it cannot read at all still leaves a `NetworkCaptureRefusal` record naming what stopped it, because a capture that was detected and not read must never render as a capture that held no traffic. A LINKTYPE it does not decode is refused by number, with the packet count that carried it, so the reader knows which decoder is missing rather than seeing a quiet segment. A frame whose IPv4 header checksum fails with a non-zero field is refused and counted as corrupt or forged, while a zero field is offload and decodes with that stated. Where two segments claim the same stream offsets with different bytes, the first are kept and the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved — that is how a sensor is evaded. If the reader ever panics, the panic is caught and the capture leaves a refusal record carrying the panic message.

### `plugin.ntfs.badclus_parser`

**Reads.** The run list of NTFS's `$BadClus:$Bad` stream, as the MFT parser already published it. It subscribes to `FileEntry`, `RawEvidence` and `SystemArtifact` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, and it reads no bytes at all: everything it consumes is metadata. An artifact is a target when its `name` (else `file_name`) or its `source_path` (else `path`) is exactly `$BadClus:$Bad` — the whole value, or its last `/`- or `\`-separated component, compared ignoring ASCII case; anything else returns an empty list. From a target it takes `bad_cluster_runs` — an array of `[offset, length]` pairs in bytes, offset `null` for a sparse run — with `bad_cluster_runs_complete`, and, only where no producer published those, the older `data_runs` in the same shape; and, if present and non-zero, a cluster size from `cluster_size`, `allocation_cluster_size` or `bytes_per_cluster`. In the pipeline the artifact that carries them is the alternate data stream the MFT parser emits for record 8: a `FileEntry` parented to the filesystem, named `$BadClus:$Bad` with `stream_name: $Bad`, `is_ads: true`, `parent_file: $BadClus`. Its `data_runs` is the stream's LOGICAL extent, and `$Bad` has an initialized size of zero on a real volume (a Windows 11 NTFS image: `alloc=2250240000 real=2250240000 init=0`; dfir_ntfs's `ntfs_index.raw.gz`: `real=30406656 init=0`), so that list is one sparse run with every bad-cluster run dropped. The MFT parser therefore also publishes, on record 8's `$Bad` only, the attribute's raw allocated runs as `bad_cluster_runs` (coalesced, capped at 512, with `bad_cluster_runs_complete` false where the cap was hit or an `$ATTRIBUTE_LIST` extent was not resolved) and the volume's `cluster_size`; `data_runs` keeps its contract, so no resolver serves the never-initialized clusters as the stream's content. The stream's content is never parsed as run bytes.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per non-sparse run, parented to the stream artifact, with `record_type: badclus_range` (there is no `type` or `subtype` key; the database resolves the record's type through its `record_type` fallback), `stream` (the artifact's `name`, else its path), `volume_offset_bytes` and `length_bytes` copied from the run, `cluster_size_bytes`, and `description` — 'Bad cluster region at byte offset N (M bytes, K clusters)' — with `cluster_start_lcn`, `cluster_end_lcn`, `cluster_count`, `vcn_start` and `vcn_end` derived from the cluster size, which the MFT parser now publishes on `$Bad`; where no cluster size was given those five are `null`, never derived from an assumed 4 KiB. A sparse run — offset `null` — advances the virtual position and produces nothing, so a volume with no bad clusters produces no range record. Where the producer said the run list is not whole (`bad_cluster_runs_complete: false`) one further record is appended: `record_type: badclus_status`, `stream`, `ranges_reported`, and `inventory_incomplete: true` with reason `unresolved_structure` and a `_detail` saying a cluster absent from the ranges is not shown to be good. The records attach no data, raise no timeline event, and are read by no report section or frontend viewer beyond the generic records list. A malformed run list — not an array, an entry that is not a two-element array, an offset or length that is not an unsigned integer — is `ModuleError::ParsingError` naming which, an `error` row in the processing log, and no artifact. A target with neither run list publishes one `badclus_status` record with `ranges_reported: 0`, `run_list_absent: true`, and `inventory_incomplete: true` with reason `unresolved_structure` and a `_detail` saying no bad cluster could be looked for — not that the volume has none.

**Cannot.** It cannot say the offsets are device-absolute: the MFT parser's runs are relative to the filesystem window, and nothing here adds the partition's start, so `volume_offset_bytes` is a volume offset that a reader must place themselves. It cannot say a bad range was read, hashed or carved: it never touches the bytes, so it cannot say whether the marked clusters are unreadable now, held recoverable data, or were marked bad by software to hide something — the last being the reason `$BadClus` matters, and this module's whole answer to it is a list of ranges. It cannot list more than 512 coalesced ranges: the producer caps the run list there and says so, and this module then publishes the `badclus_status` record rather than the missing ranges. It cannot tell a volume with no bad clusters from a `$BadClus` record the producer never emitted: both leave no range record, and only the first leaves a `$BadClus:$Bad` stream artifact to look at. It cannot check the marking against `$Bitmap`, against the MFT's own allocation, or against `chkdsk`'s record; it cannot tell a bad cluster from a range the run list encoded oddly. Its `RawEvidence` and `SystemArtifact` subscriptions are dead in practice: no producer writes a run list on either type. It runs on the ADS the MFT parser emits for a deleted `$BadClus` record too, since it does not read `deleted`. It is graded through the producer on a real volume — dfir_ntfs's `ntfs_index.raw.gz` (gitignored; CI skips the test), unmodified (no bad cluster; the raw run list reaches this module as the one sparse run it is) and with two clusters marked bad by rewriting `$Bad`'s mapping pairs the way `chkdsk /r` does (both reported at LCN 1,000–1,001, byte offset 2,048,000) — but not on a volume on which Windows itself marked a cluster bad; none is held.

**Refuses.** It refuses to recover bad clusters from the stream's content: the `$Bad` stream's bytes are the clusters themselves, not a run list, and parsing them as runs would invent ranges from data, so a target with no run-list metadata produces only the `badclus_status` record saying it could not look. It refuses to flag a sparse run as bad, because on a healthy volume the sparse runs are the good clusters and flagging them would mark the whole disk. It refuses to assume a cluster size: with none given, every cluster-denominated field is `null` and the description counts bytes only. It refuses a malformed run list outright, with a `ParsingError` naming the fault, rather than skipping the entry it could not read. It refuses to present a run list its producer called incomplete as the whole bad-cluster map. It refuses an artifact that is not the `$BadClus:$Bad` stream, in silence. And it does not check what it produces: no ceiling of its own on the number of ranges, no check that a run lies inside the volume, no check that ranges do not overlap — a record emitted is a run copied from metadata it did not verify.

### `plugin.ntfs.i30_parser`

**Reads.** NTFS directory index streams — the `INDX` records of a `$I30` `$INDEX_ALLOCATION` attribute — and it takes them from three artifact types with three different gates. It subscribes to `SystemArtifact`, `FileEntry` and `RawEvidence`, declares `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, and does not run under the triage ingestion profile, whose enabled list names only the MFT and USN parsers among the NTFS modules. The route that carries the real workload is the `SystemArtifact` one: `seance_plugin_mft` emits one `SystemArtifact` per directory record whose `$INDEX_ALLOCATION` is non-resident, with `name: "$I30"`, `type: "IndexAllocation"`, a `parent_file` naming the directory, and a `RunListDataSource` built from the attribute's cluster runs; this module accepts it only when `type` is exactly `IndexAllocation` and `name` is exactly `$I30`. A `FileEntry` is accepted when its `name` (falling back to `file_name`) or its `path` (falling back to `source_path`) names the stream itself: a last path component, compared without case, of `$I30`, `<dir>:$I30` or `<dir>:$I30:$INDEX_ALLOCATION` — a name that merely contains `i30`, such as `vti30.dll`, is not taken. A `RawEvidence` artifact is accepted when `seance_core::file_detection::detect_file_type` reads its first 512 bytes and finds `INDX` at offset 0, or, failing that, when its `source_path` names the stream by the same exact test. Anything else returns an empty list without a word. Having selected the stream, it walks it from offset 0 to the source's `size()`: at each position it reads a 36-byte head through a looped read that tells an I/O error apart from the end of the stream — an error stops the scan with `indx_read_failed`, and fewer than 4 bytes where at least 4 remain stops it with `indx_buffer_short_read` — and a head that is not `INDX` advances the position by 512 bytes and tries again, so the whole stream is swept sector by sector and an `INDX` block the directory's own bitmap has freed is found exactly as an in-use one is. The record size is never assumed: `indx_record_size` derives it from the update-sequence count at offset 6 — `(count − 1)` × 512 bytes, NTFS's update-sequence stride, which is 512 on every volume whatever the disk's sector size (a 4Kn volume's 4,096-byte records carry a count of 9) — reconciled against `INDEX_HEADER.allocated_size` at offset 0x20 rounded up to a 512-byte multiple, within a 512-byte to 65,536-byte window, and when the two cannot be reconciled the scan stops rather than guess, because a 4 KiB guess on an 8 KiB-index volume decodes every later buffer at the wrong alignment. The whole record is then read the same way and must arrive entire; `apply_fixup` verifies the update-sequence placeholder in the last two bytes of every 512-byte sector against the USN and restores the saved bytes, and a mismatch marks the buffer torn while the sectors already restored are still parsed. Inside the buffer it reads `EntriesOffset` at 0x18 and `IndexLength` at 0x1C, both relative to the node header at 0x18, and walks entries from `0x18 + EntriesOffset` to `0x18 + IndexLength`: for each, the 8-byte file reference, the 16-bit entry length, the 16-bit attribute length and the flags word, and — where the attribute length is at least 0x42 and fits inside the entry — the embedded `$FILE_NAME`: parent reference, the four FILETIMEs (created, modified, MFT-changed, accessed), allocated and real sizes, the attribute flags, the name length and namespace bytes, and the UTF-16LE name. An entry length of zero, or one running past the used region, ends that buffer's walk. `parse_slack_space` then scans the record's free space — from `0x18 + IndexLength` to `0x18 + AllocatedSize`, bounded by the record, the range dfir_ntfs's `get_slack` reads — byte by byte for `$FILE_NAME` shapes: a non-zero name length, a namespace byte of 0–3, all four FILETIMEs between 1980-01-01 and 2108-01-01, and a non-empty decoded name with no `/` or NUL in it. Where the 16 bytes in front of a candidate lie inside the slack and form an index-entry header whose attribute length is exactly that `$FILE_NAME`'s and whose entry length is a multiple of 8 that holds it, the deleted entry's own file reference is read from them. It does not read `$INDEX_ROOT`, the directory's `$BITMAP`, or the parent `$MFT` record.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per index entry recovered, parented to the artifact it read — the `$I30` `SystemArtifact`, not the directory's `FileEntry` — with `type: "NtfsIndexEntry"`, `source: "$I30"`, a running `entry_number`, `file_name`, `file_reference` and `parent_reference` as `record-sequence` strings (an empty string where the raw reference was zero), `allocated_size`, `real_size`, `file_attributes` as `0x%08x`, `is_directory` (attribute bit 0x10), `namespace` as `posix`, `win32`, `dos`, `win32_dos` or `unknown`, `entry_flags` as a list drawn from `has_subnode` and `last_entry`, `created`, `modified`, `mft_changed` and `accessed` as RFC 3339 strings or `null` where the FILETIME was zero or out of range, `from_slack`, `buffer_index` and `entry_offset` (the absolute byte offset of the entry in the stream), and `fixup_verified`. An entry decoded from a buffer whose update-sequence check failed — including a buffer that declares no update-sequence array at all — carries `fixup_verified: false`, `content_incomplete: true` and `content_incomplete_reason: "indx_fixup_failed"`. An entry `parse_slack_space` found carries `from_slack: true`, `entry_flags: []`, an `entry_offset` pointing at its `$FILE_NAME` rather than at an entry header, and a `file_reference` read from the stale entry header in front of it where that header survives, else an empty string — never the placeholder `0-0`, which would read as MFT record 0. Every slack entry also carries `slack_status` — `copy_of_live_entry`, `reference_live_under_other_name`, `live_name_reference_unknown` or `no_live_entry` — set against the live entries decoded from the same stream, and `stale_copy_of_live_entry` (`true`, `false`, or `null` where the reference is gone and the name is live). On the graded volume the header in front of the first stale entry of a buffer is the directory's new end-of-index marker, written over it, so that entry's reference is genuinely gone. Where the scan stopped before the end of the stream, any buffer was torn, or any buffer read whole could not be walked, one further `ParsedRecord` is appended: `type: "I30ScanStatus"`, `record_type: "i30_scan_status"`, `name: "<source> (partially recovered)"`, the shared pairs `content_incomplete` and `inventory_incomplete`, each with a `_reason` — the stop reason (`indx_read_failed`, `indx_buffer_short_read`, `indx_record_size_unresolved` or `indx_buffer_truncated`), else `indx_buffer_unparsable` when a buffer could not be walked, else `indx_fixup_failed` — and a `_detail` sentence giving the torn and unparsable counts and saying that names absent from these entries are not evidence that no such file existed; `torn_buffers`, `buffers_unparsed` and `entries_recovered` counts; and the same sentence as `message`. It emits no `TimelineEvent` — the four `$FILE_NAME` timestamps live on the record and nowhere else — no hash, no `FileEntry`, and no link from an index entry to the `FileEntry` the MFT parser produced for the same record. In the processing log a stream that yielded nothing and an artifact it declined are the same zero-yield row. A selected artifact with no data source yields one `I30ScanStatus` named `<source> (not read)` with `read_incomplete` `volume_not_in_evidence` (the `$I30` stream the MFT parser emits from a bare `$MFT`, which carries `volume_not_in_evidence: true`) or `no_data_source`, `parent_file` where the stream names one, `entries_recovered: 0`, and both shared pairs with reason `unresolved_structure` and a `_detail` saying the directory's names are unknown, not absent.

**Cannot.** It cannot recover a deleted entry's file reference once NTFS has written over the header in front of it, which on the graded volume is what happened to the first stale entry of each buffer; it cannot recover a stale name whose four timestamps are not all inside 1980–2108 — zeroed, or set earlier by a tool — because that window is what keeps a byte-by-byte shape test from reading fragments as names (it rejected a one-character `h` on the graded volume); and it cannot recover a stale `$FILE_NAME` whose fixed part or name has been partly overwritten, since it requires both whole. It cannot prove a slack name is deleted: `no_live_entry` means only that nothing live in the decoded buffers matches it by reference and name (compared exactly, case included) — the resident `$INDEX_ROOT`, a buffer not read and the `$BITMAP` are not consulted — and a name whose reference was overwritten but is live is left undecided (`live_name_reference_unknown`); on the graded volume the two copies of the live `AAAAAAAAAAA.txt` in `test_dir`'s slack are labelled copies and `BBBBBBBBBBBBB-del.txt` `no_live_entry`. It cannot tell a live entry from a stale one: it does not read the directory's `$BITMAP`, so an `INDX` block the file system has freed — whose entries may all describe deleted files — is decoded as ordinary entries with `from_slack: false`, indistinguishable from the current directory listing. It cannot see a small directory: entries held in a resident `$INDEX_ROOT` never reach this module, because the MFT parser emits a `$I30` `SystemArtifact` only for a non-resident `$INDEX_ALLOCATION`, and nothing in the tree decodes `$INDEX_ROOT` entries. It cannot name the directory: the record carries the entry's `parent_reference` and nothing else, the `parent_file` the MFT parser put on the `SystemArtifact` is not copied down, and no path is built. It cannot say that part of one buffer was lost: an entry whose declared length is zero or overruns the used region ends that buffer's walk, and the entries after it in that buffer are neither decoded nor counted. Its slack heuristic does not check that the parent reference points at a directory. It does not check the entry's file reference against the MFT, does not de-duplicate an entry that appears in several buffers or against the `FileEntry` for the same record, publishes the `$FILE_NAME` timestamps without saying they are `$FILE_NAME` — the set that Windows updates only on rename and that a timestomping tool leaves alone — and emits no timeline event from any of them. A `$I30` stream exported under another file name (`Users_I30.bin`) is taken only as `RawEvidence` whose first bytes are `INDX`; as a `FileEntry` it is not recognised. A selected stream is swept sector by sector for `INDX` magic, 36 bytes at a time, however large it is. Its ceilings are the record-size window of 512 to 65,536 bytes and nothing else: there is no cap on the number of buffers, entries or slack candidates, and no cancellation or progress hook.

**Refuses.** It refuses to guess a record size. Where the update-sequence count and `allocated_size` cannot be reconciled to one plausible size — both fields implausible, or two USA candidates neither of which the record confirms — the scan stops with `indx_record_size_unresolved` rather than decode the following buffers at a guessed alignment, since a wrong alignment yields plausible-looking names and dates that belong to nothing. It refuses to parse a buffer it did not read whole: a record that would run past the end of the stream stops the scan with `indx_buffer_truncated`, and a `read_full` that returns fewer bytes than the record size stops it with `indx_buffer_short_read`, because a zero-padded `INDX` buffer parses into fabricated entries. It refuses to present an entry from a torn block as a verified directory record: a buffer whose update-sequence check fails is still decoded, but every entry from it carries `fixup_verified: false` and the `content_incomplete` pair, and the buffer is counted into the `I30ScanStatus` record, so a spliced name or timestamp cannot be read as a clean one. It refuses to let a stopped or torn scan pass as a complete listing: the status record exists because a name absent from a partial index is otherwise indistinguishable from a file that never existed in that directory. It refuses an entry whose `$FILE_NAME` attribute is shorter than 0x42 bytes, whose name length is zero or whose name runs past the attribute; and it refuses to underflow on a hostile entry length below 16, testing `attr_len + 16 <= entry_len` rather than subtracting. It refuses a slack candidate whose timestamps fall outside 1980–2108 or whose name holds `/` or NUL, and it refuses to publish a file reference for a slack entry whose header did not survive rather than print a placeholder. It refuses to let a selected stream with no data source pass as skipped or as an empty directory: it publishes the unread `I30ScanStatus` instead . Everything else it declines, it declines in silence: an artifact that fails the name, type or magic gate returns an empty list and leaves only the zero-yield row that a genuinely empty stream also leaves. The unit tests pin the recovery of a full 4 KiB block, the walk of two 8 KiB records at their own alignment, the stop on an indeterminate record size, the torn-block marking, the `name`-keyed `FileEntry` gate, the 512-byte update-sequence stride, a mid-stream read error as a stop, an unparsable buffer counted, and the status record's shared pairs. The slack pass is graded on a real volume — dfir_ntfs's `ntfs_index.raw.gz`, walked through the MFT parser as the pipeline walks it — where it recovers the deleted `BBBBBBBBBBBBB-del.txt` from `test_dir`'s index, exactly the three names dfir_ntfs's own carver finds in that buffer, and `test_dir` from the root's slack with its reference 39-1 read from the surviving header. That image is in the gitignored `reference/` corpus, not the committed tree; CI skips the test.

### `plugin.ntfs.logfile_parser`

**Reads.** The NTFS transaction log — the Log File Service's restart area and its ring of `RCRD` record pages — and it accepts the bytes only when they identify themselves. It subscribes to `FileSystem`, `FileEntry`, `RawEvidence` and `SystemArtifact` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, and it is not in the triage profile's enabled list. For a `FileEntry`, `RawEvidence` or `SystemArtifact` it requires a data source and asks `seance_core::file_detection::detect_file_type` for the first 512 bytes: only `NtfsLogFile` — the four bytes `RSTR` at offset 0 — passes, and passing sets the `content_confirmed` flag that decides whether a later failure is recorded. The `$LogFile` it ordinarily sees is the `FileEntry` for MFT record 2 that `seance_plugin_mft` emits with a run-list data source. For a `FileSystem` artifact the gate is different and weaker: a `subtype` other than `ntfs`, or a `filesystem_type` other than empty or `NTFS`, declines it; otherwise the module attempts to parse the volume's own data source from offset 0, where the boot sector is, and nothing confirms the content. `parse_logfile` then reads a 64-byte probe with `read_full` (at least 32 bytes must arrive); if it begins `RSTR` or `CHKD` and the 32-bit system page size at offset 16 is 512..=65,536 and a multiple of 512, that is the page size, otherwise 4,096 is used. Page 0 and page 1 are each read whole or not at all, and the first that parses as a restart page is used (`restart_page_used` 1 or 2). `apply_usa_fixup` runs first on a private copy: the page must be two or more whole 512-byte sectors, the USA offset 8..=506, the count exactly sectors + 1, and a `CRC4` marker four bytes past the array refuses the page as a DAX-protected variant; every sector's trailing two bytes must equal the sequence number and are replaced from the array. From the fixed-up page come the signature, `chkdsk_lsn`, system and log page sizes (both validated), the restart-area offset (≥ 8, a multiple of 8, inside the page), major and minor versions, and from the restart area `current_lsn`, `log_clients`, `flags`, `seq_number_bits`, `restart_area_length`, the client-array offset, the log `file_size`, `record_header_length` and `log_page_data_offset`, plus up to 64 client records of 160 bytes each with a name of at most 128 bytes. The logging area starts at twice the system page size and ends at the lesser of the declared `file_size` (or the source size when that is ≤ 0) and the source size. Each log page is read whole; one that begins `RCRD` or `CHKD` is fixed up and walked, and any other signature is passed over silently. Within a page, records start at the restart area's data offset when it is at least 40, less than the page and 8-aligned, else at 0x40; the free-space offset at 24 bounds the walk when it is sensible; each LFS record header — at least 48 bytes — yields `lsn` (zero ends the page), `client_previous_lsn`, `client_undo_next_lsn`, `client_data_length`, `client_id`, `record_type`, `transaction_id` and `flags`; and for `record_type` 1 with at least 32 bytes of client data available the NTFS operation header is decoded: redo and undo operation codes, offsets and lengths, target attribute, LCNs-to-follow, record offset, attribute offset, MFT cluster index, target VCN, and the first target LCN where one follows. Cross-checked against dfir_ntfs, libfsntfs and Windows Internals; no specification is vendored.

**Produces.** `ParsedRecord` artifacts only, all parented to the artifact it read. One per significant record — an NTFS client record whose decoded redo or undo operation code is non-zero — with `type: "NtfsLogFileRecord"`, `source: "$LogFile"`, a running `record_number`, `lsn` as `0x%016x`, `page_number` (the page's index from the start of the file, so the first record page of a 4 KiB-page log is page 2), `operation` (the redo code's name from a 38-entry table, `Unknown` past 0x25), `redo_operation` and `undo_operation` as numbers, `undo_operation_name`, `redo_data_length`, `undo_data_length`, `target_attribute`, `target_vcn`, `target_lcn` (`null` where no LCN followed), `transaction_id`, `ntfs_record_type` and `multi_page`. A record whose client data continues past the page carries `content_incomplete: true` with `content_incomplete_reason: "multi_page_record_not_reassembled"`, because its operation codes were read from the first-page fragment. Where the walk did not cover the whole logging area intact — any torn page, any page left part-walked, a page or record cap, a short read, or a declared size beyond the source — one `LogFileParseStatus` record precedes the journal records: `record_type: "logfile_parse_status"`, `name: "$LogFile (partially parsed)"`, the `content_incomplete` and `inventory_incomplete` pairs with the reasons joined by commas from `torn_pages_skipped`, `page_read_short`, `page_records_not_fully_walked`, `source_shorter_than_declared_log`, `page_scan_cap` and `record_cap`, the same sentence under `content_incomplete_detail`, `inventory_incomplete_detail` and `message`, and the counts `torn_pages`, `pages_part_walked`, `pages_scanned` and `records_parsed`. Where the bytes were confirmed as a transaction log and `parse_logfile` failed outright, the only output is a `LogFileParseStatus` named `$LogFile (not parsed)` with both pairs set to `unresolved_structure`, all four counts stated as 0, `parse_error` carrying the parser's message, and a sentence saying no journal operations from it are in the case and that this is not evidence none occurred. It emits no `TimelineEvent`, no `FileEntry`, and nothing from the restart page: the LSNs, versions, client names and `chkdsk_lsn` it decodes are logged at `info!` and published nowhere. `process` never returns an error, so this module has no `error` row in the processing log; an artifact it declined, an NTFS volume whose bytes are not a log, and a log with no significant record all leave the same zero-yield row.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell you what was renamed, deleted or written. The record is the operation code, its target VCN and LCN, an attribute index and a transaction number; the redo and undo payloads — where the `$FILE_NAME` of a rename, the index entry of a deletion, the bytes of a resident write actually are — are measured (`redo_data_length`, `undo_data_length`) and never decoded or published, and the `redo_offset`, `undo_offset`, `record_offset`, `attribute_offset`, `mft_cluster_index`, `lcns_to_follow`, `client_id`, `client_previous_lsn`, `client_undo_next_lsn` and `flags` fields it decodes are dropped before the record is built. No file name, no MFT record number and no path is on any record, so `COMPARISON.md`'s ✅ beside suites that render `$LogFile` as named file events describes a depth this module does not reach. It cannot date anything: LFS records carry no timestamp, it derives none, and it emits no timeline event. It cannot reassemble a transaction: the LSN chain (`client_previous_lsn`, `client_undo_next_lsn`) is read and discarded, a record that spills into the next page is decoded from its first fragment only and abandons the rest of that page, and the operations later in that page are never emitted — counted as `pages_part_walked`, not recovered. It cannot separate the current cycle of the ring from the previous one: page LSNs are not compared with the restart area's `current_lsn` or the sequence-number bits, so a record from before the log wrapped is published beside one from after it with nothing to tell them apart. It cannot find the `$LogFile` on a volume: the `FileSystem` subscription reads the volume's own bytes from offset 0, which is the boot sector, fails to find a restart page, and — the bytes never having been confirmed — returns nothing; the test `an_ntfs_volume_that_is_not_a_logfile_is_passed_over_silently` pins that this route yields nothing, so every `FileSystem` artifact costs two page reads for no output. It cannot recognise a log whose first page is `CHKD`: `detect_file_type` claims only `RSTR`, so a chkdsk-repaired log with a `CHKD` primary page is not a `$LogFile` to the gate even though `parse_restart_page` would accept it. It cannot read a DAX-protected page (`CRC4`), which it counts as torn rather than as unsupported. It cannot count what it skipped: a log page whose signature is neither `RCRD` nor `CHKD` is passed over and included in `pages_scanned` as though walked; a client record shorter than 32 bytes, or any record whose type is not 1, gets no operation and is silently excluded from `records_parsed`'s significant subset; and a page whose free-space offset is implausible is walked to its end, so stale records past the real free-space boundary are published as journal records. A record whose `client_data_length` is zero or not a multiple of 8 ends the page. Its ceilings are 4,096 records per page, 1,048,576 pages and 500,000 records in total, a 65,536-byte page, 64 clients and 128-byte client names; each cap is reported as a reason only when a whole page was still waiting. The processing-log counterpart of all this is that `process` never errors, so the only place a failed parse of a confirmed log is recorded is the status record itself. Its real-corpus baseline is one fixture: `test_data/LogFile_10.bin` decodes to a status record and exactly 124 significant records, and the test skips when the gitignored corpus is absent; `LogFile_7.bin`, `LogFile_10_large.bin`, `HD001_LogFile.dat` and `HD002.0_LogFile.dat` are run for absence of panic and nothing is asserted about their content.

**Refuses.** It refuses to answer a confirmed transaction log with silence. When the bytes began `RSTR` and no restart page parses — or the page sizes are invalid, or the page-size arithmetic overflows — it publishes a `LogFileParseStatus` naming the error, with every count stated as 0 rather than omitted, because a case with no journal records must be distinguishable as "the journal was never read" and not read as "the journal recorded no renames or deletes". It refuses, by the same token, to put that disclosure on every NTFS volume: a `FileSystem` artifact whose bytes were never established to be a log fails in silence, since a warning that fires everywhere discloses nothing. It refuses to read a torn page: a record page whose update-sequence check fails is skipped whole and counted in `torn_pages`, never decoded with the placeholder bytes in place, and the same fixup failure on both restart pages refuses the whole log. It refuses to parse a partially delivered page: a restart page or record page that `read_full` cannot fill is not parsed with its zero tail, and a short read inside the logging area stops the walk with `page_read_short` rather than treating the short page as the end of the log. It refuses to walk past a record it cannot step over — a client data length of zero or not a multiple of 8, a data end that overflows, or a next offset that does not advance — ending the page and counting it part-walked instead of guessing the next record's position. It refuses to let a size the restart area declares run past the evidence: the walk is bounded by the source and the shortfall is stamped `source_shorter_than_declared_log`, so pages lost in acquisition are not read as pages that never held an operation. It refuses a system or log page size outside 512..=65,536 or not a multiple of 512, a USA offset outside 8..=506, a USA count that does not match the page's sector count, and a restart-area offset that is not 8-aligned. It refuses `Noop`-only records and LFS-internal records — a client restart area, or anything not of type 1 — as artifacts, since they carry no operation. And it refuses to raise a `ModuleError` for any of this: the one artifact whose content it confirmed and could not read gets a record, and every other refusal — a non-NTFS file system, a file that does not begin `RSTR`, an artifact with no data — is an empty list and a zero-yield row that reads exactly like a log with nothing in it.

### `plugin.ntfs.mft_parser`

**Reads.** The `$MFT`, either as the whole NTFS window of a volume or as a bare `$MFT` file — and a loose file is accepted as one on nothing more than the four bytes `FILE` at offset 0. On a volume it takes the cluster size, the MFT record size and the `$MFT`'s own cluster from the boot sector rather than assuming them, parses record 0 there, and reads the table through record 0's own `$DATA` run list — the `$MFT` and nothing else of the volume. When the table's record 0 does not parse it reads the copy at the boot sector's `$MFTMirr` cluster instead and says so on the summary; when record 0's `$ATTRIBUTE_LIST` names extension records past the first sixteen it reads up to 65,536 records of the table through the runs already found to resolve them. It used to step the whole volume window a record at a time and publish every slot that began `FILE`, which put `$MFTMirr`'s copies and every older record a shadow copy's diff area preserves on the case as live files. A bare `$MFT` has no boot sector to ask, and falls back to 4,096-byte clusters and 1,024-byte records. Every record slot is read twice: a first pass builds the record-number-to-name-and-parent map that paths are reconstructed from, and the main pass reads the record itself. Inside a record it reads seven attribute types and no others — the first 32 bytes of `$STANDARD_INFORMATION`, which is the four FILETIMEs, and, in the 72-byte NTFS 3.x form, the `security_id` at 0x34; `$FILE_NAME`; `$ATTRIBUTE_LIST`; `$DATA`, resident and non-resident; `$INDEX_ROOT`, for its presence only; the run list of `$INDEX_ALLOCATION`; and a `$LOGGED_UTILITY_STREAM` named `$EFS` — and follows a resident `$ATTRIBUTE_LIST` into the extension MFT records it names for the `$DATA` extents and the `$INDEX_ALLOCATION:$I30` extents they hold, checking each one's own record number (an NTFS 3.1 header carries one; a 3.0, Windows 2000, header does not), its sequence, and that its base reference names the file that listed it before trusting it. The record number at header offset 0x2C is read only from a 3.1 header, one whose update sequence array starts at 0x30: in a 3.0 header that offset is inside the array. On a whole volume it also reads the contents of `$Bitmap` (record 6) through its run list and the boot sector at offset 0.

**Produces.** One `FileEntry` per record that carries a resident `$FILE_NAME`: the name, the reconstructed absolute path or a placeholder under `/$OrphanFiles` with the `orphan_reason` that put it there, `record_number` **and** `sequence_number` (both halves of the file reference, because the record number alone cannot tell "still that file" from "that slot now holds another"; on a volume the record number is the record's slot in the table, which is what a file reference indexes, and a header that names another number is carried beside it as `header_record_number`; from a bare `$MFT` it is the header's own number, except for an NTFS 3.0 record, whose header has none, which is numbered by its slot and says so with `record_number_source: slot`), the `mft_offset` (on a volume, the byte offset in the volume the table's runs put the record at), the logical size, and the file's content either as inline base64 for resident `$DATA` or as a list of byte runs into the filesystem window with `data_runs_complete` beside it. Those runs are reduced to the file's logical extent — cluster slack past `real_size` dropped, the never-written range `[initialized_size, real_size)` turned into a sparse hole — so what is hashed and served is the file rather than the clusters, and an LZNT1-compressed stream is instead published with a `compression`/`compression_unit_bytes` descriptor and reconstructed in memory up to 256 MiB. Beside the base file it emits one `FileEntry` per alternate data stream, named `basefile:stream` and parented to the filesystem because its runs are filesystem-relative, a `$I30` `SystemArtifact` per `$INDEX_ALLOCATION` — including one held wholly or partly in extension records, flagged `content_incomplete` (`unresolved_structure`, with no data source when nothing was recovered) when a listed extent could not be trusted — and one `TimelineEvent` for each of the eight timestamps it writes, each labelled with the attribute it came from (`SI_Created` through `FN_Accessed`) and carrying the timestomping verdict. An entry whose `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` is the 72-byte form carries its `security_id` as found — 0 included, which is no `$SDS` key — the key into `$Secure:$SDS` that the descriptor records and the USN journal also carry ; the file's page joins it to the descriptor from the same volume's store (see `plugin.windows.secure_sds`). Record 8's `$BadClus:$Bad` stream also carries its raw allocated runs as `bad_cluster_runs`, with `bad_cluster_runs_complete` and the volume's `cluster_size`, because its `data_runs` — the logical extent of a stream whose initialized size is 0 — is one sparse run with every bad cluster dropped. On a volume it also emits one `SlackSpace` region per live file whose slack holds any non-zero byte — the bytes from the file's logical end to the end of the cluster holding its last byte, read from the unnamed `$DATA`'s allocation runs — parented to the `FileSystem`, naming the file (`parent_file`, `parent_path`, `owner_artifact_id`) and stating that slack is allocated, not free space and not the file's content; only an in-use, non-directory, non-resident, uncompressed, unencrypted `$DATA` whose run list is complete from VCN 0 is offered, an all-zero tail is counted and not emitted, at most 250,000 regions are emitted per volume, and one `slack_space_summary` record counts what was offered, emitted, zero, unreadable and past the ceiling, and as `files_not_located` every live file with a tail that was not offered because its runs were compressed, encrypted, incomplete or shorter than its size. On DFTT #3 the region for `file-n-4.dat` covers the published `n-slack` bytes at image offset 4,128,229. Clusters allocated to a file past the one holding its last byte are not in the window. From a bare `$MFT` every non-resident stream — unnamed `$DATA`, alternate data stream, compressed or not — and every `$I30` stream is published with its run list and **no data source**, stamped `content_incomplete` with reason `unresolved_structure`, `volume_not_in_evidence: true` and a `_detail` sentence, because the clusters its runs name are on a volume that was not supplied and the same offsets in the `$MFT` file are other MFT records; only resident content is served. Every entry carries the `$SI`/`$FN` comparison as `timestamp_indicators`, each graded strong or weak and each weak one naming the ordinary operation that also produces it, with `timestomp_suspected` set only by a strong one. A record not in use is marked `deleted` with `deleted_recovery_source: mft`; an EFS file is marked `content_ciphertext: ntfs_efs`; and where records were unreadable or torn it emits an `mft_parse_summary` `ParsedRecord` carrying both counts against the total record slots — the same record says, on a volume, when the table was found other than whole from its own record 0: `mft_record0_source: mftmirr_record_0`, `mft_runs_complete: false` with the `mft_record_slots_unreached`, or `mft_located: false` with the reason — plus, on a volume, a downsampled `allocation_map` from `$Bitmap` and one `NtfsBootSector` record. Since `ROADMAP` §5.4 it also emits one `UnallocatedSpace` region per run of clusters that `$Bitmap` proves free, which is what points the automatic carver at a volume's free space — before it, the only regions in the product were the gaps a partition table leaves, so the free clusters inside a filesystem were never carved automatically at all. The regions' offsets are relative to the **volume**, which each one states on itself, and the `allocation_map` carries the pass's own arithmetic: how many runs were found, how many became regions, the bytes they cover, and the bytes any ceiling declined. The two ceilings default to 4,096 regions and 128 GiB of free space per volume; a lab changes them with `SEANCE_FREE_REGION_CAP` and `SEANCE_FREE_BYTE_CAP`, and the record publishes the ceilings actually applied with `free_region_cap_source` and `free_byte_cap_source` saying whether each was the default or configured.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell you what a deleted entry's bytes are. A clear IN_USE bit establishes that the record was free when the image was taken and nothing else — not when it was deleted, not by what, and not that the clusters its runs name still hold its own content, which is why every such entry carries `deleted_content_caveat: clusters_may_be_reallocated` and is stamped `content_incomplete`. It reads seven attribute types, so it cannot say where a junction, symlink or deduplicated file points (`$REPARSE_POINT` is never decoded), cannot report an object id, an extended attribute or a per-file security descriptor, and reads nothing of `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` past byte 32 but the `security_id` — the DOS attribute flags, the owner id, the quota charge and the update-sequence number are on no record it emits. It does not resolve a **non-resident** `$ATTRIBUTE_LIST` at all, flagging the file's runs incomplete instead, and it publishes only one name per record — Win32 or POSIX in preference to the DOS 8.3 alias — so a hard link's second name and second path are not emitted, and a record whose `$FILE_NAME` is absent or non-resident produces no entry whatsoever. Its caps are real limits and each one flags the record it truncates: 100 attributes per record, 64 extension MFT records per file, 10,000 runs per attribute list, 1,024 `$ATTRIBUTE_LIST` entries, 512 runs persisted in metadata, 255 path hops, a compression-unit exponent above 6 refused as corrupt, and 64 MiB of `$Bitmap` read into 65,536 buckets. It reads `$MFTMirr` only for record 0, and only when the table's own record 0 does not parse, so no other record this parser had to skip is recovered from the mirror, and a mirror copy of record 0 older than the table can name runs the table has since outgrown. It does not recover `FILE` records that lie outside the table — an older copy in free space, in slack, or in a shadow copy's diff area is not read at all (the VSS module publishes the records a shadow copy's own `$MFT` holds that differ from the live one). And when a volume's `$MFT` cannot be located — no NTFS boot sector, or neither record 0 nor its mirror copy parses — it reads no record rather than scanning for signatures, so a volume with a destroyed record 0 and mirror yields no file inventory from this module. It cannot stop a re-serve from reading a bare `$MFT`'s bytes: it attaches no data source to a non-resident stream there, but the API's content resolver applies any published `data_runs` against the artifact's parent chain, and for a bare `$MFT` that chain ends at the `$MFT` file (open in the resolver). And its timestomping verdict is deliberately narrow — a tool that rewrites a single `$SI` field at full precision leaves a weak indicator and no verdict, which is the price of the rule that took 4,054 verdicts on a stock Windows XP install to 0 with all 4,054 observations kept. Its NTFS 3.0 (Windows 2000) handling — slot numbering of a bare `$MFT` and extension-record resolution — is graded on one real Windows 2000 Professional SP3 volume against The Sleuth Kit (every one of its 6,604 records numbered by slot, the paths of all 6,578 names TSK lists, and the cluster lists of the four files whose attributes continue in extension records), but that volume holds metadata only: no resolved file's content was hashed, it has no non-resident `$ATTRIBUTE_LIST`, and it is one volume.

**Refuses.** It refuses to publish a `FILE` record that is not in the volume's `$MFT`: a copy found anywhere else on the volume is not a live record, and publishing it under the number in its header made record 77 of dfir_ntfs's Server 2003 shadow-copy volume — deleted, sequence 2 — a live file a second time from an in-use copy at volume offset 2,208,768, published every record of that volume four to five times (405 entries for 87 records) and let whichever copy was read first name a directory in every path beneath it. It refuses to read a record whose update-sequence-array fixup failed: the tail of every sector still holds the placeholder rather than the record's own bytes, so names, MACB times and cluster runs decoded from it are partly invented, and a fabricated name here becomes a fabricated path for every file beneath it — such records are skipped, counted, and their count published on the `mft_parse_summary` record so their absence is visible. It refuses to walk a parent hop whose record is missing, holds a sequence number the reference does not name, or is not a directory; the file is filed under `/$OrphanFiles` with the reason, because following the record number alone put 1,419 entries on the NIST Data Leakage image underneath a `.lnk`. It refuses to attach the on-disk compressed clusters as a compressed stream's content when it cannot reconstruct the plaintext — over the 256 MiB ingest cap, on a decompression failure, with no run list, or with an out-of-range compression exponent — because hashing and indexing them under the file's name produces bytes that are not the file's and a digest that matches nothing; each of the four gets its own reason code rather than one label that claims the data is merely too large. It refuses to fabricate volume geometry: a bare `$MFT` gets no allocation map at all, a short `$Bitmap` read never shrinks the volume (the boot sector's cluster count stands and the shortfall is published as `allocation_map_incomplete`), and an unreachable backup boot sector is recorded as unassessed rather than as a mismatch. It refuses to call the tail of a short `$Bitmap` free: a bitmap read short leaves a run of zero bytes and a zero bit means free, so no free-space region is ever emitted past the last cluster the bytes it actually held can speak for, and those clusters are published as unassessed instead. Nor does it claim that a cluster the bitmap calls free was never written to — that is the reason to carve it — nor that nothing holds it now, since a shadow copy may and `$BadClus` may; and the unused tail of a live file is slack, is not free space, and gets no free region — it gets a `SlackSpace` region of its own type, so no free-space total can count it. And it refuses to re-parse its own output — any artifact carrying a `record_number`, which every entry it publishes (its own `$MFT` among them) carries, returns nothing. The name is not the test: an exported `$MFT` ingested under that name carries no `record_number` and is parsed.

### `plugin.ntfs.usnjrnl_parser`

**Reads.** The `$UsnJrnl:$J` change-journal stream of an NTFS volume, **selected by name and never by content**. It subscribes to `FileEntry`, `RawEvidence` and `SystemArtifact` and asks for random access; `usn_journal_stream_label` then reads five metadata keys — `stream_name`, `name` (falling back to `file_name`), `source_path` (falling back to `path`) — and accepts the artifact when `stream_name` is `$J`, or when the last segment of the name or the path, split on `/`, `\`, `:` or `_` and stripped of a trailing `.bin`, is `$J`, or is `J` in a string containing `UsnJrnl`. That covers the ADS spelling the MFT parser publishes (`$UsnJrnl:$J` with `stream_name` `$J`) and the exported-file spellings (`…/$Extend/$UsnJrnl/$J`, `…/$UsnJrnl_$J`); and for a `RawEvidence` artifact only, it additionally accepts any input whose name or path merely contains `UsnJrnl`, which is how a loose dump an examiner added by hand is taken. The gate used to read `file_name` alone, which the MFT parser never writes, so a normal NTFS ingest produced no USN history at all while every unit test passed. Nothing about the bytes is checked before they are walked. At most 536,870,912 bytes (512 MiB, `MAX_USN_BYTES`) are staged; `$J` is a sparse stream whose purged head reads back as zeros while live records accumulate at the tail, so when the stream is larger than that the window begins at exactly `size − 536,870,912` and the earlier bytes are never opened. Short reads are looped until the window is full and a premature EOF truncates the buffer — unread bytes are never treated as zero records — while a read error aborts the whole parse. The walk is a flat forward scan of that buffer: a four-byte little-endian `RecordLength`; a length of zero is padding and advances 8 bytes; a length that is not a multiple of 8, or below 60, is counted and advances 8 bytes; a length running past the buffer ends the walk. `MajorVersion` at offset 4 dispatches to one of three readers and nothing else is tried. V2 and V3 share a layout — a 64-bit file reference and parent reference at 0x08 and 0x10 for V2, both widened to 128 bits at 0x08 and 0x18 for V3, shifting every later field by 16 — from which it reads the USN, the update FILETIME, the 32-bit reason bitmask, `SourceInfo`, the security id, the file attributes, and the name's byte length and offset, decoding the name as UTF-16LE from that offset within the record. V4 (`USN_RECORD_V4`, [MS-FSCC] 2.3.58) is read on its own 64-byte header: the two 128-bit references, the USN, the reason, `SourceInfo`, `RemainingExtents` at 0x38, `NumberOfExtents` at 0x3C and `ExtentSize` at 0x3E, then that many entries of that stride from 0x40, each an eight-byte signed offset and an eight-byte signed length.

**Produces.** One `UsnJournalEntry` `ParsedRecord` per decoded record (`record_type` `usn_journal`), parented to the stream it was read from, carrying the USN as a decimal string, the file name, the file and parent references, the raw reason bitmask as `0x%08X` alongside `reason_names` — the 24 documented reason flags the record's bits select, from `DATA_OVERWRITE` through `DESIRED_STORAGE_CLASS_CHANGE` and `CLOSE` — a single `primary_operation` reduced from those bits, `source_info` as raw hex, the `major.minor` version and the record's declared length. A V2 or V3 record also carries the security id as a bare integer, the file attributes as raw hex, and the update time as an RFC 3339 string, omitted entirely where the FILETIME was zero, before 1970 (11,644,473,600 seconds of FILETIME epoch difference) or at or past the year 10000 (253,402,300,800 Unix seconds) — never rendered as a 1970 date. A V4 record instead carries its changed byte ranges as `extents`, each an offset and a length, with `remaining_extents`, and `extents_complete`; where `RemainingExtents` is non-zero the record is stamped `content_incomplete` with reason `v4_extents_continue_in_later_records`, because otherwise its extent list reads as the complete set of byte ranges that change touched. Then one `TimelineEvent` per record that has a timestamp, stamped `USN Journal Entry` to whole seconds, its `short_desc` reading `USN: <primary_operation> on <file name>` and its details carrying the USN, the full reason-name list, the file name, the file reference and the numeric attributes. Where the parse fell short of the stream in any way, one `UsnJournalWindow` status record (`record_type` `usn_journal_status`) states which way: the stream's logical size, the offset the window began at, the bytes parsed, the records parsed, the count of unusable record lengths, the count of records that would not decode, whether the window ended mid-record, and a single `content_incomplete_reason` of `cap_reached`, `short_read` or `unresolved_structure` in that precedence — with the sentence that a rename or delete absent from these entries is not evidence that it did not happen. No status record is emitted when nothing fell short — but that silence has two causes and does not separate them: a journal read whole with every record decoded, and a journal that was read whole and held nothing at all, a wholly purged or deliberately cleared `$J` whose zero bytes are stepped over as padding and counted nowhere. In the second case the module produces no artifact of any kind.

**Cannot.** **A USN record proves that NTFS wrote a change record, and nothing more.** It cannot say who made the change: the journal carries no user, no SID, no session and no process, and the `SecurityId` it does carry is published as a bare integer and never resolved to an owner — this product can resolve one, from `$Secure:$SDS` in a separate module, and nothing joins a journal entry to it. `SourceInfo` — the field that distinguishes a change made by a background service, a replication agent or a backup from one made by a person — is published as raw hex and decoded into words nowhere. It cannot say a file existed with that name at that path: there is no path in these records at all. The parent is a reference, never resolved against the MFT, so a record names a file name and a number; and the name is the journal's own bytes decoded UTF-16LE lossily, so invalid code units become U+FFFD with no marker. It cannot pair a rename. `RENAME_OLD_NAME` and `RENAME_NEW_NAME` are separate records and nothing joins them, so the journal's account of "X became Y" is two rows the examiner must pair, and `primary_operation` flattens both to `RENAME` with the direction visible only in `reason_names`. It cannot give a V4 record a name or a time — it has neither, and inventing one from the extent bytes at the V3 offsets is refused — and it does not pair a V4 range record with the later V3 close record that would carry them, so a V4 record's subject file is identified by reference number alone and appears on no timeline. A V4 extent is published exactly as read, a signed offset and a signed length, with no check that either is sensible, and the number of ranges a record may declare is bounded only by the record's own length. `primary_operation` is a one-label reduction in a fixed precedence — create, delete, rename, data-modify, security-change, close — so a record carrying both a create and a delete bit reports only the create, which is what the delete-against-a-live-MFT-record comparison selects on, and any record whose bits fall outside those six reports `UNKNOWN` even where `reason_names` names the change (a `BASIC_INFO_CHANGE`-only record reads `UNKNOWN`). Reason bits outside its table of 24 are not named and not counted, surviving only in the raw hex. It cannot tell one kind of missing timestamp from another: zero, pre-1970 and year-10000-or-later all render as an absent field, with no reason and no count, so a timestomped record and a corrupt one are indistinguishable on the record — and a record with no timestamp produces no timeline event, so the timeline holds fewer entries than the journal holds records without that being a shortfall in the reading. What does reach the timeline is stamped to whole seconds, so the 100 ns precision on the record itself cannot order two changes inside one second.
