A name it could not read reads as a name the journal did not hold: a name length that is odd, or a name whose offset and length run past the record's declared end, yields an empty `file_name` with no error, no counter and no marker, and the declared name length is never published. The file reference's form depends on its data and is unlabelled: a reference whose high 64 bits are zero — every V2 reference among them — is printed as decimal `record-sequence`, while a 128-bit reference is printed as hexadecimal `LO-HI`, and only the record's `version` field distinguishes them. It cannot tell you how much history the journal discarded. The purged, deallocated head is walked eight bytes at a time as zero-length padding and never counted, the `journal_size` it reports is the sparse logical size and not the live history, and `$Max` — which holds the maximum size and allocation delta the volume was configured for — is never read, so nothing says how much retention the journal had. A journal that is entirely zero is therefore read as a journal that recorded nothing, and it produces no entries, no status record and no artifact at all. It performs no continuity check on the USN values themselves: a gap in the sequence, which is what an overwritten or deliberately cleared region looks like, is not detected, not counted and not reported. It cannot be reached at all except by name: an unrecognised spelling of the stream is skipped silently, with no artifact and no decision recorded, and a stream it does recognise but that arrives with no data source is filed under the run's declined inputs — indistinguishable from an artifact this module was never interested in. A read error is worse: the whole window is buffered before anything is parsed, so an I/O error at any byte discards every record already read and returns before one artifact is built. One unreadable byte therefore renders up to 512 MiB of journal as a volume with no USN history, and the only trace is an error row in the run's processing log — there is no refusal record of the kind the capture and prefetch readers publish. Its ceilings: 536,870,912 bytes staged, and when that applies the parse begins at that exact byte offset with **no search for a record boundary** — its only resynchronisation is the 8-byte step and three plausibility tests (a length that is a multiple of 8, a length of at least 60, and a major version of 2, 3 or 4), so the first record in a capped window may be read from mid-record bytes; 60 bytes minimum per record, 76 for a V3 and 64 for a V4, below which the record is counted undecodable; 16 bytes minimum per V4 extent entry, checked only where the record declares at least one. There is no cap on records emitted. Of these, only the byte cap reaches the status record, and it reaches it as a window start rather than as a limit; the record-size minima appear on nothing, only their consequences as two counts. And where the length test fails it resynchronises 8 bytes on rather than stopping, so an unknown span of the journal is stepped over and the records inside it are missing from the case, not absent from the volume's history — counted as `invalid_record_lengths`, with neither the offset nor the reason published for it or for any undecodable record; both go to the log alone. A window ending in fewer than eight bytes drops them without a mark of any kind.

**Refuses.** It refuses to read `$UsnJrnl`'s other streams as change history — with one gap it is better to state than to imply away. A `stream_name` of `$Max`, or a name or path ending `:$Max`, is declined; so is the base `$UsnJrnl` record with its unnamed `$DATA`, which simply does not name the `$J` stream. Neither holds USN records, and decoding them would either fail the module or invent history. But for a `RawEvidence` input the loose-dump rule accepts anything whose name or path contains `UsnJrnl`, so a hand-added dump spelled `$UsnJrnl` or `$UsnJrnl_$Max` is accepted and walked; only the `:$Max` spelling and the `stream_name` key are refused there. It refuses to guess at a record version: a major version other than 2, 3 or 4 is not read at nearby offsets but counted undecodable, with the version number in the log. It refuses to read a V4 extent array it cannot trust — an `ExtentSize` under 16 bytes cannot hold an offset and a length, and a declared extent count whose array runs past the record is a truncated record — and in both cases errors rather than reading the extents it can see, because a partial range list presented as a range list is a false statement about which bytes of a file changed. It refuses to fabricate a V4 timestamp or file name, leaving both empty, and refuses to put a record with no time on the timeline at all rather than dating it 1970. It refuses to treat unread bytes as zeros: a short read truncates the buffer and is published, and a genuine I/O error fails the module closed — though closed here means nothing at all is published, not that a refusal is. It refuses to report a partial parse as a whole one, which is the shape of the whole reader — the byte cap, a short stream, a window ending mid-record, an unusable record length and an undecodable record body are each counted and published, because history missing from this journal is read as "this file was never renamed, never deleted". It emits no status record when nothing fell short; that silence is not a claim that history was held, because a journal whose bytes are all zero falls short of nothing and holds nothing.

### `plugin.os.freedesktop_thumbnails`

**Reads.** Every file it is handed, and it decides by content, not by name. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent` with `InputCapability::Stream`, is not in the triage profile, and has no name or path gate at all: for every artifact with a data source it calls `read_capped`, which allocates the lesser of the declared size and 64 MiB and reads that much, and only then checks the first eight bytes for the PNG signature `89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A`. A file that is not a PNG yields nothing after that read. A PNG is walked chunk by chunk from offset 8 — a 32-bit big-endian length, a four-byte type, the data, and four bytes of CRC that are skipped and never verified — until an `IDAT` or `IEND` chunk is met, which is what proves the whole header was present, or until a chunk's declared length runs past the bytes held, which ends the walk short. In `tEXt` chunks only, the keyword before the first NUL and the text after it are read, and four keywords are kept: `Thumb::URI`, `Thumb::MTime`, `Thumb::Mimetype` and `Software`; `zTXt` and `iTXt` chunks, which carry the same keys compressed or in UTF-8, are not read, and no other `Thumb::` key (`Thumb::Size`, `Thumb::Image::Width`, `Thumb::Image::Height`, `Thumb::Document::Pages`, `Thumb::Movie::Length`) is kept. The URI is what makes it a thumbnail: a PNG with a `Thumb::URI` is one, and the file's MD5-of-URI name, the `normal/`, `large/`, `x-large/`, `xx-large/` or `fail/` directory it sits in, and the `.cache/thumbnails/` path are used for nothing except one decision — whether a PNG whose header was cut short and carries no URI is worth a marker (see Produces). The pixel data is never decoded and the thumbnail image is not attached to anything.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per PNG carrying a `Thumb::URI`, parented to the file artifact, with `type: "FreedesktopThumbnail"`, `subtype: "freedesktop_thumbnail"`, `uri` verbatim, `original_path` (the URI with a leading `file://` removed and percent-decoded), `name` (that path's last component), `source_mtime` as a signed integer only where `Thumb::MTime` parsed as one, `mime_type` from `Thumb::Mimetype`, and `software`. Where the chunk walk did not reach `IDAT` or `IEND` — because the read was short or because the file itself ends inside its header — the record also carries `content_incomplete: true`, `bytes_read`, `declared_size` and a `content_incomplete_reason` of `cap_reached` or `short_read` when the bytes never arrived and `unresolved_structure` when every declared byte did and the structure still ended early, since a missing `Thumb::MTime` on such a record means "not read", not "not written". Where the header was cut short and no URI was found, one `DesktopArtifactParseStatus` record is produced instead — `artifact_kind: "FreedesktopThumbnail"`, `entries_emitted: 0`, the byte counts and the same three-way reason — but only where something says the PNG could be a thumbnail: a `Thumb::MTime` or `Thumb::Mimetype` already read, no `path` metadata at all (a loose or carved file), or a `path` containing `/.cache/thumbnails/` or `/.thumbnails/`; a cut PNG at any other known path yields nothing, because on the NIST Data Leakage image Windows Installer's `/Config.Msi/*.rbf` rollback files each gained a thumbnail marker this way. A whole PNG with no URI yields nothing, so an ordinary image never gains a finding. It emits no `TimelineEvent` — `source_mtime` is the original file's modification time and goes on the record only — no image data, no hash of the thumbnail, and no path of its own. `process` never returns an error.

**Cannot.** It cannot avoid reading everything. With no name, path, extension or size gate ahead of the signature check, every `FileEntry` and `FileContent` artifact in the case is read up to 64 MiB through `read_capped` before the first eight bytes are examined — a 60 MiB executable, a database, a video's first 64 MiB — so this module costs a full read of the evidence's files to find PNGs, and every byte of it is discarded for anything that is not one. It cannot read a thumbnail whose keys are in `zTXt` or `iTXt`: only `tEXt` is decoded, and a thumbnailer that wrote its metadata compressed or as UTF-8 produces a PNG this module calls an ordinary image and says nothing about. It cannot recover the thumbnail's size class, the `fail/<thumbnailer>/` marker that records a file the thumbnailer could not render, the width and height, the document page count or the movie length, since none of those keys is kept and the directory is not read. It cannot verify the file: the CRC of every chunk is skipped, the file name is not checked against the MD5 of the URI the spec derives it from, and a PNG whose `Thumb::URI` was edited is a thumbnail of whatever the edit says. It cannot say when the thumbnail was made — the PNG's own `tIME` chunk is not read and the file's timestamps are not carried — so `source_mtime` dates the original file, not the viewing of it, and no timeline event is emitted for either. It cannot say whether the original still exists, and it cannot show the image: the pixels are not decoded, not attached, and not hashed. It cannot resolve a non-`file://` URI, which is percent-decoded and published as a path regardless of scheme. It cannot name the user, and carries no path on the record. Its cap is 64 MiB, and a PNG larger than that whose header lies within the first 64 MiB is parsed whole and stamped `cap_reached` anyway, because the stamp follows the byte count, not the walk. Its `content_incomplete` stamps carry no `content_incomplete_detail`, so the examiner-facing incompleteness reader shows the reason code without the sentence that lives in `message`.

**Refuses.** It refuses to call a PNG a thumbnail on the strength of its location: the URI in the header is the only thing that makes one, and a whole PNG without it — in the thumbnail cache or anywhere else — yields nothing rather than a finding on every image in the evidence. It refuses, equally, to let a cut thumbnail vanish: a PNG whose header the walk did not finish is reported as possibly-a-thumbnail when its path, the absence of a path, or a `Thumb::` key already read makes that plausible, because a thumbnail of a deleted file is the kind of evidence that disappears without trace otherwise. It refuses to name the wrong fault for that shortfall: a file delivered whole that ends inside its own header is `unresolved_structure`, a property of the evidence, and only bytes that never arrived are `short_read` or `cap_reached`, because the wrong reason sent an examiner after an acquisition fault that did not exist. It refuses to publish a `source_mtime` that did not parse as an integer, and refuses to parse the pixel data or any chunk beyond the header. It refuses to panic: a chunk length that overflows or overruns ends the walk. Every refusal is silent — an empty list and a zero-yield processing-log row — and no record says a candidate was passed over. The tests pin the URI and MTime read, silence on an ordinary PNG, the marker on a cut PNG in a cache path, silence on a cut PNG at a known non-cache path, and the absence of any stamp on a whole thumbnail; no thumbnail from a real desktop is in the tree.

### `plugin.os.linux_trash`

**Reads.** A Freedesktop Trash `.trashinfo` record — the small INI file the desktop writes beside the trashed file's copy in `~/.local/share/Trash/info/` or a volume's `.Trash-<uid>/info/`. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent` with `InputCapability::Stream` and is not in the triage profile. The gate is the artifact's `name` metadata, reduced to its last `/`-separated component and lower-cased, ending in `.trashinfo`; the `path` is not consulted, so a `.trashinfo` anywhere on any file system passes and one the ingest named otherwise does not. An artifact with no data is passed over. The content is read through `read_capped` up to 64 MiB, a shorter result than the declared size being remembered as a short read, decoded lossily as UTF-8, and scanned line by line for `key=value` pairs: a trimmed key of `Path` sets the raw path and `DeletionDate` sets the date, the last occurrence of each winning, and every other line — including the `[Trash Info]` section header, which is never checked for — is ignored. The path is percent-decoded (`%XX` with two hex digits; a malformed escape is passed through verbatim) and the bytes re-read lossily as UTF-8. The date is kept as the string found and, in addition, converted to Unix seconds by a hand-written ISO-8601 reader: `YYYY-MM-DD` then `T` or a space then `HH[:MM[:SS]]`, month 1–12 and day 1–31 checked but not against the month, fractional seconds dropped, a trailing `Z` or `z` meaning UTC, a `±hh:mm`, `±hhmm` or `±hh` offset subtracted to reach UTC, and a value with no designator treated as UTC. It does not open the trashed file itself, the `files/` sibling, the `directorysizes` file, or the trash directory.

**Produces.** Exactly one `ParsedRecord` per `.trashinfo` that carries a `Path=` line, parented to the file artifact, with `type: "TrashEntry"`, `subtype: "linux_trash"`, `original_path` (percent-decoded), `name` (the last path component of that), and where a `DeletionDate=` line was found `deletion_date` (the string as written) and, where that string parsed, `date` as Unix seconds. Where the read fell short of the declared size the record itself carries `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason` of `cap_reached` or `short_read`, `bytes_read` and `declared_size`, because the `DeletionDate` line may lie past the point the source stopped and a missing date must not read as a record the desktop wrote without one. Where no `Path=` line was found and the read was short, one `DesktopArtifactParseStatus` record is produced instead — `artifact_kind: "linux_trash"`, `entries_emitted: 0`, the byte counts, the reason — so a deleted file whose record was cut before its path is not erased from the case; where no `Path=` line was found and the file was read whole, nothing is produced, because a whole file with no path is not a trash record. It emits no `TimelineEvent`, no link to the trashed content in `files/`, no statement of whether that content still exists, and no hash. `process` never returns an error, and a declined artifact leaves only a zero-yield processing-log row.

**Cannot.** It cannot give you the deletion time in UTC, though `date` looks like it does. The Freedesktop Trash specification says `DeletionDate` is written in the user's local time with no zone designator, and `parse_iso8601_to_unix` treats a designator-less value as UTC, so `date` is the local wall clock re-labelled as UTC and is wrong by the machine's offset from it — up to fourteen hours — while the unit test `trashinfo_decodes_path_and_parses_date` pins exactly that reading (`14:30:00` → `1672929000`, the UTC epoch). The verbatim `deletion_date` string is on the record and is the value an examiner should quote. It cannot say who deleted the file: the `.Trash-<uid>` directory name, the owning user, and the trash directory's path are not read, and the record carries no path of its own, only its parent artifact's id. It cannot say where a relative path points: on a non-home volume the spec allows `Path` relative to the volume's root, and the module publishes the string as decoded without resolving it. It cannot say whether the file is still in the trash, whether `files/<name>` exists or matches, whether the trash was emptied, or what size the trashed item was; it does not pair the info record with its content, does not read `directorysizes`, and does not carry the `.trashinfo` file's own timestamps. It cannot validate the record: the `[Trash Info]` header is not required, a key appearing twice takes the last value silently, and a `Path` that is not percent-encoded as the spec requires is accepted as-is. Its date reader checks day 1–31 against no month, accepts `2023-02-31`, and returns nothing — no `date` key, no note — for a value it cannot read, so a malformed date and an absent date look alike. Its cap is 64 MiB, on a file that is normally under a hundred bytes. And the `content_incomplete` stamp on a short record carries no `content_incomplete_detail`, which is the only key the examiner-facing incompleteness reader displays as a sentence, so what the examiner sees is the reason code alone.

**Refuses.** It refuses to erase a deleted file over a short read. A `.trashinfo` whose bytes stopped before the `Path=` line still yields a `DesktopArtifactParseStatus` record naming the file and the shortfall, because returning nothing would remove that deletion from the case; and one whose `Path=` arrived but whose `DeletionDate=` may not have is stamped `content_incomplete` so the absent date is not read as a record the desktop wrote undated. It refuses to name the wrong fault: the reason is `cap_reached` when the declared size exceeds the 64 MiB cap and `short_read` only when the source itself stopped, since a hard-coded `short_read` once sent an examiner after a broken image that did not exist. It refuses a file read whole that carries no `Path=` line — that is not a trash record, and it produces nothing rather than a record with an empty path. It refuses to guess at a date it cannot parse: no `date` key is written, and the original string is kept verbatim. It refuses any file whose name does not end `.trashinfo`, in silence. It refuses to panic on malformed input, returning an empty list instead. The tests pin percent-decoding, the naive and offset date readings, the short-read marker on the record, the cap-versus-short distinction, and the two no-path outcomes; no `.trashinfo` from a real desktop is in the tree.

### `plugin.os.recent_files`

**Reads.** The GTK recently-used list — `recently-used.xbel`, the XBEL bookmark file GTK applications keep in `~/.local/share/` — and it identifies it by name alone. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent` with `InputCapability::Stream`, is not in the triage profile, and accepts an artifact only when its `name` metadata, reduced to its last `/`-separated component and lower-cased, is exactly `recently-used.xbel`; the `path` is not consulted, and `.recently-used.xbel` (the older dotfile location) or a `.xbel` under any other name is not accepted. An artifact with no data is passed over. The content is read through `read_capped` up to 64 MiB, a shorter result than the declared size being remembered as a short read, and decoded lossily as UTF-8. It is not parsed as XML. The text is scanned for each occurrence of the literal `<bookmark ` and the `>` that ends that start tag; from the tag text four double-quoted attributes are pulled by a `key="` search — `href`, `added`, `modified` and `visited` — and the five predefined XML entities are unescaped in each. The region from the end of that tag to the earlier of the next `<bookmark ` or the next `</bookmark>` is then searched for the first `<bookmark:application ` tag and its `name` attribute. The `href` has a leading `file://` stripped and is percent-decoded. Nothing else in the file is read: not the `<mime:mime-type>`, not the `<bookmark:groups>`, not the application's `exec`, `modified` or `count` attributes, not a second application on the same bookmark, and not single-quoted attribute values.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per `<bookmark ` tag found, parented to the file artifact, with `type: "RecentFileEntry"`, `subtype: "recent_file"`, and, each only where present, `uri` (the `href` with `file://` removed and percent-decoded — other schemes are left intact), `added`, `modified` and `visited` as the attribute strings verbatim (ISO-8601 text as GTK wrote it, not converted to an epoch and not published under `date`), and `application`, the `name` of the first `<bookmark:application>` in the bookmark's region. `name` is the last path component of the URI, or the literal `recent file` where there was no `href`. Where the read fell short of the declared size, one `DesktopArtifactParseStatus` record is appended with `artifact_kind: "Recently-used bookmarks"`, the count of entries emitted, the byte counts, `max_text_bytes`, and a reason of `cap_reached` or `short_read`. It emits no `TimelineEvent`, no user attribution, no path of its own, and no hash. `process` never returns an error; a file it does not claim, an artifact without data and a file with no bookmarks all leave the same zero-yield processing-log row.

**Cannot.** It cannot put a recent file on the timeline: `added`, `modified` and `visited` are copied as strings and never parsed, so no epoch, no `date` key and no `TimelineEvent` is produced, and a viewer that sorts by time has nothing to sort on. It cannot say which application last opened a file when more than one is listed: only the first `<bookmark:application>` in the region is read, its `modified` and `count` attributes — the number of times and the last time that application opened the file — are never read, and the second and later applications are dropped without a note. It cannot read the MIME type, the groups, or a `private` flag. It cannot parse XML: an attribute in single quotes is missed, an attribute value ends at the first literal `"` (an escaped `&quot;` survives and is unescaped to `"`), a literal `>` inside an attribute value ends the tag early because the tag is cut at the first `>` after `<bookmark `, a `<bookmark ` inside a comment is a bookmark, and an `href` whose value contains an entity other than the five predefined ones is published with the entity in it. Its region logic stops at the next `<bookmark ` as well as at `</bookmark>`, which is what makes a self-closing bookmark work, but it also means the first application of a bookmark that closes late can be attributed to the wrong entry when the document is malformed. It cannot say whose list this is — no path, no user — and cannot see a list under the older `.recently-used.xbel` name or any application's private XBEL. It cannot distinguish a file that no longer exists from one that does; the URI is a string it never resolves. Its cap is 64 MiB. And its status record carries its sentence in `message`, not in `content_incomplete_detail`, so the examiner-facing incompleteness reader shows the reason code and no sentence.

**Refuses.** It refuses to let a short read pass as the whole list: the recently-used file is an inventory of every document the desktop saw opened, so a read that returns fewer bytes than the source declares appends a `DesktopArtifactParseStatus` record carrying the number of entries that were emitted and the bytes that were and were not read, with `cap_reached` distinguished from `short_read`. It refuses to invent a field: a bookmark with no `href` gets no `uri`, no `name` beyond the literal `recent file`, and no attempt at a path; an attribute that is absent is absent from the record rather than empty. It refuses to convert a timestamp it has not parsed — the strings are published as found. It refuses any file not named exactly `recently-used.xbel`, in silence, and refuses to fall back to the `path`. It refuses to panic: a truncated tag, a bookmark with no closing `>`, or non-UTF-8 content ends the scan or is decoded lossily and returns what was found. The test `xbel_yields_uri_and_application` pins the URI, the three attribute strings and the application name from a synthetic document; `a_short_read_xbel_emits_an_incomplete_marker` pins the marker. No real GTK file is in the tree.

### `plugin.os.shell_history`

**Reads.** A user's shell history file, chosen by its name alone. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent` with `InputCapability::Stream`, and it is not in the triage profile. The gate is the artifact's `name` metadata — not its `path` — reduced to its last `/`-separated component and lower-cased, which must be one of exactly five strings: `.bash_history`, `.zsh_history`, `.sh_history`, `zsh_history` or `bash_history`. An artifact with no data source is passed over. The content is read through `read_capped` up to 64 MiB (`MAX_TEXT_BYTES`), and a result shorter than the source's declared `size()` is remembered as a short read. The bytes are decoded as UTF-8 lossily and split on line endings, empty lines skipped, each line numbered from 1 over the whole file including the lines that carry no command. Three line shapes are recognised. A line beginning `: ` with a `;` after it is a zsh `EXTENDED_HISTORY` entry, `: <epoch>:<elapsed>;<command>`: the text before the first `:` of the metadata is parsed as a signed 64-bit epoch, the command is everything after the first `;`, and the shell is recorded as `zsh` whatever the file was called; a line with the prefix but no `;` falls through to the plain-command path, and a line with the prefix and `;` but an empty command is dropped with no record at all. A line beginning `#` whose remainder, trimmed, parses as a signed 64-bit integer is a bash `HISTTIMEFORMAT` stamp and is held for the next command line; any other `#` line is a command. Every other non-empty line is a command, dated by the held stamp if there is one and undated otherwise, with the shell taken from the file name — `zsh` where the lower-cased basename contains `zsh`, `bash` for everything else including `.sh_history`. It reads no `HISTFILE` setting, no `fish_history`, no `.python_history`, `.mysql_history`, `.psql_history`, `.lesshst`, `.viminfo`, `.histfile` or `.zhistory`, no `HISTTIMEFORMAT` value, and nothing about which account the file belongs to.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per command line, parented to the file artifact, with `type: "ShellHistoryEntry"`, `subtype: "shell_history"`, `shell` (`bash` or `zsh`), `command` (the line verbatim, or the text after the `;` of a zsh extended entry), `line_number`, `date` as Unix seconds only where a zsh entry carried an epoch or a bash `#<epoch>` line preceded the command — the key is absent, not null, otherwise — and `name`, the command cut to its first 80 characters with `...` appended when longer. Where the read fell short of the declared size, one further `ParsedRecord` follows the entries: `type: "DesktopArtifactParseStatus"`, `subtype: "desktop_artifact_incomplete"`, `artifact_kind: "Shell history"`, `file_name`, `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason` of `cap_reached` when the declared size exceeds 64 MiB and `short_read` otherwise, `entries_emitted`, `bytes_read`, `declared_size`, `max_text_bytes`, a `name` of `Shell history (partially parsed): <file>` and a `message` saying entries past that point were not extracted. It produces no `TimelineEvent` — a dated command is on the record and not on the timeline — no path, no user name, no host, and no hash. `process` never returns an error: a file it does not claim, an artifact without data and an empty history all leave the same zero-yield row in the processing log.

**Cannot.** It cannot say whose commands these are: the record carries neither the file's path nor a user name, and the only link to the account is the parent artifact's id, so a listing exported on its own names no one. It cannot date a plain bash history at all, and says nothing about the fact — most `.bash_history` files have no `#<epoch>` lines, and an undated command is simply a record without a `date` key, indistinguishable from one whose stamp line was malformed. It cannot tell a timestamp from a comment: any `#` line whose remainder is an integer — `#1`, `#2024`, a commented-out number — is consumed as a bash timestamp and applied to the next command, and a negative integer is accepted as an epoch before 1970; conversely a `#` line that is not an integer is published as a command. It cannot reassemble a multi-line command: zsh writes continuation lines with a trailing backslash and bash writes each line of a here-document or a `for` loop as its own history line, and each becomes its own record with its own `line_number`. It cannot un-metafy zsh: zsh stores bytes above 0x7F with a 0x83 escape, which this reader does not reverse, so a non-ASCII command from a zsh history is published mangled by the lossy UTF-8 pass. It cannot see a history that was moved: `HISTFILE` is not read, `.zhistory`, `.histfile` and `fish_history` are not in the name list, and `.sh_history` is labelled `bash` whatever shell — ksh, typically — wrote it. It cannot say whether the history is complete beyond the byte count: `HISTSIZE` truncation, `history -c`, `HISTIGNORE` and `HISTCONTROL=ignorespace` all leave a shorter file that reads as the whole record, and the module has no way to mark that absence. It cannot recover a deleted or unallocated history — it reads the file it was handed and nothing else. Its cap is 64 MiB of text, stated on the status record; a file over it is read to the cap and stamped `cap_reached`. The status record's sentence lives in `message`, which the examiner-facing incompleteness reader (`frontend/src/lib/incompleteness.ts`) does not display — it reads `content_incomplete_detail`, which this module does not write — so the reader shows the reason code without the sentence; the LogFile parser had the same defect and was fixed.

**Refuses.** It refuses to let a short read pass as a full history. A history is an inventory — every command a user typed that survived — and a prefix of one emitted without comment reads as the whole, so a read that returns fewer bytes than the source declares appends a `DesktopArtifactParseStatus` record with the byte counts and the reason, distinguishing a file over the parser's own cap (`cap_reached`) from a source that stopped early (`short_read`) so an examiner is not sent looking for an acquisition fault that is a parser cap. It refuses a file by any name but the five it lists, however history-like its content, and refuses the `path` as a fallback: a history file the ingest named differently is not parsed. It refuses to invent a date: a command with no stamp gets no `date` key rather than a placeholder, and a zsh metadata field that does not parse as an integer yields a record with the command and no date. It refuses to panic on anything: malformed input returns an empty list. Everything it declines it declines in silence — an empty list, a zero-yield processing-log row, and no record saying a candidate was passed over. The tests pin the zsh extended form, the bash stamp form, the undated plain line, and the presence and absence of the incompleteness marker; there is no real history fixture in the tree.

### `plugin.recovery.file_carver`

**Reads.** Raw bytes, and nothing else. It scans the data source of a `FileSystem` or `UnallocatedSpace` artifact sequentially in 512-byte blocks through a 1 MiB read-through buffer, testing each block against the 364 built-in format signatures `seance_carving::formats::register_all` registers, plus any user-declared header/footer signatures supplied as a JSON custom-defs document. It reads no filesystem metadata through a file system: no directory entry, no inode, no allocation bitmap, no MFT record. The one metadata it reads is found as bytes: the ext2/ext3 pointer blocks lying in line with a carve, read to rebuild that carve without them and used only once every entry names exactly the blocks after it. A raw pattern match is never acted on by itself — the signature's own `header_check` must confirm it from the start of the block first, because a loose signature such as a one-byte OpenPGP packet tag matches random data about 1.5% of the time. It takes the region's position in the parent evidence from the input artifact's own `offset_bytes` and from nowhere else, so without that key it reports no absolute offsets. It is opt-in (`ExecutionMode::OptIn`), and in the product it is normally driven by the one-click `carve_source` route, which enqueues it against every `FileSystem` and `UnallocatedSpace` descendant of a source.

**Produces.** One carved `FileEntry` per surviving candidate, carrying the name of the signature that matched, the recovered size, the offset within the scanned region, the absolute offset in the parent evidence where the region declared one, and md5 plus sha256 computed over exactly that window — or, for a carve rebuilt without in-line ext2 pointer blocks, over the rebuilt run list it records as `data_runs` with `carving_reconstruction: ext2_indirect`, which is also what the content route serves. Each also carries a manufactured name of the form `carved_00000200.bmp` — the hex offset it was found at and the signature's extension — and `carving_validated`, which is `true` when the signature's `data_check` found its terminator, `false` for a heuristic extent (interrupted by a new unsized header that survives its own `data_check` on that block; or cut at the start of a header-sized object met inside it when no terminator of its own is found past that object — the object is recorded without ending the running carve, which keeps its whole extent when its own terminator lies beyond the object; or clamped at the end of the source, stopped by the signature's own size cap, or abandoned when the structure stopped making sense), and absent entirely when the size came straight from the header and nothing was validated. Beside them, one `CarvingSummary` per region giving the number carved, the number of raw candidates, how many were dropped as overlapping and how many as too small, the bytes scanned, whether the scan was cancelled, a per-signature breakdown of counts and byte totals, and the 50,000-file cap together with whether it was reached.

**Cannot.** A carved object cannot tell you its name, when it was created, modified or accessed, where in a directory tree it lived, or whether it was allocated: the name on the record is manufactured from the offset, the bytes hold no timestamps, and it raises no timeline event. It cannot separate a deleted file from a live one, because it reads no allocation bitmap — pointed at a whole `FileSystem` it carves allocated and freed content alike. It cannot see a file whose header does not begin on a 512-byte block boundary, and it cannot carry two recoveries at once: the engine holds a single `active` recovery, so a confirmed second unsized header ends the first and records it as a heuristic extent (a header-sized object is recorded beside it without ending it). A second header counts as confirmed only once it passes its own signature's structural check on its header block; for a magic of four bytes or fewer that check reads what the format's specification puts there (a PDF version, a ZIP local header's method and name, a JPEG's first segment, a TIFF directory — read from the source where it lies, however far past the header block, and every registration of the TIFF magic applies it — a PST client magic, and so on). A stray magic can still cut a carve short in these cases, which are all the cases a survey over four kinds of filler finds: a TIFF-style header whose directory lies past the end of the source, which cannot be refuted; and three whose check passes text, measured on prose — a script's `#!` (`TXT`), a Zstandard skippable frame, whose payload is free, and `HDF4`, whose descriptors prose makes in range. The survey does not reach three further ways through, which stand beside that list: a stray TIFF-style directory that passes by chance (its every entry must carry one of the 16 defined field types, so a one-entry directory of random bytes passes about once in 4,096); a directory whose count can be read but none of whose entries lies wholly inside the source, which is unknown, not refuted; and a source read that fails, which is also unknown. A genuine TIFF whose directory lies in a fragment not contiguous with its header is refuted as if stray: it is carved as part of the running carve and does not start its own. Five signatures with neither a public layout past their magic nor a sample (`CAM`, `DIM`, `Papyrus`, `QuarkXpress`, `TIB`) are weak headers: they may start a carve when none is running but never end one, so their magic inside another file's body does not split that file. The cost is stated: a genuine file of theirs met while a carve is running does not start its own carve, and wherever the running carve stops before that file ends — at its own terminator, its structure check or its size cap — the rest of that file is recovered by nothing. PhotoRec's disabled-by-default `dovecot` layout (80 KiB of zeros) is not carried . A whole EVTX log is sized by walking its consecutive 64 KiB `ElfChnk` chunks from offset 4,096, not by the header's chunk count, which real logs contradict both ways; the count is not recorded on the carve . A Parquet file is sized from its trailing `PAR1` and the footer length before it, checked against the Thrift `FileMetaData` version field where the footer begins; a stray `PAR1` in column data passes that check about once in 32,768 times, a Parquet file stored inside another file's column is sized as the inner file if its footer passes first, and a file not contiguous in the source is not found. A Parquet carve so sized carries no `carving_validated` flag: the size was read from the file's structure, not confirmed by a second route. A BPG is carved to its declared length up to 64 MiB. A PE with no certificate table ends at its last section: a self-extractor's payload or other data appended after it is neither carved nor flagged, and an absent `carving_validated` on a PE means the size came from the headers, not that nothing follows. A carve that ended short of the minimum size its signature expects (a truncated `.clip`, `.abr`, `.axx` or `.ds_store`) is published marked `carving_below_minimum: true` with `carving_validated: false` and counted in the summary as `total_below_minimum`; it records that a header was found and the bytes ended early, not a recovered file, and one under 16 bytes or overlapping a recorded file is not published. It reassembles one kind of fragmented file and no other: a carve that runs across the ext2/ext3 pointer blocks the allocator writes in line with a file (the indirect block after its twelfth block; the double-indirect block and the indirect blocks under it) is rebuilt without them, and only once every pointer entry has been read and names exactly the blocks the in-line layout puts after it. Such a carve carries `carving_reconstruction: ext2_indirect`, the pointer blocks skipped, the block size and the `data_runs` the content route serves, which are the bytes hashed. When the carve's own walk read a pointer block as content and the file had to be sized again through the layout, `carving_validated` is the flag of that second walk, so it describes the end the published file has, not the end the raw carve stopped at. On DFTT #12 all ten files in the answer key carve byte-exact (`VALIDATION.md` `DFTT-12`). It does not follow pointers to content the allocator placed elsewhere, rebuild a triple-indirect file (over 64 MiB at 1 KiB blocks), or reassemble any other file system's fragments, and reordering non-sequential fragments (`FC-CA-09`) is on this project's deliberately out-of-scope list. Its caps are hard: 50,000 files per artifact, candidates under 16 bytes dropped, each signature's own `max_file_size`, at most 16 MiB read back to refine an extension from content, and at most the last 8,192 bytes examined when confirming an end. `carving_validated: true` is not an independent confirmation — only four of the 364 signature modules (`jpeg`, `pdf`, `cpio`, `parquet`) implement `verify_footer`, and Parquet's is not reached on the engine's path because a Parquet carve is sized, not stopped; for every other format it means the same walk that chose the end agreed with itself. It does not carve file slack itself: the `SlackSpace` regions the filesystem parsers publish are carved by `plugin.recovery.unallocated_carver`, and `carve_slack_for_file` remains only for a caller that holds the geometry; nor can it say a region held nothing, since a region where no signature matched produces no record whatever, leaving a region carved and empty indistinguishable from one never carved.

**Refuses.** It refuses to publish digests that do not cover the whole window it declares: where the carved window reads short, md5 and sha256 are withheld and the record carries `hash_skipped: short_read`, the bytes actually hashed and `content_incomplete`, because otherwise a 64-byte prefix would verify as the 256-byte carved file . It refuses to examine a byte it did not read — the block scan is bounded to the bytes actually returned, a tail window that reads short leaves the validation verdict unknown rather than positive, and slack that exists geometrically but is zero-filled yields nothing. On cancellation it refuses to emit the recovery still in flight, because its extent past the scanned range was never looked at and publishing it would fabricate evidence. It refuses to let a truncated carve read as a complete one: hitting the file cap or being cancelled stamps the summary `content_incomplete` with the reason, while a run that finished carries no marker, so the two are distinguishable. Equally, it refuses to make a real object vanish — a carve stopped by the signature's size cap, by the end of the source, or by a `data_check` error is emitted as the extent recovered and marked not validated, rather than dropped in silence. For an artifact with no data source, or one of zero length, it produces nothing at all.

### `plugin.recovery.unallocated_carver`

**Reads.** Free space and file slack, and nothing else. It subscribes to `ArtifactType::UnallocatedSpace` and `ArtifactType::SlackSpace`: one region per live file whose last cluster's unused tail holds any non-zero byte, published by the NTFS, FAT, exFAT, ext4, HFS+ and APFS parsers and hanging off the `FileSystem`. In a slack region it scans only from the first 512-byte boundary of the volume past the owner's logical end — under the volume's current cluster size no file begins in slack, since a file starts on a cluster boundary and the start of that cluster is the owner's content, so a header there is part of a former file's content or was placed there, unless the volume was reformatted with larger clusters or once held another file system, when a former file may start at an old boundary inside the cluster (the 512-byte step reaches such a start) — and it reads the region's `parent_file`, `parent_path` and `owner_artifact_id`. For `UnallocatedSpace` there are **two** producers of that type. `plugin.disk.partition_parser` emits one region per free sector run an MBR or GPT table leaves between or around its partitions, down to a floor of 512 bytes, hanging off the raw evidence. Since `ROADMAP` §5.4 `plugin.ntfs.mft_parser` emits one region per run of clusters a volume's `$Bitmap` proves free, hanging off the `FileSystem` artifact — which is where nearly everything an examiner carves for actually is, and which was never carved automatically before. From the region it reads the bytes through a 1 MiB read-through buffer and exactly one metadata field, `offset_bytes`, which is what turns a position in the region into a position in **that region's parent**; the `sector_size`, `partition_scheme`, `small_gap` and `trailing` flags the partition parser puts beside it are never read, and neither are the `filesystem`, `first_cluster`, `clusters` and `free_means` fields the bitmap route puts there. Because the parent differs between the two producers, so does what `carving_offset_absolute` is absolute **to**: an offset in the evidence for a partition gap, an offset in the volume for a free-cluster region — which is why the region states its own `offset_basis` in words. Against every 512-byte block of that window it runs the 364 format signatures `seance_carving::formats::register_all` registers, confirming each pattern hit with the signature's own `header_check` before acting on it, because a loose one-byte magic matches random data about one block in seventy. It reads no filesystem structure through a file system: no allocation bitmap, no directory entry, no MFT record, no inode. The ext2/ext3 pointer blocks lying in line with a carve are read as bytes, to rebuild that carve without them.

**Produces.** One carved `FileEntry` per surviving candidate, named for its own offset in the region, carrying the signature that matched, the offset within the region, the absolute offset in the parent evidence where `offset_bytes` was present, the recovered length, and md5 and sha256 computed over that exact window for chain of custody. Each also carries a three-state validation flag: confirmed, where the signature found its terminator and any independent footer check agreed; not validated, where the extent was a heuristic — interrupted by the next unsized header that survives its own data check, cut at a header-sized object met inside it when no terminator of its own follows that object, capped, or cut by a structure that stopped making sense; and absent, where the size came straight from the header and nothing checked it. Beside them one `CarvingSummary` record per region, holding what was emitted, how many raw candidates the scan produced, how many were dropped as overlapping or as under sixteen bytes, the bytes actually scanned, a per-signature breakdown of count and total size, and whether the run was cancelled or hit the file cap. The summary says plainly when the carved set is not everything recoverable: a cap, a cancellation or a scan that read short of the region's end stamps `content_incomplete` with its reason (`cap_reached`, `unresolved_structure`, `short_read`), and a run that finished carries no such marker, so an honest complete carve is distinguishable from a truncated one.

**Cannot.** It reaches **slack** only where a `SlackSpace` region was published: on NTFS, FAT and exFAT, for a live file whose allocation is fully described and whose tail is not all zeros, up to 250,000 regions a volume; slack on any other file system, a deleted file's former slack, and clusters allocated past the one holding a file's last byte are not reached. A carve from slack can be no longer than the slack window, under one cluster — at most about 3.5 KiB on 4 KiB clusters — so an executable in slack is found only when it is that small or its header alone is enough to size it. On free space itself the position changed: an "unallocated" region is now either a statement of the partition table or one of a filesystem's own allocation bitmap, and the region says which on itself, so this module carves the free clusters inside a volume as well as the gaps between partitions. It still never runs on a partition holding no filesystem, which is a `Partition` artifact and gets no region. Where a bitmap could not be read in full, the tail it could not speak for is reported as unassessed and no region covers it, so this module is never pointed at address space nobody assessed. It cannot tell you when a carved object was deleted, or that it was deleted at all: it emits no timestamp of any kind and knows no name for the object beyond its own offset, so bytes left by an earlier partitioning, by installer payload no filesystem ever referenced, or by a volume since resized read exactly like bytes from a deleted file. It cannot establish where a carved file ends — the extent is a declared length or a heuristic, and the PE signature's `max(PointerToRawData + SizeOfRawData)` overshot the true end of all 231 signed executables carved from unallocated space on `LenovoFinal.E01`, by between 8 and 97,824 bytes. It cannot find a header that does not begin on a 512-byte boundary measured from the region's start, and it reassembles no fragmented file but one: a carve across the ext2/ext3 pointer blocks written in line with a file is rebuilt without them once every pointer entry is verified (`carving_reconstruction: ext2_indirect`, with the `data_runs` served). Every other carve is one contiguous run forward from its header, and that run can still be cut short where the free space holds, on a block boundary, the magic of a TIFF-style header whose directory lies past the end of the source, or, in text, a script's `#!` (`TXT`), a Zstandard skippable frame or an `HDF4` header, whose checks prose passes; those are all the cases the survey finds. The magic of `CAM`, `DIM`, `Papyrus`, `QuarkXpress` or `TIB` never ends a running carve, so a genuine file of theirs met inside one does not start its own carve, and its bytes past the point where the running carve stops are not recovered. A genuine TIFF whose directory lies in a fragment not contiguous with its header is likewise absorbed rather than carved on its own. It stops at 50,000 files per region, drops anything under sixteen bytes, and drops any candidate beginning inside the previous survivor's extent — those last two are counted in the summary, not emitted, so a small object genuinely embedded in a larger carve is a number rather than a file. A free region that was scanned and held nothing still gets its `CarvingSummary`; a slack region scanned cleanly to its end that held nothing gets none — one per live file would bury the case — so for slack its own output cannot distinguish a region scanned and empty from one never carved, and the volume's `slack_space_summary` says only that the regions were produced for it. A slack region whose scan was cancelled or read short does get a summary, stamped `content_incomplete`, so a stop part-way through is never silent.

**Refuses.** It refuses whole live filesystems. `subscribes_to` names `UnallocatedSpace` and `SlackSpace` and nothing else, and a test asserts `FileSystem` is absent from it, because carving every allocated byte of a disk automatically is a cost the examiner should choose — `plugin.recovery.file_carver` is where that choice is made. It refuses to publish an md5 or sha256 for a carved window it could not read to the declared length, recording `hash_skipped: short_read` with the bytes it did hash and a `content_incomplete` reason instead, because digests over a prefix would let a partial read verify as the whole carved file. It refuses to emit an unfinished recovery when the run is cancelled: the extent past the point the scan reached was never examined, and publishing it would fabricate evidence. It refuses to examine the unread tail of a short block, and refuses to call a footer validated on a tail it could not read in full — that outcome is recorded as unknown rather than as a pass. And it refuses to honour a header-declared size that runs past the end of the region, clamping the window to the bytes that exist and marking the carve not validated rather than declaring a length it does not have.

### `plugin.search.indexer`

**Reads.** Every artifact the pipeline routes to it — the nine types it declares, from `RawEvidence` down to `ParsedRecord` — read as two things: the artifact's own metadata JSON, and, for a `FileEntry` or `FileContent` that arrives carrying a resolvable data source, the first 16 MiB of that file's bytes (`CONTENT_INDEX_CAP`). Those bytes are turned into text by a `strings`-style pass run three times over the same buffer — UTF-8, then UTF-16LE, then UTF-16BE — keeping any run of at least four characters (`MIN_STRING_LEN`) and discarding shorter ones, which is the bound that stops a binary file filling the index with two-character noise. The bytes it sees are the file's logical content and not its allocation: the data source trims trailing cluster slack rather than serving it, so slack is outside the search universe before this module is reached. It opens no image and reads no evidence of its own; it sees only what a producing module already attached, and it indexes inline on the ingest worker, handing each finished document to one writer thread across a channel bounded at 512 documents so a producer waits for the indexer rather than piling gigabytes of buffered content behind it.

**Produces.** It produces no artifact at all: `process` returns an empty vector, and its entire output is a document in the Tantivy index. One document per artifact, carrying the artifact id, the case id, the coarse `artifact_type`, the display name the record's own metadata implies, `record_kind` — the record's `type` discriminator where it has one and the artifact type where it does not, which is what a pivot groups its hits by — and a multi-valued `content` field holding the metadata JSON and then the text extracted from the file's bytes. Where the indexed text is only part of the file it appends `seance_index_incomplete` and a reason: `cap_reached` when the file is larger than the 16 MiB bound, `short_read` when the source stopped early or errored part-way. That token is the only thing it ever says about its own coverage, and it exists because a query that misses is otherwise identical whether the word is absent from the evidence or merely past the point indexing stopped. To an examiner it is never a record in the case; it is the reason a search finds a term.

**Cannot.** It cannot find Chinese, Japanese kanji or Korean text stored as wide characters, nor any UTF-16 character outside the set it can vouch for — ASCII, the Latin-1 letters U+00C0–U+00FE less `×` and `÷`, and letters of one of Greek, Cyrillic, Cyrillic Supplement/Armenian/Hebrew, Arabic or kana (U+3041–U+30FF) per run (`UTF16_SCRIPT_BLOCKS`), a word being split where its alphabet changes — so no Latin Extended letter (`Ł`, `ř`, `İ`, `ş`, `ệ`), no Indic, Thai or other script — which is what remains of `SEARCH-002`. CJK and Hangul are excluded by decision; the rest (a ligature such as U+FB01, any other script) is the open remainder, not decided. On NIST CFTT's Forensic String Search key that is 60 of the 710 assessable expectations (東京, 中国, 中國 and 서울 by decision, and the `ﬁ`-ligature `inﬁnity`, 12 rows each), down from 228 when only ASCII was taken; a prediction about reach, measured on the key, not a graded result. Every search response and export carries a `universe` statement built from these same constants that says so, names the timeline and backfill gaps below, and names the byte sweep, which searches those terms. That coverage is this build's text extractor (version 2); the index records per case which extractor versions built its file documents, and a case an earlier build ingested — whose extractor read UTF-16 as ASCII only — is told so in its statement, with the fact that the backfill cannot repair it (it adds metadata only) and a re-ingest can. A fuzzy search is stated as approximate, not exact-form. It does no Unicode normalisation, of the indexed text or of the query: matching is case-insensitive (both are lowercased) but otherwise exact-form, so a precomposed (NFC) `mañana` does not find the same word stored decomposed (NFD, `n` followed by U+0303), nor the reverse; each form finds itself, and a combining mark is indexed with the letter it follows in UTF-8 text and in UTF-16 text (U+0300–U+036F after any character, or a mark of the run's own block). The kana block's high byte is ASCII `0`, so 8-bit hex text with a `0` in every other byte (`0D0A0D0A`, `0x0A0B0C0D`) is byte-identical to UTF-16 kana and is indexed as kana; a kana search can hit it, and how often is not measured. Digit text (`01020304`) is not, because units below U+3041 are refused. It indexes file bytes for `FileEntry` and `FileContent` only, so a term living solely in unallocated space, in slack, or past the 16 MiB cap is not in the search universe — 134 of that key's 921 expectations are unallocated and this tool offers no search of them. It declares `TimelineEvent` among its subscriptions and never receives one, because the pipeline does not re-dispatch a timeline event: one measured case indexed 8,134 of its 11,390 artifacts, and the 3,256-row difference is exactly its timeline. It cannot tell an examiner that a case was never indexed, because `index_incomplete` is raised only by a non-zero write-failure count or by a schema rebuild, and an ingestion profile that leaves this module out yields a case with no documents and no such mark. It cannot reconstruct file text for a document the backfill adds, since an artifact loaded from the database carries no data source, and it does not withhold a recovered credential's value from the index, so the workspace index holds in the clear what the API releases only through the audited reveal.

**Refuses.** It refuses to treat Séance's own prose about an artifact as words the evidence contains: `timestamp_indicators` and `timestomp_reasons` are stripped from the indexed text (`NOT_EVIDENCE_TEXT`), because on one measured image the MFT parser's timestamp explanations put `preserves the source` on 4,026 artifacts and made a search for `rename` return 1,386 hits, not one of them because the word was in a file — the values stay in the metadata the API serves and the UI renders, they are simply not indexed as evidence text. It refuses to accept a UTF-16 code unit it cannot vouch for structurally, because two arbitrary bytes carry no check digit and accepting any alphabetic unit filled the index with runs like `懿戀㴀Ø揞搀`: a unit must have a zero high byte, or share one high byte with every other non-ASCII unit of its run from the short list of single-block alphabets, and a run that changes block is broken there. On a fixed pseudo-random megabyte that rule yields no non-ASCII run at all; structured binary is not measured. It refuses `ÿ` (U+00FF), whose unit is `0xFF` beside `0x00`, the commonest padding in a binary file. The exclusion of CJK and Hangul is pinned by `cjk_and_hangul_utf16_text_is_still_not_found_and_that_is_search_002`, a test written to fail the day it changes so the limit cannot be lifted without the statement of it being rewritten. It refuses to read an invalid UTF-8 byte as Latin-1, because `0xFF` read that way is an alphabetic character and padding bytes either side of a short string joined it into a run long enough to pass the minimum, putting `cat` in the index as though the evidence held it. And when tantivy has killed the writer it refuses the write instead of dropping it quietly: the caller is told in as many words that this write did not happen, the count reaches `pending_index_failures`, and every search served while that is non-zero is marked `index_incomplete` with its totals as a floor.

### `plugin.windows.amcache_parser`

**Reads.** `Amcache.hve` and the Windows 7 `RecentFileCache.bcf` that preceded it, out of the file A shadow-copy prior version of the file (a `VssPriorVersion` `ParsedRecord`) is read too and named by its `file_name`, since its `name` carries a `[shadow copy ...]` label; everything it yields repeats the snapshot id, label and creation time, and its transaction logs are not searched. entries and system artifacts the module subscribes to, selected **by name first**: the artifact's `name` metadata, lower-cased, must contain `recentfilecache.bcf`, or else `amcache`, and a file whose name contains neither is handed back untouched. A name carrying `amcache` is then put to a content probe and must be detected as a registry hive — `regf` at offset 0 — while a `.bcf` is put to no content probe whatever. Up to 512 MiB (`MAX_AMCACHE_BYTES`) is staged into memory through `read_capped`, which loops over short reads and keeps only what it actually got. Before the hive is opened its base block is inspected: mismatched sequence numbers, or an XOR-32 checksum at offset 0x1FC that does not verify, mark it dirty, and `.LOG1` and `.LOG2`, else `.LOG`, are looked for beside it both on the filesystem and as siblings inside the evidence container. The hive is then opened by the reader every hive-reading plugin shares, which requires `regf` and a full 4,096-byte base block and enforces version, file type, file format, declared-size alignment, clustering factor and base-block checksum, tolerating exactly two things: a mismatched sequence pair, and a base block declaring more hive-bin data than the buffer holds. The walk goes root → the first child named `Root` → its children, and reads **exactly two** of them: `InventoryApplicationFile` and `File`; the older of the two corpus hives carries both. If no `Root` is found, or the walk under it produced nothing, the same two names are looked for directly beneath the hive root. Under `InventoryApplicationFile` each subkey is one file entry, and seven values are read, by either spelling — `LowerCaseLongPath`/`15`, `FileId`/`101`, `Size`/`6`, `LinkDate`/`f`, `ProgramId`/`7`, `Publisher`/`1`, `Version`/`5` — plus the entry key's own last-written FILETIME; `FileId` has its four-zero prefix stripped to leave the 40-hex SHA-1. Under `File` the walk descends two levels — a volume-GUID container, then the entries inside it — and reads `15` and `101` and nothing else. A `.bcf` is read as a 20-byte header when its first four bytes are `0xDEADBEEF` and as a 4-byte header on **any other** signature, then as a flat sequence of records, each a little-endian `u32` byte count and that many bytes of NUL-terminated UTF-16LE path.

**Produces.** One `AmcacheEntry` `ParsedRecord` per entry, in three shapes. From `InventoryApplicationFile`: the lower-case long path, the SHA-1 Amcache recorded for the file, the size, the raw `LinkDate` string, `key_last_written` — the entry key's own write time, converted to RFC 3339 — the `ProgramId`, the publisher, the version, the subkey's own name, and a `link_date_plausible` judgement on every `LinkDate` that parsed, with `link_date_note` giving the reason where the judgement is false. From `File`: the path, the SHA-1 and `format: legacy_win8`, and nothing else. From a `.bcf`: the path and `format: win7_recentfilecache`. Every record parsed out of a hive carries that hive's recovery state (`hive_dirty`, `logs_replayed`, `log_files`, `replay_reason`, `hive_truncated`) and the walk's own census (`walk_subkey_errors`, `walk_value_errors`, `walk_record_errors`, `walk_cap_reached`), written whether or not anything was missed, so a clean walk and an uncounted one cannot render alike; a `.bcf` record carries no hive state — there is no hive — and carries the census only when the `.bcf` walk was **not** clean. One `TimelineEvent` per surviving `LinkDate`, labelled `Amcache LinkDate (PE link time)` so it reads as a build attribute of the binary and not as host activity: on the plaso `win10-Amcache.hve` that is 26 events from 30 `LinkDate`-bearing entries, and on the older corpus hive — 247 `InventoryApplicationFile` entries, none of which holds a `LinkDate` value, and 1,120 legacy entries, whose shape has no `LinkDate` field at all — it is none. Where a file this module recognised yielded nothing, it produces a status record instead of silence: `registry_hive_parse_status` with `parse_failed` and the parser's own words when the hive was rejected or the parser panicked; `registry_hive_parse_status` when a hive that was truncated, or dirty with its logs found beside it, or walked incompletely, produced no entries; `amcache_parse_status` with `bytes_read` and `declared_bytes` for a `.bcf` that was too short to hold a header or was not read to its end.

**Cannot.** **It cannot tell you that a program ran.** Nothing in the keys it reads records an execution: there is no run count, no last-run time, no user and no session in any of the seven values, and this module asserts none. What an `InventoryApplicationFile` entry establishes is that the file was present on the machine and inventoried, with that path, that SHA-1 and that size, at or before the time the key was written. It cannot say when a program was installed, or what the program was, although the hive says so: the `ProgramId` is carried on the record and never resolved, and `Root\InventoryApplication` — which maps that id to `Name`, `Publisher`, `Version`, `Source`, `InstallDate`, `RootDirPath` and `UninstallString` — is not read at all, 75 entries of it in the Windows 10 corpus hive and 74 in the older one. Of the fifteen keys beneath `Root` in that older hive it reads two; `InventoryDriverBinary` (311 entries), `InventoryDevicePnp` (194), `Orphan` (78), `Programs` (26), `InventoryDeviceContainer` (18), `DeviceCensus` (16) and the rest are not opened, and the sixteen keys of the Windows 10 hive are read the same two ways. Inside an entry it reads seven values and discards every other one uncounted — `Name`, `LongPathHash`, `BinaryType`, `BinFileVersion`, `BinProductVersion`, `ProductName`, `ProductVersion`, `Language`, `IsPeFile`, `IsOsComponent` and `Usn` are all present in the corpus and none reaches a record. It consults no value's declared registry type anywhere: every text field is decoded as UTF-16LE whatever the hive says it is, and `Size` is read as an 8-byte little-endian integer falling back to 4, so a `Size` the hive stored as text is reported as an integer of that text's bytes — in the older corpus hive all 247 `InventoryApplicationFile` entries store `Size` as `REG_SZ` (`"0x7fac0"`, 522,944 bytes) and all 247 records carry a size of 28,710,683,855,552,560 with no value error counted. It cannot say, of any one record, whether a field it shows as empty was absent from the key or failed to read: both render as `""`, and the value-error count is per hive, not per entry — all 247 entries of that hive report `publisher: ""` because the key holds no `Publisher` at all. A legacy `File` entry gets no time and no volume from it: the entry key's write time is not read on that path, the `REG_QWORD` value `17` that every one of the 1,120 legacy entries in the corpus carries is not read either, nor is `100`, nor the `6`, `f`, `5` and `7` that 11 of them carry, and the volume-GUID container is walked but its name discarded, so the record does not say which volume the file was on. A `.bcf` entry is a path and nothing else — no hash, no size, no time, no timeline event — and because there is no content check on that path, a file merely *named* `RecentFileCache.bcf` is decoded whatever it holds: on an unrecognised signature a 4-byte header is assumed and whatever UTF-16 decodes out of the remainder is emitted as paths. It puts no timeline event on `key_last_written`, the one time the examined machine itself wrote; the only event it makes is the vendor's PE link time. It cannot replay a transaction log. `Amcache.hve` is written continuously on a running machine, so a live copy is usually dirty and its newest entries sit in `.LOG1`/`.LOG2`; those are detected and named, `logs_replayed` is always `false`, and the absence of a program from the listing is therefore not evidence that the program was never there. It cannot report a time more finely than one second, and a FILETIME below 116,444,736,000,000,000 — the 1970 epoch — is reported as no time rather than as a pre-epoch date. It cannot read a `LinkDate` written in any form but `MM/DD/YYYY HH:MM:SS`: anything else stays on the record as text and produces no event. Its judgement on a `LinkDate` is one-sided and needs a time the key may not hold: only a `LinkDate` *later* than the key's write is refused, so an impossibly early one is placed on the timeline, and where the entry key records no write time at all the comparison is not made and the `LinkDate` is stamped `link_date_plausible: true` unchecked. And it cannot exceed its bounds: 512 MiB of any one input, after which the hive is a prefix — and because a hive's keys are spread across the whole file, a prefix is an arbitrary subset and not the first *n* entries; 4,096 bytes minimum, below which the file is not read as a hive; 250,000 entries per hive (`MAX_AMCACHE_ENTRIES`), counted across `InventoryApplicationFile` and `File` together and counting records emitted rather than subkeys examined; 50,000 `.bcf` records (`MAX_BCF_ENTRIES`); 20 bytes minimum for a `.bcf`; and 2,048 bytes, or 1,024 UTF-16 code units, for one `.bcf` path. Each of those is stamped on what it emits, never silent.

**Refuses.** It refuses to place a `LinkDate` later than the write of the key that records it on the timeline. `LinkDate` is the PE header's link timestamp copied into the hive, a binary cannot be linked after the record describing it was written, and on Windows 10 and later Microsoft's binaries carry a reproducible-build hash in that header field rather than a time: on DFIR Madness Case 001 those led the case timeline as events dated 2090, 2077 and 2049. Such a value stays on the record with `link_date_plausible: false` and a note naming both times and the reason — 4 of the 30 `LinkDate`s in `win10-Amcache.hve`. It refuses to emit a timeline event for a `LinkDate` it could not convert, because the timeline insert accepts only Unix seconds or RFC 3339 and silently dropped anything else; the raw string is kept regardless. It refuses to call an undecodable `Size` zero — a fabricated 0-byte size is a claim about the file that the evidence does not make — and counts the failure as a value error instead. It refuses to return nothing for a file it recognised: a hive that would not parse or panicked the parser, a hive that parsed to no entries while truncated, or dirty with its logs beside it, or walked incompletely, and a `.bcf` too short to hold a header or stopped before its end, each produce a status record saying so, because an empty return is indistinguishable from a machine on which nothing was ever installed. It refuses to read past a `.bcf` record whose declared length is zero, above 2,048 bytes, or past the end of the file: the stream is sequential, so everything after such a record is unreachable, and the walk stops and counts it rather than resynchronising on a guess. It refuses to emit an `InventoryApplicationFile` entry that names neither a file nor a hash, and a legacy `File` entry that names no file — on that path a hash without a path is not emitted. It refuses to let one stage's incompleteness reason erase another's — the hive's state and the walk's tally are merged into a single `+`-joined reason, because a capped walk on a hive that was not read in full is two different pieces of missing evidence with two different follow-ups. And it refuses to read a file whose name metadata names neither artefact, or one named Amcache that is not a registry hive by its first four bytes; that refusal is silent and produces no record, on the footing that a file which is not this artefact belongs to another module.

### `plugin.windows.asep`

**Reads.** What Windows will execute at boot or logon, read from evidence other modules have already produced and from three kinds of file on the volume, for thirty-one autostart categories in one table (`rules::CATEGORIES`: Run/RunOnce keys, Startup folder items and redirections, Winlogon Shell/Userinit/notification packages/Taskman-GinaDLL-AppSetup, IFEO debuggers, AppInit_DLLs, AppCertDlls, BootExecute, KnownDLLs, Active Setup, services and drivers, LSA authentication/notification/security packages, print monitors and processors, netsh helpers, Winsock providers, network providers, COM servers outside the system directories, shell extensions, Browser Helper Objects, scheduled tasks and TaskCache registrations, WMI auto-recover MOFs, installed shim databases, default file associations, and WMI event subscriptions). It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `SystemArtifact` (the volume as it is walked) and to `ParsedRecord` (the `RegistryHive` records the registry plugin produces; its own records are ignored on re-entry) with `InputCapability::Stream`. Every non-directory file's path is noted in an evidence index of executable basenames (up to 400,000 names, 8 paths each) and, for a file named `SOFTWARE`, `SYSTEM`, `SAM`, `SECURITY`, `DEFAULT`, `COMPONENTS`, `DRIVERS`, `NTUSER.DAT` or `USRCLASS.DAT`, in a hive-path index of up to 4,096 entries. A `RegistryHive` record's `all_values` array is scanned (up to 2,000,000 values, 50,000 entries per hive, 50,000 service keys, 500,000 CLSID registrations) against the category rules for the hive kind its `hive_type` names, with the profile taken from the hive file's own path (`/users/<name>/`, `/documents and settings/<name>/`, the SYSTEM or .DEFAULT profile) and never guessed. A multi-string list — the Session Manager execute lists, the three LSA package lists, WMI auto-recover MOFs — is read element by element from the value's `value_data_list` array; only a record that carries no such array has its `" | "`-joined rendering split, which is ambiguous where an element holds that separator. A file under a Startup folder path (`desktop.ini` excluded) is an entry; a `.lnk` there is read up to 4 MiB and its shell-link target decoded. A file under `\Windows\System32\Tasks\`, `\SysWOW64\Tasks\` or `\Windows\Tasks\` is a task definition by construction: a `.job` is Task Scheduler 1.0 and not decoded; anything else is read up to 8 MiB, must carry the 2004/02 task namespace within its first 4,096 bytes, is decoded from its UTF-16 or UTF-8 encoding and parsed with a bounded reader (64 levels, 200,000 events, 512 triggers, 64 actions, 8,192 characters per text). A file at `\wbem\Repository\OBJECTS.DATA` (or `\wbem\Repository\FS\OBJECTS.DATA`, the XP form) is the CIM repository: it is read up to 512 MiB and scanned page by page — each 8,192-byte page's descriptor table (id, offset, size, CRC-32) parsed, descriptor-listed records within a page tried as class definitions so the property tables (name, CIM type, state-bit index, value offset, superclass, default-value block) come from the file itself, then the class-name hash strings (SHA-256 of the upper-cased UTF-16LE name, or MD5 where the file's records verify under it) of `__EventFilter`, `__FilterToConsumerBinding`, `CommandLineEventConsumer`, `ActiveScriptEventConsumer`, `NTEventLogEventConsumer`, `LogFileEventConsumer`, `SMTPEventConsumer` and any consumer class a decoded binding names searched for, each hit classified as an allocated instance (at a descriptor's start), a key path inside another record (counted, never an instance) or a record in bytes no descriptor points at (recovered); an instance block is accepted only when it verifies end to end against a candidate definition, and XP's CRC-32s are checked. The page mapping beside the file (`MAPPING1/2/3.MAP`, or `OBJECTS.MAP` on XP, reached by name through the neighbour bundle the filesystem walker attaches in a `wbem\Repository` directory, or on disk) is read when present (HUNT-195): each section's signature, counts and `0xDCBA` footer are checked, a mapping that accounts for a different number of physical pages than the file has is refused, and the well-formed file with the highest sequence number is used. The pages are then walked in logical order: a record running past its page is read on into the next logical page the mapping names, a continuation page's first bytes are not read as a descriptor table, and every record is labelled by its page — mapped (with its logical page), unmapped, or past the whole pages the mapping covers. A record no descriptor table lists is residue even in a mapped page and is never called current or in force. A mapping file whose name occurs twice in its directory is withheld by the bundle and reported as withheld, not as not found. The index (`INDEX.BTR`) beside the file is read too where the mapping is a `MAPPINGn.MAP` (HUNT-195): it is refused unless it holds exactly the pages the mapping accounts for, and it is walked as a tree from its root page (the logical page in the fourth field of the first entry of its mapping section), never by reading every mapped page, since pages the tree no longer reaches stay mapped and keep stale references. A page must carry its signature and its own logical number and may be reached once; every count is checked against the bytes left. A descriptor-listed record in a mapped page is then either named by the index (by its logical page, descriptor id and size) or listed but not indexed, which is deleted or unlinked and is published as `RecoveredAsepEntry` with `evidence_state: "unlinked"`. A Windows Server 2003 R2 SP2 repository, whose `MAPPINGn.MAP` holds two sections of four-byte entries (the data section then the index section) and whose index root is named by the header of its logical page 0, is read the same way, and every record of the one held (189, a stock install's sixty-odd MCA subscriptions and one planted) is named by its index and is the set python-cim lists. The single-section Windows XP form (`OBJECTS.MAP` with its `INDEX.MAP`) is read the same way, its index walked from the root named by index page 0: every one of the six records of the 2004 XP repository held is named by its index and is the set python-cim lists on the same bytes. An `INDEX.MAP` that is missing, refused or of another sequence number leaves the index unread, said so.

**Produces.** One `AsepEntry` per autostart entry — or `RecoveredAsepEntry` for a WMI record found in unreferenced bytes, with `evidence_state: "recovered"`, or in a page the mapping maps to no logical page, with `evidence_state: "superseded"` — carrying `category`, `category_label`, `mitre_technique`, `mitre_technique_name`, `mitre_tactic: "TA0003 Persistence"` and a `mitre_note` where the mapping is approximate, `category_source` (`registry`, `filesystem`, `wmi_repository`), `category_locations`, `entry_name`, `asep_location`, `asep_location_kind`, `asep_value_name`, `hive`, `scope` (`HKLM`, `HKCU`, `filesystem`), `user`, `image_path`, `command`, `arguments`, `working_dir`, `command_split_basis`; when the command runs `powershell` or `pwsh` with an `-EncodedCommand` parameter (any prefix of the name, or `-ec`), `powershell_encoded_command_parameter` and either `powershell_encoded_command_decoded` (the argument read as base64 of UTF-16LE text, with a basis saying it is what the command carries, not that it ran) or `powershell_encoded_command_undecodable` with the reason and no script; a `runs_when` sentence (for a WMI binding: which filter's query in which namespace triggers which consumer and what it executes or that it executes nothing), `enabled` with `enabled_basis`, `installed_time` with `installed_time_source` and `installed_time_status: "recorded"` — or null with `installed_time_status: "unavailable"` and the reason, which for every registry entry is that the parsed hive record carries no per-key last-write times — and `timezone: "local"` when the
