source records wall clock; `read_status: "parsed"` or `"unread"` with a reason; `incomplete`/`incomplete_reason` and, when set, the standard `content_incomplete` pair with reason `cap_reached`, `short_read` or `unresolved_structure`; `observations` as neutral `{code, statement}` facts with an `assessment_note` that this module does not determine whether an entry is unwanted; and the target resolution — `target_exists` as `observed_at_path`, `observed_by_name_only`, `not_observed`, `no_file_index`, `unresolved_variable` or `not_applicable`, with `target_exists_basis`, `target_lookup_path`, `target_path_expansion`, `target_observed_paths` (and `_truncated`), `target_index_executable_names` and `target_index_capped`; for a bare program name (no directory, drive or variable — `cscript`, `rundll32.exe`) also `target_search_path_candidates` (a WMI `CommandLineEventConsumer`'s `WorkingDirectory` first where it records one, then `\Windows\System32`, `\Windows\SysWOW64`, `\Windows`), `target_search_rule` naming the extension rule applied — `create_process_exe_only` for that consumer, whose properties are `CreateProcess` parameters (only `.exe` appended to a name with no extension), `full_path_required` for a service's `ImagePath` (where no `ServiceDll` is reported), which `CreateService` documents as a fully qualified path, and an Image File Execution Options `Debugger` value, which Microsoft's service-debugging guidance says to set to the debugger's full path (no general specification of the value was found, and the basis names that scope), so the basis says a bare name is outside that contract and its resolution is undocumented — naming the service control manager for a service (`Type` 0x10 to 0x60, including a per-user instance with the 0x80 bit, such as 0xD0 or 0xE0), the kernel for a driver (`Type` 0x1, 0x2 or 0x8, or `Start` 0 or 1), and either when `Type` does not say, which includes the reserved `SERVICE_ADAPTER` 0x4 — and tries the shell's list as leads only, with `\Windows\System32\drivers` and `.sys` added for an entry that is or may be a driver, and a `target_path_expansion` naming the candidates as leads, never the search path, `shell_pathext` for every other source (the shell's `.com`, `.exe`, `.bat`, `.cmd`, appended to a name with no executable extension, a rule whose use by those launchers is stated as not established) — `target_search_path_directory` naming the directory that answered, and `target_search_path_resolution` — `observed_on_search_path`, `observed_in_working_directory` (worded apart because `CreateProcess` searches the launching process's current directory, not the new one's, so a copy there is where a planted program would sit, not proof it was the one loaded), `search_path_convention_not_observed` when `target_lookup_path` is only the first candidate, or, under `full_path_required`, `lead_candidate_observed` (with `target_exists: observed_by_name_only`, never `observed_at_path`, because the launcher's resolution is undocumented and the file is a lead, not the one it is established to load) or `lead_candidate_not_observed` (a miss, or no file index). A WMI entry (`category: wmi_event_subscription`) also carries its class, offset, size, page, record id, provenance, checksum status (`verified`, `mismatch` with the stored and computed values, `not_stored` on Windows 7+ which store zero, `not_applicable`), hash form, both header FILETIMEs raw and RFC 3339 — the later being `record_time` under source `wmi_record_filetime_later_of_two`, **not** `installed_time` (which is null with `installed_time_status: "unavailable"`): on a Windows 11 repository where instances were planted at known times, each carried a time before it was created, by 76 minutes, 6 minutes and 3 seconds in three waves, so the record time is the repository's previous commit and the subscription was made no earlier than it, how much later not being stated (one machine, one build) — every property with value, state and CIM type, `CreatorSID` rendered, the data block's printable strings, the class-definition offset used, decode notes, `mapping_read`, `record_page_state`, `repository_liveness` and a `scan_basis` sentence — naming the mapping file and sequence number and where the record stands in it (listed in a mapped page, residue in one, in an unmapped page, or past the mapping) and that whether the index names it (`indexed`, `listed_not_indexed`) or that the index was not read and why, or, with no mapping, that the index and mapping were not read and liveness is not established; an undecodable record is emitted with `read_status: "unread"` and the reason, never dropped, and a binding whose filter or consumer does not resolve is marked incomplete. A binding resolves each end to the copy that stands best in the mapping (listed and indexed, then listed but not indexed, then residue, then past the mapping, then unmapped; by offset within each), saying `binding_filter_record_current` and `binding_consumer_record_current`, and an end found only as a copy the mapping does not establish as current marks the binding incomplete; a filter's or consumer's bound list counts only bindings the mapping establishes as current, with the rest in `filter_bound_consumers_not_current` / `consumer_bound_filters_not_current`. One `TimelineEvent` per entry with an `installed_time`, `timestamp_desc: "Autostart Entry Installed/Modified"`, the source in `full_details`, and `timezone` where local; a WMI entry, which has only a record time, gets one with `timestamp_desc: "WMI repository record time (the subscription was made no earlier than this)"`. One `AsepCoverage` per hive record (with the hive, its path, profile, values and keys totals, per-category rows of `status` — `examined` with a count including zero, `examined_partial` with a partial reason, `not_applicable_to_hive` naming the hive that can carry it, `examined_from_another_source` for the filesystem- and WMI-backed categories pointing at their own record and saying that without one the category is unexamined, or `unexamined` with the reason — plus `unexamined_categories`, `examined_and_empty_categories`, scan notes and caps), and one `AsepCoverage` per `OBJECTS.DATA` (`hive: "OBJECTS.DATA"`, `hive_kind: WMI_REPOSITORY`, a `wmi_scan` block of bytes scanned, pages, trailing bytes, descriptor records, class definitions seen, classes scanned/added-from-bindings/without-definition, signature hits, hits inside other records, unreferenced hits, descriptors tried as class definitions and skipped for spanning pages, records matched/decoded/undecodable/spanning pages, the 4,096-record cap, `index_walked` and `index_read` with the reason when unread, the index's data references and pages visited, descriptors listed but not indexed and subscription records indexed or listed but not indexed, `mapping_read` with the mapping file and sequence number used, the older, refused (with reasons) and not-found mapping files, logical/mapped/continuation/unmapped page counts, descriptors reassembled (with the CRC-32s verified and mismatched on the reassembled records, where the file stores them), unresolved and in unmapped pages, records in unmapped pages, and a note when the 512 MiB ceiling or a short read cut the scan) — emitted even when the file could not be read, with the category unexamined.

**Cannot.** It cannot say when a registry entry was installed: the parsed hive record carries values, not per-key last-write times, so every registry-backed entry's `installed_time` is null with that reason, and no registry entry reaches the timeline. It cannot say a target is absent: `not_observed` means the name was not among the files enumerated so far, `no_file_index` that no filesystem was walked, and the index is capped at 400,000 basenames and 8 paths each with the cap stated on the record. It cannot decode a Task Scheduler 1.0 `.job`, a Winsock `WSAPROTOCOL_INFO` blob (the entry is present, the provider DLL path is not read), or a `UserChoice` hash (a MAC Windows verifies with a key that cannot be recomputed offline, so a tampered association is not distinguishable here and no record claims it is). Its WMI scan reads the index (`INDEX.BTR`) only for a `MAPPINGn.MAP` repository found beside the file; on an XP repository, or when the index is missing, withheld or refused, a record in a mapped page is current only on its page's own descriptor table, not on the index naming it. The index is graded on four real Windows 7 and Windows 10 repositories (`WMI-4`); no real subscription record is listed but not indexed in any of them, so that standing is pinned on a synthetic index only, and the 23 and 4 descriptors that are listed but not indexed there carry no subscription-class record the scan matched. Without the mapping beside the file (none found, refused, or a source that cannot look beside itself — each stated on the coverage record) it cannot say whether a record is live: an allocated instance may be a superseded copy, it skips descriptors whose size runs past their page (427 of 11,548 on the Lone Wolf image), so a class definition that spans pages is never collected and its instances read as "no class definition found" — counted as `descriptors_spanning_pages` — and it cannot decode a page-spanning instance. Through the mapping, on the whole Lone Wolf, Data Leakage and CFReDS XP repositories every spanning record was reassembled (364, 180 and 84; `WMI-2`; on XP, which stores a CRC-32, the scan checks each reassembled record against it and counts `reassembled_checksums_verified` / `_mismatched` — all 84 match), but a spanning record in an unmapped page still cannot be followed, and `MAPPING.VER` is not read — no repository here holds one. A deleted `OBJECTS.DATA` reaching the module has its records labelled allocated. It cannot decode a dynamic-property form, an unknown CIM type or an ambiguous pair of definitions, and reports each as unread with the reason; a page-spanning XP record not read whole through the mapping with a stored checksum is labelled `not_applicable`, whose documented meaning is "no descriptor", which is ambiguous rather than false. The MD5-on-XP / SHA-256-from-Vista split is reference-sourced for Vista and 8.x: Windows 10, Windows 7 and Windows XP repositories were observed, and the Windows 7 one stores the zero checksum the reference describes. Instance decoding is graded on real `__EventFilter`, `__FilterToConsumerBinding`, `NTEventLogEventConsumer`, `MSFT_UCScenarioControl` and — Windows 7's stock `BVTConsumer`, `WMI-1` — and the attacker-planted `Windows Update` consumer of the HTB "Perseverance" repository, graded against its published write-up and an independent parse, `WMI-3` — `CommandLineEventConsumer` records; no real `ActiveScriptEventConsumer`, `LogFileEventConsumer` or `SMTPEventConsumer` instance has been met, and a decoded record of those classes says so. A command line whose first token is a bare program name (`cscript KernCap.vbs`) is split at that token with `command_split_basis: bare_program_name_first_token`, and the name is resolved against the consumer's recorded `WorkingDirectory` and the system directories only: the launching process's own directory (the WMI host's is not recorded in the repository), its current directory and `PATH` need a live environment and are not modelled, so a search-path hit does not rule out an earlier match there; a working directory holding an unexpanded variable is named as not searched; and a bare COM server name is never excluded as in-System32 on the convention alone. Its WMI timeline events are dated by the later of two header FILETIMEs, which is a record time that bounds the subscription's creation from below and is not the creation time, and are labelled so. It does not accuse: no score, no verdict, no "suspicious" flag exists in the record, and an observation that an image resolves outside the system directories is a fact, not a finding. It reads the registry only through the registry plugin's records, so a hive that plugin did not parse, or a `RegistryHive` record with no `all_values`, leaves every registry category of that hive unexamined and says so. It does not read the SOFTWARE hive's `TaskCache` binary `Actions`/`Triggers`, the `Explorer\Shell Folders` redirection targets' contents, or a service's `Parameters\ServiceDll` beyond the value itself, and it does not expand environment variables in a target path (`unresolved_variable`).

**Refuses.** It refuses to let "checked and empty" and "never checked" render the same: every category is reported for every hive, a count of zero means the locations were read and empty, and a category not read is `unexamined` with the reason — because an implant that survives through a family the report omits survives the examination too. It refuses to drop an entry it could not decode: a `.job`, an unreadable task definition, an empty or foreign file in the task store, and an undecodable WMI record are each emitted `unread` with the reason, and a WMI repository that could not be read still yields a coverage record with the category unexamined. It refuses to emit a timestamp it did not read from evidence — never the hive's own time, never an epoch — and refuses to present a local wall-clock time as UTC. It refuses to guess a profile for a hive whose path was not seen, saying so in the scan notes, because an unattributed HKCU Run key reads as if it applied to everyone. It refuses to claim a target is absent from the volume. It refuses to decode WMI class layouts from a table in the code — the two real repositories each hold two different `ActiveScriptEventConsumer` definitions — reading them from the file, and refuses an instance block that does not verify end to end. It refuses to report a hash string found inside another record's key path as an instance. It refuses to present a WMI record as live beyond what the page mapping establishes, stamping `scan_basis` on every one and `index_walked` on the coverage saying whether the index was read, and `mapping_read` whether the page mapping was used; it refuses to attach a superseded or residue copy's command line to a binding when a current copy of the same consumer was found, and to call a binding in force when an end was found only as such a copy; and it refuses to use a mapping that does not account for the file's page count. It refuses to verify a checksum Windows 7+ stores as zero, reporting `not_stored`. It refuses to accuse. And it refuses to fan out on its own output.

### `plugin.windows.bits`

**Reads.** The binary Background Intelligent Transfer Service queue, `qmgr0.dat` / `qmgr1.dat` under A shadow-copy prior version of the file (a `VssPriorVersion` `ParsedRecord`) is read too and named by its `file_name`, since its `name` carries a `[shadow copy ...]` label; everything it yields repeats the snapshot id, label and creation time, and its sidecars are not searched. `%ALLUSERSPROFILE%\Microsoft\Network\Downloader\` (Windows XP to 8.1, Server 2003 to 2012 R2). It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent` and chooses a file by content — the header GUID `{C82BF713-9940-4A12-9F1A-3AAEBD894EEA}` at offset 16 or 24 followed by the queue GUID `{005F4447-BDA9-44BA-9851-C47BB6C07ACE}` — or by the name `qmgr0.dat` / `qmgr1.dat`. Up to 64 MiB is read whole. The layout is undocumented; the reading is a clean-room one, measured on the bytes of two real queues (NIST CFReDS Data Leakage, Windows 7; DFIR Madness case 001 DC01, Server 2012 R2) and nothing else. It walks each queue (queue GUID, a u32 job count bounded at 100,000, the jobs, the queue GUID again) to the closing header and file GUIDs. A job runs from its 16-byte delimiter to the next occurrence of the same delimiter; inside it the job type, priority and state (u32 each), the job GUID, the name, description, notify command, notify arguments and owner SID (u32 UTF-16 counts, at most 32,768 units) and the notify flags are read in that order. The stretch after them, holding notification and security data, is not decoded. The file list follows the GUID `{7756DA36-516F-435A-ACAC-44A248FFF34D}`: a u32 count and, per file, the local path, the remote URL, the temporary path, a u64 bytes-transferred and a u64 bytes-total (all ones is "size unknown"), then a tail of volume and range data that is walked to reach the next file. The order of the two byte counts was inferred from the bytes: a completed job holds them equal, a pending one holds 0 and all ones. The job's times are the first run of three plausible FILETIMEs (1995 to 2100) followed by a fourth that is plausible or zero, in the first 96 bytes after the second file-list GUID — located by shape, not by a measured offset, because the trailer's length changes when a job carries an error. Every DPAPI blob in a job (provider `{DF9D8CD0-1501-11D1-8C7A-00C04FC297EB}`) has its own description and master-key GUID read. Bytes past the live structure's closing GUIDs — earlier states of the file — are scanned byte by byte for three length-prefixed strings whose second is an HTTP(S), FTP, file or UNC source (a `\\?\` or `\\.\` device path is not one) and whose first and third contain a backslash. It also reads the Windows 10+ queue `qmgr.db`, an ESE database, chosen by content (the ESE signature) and then kept only when it has both a `Jobs` and a `Files` table carrying `Id` and `Blob` columns — every other ESE database (SRUM, WebCache, UAL, the Search index) yields nothing. A database up to 64 MiB is copied to a temporary file for libesedb in 8 MiB chunks, not buffered whole; only a database with those tables is read back into memory, and both tables are walked. A `Jobs` blob is a 16-byte GUID and then the same job header the `.dat` file carries, and only that header is read — the rest of the blob, which holds the job's file list and times, is not decoded; a `Files` blob is a short prefix and then the same file record. Both are located by shape in the blob's first 64 bytes. These layouts were read off record images in real bytes — a `Jobs` record in LoneWolf's `edb00001.log`, `Files` records in its database's unreferenced pages — and have not been run on a row a table walk returned, because the only real `qmgr.db` held has none. The ESE header's database state (offset 52) and page size (offset 236) are read, and the whole database is byte-scanned for file records that no decoded row holds.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` `BitsJob` (`subtype: bits_job`) per decoded job, with `job_id`, `job_name`, `description`, `notify_command`, `notify_arguments`, `owner_sid`, `notify_flags`, the raw `job_type` / `priority` / `state` and their names from Microsoft's documented `BG_JOB_TYPE` / `BG_JOB_PRIORITY` / `BG_JOB_STATE` numbering, `files` (local path, remote URL, temporary path, bytes transferred, bytes total or `unknown`, volume), `remote_urls`, `queue_index` and the job's byte `offset`. Of the four trailer times the first two are labelled `creation_time` and `modification_time` by position — ANSSI's `bits_parser`, run as a black box, reads the same two the same way on the Data Leakage jobs — and the third and fourth are `unnamed_time_3` / `unnamed_time_4`; an unset one is `unavailable`, and `times_basis` says all this on the record. `credentials_present` / `custom_headers_present` come from the blobs' own descriptions, listed in `dpapi_blobs`, and `secrets_decrypted` is always `false`. One `BitsCarvedFileTransfer` (`recovery_method: stale_region_carve`) per distinct record found past the live structure, with its offset and a count of identical copies. One `BitsQueueFile` summary per file: the `file_guid` (the file's first 16 bytes, not the header GUID) and `header_guid_offset`, each queue's declared and decoded job count, the live structure's end and a status — `queue read, N job(s)` or `queue partly read, N job(s) decoded`. Every `BitsJob` carries `files_read` and `times_read`. From a `qmgr.db`: `BitsJob` per decoded `Jobs` row (`source_format: qmgr_db`, `row_id`) carrying the job header's fields only — `files_read` and `times_read` are `false`, there is no `file_count`, `files` or `remote_urls`, `creation_time` and `modification_time` read `not_read`, and `content_incomplete` says the file list and times were not decoded and that the database's file rows are not linked to the job; `BitsFileTransfer` per decoded `Files` row, not tied to any job, `BitsCarvedFileTransfer` (`recovery_method: database_byte_scan`, with its offset and page) per record the scan found and no row holds, and one `BitsQueueDatabase` summary with the row counts and `database_state` (`dirty_shutdown`, `clean_shutdown`, …) and `file_rows_linked_to_jobs: false`.

**Cannot.** It does not read a `qmgr.db` job's files or times: the `Jobs` blob past the job header is not decoded, and a `Files` row is not linked to the job that owns it. It does not replay ESE transaction logs: a `qmgr.db` copied from a running machine holds its recent state in `edb*.log`, which is not read, so its tables can read empty when the queue was not. It does not read the log files at all. Neither `qmgr.db` blob decoder has been run on a row a real table walk returned. It does not decrypt credentials or custom headers, and says so on every job. It does not decode the notification and security data between the job header and the file list, the file records' range tail, the error block a failed job carries, or what the third and fourth trailer times record, and it reports no transfer-completion time. It does not attach a stale trailer's times to the records carved beside it. It cannot say which of `qmgr0.dat` and `qmgr1.dat` is the newer: Windows writes them in turn, and each is reported as it reads. A carved record is not a job: the header that owned it — name, owner, state, times — was overwritten, so it shows a transfer was once queued, not that it still was, and the record says so. The layout was measured on two queues, one with jobs (Windows 7) and one empty (Server 2012 R2); a job written by another build is read by the same rules, and a record that does not fit them is reported incomplete rather than guessed at.

**Refuses.** It refuses to read a file named like a queue that does not open with the header and queue GUIDs, and one over 64 MiB, and gives it a `BitsQueueIncomplete` record (`status: NotDecoded`) saying no job was read — never a summary that reads as an empty queue. A walk that stops early (a count larger than the file, a job with no closing delimiter, a missing closing GUID) keeps what it decoded, stamps `content_incomplete` on the summary with the reason and offset, and emits a standalone `BitsQueueIncomplete` (`status: QueueWalkIncomplete`). A job whose file list or times cannot be found carries `content_incomplete` with the reason. A `qmgr.db` whose header says dirty shutdown, whose walk fell short or whose row blobs did not decode stamps `content_incomplete` on its summary with the reason — for dirty shutdown, that the transaction logs hold changes not in the file — and emits a `BitsQueueIncomplete` (`status: DirtyDatabase` or `TableWalkIncomplete`). A file named `qmgr.db` gets `status: NotDecoded`, saying no job was read, when it cannot be read, is not an ESE database, cannot be staged to a temporary file, will not open in libesedb, or opens but lacks the `Jobs` and `Files` tables; the same failures on an ESE file of any other name yield nothing.

### `plugin.windows.clipboard`

**Reads.** The on-disk part of Windows clipboard history — the store under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Clipboard\` — and it chooses files by path. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess` and `ExecutionMode::Automatic`, and is not in the triage profile. An artifact whose `is_directory` is `true` is passed over; the path is taken from `path`, else `full_path`, else `relative_path`, and an artifact with none is passed over. `layout::classify` splits the path on `/` and `\`, finds the first run of components equal, case-insensitively, to `microsoft`, `windows`, `clipboard`, and requires the next component to be `pinned` or `historydata` — a path that merely mentions clipboard, or the `Microsoft\Clipboard` folder, is not the store. A last component of `metadata.json` is the inventory. Any other last component that is not itself GUID-shaped (36 characters of hex and four hyphens, braces optional) is a payload, attributed to the nearest GUID-shaped ancestor folder as its item id, lower-cased; a payload with no GUID ancestor is not classified. The payload's file name is base64-decoded — standard, no-pad, URL-safe and URL-safe-no-pad alphabets tried in turn, up to 256 bytes — into the clipboard format name it encodes (`VGV4dA==` is `Text`, `Qml0bWFw` is `Bitmap`, `TG9jYWxl` is `Locale`), accepted only when the result is printable ASCII. For the inventory, up to 8 MiB is read with `read_full` and parsed by `serde_json`; the document is then walked to depth 32 — arrays and objects alike — and every object carrying one of seven id spellings (`itemId`, `id`, `ItemId`, `Id`, `guid`, `Guid`, `identifier`) or one of eleven time spellings (`timestamp`, `Timestamp`, `time`, `Time`, `pinnedTime`, `PinnedTime`, `lastModified`, `LastModifiedTime`, `createdTime`, `CreatedTime`, `dateTime`) is an item, with `source`, `Source`, `origin`, `Origin` or `deviceId` as its source; up to 4,096 items are kept. A time is read as RFC 3339 text, or as a number: above 10^17 a Windows FILETIME, above 10^12 Unix milliseconds, otherwise Unix seconds, and any reading — numeric or RFC 3339 text — outside 2018-01-01 to 2100-01-01 is dropped. For a payload, the first 16 KiB is read and `envelope::inspect` checks for a DER `SEQUENCE` whose first element is an OID: `1.2.840.113549.1.7.3` (CMS enveloped data) is a protected payload, whose first 8 KiB are then scanned for `SID=` in ASCII or UTF-16LE followed by an `S-1-` value of up to 512 descriptor characters; another OID is named in dotted form; anything else is `not_der`, or `too_short` under four bytes. The file system's `created`, `created_time`, `birth_time`, `modified`, `modified_time`, `accessed` and `accessed_time` keys on the payload's own artifact are copied. Nothing under `%ProgramData%\Microsoft\Windows\ClipSVC` is read; that is Store licensing.

**Produces.** Three kinds of artifact, every one stamped `analysed_by: plugin.windows.clipboard`, `analysed_by_version: 0.1.0`, `analysed_os: windows` and a `scope_note` saying that Windows keeps most clipboard history in the `cbdhsvc` service's memory and that absence here is not evidence nothing was copied. From an inventory: one `ParsedRecord` per item found, `type` and `record_type` `WindowsClipboardIndex`, `subtype: "clipboard_index_entry"`, `name: "Clipboard item <id>"`, `clipboard_store` (`pinned` or `history_data`) with a `store_meaning` sentence, `source_path`, `item_id`, `clipboard_source`, and where a time was read `timestamp` in UTC RFC 3339, `timestamp_field` (which spelling it came from) and `timestamp_interpretation` (`rfc3339`, `windows_filetime`, `unix_milliseconds` or `unix_seconds`), the whole object as `inventory_entry`, and `index_truncated: true` when the 4,096-item cap was hit; plus one `TimelineEvent` per dated item with `timestamp_desc: "Windows Clipboard"`, `source_module`, a `short_desc` of `Clipboard item <id> recorded in the <store> store` and a `full_details` JSON string carrying the id, store, source, `timestamp_field`, interpretation and path. An inventory that does not parse as JSON yields one `WindowsClipboardIndex` record named `Clipboard inventory (unreadable)` with `parse_failed: true` and a `parse_failure` sentence, rather than nothing. From a payload: one `ParsedRecord`, `type` and `record_type` `WindowsClipboardItem`, `subtype: "clipboard_payload"`, `name: "Clipboard <format> — <item>"`, the store pair, `item_id`, `source_path`, `payload_file_name`, `payload_bytes` (the declared size), `clipboard_format` with a `format_meaning` sentence for `Text`, `Bitmap`/`PNG`/`DIB`/`DIBV5`, `HTML Format`, `Locale`, `UnicodeText` and the file-drop formats, or a `clipboard_format_note` when the name did not decode; `content_encrypted` (true only for CMS enveloped data), `payload_encoding` (`cms_enveloped_data`, `der_other_content_type`, `not_der`, `too_short`), a `content_statement` sentence, and for a protected payload `protected_to`, `protected_to_sid` (the value after the `SID=` prefix, in any letter case — the same test the header scan admitted it under), `protected_to_encoding`, a `protected_to_recovery` sentence saying the descriptor was found by scanning the header and not by parsing the CMS recipient structure, and a `decryption_requirement` naming the DPAPI master key or domain root key it would take; and `filesystem_times` where the payload artifact carried any. No plaintext of any payload is ever produced, and no `TimelineEvent` is made from a payload or its file times. `process` never returns an error.

**Cannot.** It cannot read a single clipboard item's content, and does not try: every payload Windows writes is CMS enveloped data from `NCryptProtectSecret`, the key material is the user's DPAPI master key or a domain root key over RPC, and the module holds neither, attempts no decryption, and publishes no plaintext. It cannot see the clipboard history that matters most: the unpinned items live in `cbdhsvc`'s memory and are cleared at sign-out, so what reaches this module is the pinned set and, where sync is on, some history items — the `scope_note` on every record exists because two pinned items must not be read as two things copied. It cannot vouch for the inventory's field names: the crate says in terms that no source available to the project sets out `metadata.json`'s schema and that the project holds no Windows 11 image to read one from, so the seven id spellings and eleven time spellings are guesses walked tolerantly, `timestamp_field` records which one matched, the whole object is kept verbatim so a later version can re-read it, and no record carries a validation stamp saying the parser has never met the real artifact — which the Sticky Notes and macOS memory modules do carry. So `README.md`'s "when each item was pinned" is the first plausible time field found under any of those names, not a field known to be the pin time. It cannot recover a descriptor reliably: `protected_to` comes from a substring scan for `SID=` in the first 8 KiB, not from the CMS recipient structure, a descriptor written as `LOCAL=user`, `WEBCREDENTIALS=` or a `SDDL=` rule is not found, and the record says so. It cannot decode a payload's format beyond its name, and a format Windows registered at run time (`AcmeCorpInternalFormat`) gets a name and no meaning. It cannot date a pinned item from the folder that dates it: the doc comment on `filesystem_times` says the item folder's creation time is the pin time, but directories are passed over at the top of `process`, so what travels is the payload file's own timestamps under whichever key the file-system parser used, and nothing compares them to the inventory's figure. It cannot say which machine a synced item came from beyond the raw `source` string. Its ceilings are 8 MiB of inventory, 4,096 items, depth 32, 16 KiB of payload header, an 8 KiB descriptor window, 512 descriptor characters and a 256-byte format name; a time outside 2018–2100 is dropped without a note, and the FILETIME/millisecond/second reading is chosen by magnitude alone, so a genuine value in the wrong band is misread by orders of magnitude and labelled with the reading that was made.

**Refuses.** It refuses to produce plaintext. The test `an_encrypted_payload_never_yields_plaintext_and_says_it_is_encrypted` pins that a protected payload's record carries `content_encrypted: true`, no decrypted content, and the sentence naming what decryption would need, because clipboard text — a password, a message, an address — is exactly the evidence nobody would think to doubt, and a guessed plaintext would survive into a statement. It refuses to attach a clipboard finding to a file that is not in the store: a path must run `Microsoft\Windows\Clipboard\{Pinned|HistoryData}\…`, and `C:\Users\jo\Documents\clipboard\Pinned`, `Microsoft\Clipboard\Pinned` and `Windows\Explorer\Pinned` are all refused, as is a payload with no GUID-shaped item folder above it and the GUID folder itself. It refuses to go quiet on an inventory it cannot read: a `metadata.json` that is not JSON yields a record saying so, because silence would read as "this user pinned nothing", a claim about the custodian the parser has not established. It refuses to present a scanned value as a parsed one — `protected_to_recovery` says the descriptor came from a header scan — and refuses a descriptor that does not begin `S-1-`. It refuses to render an implausible value as a date: zero, negatives, and any number or RFC 3339 string outside 2018–2100 leave the item with no timestamp and no timeline event, and a string that is not RFC 3339 does the same. It refuses to treat a payload that is not DER as nothing: `not_der` is published with a sentence saying the file has either been altered or is not what its location implies and is worth looking at directly. It refuses to panic on hostile payloads — a DER length of more than four bytes, an OID that overflows, a truncated envelope — all pinned by `hostile_payloads_are_handled_without_panicking`. Everything it declines — a directory, an artifact with no path, a path outside the store — is an empty list and a zero-yield processing-log row. Every fixture is synthetic; no clipboard store from a real Windows machine is in the tree.

### `plugin.windows.evtx_parser`

**Reads.** Windows event logs in the EVTX binary-XML format, in two passes over one input. It subscribes to `FileEntry`, `SystemArtifact` and — for a shadow-copy prior version only, whose output repeats the snapshot id, label and creation time — `ParsedRecord`, with `InputCapability::Stream`; an artifact with no data source yields nothing. It reaches an input in one of three ways: `seance_core::file_detection::detect_file_type` recognises the `ElfFile` header; the name ends `.evtx`; or an `ElfChnk\0` signature sits somewhere in the first 64 KiB of a file at least 545 bytes long — every other file is left alone. A chunk lying on its own in free space reaches it as the `FileEntry` the carver emits for the `EVTX chunk (Windows event log)` signature (one fixed 64 KiB extent, `.elfchnk`). The intact pass runs only on a detected header: the `evtx` 0.8.5 crate opens the file over a `SourceCursor`, and the walk proceeds chunk by chunk through `find_next_chunk`, each 64 KiB chunk at file offset 4,096 + 65,536 × n, with each chunk's header advance and each chunk's decode wrapped in `catch_unwind` because the upstream decoder can panic on a malformed record (an integer overflow on a length prefix, found by replaying this crate's own stored fuzz reproducer); before a chunk is handed to the decoder, its string table (64 buckets at 0x80) and template table (32 buckets at 0x180) are walked and refused if a chain cycles or runs longer than the chunk can hold, since a loop is not a panic and nothing could catch it. Each record's binary XML is rendered to text and read with `quick_xml` under an `XmlGuard` (256 attributes per element): from `System`, `EventID`, `EventRecordID`, `Computer`, `Channel`, `Level`, `Task`, `Keywords`, `Provider@Name` and `Security@UserID`; from `EventData` every `Data@Name` (unnamed ones numbered `Data1`…) and from `UserData` every child element, duplicates suffixed `_2`, `_3` rather than overwritten. The record's `TimeCreated` FILETIME is kept to 100 ns. The recovery pass then runs on every input, live or not (`recovery.rs`): `ElfChnk\0` signatures are found anywhere in the input by a 4 MiB windowed scan under a 2 GiB bound, at most 16,384 chunks acted on, the header CRC32 (bytes 0..120 and 128..512) and the data CRC32 (512..free-space offset) verified separately with a chunk whose flags say no CRC was written marked `absent` and a truncated one `unverifiable_truncated`; every chunk the intact walk did not fully decode is re-read by a walker that trusts neither the free-space offset nor the header tables, discarding tables that will not walk; each chunk's slack past the free-space offset is decoded against a copy whose live region is poisoned so a reference into rewritten bytes fails rather than reads; records with the `**\0\0` magic outside every chunk are decoded in an inferred 64 KiB window under a synthesised header when the carved chunks agree on a grid phase; and a template pool keyed by template id and a hash of the sentinel-rendered, name-resolved definition (at most 4,096 templates) revives a record whose own definition is gone. Substitution arrays are re-bound value by value from the descriptor table. At most 500,000 records are recovered. A record-header FILETIME outside 1980..2200 is refused as a date.

**Produces.** From the intact pass, one `EvtxLogEntry` per decoded record — `event_id` and `event_record_id` as numbers or null (never 0 for an unreadable one; the text that defeated the parser travels as `event_id_raw`/`event_record_id_raw` with `content_incomplete: true`, reason `unresolved_structure`, and a sentence saying 0 is itself a valid Windows identifier), `timestamp` in whole Unix seconds, `timestamp_subsec_nanos`, `timestamp_utc` as RFC 3339 with full sub-second precision, `computer_name`, `provider_name`, `channel` (`Unknown` when absent), `level` and `level_description` (Critical/Error/Warning/Information/Verbose/Unknown), `task`, `keywords`, `user_sid`, `event_data` as a name→value map, `short_desc` from a table of about forty well-known channel/ID pairs (Security 4624, 4625, 4634, 4648, 4672, 4688, 4689, 4720–4726, 4732, 4733, 4756, 4768, 4769; System 1074, 6005, 6006, 6009, 7045; Application 1000, 1001; WLAN-AutoConfig 8000–8003; …) else `<provider> Event ID <n>`, `full_event_xml`, and any `XmlGuard` findings (attributes truncated, duplicated or unparseable) — plus one `TimelineEvent` per record, parented to its entry, with the RFC 3339 timestamp (so the nanoseconds reach `timeline_events.timestamp_subsec_nanos`), `timestamp_desc: "EventTime"`, `short_desc: "<desc> on <computer>"` and `full_details` carrying the same unreadable-ID stamp. When anything was lost, one `EvtxParseStatus` (`content_incomplete: true` with a comma-joined reason from `chunk_walk_aborted_after_decode_panic`, `records_failed_to_parse`, `chunks_skipped_after_decode_panic`, `chunks_unreadable`, `chunk_truncated_at_end_of_file`; `inventory_incomplete: true`; `events_parsed`; `records_failed` exact per record; `chunks_skipped`, `chunks_unreadable`, `chunks_partially_recovered`, `chunks_read` as counts of 64 KiB chunks, each of which may have held many events; `walk_aborted` and `counts_are_floor` when a chunk header panicked and the remainder of the file was never read; `chunks_truncated_at_eof`, `truncated_chunk_offset` and `truncated_chunk_bytes_present` when the file ends inside a chunk whose bytes open with `ElfChnk\0`, a chunk the walk cannot read and the recovery pass does; and a message saying absence from the case is not evidence nothing was logged). From the recovery pass, one `EvtxRecoveredLogEntry` per recovered record — a different type from a live entry, with `recovered: true` and a mandatory `recovery_source` of `carved_chunk`, `chunk_slack` or `loose_record`, `record_offset`, `record_size`, `record_trailer_valid`, `record_header_event_record_id`, `chunk_offset`, `chunk_header` (`present`, `tables_discarded`, `synthetic`), `chunk_header_checksum` and `chunk_data_checksum` (`valid`, `failed`, `absent`, `unverifiable_truncated`, `none`, and `not_applicable` on a slack record, which also carries `containing_chunk_header_checksum`, `containing_chunk_data_checksum` and a `chunk_checksum_note` saying no checksum covers its bytes), `chunk_truncated`, `template_id`, `substitution_count`, the three timestamp forms or nulls with `timestamp_unreadable_reason`, `rendered_with_borrowed_template` and a `borrowed_template` object (`template_id`, `guid`, `text_hash`, `from_chunk_offset`, `candidates`, `ambiguous`, `guid_confirmed`), `partial`, `incomplete_substitutions` (each with `index`, `position`, `reason`, `values_without_names`), `full_event_xml` holding `<SeanceIncomplete substitution="N"/>` markers where a value did not bind, `own_decode_failure`, `record_id_also_read_live`, a `recovery_note` in words, the parsed System fields when the XML parsed, and `content_incomplete: true` with reason `unresolved_structure` and a detail naming the unbound indices or the failure when partial — plus a `TimelineEvent` with `timestamp_desc: "EventTime (recovered)"` and `[recovered]` in its description only when the header time was plausible. One `EvtxRecoveryStatus` when there is something to say (always on a headerless input, where "looked, found nothing" is a finding): `bytes_declared`, `bytes_scanned`, `scan_bound_hit`, `short_read`, the chunk tallies (`chunks_found`, `_checksum_valid`/`_failed`/`_absent`/`_unverifiable`, `_truncated`, `_live_skipped`, `_nested_skipped`, `_tables_discarded`, `_unopenable`, `_bound_hit`), the record tallies (`records_recovered`, `_partial`, `_header_only`, `_borrowed_template`, `_already_live`, `_bound_hit`), `loose_records_found`, `loose_windows`, `loose_records_unlocatable`, `templates_pooled`, `template_pool_bound_hit`, the `limits` in force, a `chunk_listing` of up to 1,024 chunks of note by offset (checksum states, truncation, header state, unopenable, `read_live_whole`, records and slack records recovered) with `bound_hit` and `omitted`, `inventory_incomplete` and `counts_are_floor` when any bound was hit, `content_incomplete` with reason `cap_reached` and/or `short_read`, and a message stating every bound with the number it stopped at.

**Cannot.** It cannot decode what the upstream `evtx` crate cannot: a record whose value the decoder refuses is counted under `records_failed` and lost, and one confirmed case is event 4739's `EventData` in plaso's `System2.evtx` record 216. Its intact walk cannot read a partial chunk — `find_next_chunk` stops at `(size − 4096) / 65536` — so a tail chunk the file ends inside is counted on `EvtxParseStatus` and its records are read only by the recovery pass; a tail that does not open with the chunk magic is not counted as a chunk. It cannot verify a live record's chunk checksum: the intact pass never validates CRCs, so a chunk with a failed checksum whose records were emitted live is named only in the recovery status's `chunk_listing`. No checksum covers a slack record's bytes, so nothing verifies one. It cannot render an embedded `EventData` fragment whose element names lie in rewritten bytes: the scalar values are listed under `values_without_names` without their structure. It cannot locate a substitution array behind a corrupt inline template-definition size, and cannot infer a window for a loose record with a back-referenced template when the carved chunks do not agree on a 64 KiB grid phase (`loose_records_unlocatable`). A borrowed template with more than one pooled rendering under its id is a choice, flagged `ambiguous`, not a certainty; `record_id_also_read_live` is an inference that the slack record is an earlier write, left to the examiner. Its `short_desc` table names about forty event IDs; every other event is `<provider> Event ID <n>`, and it does not resolve message strings from the provider's resource DLL, so `event_data` is name→value with no rendered message. It cannot say who a SID is. Its bounds — 2 GiB scanned, 16,384 chunks, 500,000 records, 4,096 pooled templates, 1,024 listed chunks — are each stated with the number on the status when hit. A `TimelineEvent` is never emitted for a recovered record whose header FILETIME is outside 1980..2200. It reads one file; it does not stitch a log across its archived `Archive-*.evtx` siblings or the `.evtx` in a volume shadow.

**Refuses.** It refuses to present a recovered record as a live event: every one leaves as `EvtxRecoveredLogEntry` with a mandatory `recovery_source`, a distinct `record_type`, and a note stating which chunk, what state its header was in, whether its checksums held, whether its template was its own and which substitutions — by index — did not bind, because an examiner filtering by type must not pick up a carved or slack event as one the machine logged in its current state. It refuses to write 0 for an `EventID` or `EventRecordID` it could not read, leaving null and the raw text with the incompleteness pair, and stamping the same inside the timeline event's `full_details`, the one field that survives the insert. It refuses to let a single bad record lose a whole log: chunks are isolated under `catch_unwind`, records decoded before a fault survive it, and a chunk whose tables would loop the decoder is refused before it is handed over. It refuses to resume after a chunk-header panic at an unknown offset, declaring `walk_aborted` and every count a floor rather than reading from a guess. It refuses to fold a chunk-sized loss into a record count: `records_failed` is exact, the chunk figures are chunks, and the message says so. It refuses to drop the sub-second part of a FILETIME, because same-second order is what decides whether a process started before or after the logon it is attributed to. It refuses to read a reference from a slack record into bytes the chunk has since rewritten, poisoning the live region so the read fails rather than fabricates. It refuses to render a date from a header FILETIME outside any plausible range. It refuses to trust a carved chunk's free-space offset or header tables. It refuses to pool a template by id alone, keying on the hash of its rendered text as well. And it refuses to present a short read as a complete scan: `bytes_declared` sits beside `bytes_scanned` and `short_read` says the bytes past the read were not examined.

### `plugin.windows.jumplist_parser`

**Reads.** Windows jump lists, selected by name and by nothing else: the artifact's `name` (for a shadow-copy prior version, its `file_name`, since its `name` carries a `[shadow copy …]` label; what such a version yields repeats the snapshot id, label and creation time) is lower-cased and tested for the suffixes `.automaticdestinations-ms` and `.customdestinations-ms` — four spellings are pinned by test, because matched by exact case an acquisition whose tool folded case recovered zero jump lists in silence (CR-044) — and no content probe takes part in the decision. It subscribes to `FileEntry` with `InputCapability::Stream`. The hex digits in front of the extension are the AppID; `appid` resolves it against a table of 41 applications whose IDs this build computes as the CRC-64 of the documented AppUserModelID or known-folder path, 19 of them cross-checked against an independently published ID and 22 computed with no independent confirmation, and the record says which basis applies. For an `automaticDestinations` file the first 512 bytes are read through the looping `read_exact_or_fail`, and all **eight** bytes of the OLE compound-file signature `D0 CF 11 E0 A1 B1 1A E1` are compared (an earlier reading compared four while claiming eight); a file too short to hold the header is not refused but scanned as a fragment. The file is then staged with the shared capped read to 256 MiB (`MAX_JUMPLIST_BYTES`), which returns only the bytes delivered, and the OLE structure is read through the `cfb` crate in its permissive mode — header, FAT, mini-FAT and root directory. From the directory it takes the `DestList` stream and every stream whose name is hexadecimal (a numbered shortcut stream), reading the lowest-numbered up to 10,000 streams, each under a 16 MiB ceiling, and `DestList` under 64 MiB, through the allocation tables so a scattered stream is followed. `DestList` is decoded from its 32-byte header (format version, entry count, pinned count, last entry number, last revision) in two layouts: version 1 (Windows 7/8) with a 114-byte fixed part per entry, and versions 2–4 (Windows 10+) with a 130-byte fixed part carrying the additional 32-bit field at offset 116 and four trailing bytes; each entry's DROID and birth-DROID volume and file identifiers, NetBIOS hostname, entry number, FILETIME, pin status and UTF-16 path are read, up to 100,000 entries. Where the directory cannot be read — the `cfb` open fails, or the header was short — the staged bytes are scanned one byte at a time for the eight-byte MS-SHLLINK signature `4C 00 00 00 01 14 02 00` and each hit sized by walking the shortcut per MS-SHLLINK (the 76-byte header, `LinkTargetIDList`, `LinkInfo`, up to five `StringData` strings, the `ExtraData` chain to its terminal block); every offset at which the whole signature fits is tested, the last eight bytes included, and the scan resumes at the end of each carve. A `customDestinations` file has no directory and is only scanned; its version header, entry count and `0xBABFFBAB` footer are not read.

**Produces.** When the directory reads: one `FileEntry` of `type: "JumpListStream"` per numbered stream read, named `<file>_stream_<hex>.lnk`, carrying the stream's bytes on an in-memory data source so the shortcut reader (`plugin.windows.lnk_parser`), the hasher, the file analyser and the search index see it, with `recovery_method: "ole_directory"`, `stream_name`, `stream_declared_len`, `stream_read_len`, a `stream_read_note` where the read fell short, `source_offset` with its basis only where the stream's bytes lie contiguous at a signature in the file (else `source_offset_unavailable`), the AppID attribution (`app_id`, `application`, `application_identifier`, `application_basis`, or `application_unknown` / `app_id_unavailable`), and its `DestList` correlation — `matched` with `dest_list_entry_number`, `dest_list_mru_position`, `dest_list_path`, `dest_list_last_recorded_time` (null when the FILETIME is the unset sentinel or out of range), `dest_list_pinned`, and the version 2+ field as `dest_list_offset_116_unknown_possibly_access_count` with a note that its meaning is not established; `no_dest_list_entry` when the list names no entry with that number; `dest_list_unavailable` when there is no list. One `ParsedRecord` of `type: "JumpListDestListEntry"` (`record_type: "jumplist_destlist_entry"`) per DestList entry — format version and layout, `offset_in_dest_list`, `mru_position` with a basis sentence saying the libyal documentation does not state the order and that most-recently-used-first is what real files show and how plaso and JLECmd read it, `entry_number`, `stream_name`, `lnk_stream_present` and `lnk_artifact_name`, `path` (with a note when UTF-16 units did not decode), `hostname`, the four DROID identifiers, `last_recorded_time` or `last_recorded_time_unavailable` with the raw value, `last_recorded_time_raw_filetime`, `pin_status`, `pinned` (`false` for −1, `true` with `pinned_position` for 0 and above, null with a note for anything else), and the offset-116 field or `offset_116_unavailable` on a version-1 entry — plus one `TimelineEvent` (`timestamp_desc: "Jump list entry last recorded"`) per entry with a valid time. Always last, exactly one `ParsedRecord` of `type: "JumpListDestList"` (`record_type: "jumplist_destlist"`) per file: `ole_directory_read`, `recovery_method`, `lnk_streams_in_directory`, `other_directory_entries`, `dest_list_present` (null with a note when the directory was never read), `dest_list_declared_len`, `dest_list_empty` for the empty stream Windows writes on a list with no entries, the header fields, `entries_read`, `lnk_streams_read`, `lnk_streams_unread` with each stream's reason, `entries_without_stream`, `streams_without_entry`, and `content_incomplete` with `content_incomplete_reason` (the first), `content_incomplete_reasons` (all), the joined detail on both `_detail` keys and the `inventory_incomplete` pair whenever anything fell short — a partial staging, no `DestList` in the directory, a `DestList` not read in full or not decodable, a truncated entry, the entry cap, more numbered streams than the 10,000 read, or streams that would not read; otherwise a message that everything was read in full. On the carve fallback: one `FileEntry` of `type: "JumpListCarvedShortcut"` per signature hit, named `<file>_stream_<offset>.lnk` or `<file>_entry_<offset>.lnk`, with `recovery_method: "signature_carve"`, `source_offset`, a `length_note` when the structure could not be walked and up to 4,096 bytes were taken, stopping short at the next signature, the attribution, and `dest_list_correlation: "dest_list_unavailable"` with a note naming the directory error; the `JumpListDestList` summary with `ole_directory_read: false`, `ole_directory_error`, `shortcuts_carved` and an `unresolved_structure` shortfall; and one `JumpListCarveStatus` (`links_carved`, `max_carved_links: 10000`, `bytes_scanned` — the bytes from the start of the staged buffer that were tested — `carve_complete`, the incompleteness pairs with `short_read` for a fragment, `cap_reached` or `short_read` for a scan that stopped, or none and `carve_complete: true` when the whole file was scanned and held nothing). A `customDestinations` file yields its carved shortcuts and, in the same circumstances, the carve status. It emits no parsed record for a shortcut's own contents: every target path, argument and date is `plugin.windows.lnk_parser`'s reading of the stream bytes. When the directory was read, it also walks the compound file's own allocation tables — header, DIFAT, FAT, the root entry's mini stream and the mini-FAT, as [MS-CFB] defines them — and scans every run of sectors and mini-sectors marked `FREESECT` for the shortcut signature; each hit whose bytes are not a prefix of a live stream is a `FileEntry` `JumpListCarvedShortcut` with `recovery_method: "unreferenced_sector_carve"`, `sector_kind` (`sector` or `mini_sector`), `sector_index`, `source_offset`, `dest_list_correlation: "none"` and a note that nothing ties it to a DestList entry, and a `validation_note` that no real jump list examined has yet held one; the summary carries `shortcuts_carved_from_unreferenced_sectors`, `unreferenced_sector_scan`, a sentence naming how many free sectors were scanned, and `unreferenced_sector_cap_reached`. That carve stops at 10,000 shortcuts; when it stops there with a further signature found, the sentence says the count is a floor, the summary carries `max_carved_links`, and the DestList record is stamped `content_incomplete` with reason `cap_reached`.

**Cannot.** It cannot say which stream a shortcut found in a free sector belonged to, when it was freed, or tie it to a DestList entry: the allocation tables record none of that. That carve is pinned on compound files written and edited by the `cfb` crate; 30 real jump lists were checked (Data Leakage 10, LoneWolf and DC01 18, plaso 2) and none held a freed shortcut, so it has not yet recovered one from real evidence. Bytes in a free sector that do not begin with the shortcut signature — a shortcut whose first sector was reused — are not reassembled. It cannot name an AppID outside its table of 41, reporting `application_unknown` and never guessing, and 22 of those 41 rest on a computed CRC-64 with no independent confirmation, which the record states. It cannot say what the version 2+ field at offset 116 is: libyal lists it as "Unknown (access count?)" and plaso as `unknown5`, so it is reported under that name and not asserted to be an access count; nor does it surface the remaining undocumented bytes of a version 2+ entry. It cannot say whether a pinned position is current — the pin field is read as stored. Its most-recently-used order is an observed convention, stated as such. On the carve fallback it inherits the scan's limits: after a hit whose structure walks, the scan resumes past the walked length, so a signature lying inside a walked shortcut is not carved separately; a shortcut that does not walk is carved up to 4,096 bytes or the next signature with a `length_note`, and may be cut short or carry bytes of what follows; and the carve status carries one reason, the later finding overwriting the earlier. It cannot find a jump list that is not named as one. Its ceilings are 256 MiB staged per file, 10,000 numbered streams read, 16 MiB per stream, 64 MiB for `DestList`, 100,000 DestList entries and 10,000 carved shortcuts, each stated on the summary or status record with its number when reached.

**Refuses.** It refuses a `DestList` whose format version is not 1 through 4, naming the version it found rather than decoding a layout it was not written to. It refuses to guess the application: an AppID not in the table is reported as unknown, and a known one carries the basis on which it is known. It refuses to carve an `.automaticDestinations-ms` file whose first 512 bytes were read and do not carry the full eight-byte OLE signature, even when shortcut signatures are plainly visible further in, leaving an `unresolved_structure` status record instead; a fragment too short to hold the header is scanned, and its status record says the container was not corroborated. It refuses to let silence stand for a finding: a scanned file with nothing in it leaves the positive record, and every shortfall — partial staging, missing or truncated `DestList`, unread streams, caps — is a token from the shared vocabulary with a sentence on the `_detail` keys the examiner-facing reader shows. It refuses to invent a source offset for a stream the allocation table scatters, and refuses to report a null or out-of-range FILETIME as a date. It refuses to read a zero-padded tail as content, staging only the bytes delivered. It refuses to invent a length for a malformed shortcut. It refuses an artifact whose name matches neither suffix, silently, and one whose name it has claimed but that arrived with no data source with `InvalidInputFormat`.

### `plugin.windows.lnk_parser`

**Reads.** Windows shortcuts — MS-SHLLINK Shell Link files — selected **by name and only by name**: the artifact's `name` metadata (for a shadow-copy prior version, its `file_name`, since its `name` carries a `[shadow copy …]` label; everything such a version yields repeats the snapshot id, label and creation time) is lower-cased and must end `.lnk`. There is no content probe and no magic-based discovery, so what reaches this reader is whatever the case named that way, wherever it sat — a file-system entry with that extension, the shortcut streams `plugin.windows.jumplist_parser` carves out of a jump list and hands on as `<jumplist>_stream_<offset>.lnk` and `<jumplist>_entry_<offset>.lnk`, or the carver's own `carved_<offset as eight hex digits>.lnk`. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and declares `InputCapability::Stream`, a declaration nothing in the orchestrator branches on. The whole file is staged into memory through `seance_core::io::read_capped` under a 16,777,216-byte ceiling (16 MiB) — real shortcuts are kilobytes — and how many bytes actually arrived is compared against the data source's own `size()` before the header is read, because the LinkInfo path strings are reached by offsets into that buffer and an offset into bytes that were never read yields an empty string. It then walks the 76-byte ShellLinkHeader, taking `HeaderSize`, the `LinkCLSID`'s first four bytes, `LinkFlags` at 0x14, `FileAttributes` at 0x18 and the three FILETIMEs at 0x1C, 0x24 and 0x2C — the remaining twelve bytes of the 16-byte CLSID are skipped explicitly, because a four-byte skip read the flags and every timestamp twelve bytes early. From `LinkFlags` it takes `HasLinkTargetIDList` (0x01), `HasLinkInfo` (0x02), `HasName` (0x04), `HasRelativePath` (0x08), `HasWorkingDir` (0x10), `HasArguments` (0x20), `HasIconLocation` (0x40) and `IsUnicode` (0x80). The `LinkTargetIDList` is skipped by its own 16-bit size. In `LinkInfo` it reads `LinkInfoSize`, `LinkInfoHeaderSize`, `LinkInfoFlags`, `LocalBasePathOffset`, `CommonNetworkRelativeLinkOffset` and `CommonPathSuffixOffset`, and the two Unicode offsets only when the LinkInfo header is 0x24 or larger, because an ANSI-only LinkInfo has no such fields. Where the flags say `VolumeIDAndLocalBasePath` it takes the local base path, Unicode form first; **otherwise**, where they say `CommonNetworkRelativeLinkAndPathSuffix`, it walks the `CommonNetworkRelativeLink` at its offset, reads `NetNameOffset` at +0x08 and the Unicode `NetNameOffset` at +0x14 when the ANSI offset is greater than 0x14, and takes the share name. `CommonPathSuffix` is taken from whichever of its two offsets is non-zero, with no flag consulted, and joined to the base with a single backslash inserted only when both sides are present and neither already carries one. Then StringData, read in order from the cursor, each a 16-bit character count followed by UTF-16LE or ANSI bytes: `NAME_STRING`, `RELATIVE_PATH`, `WORKING_DIR`, `COMMAND_LINE_ARGUMENTS` and `ICON_LOCATION`. ANSI fields — the shape a shortcut written without `IsUnicode` has — are decoded through CP1252 by `seance_core::codepage::decode`, which also reports whether any byte at 0x80 or above had to be interpreted at all.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` of type `LnkFile` per shortcut, carrying `target_local_path` (the assembled LinkInfo path — local base plus suffix, or `\\server\share` plus suffix for a network target), `relative_path`, `arguments`, `working_dir`, `icon_location`, the raw `flags` and `attributes` words, and `target_created`, `target_accessed` and `target_modified` as RFC 3339. The four string fields are always present: each is the empty string when its `LinkFlags` bit is clear, so a shortcut that carried no arguments and a shortcut whose argument bytes were never read hold the same value. The record carries no name and no path of its own; the shortcut it came from is identified only by the record's parent. And up to three `TimelineEvent` records, one per timestamp, each with its own `timestamp_desc` — `LNK Target Created`, `LNK Target Accessed`, `LNK Target Modified` — because all three once carried one shared label and a timeline filter could not separate the target being created from its being opened; only the prose differed, and prose is not filterable. Each event names the `target_path` it concerns, falling back to the relative path and then to the shortcut's own lower-cased file name, and the `lnk_source` it came from, also lower-cased. Where any string on the record came from an ANSI byte outside ASCII, the record carries `path_decode: "cp1252"`, so the path is not quoted as literal text; the stamp is written once for the record and does not say which field was interpreted. Where every byte was ASCII, or the strings were UTF-16, no such stamp is written, because a stamp on those would cry wolf on the overwhelming majority of real paths. Where the staged bytes fell short of the size the data source declared, the record carries `content_incomplete`, `content_incomplete_reason` (`cap_reached` or `short_read`), `bytes_read` and `declared_size`. A shortcut whose declared bytes exist but which could not be staged as far as its 76-byte header leaves a second record type instead, `LnkParseStatus`, naming the shortcut as `<name> (not parsed)`, the reason, the bytes read and the bytes the data source declared, and stating in words that the absence of a target is not evidence the shortcut pointed nowhere.

**Cannot.** **A target path in a shortcut establishes the path a shortcut points at, and nothing more.** It does not establish that the file was there, that it is there now, that it was ever opened, or that it was opened on this machine: a shortcut can be authored anywhere and copied in, shipped by an installer, or written by hand. This reader examines only the shortcut's file name, never the directory it sat in, so it cannot tell an automatic `Recent` shortcut — the kind whose existence is evidence of an open — from a desktop or Start Menu one, and it draws that distinction nowhere on the record. It cannot report that name as it was written, either: the name is lower-cased before use, and `NeroInfoTool.lnk` is reported as `neroinfotool.lnk` in `lnk_source` and wherever the name stands in for a missing target. The three timestamps are the **target's** created, accessed and written times **as the shortcut last recorded them**, not the shortcut's own; the moment the user opened the file is the shortcut file's own modification time in the file system, which this module does not read and does not emit. A target FILETIME before 1970-01-01, and one at or past the year 10000, are both treated as the unset sentinel: no field, no timeline event, and no note that a value was there. It resolves nothing: no `FileEntry` is emitted for the target, no correlation to an MFT record is made, and the target is not hashed or identified. It cannot say the file carried the Shell Link CLSID — only four of the GUID's sixteen bytes are tested, and the remaining twelve are skipped unverified, so a file matching `0x00021401` alone is parsed and produces a record. It reads no `ExtraData` block at all — the walk stops at the end of StringData — so the `TrackerDataBlock`'s NetBIOS machine name and its two droid GUIDs, the `PropertyStoreDataBlock`, `KnownFolderDataBlock`, `SpecialFolderDataBlock`, `EnvironmentVariableDataBlock`, `IconEnvironmentDataBlock`, `ConsoleDataBlock`, `ShimDataBlock`, `DarwinDataBlock` and `VistaAndAboveIDListDataBlock` are all unread; a shortcut whose only statement of its target is an environment-variable block therefore reports no target. It does not decode the `VolumeID`: the volume serial number, the drive type and the volume label are not read, so it cannot say which volume the target was on, and it cannot distinguish a fixed disk from removable media. It does not decode the `LinkTargetIDList` — the shell item list is skipped by its size — so the PIDL's own copies of the target's name, its MFT entry and sequence number and its per-item timestamps are not recovered, and a shortcut with a shell item list and no LinkInfo yields no target path. It cannot report a UNC share for a LinkInfo that declares both `VolumeIDAndLocalBasePath` and `CommonNetworkRelativeLinkAndPathSuffix`: the local base path is taken and the network structure is never walked. `NAME_STRING`, the shortcut's description, is read only to advance the cursor and is discarded. The header's `FileSize` (the target's length when the shortcut was written), `IconIndex`, `ShowCommand` and `HotKey` are read and not emitted, so it cannot tell you the target's recorded size, the window state, or the hotkey a shortcut was bound to; `FileAttributes` is published as the raw word and not decoded. It assumes one ANSI code page and one only: CP1252. A shortcut written on a machine running a Cyrillic, Greek or Japanese ANSI code page is decoded against the wrong table and the record still says `cp1252`, and the same bytes then name a different file; five CP1252 byte values are undefined in that table — 0x81, 0x8D, 0x8F, 0x90 and 0x9D — and become U+FFFD, and Unicode strings are decoded lossily, so an unpaired surrogate becomes U+FFFD too, with nothing on the record saying so in either case. And its declaration of a short read protects the LinkInfo path strings only: those are reached by offset and come back empty, but the StringData fields and the LinkInfo header are read sequentially, so a shortcut truncated inside either errors out and produces **no record at all** — neither the `LnkFile` with `content_incomplete` nor the `LnkParseStatus`. A corrupt `LinkInfoSize` has the same effect, by parking the cursor past the staged bytes. Its bounds are: 16,777,216 bytes staged per file, a 76-byte floor, four of sixteen CLSID bytes verified, a `LinkTargetIDList` skipped by a 16-bit size and so at most 65,535 bytes of shell items, StringData fields of at most 65,535 characters each, and at most three timeline events per shortcut.

**Refuses.** It refuses any artifact whose name does not end `.lnk`, whatever its content — a shortcut renamed, or one whose name the case did not record, is never examined, and this refusal is silent. It refuses to work from an artifact with no data source at all: that is an error naming the missing input, not an empty result, because a shortcut the case knows of and cannot open is not a shortcut with nothing in it. It refuses to parse a file whose `HeaderSize` is not exactly 76, **or** whose CLSID does not begin `0x00021401`: either failure is enough, the reason is logged with both values, and no record is produced — including no `LnkParseStatus`, even where the bytes were on record and the read fell short. It refuses to read a file shorter than the 76-byte header as a shortcut. Where such a file's bytes were on record and the read fell short, it refuses to let it vanish into that same silence: a `LnkParseStatus` record is produced instead, so that the shortcut's presence in the evidence survives the failure to read it and the absence of a target is not read as a shortcut that pointed nowhere. It refuses to present a blank LinkInfo target as a fact — a record whose path strings sat in bytes that were never read carries `content_incomplete` with the reason, the bytes read and the size declared, so "the shortcut had no target" and "the target was not read" are not the same record. It refuses to publish an unset FILETIME as a date: zero, anything before 1970 and anything at or past the year 10000 produce no field at all and no timeline event, rather than an empty string where an examiner reads a timestamp. It refuses to fabricate a path separator, inserting a backslash between base and suffix only when both are present and neither supplies one. It refuses to stamp a code page on a string it never interpreted — an all-ASCII ANSI path and a UTF-16 path both carry no stamp — and equally refuses to report an interpreted ANSI path without one, because `String::from_utf8_lossy` turned every accented byte into U+FFFD and reported `\\fileserver\Röntgen\scan.pdf` as a share and a file that match nothing an examiner can search for. And it refuses to pull an unbounded file into memory on the strength of its name: past 16 MiB the read stops and the shortfall is declared as `cap_reached`.

### `plugin.windows.prefetch_parser`

**Reads.** Windows prefetch files, selected by content and never by name or the `.pf` extension (a shadow-copy prior version, is read too and everything it yields repeats the snapshot id, label and creation time): `seance_core::file_detection::detect_file_type` reads the first 512 bytes of the artifact and calls a buffer prefetch when it opens with the four bytes `MAM\x04` — the Xpress-Huffman wrapper Windows 10 and 11 write — or with a version of 17, 23, 26, 30 or 31 followed by `SCCA` at offset 4. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `SystemArtifact`, so a prefetch file recovered from a carve or lifted out of a shadow copy is read on the same terms as one found in `C:\Windows\Prefetch`. A `MAM\x04` file's declared uncompressed length is read from offset 4 and checked before anything is allocated, then the body from offset 8 is inflated by the pure-Rust `xpress-huffman` decoder and parsed as SCCA. Inside SCCA it reads the fixed 60-byte UTF-16LE executable-name field at 0x10, stopping at the first NUL or at 30 code units; the last-run FILETIME array — one slot at 0x78 on version 17, one at 0x80 on version 23, and eight consecutive slots from 0x80 on versions 26, 30 and 31; the run counter at 0x90 (v17), 0x98 (v23) or 0xD0 (v26, v30, v31); and six section pointers and nothing else — the file-metrics array at 0x54 and 0x58, the filename-strings section at 0x64 and 0x68, and the volume-information array at 0x6C and 0x70. One metrics entry is 20 bytes on v17 and 32 bytes on every later version, and the only two fields read from it are the filename offset and length, at entry+0x8/+0xC (v17) or entry+0xC/+0x10 (later), used as a **code-unit** count into the strings section, not a byte count (capping a unit count with a byte length shortened names, and a shortened path is a different file from the one the record names). A volume entry is 40 bytes on v17, 104 on v23 and v26, and 96 on v30 and v31; from each it reads the device-path offset and character count at entry+0x0/+0x4 — an offset relative to the start of the volume section — the volume creation FILETIME at entry+0x8 and the serial number at entry+0x10. On versions 30 and 31 the run counter is read twice, at 0xD0 and at 0xC8, because Windows 10 build 1607 moved that field without changing the version number: 0xD0 is used whenever it holds a value between 1 and 1,000,000, and 0xC8 is used only when 0xD0 does not and 0xC8 itself does.

**Produces.** One `PrefetchEntry` `ParsedRecord` per file, parented to the file it was read from, carrying the executable name, the run count, the last execution time, the referenced-file count and the full list of referenced filename strings, the version label the version number maps to (`WindowsXp2003`, `WindowsVista7`, `Windows8`, `Windows10`, `Windows11`), and one entry per referenced volume with its device path, serial number and creation time. Both FILETIMEs are emitted as RFC 3339 strings and are null where the value is zero, pre-1970 or at or past the year 10000, never as a bare 100-nanosecond integer a reader could take for Unix seconds . Then one `TimelineEvent` per last-run slot that is non-zero **and** converts to a time inside that range, stamped `Program Last Executed` to whole seconds, carrying the executable name, the run count and — where more than one slot survived — that slot's position in the array, so three usable slots read as "execution 1 of 3". Where the source could not deliver the file to its declared length, every record it produced carries `content_incomplete`, `inventory_incomplete`, the bytes read, the declared size and the reason `short_read`, because the SCCA sections are addressed by offset and a short buffer makes the run times and the referenced-file list a floor rather than the whole record . Where the file was identified as prefetch and not decoded, it produces a `PrefetchParseStatus` record instead, naming the file and stating whether it was never read (`size_cap_exceeded`), read short before parsing (`short_read_before_parse`) or read and undecodable (`parse_failed`); on the two decode failures it says in words that the program it records was executed and that no execution time or loaded-file list from it is in this case.

**Cannot.** It cannot say who ran the program. A prefetch file carries no user account, no SID and no session, so nothing in these records attributes an execution to a person; and it cannot say a person ran it at all — the file exists because Windows prepared that image for execution, which a service, a scheduled task or another program's child process does as readily as somebody at the keyboard. It cannot give the executable's full path: the name field holds at most 30 UTF-16 code units of the image name, the volume is recorded separately, no path is assembled from the two, and while the referenced-file list often holds full paths, nothing in the record marks which of them is the image. It cannot tell you which prefetch file on disk it read from its own record — the `PrefetchEntry` carries no source filename, and the eight-hexadecimal-digit path hash in a `.pf` name is never read or checked, so two prefetch files for images of the same name are told apart only by the artifact they hang from. It cannot give more than eight execution times, and on versions 17 and 23 no more than one: a run count of 400 with eight times means the other 392 executions have no recorded moment, and a file whose slots are zero yields fewer events than its run count without that being a shortfall in the reading. It cannot distinguish an unset time from an out-of-range one: zero, anything before 1970 and anything at or past the year 10000 are all dropped to null and produce no event, with no reason recorded. It cannot state a run count it is sure of. Above version 26 the count is read at whichever of two offsets holds a value between 1 and 1,000,000 and the record does not say which; where neither does, the 0xD0 value is reported as it stands; and on versions 17, 23 and 26 the field is reported exactly as found, with no plausibility test at all — so a zero, which the format cannot hold, or a 32-bit absurdity, is published as a run count with no marker. It cannot give the timeline better than whole seconds, and it cannot say which slot an event came from or which execution is the earliest: the ordinal is the slot's position in the array, in file order. It cannot date the first execution, it reads nothing else from a metrics entry — the MFT file reference included — and it produces no directory-strings list: the prefetch directory array is deliberately not emitted. It cannot guarantee that a referenced name is whole: a declared length longer than the strings section is clipped to what the section holds with no marker, and an entry whose declared offset lies past that section yields an empty string that is still counted, so the referenced-file count counts entries, not names. It cannot confirm a version label names the operating system that wrote the file — the label is a mapping from the version number alone, and the 1607 layout change is itself proof that one version number covers more than one build. It cannot read a format version outside 17, 23, 26, 30 and 31, and an uncompressed file carrying any other version is not recognised as prefetch at all, so no record of it — not even a refusal — reaches the case. It cannot emit the referenced files as artifacts: they are strings, not `FileEntry` records, so no hash, signature or existence check is run against them here. Its ceilings are 16,777,216 bytes of input, the same figure as the ceiling on a `MAM` blob's declared uncompressed size, 1,000,000 declared metrics entries and 10,000 declared volume entries. And no compressed Windows 10 or 11 prefetch file has been decoded against a known answer in this crate's tests: the `MAM` path is pinned for refusal and for not panicking, and for nothing else. It cannot tell you that a program never ran: it reads the files it is handed, it knows nothing about whether prefetching was enabled on the machine or whether a `.pf` was deleted, and the absence of a prefetch file is not evidence of the absence of an execution.

**Refuses.** It refuses to publish an execution record from a file whose parse failed, and it refuses to be silent about that file. A version 26, 30 or 31 file cut short inside its eight-slot last-run array fails the whole parse rather than reporting the slots that survived: the run counter sits past the array in every supported layout, so a buffer too short for a slot is too short for the counter and the parse closes — a `PrefetchEntry` naming two executions for a program that ran eight, with no sign that six slots were never read, is the answer this refusal exists to prevent. A file the source could not deliver in full but whose readable prefix parses is published, stamped incomplete on every record, rather than refused. Every file that failed to decode leaves a `PrefetchParseStatus` record, because producing nothing would make a prefetch file that exists indistinguishable from a machine where the program was never run, and "prefetch shows no trace of it" is exactly the conclusion that would be drawn. It refuses a file past 16,777,216 bytes before reading it into memory, and records the refusal with the size it saw.
