It refuses a `MAM` blob declaring an uncompressed size of zero or above that same ceiling, before handing anything to the decompressor, because the decoder allocates to the declared size and a lie in that field is otherwise an out-of-memory kill of the worker — the defect that retired the previous third-party parser, whose metrics reader allocated against an attacker-controlled count and could be driven to hundreds of gigabytes from a 267-byte file. It refuses a declared metrics count above 1,000,000 or a volume count above 10,000, any section whose declared offset and length run past the end of the buffer — including a section declaring no entries at all, which is refused whole rather than reported as empty — and any header arithmetic that overflows: each a clean error, never a panic, checked against the real buffer length before a slice or an allocation is made, and pinned by parsing every truncation of a known-good file and by a fuzz target with its reproducer corpus. It refuses a buffer with no `SCCA` at offset 4 after decompression, and a `MAM\x04` header shorter than eight bytes is not treated as compressed and fails that same check. A non-prefetch file and an artifact with no data source are passed over without a record, since this module is offered every file in the case and a word about each would be noise.

### `plugin.windows.rdp_bitmap_cache`

**Reads.** The Remote Desktop client's persistent bitmap cache under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Terminal Server Client\Cache\`. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent`. A `Cache####.bin` is chosen by its first eight bytes, `RDP8bmp` and a NUL, or by that name; a `bcache*.bmc` by name. The `.bin` layout was measured on one real file (DFIR Madness case 001 DC01, Server 2012 R2, version 4): a 12-byte header (the magic and a u32 version), then tiles back to back, each an 8-byte key, a u16 width, a u16 height and `width x height` four-byte pixels, blue, green, red and a fourth byte that is zero on every pixel of that file and is dropped. The walk reads each tile header at the offset the previous tile ends, up to 65,536 tiles, and reads each tile's pixels from the file.

**Produces.** One `FileEntry` per tile, `type: RdpCacheTile`, named `<file>_tile_NNNNN.png`, carrying a PNG re-encoding of the tile's pixels (8-bit RGB) as its content — so the gallery, hashing and OCR reach it — with `tile_index`, the `key` as hex in file order, `width`, `height`, `source_offset` and a `derived_note` saying the PNG bytes are Séance's and the pixels the cache's. One `FileEntry` collage per cache file (`RdpCacheCollage`, named `<file>_collage_cache_order_not_a_reconstruction.png`), holding every tile in cache order, 64 cells of 64 px across, with `reconstruction: false`, `first_tile`, `last_tile`, `tiles_placed`, `cells_blank` (a tile that could not be read back leaves its cell black, so no later tile moves into its place) and the `collage_note`, which opens "not a reconstruction". The collage is written one band of 64 cells at a time. One `RdpBitmapCache` summary with the version, tile and collage counts. An empty `.bmc` yields a summary reading `empty file (0 bytes)`.

**Cannot.** It does not reconstruct screens: no tile edges are matched and the collage's layout is the file's order, which is not screen position. It does not decode the legacy `.bmc` format — no real non-empty `.bmc` has been examined. It has read one real `.bin` (5,304 tiles, all 64 x 64); other versions and tile sizes are walked by the same rules. It cannot say which remote host or session a tile came from, or when it was drawn: the cache records neither.

**Refuses.** It refuses a file named like a cache without the `RDP8bmp` magic, or shorter than its header: it gets an `RdpBitmapCacheIncomplete` (`status: NotDecoded`) and no tile. A non-empty `.bmc` gets the same, saying the format is not read. A tile declaring a side of 0 or over 64, a trailing partial tile, or the 65,536-tile cap stops the walk: the tiles before it are kept and the summary is stamped `content_incomplete` with the offset and reason; the partial tile is not emitted.

### `plugin.windows.recycle_bin_parser`

**Reads.** Windows Recycle Bin metadata: the `$I` records Vista and later write beside each `$R` file, and the legacy `INFO2` table of Windows 2000/XP. It subscribes to `FileEntry` only, with `InputCapability::Stream`, and is not in the triage profile. The gate is the artifact's `name` metadata alone, upper-cased: a name beginning `$I` but not `$ID`, or a name equal to `INFO2`; the `path` is never read, so nothing checks that the file lies under `$Recycle.Bin\<SID>\` or `RECYCLER\`, and no SID is recovered. An artifact with no data is passed over. The content is read through `read_capped` up to 64 MiB (`MAX_RECYCLEBIN_BYTES`), and `ReadExtent::measure` records how many bytes arrived against the declared size, with a reason of `cap_reached` when the file is over the cap and `short_read` when the source delivered less. Fewer than eight bytes cannot hold a header. For a `$I` file the first eight bytes are a little-endian version: 1 (Vista to Windows 8) gives a fixed 544-byte record — size at 8, deletion FILETIME at 16, a 520-byte UTF-16LE path field at 24 — and 2 (Windows 10 1709 and later) gives size at 8, FILETIME at 16, a 32-bit path length at 24 counted in UTF-16 characters including the terminator (it was once read as bytes and halved every path), and the path from 28. `decode_utf16le` stops at the first NUL. For `INFO2`, the record size is the 32-bit field at offset 12 of the 20-byte header and must be 1..=4,096 and at least 280; records are walked from offset 20 while a whole one fits, and from each come the FILETIME at 268, the 32-bit size at 276, and the path — the UTF-16LE field at 280 when the record is 800 bytes or more and that field is non-empty, else the 260-byte ANSI field at 0 decoded as CP1252 through `seance_core::codepage::decode`, which reports whether any byte outside ASCII was substituted. The record number at 260 and the drive number at 264 are not read, and neither is the `$R` file, the directory, or the SID.

**Produces.** For each decoded record, one `ParsedRecord` parented to the file artifact with `type: "RecycleBinEntry"`, `original_path`, `deleted_time` as RFC 3339 or an empty string where the FILETIME was zero or out of range, `file_size`, a `short_desc` of `Deleted: <name>` (or `Deleted (legacy): <name>` from `INFO2`), and either `recycle_bin_path` (the `$I` file's name) with `version` 1 or 2, or `format: "INFO2"`; an `INFO2` record whose ANSI path held a non-ASCII byte also carries `path_decode: "cp1252"` so the string is read as this build's decoding under an assumed code page and not as text off the disk. Where the record has a deletion time, one `TimelineEvent` follows it, parented to the record, with `timestamp_desc` `File Deletion` or `File Deletion (INFO2)`, `source_module`, the `short_desc`, and `full_details` carrying the path and size. A `$I` whose declared path did not fit in the bytes read carries `original_path_truncated: true`; a `$I` read short of its declared size carries `bytes_read` and `bytes_declared`; either or both set `content_incomplete: true` with the reasons joined by commas from `original_path_truncated`, `short_read` and `cap_reached`. Where the file could not be decoded at all — fewer than eight bytes with a shortfall or a non-empty fragment, an unknown `$I` version, a `$I` too short for its version, an `INFO2` header or record size that fails, or an `INFO2` table read short or ending inside a record — one `RecycleBinParseStatus` record is produced with `record_type: "recycle_bin_parse_status"`, `name: "<file> (partially parsed)"`, `content_incomplete: true` with a reason of `unresolved_structure`, `short_read` or `cap_reached`, `inventory_incomplete: true`, `entries_parsed`, `bytes_read`, `bytes_declared` and a `message` sentence; for a cut `INFO2` table it follows the records that were decoded. A zero-length source produces nothing at all. `process` never returns an error; a name it does not claim leaves only a zero-yield processing-log row.

**Cannot.** It cannot say whose Recycle Bin this is: the `$Recycle.Bin\<SID>` folder that attributes a deletion to an account is not read, the path is not on the record, and the only link to the user is the parent artifact's id. It cannot pair a `$I` with its `$R`: the record does not say whether the deleted content still exists, was restored, or was emptied — and a `$I` that survives after the bin was emptied is a deletion that happened, not a file that is still recoverable. It cannot tell a Recycle Bin record from a file that merely starts with `$I`: the gate is the name alone, so a file named `$Install.log` or `$Image.bin` anywhere in the evidence is read as a `$I` record, and when its first eight bytes are not 1 or 2 the module publishes a `RecycleBinParseStatus` stating that "the file it describes was deleted" — a deletion claim about a file that was never in a Recycle Bin. It cannot verify a record it decoded: a v2 `$I` whose declared path length is small and whose bytes are garbage yields a garbage path, no FILETIME plausibility check is applied beyond the year-10000 bound, and a `$I` from one bin dropped into another is read as-is. It cannot read `INFO2` fully: the record number and drive number are dropped, a record whose ANSI and Unicode paths both decode empty is skipped without a count, and the code page is assumed CP1252 with the assumption recorded but no alternative offered, so a Cyrillic or Japanese bin's ANSI paths are published under the wrong table and labelled only as decoded. It cannot see a deleted `$I`: it reads the `FileEntry` it is handed, and a `$I` recovered from unallocated space reaches it only if a carver named it `$I…`. An empty `deleted_time` string, rather than a null, is what a zero FILETIME becomes, and no timeline event is made for it. Its status record sets `inventory_incomplete: true` with no `inventory_incomplete_reason`, so the completeness census, which groups by that reason, files it under a null reason; and both the status record's `message` and the entry's `content_incomplete` carry no `content_incomplete_detail`, so the examiner-facing incompleteness reader shows the reason code and none of the sentences the module writes. Its cap is 64 MiB. Its real-corpus checks are three gitignored fixtures — `$I103S5F.jpg`, `$II3DF3L.zip` and an `INFO2` — of which only the first asserts a non-empty path.

**Refuses.** It refuses to let a deletion vanish because its record would not decode. A `$I` this build cannot read — an unknown version, a header too short for its version, a fragment of fewer than eight bytes that still declared more or held something — yields a `RecycleBinParseStatus` saying the file it describes was deleted but its path, size and time are absent from this case, because "no record of deletion" is an argument made in court and silence here would make it. It refuses to publish a shortened path as a real one: a v2 record declaring a longer path than the bytes hold is stamped `original_path_truncated`, and a v1 record short of 544 bytes with no terminator in its path field is stamped the same, since `C:\Users\bob\Documents\rep` reads as a directory that never existed. It refuses to report a table as whole when it was not: an `INFO2` read short of its declared size, or delivered whole but ending inside a record, gets a status record after the entries that were decoded, with `short_read`/`cap_reached` kept distinct from `unresolved_structure` because the first two send an examiner after an acquisition fault and the third is a fault in the artifact. It refuses an `INFO2` record size of zero, above 4,096, or below the 280 bytes the layout needs, with a status record rather than an empty listing that would read as an empty bin. It refuses to render accented bytes as U+FFFD — `José` is decoded under CP1252 and the assumption is stamped as `path_decode` — because a path naming no user and no file matches nothing an examiner searches for. It refuses a zero-length source in silence, since there is no fragment and no shortfall to be honest about. And it refuses nothing else: `process` never errors, a file the name gate passes is always answered with either entries or a status record, and a file the gate does not pass is answered with an empty list and a zero-yield row.

### `plugin.windows.registry_parser`

**Reads.** Windows registry hives — `SYSTEM`, `SOFTWARE`, `SAM`, `SECURITY`, `NTUSER.DAT` and `UsrClass.dat` — through this project's own zero-dependency hive reader, under a 512 MiB ceiling per hive. A hive that is a shadow-copy prior version (a `VssPriorVersion` `ParsedRecord`) is read too, and every record it yields repeats the snapshot id, label and creation time, and each timeline event's text begins `[shadow copy <time>]`; its transaction logs are not searched. A hive whose keys carry layered-key bits (base-block minor version 6; a Windows container's differencing hive) is reported as what it is, `differencing_hive` with `layered_keys` counts and a statement that it is one layer's changes and not a registry — a tombstoned key was deleted there and a key it does not list says nothing — and each such key carries `layer_semantics`; the merge of a base hive and its layers is not built. The hive's minor version is always recorded. Where a hive is dirty and its `.LOG1`/`.LOG2` transaction logs are reachable, it replays the pending pages into an in-memory copy first, and every record drawn from a dirty hive that could NOT be replayed says so. Beyond the live key tree it reads two things more. Every `nk` cell in the hive's bins, up to 200,000, for the key-write timeline and for the live-cell map the recovery path resolves against. And the hive's free space: `seance_hive::Hive::unallocated_cells` walks the bins bounded by the base block's declared data size (Windows grows a hive file in 256 KiB steps, and the zeros past that size are not a broken chain) for `nk` and `vk` cells a deletion marked free but never overwrote, examining up to 200,000 unallocated cells. The shell-item ID list inside a `RecentDocs`, `OpenSavePidlMRU` or `LastVisitedPidlMRU` value is walked through `seance_shell_item::walk_id_list_detail` one item at a time: each item's own name from its documented field, the deepest item's FAT times, and the deepest item's MFT file reference where a version-7+ `BEEF0004` extension block carries one.

**Produces.** Every key and value the walk reached, and on top of that the registry-resident artifacts: UserAssist, BAM/DAM, MUICache, the shell most-recently-used lists, typed URLs and paths, outgoing RDP destinations — one record per destination, joining every `Default` `MRUn` naming it to its `Servers` subkey by host name compared case-insensitively with an explicit `:3389`, the client's default port, treated as no port, with `destination` (the join key), `hosts_as_stored` (every spelling joined), `ip_to_name_join_attempted: false`, `mru_position`, `mru_positions`, `username_hint`, `in_mru_list`, `in_servers_key`, and each key's path and last-written time carried separately as `mru_key_*` and `servers_key_*`, each time naming in its `*_last_written_scope` whether it dates the `Default` key that holds every MRU entry or the destination's own `Servers` subkey; a host in only one key is still one record, the other key's fields null, and a destination with more than one `Servers` subkey carrying `servers_keys` (each subkey's `host`, `path`, `last_written`, `last_written_scope` and `username_hint`), `servers_key_count` and `username_hints` — installed programs, USB mass-storage devices with their install and connection times, per-interface network configuration, the `MountedDevices` drive-letter table, the Windows Search service's configuration, the local accounts from SAM's `F` and `V` values, and the security descriptor on every key. Beside each family, a coverage record naming what that family does and does not include. Each value in the hive record's `all_values` carries its rendering in `value_data` — a `REG_DWORD_BIG_ENDIAN` as the big-endian number it is — and its stored bytes in `value_data_b64`: always for a value of up to 64 bytes, and for a larger one while the hive's 256 MiB cap on published value bytes holds, the cap stated on the hive record as `value_bytes_budget_bytes` with `value_bytes_complete`, `value_bytes_omitted` and `value_bytes_detail`, and a value past it marked `value_data_b64_omitted`; a `REG_MULTI_SZ` also carries its elements as the array `value_data_list`. A recovered value carries the same fields, and a recovered default value is named `(Default) (recovered)` with its empty `value_name` kept. A `CIDSizeMRU` or `FirstFolder` entry is read as the program name or path it holds, with the bytes after it published whole as `value_tail_bytes_base64`, `value_tail_bytes_len` and `value_tail_all_zero`. A shell MRU entry now carries `shell_item_name`, `shell_item_path` with `shell_item_path_basis`, `shell_item_created`/`shell_item_modified`/`shell_item_accessed` with a `shell_item_time_scope` and note, `shell_item_mft_entry` and `shell_item_mft_sequence` (the same field names as the shortcut reader), `shell_items_total`, `shell_items_unread`, `shell_item_parsed` (per item — a type this build does not know, or an instance too short for its fields, reports `false` for that item alone), `shell_item_bytes_len`, and either `content_incomplete` when the tail could not be walked as an ID list at all or k of n items were not decoded (the detail says which), or `shell_item_decode_scope` stating exactly which fields were read and that other extension blocks were not; a file reference that is all zero — every one of the 38 `RecentDocs` items in plaso's `NTUSER-WIN7.DAT` — is published as `shell_item_mft_reference_zero: true` with a note, never as entry 0 sequence 0, which would name `$MFT`. From free space, one `RecoveredRegistryKey` per recovered `nk` and one `RecoveredRegistryValue` per recovered `vk` — distinct types, `evidence_state: "recovered"`, `recovered: true`, `recovered_from` the bin offset, never added to the hive record's `all_keys`/`all_values` — plus one `TimelineEvent` per recovered key with a readable time under `timestamp_desc: "Recovered Registry Key Last Written"`. A recovered key carries `key_name`, `bin_offset`, `parent_offset`, `last_written` and its FILETIME, `subkey_count_declared` and `value_count_declared` (none of its freed lists is followed), `key_path` rebuilt through live and other recovered `nk` cells with `key_path_is_inference: true`, `key_path_basis`, `key_path_complete` and `key_path_parent_offset_unresolved` when the chain breaks, `live_key_with_same_name_under_parent` with `live_namesake_note` flagging an earlier version of a live key rather than a deletion, and a `recovery_note`. A recovered value carries `value_name`, `value_type`, `raw_data_size_declared`, `data_read` and `data_basis` — inline in the freed `vk` cell itself, declared empty (a zero size field the reader answers without following the offset), or read from a data cell that is still allocated and may have been reused since — or `data_unread_reason` for a freed data cell, `value_data` rendered by the same formatter as a live value, a `key_association_note` that no key is inferred for it, and `tombstoned`. The hive record's `recovered_cells` summary carries `keys`, `values`, `undecodable` with `undecodable_cells[]` (offset, signature, reason), `examined_cap: 200000`, `examined_capped`, `walk_incomplete`, `records_cap: 50000`, `records_capped`, `complete`, `incomplete_reason` naming the number hit, and `basis`.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell you that a program ran from MUICache, a shell MRU or a file association, and every such record carries `execution_evidence: false` with the reason — the shell writes those for a properties dialog and a context menu too. It cannot tell you an outgoing RDP connection succeeded: the client stores a destination because it was typed. It joins RDP keys by the host as typed less a `:3389`, so an IP address and a host name for the same machine stay two records (the hive holds no evidence they are one machine), a non-default port is its own destination. A destination with more than one `Servers` subkey (`host` and `host:3389`) is one record listing every subkey in `servers_keys` with its own path, time and `UsernameHint`, counted as `servers_key_count`, every distinct hint in `username_hints`; the `servers_key_*` scalars are the first subkey seen, and `username_hint` the first non-null hint, which can be a later subkey's than `servers_key_path` — `join_basis` says so. That case is pinned on a synthetic capture only: no graded hive held two `Servers` spellings of one host. Outgoing RDP and the BAM per-SID decode were graded against real hives (`RDP-1`: three user hives; `BAM-1`: three Windows 10 `SYSTEM` hives, 117 executions, with `is_current_control_set` read from `Select\Current`); a populated `dam` key and an `MRU1`-or-later RDP entry have not been met. It cannot date an individual entry on a key that carries only the key's own last-write time, so that time is reported once, scoped to the key, and raises no per-entry timeline event — stamping it on each entry would date all 131 entries of a real `MUICache` to the most recent one. It does not decode every shell item type: `0xEE` and the other types this build does not know are reported unread by count, a users-property-view item (`0x00` class with the `1SPS` signature) is named and nothing is claimed read from it, and only the deepest item's times and file reference are read, so 28 of the 75 tailed entries in plaso's `NTUSER-WIN7.DAT` carry one unread item. It does not interpret the bytes after a `CIDSizeMRU` or `FirstFolder` name — 72 bytes on each of the nine `CIDSizeMRU` values there — and discloses them as undecoded when they are not all zero. `hive_type` is the ingested file name upper-cased, not a classification of the hive. It does not decode `Tcpip6`, and says that rather than letting its absence read as an absence of IPv6 configuration. A recovered key's path is an inference from a parent offset that may have been reused since the deletion, and its `key_path_complete: false` and `live_key_with_same_name_under_parent: false` are judged against a live-cell map that stops at 200,000 `nk` cells — past that cap they read as slot reuse and no namesake when the truth is that the map stopped short, and the recovered record carries nothing tying it to the hive record's `key_timeline_complete`. It does not infer a freed `vk`'s key, does not read a freed data cell, reads an allocated data cell that may since have been reused and says so, and follows none of a recovered key's subkey, value or security lists. A recovered cell's absence is not evidence none was deleted: a cell overwritten since deletion leaves nothing to recover, and the walk examines at most 200,000 unallocated cells and emits at most 50,000 records, each ceiling stated on the summary with its number. It does not yet merge layered keys: the hive reader can merge a minor-version-6 (differencing) hive with the base hive it layers onto — tombstones, supersedes and inherited class names, graded on two real Windows container chains against the PATH their Dockerfiles set — but this module does not find a container's layers or put them in order. So a differencing hive in evidence, as Windows containers and Windows Sandbox write, is walked on its own as an ordinary hive: its records are one layer's changes, not the registry the container saw. A key that layer marks deleted is reported as present, and a key it inherits from the base is absent.

**Refuses.** It refuses to present a DHCP lease field as a time unless the lease's own arithmetic agrees that it is one, because what those counters hold is not fixed across Windows versions and a boot-relative counter rendered as a 1970 date puts a wrong day on a report. It refuses to decode a device property on the length of its payload rather than its declared type code — an eight-byte string would otherwise become a connection time in 1601. It refuses to dispatch a UserAssist entry on the `Version` its key declares, dispatching on the data length instead, because a real hive has a 1,612-byte session record under a key declaring the 72-byte version. It refuses to publish a zeroed MFT reference as entry 0 sequence 0. It refuses to give a stale MRU value a position `MRUListEx` does not record, and refuses to skip an index naming a value that does not exist silently. It refuses to fold a recovered key or value into the live listing: each is its own record type, so a viewer or an export cannot include a deleted key by forgetting to check one flag. It refuses to follow a freed key's subkey, value or security lists, or a freed value's data cell, because those cells may have been reused and reading them would attribute another key's data to this one. It refuses to present a rebuilt path as a fact, labelling it an inference with the offset at which the chain broke. And it refuses to claim the root key's parent from its parent field, which on real hives is not `0xFFFFFFFF` (plaso's SAM root points at `0x4f8`), ending the chain on the `KEY_HIVE_ENTRY` flag instead so every path in the hive does not gain a bogus prefix.

### `plugin.windows.sdb_parser`

**Reads.** Windows application-compatibility shim databases — `sysmain.sdb` and any custom `.sdb` — by the `sdbf` or `zdbf` magic at byte 8, not by extension.

**Produces.** The database's own identity, one record per shimmed executable, and a census of every tag the walk met including the ones this build does not name.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell you that a shimmed executable ran. A shim entry is a rule about how a program would be run if it were, and reading it as execution evidence is the standard error with this artifact. It cannot decode a tag whose payload runs past its parent's declared end — which happens nine times in Microsoft's own shipped files — and reports the tag with no value rather than choosing between two readings that both fabricate.

**Refuses.** It refuses to produce anything at all for a file named `.sdb` that does not carry the magic: inventing a parse failure would put a statement in the case about something that is not evidence.

### `plugin.windows.search_index`

**Reads.** The Windows Search index, `Windows.edb`, an ESE database, chosen by content (the ESE signature; a shadow-copy prior version, is read too, named by its `file_name`, and everything it yields repeats the snapshot id, label and creation time and states that its sidecars were not searched; a `ParsedRecord` that is not a prior version is declined) and kept only when it carries a `SystemIndex_PropertyStore` (Windows 10) or `SystemIndex_0A` (Windows 7) table with an `System_ItemPathDisplay` column — so SRUM, WebCache, UAL and the BITS queue yield nothing here. The database is copied to a temporary file (up to 4 GiB) for libesedb in 8 MiB chunks — only its first 4 KiB header is held in memory — and the one table walked row by row. A Windows 10 column name's numeric prefix (`4428-`, `15F-`) is removed. Forty-six named properties are read — path, URL, names, type, size, attributes, the modified, created, accessed, imported, item and gather times, owner, computer, folder/deleted/attachment flags, link and Internet Explorer targets, title, subject, author and the mail sender, recipients, dates, attachment flag and read state, and the auto-summary — and nothing else. The two layouts were measured on real files (CFReDS Data Leakage, Windows 7; LoneWolf, Windows 10 1709): an 8-byte time or size is big-endian in the Windows 7 layout and little-endian in the Windows 10 one, taken from the layout, not guessed per value. Eight `0x2A` bytes (a size) or `0x2A2A2A2A` (attributes) mean not set. A Windows 7 binary text value is de-obfuscated (each byte XORed with a byte of `0x05000113 ^ length` and with its index — the key libyal's published format notes give, checked on every such value in the Data Leakage index) and decoded by its first byte: 1 is eight-bit text, 0 is runs of a count, a high byte and that many low bytes. Multi-valued values are read member by member and long values as UTF-16. When libesedb's first count of the table's rows fails on a page that is not a leaf, the count it gives on a second call is used and kept as a floor.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` `WindowsSearchItem` per row: `item_id` (`DocID` or `WorkID`), `path`, `schema_variant` (`windows7_systemindex_0a` or `windows10_propertystore`), `properties` keyed by property name with times in UTC RFC 3339, `properties_not_decoded` naming each property present on the row but not decoded and why, an `index_note` that a row is not evidence the item still exists, and `timestamp` from the modified or received time. One `WindowsSearchIndex` summary: the layout, the item count, how many values were not decoded, and `database_state`.

**Cannot.** It does not decode the Windows 7 text forms whose first byte is 2 or 3 (a Huffman-table form) — 10 of the 113 auto-summaries in the Data Leakage index — and reports each by property and type rather than rendering it. It reads 46 properties, not all of the several hundred the table can carry, and not the gather tables (`SystemIndex_Gthr`), the word lists or the content index. It does not replay transaction logs, so the last items the indexer wrote may be absent from a database copied from a running machine. Where libesedb cannot walk every page of the table's tree, the items it reached are a floor, and the summary says so. It does not read Windows 11 22H2+'s SQLite `Windows.db`. It has read two real indexes, one per layout; other builds are read by the same rules.

**Refuses.** It refuses a `Windows.db` that is SQLite: it gets a `WindowsSearchIndexIncomplete` (`status: NotDecoded`) saying the Windows 11 form is not read. A file named `Windows.edb` that cannot be read, is not an ESE database, cannot be staged, will not open in libesedb, carries neither property table, or is over 4 GiB gets the same, saying no item was read; those failures on an ESE file of any other name yield nothing. A dirty-shutdown database, a walk that fell short, the first-count failure above, or the 2,000,000-row cap stamps `content_incomplete` on the summary with the reason and emits a standalone `WindowsSearchIndexIncomplete` (`status: DirtyDatabase` or `TableWalkIncomplete`).

### `plugin.windows.secure_sds`

**Reads.** The NTFS `$Secure:$SDS` stream — the one volume-wide store of security descriptors that NTFS 3.0 and later keep in place of a descriptor in every MFT record — and it accepts that stream only when its provenance says it is the store. It subscribes to `FileEntry`, `SystemArtifact` and `RawEvidence` with `InputCapability::Stream`; it deliberately does not subscribe to `FileSystem`, because locating MFT record 9 in a raw volume is the MFT parser's job and a second locator could disagree with the first. The gate reads `is_directory` (true declines), a name (`name`, else `file_name`) and a path (`path`, else `source_path`). Where `stream_name` equals `$SDS` case-insensitively — the shape `seance_plugin_mft` emits for every named `$DATA` stream, with `name` `$Secure:$SDS`, `parent_file` `$Secure` and `path` `<path>:$SDS` — the artifact is accepted only if `parent_file` is `$Secure` case-insensitively or the lower-cased last path component of the name or path starts with `$secure:`. Otherwise it is accepted only if that lower-cased last component of the name or the path is exactly `$sds`, `$secure:$sds`, `$secure_$sds` or `$secure.$sds` — the spellings MFTECmd and `icat`-style exports produce. Anything else, including another file's alternate stream that happens to be called `$SDS` and the `$Secure` file itself, yields nothing. The bytes come from the artifact's own data source through `read_capped` with a ceiling of 67,108,864 bytes (64 MiB); nothing is spilled to disk. The scan then walks 16-byte-aligned offsets: at each, a 20-byte entry header of little-endian `u32 hash`, `u32 security_id`, `u64 declared offset`, `u32 entry size`. A `security_id` of 0 or an entry size of 20 or less is inter-block padding and the walk steps to the next 16-byte boundary; an entry size above 65,536 is refused as oversize and counted; after 1,000,000 entries the walk stops. The descriptor body (`entry size` minus 20 bytes) is decoded by `seance_core::secdesc::parse_security_descriptor`, the same decoder the registry reader uses for `sk` cells: revision must be 1, control must carry `SE_SELF_RELATIVE` (0x8000), owner and group SIDs are read at their declared offsets (revision 1, at most 15 sub-authorities), the DACL is read only when `SE_DACL_PRESENT` (0x0004) is set and the SACL only when `SE_SACL_PRESENT` (0x0010) is, each ACL to a ceiling of 4,096 ACEs, and each ACE's trustee SID is located at header+8 for the thirteen basic ACE types (0x00–0x03, 0x09, 0x0A, 0x0D, 0x0E, 0x11–0x15) or after the object-type GUIDs its object flags declare for the eight object types (0x05–0x08, 0x0B, 0x0C, 0x0F, 0x10). A body that will not decode, or an entry whose declared size runs past the end of the stream, is retried from its 256 KiB (262,144-byte) mirror — the copy 262,144 bytes after or before it — and taken from there only if the mirror's hash, id and size all match. Later copies of an id already seen are counted as duplicates and discarded, except that a copy that decodes replaces an earlier one that did not.

**Produces.** One `NtfsSecurityDescriptorStore` record and one `NtfsSecurityDescriptor` record per unique `security_id`, every one a `ParsedRecord` parented to the input artifact with its case id, and nothing else: no timeline events (a descriptor carries no timestamp, and the module's tests pin that none is invented), no data sources, no artifact for a stream it declined. The store record (`subtype: ntfs_secure_sds_store`, `source_module: plugin.windows.secure_sds`, `name: $Secure:$SDS descriptor store`) carries `source_stream`, `stream_size_bytes` (the data source's declared size), `bytes_scanned`, `security_block_size_bytes` (262,144), `unique_security_ids`, `duplicate_copies`, `mirror_recoveries`, `undecodable_descriptors`, `entries_past_end_of_stream`, `entry_cap_reached`, `oversize_entries_refused` with an `oversize_entries_note` when non-zero, `read_incomplete` (`cap_reached` when the stream exceeds 64 MiB, `short_read` when the source returned fewer bytes than it declared), and `store_listing_incomplete`, true whenever a read fell short, the entry cap stopped the walk or any header was refused as oversize; its `short_desc` ends `; INCOMPLETE - not the whole store` in the same cases. The same facts are stamped in the shared vocabulary that `frontend/src/lib/incompleteness.ts` and the completeness census read: a short or capped read sets `content_incomplete` with `content_incomplete_reason` `short_read` or `cap_reached` and a `_detail` giving the bytes read, and any of the listing gaps sets `inventory_incomplete` with the read's reason (else `cap_reached`) and a `_detail` naming the counts and saying that an id absent from the listing is not shown absent from the volume; a whole store carries neither. A stream that passed the gate with no data source — which is what the MFT parser emits for `$Secure:$SDS` from a bare `$MFT` — produces the store record alone, with `bytes_scanned` and `unique_security_ids` 0, `read_incomplete` and both shared pairs carrying the producer's own `content_incomplete_reason` where it stamped one, else `unresolved_structure`, with `read_incomplete` naming the cause (`volume_not_in_evidence` or `no_data_source`), `store_listing_incomplete: true`, and a `short_desc` beginning `$SDS: NOT READ`. An empty stream still produces the store record, with zero counts. Each descriptor record (`subtype: ntfs_security_descriptor`, `name: Security id <n>`) carries `source_stream`, `security_id`, `descriptor_hash` (the header's hash, published as read), `sds_offset` (where the entry was found), `sds_declared_offset`, `entry_size`, `sds_offset_mismatch: true` when the declared offset is neither the found offset nor exactly 262,144 bytes either side of it, and `recovered_from_mirror` (with `mirror_offset`, `primary_copy_offset` and `primary_copy_error` when true). A decoded descriptor adds `descriptor_revision`, `control_flags` with `control_flags_hex` and `control_flag_names`, `owner_sid` and `group_sid` as `S-1-…` strings with `owner_name` / `group_name` only where the SID is in the well-known table (`Everyone`, `Local System`, `Administrators`, …) or is a domain SID whose RID is below 1000 and in the well-known RID table (rendered `Domain Users (RID 513)`), or `owner_error` / `group_error` where an offset was set but the SID would not read; `dacl_state` and `sacl_state`, each one of `absent`, `null`, `present` or `unreadable`, and for a present ACL its `_revision`, `_declared_ace_count`, `_ace_count`, `_truncated` with `_truncation_reason`, and the `dacl` / `sacl` array of ACEs — each with raw `ace_type`, `flags` and `ace_size`, and — only where the ACE body ran to at least 8 bytes — `access_mask`, beside `ace_type_name`, `effect` (`allow`, `deny`, `audit`, `alarm`, `mandatory_label`, …), `flag_names`, `inherited`, `access_mask_hex`, `access_mask_desc` (composites such as `Full Control (0x001F01FF)`, else the named file-right bits with any unnamed residue stated) and `access_rights` — the three present only with `access_mask` — `sid` and `sid_name`, `object_flags` for object ACEs and `ace_error` where the body would not decode; then `integrity_level` from the first mandatory-label ACE in the SACL, `dacl_protected`, `sacl_protected`, `dacl_auto_inherited`, `no_dacl_full_access` (true for an absent or NULL DACL — every principal has full access — and false for an empty one, which grants nobody anything), `descriptor_partial`, `permission_summary` and a `short_desc` built from it. A descriptor that would not decode from any copy carries `security_descriptor_error` and its `short_desc` says so, so the id reads as unresolvable rather than absent.

**Cannot.** It cannot say who owned or could read any particular file. The key is now on both sides — `seance_plugin_mft` publishes each record's `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` `security_id` on its `FileEntry`, the USN journal carries it on every V2/V3 record, and the descriptor records carry it — and on dfir_ntfs's `ntfs_index.raw.gz` volume every non-zero `security_id` the MFT parser publishes names a descriptor this module decodes from the same volume (one record, `$Repair`, really holds 0, which is no key). The join is performed on one surface only, the web UI's file page: its Inspector looks up the descriptor with the file's `security_id` under the `$Secure:$SDS` stream entry that shares the file's parent — the volume or bare `$MFT` the MFT parser read both from, because ids on two volumes are unrelated — and shows the owner, group and ACEs with the stream, hash and offset they came from, or says which of no id, id 0, no store examined, store not read, or no such descriptor applies. No record, report, export or REPL command carries the join, so a file grid or a report still shows no owner; and the crate's own front matter about recovering a deleted file's owner describes what NTFS makes possible, not what this tree presents. It cannot name an account: the only names it has are the fixed well-known-SID table and the well-known RIDs below 1000, so every ordinary user (`S-1-5-21-…-1001` and up) is published as a bare SID with no `owner_name`, and an absent `owner_name` means "not in the table", never "unknown user"; the SAM is not consulted. It does not read `$SII` or `$SDH`, so it cannot use the volume's own index to find an entry or check the hash the index holds; `descriptor_hash` is published from the header and is never recomputed from the descriptor bytes, so a descriptor whose body no longer matches its hash is not detected. `duplicate_copies` counts copies and does not compare them: where the primary decodes, its mirror is discarded unread, and a mirror that disagrees with its primary is invisible. The mirror retry at the point of failure fires only when the mirror's hash, id and size all equal the primary's, but the forward walk heals by `security_id` alone: a later copy with the same id whose body decodes replaces a primary that failed, stamped `MirrorRecovered`, whatever its hash or size. Only a damaged `security_id` defeats recovery, and then the two copies stand as two ids rather than being lost. Descriptor decoding is bounded by what `seance_core::secdesc` models: an ACE type outside the twenty-one whose layout it models (0x04, the compound ACE, is named but not modelled) is published with `ace_type`, `flags` and `access_mask` but no trustee and an `ace_error` saying its layout is not modelled; the conditional expression of a callback ACE (0x09, 0x0A, 0x0D, 0x0E, 0x0B, 0x0C, 0x0F, 0x10), the object-type and inherited-object-type GUIDs of an object ACE, the attribute data of a resource-attribute ACE and the policy id of a scoped-policy ACE are not decoded; access masks are described with the file-object vocabulary only, which is right for `$SDS` and would be wrong for anything else fed through this module; `permission_summary` lists at most 12 ACEs of an ACL and then `+N more`. A descriptor that parses but with an unreadable owner, group or ACL, a truncated ACL or an ACE body error is published as decoded with `descriptor_partial: true`; a caller reading only `owner_sid` will not see that the DACL beside it is `unreadable`. Nothing here distinguishes a NULL DACL from a deliberately world-open one beyond the `dacl_state` value — both are what NTFS says, and the module says only what NTFS says. It cannot tell a hand-extracted file that is itself truncated from a complete store: `stream_size_bytes` is whatever the data source declares, so an export cut short before it reached this module reads as a whole store that happens to be small, with `store_listing_incomplete: false`. A single descriptor's own damage — `descriptor_partial`, `dacl_truncated`, `owner_error` — is still stamped only in this module's words, not in the shared pair, so a partial descriptor is not counted by the completeness census. The ceilings are 64 MiB of stream, 1,000,000 entries, 65,536 bytes per entry, 4,096 ACEs per ACL and 15 sub-authorities per SID; a store past any of them is reported short, with the count, but never read past it. The `$Secure:$SDS` stream itself reaches this module only through the alternate-stream `FileEntry` the MFT parser emits, so a volume whose `$Secure` record the MFT parser could not resolve yields no store record and no statement that the store was not examined.

**Refuses.** It refuses to parse a stream that merely bears the name. A `$SDS` alternate stream on any file other than `$Secure`, a bare `$Secure`, the sibling `$SDH` stream, a directory, or an artifact with no name at all returns an empty list — silently, because inventing owners and ACLs for a user file that happens to carry a stream of that name would attribute permissions to real files that never had them (pinned by `a_stream_named_sds_on_a_file_other_than_secure_is_left_alone`). A stream that does pass the gate but carries no data source is not refused and not declined: it produces the unread store record described above, because returning nothing would look identical to a volume with no descriptors — which `$Secure` can never be. Every failure is refused into the record rather than out of it. An entry header declaring more than 65,536 bytes is refused before any read is sized from it — sizing a buffer from a hostile length is how a parser becomes an out-of-memory — and the refusal is counted in `oversize_entries_refused`, spelt out in `oversize_entries_note` as ids that are NOT in this listing, and folded into `store_listing_incomplete`. An entry whose declared size runs past the end of the stream is refused as `EntryPastEndOfStream`, counted in `entries_past_end_of_stream`, retried from its mirror, and published either recovered or with that error against its `security_id`. A body with a revision other than 1, without `SE_SELF_RELATIVE`, shorter than its 20-byte header, or with an owner, group or ACL offset outside the entry is refused by the decoder with an error that names the field and the offset, and the record still goes out carrying `security_descriptor_error` so the id is visible as unresolvable. A SID with more than 15 sub-authorities, an ACL whose declared size is smaller than its own 8-byte header, and an ACE whose size is smaller than 4 bytes or runs past its ACL are each refused at that point with the reason recorded (`owner_error`, `dacl_error`, `dacl_truncation_reason`), the rest of the descriptor still decoded. A short read from the data source is not padded: the walk covers only the bytes that arrived, `read_incomplete: short_read` is stamped, and the descriptors that were readable are still extracted. The walk itself cannot be made to spin — every step advances to at least the next 16-byte boundary, so any input, hostile or valid, terminates in at most `len / 16` steps — and after 1,000,000 entries it stops with `entry_cap_reached: true` rather than continuing into an unbounded allocation.

### `plugin.windows.setupapi_log`

**Reads.** Windows device-install logs — `setupapi.dev.log` and its siblings under `%WINDIR%\INF` — recognised by their first line, `[Device Install Log]`, and never by their file name. A file merely named like one produces no record at all.

**Produces.** One record per section of the log that concerns a device: the section kind, the device instance id, the start and end times as the log wrote them, the exit status, and the command that drove the install where the log names one. Beside them one coverage record per log carrying the header, the boot sessions in file order, and a complete histogram of every section kind — including the driver-store housekeeping that is most of them.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell you what time zone any of these times is in. No offset is recorded anywhere in the file, so the times are reported exactly as written, are never converted, and raise no timeline event: placing a local time on a UTC timeline moves the event by an offset nobody recorded. It cannot tell a device that was connected from one whose driver was merely staged, beyond what the section kind says. It does not read the log's body lines as evidence of anything except the device ids and the command they carry.

**Refuses.** It refuses to reorder the boot sessions, even though they are not in chronological order on real evidence — one measured log has a session 9 hours 19 minutes earlier than the one before it — because the file's order is the order the machine wrote them. It refuses to clamp or drop a section that starts before its own boot session, which on real evidence is Windows Update replaying an earlier-clock install.

### `plugin.windows.shellbags`

**Reads.** A Windows per-user registry hive, selected **by file name and nothing else** — an artifact A shadow-copy prior version of the file (a `VssPriorVersion` `ParsedRecord`) is read too and named by its `file_name`, since its `name` carries a `[shadow copy ...]` label; everything it yields repeats the snapshot id, label and creation time, and its transaction logs are not searched. whose `name` metadata, lower-cased, ends in `usrclass.dat` or `ntuser.dat`. Up to 512 MiB (`MAX_HIVE_BYTES`) is staged through `seance_core::io::read_capped`, which stops at the first zero-length or failed read and returns what it had, so an I/O error becomes a short buffer rather than a failure. Before anything is parsed, `seance_hive_util::hive_state::inspect` judges the base block — and only judges it at all where the buffer holds at least 0x200 bytes, opens with `regf`, and declares `file_type` 0 at offset 0x1C: the two sequence numbers at offsets 4 and 8, and the XOR-32 checksum at 0x1FC, **either** of which failing marks the hive dirty. It then looks for a `.LOG1` and a `.LOG2` beside the hive — under the `source_path` metadata or the data source's underlying path on the local filesystem, or as a sibling inside the evidence container — and for a `.LOG` only where neither of those was found. The logs are found by name; none of them is opened. The hive is then opened through `seance_hive_util::open_hive`, which requires the `regf` signature and a whole 4,096-byte base block, runs the header parse under `catch_unwind`, and **deliberately tolerates** both mismatched sequence numbers and a base block declaring more hive-bin data than the buffer holds, because refusing either lost whole hives in the field. Three paths are then walked from the root key, one name component at a time, matched with ASCII-only case folding: `Local Settings\Software\Microsoft\Windows\Shell\BagMRU` (UsrClass), `Software\Microsoft\Windows\Shell\BagMRU` (NTUSER) and `Software\Microsoft\Windows\ShellNoRoam\BagMRU` (XP). All three are tried on every hive, and each found is parsed independently of the others. Inside a `BagMRU` key the walk collects only those values whose names parse as a decimal `u32`, each holding one shell item's bytes, and then iterates the key's subkeys: a subkey whose name matches a numbered value is the folder that value describes, and the walk descends into it, building the path as `ROOT:<registry path>` then one `\`-joined folder name per level. Each shell item's own bytes are decoded by its type byte at offset 2 — root folder (`0x00`), GUID folders (`0x1E`, `0x1F`, GUID at 4..20), drive and volume items (`0x20`–`0x2F`, an ASCII run at offset 3), file entries (any type whose `& 0x70` is `0x30`, which is `0x30`–`0x3F` **and also `0xB0`–`0xBF`**, plus `0x52` compressed folders), network items (`0x41`, `0x42`, `0x43`, `0x46`, `0x47`, `0xC3`, a run at offset 5), URI/FTP (`0x61`, offset 6), control panel (`0x71`) and delegate folders (`0x74`, inner GUID at 14..30). For a file entry the walk scans the item from offset 4 for the little-endian `0xBEEF0004` signature and takes the first match whose block version is 3, 7, 8 or 9 and whose long-name-offset field is non-zero; the position of the UTF-16LE long name is then **computed** by libfwsi's field walk — 18 base, plus 18 for the v7+ file-reference block, plus 2 for the localized-name-offset field, plus 4 at v9 and 4 at v8 — and that long name is preferred over the ASCII short name at offset 14.

**Produces.** One `ShellBagEntry` `ParsedRecord` per bag, carrying the reconstructed `path`, the `folder_name` the shell item decoded to, and the `slot` — the numbered value and subkey it came from — parented to the hive file's artifact. Where the shell item is a file entry (`type & 0x70 == 0x30`) of at least 12 bytes and its DOS date field is non-zero and in range, a `TimelineEvent` follows it with the `timestamp` as RFC3339, `timestamp_desc` "ShellBag Modified (FAT)", `timezone` `"local"`, `short_desc` "ShellBag: <path>", the path, and `source_module` `plugin.windows.shellbags`. Every record emitted from a successful walk is stamped with the hive's recovery state: `hive_dirty`, `logs_replayed` (always `false`), `log_files` naming the transaction log files found beside the hive, `replay_reason` (`clean`, `dirty_but_no_logs_found`, or `replay_not_supported_by_this_parser`), and `hive_truncated`, with `hive_bytes_read` and `hive_declared_bytes` added when the load was short, and `content_incomplete` with a `content_incomplete_reason` (`hive_not_read_in_full` or `replay_not_supported_by_this_parser`, joined with `+` to any reason an earlier stage stamped) when what was parsed is known not to be the whole hive. Where the bag tree nests deeper than the walk will go, a `ShellBagWalkTruncated` record (`record_type` `shellbag_walk_truncated`) names the path the walk stopped at, reports `max_depth: 256`, and gives the reason `bagmru_depth_limit`. Where a hive that is dirty **with its logs found beside it**, or that was loaded short, yielded no bags at all — including one that would not open — a `RegistryHiveParseStatus` record (`record_type` `registry_hive_parse_status`) carries the hive name and the sentence that the absence of entries below it is not evidence that none exist.

**Cannot.** It cannot tell you **when** a folder was browsed. The last-write time of the `BagMRU` key — the timestamp shellbag analysis normally rests on — is not read, even though the hive reader exposes it as `KeyNode::last_written_filetime()`, and a `ShellBagEntry` carries no timestamp field of any kind. The only time this module emits is the FAT/DOS last-modified stamp embedded in a file-entry shell item: two-second granularity, seven bits of year from 1980, host local wall clock with no zone recorded, which is why it is tagged `local` rather than rendered as a false zero offset. That is the item's recorded last-modified stamp, not the time the folder was opened, and it is the only field in the item this module dates: for every other class — root folders, GUID folders, volumes, network locations, URIs, control panel, delegate folders, and compressed folders (`0x52`, whose name *is* read as a file entry) — no timestamp is read and no event is emitted. From the `0xBEEF0004` block it reads only the version, the presence flag and the name: everything else in the block, including the 18-byte file reference in a version 7 or later block that names the folder's MFT entry, is stepped over. It cannot order the bags: `MRUListEx` is not a decimal name, so it is never read, and nothing in a record says which sibling was browsed most recently. It cannot reach the view itself: `NodeSlot` is likewise skipped, and the `Bags\<n>\Shell` keys holding the window size, position, view mode and sort column are not walked at all. It cannot say that a folder no longer exists: no record is compared against a file system and no entry is marked deleted. It cannot say whether the item was a file or a folder, or how large it was: the size field at offset 4 and the attribute field at offset 12 are never read. It cannot attribute the browsing to an account — the record carries no SID, no user name and not even the hive's name, and the only link back to the hive the bag came from is the artifact's parentage. It cannot name every folder it finds: 13 GUIDs are mapped to names and any other is reported as `GUID:{…}`; a control panel item is always the literal `ControlPanel` and a root folder always `ROOT`, so neither says which; an unrecognised type byte becomes `UnknownType_0xNN`; an item under 3 bytes becomes `INVALID`; a short item degrades to a fixed string (`SystemFolder`, `DelegateFolder`, `Volume`, `NetworkLocation`, `URI`); a file entry with no long-name block and a zero byte at offset 14 becomes `Unparsed`; and a `0xBEEF0004` block at a version other than 3, 7, 8 or 9 is skipped so the entry falls back to its short name. The long-name search is a byte scan that takes the first plausible signature anywhere in the item and reads the name at a position it computes rather than at the offset the block states, and it validates nothing it finds there. Short names, volume labels, network names and URIs are read as bytes and passed through `from_utf8_lossy`, so a non-ASCII name with no long-name block is returned mangled. It cannot report a bag whose numbered value and numbered subkey do not both exist and both read: the record and the descent alike happen only where the subkey's name matches a value in the same key, so a subkey with a missing, unreadable or undecodable parent value is neither listed nor walked into, its whole subtree is lost, and nothing marks the loss. Its ceilings are: 512 MiB of hive staged; a `BagMRU` walk that descends to depth 256 inclusive and stops below it — 257 levels of key, while the record it emits reports `max_depth: 256`; 255 bytes of short name; 260 UTF-16 characters of long name; 260 bytes of network name and of URI; and 25 bytes of drive string. It cannot tell an unflushed hive from a corrupt one: a base block whose XOR-32 checksum does not verify is reported `hive_dirty` exactly as mismatched sequence numbers are. It cannot confirm that a named transaction log is a transaction log — the logs are found by suffix and never opened. And it cannot replay one. A hive lifted from a running machine keeps its newest writes in `.LOG1`/`.LOG2`; replay lives in the registry plugin (`seance_plugin_registry::reglog`), this module cannot reach it, and so every record it emits says `logs_replayed: false` — the most recent folder a user opened may exist only in a log this parser did not read. Two silences remain that it cannot qualify: a dirty hive whose logs were **not** carried into the evidence is not marked `content_incomplete` and, if it yielded no bags, produces no status record at all; and a hive that opens but whose root key will not read returns a `ModuleError::ParsingError` with no disclosure record, even when the hive was already known to be short or dirty.

**Refuses.** It refuses any file whose name does not end in `usrclass.dat` or `ntuser.dat`, and returns nothing at all for it — a `SYSTEM` or `SOFTWARE` hive, and equally a per-user hive recovered under another name or carved out of unallocated space, is never examined for bags. It refuses a hive artifact with no data source, answering `InvalidInputFormat` rather than an empty result, because "no bags" and "nothing was read" are different answers. It refuses to parse a file that is not a hive: shorter than the 4,096-byte base block, or without the `regf` signature; and it refuses to be crashed by one — a `UsrClass.dat` that was not a hive once panicked the reader of the day while it was reporting the bad signature, so the header parse runs under a `catch_unwind` in `seance_hive_util` and a panic becomes an error. It refuses to invent a recovery warning for something that is not a primary hive: a buffer under 0x200 bytes, one without the `regf` signature, or one whose `file_type` at 0x1C is not 0 — a transaction log fed in directly — is reported as not dirty rather than as unflushed. Conversely it refuses to *reject* a hive for being dirty or short: the sequence-number match and the declared-length check are both dropped at open, because enforcing them cost an entire domain-controller hive and a 48 MB `SOFTWARE` hive to a 216 KB shortfall; what was tolerated is stamped instead. It refuses to descend past 256 levels of `BagMRU`, because the walk follows on-disk cell offsets and does not detect a cycle, and it refuses to do so silently: past the cap it emits a record naming the path, because a bag list that ends mid-tree with nothing marking the cut reads as "the user browsed no further" for folders the tool simply would not walk. It refuses to invent a timestamp: an item class with no DOS date field at that offset, an item under 12 bytes, a zero date, or a date and time that do not resolve to a single real instant produce no timeline event rather than an epoch or a guess. It refuses to read a `0xBEEF0004` long name whose long-name-offset field is zero, treating that field as the presence flag. It refuses to claim a recovery it did not perform: `logs_replayed` is `false` on every record it emits and the reason is stated as `replay_not_supported_by_this_parser`. It refuses to erase an incompleteness reason another stage already recorded: reasons are merged and `+`-joined, because a plain overwrite once left a capped walk on a dirty hive reporting only "the hive was not read in full" and the examiner lost the fact that the walk itself had stopped. And it refuses to return nothing from a hive it knows it did not read in the state it was captured in — dirty with its logs present, or loaded short — because nothing is exactly what a clean, whole, genuinely empty hive returns, and "this user opened no folders" is the one conclusion that must not be reachable by silence. The converse is refused just as firmly: a hive read in full that simply holds no bags emits no status record, because a disclosure there would put a false gap in the case.

### `plugin.windows.shimcache_parser`

**Reads.** A Windows registry hive, chosen by two gates that must both pass: the content probe A shadow-copy prior version of the file (a `VssPriorVersion` `ParsedRecord`) is read too and named by its `file_name`, since its `name` carries a `[shadow copy ...]` label; everything it yields repeats the snapshot id, label and creation time, and its transaction logs are not searched. `detect_file_type` must answer `RegistryHive`, which it does on the four bytes `regf` at offset 0 and on nothing else, and the artifact's `name` metadata must contain the string "system", case-insensitively. Neither gate asks whether the file is a *primary* hive, so a `SYSTEM.LOG1` transaction log and a `SYSTEM.sav` both pass it. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `SystemArtifact` and declares itself a stream reader. Up to 512 MiB (`MAX_HIVE_BYTES`) is then staged with `read_capped`, a best-effort read: a short one keeps the prefix, and the shortfall is measured against the source's declared size. Before any parsing the base block is inspected by `seance_hive_util::hive_state` — the two sequence numbers and the XOR-32 checksum over the first 0x1FC bytes decide whether the hive was cleanly flushed — and `SYSTEM.LOG1`, `SYSTEM.LOG2`, or failing both `SYSTEM.LOG`, are probed for beside it, on the local filesystem or as siblings inside the evidence container; their existence is all that is taken from them, and their contents are never read. The hive is then opened leniently: a mismatched sequence pair and a base block declaring more hive-bin bytes than the buffer holds are both tolerated and reported, while the buffer must be at least the 4,096-byte base block, and the major version (1), the minor version (1 to 6), the file type (0, meaning a primary hive), the file format (1), the clustering factor (1, 2, 4 or 8), the declared-size alignment and the base-block checksum are every one still enforced. From the root key the walk visits three control sets by name, case-insensitively — `ControlSet001`, `ControlSet002` and `CurrentControlSet` — and under each takes `Control\Session Manager` and reads the `AppCompatCache` value; failing that, an `AppCompatCache` subkey's value of the same name, then an `AppCompatibility` subkey's. Every key node, value node and `ri` sublist the hive reader refuses along the way is counted. The value's own first four bytes choose the layout: 0x30 or 0x34 is Win10, 0x80 is Win8/8.1, 0xBADC0FEE is Win7, 0xBADC0FFE is Vista; a first field that is none of those is still read as Win10 when a `10ts` or `00ts` entry signature really sits at offset 0x30 or 0x34. Win8.0, 8.1, 10 and 11 are one signature-tagged record stream — a four-byte signature, four bytes this reader does not interpret, a `u32` entry data size whose total on-disk length is that plus twelve, a `u16` path size, the path in UTF-16LE, then a FILETIME — begun at offset 128 on Win8/8.1 and, on Win10, at the header-size field where it reads 0x30 or 0x34, at 0x34 where a signature sits there, and at 0x30 otherwise. Win7 and Vista are fixed-width records after a 128-byte and an 8-byte header respectively, the declared entry count in both at offset 4 of the value, 48 bytes wide on x64 and 32 on x86, the width settled by whether bytes 4 to 8 of the first record are zero padding, and the path not inline but at an offset into a strings area following the records.

**Produces.** One `ShimcacheEntry` parsed record per decoded entry, carrying the path as the record's UTF-16LE decodes up to its first NUL, the FILETIME the record holds as an RFC 3339 `last_modified`, the tri-state `exec_flag`, `data_size` (the record's own on-disk length — the fixed-width layouts report the 48 or 32 bytes the record is), `position` as the entry's 1-based place in the list of entries decoded from that value, the `control_set` it was read from and the `format_version` that was detected. One `TimelineEvent` per entry whose FILETIME decoded, timestamped at that time, described as "Shimcache LastModified", naming the path, the `exec_flag`, the position and the control set, so two control sets holding the same binary do not become one indistinguishable pair of rows. Where a cache value decoded no entries at all, or where its layout matched no known version, a `ShimcacheParseStatus` record (`record_type` `shimcache_parse_status`) states the control set, the value's byte length, the entries decoded, the version where one was detected, `format_status` `format_unrecognised` where that applies, and the sentence that an AppCompatCache value is present in this control set but no execution entries were decoded from it, and that this is not evidence that nothing ran. Where the hive could not be opened or walked, where the navigation lost key or value nodes and nothing else was produced, or where the hive reader panicked — the panic is caught — a `RegistryHiveParseStatus` record (`record_type` `registry_hive_parse_status`) carries `parse_failed`, the failure detail, and the statement that the absence of execution entries is not evidence that nothing ran. Where a hive that is dirty or was not read in full held no AppCompatCache at all, a second `registry_hive_parse_status` record is emitted rather than silence; it carries no `parse_failed`, and says instead that this hive yielded no records and was not read in the state it was captured in. Every record is stamped with what the hive was: `hive_dirty`, `logs_replayed` (always false), `log_files`, `replay_reason`, `hive_truncated`, and `hive_bytes_read` against `hive_declared_bytes` where the load was short. Every record of an incomplete walk additionally carries `walk_cap_reached`, `walk_stopped_early`, `walk_undecodable_records` and, where the format declares one, `declared_entries` — with `content_incomplete` and a `content_incomplete_reason` of `cap_reached` or `unresolved_structure`, and the same pair again under `inventory_incomplete` — merged with the hive's own `hive_not_read_in_full` or `replay_not_supported_by_this_parser`, never overwriting it, because "the walk stopped at its entry cap" and "the hive was not read in full" are two different things to follow up. No entry record names the hive it came from; only the two `registry_hive_parse_status` routes carry `hive_name`.

**Cannot.** **It cannot say that a program ran.** An entry in the application-compatibility cache means Windows looked at the file; it is not a record of execution, and this project's findings layer will not build an execution claim out of one (`seance_plugin_findings/src/cross_view.rs`). Nor can it say a program did *not* run: on Win8.0, Win8.1, Win10 and Win11 — every modern machine — the signature-tagged record carries no insertion-flags field this parser reads, so `exec_flag` is null and nothing is known either way. Only the Win7 and Vista fixed-width records yield a flag at all, read as bit 0x2 of the insertion-flags field, and even that flag's meaning varies by Windows version. The timestamp is not a run time: it is the last-modified time the cache recorded for the file, so an entry's timeline row is placed at the file's modification, not at any act of a user. Where that FILETIME is zero, pre-1970 or beyond the year 10000 it decodes to nothing, `last_modified` is written as an empty string and the entry gets no timeline event. It cannot replay the transaction logs. The AppCompatCache value is written by Windows at shutdown, so on a hive lifted from a running or crashed machine the cache can predate the most recent executions entirely, and everything the machine did since it last booted is in memory rather than in this value — that is what `plugin.memory.windows`'s `amcache_shim` stage exists for, and this module cannot reach it. It cannot read a buffer shorter than the 4,096-byte base block, and it cannot read past 512 MiB of a hive; a registry hive's cells are spread across the whole file, so a prefix is an arbitrary subset and not "the first N keys". It cannot read a `regf` file at all unless its base block passes every structural check — major version 1, minor version 1 to 6, file type 0, file format 1, clustering factor 1, 2, 4 or 8, an aligned declared size and a verifying checksum — and a failure there costs every key in the hive, leaving only a parse-failure record. It cannot walk more than 1,024 Win7 or Vista records (`MAX_WIN7_ENTRIES`); a header declaring more has its excess reported as a cap reached, and the declared count is carried so the shortfall is arithmetic an examiner can do. The signature-tagged stream has no entry cap of its own, being bounded only by the value's length — and it declares no entry count either, so where such a walk stops short there is no figure to measure the shortfall against. It cannot look in `ControlSet003` or any higher-numbered control set, only the three names above; where `CurrentControlSet` aliases one of the numbered sets the duplicate is suppressed by comparing the raw value bytes, so a one-byte difference emits both. It cannot resolve a path the strings area no longer holds, or one the record's bounds put outside the value: such a record is counted in `walk_undecodable_records` as a lost program name, never presented as an empty slot — and because those records are counted rather than emitted, an entry's `position` is its place among the entries that decoded, not its slot in the cache. It cannot carry a path past an embedded NUL, and an unpaired surrogate is replaced rather than preserved. It cannot confirm that a record's path came from inside that record: in the signature-tagged stream the path and the FILETIME are bounded against the end of the cache value and not against the record's own declared length, so a record whose path size exceeds its entry data size reads the following record's bytes into its path and takes that record's bytes as its timestamp, with nothing recorded to say so; and in the fixed-width layouts a path offset is accepted anywhere inside the value, zero included, so a damaged record can yield a path decoded out of the record array. It cannot report a trailing remnant of one to thirteen non-signature bytes as a truncated walk: fourteen bytes are needed to read a record's header, and the walk ends there without setting `walk_stopped_early`. It cannot mark the records it did produce when the navigation lost nodes: the count of refused key nodes, value nodes and `ri` sublists becomes a status record only where the hive produced nothing at all, so a hive whose `ControlSet002` was unreadable but whose `ControlSet001` parsed emits its entries with no sign of the loss. It cannot say whether a buffer under 0x200 bytes, or one whose base block is not a primary hive's, was cleanly flushed: `hive_dirty` reads false in both cases rather than unknown. It cannot say what the file was — the cache holds a path, a time and, sometimes, a flag: no hash, no size, no signer, no file contents, and `data_size` is the record's length and not the file's. It cannot say whether the path still exists on the volume, was deleted, or ever existed. It cannot say which entries Windows evicted from a cache that was already full. It cannot read the opaque data blob that follows the FILETIME in the signature-tagged layout. Its Vista reader has never been validated against a real Vista hive; on a layout mismatch the path bounds checks fail and no entries are emitted. And the record width for Win7 and Vista is decided by a single four-byte test on the first record, so a cache whose first record has a non-zero where the x64 layout puts padding would be walked at the 32-byte stride.

**Refuses.** It refuses every artifact that carries no data, every file whose first four bytes are not `regf`, and every `regf` file whose name does not contain "system": for those, nothing at all is produced — no record, no status row. It does not refuse a file at that gate for failing to be a primary hive; a `SYSTEM.LOG1`, which begins `regf` too, is refused later by the base block's file-type field and leaves a parse-failure record rather than silence. It refuses to stop at the first control set that yields entries: a SYSTEM hive keeps the previous boot's control set alongside the current one, and its cache can name programs since purged from the live set, so stopping at the first hit would discard that history while still reporting a successful parse. It refuses to guess a cache layout: a value whose signature matches no known version, and which carries no `10ts`/`00ts` entry signature at either header offset, is reported as present and unrecognised with zero entries decoded, because walking arbitrary bytes with the Win10 reader would invent execution records and a fabricated record is worse than a stated gap. It refuses to write `exec_flag: false` for a format that has no flag it can read — the parser once hard-coded `false` on every Win8-and-later entry, which asserted "this program was never executed" about every entry of every modern hive without having looked, and an examiner cannot tell a fabricated negative from a measured one. It refuses to report the fixed-width layouts' `data_size` as the zero it once carried: the record is its width, and the width is a fact. It refuses to treat a stream that stopped on non-zero bytes as the end of the cache: that is `walk_stopped_early`, records left unread. Equally it refuses to flag the zero padding that legitimately ends a fixed-size cache value as a truncated walk, because a false incompleteness marker on every healthy cache teaches examiners to ignore the marker. It refuses to answer "there is no AppCompatCache in this hive" when the navigation itself lost key or value nodes and nothing else was produced: the refused node can be the control set holding the cache, so the outcome becomes an unreadable hive, not an absent cache. It refuses to return nothing when a SYSTEM hive was recognised but could not be parsed, or when the hive parser panicked on it — the panic is caught and reported as a status record — because an empty result reads as a machine on which nothing ever ran. For the same reason it refuses to be silent when a dirty or short-loaded hive yielded no cache at all. And it refuses to let one limit hide another: a capped walk on a hive that was not read in full states both reasons.

### `plugin.windows.srum_parser`

**Reads.** An ESE database, and it decides on content alone (a shadow-copy prior version, is read too and everything it yields repeats the snapshot id, label and creation time and states that its sidecars were not searched; a `ParsedRecord` that is not a prior version is declined before its data is touched). It subscribes to `FileEntry`, `SystemArtifact` and `ParsedRecord` with `InputCapability::Stream`, ignores the artifact's name and every other metadata key, returns nothing for an artifact with no data source, and runs `seance_core::file_detection::detect_file_type` on the source: that reads up to 512 bytes from offset 0 and calls the file an ESE database when at least 8 bytes arrived and bytes 4–7 are `EF CD AB 89` — the ESE header magic. Every ESE file in a case therefore reaches this module: `SRUDB.dat`, but also `WebCacheV01.dat`, `Windows.edb`, `Current.mdb` and the rest. libesedb — the C library, linked in-process through the `libesedb` 0.2 crate — opens only a path, so the database is staged: the source's declared size must be at most 2,147,483,648 bytes (2 GiB), a buffer of exactly that size is filled with `read_exact_or_fail` (a short read fails the stage rather than writing a prefix), and the bytes are written to `seance_srum_<uuid>.dat` in the system temporary directory under a `TempSpill` guard that removes the file when it drops, including on a panic the orchestrator catches. Inside the database it opens tables by exact name: `SruDbIdMapTable`, whose `IdIndex` and `IdBlob` columns build the integer-to-name map (`IdType` is read and discarded); `{D10CA2FE-6FCF-4F6D-848E-B2E99266FA89}`, application resource usage, reading `TimeStamp`, `AppId`, `UserId`, `ForegroundCycleTime`, `BackgroundCycleTime`, `FaceTime`, `ForegroundBytesRead`, `ForegroundBytesWritten`, `BackgroundBytesRead`, `BackgroundBytesWritten`, `ForegroundContextSwitches` and `BackgroundContextSwitches`; `{973F5D5C-1D90-4944-BE8E-24B94231A174}`, network data usage, reading `TimeStamp`, `AppId`, `UserId`, `InterfaceLuid`, `L2ProfileId`, `L2ProfileFlags`, `BytesSent` and `BytesRecvd`; `{DD6636C4-8929-4683-974E-22C046A43763}`, network connectivity, reading `TimeStamp`, `AppId`, `UserId`, `InterfaceLuid`, `L2ProfileId`, `ConnectedTime` and `ConnectStartTime`; and `{FEE4E14F-02A9-4550-B5CE-5FA2DA202E37}`, energy usage, reading `TimeStamp`, `AppId`, `UserId`, `BatteryLevel`, `DesignedCapacity`, `FullChargedCapacity` and `ChargeLevel`. Column names are matched case-insensitively; a column the table lacks is recorded once in `missing_columns` and its values read as 0. Timestamps come from `seance_ese_util::value_to_datetime`: a `DateTime` cell is a FILETIME, an `I64` or `Currency` cell is taken as FILETIME ticks, and 0, a negative tick count or any value before 1970 becomes no timestamp. Counters and ids are coerced with checked conversions (`to_u64`, `to_u32`, `to_i64`, `to_i32` into `u64`; `to_u32` into `u32`), so a negative or out-of-range cell is not a number. An `IdBlob` that is text is taken as is; a binary one is decoded as UTF-16LE only if it is at least 2 bytes, even-length, its first unit is not NUL, and every character up to the first NUL is ASCII-graphic, space or one of `\ / . - _ : { }`, else if it is 8 bytes or more and its first byte is 1 it is rendered as a SID string, else it is hex-encoded; a cell that is neither text nor binary falls back to the cell's own `to_string()`.

**Produces.** For each of the four usage tables that exists and yields at least one row, one `ParsedRecord` parented to the input artifact holding the whole table: `type` `SrumAppResourceUsage`, `SrumNetworkDataUsage`, `SrumNetworkConnectivity` or `SrumEnergyUsage`, `table_name` (the GUID), `record_count`, and a `records` array of one object per row — `app` and `user` resolved through the id map or rendered `Unknown(<id>)`, `app_id`, `user_id`, `timestamp` as RFC 3339 or `null`, and that table's counters by the names above (`interface_luid`, `l2_profile_id`, `l2_profile_flags`, `bytes_sent`, `bytes_recvd`, `connected_time`, `connect_start_time`, `battery_level`, `designed_capacity`, `full_charged_capacity`, `charge_level`). These table records carry neither `name` nor `source_module`. For each application-resource and network-data row with a timestamp, and each connectivity row with a `ConnectStartTime`, one `TimelineEvent` parented to the table record: `timestamp_desc` `SRUM App Resource Usage` (`short_desc` `App usage: <app> (user: <user>)`, `full_details` with `face_time` and the four I/O counters summed as `total_io_bytes`), `SRUM Network Data Usage` (`Network: <app> sent=<n> recv=<n>`, `full_details` with `app`, `bytes_sent`, `bytes_recvd` and `interface_luid`), or `Network Connection Start` (`Connected: <app> (<n>s)`, `full_details` with `app`, `connected_time_seconds` and `interface_luid`), each stamped `source_module: plugin.windows.srum_parser`. Energy rows produce no timeline event.
