Where a walk fell short — rows libesedb would not decode, a column the table lacks, a cell that would not coerce, or a table whose columns or records could not be enumerated at all — the table record and every timeline event under it carry `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason: unresolved_structure`, `rows_skipped`, `values_defaulted`, `missing_columns` when any and `walk_unreadable` (`columns` or `records`) when the walk never started; and a standalone marker is emitted, `type` `SrumIdMapIncomplete`, `SrumAppResourceUsageIncomplete`, `SrumNetworkDataUsageIncomplete`, `SrumNetworkConnectivityIncomplete` or `SrumEnergyUsageIncomplete`, `subtype: parse_incomplete` (set on the artifact as well as in the metadata), `status: TableWalkIncomplete`, with `table_name`, `rows_emitted`, the same counts, a `content_incomplete_detail` sentence stating what the absence of rows does and does not mean, the same sentence again under `detail`, and a `name` of the form `SRUM <table>: incomplete - <detail>`. The marker's `type` is deliberately not the table's, so grouping by type cannot file it as a usage row, and it is emitted even when the walk recovered nothing — the case where the table's own record is not emitted at all. When SRUM tables are present but every one yielded nothing and no marker was raised, one `SrumDatabase` record with `status: Detected`, `source: SrumParser`, `srum_tables_present` and a `note` saying the standard tables were present but yielded no rows says the database was recognised. When the file holds none of the five tables, nothing at all is produced : a WebCache or Search index must not be filed as resource-usage evidence.

**Cannot.** It cannot say when anything happened within the hour. SRUM flushes its in-memory counters to `SRUDB.dat` on a roughly hourly cadence, so `TimeStamp` is the moment a row was written, not the moment the application ran or the bytes moved; the module publishes it as the event's timestamp with no qualification on the record. It cannot name a user: the id map yields a SID string (`S-1-5-21-…`) and nothing joins it to the SAM or a profile, so `user` is a SID or `Unknown(<n>)`. It cannot render an application name that contains a non-ASCII character: the UTF-16LE decode accepts only ASCII-graphic text, so a path through a user's accented profile name fails that test, is not a SID, and is published as the hex of its UTF-16 bytes. It does not read `IdType`, so an id that was in the map under a different kind is resolved regardless. `interface_luid` is a raw LUID and `l2_profile_id` a raw integer — neither is joined to the interface list or the network-profile (SSID) list in the SOFTWARE hive — so a connectivity row names a number, not a network. It reads exactly the four provider tables named above plus the id map: the further providers a Windows 10 or 11 `SRUDB.dat` carries — push-notification, application-timeline, long-term energy and others — are not opened and their presence is not recorded, so `COMPARISON.md`'s "all 5 tables" describes what is read, not what SRUM holds. A NULL cell is indistinguishable from an undecodable one: both read as 0, both count in `values_defaulted`, and either marks the whole table record and every event under it `content_incomplete` with reason `unresolved_structure` — a table where one column is legitimately unset on every row is reported exactly like a damaged one. `BatteryLevel` is absent on most builds, so most energy records carry `missing_columns: ["BatteryLevel"]` and are incomplete by construction. It applies no transaction log: `SRUDB.jrs`, `SRUDB.log` and the `SRU*.log` set are neither read nor named, so a database captured with unflushed transactions is read as libesedb finds it, and libesedb's dirty-shutdown state is not published. Nothing is verified — no ESE page checksum result is exposed. The table record holds every row in its own metadata with no cap, so a 400,000-row table is one JSON blob, and each of those rows with a timestamp is its own timeline artifact. libesedb runs in this process, not in a helper: a crash in the C library on hostile evidence takes the worker with it (the orchestrator catches a panic, not a segmentation fault), and every byte of the database — up to 2 GiB — is first buffered in memory and then written to the temporary directory, which a WebCache or `Windows.edb` pays too, once here and once again in `plugin.windows.sum`. The four I/O counters are summed into `total_io_bytes` with unchecked `+`; the workspace builds with `overflow-checks = true`, so four hostile values summing past 2^64 panic, the orchestrator catches it, and the whole database's output is lost rather than one row's total. `record_count` is the number of rows published, never the number the table held; the difference is `rows_skipped`. A partially read id map is reported first, and from then on every unresolved id in every table is `Unknown(<n>)` — the marker `SrumIdMapIncomplete` is the only thing that says why. And the gate is the ESE magic only: a `SRUDB.dat` whose first 8 bytes were overwritten is not opened, and nothing records that a file by that name was passed over.

**Refuses.** It refuses to stage a database it cannot read whole. A source whose declared size exceeds 2 GiB is refused before any buffer is allocated with `ModuleError::ParsingError` ("too large to buffer safely"), and a source that returns fewer bytes than it declares is refused with a `ParsingError` naming "SRUM database" rather than written short: libesedb opens a truncated ESE file willingly and hands back the rows it can still reach, which would publish a fraction of an hourly usage history as the whole of it. Both refusals are error rows in the processing log, and both apply to every ESE file in the case, so a `Windows.edb` over 2 GiB draws an error row from this module on every ingest without being SRUM at all. A file libesedb will not open is refused the same way, the library's message carried in the error. A table whose column list or record cursor will not open is refused into a marker (`walk_unreadable: columns` or `records`) that says in words that the absence of rows says nothing about what the table held — because an unopenable network table otherwise reads as a machine that never used the network. A row libesedb will not decode is skipped and counted, never partially published. It refuses to claim SRUM for a database that has none of SRUM's tables and refuses to fabricate a timestamp: a zero, negative or pre-1970 FILETIME publishes `timestamp: null` and no timeline event. It refuses to read the `EventTimestamp` column in place of a missing `BatteryLevel`, a fallback it once had that turned a FILETIME into a battery percentage that never fit and published a flat battery drawn from a clock. What it does not refuse: a non-ESE file is not an error but an empty result, and a `SRUDB.dat` recognised by name but not by magic is passed over in silence.

### `plugin.windows.sticky_notes`

**Reads.** `StickyNotes.snt`, an OLE2 compound file holding one storage per note, and the newer app's `plum.sqlite` together with its `-wal`, which on the app version compared holds the whole database. Each is recognised by its own magic bytes. The database and its `-wal` are copied to a temporary directory and the copy is opened read-only; the evidence is never opened in place.

**Produces.** One record per note, with its text, its stored times, its `source_format` (`snt_compound_file` or `plum_sqlite`, on every note of either form), and — for the compound-file form — every stream in its storage with that stream's name and declared length. A `plum.sqlite` note also carries its rowid, its text with the app's per-paragraph `\id=<guid>` prefixes removed and the stored text beside it, and its times converted from .NET ticks with the ticks kept, as the file holds them and uncorrected for any clock error. A note deleted from `plum.sqlite` is reported as recovered from the newest write-ahead-log frame still holding it, with the frame number and its byte offset.

**Cannot.** The `plum.sqlite` reader has been compared against one LAB-MADE database, written by the real Sticky Notes app 6.1.4.0 on the project's Windows 11 test machine (schema `user_version` 13, `PLUM-1`), and against no seized or public one. Records from a `user_version` 13 store say exactly that; the file does not record the app version, so another version writing the same schema has not been compared, and a store at any other `user_version` carries the never-validated stamp. It cannot give a deletion time: the app sets no tombstone, so a deleted note's deletion is inferred from its row being absent from the latest committed state, and says so. It does not recover a deleted note once its WAL frames have been checkpointed and reset away, because it does not read page free space, and it does not report earlier text versions of notes that are still live. It does not interpret ink, images or sync fields. The `StickyNotes.snt` reader has been run against one real file — Windows 7, one plain-text note, the NIST Data Leakage case (`SNT-1`) — and its records say exactly that and no more: a file with several notes, a note with a picture, and a Windows 8 or pre-Anniversary Windows 10 file have not been met. It does not interpret the `Metafile` stream or a note's non-RTF streams, only lists them. It cannot tell an unset directory-entry timestamp from a note genuinely created at the Unix epoch, because the reader it uses exposes a wall-clock instant and no raw value; both read as absent, with the reason. It does not render an embedded picture or object as text.

**Refuses.** It refuses to skip a storage whose streams it does not recognise: such a storage is listed with every stream named and measured, because a note that would not read is not the same as no note. It refuses to read a zero-length stream descriptor by following its offset, which on real files points at the next payload and would publish one field's text as another's.

### `plugin.windows.sum`

**Reads.** The Windows Server User Access Logging databases — `SystemIdentity.mdb`, `Current.mdb` and A shadow-copy prior version of the file (a `VssPriorVersion` `ParsedRecord`) is read too and named by its `file_name`, since its `name` carries a `[shadow copy ...]` label; everything it yields repeats the snapshot id, label and creation time, and its sidecars are not searched. the archived `{GUID}.mdb` from `System32\LogFiles\SUM` — and it identifies them by schema, not by name, because the client-access tables are named after role GUIDs and the archives are named after GUIDs too. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, returns nothing for an artifact with no data source or with `is_directory: true`, and otherwise runs `detect_file_type` on the source: bytes 4–7 of the first read must be `EF CD AB 89`, the ESE header magic. Every ESE file in the case therefore reaches it, `SRUDB.dat` and `WebCacheV01.dat` included. The database is staged for libesedb exactly as the SRUM reader stages its own: declared size at most 2,147,483,648 bytes, filled with `read_exact_or_fail` so a short read fails rather than writing a prefix, written to `seance_sum_<uuid>.mdb` in the system temporary directory under a `TempSpill` guard that removes it on drop. Six tables are opened by exact name and read only where present: `ROLE_IDS` (`RoleGuid`, `RoleName`, `ProductName`), read first so client rows in the same database resolve to names; `SYSTEM_IDENTITY` (`CreationTime`, `SystemDNSHostName`, `SystemDomainName`, `SystemManufacturer`, `SystemProductName`, `SystemSerialNumber`, `OSBuildNumber`, `OSMajor`, `OSMinor`, `SystemTimeZone`); `CHAINED_DATABASES` (`Year`, `FileName`); `ROLE_ACCESS` (`RoleGuid`, `FirstSeen`, `LastSeen`); `DNS` (`HostName`, `Address`, `LastSeen`); and `VIRTUALMACHINES` (`VmGuid`, `BIOSGuid`, `CreationTime`, `LastSeenActive`, `SerialNumber`). Then every other table in the database is enumerated and its column list examined: a table carrying both `AuthenticatedUserName` and `TotalAccesses` is a per-role client-access table and is read — `AuthenticatedUserName`, `Address`, `RoleGuid`, `TenantId`, `TotalAccesses`, `InsertDate`, `LastAccess`, and whichever of `Day1` … `Day366` exist. Column names match case-insensitively. GUID columns are rendered by `seance_core`'s mixed-endian formatter from 16 raw bytes or a `Guid` cell, or taken from text with surrounding braces stripped. An address column of exactly 4 bytes is dotted-quad IPv4, exactly 16 bytes is eight colon-separated hex groups, text is taken trimmed, and any other length is left undecoded. Text columns are taken as-is, or from a binary cell only when it decodes as ASCII-only UTF-16LE, trailing NULs and whitespace trimmed, empty dropped. Timestamps go through `value_to_datetime` (a FILETIME `DateTime` cell or `I64`/`Currency` ticks; 0, negative or pre-1970 is no timestamp). `TotalAccesses` is coerced with checked conversions and defaults to 0 with `values_defaulted` counted when the cell will not coerce; the `DayN` cells are read the same way and a day is listed when its value is greater than 0.

**Produces.** `ParsedRecord` artifacts, all parented to the database artifact, each with a `type`, a `subtype` and a `name`, and every field omitted rather than emitted as null or an empty string when it could not be read — an account whose name would not decode is not an account with a blank name. `UalClientAccess` (`subtype: ual_client_access`) per client-table row: `source_table` (the table's GUID name), `authenticated_user`, `client_address`, `role_guid`, `role_name` where `ROLE_IDS` in this same database maps the GUID case-insensitively (the `RoleName`, else the `ProductName`), otherwise `role_name_unresolved: true` with a `role_name_unresolved_reason` saying the mapping lives in `SystemIdentity.mdb`, `tenant_id`, `total_accesses`, `insert_date` and `last_access` as RFC 3339, `timestamp` as `insert_date` in Unix seconds, `active_day_count` and `active_days` (the day-of-year numbers with a non-zero count), and `name` of the form `<user> from <address> accessed <role>`. `UalRoleId` (`ual_role_id`) with `role_guid`, `role_name`, `product_name`; `UalSystemIdentity` (`ual_system_identity`) with `dns_host_name`, `domain_name`, `system_manufacturer`, `system_product_name`, `system_serial_number`, `system_timezone`, `os_build_number`, `os_version` as `major.minor` when both are present, `creation_time` and `timestamp`; `UalChainedDatabase` (`ual_chained_database`) with `year` and `file_name`, so an examiner holding one year knows the others exist; `UalRoleAccess` (`ual_role_access`) with `role_guid`, `role_name`, `first_seen` (also `timestamp`) and `last_seen`; `UalDnsRecord` (`ual_dns`) with `host_name`, `address`, `last_seen`; `UalVirtualMachine` (`ual_virtual_machine`) with `vm_guid`, `bios_guid`, `serial_number`, `creation_time`, `last_seen_active`. A walk that fell short stamps every record it produced with `content_incomplete: true`, `content_incomplete_reason: unresolved_structure`, `rows_skipped`, `values_defaulted`, `missing_columns` and `walk_unreadable`, and emits one `UalTableIncomplete` marker (`subtype: parse_incomplete`, `status: TableWalkIncomplete`) per table naming `table_name`, `rows_emitted` and a `content_incomplete_detail` sentence — for an unreadable client table, that the absence of access records "says nothing about who reached this role". Last, one `UalSummary` (`ual_summary`) with `tables_parsed` and `client_access_records`. No `TimelineEvent` is produced by this module — the `timestamp` fields sit on `ParsedRecord`s, which the database does not project onto the timeline — and none of these records carries `source_module`. When the database holds none of the six named tables and no client-shaped table, nothing at all is produced: no summary, no marker, because a "0 client access records" summary emitted for every WebCache in the case would put a UAL finding in a report for a machine that never had the feature.

**Cannot.** It cannot put an access on the timeline: it emits no `TimelineEvent`, so the accesses it recovers are read on the record surface and never beside the event log or the MFT. It cannot say what an access was: UAL counts authentications to a role, and `total_accesses` is that count, not a session, a file or a command. It cannot place an access within a day: `active_days` lists the day-of-year numbers whose `DayN` count was non-zero and discards the counts themselves, so the per-day access totals the table holds are not published, and `insert_date` / `last_access` are the only instants. Days are numbered 1–366 within the year the database covers, and the year is not on the client record — it is on the `CHAINED_DATABASES` row of a different file, or implied by which database this is — so a bare `active_days: [45]` does not say which 14 February. It cannot resolve a role name across files: the GUID-to-name map is built from the `ROLE_IDS` of the database being parsed, and the role names live in `SystemIdentity.mdb` while the client tables live in `Current.mdb` and the archives, so on an ordinary ingest every client row carries `role_name_unresolved: true` and the reason it gives; the reason text is fixed, so a GUID that `ROLE_IDS` in this same database simply does not list gets the same sentence claiming the mapping was absent. It cannot name a tenant beyond its GUID. It decodes an address of 4 or 16 bytes only; any other length is dropped without a note, and an IPv6 address is rendered as eight uncompressed groups with no zone. A user name stored as a binary cell with any non-ASCII character is dropped, silently, because the binary-to-text path accepts ASCII only. A NULL `TotalAccesses` cell is indistinguishable from an undecodable one: both publish 0, both count in `values_defaulted`, and either marks every record of that table `content_incomplete` with reason `unresolved_structure`. It applies no transaction log (`SUM\*.log`, `*.jrs`, `*.chk`), so a database imaged mid-write is read as libesedb leaves it and its dirty-shutdown state is not published. Nothing is verified: no ESE checksum result reaches a record. libesedb runs in this process, and every ESE file in the case — including ones this module will discard — is buffered whole (up to 2 GiB) and written to the temporary directory once by this module and once by the SRUM reader. The client-table test is two column names, so a foreign ESE table that happens to carry `AuthenticatedUserName` and `TotalAccesses` would be read as a role, and a UAL build that renamed either column would hide every client table with no marker saying so. `os_version` needs both `OSMajor` and `OSMinor`; a build with one is published with neither. And detection is the ESE magic only: a `Current.mdb` whose first 8 bytes were overwritten is passed over in silence, and nothing records that a file of that name was seen.

**Refuses.** It refuses to stage a database it cannot read whole: a source declaring more than 2 GiB is refused before allocation, and a source that returns fewer bytes than it declares is refused rather than written short, both as `ModuleError::ParsingError` rows in the processing log — the second because libesedb opens a truncated file willingly and would publish a fraction of a three-year access log as the whole of it. A file libesedb will not open is refused with its message. A table whose column list or record cursor will not open is refused into a `UalTableIncomplete` marker with `walk_unreadable`, so that an unreadable client table is not read as a role nobody ever accessed — in an intrusion report the difference between "no evidence of access" and "we could not read the access log". A row libesedb will not decode is skipped and counted, never partially published. It refuses to emit a `UalSummary`, or anything, for an ESE database with no UAL tables, and refuses to read a table as a client table on one of its two identifying columns alone (pinned by `a_partial_client_schema_is_not_enough`). It refuses to invent a timestamp from a zero or pre-1970 FILETIME, an OS build from a cell that will not decode (`SYSTEM_IDENTITY` numbers are read without defaulting, because a build reported as 0 is a claim about the machine), an address from a byte length it does not model, or a name from a cell that would not decode — each is omitted from the record. What it does not refuse: a non-ESE file is an empty result, not an error; a directory is skipped; and a `{GUID}.mdb` that libesedb opens but that carries nothing UAL-shaped is passed over without a word.

### `plugin.windows.thumbcache`

**Reads.** A Windows thumbnail cache — `thumbcache_32.db`, `thumbcache_256.db`, `thumbcache_1600.db` and the rest of the family in `AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer` — recognised by content and by nothing else (a shadow-copy prior version, is read too and everything it yields repeats the snapshot id, label and creation time and states that its sidecars were not searched; a `ParsedRecord` that is not a prior version is declined before its data is touched). It subscribes to `FileEntry`, `FileContent` and `ParsedRecord` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, runs automatically, declines an artifact with `is_directory: true` or with no data source, and reads the source's first 4 bytes: they must be `CMMM`, the signature shared by the file header and every cache entry. The name is not consulted — a `thumbcache_` basename is described in the crate as a soft hint and is not read by the code at all. The whole file is then loaded into memory up to a ceiling of 1,073,741,824 bytes (1 GiB), looping over short reads and keeping whatever arrived. The first entry is not taken from the header's `first_cache_entry` field: from byte 24 (the Vista/Windows 7 header length) the buffer is scanned byte by byte for the next `CMMM`, and the walk starts there, so a header of any later length is stepped over without being decoded. Each entry is read from a fixed 28-byte prefix: `CMMM` at 0, `u32 cache_entry_size` at 4, `u64 entry_hash` at 8, `u32 identifier_string_size` at 16, `u32 padding_size` at 20 and `u32 data_size` at 24, all little-endian. The entry's variable regions are located from its end rather than from any fixed header length: the identifier starts `identifier + padding + data` bytes before the entry's end and the thumbnail data starts `data_size` bytes before it, which is what lets the same reader walk the Windows 7 layout (whose fixed header continues with an unknown field and two checksums) and the Windows 8 and later layout (which adds width and height ahead of the checksums) without modelling either. The identifier is decoded as UTF-16LE with trailing NULs trimmed, an odd trailing byte dropped; the thumbnail's format is classified from its first bytes — `FF D8 FF` is `jpeg`, `89 50 4E 47` is `png`, `42 4D` is `bmp`, anything else including no bytes at all is `unknown`. The walk advances by `cache_entry_size` and stops at 100,000 entries, at an entry whose declared size is below 28 bytes or overflows, at an entry that runs past the loaded bytes, at bytes that are not `CMMM`, or at fewer than 28 bytes remaining; trailing bytes that are all zero are the cache's own free space and end the walk cleanly, anything else non-zero ends it as a shortfall.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per cache entry the walk could make sense of, parented to the cache file's artifact: `type: ThumbcacheEntry`, `subtype: thumbcache`, `entry_hash` as 16 lower-case hex digits of the 64-bit cache key, `identifier` only when the entry's identifier string decoded to something non-empty, `data_size` (the thumbnail's byte length as the entry declares it), `image_format` (`jpeg`, `png`, `bmp` or `unknown`) and `name` of the form `thumbcache <hash>`. The record carries no data source and no offset: the thumbnail bytes themselves are not attached, exported or previewed by this module. No `TimelineEvent` is produced — a cache entry carries no timestamp — and nothing joins the entry to the file it was rendered from. Whenever the walk stopped before the end of the loaded bytes, or stepped over an entry, one further `ParsedRecord` follows: `type: ThumbcacheParseStatus`, `record_type: thumbcache_parse_status`, `name: thumbcache (partially parsed)`, the standard pair `content_incomplete: true` with `content_incomplete_reason`, `inventory_incomplete: true`, `entries_parsed`, `entries_skipped`, `stopped_at_offset` (the byte offset within the loaded buffer where the walk gave up, so an examiner can carve the remainder by hand, or null when the walk ran to the end but skipped entries), `max_entries` (100,000) and a `message` saying thumbnails past that point are absent from this case. The reason is one of `entry_cap` (an entry was waiting when the 100,000 cap was reached), `invalid_entry_size` (a declared size below 28 bytes or one that overflows, after which the stride to the next entry is unknowable), `truncated_final_entry` (an entry runs past the loaded bytes, or a non-zero stub shorter than a header ends the file), `entry_signature_mismatch` (non-zero, non-`CMMM` bytes where an entry header should be — one corrupt entry, or a stride this parser computes differently), `entry_header_unreadable` (a guard the bounds check should make unreachable), `short_read` (the source handed over fewer bytes than were asked for — given in place of `truncated_final_entry` when the torn entry sits at the end of such a read, because the read and not the file tore it), `file_read_capped` (the file is over the 1 GiB cap and every byte up to it arrived), or `inconsistent_entry_fields` when nothing stopped the walk but at least one entry's `identifier + padding + data + 28` exceeded its own `cache_entry_size` and was stepped over. A cache parsed to its end with nothing skipped carries no status record, so its absence is the claim of completeness. Where the walk finds no `CMMM` after the header at all, the result is empty with no status record — an empty cache and a cache whose entries could not be found look the same here.

**Cannot.** It cannot show a thumbnail. The record holds the entry's byte count and a format guess from its first bytes, but no data source, no offset into the cache and no export, so the image that proves a picture existed on the machine cannot be opened from the record this module writes; an examiner who needs the pixels must carve the cache by hand using nothing this record gives them beyond the file. It cannot say which file a thumbnail belonged to: `entry_hash` is the cache key and `identifier` is whatever string the entry stored, and nothing here or elsewhere in the tree resolves either to a filename, so "evidence that a file or folder existed" is evidence that some file did, unnamed. It cannot date anything: no entry carries a timestamp and no timeline event is written. It cannot tell an empty entry from an unrecognised one: a `data_size` of 0 — an entry whose thumbnail was removed, or a placeholder — classifies as `unknown` exactly as a format outside JPEG, PNG and BMP does. It does not read the width and height the Windows 8 and later entry header carries, either checksum (the data checksum over the thumbnail, the header checksum over the entry), the unknown field that follows the sizes, or the file header's version, cache type, first-entry offset, next-available offset or entry count, so it cannot verify an entry or compare its own count to the cache's declared one. The three size fields are read at offsets 16, 20 and 24 of every entry, the Windows 7 and later arrangement; no version is detected, so an entry laid out differently — Windows Vista's, which the published format descriptions place an 8-byte extension string ahead of those sizes — reads those fields from the wrong bytes, and each such entry is stepped over as `inconsistent_entry_fields` while the walk goes on, so a Vista cache reports its whole population as skipped rather than as a layout this parser does not model. `image_format` is a three-signature sniff of the first bytes: a thumbnail Windows stored in another encoding is `unknown`, and a JPEG whose first bytes are damaged is `unknown` too. The header scan for the first `CMMM` is a byte-wise search from offset 24, so a header field that happens to contain those four bytes would start the walk inside the header. Its ceilings are 1 GiB of file, all of it held in memory at once, and 100,000 entries; past either the status record says so. The cap reason is `file_read_capped`, not the standard `cap_reached` the rest of the tree uses (`short_read` is the standard word). And because the gate is the first four bytes only, a cache whose signature was overwritten yields nothing and no record that a file by that name was passed over, while any unrelated file beginning `CMMM` is walked as a cache.

**Refuses.** It refuses to read past what it can locate. An entry declaring a `cache_entry_size` below its own 28-byte header, or one that overflows the offset arithmetic, ends the walk with `invalid_entry_size` rather than guessing a stride, because every entry after it would then be found by luck. An entry that runs past the loaded bytes ends the walk with `truncated_final_entry` rather than being read short, and a non-zero stub shorter than a header at the end of the file is reported the same way instead of being taken as free space; only all-zero trailing bytes are accepted as the cache's normal in-place growth, and claiming incompleteness for those would cry wolf on every cache (pinned by `trailing_zero_fill_is_free_space_not_an_incomplete_parse`). Bytes that are neither `CMMM` nor zero where an entry should begin end the walk with `entry_signature_mismatch` rather than being skipped over to the next signature, since later bytes may hold entries this walk will never reach and a silent stop turns them into thumbnails that never existed. An entry whose identifier, padding and data lengths do not fit inside its declared size is refused as a record — no `identifier` or `data_size` is published from contradictory fields — but its stride is still trusted, the walk continues, and the entry is counted in `entries_skipped` so the case carries the fact that the cache holds a thumbnail it does not (pinned by `an_entry_whose_size_fields_contradict_each_other_is_counted_as_skipped`). The 100,000-entry cap ends the walk with `entry_cap` only when another entry was actually waiting. Every one of these produces the status record; none of them fails the module — `process` never returns an error, so nothing from this module ever reaches the processing log as an error, and every prefix of a valid cache parses without panic (pinned by `truncated_entry_does_not_panic`). A file whose first four bytes are not `CMMM`, an empty file and a directory are declined in silence, with no artifact and no error.

### `plugin.windows.timeline_activity`

**Reads.** The Windows 10/11 Timeline — the per-user `ActivitiesCache.db` the ConnectedDevicesPlatform A shadow-copy prior version of the file (a `VssPriorVersion` `ParsedRecord`) is read too and named by its `file_name`, since its `name` carries a `[shadow copy ...]` label; everything it yields repeats the snapshot id, label and creation time, and its sidecars are not searched. service writes — selected by basename, magic and then structure. It subscribes to `FileEntry` and `FileContent` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`, lower-cases the last path segment of the artifact's `name` and acts on exactly `activitiescache.db`; a directory entry or an artifact with no data source yields nothing. The first 16 bytes are read with a looping `read_full` and must be `SQLite format 3\0`. The file is spilled by `TempDb::spill` under a 2 GiB cap (`MAX_DB_BYTES`) with its `-wal` sibling where the source can open one — a live cache routinely holds its newest activities only there — and the copy opened read-only. The structural gate has three answers per table: `probe_table` must list `Activity` and `Activity_PackageId`, an absent table in a readable catalogue meaning "not a Timeline schema", a catalogue that will not answer meaning damage; then `Activity`'s columns are read through `PRAGMA table_info` and must include the three signature columns `ActivityType`, `Payload` and `StartTime` (`ClipboardPayload` and `CreatedInCloud`, added in 1903, are deliberately not required). `Activity_PackageId` is read whole (`ActivityId`, `Platform`, `PackageName`) into a map keyed by the same GUID rendering as `Activity.Id` — a TEXT GUID as is, a 16-byte BLOB formatted in Microsoft's mixed-endian layout. `Activity`, and `ActivityOperation` when present, are walked with a projection of exactly those of seventeen known columns that exist (`Id`, `AppId`, `ActivityType`, `ActivityStatus`, `Group`, `Payload`, `ClipboardPayload`, `StartTime`, `EndTime`, `LastModifiedTime`, `ExpirationTime`, `LastModifiedOnClient`, `CreatedInCloud`, `IsLocalOnly`, `PlatformDeviceId`, `OperationType`, `OperationOrder`), with no row limit. `AppId` is parsed as a JSON array of `{application, platform}` entries; `Payload` as a JSON object (`displayText`, `appDisplayName`, `description`, `activationUri`, `contentUri` percent-decoded, `reportingApp`, `activeDurationSeconds`, `userTimezone`, `devicePlatform`); `ClipboardPayload` as a JSON array whose first entry with `content` is base64-decoded, and read as UTF-8 text only when its `format` is `Text`. Every timestamp column is Unix seconds and is fail-closed: a non-positive value is omitted, never 1970.

**Produces.** One `WindowsTimelineActivity` (`subtype: "windows_timeline_activity"`, `platform: "Windows"`, `source_table`) per row of `Activity` and `ActivityOperation`: `activity_id`; `executable`, resolved in WxTCmd's preference order from the row's `AppId` entries then its package-map entries — a `windows_win32` path, else an `x_exe_path` with a leading Known-Folder `{GUID}` rewritten to its name from a table of twenty (`%ProgramFiles%`, `%WinDir%\System32`, `%LocalAppData%`, `Downloads`, …) and any other GUID left verbatim, else `windows_universal`, else the first entry; `app_display_name`; `app_id_raw` up to 64 KiB with `app_id_raw_truncated` always stated and `content_incomplete: true`, reason `app_id_raw_capped`, when it was cut; `activity_type` and an advisory `activity_type_label` (2 Notification, 3 Mobile backup / Azure auth, 5 Open app / file / webpage, 6 App in focus, 10 Clipboard, 11/12/15 System operation, 16 Copy/paste, else `Type n`); `activity_status`, `group`, `display_text`, `description`, `content_uri`, `activation_uri`, `reporting_app`, `payload_binary` (true when `Payload` is not a JSON object); for a clipboard-typed row or any row whose clipboard decoded to text, `has_clipboard`, `clipboard_text` capped at 8 KiB with `clipboard_text_truncated` always stated and `content_incomplete: true`, reason `clipboard_text_capped`, when cut, `clipboard_bytes` and `clipboard_format` — a non-`Text` format such as a bitmap yields the format and byte count and never fabricated text; `date`/`start_time`/`start_time_iso`, `end_time`/`end_time_iso`, `duration_seconds` (only when the end is after the start), `active_duration_seconds`, `last_modified_time`, `last_modified_on_client`, `created_in_cloud` as the raw value (0 meaning local), `expiration_time`, `is_local_only`, `platform_device_id`, `device_platform`, `user_timezone`, `packages` (the `Activity_PackageId` entries), `operation_type` and `operation_order`; a `name` of the display text, else the executable, else the app name, else `Windows Timeline Activity`; and a `short_desc` of `<app> — <display text> (focus Ns)`. One `TimelineEvent` per record with a positive `StartTime`: `timestamp`, `timestamp_desc: "Windows Timeline Activity"`, `source_module`, `short_desc`, `filename` (the content URI, else the display text), `user_timezone`, and `full_details` as a JSON string of the activity's key fields including any clipboard text. Where any row of either activity table or of `Activity_PackageId` would not decode, or a query would not prepare or run, every record is stamped `content_incomplete: true` with `unresolved_structure` merged into any reason already present (never overwriting a cap reason) and `inventory_incomplete: true`, and one `WindowsTimelineParseStatus` `RowsNotDecoded` marker is appended with `activity_row_errors`, `package_row_errors`, `records_recovered` and a sentence saying the activities listed are a floor. A recognised database that could not be staged or opened, whose catalogue would not answer, or whose `Activity` column list would not read yields one `WindowsTimelineParseStatus` `DatabaseUnreadable` record with both pairs. Every record from a short-staged or WAL-refused copy is stamped `content_incomplete: true` with its reason and one `SqliteSpillIncomplete` marker is appended, even when nothing parsed.

**Cannot.** It cannot see past 8 KiB of a clipboard entry, and says so on the record, because clipboard contents are often the evidence itself and a silently shortened capture reads as the whole thing an examiner would quote. It cannot show a non-text clipboard entry — a bitmap is a format and a byte count. It cannot resolve an executable a Known-Folder GUID it does not know prefixes, leaving the GUID verbatim, and its `activity_type_label` is advisory: the meanings are the community's reading of undocumented values, and an unfamiliar type is `Type n`. It cannot read a `Payload` that is not a JSON object beyond flagging `payload_binary`. It does not read the `Activity_PackageId` `ExpirationTime`, the `Manifest`, `Metadata`, `AppSettings`, `ManualSequence`, `DataEncryptionKeys` or `LocalCache` tables, `MatchId`, `OriginalPayload`, `OriginalLastModifiedOnClient`, `Tag`, `Priority`, `ETag`, `PackageIdHash` or `UserActionState`, so a synced activity's origin and an ActivityOperation's queued cloud state are only what the raw columns above carry. Its `TimelineEvent` is dated by `StartTime` alone; an activity with no positive start has a record and no event. It cannot tell which user the cache belongs to — the `\Users\<name>\...\ConnectedDevicesPlatform\<id>\` path is not parsed — nor which device a synced-in activity came from beyond `platform_device_id`. It has no row cap and no `CapCounter`. It recovers no deleted rows.

**Refuses.** It refuses to return an empty history from a store it could not read: a catalogue that will not answer or a column list that will not read is `DatabaseUnreadable`, and only a readable catalogue without the Timeline tables, or an `Activity` without the three signature columns, is passed over in silence. It refuses to surface a non-positive timestamp as 1970-01-01, omitting `date`, `start_time`, `end_time`, `last_modified_time`, `expiration_time` and the ISO strings instead, and refuses to emit a `TimelineEvent` without a valid start. It refuses to fabricate clipboard text from a non-text format or a base64 payload that will not decode. It refuses to let a cut clipboard or `AppId` read as short by nature, stating `_truncated` on every record and `cap_reached`-class reasons only when a cut happened. It refuses to let a walk's incompleteness overwrite a record's own cap reason, merging the two with `+`. It refuses to let a dropped activity or package row vanish, counting each and stamping every record, because a dropped package row removes the application name from an activity that stays. It refuses to guess a Known-Folder name. And it refuses to present a partially staged cache as whole, stamping every record — and an empty result — with the spill's incompleteness.

### `plugin.windows.vss_enumerator`

**Reads.** The Volume Shadow Copy catalog and stores that Windows keeps inside an NTFS volume, following the layout libvshadow documents. It subscribes to `FileSystem` and `RawEvidence` with `InputCapability::RandomAccess`. A `FileSystem` artifact is taken only when its `subtype` is exactly `ntfs` (the partition parser lower-cases the detected type into that key), or, with no `subtype` at all, when its `filesystem_type` is `ntfs` case-insensitively or is absent; a `RawEvidence` artifact is not gated at all. Either must carry a data source. Offsets are volume-relative: it reads 512 bytes at offset 7,680 (0x1E00) with `read_exact_or_fail` — a short read fails the parse rather than leaving a zero tail that would read as a zero catalog offset — and takes from that block a 16-byte identifier, `u32 version`, `u32 record_type`, two `u64` offsets, the `u64 catalog_offset` at +48, `u64 max_size`, and the volume and storage-volume GUIDs at +64 and +80. Only `record_type == 1` is accepted; the identifier GUID is not checked. On a whole-disk `RawEvidence` image the bytes at 0x1E00 are the disk's, not a volume's, so a catalog is found on raw evidence only when the evidence is a bare volume image; in ingestion the partition parser's windowed `FileSystem` artifact is the route. The catalog is a singly linked chain of 16,384-byte blocks from `catalog_offset`: each block is read whole with `read_exact_or_fail`, its 128-byte header yields `next_offset` at +40 (the header's own record type is not checked), and the 128-byte entries that follow are typed by their first `u32` — byte 4 is the snapshot priority, so reading 8 bytes here once folded a non-zero priority into the type. A type-2 snapshot entry gives the store GUID at +16, `volume_size` at +8, stack position at +32, attribute flags at +40 and the creation FILETIME at +48; a type-3 store entry gives the diff-area (block list) offset at +8, store GUID at +16, store header offset at +32, block-range-list offset at +40, bitmap offset at +48 and previous-bitmap offset at +72; type 1 is unused and skipped. The chain walk keeps a visited set and a bound of 100,000 blocks. Entries are keyed by store GUID, snapshots and stores matched on it. For each snapshot with a store entry, `VssStore::build` (`vss_source.rs`) reads the diff-area table chain (16 KiB shadow blocks prefixed by the diff-area GUID `3808876b-c176-4e48-b7ae-04046e6cc752`, type 3, self-offset at +32, next at +40, 32-byte entries from +128: original volume offset, offset in store, data volume offset, flags, allocation bitmap), the store bitmap chain and the previous-bitmap chain (type 6 blocks, sized from `volume_size`), all bounded at 100,000 blocks each, and links the store to the nearest higher-numbered store that built, the live volume last. Separately, `parse_block_list` re-walks the diff area to count regular entries, and the store header's 128 bytes are read for a `u32` version at +16. Then it reads the live volume's `$MFT` once and each rebuilt snapshot's `$MFT`: the NTFS boot sector gives the cluster size, record size and `$MFT` cluster, the first 16 records give record 0's own `$DATA` runs, and the `$MFT` those runs describe is parsed by the MFT module itself (`seance_plugin_mft::volume_mft`, which hands it to `MftParser::process` as a bare `$MFT`), so a record is decoded exactly as the live volume's `FileEntry` is. Of each record it compares the sequence number, the in-use flag, the name, the reconstructed parent path, the size and the four `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` and four `$FILE_NAME` timestamps.

**Produces.** One `ParsedRecord` per type-2 catalog entry, `type: VssSnapshot`, `subtype: vss_snapshot`, `name: Shadow Copy <guid>`, parented to the volume artifact, with `snapshot_id` and `store_id` (both the store GUID, mixed-endian), `volume_size`, `creation_time` as `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS UTC` or the string `unknown` for a zero or pre-1970 FILETIME, `store_header_offset`, `block_list_offset`, `bitmap_offset`, `stack_position`, `store_version` (null when the store header could not be read whole, with `store_header_incomplete: true` and reason `short_read`), `multi_device` (true when the volume header's storage-volume GUID differs from its volume GUID), `modified_blocks` (the count of regular — not forwarder, overlay or ignore — diff-area entries, with `diff_area_incomplete: true` and reason `unresolved_structure` when that walk failed and the count is 0 by default), `content_reconstruction` (`reconstructed` or `unavailable_requires_store_chain`), `store_chain_complete` and `source: VssEnumerator`. A snapshot whose store built carries a live `VssDataSource` as the artifact's data: a read at any volume offset is translated block by block through the store's diff-area entries (regular, forwarder and overlay, with per-sector allocation bitmaps), falls through the chain to older stores and then to the live volume for blocks the snapshot did not preserve, serves nullified sectors as zeros where the store's `0x400` flag says so, and fails a read rather than zero-filling when a present sector cannot be read whole. That source is virtual — it cannot be expressed as data runs — so it does not survive the database; `seance_api`'s content resolver rebuilds it on demand through `reconstruct_snapshot_content` from `stack_position`, and a test proves the rebuilt bytes match the ingest-time ones. Where the reconstruction serves bytes that are not the whole snapshot, the record carries `content_incomplete: true` with reason `vss_store_chain_gap` (a store between this one and the live volume did not build, so part of the image is dated to the wrong moment), `vss_diff_storage_on_other_volume` (the diff area lives on a volume this image is not, so every block preserved there falls through to the live volume) or `vss_diff_area_unreadable` (a store built but the count walk failed, so the two parses disagree). When the catalog chain looped or hit the block bound, every snapshot record gains `inventory_incomplete: true`, `inventory_incomplete_reason` (`unresolved_structure` or `cap_reached`) and `catalog_walk_complete: false`, and one `VssCatalogStatus` record (`subtype: vss_catalog_incomplete`, `snapshots_listed`, the standard pairs with a `detail` sentence and a `message` that absence is not evidence of never having existed) follows; a catalog that could not be read at all after a valid header produces that record alone . Each snapshot record also carries `prior_versions`: `status: compared` with `records_compared`, `snapshot_mft_record_slots`, `live_mft_record_slots`, `records_differing`, `prior_versions_published`, `prior_versions_unpublished` and the two caps, or `status: not_compared` with the `reason` (no store chain built, or a `$MFT` that could not be located), so an empty prior-version list never reads as "nothing changed". For every snapshot record that differs from the live record at the same record number — a different sequence number (the slot was reused: the snapshot holds another file), in-use flag, name, parent path, size or `$SI`/`$FN` timestamp, or a record the live `$MFT` does not publish — one `ParsedRecord`, `type: VssPriorVersion`, `subtype: vss_prior_version`, parented to its `VssSnapshot` record, never a `FileEntry`: `name` is the file name suffixed `[shadow copy <creation time>]`, `is_snapshot_version: true`, `provenance: vss_snapshot`, `snapshot_label` beginning `SHADOW COPY VERSION, not the live volume`, `vss_snapshot_id`, `vss_creation_time`, `vss_stack_position`, `record_number`, `sequence_number` and `live_sequence_number`, `absent_from_live`, `in_use_in_snapshot`, `snapshot_path` and `live_path`, `differences` (one `{field, live, snapshot}` per differing field, or one `{field: record}` when the live `$MFT` has no such record), `changed_fields`, `snapshot_times`, `size`, and the snapshot record's own `data_runs` / `data_runs_complete` / `resident_data_b64` and compression or EFS descriptors. Its content is the snapshot's: at ingest the runs are served over the rebuilt snapshot stream, and from the database the content resolver applies the parent `VssSnapshot` step first, so the runs resolve against the rebuilt snapshot and never against the live volume (graded on the Server 2003 image, record 79 of stack 1: the snapshot's 7,106 bytes of `1` are served while the live clusters hold another file's `3`s; `a_prior_version_is_served_from_the_snapshot_not_the_live_volume` and `a_vss_prior_version_resolves_against_the_rebuilt_snapshot`). The bare parse's `volume_not_in_evidence` stamp is removed and what is still true is re-stated as `content_incomplete`: `encrypted` for EFS, the snapshot's own reason when its bytes are not the whole snapshot, `unresolved_structure` with `deleted_content_caveat` for a record not in use in the snapshot, or `unresolved_structure` for a run list known short. No `TimelineEvent` is written for a snapshot's creation time or a prior version's timestamps (the timeline projects only `FileEntry`), and no `FileEntry` is produced from a snapshot.

**Cannot.** It does not walk a shadow copy as a file system. What it reads of a snapshot is its `$MFT`, and what it publishes is only the records that differ from the live volume's: a file unchanged since the snapshot has no prior-version record (the live `FileEntry` stands for it), and nothing is read from a snapshot's `$I30` indexes, `$UsnJrnl`, `$LogFile`, `$Bitmap`-unallocated space or slack, so a file whose only trace in the snapshot is a directory-index entry or a carvable remnant is not found. Records are compared by number, not followed through `$ATTRIBUTE_LIST` history; a record the live `$MFT` still holds but the MFT parser does not publish (no `$FILE_NAME`) counts as absent from live. The parent path is the path reconstructed inside each `$MFT`, so a renamed ancestor makes every descendant differ in `parent_path`. Last-access times are compared, so a volume with access updates on shows many records that differ only in `accessed`. The full per-snapshot walk — each rebuilt snapshot a child `FileSystem` walked by every NTFS module with its provenance — stays open as an opt-in , because N snapshots cost N full walks. Its caps are 1,048,576 `$MFT` records compared per `$MFT` and 10,000 prior versions published per snapshot; past either, the snapshot record carries `inventory_incomplete: true`, reason `cap_reached` and an `inventory_incomplete_detail` naming the count left out, and a `$MFT` whose own run list is incomplete (an `$ATTRIBUTE_LIST` on record 0 whose extension records lie past the first 16) is compared only over its known extent and says so the same way. The live and each snapshot `$MFT` are parsed whole in memory, the same cost as the live MFT parse. The whole-volume byte stream stays reachable through the API's content resolver. It cannot date anything on the timeline: `creation_time` is a display string on the record, not an event, and a prior version's timestamps are not timeline events. Its `creation_time` is the FILETIME the catalog entry carries and is not cross-checked against the store header. It cannot tell an unset FILETIME from a damaged one: both are `unknown`. `modified_blocks` counts only regular diff-area entries from a second, independent walk (`parse_block_list`) with different stopping rules from the store's own (`read_diff_area` additionally refuses unaligned offsets and unknown flag bits and stops the table there), so the count can differ from what the store serves, and the count is 0 both for a snapshot with no diff area and for one whose walk failed — only `diff_area_incomplete` separates them. Forwarder and overlay entries are served but never counted. A snapshot with no type-3 store entry — a legitimate state for a shadow copy with no diff area yet — is listed with every offset 0, `store_version` null and `content_reconstruction: unavailable_requires_store_chain`, and the same label is given to a snapshot whose store failed to build for any reason, so the record cannot tell "no store" from "store unreadable"; the build error goes only to the log. Nullified sectors are served as zeros, indistinguishable from sectors that held zeros. Blocks the snapshot did not preserve are served from the live volume by design, so the image is point-in-time only where the store says it is, and a live volume that has been wiped or re-imaged since the snapshot changes what the snapshot reads. Two catalog entries with the same store GUID silently keep the last one seen. The volume header GUID, the catalog block record type, the store header's identifier and the block-range list are not validated or read. It reads the `storage_volume_identifier` and warns when it differs, but cannot follow it: a diff area on another volume is never opened even when that volume is also in the case. Its ceilings are 100,000 catalog blocks, 100,000 diff-area tables and 100,000 bitmap blocks per chain — a bitmap chain can therefore hold up to 1.6 GiB in memory per store, two bitmaps per store — and no bound on the number of stores. And on a whole-disk image handed in as `RawEvidence` it looks at 0x1E00 of the disk, finds no header, and says nothing.

**Refuses.** It refuses to read a structure short. The 512-byte volume header, every 16 KiB catalog block, every diff-area table block in the count walk and in the store build, every bitmap block and the 128-byte store header are read with `read_exact_or_fail`, which loops over a source that legally answers in pieces (the store build once failed on any source returning under 16 KiB per call — pinned by `store_metadata_reads_survive_a_legal_short_read_and_fail_on_a_real_one`, and graded on `dfir_ntfs`'s Windows 10 and Server 2003 images through a 4 KiB-per-call source, every listed block matching its published MD5, in `tests/real_vss_test.rs`), so a source that ends inside one fails that read rather than leaving a zero tail that would parse as a zero catalog offset ("no shadow copies"), a zero `next_offset` ("the catalog ends here") or an empty table (pinned by `volume_header_short_read_fails_closed` and `catalog_block_short_read_fails_closed`). A volume header that fails to read, or whose `record_type` is not 1, or whose `catalog_offset` is 0, ends the module with an empty result and a debug line — a volume with no VSS is the ordinary case and is not an error. A catalog that fails after a valid header is refused into a `VssCatalogStatus` record rather than an empty list, because an empty list reads as a volume with no shadow copies. A catalog chain that loops back on itself is stopped by the visited set and reported as `unresolved_structure`, and one longer than 100,000 blocks is stopped and reported as `cap_reached`, each stamped on every snapshot listed and on the status record, since a self-referential chain from hostile evidence would otherwise hang the worker beyond what `catch_unwind` can catch. A diff-area or bitmap chain is stopped, without a record, at the first block whose GUID, type or self-offset does not match, or at 100,000 blocks. In the served bytes, a present sector that cannot be read whole from the underlying volume refuses the read with `UnexpectedEof` naming the offset rather than zero-filling (pinned by `read_block_fails_closed_on_present_sector_short_read`), and a read at or past `volume_size` returns zero bytes. A snapshot whose store did not build is refused a data source entirely rather than served from the live volume under the snapshot's name, and one that does serve bytes while its chain has a gap, its diff storage lies on another volume, or its diff area would not walk is stamped `content_incomplete` with the specific reason, because a point-in-time image with present-day bytes mixed in, unmarked, is the most dangerous output this module can produce. `process` itself never returns an error: every refusal above is either an empty result or a record.

### `plugin.windows.wlan_profiles`

**Reads.** A Windows WLAN profile document, recognised by its root `WLANProfile` element and the `microsoft.com/networking/WLAN/profile/v1` namespace in its first four kilobytes — not by its path, so a profile exported to a desktop or carved out of free space reads the same as one under `ProgramData\Microsoft\Wlansvc\Profiles\Interfaces`. It walks the document by element name and by the path to each text node, because `<name>` appears twice in the schema at different depths.

**Produces.** One `WifiNetwork` record with subtype `windows_profile` per profile — the same record type the macOS known-networks parser emits, so both platforms' answers to 'where has this machine been' sit together. It carries the SSID in both the hex and text forms the document gives, whether the network was hidden, the authentication and encryption, whether the machine was configured to join it automatically, and the pre-shared key where the file holds it in the clear. Where the key is DPAPI-protected it names the master key GUID the blob was encrypted under and what recovering it would require. Where the path shows it, the interface GUID of the adapter the profile was configured on is on the record.

**Cannot.** It cannot say when the machine joined the network, or that it ever did. The profile carries no timestamps at all: it states that the machine was configured to join, and the join history is in the `Microsoft-Windows-WLAN-AutoConfig/Operational` event channel and the `NetworkList` registry keys, neither of which this module reads. It does not decrypt a protected key: that needs the boot key from the SYSTEM hive, the `DPAPI_SYSTEM` secret from the SECURITY hive and the master-key file under `Windows\System32\Microsoft\Protect\S-1-5-18\User` (where the one real profile graded, LoneWolf's, has it), and this build reads none of them. It has been graded against that one real Windows 10 profile (`WLAN-1`, a WPA2-Personal network with a protected key); an open, 802.1X or hidden-network profile from a real machine has not been met. It does not read the Windows XP-era binary WZCSVC profiles, which are registry values rather than XML. It reads at most one megabyte per file and 10,000 elements per document.

**Refuses.** It refuses a document it cannot walk to a profile name or an SSID, and a file past its staging ceiling, and each refusal leaves a `WifiNetworkIncomplete` record naming which of the two applies -- because 'there was no wireless profile here' and 'there was one and it was not read' must never render the same. It refuses to read a document that ends inside an element as a whole one: that is reported as a PREFIX of a profile rather than as a profile with fewer fields. It refuses to pass over an element it does not read, counting it by name on the record instead. And where the SSID's hex and text forms disagree it refuses to choose silently: both are reported and the disagreement is stamped, with the network filed under the hex form where those bytes render as text -- they are what the radio used -- and under the text form where they do not, since an SSID that is not valid UTF-8 cannot be rendered as a name at all. It also refuses to publish a key the document did not say was in the clear: a profile carrying keyMaterial and no `protected` element is reported as protection-not-stated, with whether the material is a DPAPI blob, rather than having a blob's hex published as a passphrase.
